Description:
## Overview

In Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard, by local report the largest graveyard in Asia, the oldest seat belongs not to the dead in general but to one man in particular: Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri, a scholar and Qur'an-teacher who built a mosque, a madrasa and a library on this ground while he was still alive, and who was buried beside his own mosque when he died in 1630. It is reported that the graveyard grew up around his tomb over the following centuries, as generation after generation asked to be laid to rest near him, and not the other way around. The graveyard is reported to cover some 475 kanals.

Three older books on the saints and monuments of Lahore know the tomb and set it in the same graveyard. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, written in 1875, gives him a full entry as "شیخ محمد طاہر لاہوری قادری و نقشبندی", Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Lahori, Qadiri and Naqshbandi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 59–60, folios 47–48), and its appendix lists his tomb in the Miani graveyard, "قبرستان میانی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 288, folio 276). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* opens its chapter on the Miani graveyard with "فصل در ذکر مقبرہ حضرت شیخ طاہر بندگی", the section on the tomb of Hazrat Shaikh Tahir Bandagi (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 186). And Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* calls his the first and largest enclosure of the Miani graveyard, a walled precinct holding thousands of graves, old and new (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). The three books spell his name in several ways, name his Sufi order in several ways, and differ from what is reported at the shrine and from one another on the day and year of his death, on who gave him the name Bandagi, and on how the graveyard came to be; those differences are set out side by side below.

## The Life of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri

He was born in Lahore in 1576 CE. His father, Fazlullah, gave him his early education, and he went on to memorize the Qur'an. For advanced learning he became a disciple (*mureed*) of Hazrat Shah Sikandar, who is credited with giving him the name "Tahir Bandagi" and is reported to have told him, "you are meant for the spiritual reformation of people; simply remain devoted to the service of humanity at all times."

Lahori names the same master more fully: Shah Sikandar, son of Pir Kamal Kaithali, whose *murid* and *khalifa* Shaikh Muhammad Tahir was, and under whom he first completed his training (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). Chishti credits the title to another man. He writes that it came from "حضرت لال کمال شاہ[OCR?] ساکن کیتھل[OCR?]", a Hazrat Lal Kamal Shah of Kaithal (the reading of both names uncertain in the printed text), and that "سو اب تک طاہر بندگی مشہور ہیں", he is known as Tahir Bandagi to this day (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 189). Kanhaiya Lal makes him the *murid* of "شاہ کمال کیتہلی [OCR?]", Shah Kamal Kaithali, in the Qadiri family (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

It is also reported that there was a real trial in his life: a period in which he became enamored of a Hindu woman and stepped back from his religious work. His well-wishers are said to have appealed to Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani on his behalf, after which he returned to his path and formally became Mujaddid Alf Sani's disciple as well, later teaching Mujaddid Alf Sani's own children. The episode is told plainly, as part of his story rather than something to smooth over. Chishti tells the episode at length, and it is given under Legends and Miracles below.

The books record the bond with the Mujaddid in several forms. Lahori writes that after his training under Shah Sikandar he attended "امام ربانی مجدد الف ثانی پیر احمد فاروقی سرہندی", the Imam-e Rabbani, Mujaddid Alf Sani, Pir Ahmad Faruqi Sirhindi, gained great benefits from him, and came to Lahore at the Mujaddid's direction to guide the people, where thousands reached high stations through him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). The edition's modern editor separately names him a *khalifa* of the Mujaddid, extremely strict in the *shariah*, who died in 1040 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44, حاشیہ 1). Chishti calls him a *murid* of "حضرت شیخ احمد سرہندی", writes that he first taught the Mujaddid's sons "حضرت شیخ محمد معصوم اور شیخ محمد سعید [OCR?]", Hazrat Shaikh Muhammad Masum and Shaikh Muhammad Said, and says that the *qutbiyat* of Lahore was conferred on him by the Mujaddid, "قطبیت لاہور کی [illegible] حضرت مجدد سے اونکو عطا ہوئی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187). Kanhaiya Lal calls him a *khadim* of Shaikh Ahmad in the Mujaddidi silsila (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

Kanhaiya Lal writes that he came "شہر سرہند سے", from the city of Sirhind, and settled at the site in the time of "شاہ جہانگیر بادشاہ" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88); elsewhere he places him in the Shah Jahan era, "خاندان قادریہ مین ایک خدا پرست صاحب کشف و کرامت شاہجہانی عہد مین تہا", a God-worshipping man of *kashf* and *karamat* of the Qadiri family in the time of Shah Jahan, and adds that he was accomplished in the outward sciences too (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). Chishti, in a passage much damaged in print, says he lived inside the walled city, in a quarter printed "محلہ شیخ اسحاق[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191).

Lahori calls him the *qutb* of his age in the Qadiri silsila, "اپنے عہد کے قطب وقت", and says of him "کوئی سائل دین و دنیا کا جو ان کے دروازے پر آیا خالی نہ گیا": no seeker of faith or of the world who came to his door went away empty (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). He lived, Lahori writes, by his pen: "کتب احادیث و تفاسیر کی کتابت حضرت کرتے اور ہدیہ کر کے گزارہ اوقات کرتے", he copied out books of hadith and *tafsir* and subsisted by presenting them, and his nights passed in instructing his attendants and in worship (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). Chishti, too, has him live on copying hadith and *tafsir* and accept no "نذر و نیاز [OCR?]", no votive offerings (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187). Lahori records a refusal of patronage: "یہ حضرت تمام عمر کسی دولت مند کے پاس نہ گئے اور نہ ان کو اپنے دربار میں بار دیا", all his life he went to no rich man, nor admitted the rich to his own *darbar* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47).

It is reported that in his later years he married twice, to Mah-e-Khanam and to Ismatullah, the latter the daughter of an Afghan king, and that he spent his nights absorbed in remembrance (*zikr*) rather than in the comforts that came with his following. He is described as periodically fasting and practicing self-denial for stretches of fifteen to twenty days, and as never allowing the crowds who gathered around him to produce pride. Chishti records the graves of two wives under other names and parentage: "ماہ خاتم[OCR?] دختر مرزا امان اللہ[OCR?]", Mah Khatam, daughter of Mirza Amanullah, and "عصمت النسا[OCR?] دختر سید شہ[OCR?]", Ismat al-Nisa, daughter of a Sayyid whose name is cut short in print (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 189). He adds "اولاد حضرت کی باقی نہیں", none of his descendants remain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 189).

Of the orders in which he initiated others, Chishti writes "حضرت شیخ طاہر ہر چار[OCR?] سلسلہ یعنی قادریہ ونقشبندیہ وسہروردیہ میں بیعت لیتے تھی": that he took *bai'at* in all four (the numeral uncertain in print) silsilas, though only three are then named, the Qadiri, Naqshbandi and Suhrawardi (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 215).

He died on 8 Muharram 1040 AH, reported as 8 August 1630 CE, the two calendars agreeing exactly, at the age of 54, consistent with the reported birth year of 1576. Lahori gives the same day and adds the hour: "بروز پنجشنبہ وقت چاشت آٹھویں محرم سال ایک ہزار چالیس ہجری", on Thursday, at the forenoon hour, 8 Muharram 1040 AH; but he gives his age as fifty-six, "اور عمر چھپن برس کی پائی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). The edition's editor repeats the year, as "حضرت شیخ محمد طاہر بندگی لاہوری (ف ۱۰۴۰ھ)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 129, folio 117, حاشیہ 1). Chishti has a different day and year, "بروزِ پنجشنبہ ششم [OCR?] ماہ محرم سنہ ۱۰۴۱ [OCR?]", Thursday the sixth of Muharram, 1041, both numbers uncertain in print, and writes that he was buried at Miani, "بمقام میانی مدفون ہوئی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187); he places the death in the reign of Shah Jahan, the age and regnal year given in words that cannot now be read with confidence (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 188). Kanhaiya Lal gives the year only, 1040[OCR?] AH, without month or day (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88).

## His Khalifas and His Circle

Lahori names four *khalifas*: "شیخ طاہر کے چار خلیفہ تھے", Shaikh Tahir had four *khalifas*, Abu Muhammad Qadiri, Sayyid Sufi, Shaikh Adam Banuri and Shah Ghulan Sarmast, the last with his own *mazar* in Lahore, "موری دروازے کے باہر سرکاری باغ کے اندر", outside the Mori Gate, inside the government garden (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 279, folio 267).

Shaikh Adam Banuri, Lahori writes, came to him on foot, "پیادہ بنور سے لاہور میں آیا", walking from Banur to Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). The edition's editor quotes Adam Banuri's own Persian account, from the second volume of the *Khulasat al-Maarif*, of receiving the *nisbat-e jazba* from Shaikh Tahir Lahori, "کہ خلفائی کبار حضرت پیر است", who is among the great *khalifas* of Hazrat Pir, and of that *nisbat* having reached Tahir through Shah Iskandar son of Pira Shah Kamal Kaithali (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47, حاشیہ 1).

Chishti records the grave of Hazrat Abu Muhammad Qadiri Lahori within Shaikh Tahir's enclosure (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 190), and writes that Abu Muhammad's family were *khadims* of Shaikh Tahir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191). Chishti records that Abu Muhammad Lahori was "سلسلہ قادریہ میں مرید شیخ طاہر صاحب", a *murid* of Shaikh Tahir in the Qadiri silsila (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 215). Lahori traces a three-generation chain out of his circle: Shaikh Muhammad Fazil Qadri Batalvi was *murid* and *khalifa* of Shaikh Muhammad Afzal Kalanauri, who was *murid* of Shaikh Abu Muhammad Lahori, who was *murid* of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Lahori (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 76, folio 74).

In a footnote, Lahori's editor records Shaikh Tahir's wish to visit the *mazar* of Shah Husain to seek his help, *istimdad* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44, حاشیہ 1).

A book has also been ascribed to him. Lahori's editor writes "تذکرہ مجددیہ کے مصنف کا نام معلوم نہیں ہے", the author of the *Tazkira-e Mujaddidiya* is not known, and then reports that Muhammad Din Fauq stated it to be the work of "حضرت شیخ محمد طاہر بندگی لاہوری (ف ۱۰۴۰ھ)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 129, folio 117, حاشیہ 1). The attribution is Fauq's, given by an editor who has just said the author is unknown. Chishti, for his part, draws on a second source whose title is printed "کتاب تذکرہ محدودیہ[OCR?]" and copies from it a Persian petition, an "عرضی", from one "احقر العبد مرتب[OCR?] محمد طاہر[OCR?]" who writes "متوجہ لاہور شدم", I set out for Lahore, and names the Qadiri and Chishti orders; nearly every word of it is uncertain in print (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 188). Chishti's first source for the chapter is "کتاب تذکرۃ الاحبا [OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 186).

## The Mosque, Madrasa, and Library

The land that is now Miani Sahib Graveyard was, in Hazrat Tahir Bandagi's lifetime, gifted to him so that he could teach. On it he built a mosque, a madrasa, and a library (*kutub khana*), and taught the Qur'an there himself. One specific episode is reported from this period: Sikh raiders, believing gold was hidden inside boxes on the premises, broke in and found only books, and, on discovering this, threw the books back into the locality and left. When Hazrat Tahir Bandagi died, his resting place beside this mosque became his shrine, and rulers and disciples of the period are said to have kept it under careful administrative care from the start.

Kanhaiya Lal describes the madrasa in his own terms: "شیخ محمد طاہر نے بہت برست [OCR?] تک اس جگہ پر مدرسہ جاری رکہا اور علوم فقہ و حدیث و تفسیر طلبا کو مفت پڑہانا رہا مرید بہی بہت کئے اور سلوک کی تلقین کی", Shaikh Muhammad Tahir kept a madrasa running at this place for many years (the word uncertain in print), taught *fiqh*, hadith and *tafsir* to students free of charge, made many *murids* and gave instruction in *suluk* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88). "چونکہ محمد طاہر عالم و فاضل و فقیر کامل تہا چند سال میں ہزاروں لوگ اُسکے مرید و شاگرد ہو گئے": because he was learned, accomplished and a perfect *faqir*, within a few years thousands became his *murids* and pupils, and a magnificent settlement grew up around him (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88). Chishti likewise writes that "ہزار ہا", thousands, came to him in Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187).

Kanhaiya Lal tells of a plundering, too, though not as the survey does. After the saint's death, he writes, the quarter stayed settled "اخیر سلطنت اسلام تک", until the end of Muslim rule; then plunderers looted "ہزاروں قرآن و کتابیں", thousands of Qur'ans and books, tried to sell them, and "باہر گاؤں پہینک کر چلے گئے", threw them outside the village and went away, burning the quarter to ashes in their anger (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 85–86, folios 88–89). Of the ruined quarter, "ایک تو مزار شیخ محمد طاہر موجود ہے اور دوسری کسی قدر عمارت کہنہ مدرسہ شیخ محمد طاہر کا ابتک موجود": the *mazar* of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir still stands, and some of the old fabric of his madrasa still stood when Kanhaiya Lal wrote (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 86, folio 89).

## The Shrine

All three books place the tomb in the Miani graveyard. In Lahori's book, Shah Muhammad Muqim, travelling to Lahore, halts "جب گورستان میانی میں بجوار مزار شیخ محمد طاہر لاہوری پہنچے", when he reached the Miani graveyard, in the vicinity of the *mazar* of Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Lahori (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 64, folio 52); the editor calls the place "میانی شریف" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 64, حاشیہ 1), and fixes another grave by the shrine: "حاجی شیخ رمضان لاہوری کا مزار دربار حضرت شیخ محمد طاہر بندگی لاہور میانی صاحب کے قریب ہے", the *mazar* of Haji Shaikh Ramzan Lahori is near the *darbar* of Hazrat Shaikh Muhammad Tahir Bandagi, Lahore, Miani Sahib (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 125, folio 113). Kanhaiya Lal gives the place as lying from mauza Mazang in a direction whose printed word is uncertain, "موضع مزنگ سے بسمت نیبرت [OCR?]" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88), and lists the tomb among the buildings outside the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3). Lahori's own text calls the site a "مزار", his editor a "درگاہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262).

Kanhaiya Lal describes the fabric: "اول احاطہ مزار شیخ ظاہر بندگی [OCR?] یہ احاطہ سب سے بڑا ہے اور وسیع چار دیواری پختہ خشتی بنی ہوئی ہے جسکے اندر ہزارون قبرین قدیمہ جدیدہ ہین", first, the enclosure of the *mazar* of Shaikh Tahir Bandagi, which is the largest of all, a spacious *pakka* wall of brick, inside which are thousands of graves, old and new (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). The tomb itself stands on a platform within it: "اس کلان چار دیواری کے اندر ایک اور بڑا پختہ چبوترہ ہے جسپر پختہ چونہ گچ مزار اس بزرگ کا بنا ہے", within this great wall is another large *pakka* platform, on which this elder's *pakka* lime-plastered *mazar* is built (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

The tomb has been rebuilt. Lahori's editor writes "موجودہ مزار جناب پیر [illegible] گیلانی مدظلہ کا تعمیر کردہ ہے", the present *mazar* was built by Pir [illegible] Gilani, the name lost in print, who reports that when the old tomb was excavated for the new construction, "قدیم مزار بالکل مزار حضرت مجدد الف ثانی رح کی طرز پر بنا ہوا تھا", the old *mazar* had been built exactly in the style of the *mazar* of Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 59–60, folios 47–48, حاشیہ 2).

His walled enclosure, the *chahar-diwari*, served others as a burial ground and as a landmark. Lahori writes of Sayyid Munawwar Ali Shah Naqshbandi Suhrawardi Lahori that he died in 1264 AH and that "مرقد چار دیواری شیخ طاہر لاہوری کے اندر ہے", his tomb is inside the *chahar-diwari* of Shaikh Tahir Lahori (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 230–231, folios 218–219); that passage names no place, but the book's appendix lists the same man's tomb in the Miani graveyard, "قبرستان میانی نزد مقبرہ حضرت طاہر بندگی قادری", near the tomb of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 290, folio 278). The appendix places a Chishti beside him as well, Shaikh Haji Ramzan Lahori Chishti, "نزد مقبرہ شیخ طاہر بندگی میانی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 288, folio 276). Chishti uses the wall to locate other graves: "یہ رویہ چار دیواری مقبرہ حضرت شیخ طاہر متصل ہے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 195); "گوشہ شرقی چار دیواری حضرت شیخ طاہر میں", in the eastern corner of Hazrat Shaikh Tahir's wall (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 198); and "چار دیواری شیخ طاہر بندگی[OCR?] کے شمال", to the north of it (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 209). Kanhaiya Lal, too, sets a neighbouring enclosure by "چار دیواری شیخ طاہر" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 294, folio 297).

## Custodianship

The shrine is overseen today by its Gaddi Nasheen (current custodians), with several people formally employed as staff who reportedly consider caring for the shrine year-round to be a privilege rather than a job.

The older books name custodians of their own day, and on their line they disagree. Lahori, giving the genealogy of a Gilani family, ends it with "سید شہسوار جو اب [OCR?] سجادہ نشین مزار شیخ طاہر بندگی کا ہے", Sayyid Shahsawar, who is now (the word uncertain in print) *sajjada nashin* of the *mazar* of Shaikh Tahir Bandagi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262). His line runs back to Sayyid Abd al-Qadir Lahori, "سید عبدالقادر لاہوری", son of Sayyid Jalal al-Din Baghdadi, who settled at Lahore in Akbar's reign and married a daughter of "نواب میر کفایت خاں"; and it records one member's trade, "بہادر بن چراغ شاہ جو مہر کنی کا کام کرتا ہے", Bahadur son of Chiragh Shah, a seal-engraver (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262). The edition's editor corrects him: "یہاں شجرہ نسب درست نہیں ہے۔ بلکہ یوں ہونا چاہیے", the genealogy here is not correct, it should run thus, and gives a line that ends in "پیر شیر حسین درسی [OCR?] طاہری مد ظلہ اس وقت سجادہ نشین درگاہ حضرت شیخ طاہر بندگی ہیں", Pir Sher Husain Darsi (the reading uncertain) Tahiri, may his shadow endure, who is at this time *sajjada nashin* of the *dargah* of Hazrat Shaikh Tahir Bandagi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262, حاشیہ ۲). The *nisba* Tahiri is taken from the saint himself.

Chishti names a *sajjada nashin* as one of his informants: "زبانی سید منصور سجادہ نشین خانقاہ حضرت شیخ محمد طاہر صاحب قدس سرہ", from the mouth of Sayyid Mansur, *sajjada nashin* of the *khanqah* of Hazrat Shaikh Muhammad Tahir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 209). Elsewhere he names a "سید شاہ سوارا[OCR?]", of the descendants of Abd al-Qadir Thani, as "سجادہ نشین خانقاہ شیخ طاہر بندگی[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 649), and in further passages, badly damaged in print, a Sayyid whose name begins "سید سہسو[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 204) and a "شہسوار" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 650). He records, too, that the office itself, "عہدہ سجادہ نشینی شیخ طاہر صاحب", was disputed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 215–216).

## Devotion and Practice

A mosque stands beside the shrine where the five daily prayers are held, and visitors come both for prayer and to recite the Fatiha and make personal supplications. It is reported that some families have visited for generations, following parents and grandparents before them. The main recurring gatherings are Mehfil-e-Naat and langar, held weekly on Thursday nights and Fridays.

Daily attendance is given as 1,200 to 1,600 visitors.

It is reported that the shrine owes its continuing importance to answered prayer across generations: families who saw their petitions answered here return, and bring their children to do the same. Hazrat Tahir Bandagi is described by visitors as a "perfect saint" (*wali-e-kamil*) who was granted visions of the Prophet and of other venerable elders on multiple occasions, and the presence of Jinnat and of other noble burials nearby is offered by devotees as further evidence, in their eyes, of his spiritual standing.

The Urs falls every year on the 7th, 8th, and 9th of Muharram, drawing an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 pilgrims across the three days. The current custodians (*Gaddi Nasheen*) describe Hazrat Tahir Bandagi as someone who did not care for drumming (*dhol*) or ecstatic dance (*dhamal*), and say the Urs is kept accordingly restrained, centered on Mehfil-e-Naat and langar rather than music or dancing.

Chishti records the *urs* of his own day, "عرس یعنی فاتحہ سالیہ[OCR?] حضرت شیخ طاہر", the *urs*, that is the annual *fatiha*, of Hazrat Shaikh Tahir, kept by the *sajjada nashin* and the gravediggers in the first ten days of Muharram, on a date printed "تاریخ تیریں[OCR?] ماہ محرم", whose reading is uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 216). Kanhaiya Lal, in his first account of the saint, names no *urs*, fair, *langar*, offering, custodian or endowment (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88).

## Legends and Miracles

Several traditions are attached to the shrine, and it is reported that not all of them are agreed on even by today's visitors.

One account holds that Hazrat Tahir Bandagi, while leading Taraweeh prayers, was granted a vision of the Prophet Muhammad, who told him that whoever looked upon him, learned from him, or was buried near him would enter Paradise, offered as the reason so many notable figures chose burial around his tomb. Lahori records a promise in the saint's own words: "حضرت فرماتے تھے کہ میری وفات کے بعد جو شخص میرے احاطہ مزار میں مدفون ہو گا۔ میں نے خدا سے مانگا ہے کہ وہ جنتی ہو گا", the Hazrat used to say that whoever is buried within the enclosure of his *mazar* after his death, he has asked of God that that person shall be of Paradise (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47).

A second, more contested tradition concerns jinn. It is reported that graves near the shrine are popularly said to belong to jinn who watch over the site, and that some visitors report having seen figures in human form vanish before their eyes. But this is reportedly not universally accepted even among visitors: others say that although the graves exist, they have never personally witnessed any jinn or wild animal there, and regard the jinn stories as ignorance, pointing out, in their own study of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi's life, that he himself never taught or endorsed such beliefs. Both positions are reported as live, current opinions, not settled fact.

Chishti tells the story of his fall and return as a prophecy fulfilled. The Mujaddid, he relates, foretold that one of those present would become a *kafir*. Then, "بمقام سرہند", at Sirhind, Shaikh Tahir fell in love with a "ماہ پیشانی [OCR?]", a moon-browed beauty; he put on the "زنار [OCR?]", the sacred thread, drew the "قشقہ", the forehead mark, "قشقہ کھینچ کر", and "بتخانہ میں جا بیٹھے", went and sat in the temple, "ہندو ہو کر", having become a Hindu (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187). At this point the story gives a Persian couplet:

کافرِ عشقم مسلمانی مرا در کار نیست
ہر رگِ من تار گشتہ حاجتِ زنار [OCR?] نیست

Chishti gives no translation; the couplet turns on the words کافر, the unbeliever, and زنار, the thread he had put on (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187). The Mujaddid's sons, whom he had taught, protested, "ہمارا اوستاد کافر ہو گیا", our teacher has become a *kafir*, and invoked the "حقِ اوستادی", the right a teacher holds; the Mujaddid prayed, his prayer was answered, and Shaikh Tahir repented (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187).

Kanhaiya Lal writes that "خزینۃ الاصفیا و حدیقۃ الاولیا و تذکرہ مجددیہ وغیرہ کتب مین اس بزرگ کی کرامتین بیشمار تحریر ہین", countless *karamat* of this elder are written in the *Khazinat al-Asfiya*, the *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, the *Tazkira-e Mujaddidiya* and other books, but he narrates none of them himself (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

## In Verse

Lahori closes his entry with a chronogram quatrain on the saint, which opens:

شیخ طاہر پاک باز و پاک دین
اوج عرفان پر تھے مثل آفتاب

The quatrain is on Shaikh Tahir himself, naming him in its first line; no translation of it is given, and the year it encodes is not stated with these opening lines (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 60, folio 48).

Chishti records a *qita* on his death by "مفتی [OCR?] غلام سرور", nearly every word of which is uncertain in print (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187). Kanhaiya Lal says that the year of his death comes out of a single word, though he prints that word in two ways in two places: "سنہ ۱۰۴۰ [OCR?] ہجری میں وہ مر گیا جسکی تاریخ غم کے لفظ سے نکلی", he died in 1040 AH, whose date comes out of the word *gham*, grief (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88); and "عم [OCR?] کے لفظ سے اسکی تاریخ وفات نکلی ہے", the date of his death comes from the word printed عم, the reading uncertain (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). No fuller chronogram phrase is printed in either place.

## Setting: The Miani Graveyard

The books' accounts of the Miani graveyard speak of the graveyard as a whole, not of this shrine alone. Kanhaiya Lal writes "یہ خطہ جسکو گورستان میانی کہتے ہین لاہور سے بجانب جنوب بفاصلہ دو میل واقع ہے", the tract called the Miani graveyard lies two miles south of Lahore; it was formerly a village of the Miani people, that is of *ulama* and *fuzala*, called Panj Pir Dhera because five graves stood there before the village, "کیونکہ ڈہیرہ [OCR?] پنجابی زبان مین قبر کو کہتے ہین", since in Punjabi *dhera* means a grave (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 291–292, folios 294–295). He explains the name Miani from the learned men who lived there: "چونکہ میانا پنجابی زبان میں مولوی عالم فاضل کو کہتے ہیں اور وہی لوگ اسمیں رہتے اسواسطے اس بستی کا نام میانی مشہور ہو گیا", because in Punjabi a *maulvi*, a learned and accomplished man, is called *miana*, and such people lived there, the settlement came to be known as Miani (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88). Within the graveyard he names, besides the saint's enclosure, only the unfinished enclosure of Rani Gul Begum, "یہ عورت قوم طوایف", a woman of the courtesan caste (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

Kanhaiya Lal describes how the ground became a burial place after the ruin of the quarter: "بعد ویرانی اس محلہ کے شہر لاہور کے لوگوں نے اس جگہ کو قبرستان بنا لیا", after the ruin of this quarter the people of Lahore made the place a graveyard, where thousands of graves have been made, burials continue, and many *pakka* enclosures have been built (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 86, folio 89). In his later account he adds that for the last ten or twelve years general burial had been stopped, and that only those who had *pakka* enclosures still buried their dead there (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

Chishti's chapter carries several accounts of the place, kept side by side. In Akbar's reign, he writes, it was a village where only learned men lived, and because Punjabis call *ulama* "میاں", it was called "میانی"; its chief was "حافظ جان محمد صاحب والد حضرت ابو محمد قادری", Hafiz Jan Muhammad, father of Hazrat Abu Muhammad Qadiri, after whose death Abu Muhammad was made its head; a dispute over a point of law then emptied the village, until a Hazrat Mir Ali, the name uncertain in print, was appointed by the king and settled there, and it was peopled again (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191). He explains the second name differently from Kanhaiya Lal: a "پیر علیمہ[OCR?] صاحب" had the coffins of five elders brought and buried here, and since a grave mound is a *dher* in Punjabi, the place was called "میانی پنج ڈھیر[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191). In his account of the gravediggers, heavily damaged in print, the account passes from the reign of Shah Jahan to that of Alamgir, has the graveyard fall desolate after Muhammad Shah, and has it grow again when burials resume under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the sequence only approximately legible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 204); elsewhere he writes that the Sikhs looted mauza Miani (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 212), and "میانی[OCR?] ویران ہوئی یہ قبرستان بنا", Miani was ruined and this graveyard came to be (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 213). A passage in the same section speaks of Shaikh Tahir's grave and of very many graves, but its words are too damaged to say what it tells of how the graveyard grew (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 212).

Chishti also records the gravediggers, the *gorkans*, who served the graveyard and, with the *sajjada nashin*, kept the saint's *urs*. He lists the *gorkans* of his day as Sayyid Mansur, the *sajjada nashin*, gave them to him (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 209), and gives two statements of how their income was shared: one in which part of it reaches the *sajjada nashin* (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 209), and one in which "جو مردہ آتا ہی تو مالک میت حق گورکنی انکو دیتا ہے اور علاوہ اسکے سجادہ نشین کو بھی کچھ حتی المقدور دیتا ہی", the family of the dead pays the gravediggers their due and gives the *sajjada nashin* something besides, as they can, the *sajjada nashin* having no share in the gravediggers' income (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 213).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The day and year of his death.** The survey gives 8 Muharram 1040 AH, 8 August 1630 CE. Lahori gives Thursday, at the forenoon hour, 8 Muharram 1040 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47), and his editor 1040 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44, حاشیہ 1). Chishti gives Thursday the sixth[OCR?] of Muharram, 1041[OCR?] (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187), and returns to the date later in words largely illegible in print (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 216). Kanhaiya Lal gives 1040[OCR?] AH, with no month or day (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88; p. 292, folio 295).
- **His age at death.** The survey gives 54, consistent with its birth year of 1576. Lahori gives fifty-six (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). Chishti's figure cannot be read with confidence in print (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 188).
- **Where he came from.** The survey has him born in Lahore. Kanhaiya Lal has him come from the city of Sirhind (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88); Lahori has him come to Lahore at the Mujaddid's direction (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47).
- **Whose time he belongs to.** Kanhaiya Lal has him settle at the site in the time of Jahangir (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88) and elsewhere places him in the Shah Jahan era (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295); Chishti places his death in Shah Jahan's reign (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 188).
- **His master, and who named him Bandagi.** The survey names Hazrat Shah Sikandar as his master and as the giver of the name Tahir Bandagi. Lahori makes him *murid* and *khalifa* of Shah Sikandar, son of Pir Kamal Kaithali (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47). Chishti credits the title to Hazrat Lal Kamal Shah[OCR?] of Kaithal (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 189). Kanhaiya Lal makes him *murid* of Shah Kamal Kaithali[OCR?] (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).
- **His Sufi order.** The site names him Qadri, and its survey bibliography names the shrine Qadri Naqshbandi Mujaddidi. Lahori names him four ways: Qadiri in the contents and in a later entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3; p. 279, folio 267); "قادری و نقشبندی" in the heading of his own entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47); "شیخ محمد طاہر قادری نقشبندی" in one appendix row (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 288, folio 276); and "حضرت طاہر بندگی قادری" in another (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 290, folio 278); his editor makes him a *khalifa* of the Mujaddid (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44, حاشیہ 1). Kanhaiya Lal names him "شیخ محمد طاہر قادری و نقشبندی" in one place (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88), and in another a Qadiri *murid* of Shah Kamal and a Mujaddidi *khadim* of Shaikh Ahmad (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). Chishti has him take *bai'at* in the Qadiri, Naqshbandi and Suhrawardi orders (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 215).
- **The name Bandagi.** The survey, Chishti and Lahori's editor use it (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 186; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 129, folio 117, حاشیہ 1). Lahori's own entry heading and contents omit it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3; p. 59, folio 47); the book's persons index gives the full form "محمد طاہر بندگی لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 328, folio 316), while another reading of the same index lists four Tahirs, none of them Bandagi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 321). In Kanhaiya Lal's first account the name appears only in the contents (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88; p. 4, folio 3); in his second it appears in the text, printed "شیخ ظاہر بندگی [OCR?]" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).
- **His wives.** The survey names Mah-e-Khanam and Ismatullah, the latter the daughter of an Afghan king. Chishti records the graves of "ماہ خاتم[OCR?] دختر مرزا امان اللہ[OCR?]" and "عصمت النسا[OCR?] دختر سید شہ[OCR?]", Mah Khatam, daughter of Mirza Amanullah, and Ismat al-Nisa, daughter of a Sayyid (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 189).
- **His fall and return.** The survey says he became enamored of a Hindu woman and stepped back from his religious work, that his well-wishers appealed to the Mujaddid, and that he then became the Mujaddid's disciple and later taught his children. Chishti sets the episode at Sirhind, has him put on the sacred thread and sit in a temple as a Hindu after the Mujaddid had foretold it, has the Mujaddid's sons, already his pupils, protest, and has the Mujaddid's prayer bring him back (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 187).
- **The promise of Paradise.** The survey has the promise made to him by the Prophet in a vision during Taraweeh prayers, to whoever looked upon him, learned from him or was buried near him. Lahori has the saint himself say that he had asked of God that whoever was buried within the enclosure of his *mazar* should be of Paradise (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 59, folio 47).
- **The raid on the books.** The survey places it in his lifetime: Sikh raiders, looking for gold, found only books, threw them back into the locality and left. Kanhaiya Lal places it after his death, at the end of Muslim rule: plunderers looted thousands of Qur'ans and books, tried to sell them, threw them outside the village and burned the quarter (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 85–86, folios 88–89).
- **How the graveyard began.** The survey says the graveyard grew up around his tomb as generation after generation asked to be buried near him. Kanhaiya Lal says the people of Lahore made the place a graveyard after the quarter was ruined (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 86, folio 89). Chishti writes that Miani was ruined and the graveyard came to be (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 213).
- **Where he lived.** The survey and Kanhaiya Lal set his mosque, madrasa and settlement on the ground of the graveyard (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88). Chishti, in a damaged passage, places his residence inside the walled city (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191).
- **Why the place is called Miani Panj Pir.** Kanhaiya Lal derives Panj Pir Dhera from five graves that stood there before the village (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 291–292, folios 294–295); Chishti from the coffins of five elders brought there by a Pir and buried (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 191).
- **The date of the urs.** The survey gives the 7th, 8th and 9th of Muharram. Chishti places the *urs* within the first ten days of Muharram, on a date whose printed word is uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 216).
- **The custodians' line.** Lahori names Sayyid Shahsawar as *sajjada nashin* at the end of a Gilani genealogy (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262); his editor declares that genealogy incorrect, gives another, and names Pir Sher Husain Darsi[OCR?] Tahiri as *sajjada nashin* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262, حاشیہ ۲). Chishti names Sayyid Mansur (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 209) and a Sayyid Shah Sawar[OCR?] (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 649), and records that the office was disputed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 215–216).
- **The chronogram word.** Kanhaiya Lal derives the year of death from the word غم in one place (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 85, folio 88) and from the word printed عم[OCR?] in another (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

## Legacy

Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri's tomb is the oldest seat of the Miani Sahib Graveyard, and the books show it serving as the point by which other graves in the graveyard were found. Kanhaiya Lal writes "اس بزرگ کی بزرگی کے سب مسلمان قائل ہین اور بڑا خاندان اسکے سلسلہ کا قصبہ بٹالہ مین ہے جنکے ہزارون مرید پنجاب کے علاقہ مین ہین", all Muslims acknowledge this elder's greatness, and the great family of his silsila is at the town of Batala, with thousands of *murids* across the Punjab (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295). A Chishti and a Naqshbandi-Suhrawardi saint lie beside him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 288, folio 276; p. 290, folio 278).

Lahori's entry on him closes with a list of further sources, among them the *Zubdat al-Maqamat*, the *Hazarat al-Quds*, the *Rauzat al-Qayyumiya* and the *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 60, folio 48), and Kanhaiya Lal points his readers to the *Khazinat al-Asfiya*, the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* and the *Tazkira-e Mujaddidiya* for the many miracles told of him (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 292, folio 295).

Name: Darbar Malik Ahmad Ayaz
Sufi Saint: Malik Ahmad Ayaz (also given as "Malik Ayaz Ahmad" and "Malik Ayaz"), described in the survey as slave of Mahmud Ghaznavi, minister, and governor of Lahore
Events: *ʿurs*, annually on 12, 13 and 14 Zil Hajj (lamps lit, sheets changed, bathing, food eaten). Daily: five daily prayers at the adjacent mosque; daily offering of *diyas* and *prasād*.
Description:
## Overview

Darbar Malik Ahmad Ayaz is an active Muslim shrine in the name of Malik Ahmad Ayaz, who is reported to have been the "Slave of Mehmood Gaznavi - Governor Lahore"; it is reported that his tomb was built at this place after his death. The site's religion is reported as Islam and its affiliation as "Ahl e Sunnat - Ghaznavi silsila" (*silsila*, a chain of spiritual transmission), reproduced as recorded.

The shrine stands in Shah Alam Market, which is reported to be the largest market in Asia and to be extremely crowded; the *mazār* (tomb, mausoleum) is reported to lie near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. The site is small, and the surrounding congestion is reported to prevent many people from reaching it, gradually reducing both the figure's fame and the enthusiasm of visitors. Residents of this densely populated neighbourhood are largely unaware of the life of the figure buried there — a figure about whom, it is reported, Allama Iqbal, Kaniya Lal and other writers have written books.

The books consulted add a good deal to this reported picture, and contest some of it. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives him an entry of his own as 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', calls him the slave and beloved of Shah Mahmud Ghaznavi, follows him from tutor to the young prince who governed the Punjab to a renouncer in the company of *faqirs*, and has him die in 450 AH and lie buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 192–193). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* and Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* both make him the man who restored Lahore after Mahmud's conquest (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Annemarie Schimmel's books on Islamic mysticism and its poetry know him as the Turkish officer whose devotion made the king "the slave of his slave" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74), and Nizami-i Arudi's *Chahar Maqala*, in Edward G. Browne's translation, tells of a carousal at which Mahmud bade him cut off his curls (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). The editor of Lahori's Urdu edition, for his part, rejects the tradition that Ayaz refounded Lahore and treats the romance of Mahmud and Ayaz as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed); and the year of Ayaz's death is given three different ways.

## The Life of Malik Ahmad Ayaz

It is reported that Malik Ayaz Ahmad was educated in Georgia in 993 AD, and that when "the infidels attacked your country" he was enslaved and taken for sale to the Baghdad slave market — slave dealing being, reportedly, then the norm. Too weak to attract buyers, he was passed over until Mahmud Ghaznavi came through and asked his price. The minister questioned the purchase; the king answered that what he saw in the boy the minister could not see. The price asked was ten thousand dinars, greed having been raised in the seller's heart by the king's words; Mahmud paid it and enrolled him among his soldiers.

Tradition holds that the relation of master and slave turned into love, and that Ayaz spent his whole life in devotion to Mahmud. The story of the melon is also reported: the king, feeding him a melon cut by his own hand, tasted it himself, found it bitter, and asked why Ayaz had said nothing; Ayaz replied that having had sweetness from his master's hand all his life, he had no cause to complain of one bitter piece.

It is reported that Mahmud fought "almost 17 battles with Hindus", in which Ayaz "played the role of the mastermind", and that his faith was so firm that "he did not fall for the infidels". In one such story the king, attacking at the "Onkay temple", found the idol suspended in mid-air; Ayaz reasoned that a magnet in the temple held the clay figure up, and that demolishing the walls would bring it down of itself — which, reportedly, is what happened, to the king's satisfaction.

The king's family and ministers are reported to have mocked the closeness between the two; when the minister tested them by summoning everyone at midnight to eat, Ayaz alone appeared fully prepared, the others arriving late or intoxicated and asleep. Mahmud made him his minister, and he continued always to regard himself as a slave, each night setting aside his costly clothes and taking out the old garments in which he had been brought for sale, so as to remember his past, sit alone and please his God. The last ten years of his life, tradition holds, were largely given to the remembrance of God (*dhikr*).

In Ayaz's last days, it is further reported, Mahmud wished to hand his own place to him; Ayaz declined, asking that it go instead to one of his two sons, Saad, and the king relinquished his power. When Ayaz governed Lahore the city had been ruined by war, its systems of livelihood, food, trade and wages broken, and by his intelligence he gave it shape again and set it on its own feet. He fell suddenly ill and died; it is said he was poisoned out of resentment at the love shown him, and in some places it is said he died a natural death. His death is reported as 8 August 1041, and his mausoleum is reported to have been built then in Shah Alam Market.

## Origins and Career in the Histories

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* tells another story of his origins, and introduces it with 'گویند', 'they say': 'این ایاز خلف والی کشمیر بود', this Ayaz was the son of the ruler of Kashmir. As a small child he went with his father to a hunting ground, where 'جمعی ازعیاران آدم دزد', a band of man-stealing rogues, seized him, carried him out of that country and sold him in Badakhshan to a merchant 'بقیمت خاطرخواه', at a price to their liking; and 'ازتقدیرات قادر مطلق شاهزاده بغلامی منسوب گشت', by the decrees of the Absolute Almighty the prince was given over to slavery (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410).

The merchant, 'نظر برحسن وجمال ایاز', with an eye to Ayaz's beauty and grace, valued him above all his slaves and saw to his upbringing, and came 'بقصد تجارت ازبدخشان درغزنین', from Badakhshan to Ghazni to trade (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). In Ghazni word spread of a slave too beautiful to look at; great and small came to see him, likening him to the moon and, 'درحسن وخوبی به یوسف کنعان', in beauty and goodness to Yusuf of Canaan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410). The Sultan summoned the merchant with him, bought Ayaz 'بقیمت گران انچه سوداگر میخواست بلکه زیاده بران', at a heavy price, what the merchant asked and more, and made him 'انیس انجمن خاص وجلیس مجلس اختصاص', the intimate of his private assembly and companion of his select gathering; 'اورا برتمامی خادم وحشم برگزیده', he preferred him above all his servants and retinue (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). 'وسلطان اگرچه چندین هزار غلام داشت اماسرامد ایشان ملک ایاز بود که سلطان درکمند عشق اوگرفتاری داشت': though the Sultan had many thousands of slaves, the foremost of them was Malik Ayaz, in the noose of whose love the Sultan was caught (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410).

Bhandari sets beside this a different view, introduced with 'بعضی شعرا نوشته اند', some poets have written: 'ایاز اگرچه حسن صوری وجمال ظاهری چندان نداشت لیکن دراخلاق پسندیده طاق ... بود', that although Ayaz had no great outward beauty he was matchless in praiseworthy character, so that the Sultan's devotion was to his 'سیرت نیک خصایل', his good disposition, and not to his looks (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 408).

Nizami-i Arudi's anecdote of Sultan Mahmud and Ayaz, in Browne's translation, calls the Sultan's love for 'the Turk' 'well-known and famous'; the opening sentence is garbled in the copy consulted, and Ayaz's name before 'the Turk' cannot be read (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). Nizami's description of him can be read only in part in the copy consulted, and its reading is pieced together and uncertain: Ayaz was "not remarkably handsome, but was of sweet expression and olive complexion, symmetrically formed, graceful in his movements, sensible and deliberate in action, and mightily endowed with all the arts of pleasing" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).

Lahori's contents list him as entry no. 130, 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', in the fifth chapter, on 'miscellaneous families' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), and the entry says of him: 'یہ شخص شاہ محمود غزنوی کا غلام و محبوب تھا۔ حق جل شانہ نے اس کو دولت ظاہری و باطنی عطا کی تھی', he was the slave and beloved of Shah Mahmud Ghaznavi, and God gave him both outward and inward wealth (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 192–193).

Lahori then follows him through the reigns after Mahmud's. After Mahmud's death Masud took the throne; in his reign his son Majdud, 'جو نو جوان لڑکا تھا', a young boy, was made governor of the Punjab, and Ayaz was appointed his *atalik*, his tutor, and came with him. When Masud died and his son Maudud took the throne, Majdud rebelled and set up a separate sultanate in Hindustan. Maudud marched against him, and 'جب لاہور کا محاصرہ ہوا تو بروز عید ناگاہ مجدود بمرگ مفاجات مر گیا': when Lahore was besieged, on the day of Eid, Majdud suddenly died, and Maudud established his hold over the Punjab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). The edition's editor dates Majdud's governorship to 427–433 AH, though the reading of these figures is uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

Maudud tried hard to take Ayaz with him to Ghazni, 'مگر اس نے منظور نہ کیا اور تارک الدنیا ہو کر صحبت فقرا اختیار کی اور بزرگان لاہور سے فیض کامل حاصل کیا اور بے انتہا دولت جو اس کے پاس تھی، براہ خدا فقرا و غربا کو دے دی': but he did not agree; he renounced the world, took to the company of *faqirs*, received complete *faiz* from the elders of Lahore, and gave away the boundless wealth he had to the *faqirs* and the poor for God's sake (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193).

'آخر سنہ چار سو پچاس ہجری میں وفات پائی اور شہر لاہور کے اندر دفن ہوا': he died in 450 AH and was buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). The editor replaces the year with 449 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193), which he gives as 1057 CE on the authority of Ibn Athir, and reports Firishta as placing the death "a few days after Maudud's death" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

## Governor of Lahore and the Resettlement of the City

The restoring of Lahore takes a large place in the books. Lahori records the tradition in full: 'یہ بزرگ بانی لاہور کا بھی شمار کیا جاتا ہے', this elder is also counted the founder of Lahore. When Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi attacked Lahore and Raja Anangpal, son of Raja Jaipal, was overthrown and fled to Hind after the encounter, Mahmud's army plundered the city and all the subjects left — 'شہر میں کوئی متنفس باقی نہ رہا', not a breathing soul remained in the city. 'اس وقت ایاز نے سلطان سے اجازت لے کر اس شہر کو پھر آباد کیا اور رعایا کو دور دور سے طلب کر کے اس میں قیام پذیر کیا': then Ayaz, taking the sultan's permission, settled the city again and, summoning subjects from far and wide, settled them in it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193).

The edition's editor rejects this tradition outright (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). He calls the founding of Lahore "later writers' conjecture" and treats the romance of Mahmud and Ayaz as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times; in their place, citing Latif, he offers Ayaz as commander of the cantonment (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).

Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore*, which writes the name 'ملک ایاز' each time and never adds 'احمد' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 17, 18, 21, 23; folios 12, 13, 16, 18), tells the story through the city's walls and gates. After Mahmud Ghaznavi's sack, 'چند سال یہ شہر غیر آباد رہا آخر جب ملک ایاز[OCR?] پنجاب کے انتظام کے لئے نامور ہوا تو اُس نے شہر کو دوبارہ آباد کرنا چاہا': for some years the city stayed unpeopled, until at last Malik Ayaz, named to the administration of the Punjab, wished to people it again (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 17, folio 12).

The resettlement was licensed, not private: 'جب ملک ایاز بادشاہ کے حکم سے پنجاب کا حاکم بنا تو اُس نے اس شہر کی آبادی پر توجہ کی اور فرمان اجازت سلطان سے حاصل کیا', when Malik Ayaz became *hakim* of the Punjab by the king's order, he turned to peopling this city and obtained a *farman* of permission from the Sultan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18). He went about it with such zeal — 'اس سرگرمی سے شہر بسایا کہ چند سال میں وہ ویرانہ علما و فضلا کا معدن بن گیا' — that in a few years that wilderness became a mine of *ulama* and the learned (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18). Kanhaiya Lal makes this resettlement the event by which he divides the city's history, and the setting into which Ali Hajveri arrives, the saint whose shrine is the reported landmark for this tomb (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

Three of Lahore's gates are tied to him in the book. The settlement began from the *mohalla* 'جسکو لاہوری منڈی کہتے ہیں', which is called Lahori Mandi, and 'سب سے اول یہی دروازہ تعمیر ہوا جسکا نام لاہوری دروازہ رکھا گیا', this gate was built first of all and was named the Lahori Darwaza (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 17, folio 12). The Mori Darwaza is his victory monument: Mahmud had breached the walls at that spot, and 'ایاز نے جب بہر شہر کو آباد کیا تو فتح کی یادگار کے طور اس جگہ دروازہ قائم کر دیا', when Ayaz settled the city again he set up a gate at that place as a memorial of the victory (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13). The Bhati Darwaza dates from his settlement too, the Bhat *qaum* settling inside it 'بعد آبادی ایاز کے', after Ayaz's settlement (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13). And yet, Kanhaiya Lal adds, 'ملک ایاز کی آبادی کے بعد بھی یہ شہر کبھی ترقی اور کبھی تنزل کی حالت میں رہا': even after Malik Ayaz's settlement the city remained now in a state of progress, now of decline (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 21, folio 16). The book gives no date for his governorship.

Bhandari says the same in brief. After Sultan Mahmud Ghaznavi conquered Hindustan, 'ملک ایاز که منظور نظر سلطان و درخوبی و فراست بے همتا بود', Malik Ayaz, the favourite of the Sultan's eye and without equal in goodness and discernment, turned to restoring Lahore; he 'قلعه پخته احداث نمود', raised a fort of baked brick, and the city was rebuilt (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Bhandari says nothing of his tomb.

## The Shrine

It is reported that the tomb was built at this very place after the death of Malik Ayaz, that the Ghaznavi Sultanate built the Darbar, and that it was later maintained in good condition by "Raja Maharaja". A period of loss is also reported: the water of the Darbar was polluted, and — in wording the transcriber flags as unclear — "the area of crop was stolen for the special place of your Darbar which was spoiled by Sikh Raja Ranjit Singh", after which only the present small plot remained. It is also reported that some of the site's space was lost during the Sikh era and some to the surrounding market.

A mosque named after the figure stands in the vicinity of the Darbar, where the five daily prayers are offered. The shrine is under the supervision of the Department of Auqaf (Government Mehkama Auqaf), consistently reported as both the present custodian and the body responsible for the site's current condition.

Of the books, only Lahori and Kanhaiya Lal speak of his grave, and neither names Shah Alam Market. Lahori has him buried inside the city of Lahore and names no quarter (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). Kanhaiya Lal's table of contents lists a 'مزار ملک ایاز' at printed page ۱۶۰[OCR?], within its Islamic section for inside the city, which opens with 'مسجد بادشاہی' at printed page ۱۴۱; by the book's own classification, then, the tomb is inside the city, unlike the shrines it lists from printed page ۲۳۶ onward (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 3, folio 2). The reading of that page number is uncertain, and the line stands out of sequence in the contents (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 2–5). Beyond that line, what the book has on him is the history of the city: it says nothing of his person, his death, his burial or his darbar, and does not mention Shah Alam Market (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

Lahori's book has, in an appendix, a line for 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری قدس سرہ', placed 'اندر شہر لاہور', inside the city of Lahore, at 'چوک رنگ محل' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277). It may be the same site, but nothing in the book says so: the line gives a saint's honorific, no 'ملک' and no date, and a landmark other than Shah Alam Market. The book's index lists him as 'ایاز لاہوری | ۱۸۰', with neither 'Malik' nor 'Ahmad' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 313, folio 301), and in the copy consulted its index of persons has no entry for a Malik Ayaz (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 330, folio 318).

Chishti and Kanhaiya Lal also list a mosque of a 'خواجہ ایاز'. Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* has in its contents 'حال مسجد خواجہ ایاز', numbered ۷۲۵[OCR?] (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 6), and Kanhaiya Lal lists a 'مسجد خواجہ ایاز[OCR?]' at printed page ۲۸۱, a second Ayaz building, entered separately from the tomb (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3). The Khwaja Ayaz of Kanhaiya Lal's history is a noble of Shah Jahan's reign who served in the buildings department under Ali Mardan Khan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 278, folio 281) and as *mir-e-imarat* of Shalamar Bagh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 279, folio 282). Neither book says that this mosque is the one reported beside the Darbar.

## Devotion and Practice

Visitors come from distant places; it is reported that non-Muslims also visit and that some have made documentaries about the figure, his stories appearing in books. It is reported, in these terms, that *Diyas* (oil lamps) and *prasād* (consecrated food) are offered daily.

The *ʿurs* (death anniversary observance) is held annually on 12, 13 and 14 Zil Hajj, its activities including the lighting of lamps, the changing of sheets, bathing, and the eating of food at the site. Attendance is given as 700 to 800 people daily and 40,000 to 50,000 at the annual *ʿurs*.

The place is reportedly held spiritually important because he fought alongside the king, served the people, protected their lives and property and instilled the spirit of Islam in them; because after Mahmud Ghaznavi's death he left his residence; and because it was his habit to spend nights in the remembrance of God.

What is reported of his teachings is brief: he was generous, intelligent, loyal, hasty, daring, brave, kind and honest, a soldier and also a good and devoted person, who set the example of these qualities in his own life, and people were motivated by seeing it.

None of the books consulted describes the observances at the tomb.

## Legends and Stories

The books tell other stories of the king and his servant, each in its own setting.

Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* has a temple story of its own. At Somnath the amirs advised Mahmud to take the rajas' crores; 'جب ایاز سے پوچہا', when Ayaz was asked, he held that breaking the idol was better, for the renown it would bring among Muslim kings, and God would give more; and the sultan broke it with his own hand (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 805). The reported temple story is set at the "Onkay temple", where Ayaz's reasoning about a magnet brought the idol down. The books do not say that the two are one episode.

The reported picture of Ayaz taking out, each night, the old garments in which he had been brought for sale stands beside a story that Schimmel tells from Rūmī. She counts among 'the finest allegories ever written' one by Rūmī, "who tells the story of Ayaz, Mahmud of Ghazna's favorite slave, who looked every morning at the out-worn shoes and shabby clothes he wore before Mahmud elected him for himself; it was necessary for him to remember his former lowly state so that he could appreciate the bounty that his lord had bestowed upon him" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190). The lesson, as Rūmī concludes it in her account, is that "man should likewise remember how weak he was created, and then he will recognize his nothingness before God" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190).

Schimmel retells the story of the Huma bird as well: "One day the Huma bird passed over Mahmud's army, and everybody rushed to be touched by the Huma's shade, which, in Persian tradition, conveys kingdom. Only Ayaz went into Mahmud's shade", "for here was his true kingdom: he is like the faithful, who does not seek glory and power from anything created but only from his eternally rich, beloved Lord" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).

Nizami-i Arudi's anecdote, in Browne's translation, turns on obedience. Mahmud, Nizami writes, was a pious and God-fearing man, and "he wrestled much with his love for Ayaz so that he should not diverge" from 'the Path of the Law'. At a carousal, with the wine affecting him, Mahmud looked at 'the curls of Ayaz' and "lover-like he drew him to himself"; but the 'watchman' of the Qur'anic verse warned him not to mingle sin with love. Fearing that he could not withstand 'the hosts of Ayaz's locks', he gave Ayaz a knife and told him to cut off his curls 'in the middle' (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37). Ayaz "doubled back his locks to get the measurement, executed the king's command, and laid the two tresses before Mahmud"; "this ready obedience became a fresh cause of love", and Mahmud gave him gold and jewels 'beyond his usual wont' before falling into a drunken sleep (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).

Next morning Mahmud 'saw the clipped tresses' and was seized by remorse. No courtier dared ask him why, until the Hajib 'Ali ibn Qarib, 'his Chief Chamberlain', sent 'Unsuri in to restore his temper (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38). 'Unsuri 'extemporized' a quatrain, of which Browne's English reads in part:

*Why deem it shame a fair one's curls to shear, … When clipped the Cypress doth most trim appear* (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38)

Mahmud had the poet's mouth filled twice with 'precious stones', and drank wine to those verses until nightfall, "whereby his melancholy was dissipated" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38). The anecdote stands in Nizami's Second Discourse, on poets, and its moral is his: "improvisation is the chief pillar of the Poetic Art" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 56, folio 38).

Bhandari also carries Zulali's dream version of the tale (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 408–409).

## Ayaz in Poetry

In the poetry Annemarie Schimmel describes, the pair became a model. "More surprising is the transformation of the great warrior king of Ghazna, Sultan Mahmud, into the model of the ideal lover", she writes in *As Through a Veil*. "This conqueror of northwest India is praised for his close relationship with his Turkish officer Ayaz, who appears as the exemplar of the 'servant.'" "But the king finally became 'the slave of his slave'" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74).

In *Pain and Grace* she returns to the theme: "the warrior king and conqueror of Northwest India, Mahmud of Ghazna, was completely enchanted by the obedience and loving veneration of his Turkish officer Ayaz so that he became 'the slave of his slave'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175). She names the Persian theme as "Shah i gada, 'King and Beggar'", and notes that the word *niyaz* is "often used in the Mahmud Ayaz story for the sake of its fitting rhyme" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175).

In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* she writes that "Mahmud of Ghazna, the warrior king of Afghanistan (d. 1030), famous in political history as the conqueror of northwest India, becomes in literary tradition the model of the lover, because of his inclination toward his slave Ayaz", and that "The story of Mahmud and Ayaz is a typical expression of this kind of love and shows, at the same time, how the poets of Iran used historical facts to point out eternal truth" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). For the theme she refers to Gertrud Spies, *Mahmud von Ghazna bei Farīd ud-dīn ʿAṭṭār* (Basel, 1959), and adds that "several epics have been devoted to this topic, and lyrics abound in allusions to Ayaz" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).

Bhandari, writing in Persian, points to this literature. 'قصه عشق ونیاز سلطان وحسن وناز ایاز مشهور هست[OCR?] ودراکثر کتب مسطور علی الخصوص مولانا زلالی': the tale of the Sultan's love and *niyaz* and of Ayaz's beauty and *naz* is famous and set down in most books, above all in Mawlana Zulali (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). Verses on this love are in the 'محمود نامه ودیگر رساله', the *Mahmud-nama* and other treatises; as Bhandari's sentence runs, the Sultan himself composed them, 'سوز درونی وراز نهانی خویش بعرصه ظهور آورده', bringing his inner burning and his hidden secret into view (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409). In a digression on love he writes: 'بدرگاهش شاه ودرویش برابر ودرحضرتش خواجه وغلام همسر', at its court king and dervish are equal, and in its presence master and slave are peers (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 409).

## Setting: Shah Alam Market and Data Darbar

The reported landmark for the tomb is Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. Of that shrine, and not of this one, Schimmel writes: "His shrine, called that of Data Ganj Bakhsh, is still a popular place of pilgrimage in Lahore" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88); and "his tomb still provides a place of pilgrimage for the Panjabis" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 376, folio 345).

Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* records a memory of Partition in Lahore that may concern the same bazaar, though the book does not mention the shrine and its 'Shah Alami' is not certainly the Shah Alam Market in which the shrine is reported to stand. From his house Bishna Ram saw "the burning of the Hindu dominated market of Shah Alami, still one of the largest wholesale markets in the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 67, folio not stated). According to Ram, "The Hindus had their shops in the front, while they lived at the back. Using the gutters, the Muslims entered that area and burned everything" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 67, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His name.** The survey gives Malik Ahmad Ayaz, and also Malik Ayaz Ahmad and Malik Ayaz. Lahori names him 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری', and his contents and index give neither 'Malik' nor 'Ahmad' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 313, folio 301). Kanhaiya Lal writes 'ملک ایاز' and never 'احمد' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 17, 18, 21, 23; folios 12, 13, 16, 18), as Bhandari too writes 'ملک ایاز' (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). Schimmel prints only Ayaz, "his slave Ayaz" and "the Turkish officer Ayaz" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).
- **His origin.** The survey has him educated in Georgia in 993 AD and enslaved when "the infidels attacked your country". Bhandari reports, as something 'they say', that he was the son of the ruler of Kashmir, seized as a child at a hunting ground and sold in Badakhshan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 410). Schimmel calls him Mahmud's "Turkish officer" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74), and Nizami's anecdote calls him 'the Turk' (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).
- **Where and how Mahmud bought him.** The survey places the sale in the Baghdad slave market, where he was too weak to attract buyers, and gives the price as ten thousand dinars. Bhandari has the merchant bring him from Badakhshan to Ghazni, where his beauty drew crowds, and the Sultan pay a heavy price, what the merchant asked and more (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410).
- **His looks.** The survey's Ayaz was passed over as too weak. Bhandari's Ayaz was too beautiful to look at and likened to Yusuf of Canaan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410), though Bhandari also reports poets who wrote that he had no great outward beauty and was loved for his character (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 408). Nizami's Ayaz, in lines only partly legible in the copy consulted, was "not remarkably handsome" but "mightily endowed with all the arts of pleasing" (Nizami-i Arudi, *Chahar Maqala*, p. 55, folio 37).
- **His office.** The survey makes him a soldier, Mahmud's minister and governor of Lahore. Lahori makes him *atalik*, tutor, to Majdud, who was governor of the Punjab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193); Kanhaiya Lal makes him *hakim* of the Punjab by the king's order (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18); Bhandari, the Sultan's intimate and the foremost of his slaves (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 409–410). Schimmel gives him no office but "his Turkish officer" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 175, folio 175), and the editor of Lahori's edition makes him commander of the cantonment (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The order of their deaths.** The survey has Mahmud, in Ayaz's last days, wish to hand his own place to Ayaz, who asked that it go instead to 'one of his two sons', Saad; it also says that after Mahmud Ghaznavi's death Ayaz left his residence, and it gives Ayaz's death as 8 August 1041. Lahori has Ayaz outlive Mahmud and live on through the reigns of Masud and Maudud (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). Schimmel gives Mahmud's death as 1030 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292).
- **The year of his death.** The survey gives 8 August 1041 and names no calendar era. Lahori gives 450 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193). His editor gives 449 AH, 1057 CE, on the authority of Ibn Athir, and reports Firishta as placing the death "a few days after Maudud's death" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed). The survey's date agrees with neither year.
- **Where he is buried.** The survey places the mausoleum in Shah Alam Market, near Darbar Ali Hajveri Ganj Bakhsh. Lahori says only that he was buried inside the city of Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193), and Kanhaiya Lal's contents class the 'مزار ملک ایاز' among the buildings inside the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 3, folio 2). Lahori's appendix places a 'شیخ ایاز لاہوری قدس سرہ' at 'چوک رنگ محل', a line the book does not tie to this tomb (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277).
- **The refounding of Lahore.** The survey remembers him as the man who gave Lahore a new shape and "made a new map of Lahore". Lahori counts him the founder of Lahore, who settled it again after Mahmud's army had emptied it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 193); Kanhaiya Lal has him resettle it under a *farman* from the Sultan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18); Bhandari has him restore it and raise a fort of baked brick (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Lahori's editor rejects the tradition outright and calls the founding "later writers' conjecture" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The romance of king and slave.** The survey names "the love and romance" of king and slave as what should be remembered, and Schimmel's books trace the bond through mystical poetry (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 84, folio 74; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). Lahori's editor treats the romance as a literary growth of post-Seljuq times (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–193, folios 189–191 as printed).
- **The old clothes.** The survey has Ayaz take out his old garments each night. Rūmī's allegory, as Schimmel tells it, has him look "every morning at the out-worn shoes and shabby clothes he wore before Mahmud elected him for himself" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 221, folio 190).
- **Ayaz's counsel at a temple.** The survey's story is set at the "Onkay temple", where Ayaz reasoned that a magnet held the idol in the air and that demolishing the walls would bring it down. Chishti's is set at Somnath, where Ayaz advised breaking the idol rather than taking the rajas' crores, and the sultan broke it with his own hand (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 805). The books do not say that the two are one episode.

## Legacy

It is reported that what should be remembered is the bond between Mahmud Ghaznavi and Malik Ahmad Ayaz — in the words reported, "the love and romance" of king and slave — a slave sacrificing his life for his king, and loyalty so complete that he could answer for it before God on the Day of Judgement; poets and travellers of that era and of the present are said to have written of these qualities. He is also reported to be remembered as the person who gave Lahore a new shape, and known still because he "made a new map of Lahore".

For Schimmel, "The complete surrender of the Turkish officer Ayaz, for whom only Mahmud exists, results in perfect love of the king, who becomes, in a wonderful transformation, the slave of his slave. Ayaz is the symbol of the loving soul" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 323, folio 292). Kanhaiya Lal, for his part, makes his settlement of Lahore the turn from which the city's later history runs (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 23, folio 18).

His name also served as a figure of speech. Chishti's history says of Raja Hira Singh that 'مہاراجہ کلان اسکو اپنا ایاز خیال کرکے [illegible] فرزند کہا کرتی تہی', thinking him 'اپنا ایاز', one's own Ayaz, and calling him son (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 868).

Description:
## Overview
Darbar Mian Qurban Ali Shah is a Muslim shrine at Mint Stop, Lahore, dedicated to Hazrat Mian Qurban Ali Shah Sarkar. The site's *silsila* (Sufi order, and the lineage of spiritual transmission within it) is reported as Naqshbandī Mujaddidī, within Ahl-e Sunnat. A mosque named after the saint stands in the same courtyard as the tomb. The site has been in the charge of the government Auqaf (religious endowments) Department since 2005.

## The figure, as the tradition relates him
It is reported that Hazrat Qurban Ali Shah was born in 1341 AH in Malerkotla, India, that his given name was Qurban Ali, and that people later came to call him Mian Qurban Ali Shah in recognition of his learning. His father is named as Hazrat Mian Fazal Deen, said to have been a great religious scholar who held thousands of disciples in a relationship of *pīrī-murīdī* (spiritual mentorship) and who taught his son the whole of his education before instructing him to devote his life to preaching. Devotees relate that virtuous people and Sufis were repeatedly born into this family, and that its members kept the call of Islam alive throughout their lives.

He reportedly left his ancestral home in youth at his father's command, never returned, and preached along the way until he reached the Mint Stop area of Lahore, which he made his final abode. Tradition holds that people were drawn to his camp of their own accord; that he arranged food, drink and lodging for all who came, young and old alike; that thousands took *baiʿat* (the oath of allegiance to a spiritual guide) at his hand, often with their entire families; and that neither he nor his family ever compelled anyone's conversion, people entering Islam instead out of regard for his learning and character. Among those he brought into Islam, it is reported, were a large number of people named as "Marzaiyas (Ahmadis/Qadianis)". Devotees relate that he served people by day and spent his nights in *dhikr* (remembrance of God), and that although his bearing was that of a simple dervish he did not disclose his spiritual station. He is reported to have passed on the *gaddi* (spiritual seat) in the last part of his life, died on 25 Rabīʿ al-Thānī, and been buried at his camp.

## Reputation and *karāmāt*
It is reported that those seeking a cure for illness, the unemployed seeking work, and people caught in difficulty and worry would present themselves to him, that he would pray to God on their behalf, and that those prayers were granted without delay. Devotees still come to pray through his *waseela* (intercession) and say they do not return empty-handed. Those who met him in life are described as knowing his spiritual manifestations at first hand; others entered his allegiance on the testimony of their elders. His devotees hold that, having left the world while engaged in preaching, his standing is no less than a martyr's, and that martyrs remain alive.

## The site and its buildings
His camp itself reportedly became his shrine: after his death a shrine was raised over the burial place, and a mosque was built in his name alongside it. Beneath the tomb is a basement, closed to the general public, reportedly the room where he kept his nightly *dhikr*; it has been left in its original condition and is said to remain exactly as he left it. His special disciple is buried beside him. The Auqaf Department took responsibility for the shrine and mosque in 2005, but most maintenance and decoration is still carried out by devotees themselves. The shrine was reconstructed again in 2022. No graveyard is reported at the site.

## Regular observances
The five daily prayers are offered in the courtyard mosque. On Thursday, Friday and Sunday the large door of the shrine is kept open; on the remaining days the small door is open, and worshippers and pilgrims come throughout. Every Thursday there is a public gathering with *dhikr*, *naʿt* (devotional verse in praise of the Prophet) recitation and *langar* (free communal food); a set number of people is said to attend. No *qawwālī* is reported at the site.

## *ʿUrs*
The annual *ʿurs* (death-anniversary observance) is held on 24, 25 and 26 Rabīʿ al-Thānī. It includes drumming (dhol), the changing of the chadar over the grave, ritual washing (*ghusl*) and *langar*.

## Attendance and custodianship
Daily attendance is put at 500 to 600 people, and at the annual *ʿurs* at some 50,000 to 60,000 pilgrims. Residents of the neighbourhood around the shrine pay their respects there each morning before going to work. The custodian of record is the government Auqaf Department. It is also reported that the saint's successor in the *gaddi* was Haji Tufail, and that after Haji Tufail's death his sons hold the position of managing the site.

## Writings
It is reported that a disciple published a discourse on the saint's life a short while ago, that it became widely popular, and that readers subsequently entered the saint's allegiance in greater numbers.
