Name: Darbar Sakhi Shah Chan Charagh
Events: Annual urs; Muharram tazia procession (9 Muharram); commemorative mach bonfire
Description:
## Overview

In the crowded lanes of the old walled city of Rawalpindi stands the *darbar* of Sakhi Shah Chan Charagh, revered across the Pothohar plateau as the patron saint of the city. His very name — *Chan Charagh*, "the moon and the lamp" — carries the imagery of light that runs through everything remembered about him, and for generations the people of Rawalpindi have looked to his shrine as the spiritual heart of their town. It is a modest complex by the standards of the great Punjabi shrines, tucked among bazaars and old *havelis*, yet on the days of remembrance it draws crowds from the whole district, and its steady lamp-lit devotion has outlasted empires, partition, and the ceaseless rebuilding of the city around it.

## The Life of the Saint

The saint's given name is traditionally said to have been Shah Zaman, and he is remembered as a *sayyid* — a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad — whose lineage is traced through Imam Musa al-Kazim, the seventh Imam venerated especially in the Shia tradition. According to the accounts preserved by his devotees, his forebears came from the city of Mashhad in Iran and settled at Chakwal, in the Salt Range country south of Rawalpindi, before he made his way to the town with which his name is now inseparably linked. He is generally placed in the eighteenth century, in the twilight of Mughal power, though the datings given for him vary and the shrine is spoken of by some as being three to four centuries old; in the absence of firm documentary record these figures are best treated as traditional rather than exact.

He is said to have been the disciple of his own maternal uncle, Sayyid Shah Inayat, himself a celebrated *wali* or friend of God, and the sources describe him as a cousin or spiritual kinsman of the great Bari Imam of Islamabad, binding him into the web of saintly families that spans the Pothohar. The best-loved legend of his life tells that, on his arrival at Rawalpindi, he stumbled — or, in the more devotional telling, deliberately sat down — in a burning potter's oven, and there remained steadfast in prayer and penance amid the flames. It is from this episode that the shrine takes one of its most striking features: the great bonfire, known in the local speech as the *mach*, which is kindled at the site in commemoration and which pilgrims still gather around.

## The Shrine and its Devotional Life

The shrine complex today holds the marble grave-chamber of the saint together with the tombs of his descendants, companions, and adherents, and it incorporates an *imambargah*, reflecting the strongly Shia colouring of its devotion. The great commemorative bonfire remains a focus of ritual, and the calendar of the *darbar* is marked above all by the observances of Muharram: a *tazia* procession sets out from the shrine on the ninth of the month, and the site becomes a gathering place for the mourning assemblies that fill the old city in that season. An annual *urs*, the celebration of the saint's union with the divine, is also kept, drawing devotees who come to offer *fatiha*, tie threads of intention, and seek the *baraka* — the blessing — believed to linger about his resting place.

The saint's spiritual legacy is said to have been carried forward by a circle of disciples, among whom tradition names Sakhi Shah Raza, Qamar Ali Shah, and Sakhi Shah Sharaf; the most romantic of these stories concerns a figure remembered as Kochak Ali Sultan, described as a Mughal prince who, drawn by the light he had glimpsed in the saint, abandoned a life of ease for the path of the dervish. Such narratives, whatever their historical basis, express the enduring theme of the shrine: the exchange of worldly power for inward illumination.

## Legacy

For the inhabitants of Rawalpindi, Shah Chan Charagh is not a remote historical personage but a living presence and protector, his shrine woven into the ordinary rhythms of the old city — a place to bring newborn children, to pray in times of trouble, and to mark the turning of the sacred year. In a garrison city that has grown enormously in modern times, the *darbar* preserves a thread of continuity with the Rawalpindi of the pre-colonial and colonial past, when the walled town clustered close about its saints. It stands as a characteristic example of the small urban shrine that anchors civic identity across Pakistani Punjab, and of the particular devotional world of the Pothohar, where Sufi veneration and the mourning of the Prophet's household flow together.

## Bibliography

- *Rawalpindi District Gazetteer* (Punjab Government, colonial-era editions), for the topography and religious life of the old city.
- Reports in *Dawn* on the annual *urs* and Muharram observances at the shrine of Shah Chan Charagh, Rawalpindi.
- Local hagiographical (*malfuzat* and *tazkira*) traditions concerning Sayyid Shah Zaman "Chan Charagh" and his lineage.
- General studies of Sufi shrine culture and Muharram devotion in the Pothohar region of Punjab.

Name: Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan (born Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was his pen name/takhallus)
Events: Annual Urs (12-14 January): chadar tabdeeli, ghusl, chiraghan, Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef, Mehfil-e-Mushaira
Description:
## Overview

Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif sits within Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard, in a plot set aside beside the wider burial ground — reported to be one of the largest graveyards in Asia, holding the graves of many well-known and pious figures alongside it. The shrine holds the grave of Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan, a twentieth-century Urdu poet and spiritual teacher. It was built by his son, Kashif Wasif, after his death in January 1993, and his family is reported to have maintained responsibility for the shrine since.

## Wasif Ali Wasif — life and career

It is reported that his given name was Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was a pen name (*takhallus*) he took as an Urdu literary figure and poet, and he became known by the fuller form Wasif Ali Wasif. He was born on 15 January 1929 in Shahpur, Khushab District. His father, Muhammad Arif, was himself a teacher. His family reportedly belonged to the Khushab region and the Awan tribe, whose lineage (*shajra nasab*) is said — by the family's own account, as recorded here — to trace back to Hazrat Ali (R.A.); this is reported as stated, not independently verified.

He began his education in Khushab, passing his middle-school examination there in 1939. His father then sent him to his maternal grandfather in Jhang, a move described as transformative: his grandfather had been associated with the Muslim League and had spent time with Quaid-e-Azam. In Jhang, he passed Matriculation in 1944, Intermediate in 1946, and his B.A. in 1948, all from Government College Jhang and all in the first division. He went on to Government College Lahore for his M.A., and passed the Civil Services examination in June 1954. He is reported to have been offered a government post on the strength of this but to have declined it, turning instead toward writing and solitary devotion.

He founded an institution called "English College" in Anarkali, Lahore, which reportedly served as a gathering place for people of every background, where free food (*langar*) and offerings (*niyaz*) were continuously distributed, and where he began guiding visitors and devoting himself to their concerns. He later addressed large public gatherings — reportedly "over a thousand nights" of addresses at Lakshmi Chowk and Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, taking questions on both spiritual and worldly matters.

## Writing and teachings

He is reported to have written more than 50 books, poetic compositions, poems, ghazals, and *na'at*, in both Urdu and English, among them: *Ghumnam Adeeb*, *Kiran Kiran Suraj*, *Qatra Qatra Qulzum*, *Harf Harf Haqeeqat*, *Mukalma*, *Dil Darya Samundar*, *Ba Say Baat*, *Dareche*, *Zikr-e-Habib (S.A.W.)*, *Guftagu*, *Shab-e-Chiraagh*, *Shab-e-Zaat*, *Baray Barwey*, and *The Beaming Soul*. One saying attributed to him is reported: "You and I are equal; we must please our Lord, and one day we all have to return." His teaching is described as combining devotion to the Prophet (recitation of *na'at*) with an explicit call to patriotism — that people owed a debt of gratitude for their homeland alongside their duties to God.

## Why the shrine is significant

It is reported that people regard him as a pious servant of Allah who gave his life to serving others, and who fulfilled requests made of him without exception. Both Muslims and non-Muslims are said to visit the shrine and study his books, and gatherings held in his name reportedly draw poets, scholars, teachers, and writers. Because he is said to have died in this devoted state, visitors reportedly regard him as a martyr (*shaheed*) in the sense of one who remains, in the words reported, "forever alive with Allah" — a status attributed to popular belief rather than to any formal religious ruling.

## Devotional life and the annual Urs

Free food (*langar*) is distributed daily, and visitors come to make offerings (*niyaz*), pray, and recite Fatiha for him; his books are kept at the shrine for visiting scholars to read. Gatherings called Mehfil-e-Mustafa (S.A.W.) are also held there. The annual Urs is observed every year on 12, 13, and 14 January, with the ceremonial changing of the shrine's cloth covering (*chadar tabdeeli*), ritual washing (*ghusl*), lamp-lighting (*chiraghan*), gatherings in praise of the Prophet (*Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef*), and poetry gatherings (*Mehfil-e-Mushaira*), attended by scholars and devotees; non-Muslim attendance at the shrine is reportedly also common. Daily visitors are estimated at 1,000-1,200, rising to roughly 150,000-200,000 during the Urs. Opposite the shrine is a private library where visitors gather to read and buy his books.

## Custodianship

The shrine remains under the management of Wasif Ali Wasif's family. It is reported that offerings (*hadiya*) collected there fund its ongoing upkeep and construction work, and that devotees take part in caring for it directly.

Name: Dargah / Roza Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed
Events: Annual urs; Sufi music and remembrance
Description:
## Overview

At Jhok Sharif, in the Sujawal region of Sindh, lies the shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed (d. 1718) — a Sufi saint remembered not only for his mysticism but for a remarkable social experiment and a martyr's death. Shah Inayat gathered around him a community that farmed the land in common under the principle that the one who sows should eat, and this challenge to the entrenched order of landlords and rulers led, after a long siege, to his execution. He is honoured today as a saint, a martyr, and — in modern eyes — a pioneer of social justice, and his darbar at Jhok is a place of pilgrimage and remembrance.

The books bear out the outline of that story from several sides. Annemarie Schimmel, who devoted a study of her own to him, tells of his preaching, the denunciation at court, the siege of his *khanqah* and his execution "in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21), and records that "Large armies were sent to Jhok, which surrendered after four months' siege" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). Christopher Shackle, translating the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif, calls him "the famous Sindhi" Sufi "martyr Shah Inayat of Jhok (d. 1718)" and finds his Persian verse quoted in that great Sindhi classic (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325). Michel Boivin, writing of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh and their descendants in India, places "Sufi Shah Inayat's dargah" at Jhok Sharif and shows the dargah as a living centre of initiation, custodianship and song, finding that "most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly, often through their own Sufi Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 60, folio 47).

## The Life of the Saint

Shah Inayat belonged to the tradition of *wahdat al-wujud*, the mysticism of the unity of being, and was schooled in the Sufi currents of his age, travelling in his search for knowledge before returning to his native Jhok in lower Sindh. There, in the early eighteenth century, he established a *khanqah* whose community held and cultivated land collectively, sharing its produce — a way of life summed up in the Sindhi maxim *jeko kheré, so khaé*, "whoever sows, eats." The gathering of the poor and the landless around him, and the implicit challenge his commune posed to the great landholders (*zamindars*) and to the Mughal-appointed authorities of the region, provoked their hostility. His settlement was besieged; after a long resistance he was taken by treachery and put to death in 1718. He is remembered ever after as *Shaheed*, the martyr of Jhok.

The books know him by several forms of the name. Schimmel writes "Shah Inayat of Jhok" and calls his establishment "his Khanqah Jhok" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21); the index of her *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* enters him, with the epithet that the site's name also carries, as Shah ʿInayat Shahid, "(d. 1718)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 517, folio 486). Boivin writes "Sufi Shah Inayat" and "Shah Inayat of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 124, folio 111), and one of Shemeem Burney Abbas's informants speaks of "Shah Inayat of Jhokevale", the Shah Inayat of the people of Jhok (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 63, folio not stated). Schimmel dates him in the title of her article on him as "A Sindhi Mystic of the early 18th century" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 293, folio 293).

Of his own spiritual descent the books say little. Boivin names his master: "Sayyid Shah Mehmud Shah al-Qadiri was the Master of Shah Inayat of Jhok Sharif." That master, he writes, was "a Sufi Master from Jhok Sharif" who had been buried in Bijapur, in Karnataka (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Boivin gives no birth or death date and no chain of succession for Shah Inayat himself, though he repeatedly ties the lodge at Jhok to the Qadiri order through its *sajjada nashins*, and the chart of Sufi orders in an annex to his book sets down "Jhok Sharif (Qadiriyya)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 227, folio 214).

Boivin also counts him in a short list of masters, the "'three great Sufi teachers'", who are "Shah Inayat, Shah Abd al-Latif and Sachal Sarmast" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 49, folio 36). The name stands there without a place, and the company it keeps is the only sign that this Shah Inayat is meant. Boivin keeps him apart from an earlier poet with a similar name, "Shah Inat, a Sindhi Sufi poet of the seventeenth century", whom he dates 1623–1712 and calls Sayyid Inayat Allah Rizvi (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 105, folio 92; p. 211, folio 198); the nearness of that man's death year to 1718 does not make the two one.

## The Commune, the Siege and the Martyrdom

Schimmel's *Pain and Grace* gives the fullest account of his end among the books, and sets it in the politics of the province. "The first obvious sign of the struggle for power in the Lower Indus Valley becomes visible in 1717, when a mystical rebel was persecuted under the pretext that he tried to overthrow the established rule." She goes on: "The tragic story of Shah Inayat of Jhok, whose successful mystical preaching attracted many disciples from the mystical centers of the country, but also laborers from the neighboring big farms led his adversaries to denounce him at court; for during the confused situation in Delhi between the reign of Farrukh Siyar and that of Muhammad Shah it was easy to sow mistrust" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). Two streams of followers thus came to him, adepts from the established centres and labourers from the great farms, and it was their coming, in her telling, that turned his enemies against him.

The siege followed. "The Kalhora clan from Upper Sind, particularly active in the struggle against Inayat, soon afterwards became independent in Sind. Shah Inayat was besieged in his Khanqah Jhok, and had to surrender to the overwhelming army that came from various places in Sind and Hind. He was executed in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). Later in the same book she gives the date again in a parenthesis: "Shah Inayat of Jhok (exec. 1718)" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 228, folio 228).

In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* Schimmel tells the story a second time, placing Jhok as "not far from Hyderabad" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). There the dargah draws followers away from its neighbours: "His way of life, spirituality, and justice attracted a large number, not only of Sufi adepts, but also, according to the sources, of slaves and husbandmen from the neighboring villages." "The Sufi sheikhs and the feudal lords in the country lost large numbers of disciples and workers, whereas the dargah in Jhok flourished." She records that "A considerable amount of land was distributed among" Shah Inayat's followers "after an unjustified attack on Jhok, led by the Sayyids of Bulrri" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397); she does not say who those Sayyids were beyond the name of their place, printed so.

Then came the charge and the end: "the pious mystic was accused of conspiracy against the Mogul throne, the easiest method of blackmail, since the throne was in constant danger after Aurangzeb's death. Large armies were sent to Jhok, which surrendered after four months' siege", and Shah Inayat "was executed in January 1718" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). In *As Through a Veil* she writes that he was "called the first social reformer in Sindhi Islam, who was executed by the Moghul governor in early 1718" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157); the governor is not named. Shackle gives the same year, "(d. 1718)", and calls him "the martyred" Sufi saint (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325; p. 321).

Schimmel is careful about how much of the commune can be known. To what extent Shah Inayat "really aimed at something like a land reform in the modern sense of the word cannot be detected from the sources, which are mostly unfriendly to him; positive evaluations, on the other hand, are strongly mixed with legends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). She places his case among others in which mystical leaders of the lower Indus valley took a political part: "This was not the first time that mystical leaders in Sind, or in other parts of the Muslim world, were engaged in politics or in social reforms" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

## The Shrine

The shrine of Sufi Shah Inayat at Jhok Sharif is a revered darbar of lower Sindh, drawing pilgrims who honour the saint and martyr. The books say little of its fabric: none of them describes the tomb, its building or its date. Boivin's glossary gives the place its most precise location: "Jhok Sharif: a village with an important Sufi Centre in Taluqa Mirpur Bathoro in Southern Sindh where Sufi Shah Inayat's dargah is." In the body of his book Jhok is "a great Sufi centre located in the extreme South of Sindh", and "Jhok, contrary to Daraza, is located in Southern Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 141, folio 128; p. 60, folio 47). Schimmel names "the dargah in Jhok" as an institution that drew disciples and workers away from the neighbouring sheikhs and lords (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

The custodians of the dargah are the *sajjada nashins*, the holders of the seat, and Boivin names several. A disciple "spent many years in Jhok Sharif, and he was initiated to the Qadiri tariqa by the sajjada nashin, Sufi Abd al-Sattar Shah", who set him to "cleaning the stable of his Master's mare" and, when he had reached "the highest spiritual degree, that of salvation", allowed him to give *nam*, the initiatory name, to disciples of his own (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107; pp. 120–121, folios 107–108). Elsewhere he writes of "Sufi Hazrat Abdul Sattar Shah of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 101, folio 88), and his glossary makes the name a recurring one: "Abdul Sattar: the name of several Sufi masters at the dargah of Jhok Sharif." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 218, folio not stated). He also cites "the official website of Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115). He gives no dates for any of them.

Jhok is, for Boivin, one of three seats in Sindh whose holders still keep the lineages of Hindu Sufis now in India: "They are the sajjada nashin of Daraza, of Tando Jahaniya and of Jhok Sharif. At each of them, a great Sufi poet is attached: Sachal Sarmast, Qutub Ali Shah and Nasir Faqir" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 27, folio 14). The poet who stands third in the list, against Jhok Sharif, is Nasir Faqir, though the book does not pair the two lists in so many words; Boivin elsewhere calls Nasir Muhammad Faqir "a Qadiri who was the disciple of the Master (murshid) of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 141, folio 128), without naming that master.

The dargah's reach crosses the border. Boivin reports that "the official website devoted to Jhok Sharif claims to have a dargah in Bijapur which is affiliated with Jhok", and that under the heading 'affiliated dargahs' it names a Hazrat Soofi Abdul Malik; he adds at once that "I do not know what the relations were between Molchand and the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Boivin tells of Molchand, who after Partition "was worried that it was difficult for Hindu Sindhi Sufis to pay a visit to the Sufi places in Sindh, now in Pakistan", and of the search for the Bijapur grave of Shah Inayat's master: "he decided to look for his grave" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111). Of the pilgrimage that grew from the claimed tie to Jhok, Boivin judges that "this attempt at creating a Muslim Sufi pilgrimage from Sindh in India is unique, but, unfortunately, it does not look to be very successful." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115).

## Devotion and Practice

The shrine's annual *ʿurs* gathers devotees for prayer, Sufi music, and remembrance. Of one Sindhi Sufi poet Boivin writes: "His Sufi poetry in Sindhi is voluminous and his verses (kafis) are still a part of the main poetry, which is sung in the urs of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 59, folio 46). He gives no date, month or length for the *ʿurs*. Other Sindhi poetry is sung at Jhok too: the *kalam* of Dalpat Sufi is sung "in several dargahs located in Sindh and run by Muslim sajjada nashins, as for example in Jhok Sharif", and "It is also sung at Jhok Sharif in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 118, folio 105).

Jhok's calendar travelled with its followers. The yearly *melo* at Bijapur is kept "every year from the 17th to the 19th of Moharram, as it is celebrated in Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111); Boivin does not say whether those days at Jhok are the *ʿurs* or whose memory they keep. One Hindu Sufi path counts Shah Inayat among the four masters whose death anniversaries (*versi*) it keeps: one of the four is "Shah Inayat (from Jhok Sharif)", and "the dates… are taken as sacred: the 11, the 15, the 17 and the 27" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 122, folio 109). The list of dates is not matched to the list of names, and nothing in the book says which day is Shah Inayat's.

A performance tradition carries his name. Naseer Mirza, speaking to Abbas of Sindhi poetry, says: "The sūng—the manānā—is done on the capṛi [castanets]—this is the tradition of Shah Inayat of Jhokevale—but we do not find this in Shah Latif's poetry", and, of Shah Latif, "his moods are more mellow" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 63, folio not stated).

Omar Kasmani, writing of the Sindhi publications of the state, which until the late 1960s hardly mentioned the saint or the shrine of Sehwan, records that "other saints of Sindh (especially Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast, and Shah Inayat) were regularly featured during this time, and their annual fairs were marked by special editions" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 70, folio 53). He names no place for this Shah Inayat; only the phrase "saints of Sindh" and his companions in the list point to the saint of Jhok.

Jhok was a place of initiation for many. Boivin writes that "It was at about the age of forty that Rakhiyyal Shah adopted the Sufi path and went to the dargah of Jhok Sharif, where he stayed under the guidance of his Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 59, folio 46), the master unnamed. Rohal Faqir "was a disciple of Shah Inayat from Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94); the guru Asardas "was himself a follower of the Sufi masters of Jhok Sharif", and Dalpat Sufi was "Himself a follower of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 118, folio 105). Bedil, Boivin notes, "also visited Jhok Sharif and Daraza" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 97, folio 84). "It is interesting to observe," he concludes, "that the Sufi centre of Jhok Sharif plays a pivotal role since most of the Hindu Sufis were in touch with Jhok, directly or indirectly, often through their own Sufi Master", and "the two main Sufi traditions that were very popular among the Hindus were Daraza and Jhok." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 60, folio 47).

## Legends and Miracles

Schimmel warns that the favourable accounts of Shah Inayat "are strongly mixed with legends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397), but the books themselves record few. The one vision they tell is of Jhok rather than of its saint: a disciple, as the published *kalam* of his own path relates, "from his early childhood on, he had visions involving Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. In one of them, the founder of the Qadiriyya told him it was time for him to reach Jhok Sharif, to take nam from the Sufi Master" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107).

## In Verse

Shah Inayat wrote in Persian, and his verse is quoted in the *Risalo* of Shah Abdul Latif. Shackle's notes to his translation trace two Persian lines in it to him. The half-verse *bar khez ba-dih sāqī* is, he writes, "a half-verse from a ghazal by the martyred" Sufi saint Shah Inayat of Jhok, and he points the reader to "another quotation from this poet" elsewhere in the poem (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 321). The second is *sar dar qadam-e yār fdā shud chi ba-jā shud* (printed so, with *fdā* for *fidā*), "a verse from a poem by the famous Sindhi" Sufi "martyr Shah Inayat of Jhok (d. 1718)"; it is, Shackle adds, "one of the very few Persian quotations in the Risālo, but compare 2.49" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325).

Schimmel, too, notes that Shah Abdul Latif "has quoted a Persian line usually connected with Shah Inayat", and that "It is possible that Shah Abdul Latif alluded to his fate in some of his verses" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 26, folio 22). She gives that line in English, citing it as Sohn. II:

*The head is sacrificed at the Friend's foot, / which is in order* (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 228, folio 228)

Schimmel does not print the Persian of this line, and neither book refers to the other, so whether her English renders the line Shackle transliterates is not stated; the two stand side by side here as each book gives them.

Another Persian verse was tied to his martyrdom by a Sindhi writer, Qani. Schimmel discusses a quatrain on the 'kitchen of love' attributed to Sarmad, "one of the Sufis of 'Hallajian succession'", though it is, she says, "much older"; and "It is typical that this very verse has been quoted by Qani", in his *Maqalat ash-shuʿara*, "in connection with the martyr-mystic Shah Inayat of Jhok" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 182–183, folios 182–183, footnote 41).

Verse about him followed his death. Schimmel writes that "his fate has inspired many Sufi poets, Hindus and Muslims alike, to write touching poetry"; "he becomes 'the Hallaj of Sind' due to his death at the hands of the establishment, and to his overwhelming mystical 'state.'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 25–26, folios 21–22). Again: "Both Muslim and Hindu admirers have composed songs extolling him or describing his martyrdom"; among them was the Suhrawardi mystic Janullah of Rohri, "one of the outstanding Persian poets of Sind from the second half of the eighteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

The Sindhi poet Sachal Sarmast names him too. "Sachal also speaks of" Shah Inayat of Jhok, Schimmel writes (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157), and her translation of Sachal's litany of the afflicted includes the words "hast killed" ʿInayat "in the fighting arena"; her footnote identifies him as 'the martyr-mystic of Jhok' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 426, folio 395).

At Jhok itself, one of the holders of the seat spoke in the same language of unity. Boivin reports that "Sufi Hazrat Abdul Sattar Shah of Jhok Sharif, speaks of jam wahdat jo, 'the cup of unity'", citing a work of Nasir Faqir of 1972 (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 101, folio 88).

## Setting

The epithet 'the Hallaj of Sind' draws on a long memory in the province. Schimmel writes that Hallaj traversed Sind "shortly after 900", and that "It is moving to listen to illiterate folk musicians in remote corners of Sind" who repeat his name in ecstatic songs, and "claim that he was the true lover who paid with his life for his love" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157). Boivin agrees: "In Sindh, Hallaj is a very popular figure, and many Sufi poets mention his name in their verses" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 102, folio 89). Of Sindhi poets at large, and not of Jhok, Schimmel adds that Hindu writers composed poems in the imagery of the Muslims and "devoted ballads to the fate of famous Sufi martyrs" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387).

The Sind in which he preached was a Mughal province in a time of change. Schimmel writes that "Sind was, since 1595, part of the Mughal Empire, and although representatives of the Delhi court came there, the indigenous rulers enjoyed much freedom" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio not stated). H. T. Sorley writes that "Sind was added to the Moghul Empire by Akbar in 1592" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 18, folio 9), and dates the rule of the Kalhora as governors from 1701 (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 35, folio 26). Of the province's social order in that century Sorley writes that "The system of land tenure in Sind, so far as is known, has always been feudal", and that the Kalhora's deference to the priestly class "led to the extraordinary reverence for pirs, Sayids and holy men, which may be said to have been the predominant characteristic of eighteenth century Sind" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 163, folio 154); "The social religion of Sind was built up round the reverence of the murid for the murshid" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 166, folio 157). In southern Sind, Schimmel notes, a strong Naqshbandi influence at the beginning of the eighteenth century "changed the spiritual climate of southern Sind to a certain extent" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). These passages speak of the province, not of Jhok.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where Jhok lies.** The site's account places Jhok Sharif in the Sujawal region of Sindh, in lower Sindh. Boivin puts it in "Taluqa Mirpur Bathoro in Southern Sindh" and "in the extreme South of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206; p. 141, folio 128). Schimmel says it "is not far from Hyderabad" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).
- **Who came to him.** The site's account speaks of the poor and the landless. Schimmel's *Pain and Grace* names two streams, "many disciples from the mystical centers of the country, but also laborers from the neighboring big farms" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21); her *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* names Sufi adepts and "slaves and husbandmen from the neighboring villages" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).
- **The land.** The site's account has the community hold and cultivate land collectively, under the maxim *jeko kheré, so khaé*. Schimmel records that land "was distributed among" his followers after an attack on Jhok, and holds that how far he aimed at a land reform "cannot be detected from the sources, which are mostly unfriendly to him" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). She also observes that progressive writers tend to read figures such as Hallaj, Bishr al-Hafi and Shah Inayat of Jhok 'in the light of' modern social ideals (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 288, folio 270).
- **How the end came.** The site's account says that after a long resistance he was taken by treachery and put to death. *Pain and Grace* says that he "had to surrender to the overwhelming army that came from various places in Sind and Hind", and names the Kalhora as "particularly active in the struggle against Inayat" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* says that Jhok "surrendered after four months' siege", after he was accused of conspiracy against the Mughal throne (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). *As Through a Veil* says he "was executed by the Moghul governor" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157).
- **The date.** The site's account gives 1718. Schimmel dates the persecution to 1717 and the execution to "January 1718" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21), to "January 1718" again (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397), and to "early 1718" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157); Shackle gives "(d. 1718)" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 325). The year agrees throughout; only the start of the persecution is set a year earlier.
- **The holder of the seat.** Boivin names the *sajjada nashin* who initiated a disciple as "Sufi Abd al-Sattar Shah" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107) and elsewhere names "Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115); his glossary calls Abdul Sattar "the name of several Sufi masters at the dargah of Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 218, folio not stated). He gives no dates, and does not say whether these are one man or several.
- **The Bijapur dargah.** "the official website of Sufi Ataullah Sattari, the sajjada nashin of Jhok" claims Abd al-Malik's dargah in Bijapur as affiliated to Jhok, while "in the narrative found in Molchand's biography, there is no mention that Abd al-Malik's dargah in Bijapur is affiliated to Jhok Sharif" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 128, folio 115).
- **Boivin's article on Jhok.** Boivin's own bibliography lists his chapter 'The Sufi Centre of Jhok Sharif in Sindh (Pakistan)' as published at New York by Continuum in 2012, pages 94–109 (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220); Kasmani cites the same title from London, Continuum, pages 95–110, its first word damaged in the printed text (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 204, folio 187).
- **When Sind became Mughal.** Schimmel gives 1595 (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio not stated); Sorley gives 1592, under Akbar (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 18, folio 9).

## Legacy

Sufi Shah Inayat Shaheed holds a singular place among the saints of Sindh — a mystic of the unity of being whose commune of shared land and labour, and whose martyrdom in its defence, made him a saint of the poor and a byword for social justice. In the modern age his memory has taken on a further dimension: writers, poets, and social reformers have celebrated him as an early martyr for the rights of the peasant and the poor against feudal power, so that his shrine is honoured both as a place of mystical devotion and as a symbol of the struggle for justice. His darbar at Jhok Sharif keeps alive the memory of a holy man who joined the inward path to the cause of the landless, and who paid for it with his life.

The books show that double memory at work. Schimmel reports that he was "called the first social reformer in Sindhi Islam" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157), and that "his fate has inspired many Sufi poets, Hindus and Muslims alike, to write touching poetry", so that "he becomes 'the Hallaj of Sind'" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, pp. 25–26, folios 21–22); she also cautions that modern readers interpret him in the light of their own social ideals (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 288, folio 270). She devoted an article to him, published in the *Liber Amicorum* in honour of C. J. Bleeker at Leiden in 1969, pp. 151–70 (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 338, folio 320; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 493, folio 462). Boivin wrote his own study of the Sufi centre of Jhok Sharif (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220), and in his book Jhok stands at the heart of a network that outlived Partition: "Again, the invocation of Jhok Sharif contributes to the construction of a network of sacred territories which are all located in Sindh." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 141, folio 128).

Name: Dargah Fateh Pur Sharif
Location: Dargah Fateh Pur Sharif, Gandawah (Jhal Magsi District), Balochistan
Founded/Opened: 1359 (site/settlement); present dargah c. 1940 (after Syed Rakhyal Shah's death)
Sufi Saint: Syed Rakhyal Shah Sufi Al Qadri
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

At Fateh Pur Sharif — a small town in the Gandava plain of the Jhal Magsi District of Balochistan — stands the *dargah* of Syed Rakhyal Shah, the Qadiri Sufi poet-saint whom the people of the region remember simply as *Saeen Rakhyal*, "the Master Rakhyal." It is one of the principal shrines of Jhal Magsi, named in the district's own heritage listings alongside the *dargah* of Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari at Gandava and the shrines of Pir Lakha and Pir Chhatal Shah near Kotra. The shrine is inseparable from the verse its saint left behind — the multi-volume *Bahar al-'ishq*, "The Springtide of Love" — for Rakhyal Shah is honoured less as a miracle-worker than as a poet of divine longing whose words are still sung across the Baloch, Sindhi and Saraiki country that meets in this corner of the Kachhi lowlands.

## The Life of Saeen Rakhyal Shah

Rakhyal Shah is generally held to have lived from 1842 to 1940, a span of nearly a century across the colonial Indus frontier. Of Baloch origin and associated with the Qadiri tradition — the spreadsheet preserves his title as *Sufi al-Qadiri* — he devoted his life to the theme of *'ishq*, the love of the Divine, and became so beloved that, in the phrase of one modern scholar, "the poet himself grew to be the head of a cult." What most distinguishes him is his reach across languages: he is said to have composed in five tongues — Sindhi, Balochi, Saraiki, Urdu and Persian — a fluency that made his message intelligible to the mixed peoples of the Sindh–Balochistan borderland and that helped his fame outlast him. Around his person gathered a circle of *murids* (disciples) whose devotion would, after his death, give rise to the shrine that now bears his name.

## The Dargah and the Bahar al-'ishq

After Rakhyal Shah died in 1940, his followers raised a *dargah* over his grave at Fateh Pur, and the town — dignified with the epithet *Sharif*, "the noble" — grew into a place of pilgrimage. By local tradition the complex also preserves the memory of other holy men of Fatehpur, among them Cheezal (Chizal) Shah, whose name likewise appears among the venerated figures of the site. An annual *urs* marks the saint's death anniversary, drawing devotees who come to recite and hear his poetry; the *Bahar al-'ishq* remains the living heart of the shrine's devotional life, its couplets treasured as both scripture and song.

## Devotion and its Trials

Like many Sufi shrines of the early twenty-first century, the dargah at Fatehpur has suffered the violence of those who reject the inclusive piety it embodies. It was struck by a suicide bombing in 2005 and again, far more grievously, in October 2017, when an attack during the Thursday-night gathering killed some twenty worshippers as they performed *dhamaal*. That the target was a shrine whose saint preached love in five languages lent the atrocity a bitter irony widely remarked upon in the Pakistani press. Yet the *urs* has continued, and pilgrims have returned — an endurance that is itself part of the shrine's story.

## A Note on Dating

The dataset records a founding date of 1359 for this site. This is difficult to reconcile with the life of its principal saint: Rakhyal Shah belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and his *dargah* was built only after his death in 1940. The medieval date, if it is not simply an error, may attach to an older foundation or an earlier holy figure at the Fatehpur site rather than to the present shrine. Readers should treat the 1359 date with caution; the securely attested history of the dargah begins in the twentieth century.

## Legacy

Rakhyal Shah endures as one of Balochistan's most cherished mystic poets, and his shrine is among the rare centres of shared Baloch–Sindhi devotional culture in the province. In a region more often noted for its aridity and its hardships, the *dargah* at Fatehpur keeps alive a tradition of poetry, music and hospitality, and the saint's own vision — that love is the truest road to God — continues to answer, in the plainest way, the violence that has periodically sought to silence it.

## Overview

The Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath, in the Jhanda Bazar of the walled city of Peshawar, is among the last living Hindu temples of that ancient frontier city. A shrine of the British colonial period, dedicated in practice to *Shiva* and centred upon the veneration of the yogi-saint *Ratan Nath*, it belongs to the tradition of the *Nath* order — the sect of ascetic yogis founded in the memory of Gorakhnath — and stands today as one of only a small handful of Peshawar's temples still in regular use, alongside the nearby Kali Bari and the historic Gorakhnath temple at Gor Khatri.

None of the books consulted for this article names the temple in the Jhanda Bazar, describes its building, or records anything of its custodians or its festival. What they offer is of two kinds. Two of them speak of the figure. Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's history of Sufism in India names a 'Ratannath' among the yogis of the *Nath* movement, a contemporary of Gorakhnath and "the subject of many miraculous tales", though it tells none of the tales and gives him no place, no date and no shrine (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 354, folio 332). Michel Boivin's study of the Hindu Sufis of South Asia mentions, in a single endnote, a *dargah mandir* devoted to a 'Pir Baba Ratannath' and places it in Delhi, not in Peshawar (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6). Whether Rizvi's Ratannath, Boivin's Pir Baba Ratannath and the saint of the Peshawar temple are one and the same is not settled by either book. The rest of what the books say concerns Peshawar, its Hindu and Sikh communities and the frontier province around it; it is given below as context about the city and the region, not as testimony about this temple.

## Ratan Nath and the Nath Tradition

The temple's saint, Ratan Nath, belongs to the *Nath sampradaya*, the order of *kanphata* ('split-eared') yogis who trace their lineage to Gorakhnath and, before him, to Matsyendranath, the semi-legendary founder of the sect. The Naths, who flourished across northern India, Nepal, and the north-western frontier from roughly the early medieval centuries, practised a rigorous discipline of yoga and *hatha* austerity and revered Shiva as the *adi-nath*, the first lord and archetypal yogi. Peshawar and its region were an old stronghold of the order: the Gorakhnath temple within the Gor Khatri complex, and the ancient association of the nearby hill of *Tilla Jogian* across the Indus with Gorakhnath himself, mark this as Nath country of long standing.

Rizvi's history gives that picture of the frontier a wider frame. Writing of the Nath movement as a whole, he says: "From the eleventh century the Nath yogis began to spread throughout northern India, and from their centre at Peshawar moved to all parts of Central Asia and Iran, at the same time influencing both qalandars and sufis" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 355, folio 333). The sentence speaks of the Naths and of Peshawar as their centre; it names no building in the city, and no temple of Ratan Nath.

Ratan Nath is remembered in tradition as a wandering seeker and teacher who carried the Nath message of peace, truth, and compassion across the frontier lands; his veneration extends beyond Peshawar to shrines in the wider region, including sites in Nepal. As with many figures of the order, the details of his life are wrapped in legend and cannot be fixed with confidence to a particular century, and the tradition should be received as sacred memory rather than documented biography.

## Ratan Nath in the Books

Rizvi spells the name 'Ratannath' and gives him no 'Pir' and no 'Baba'. The whole of what his main text says of him is one clause, set inside a list of "Other names associated with the Nath cult": "Ratannath, a contemporary of Gorakhnath, and the subject of many miraculous tales" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 354, folio 332). The tales themselves are named and never told; Rizvi records no place for him, no dargah, no dates and no order beyond the Nath cult.

Rizvi returns to the figure in a footnote of his own, as a correction: "In fact Ratannath, a contemporary of Gorakhnath, was a very important figure of the movement" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354, footnote 1). The footnote stands against a statement in his main text in the same place, that "Baba Ratan Haijji [Hajji] was identified with Gorakhnath" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354). Read together, the two passages appear to set Ratannath, the Nath yogi, apart from a Baba Ratan styled *Hajji*; the footnote again names no Peshawar, no Jhanda Bazar, no dargah, no dates and no lineage.

Rizvi's index lists 'Ratannath, 332' among its run of Nath names, beside Dandanath, Dayanath, Dharamanath, Gahininath, Guganath, Minanath, Nimanath, Nivrittinath and Parasnath, again with no 'Pir', no 'Baba', no Peshawar and no date (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 482, folio 458). The same index carries a work headed 'Risala-i Rataniyya, 320', which may be related to one or other of these figures; the index does not tie it to Ratannath (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 482, folio 458).

The Baba Ratan styled *Hajji* is a different figure in Rizvi's pages, and the book does not connect him with this temple. Rizvi writes of a 'Shaikh Baba Ratan or Hajji Baba Ratan', "Born before the birth of Muhammad", made a companion of the Prophet, given *Abu'l-Riza* as his *kunniya*, said to come from Tabarhinda or Bhatinda in the Panjab, given 700/1300 as the year of his death, and buried in the Punjab (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 342, folio 320). The index lists him as 'Baba Ratan, Hajji, 320, 354', with no Nath, no Peshawar and no Jhanda Bazar (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 461, folio 437). Some traditions join the two figures into one; Rizvi's footnote reads as keeping them apart, and nothing in the books places the *Hajji* at Peshawar.

Boivin names the figure once, in an endnote on the 'paradoxical' terminology of shrines that are at once Muslim and Hindu in name: "On this 'paradoxical' terminology, see also the discussion on the 'dargah mandir' devoted to Pir Baba Ratannath in Delhi (Bouillier and Khan 2009: 571 passim)." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6). His index repeats the location, 'Pir Baba Ratannath, Delhi 201 n.6' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 247, folio 234). Boivin says nothing about Peshawar, Gor Khatri or the Jhanda Bazar, and gives the Delhi shrine no dates, no custodian and no order.

The study to which Boivin points carries the figure's divided identity in its very title. His bibliography lists it as "Bouillier, Véronique and Dominique-Sila Khan, 'Hajji Ratan or Baba Ratan's Multiple Identities', *Journal of Indian Philosophy*, 37, 2009, pp. 559–95" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220). Boivin gives no account of its contents. Three readings of Boivin's note remain open, and the book settles none: that the same figure is honoured at a separate *dargah mandir* in Delhi, that the Delhi Pir Baba Ratannath is a different figure, or that the Peshawar shrine has been placed in the wrong city.

## The Shrine at Jhanda Bazar

The dargah itself, in its present form, is a temple of the nineteenth century, raised in the Karimpura–Jhanda Bazar neighbourhood within the old walls of Peshawar when the city's Hindu mercantile community was numerous and prosperous. Its very name — *dargah*, a word borrowed from the vocabulary of the Muslim shrine — reflects the blended religious idiom of the frontier, where a Hindu yogi's shrine could be spoken of in the language of the Sufi tomb.

Boivin's endnote, though it speaks of a shrine in Delhi and not of this one, names the same doubled vocabulary: a *dargah mandir*, a shrine called by the Muslim word for a saint's tomb and the Hindu word for a temple at once, a usage he counts among the 'paradoxical' terms of the shared shrine culture he studies (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6).

After the Partition of 1947, when the greater part of Peshawar's Hindu population departed, most of the city's temples fell silent or were converted to other uses. The Dargah Pir Ratan Nath is remarkable for having survived as a functioning place of worship, tended by the small Hindu community that remained, and it is today reckoned one of the very few temples in daily use in the city, together with the Kali Bari.

The sources consulted record no builder, no founding year, no endowment and no line of custodians for the temple.

## Devotion and Practice

The temple's chief festival is *Maha Shivratri*, the great night of Shiva, when devotees gather for worship. None of the books consulted describes the festival at this temple, or any rite performed here.

Haroon Khalid's account of Pakistan's religious minorities shows Peshawar's Hindus keeping the same festival elsewhere. He records that Hindus from Peshawar came to Katas in 2010 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 47, folio not stated), and that at Shivratri in 2011 "Hindu pilgrims from Peshawar have arrived in two large buses", about a hundred people (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated); the musical band, too, "have also come from Peshawar" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 51, folio not stated). Four marriages solemnised at Katas that Shivratri, an informant told him, were of "girls from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and FATA, who suffered during the floods of 2010" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 51, folio not stated). Of the city's other great Hindu festival, one of his informants, Prem Gupta, says: "If you want to see the lights of Diwali, go to Peshawar" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated). Khalid notes that the names of his informants may have been changed. Of the province as a whole he writes that "Hindu festivals are celebrated with much pomp in these areas" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated). None of these passages names the Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath.

## Setting: Peshawar and the Frontier

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, a history composed in the reign of Aurangzeb, describes Peshawar as an old city with older names. In one place it speaks of Peshawar "در پشاور که بکتب سلف فرشاور (۴) و پرشاور و بگرام نوشته اند", that is, as the place which the books of earlier writers call Farshawar, Parshawar and Bagram; the editor's footnote to Farshawar cannot be read in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 424). In another it says: "پشاور شهر قدیم است که در کتب متقدمین پرشاور و فرشاور نیز نویسند", Peshawar is an ancient city, which the books of the earlier writers also write as Parshawar and Farshawar (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 503).

Bhandari sets at Peshawar the battle of Mahmud's first campaign, "در سنه ۳۹۱": Raja Jaipal, in his words, "راجه جیپال نیز بعزم مقابله رهگرا گشته در پشاور ... رسیده معرکه کارزار بیاراست", set out to meet the invader and, reaching Peshawar, gave battle. The book says that "پنج هزار کفار دران کارزار علف تیغ خونخوار نمود", five thousand of the raja's men fell to the sword in that fight, and that "راجه جیپال با پانزده نفر از پسر و برادر و خویش اسیر گشته بقتل رسید", Raja Jaipal was taken captive with fifteen of his sons, brothers and kinsmen and was put to death (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 424).

In his account of the suba of Kabul, Bhandari writes that "از بلده پشاور سه راه بکابل میرود", from the city of Peshawar three roads run to Kabul (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 502–501). The first is the Nikshab road, "راه نیکشاب", with many hard defiles and a long distance, over which armies pass with difficulty (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 502). The second is the "کهرپه[OCR?]" road, the reading of its name uncertain in the printed text, which joins the highway at Jalalabad, with narrow defiles, hard passes, little water and raids by Afghans, "دست بردے[OCR?] افغانان" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 502). The third, "راه علی مسجد است و خیبر", the road of Ali Masjid and the Khyber, runs eighteen kos, "هژده کروه", from the spring of Jamshid, known as Jamrud, to "دهیکه[OCR?] کنار نیلاب"; the Khyber is hard going for two kos, yet the road is easier than the others and is the one used by armies and caravans. Beyond it, Bhandari counts thirty kos without hills from "دکه[OCR?]" to "ننله[OCR?]", and forty kos, with passes not very hard, from "ننله[OCR?]" to Kabul (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 501).

Of the country round the city Bhandari writes: "تومان بنگرام[OCR?] ان مشهور به پشاور جانب هندوستان است", the district of Bangram, known as Peshawar, lies on the side of Hindustan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 504). Its grapes, peaches and melons are like those of Turan, while its heat and cold, its seasons and its rain are like those of Hindustan; its rice, "سکهد اس[OCR?]", the reading uncertain in the printed text, is better than that of Bengal, and crops and grain are plentiful (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 504). "تمام[OCR?] این تومان بنگاه افغانان مهمند و غیر ذلک است": the whole district is the home of the Mahmand Afghans and others, who "طریق مال گذاری و رعیت گیری ... دارند", who keep to the ways of paying revenue and of living as subjects (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 504–503). Twice more the city appears in his narrative of Mughal affairs: Dara sent robes of honour to "لشکرهائے پیشاور و کابل را که مهابت خان ایالت آنجا داشت", the armies of Peshawar and Kabul, whose governorship Mahabat Khan held (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 77); and after the fort of Attock had been laid out the court "متوجه پیشاور شدند", set out for Peshawar, and from that stage a farman of counsel was sent to Hakim Mirza (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 201). Bhandari names no temple and no yogi at Peshawar in any of these passages.

Rizvi, in a passage on a place called Gorakhtari, writes that "McLeod rightly locates the site in Peshawar" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389). Harish Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis, the traditional lives of Guru Nanak, brings the Guru to the city on his return from Baghdad: "He visited Kabul before reaching Peshawar" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 224, folio 246).

Peshawar appears in the literature of the Sufis too. Robert Rozehnal records that Zauqi Shah's *Sirr-i dilbaran*, a "comprehensive encyclopedia of Sufi terminology", was "Begun in Peshawar in 1923… compiled over a number of years. The text was first published by the silsila in 1951 and is now in its fifth edition (1985)." (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 106, folio 97). Zauqi Shah moved "between Agra, Jaipur, Bombay, Peshawar, Hyderabad, Ajmer, and, finally, Karachi" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 62, folio 52). A woman disciple "originally from the northwest frontier town of Peshawar", interviewed in Lahore in 2000, contrasted the shrines of her home region with Pakpattan: "I am quite used to the culture of segregation when it comes to the saints and the shrines. In the frontier, we have so many shrines where you can walk into the saint's shrines. Women can go inside, we can touch the graves. At many places there is a separate side for the women. It is not like this at Pakpattan Sharif" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 219, folio 211). She names no Peshawar shrine.

Annemarie Schimmel, describing the boldest mystical verse of the Panjab and Sind, paraphrases its vision of a oneness in which every boundary of birth and creed falls away: "the Sufi is no longer Arab, Hindu, Turk, or Peshawari; eventually Hallaj and the judge who condemned him, the lover and the theologian, are seen as nothing but different manifestations of the one divine reality" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 417, folio 386). In another book she gives the same thought in shorter form: "there is no longer Turk, Hindu, or Peshawari." (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 176, folio 158). These are her paraphrases of the poets, not their verse, and they speak of no particular shrine; the books consulted quote no verse by or about Ratan Nath.

Khalid's books give the modern city and province a human face. Peshawar, he writes, is "a city on the western border of Pakistan"; the elders of one Sikh informant, Surjeet Singh, moved there from a village in the Khyber Agency "for better economic opportunities" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 161, folio not stated), and Sikh refugees from the tribal areas "moved to Peshawar, Hassan Abdal and Nankana Sahib, and started living at Gurdwaras, just like the migrants before them" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 175, folio not stated). After the attacks of 1971, another informant, Tarvinder Kaur, told him, her family "fled to Peshawar, where there was a considerable Sikh population", staying "for a few months" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated). A man named Diyal "teaches comparative religion at Peshawar University" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 50, folio not stated).

Of the province he writes that "since partition, the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) has been home to a large proportion of religious minorities who have lived there rather peacefully. These are primarily Hindus, who form the largest minority", and that "Thousands of them are part of the main stream society, visible often in the economic and political fabric" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated). Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is among the provinces where, he writes, "most of the Hindus are scattered" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated). Of the time of Partition he says that "unlike Punjab the riots were less intense due to the influence of the Indian National Congress there. A lot of Hindus and Sikhs continued living in their ancestral lands even after the creation of Pakistan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated); and, elsewhere, that "At the time of partition, unlike Punjab, this area was spared bloodshed primarily due to the influence of the Sarhadi (Frontier) Gandhi – Abdul Ghaffar Khan", so that "several Hindus and Sikhs stayed rooted in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa because of the comparatively peaceful political situation here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 162, folio not stated). Reaching further back, he writes that "During his reign, Maharaja Ranjit Singh captured the Pathan regions of Khyber-Pakhthunkwa and the tribal areas, as a result of which several people converted to Sikhism" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 161–162, folio not stated).

In *Walking with Nanak*, Khalid notes that Nanak Panthi Hindus, "thousands of such Sikhs", live "in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Sindh in Pakistan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 98, folio 80), and that the independent "followers of Guru Nanak" who refused the Khalsa "still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 230, folio 204).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where the figure's dargah stands.** The site's account places the Dargah of Pir Ratan Nath in the Jhanda Bazar of Peshawar, and says his veneration extends to shrines in the wider region, including sites in Nepal. Boivin places the *dargah mandir* devoted to Pir Baba Ratannath in Delhi (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6), and his index gives 'Pir Baba Ratannath, Delhi' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 247, folio 234); he does not mention Peshawar. Rizvi places Ratannath nowhere (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 354, folio 332).
- **The figure's name and style.** The site's account calls him Pir Ratan Nath, and Baba Pir Ratan Nath. Rizvi writes 'Ratannath', with no 'Pir' and no 'Baba' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 354, folio 332; p. 482, folio 458). Boivin writes 'Pir Baba Ratannath' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6).
- **When he lived.** The site's account says the details of his life cannot be fixed with confidence to a particular century. Rizvi makes Ratannath "a contemporary of Gorakhnath" in both his main text and his footnote, without giving a date for either (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 354, folio 332; p. 376, folio 354, footnote 1).
- **When the Naths spread.** The site's account has the Naths flourish across northern India, Nepal and the north-western frontier from roughly the early medieval centuries. Rizvi writes that "From the eleventh century the Nath yogis began to spread throughout northern India", from their centre at Peshawar (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 355, folio 333).
- **Who Ratan was.** The site's account treats him as a Hindu yogi-saint of the Nath order. Rizvi's main text says that "Baba Ratan Haijji [Hajji] was identified with Gorakhnath" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354), while his footnote insists that "In fact Ratannath, a contemporary of Gorakhnath, was a very important figure of the movement" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354, footnote 1). Rizvi also describes a Muslim 'Shaikh Baba Ratan or Hajji Baba Ratan', a companion of the Prophet who died in 700/1300 and lies buried in the Punjab (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 342, folio 320), and the study Boivin cites is titled 'Hajji Ratan or Baba Ratan's Multiple Identities' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220). Neither book ties the *Hajji* to the Peshawar temple.
- **The name of the place at Gor Khatri.** The site's account speaks of the Gorakhnath temple at Gor Khatri. Rizvi writes of a place called Gorakhtari, which, he says, "McLeod rightly locates" in Peshawar (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389).
- **Peshawar's Hindus after 1947.** The site's account says that the greater part of Peshawar's Hindu population departed after Partition, leaving a small community. Khalid, writing of the province rather than the city, says that "A lot of Hindus and Sikhs continued living in their ancestral lands even after the creation of Pakistan", and that Hindus are the province's largest minority (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated).
- **Why the frontier was spared in 1947.** Khalid gives two reasons on two pages: the influence of the Indian National Congress (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated), and the influence of Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Frontier Gandhi (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 162, folio not stated).

## Legacy

The survival of the Dargah Pir Ratan Nath is significant out of all proportion to its modest size. It preserves, in a city more often associated in the modern imagination with the Khyber Pass and the turbulence of the frontier, the memory of a deep and ancient Hindu and yogic presence — the Nath yogis whose austerities once echoed across these hills. As a still-living shrine, it is both a place of worship for Peshawar's remaining Hindus and a fragile monument to the religious plurality of the old walled city. Efforts to document and protect the temple, including its listing among the heritage sites of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, reflect a growing recognition of its value.

The books add a thread to that memory. Rizvi, who calls Peshawar the centre from which the Naths moved into Central Asia and Iran (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 355, folio 333), counts Ratannath "a very important figure of the movement" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354, footnote 1); and the *dargah mandir* of a Pir Baba Ratannath, which Boivin knows in Delhi, carries in its name the same meeting of Muslim and Hindu vocabulary as the Peshawar temple's own (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 214, folio 201, Ch. 4 n. 6).
