Name: Gurdwara Dera Sahib
Events: Martyrdom anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev (Jeth, May-June)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Dera Sahib, known more fully as Gurdwara Dera Sahib *Patshahi Panjvin* — "of the Fifth Guruship" — stands in Lahore, just beyond the walls of the old city, and commemorates the place associated with the martyrdom in 1606 of Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth of the Sikh Gurus and the first to lay down his life for the faith. Rising in white and gold near the River Ravi, the shrine occupies an extraordinary architectural setting: it stands amid the great Mughal and Sikh monuments of Lahore, close by the Lahore Fort, the Badshahi Mosque, the Hazuri Bagh, and the *samadhi* of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. For Sikhs it is a place of profound solemnity, marking an event that transformed the character and history of their community.

Two of the books consulted name the site. Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* gives a chapter to the "Commemoration of Guru Arjan's martyrdom at Gurdwara Dera Sahib, Lahore" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 6, folio not stated), which he attended on "6th June 2011" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated), and writes that the Guru was assassinated "in Lahore, where his now Gurdwara stands by the name of Gurdwara Dera Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 198, folio not stated). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's Urdu survey of Lahore, the *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, heads a section "حال عمارت ڈیرہ گورو ارجن صاحب کا بیان", an account of the building of the Dera of Guru Arjan Sahib, though most of what follows is illegible in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 516).

A third, Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* of 1884, describes at length a *samadh* of Guru Arjan outside the city opposite the Roshnai Gate, between the fort and the *samadh* of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 205–206, folios 208–209). It never calls the building Dera Sahib, and the great well and *baoli* it records inside the enclosure leave open whether the description belongs here or to Lahore's other shrine of the Guru, Gurdwara Baoli Sahib; it is given below as Kanhaiya Lal's account, with that question beside it. The remaining books — Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* and *In Search of Shiva*, Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's history of Sufism in India, Harish Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis, Naveed Alam's translation of Shah Hussein and Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* — speak of Guru Arjan himself, not of this site, and are drawn on here for the Guru's life, death and memory.

## Guru Arjan Dev

Guru Arjan (1563–1606), son of the fourth Guru, Ram Das, and grandson of the third, Amar Das, presided over the Sikh Panth at a moment of remarkable growth and consolidation. It was he who completed the sacred tank and the central shrine at Amritsar — the Harmandir Sahib, later known as the Golden Temple — and who, in 1604, compiled the *Adi Granth*, the first authoritative scripture of the Sikhs, gathering the hymns of his predecessors together with those of Hindu and Muslim saints and installing the volume in the Harmandir with the venerable Baba Buddha as its first custodian. Under his guidance Sikhism flourished as an organised community with its own scripture, its own centre and a widening body of devotees.

Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* gives him as "5. Guru Arjan Dev (1563-1606, Guru from 1581 to 1606)" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289), and Dhillon as "Arjan Dev (Guru from 1581 to 1606)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 240, folio 265). *A White Trail* calls him "the fifth Sikh Guru of Sikhism and the son of the fourth Sikh Guru, Guru Ram Das" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 198, folio not stated), appointed by his father as the next Guru (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated). Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, a Persian chronicle composed under Aurangzeb, records the succession in a line: "بعد ان گورو ارجن خلف او سجاده نشین گشته بعد مدت بست و پنج سال رخت هستی بربست", that after Ram Das his son Guru Arjan became *sajjada-nishin* and, after twenty-five years, departed this life (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).

## The Succession and Prithi Chand

The books tell the succession as a contest with his elder brother. In *Walking with Nanak* Arjan is the brother of Prithi Chand (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 38, folio 20), preferred when "his father, Guru Ram Das, appointed his younger son" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25). Prithi Chand hid the letters Arjan wrote from Lahore to Ram Das, who "disowned Prithi Chand" and "A few days later … appointed Arjan as the next Guru" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 253–254, folio 227 / folio not stated). "Sikh tradition finds the root of the conflict to be Arja[n]'s trip to Lahore and the machinations of Prithi Chand", and Prithi Chand then "approached Mughal authorities to get him his rightful share" of the property, "and hence began the tumultuous relation … between the Mughals and the Sikhs" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248).

Chishti tells the same story with more detail. Guru Arjan produced two letters that had been withheld in Prithi Chand's "جامہ", and Prithi Chand was "نہایت شرمندہ". Guru Ram Das, on the advice of one who from the beginning had seated each Guru on the *gaddi* with his own hand, made Arjan Guru, asked him for a fourth *pauri* so that the name of the four *pauris* should be remembered until the Day of Judgement, and, when Arjan composed it at once, seated him on the *gaddi* as "قائم مقام ہمارے"; his fame spread "عرصہ قلیل مین" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 505). The verse he composed is given below, under *In Verse*.

In Chishti's account Prithi Chand "بدرجہ کمال دشمنی رکھتا تھا", and slandered Arjan before Jahangir even in Ram Das's lifetime, complaining through Jahangir's *diwan*, himself an enemy, while Nawab Wazir Khan defended Arjan as "با خدا آدمی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 499). Arjan admonished his brother again and again, and the harassment went on (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 506). Prithi Chand came against Amritsar with "چند دلال سلطنتی[OCR?] افغان", some Afghans, intending, "با ارادہ قتل گورو صاحب", to kill the Guru, and the Guru hid in the village of "موضع ڈوالی[OCR?]", which is "(جو امرت سر سے چند کوس ہے)", a few kos from Amritsar; the Afghans died on the road (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 507). Prithi Chand petitioned the court with Chandu Lal's support; a *mir* sent to arrest the Guru was killed near Ambala by four servants he had dismissed, the rumour spread that this had happened through the Guru's blessing, Chandu Lal was rebuked and the Guru held "بری الذمہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509).

## The Granth and the Community

The compilation of the scripture is the act the books credit to him most often. Rizvi writes that "The fifth Guru, Arjan Dev" "collected the inspiring hymns written by Guru Nanak and his disciples in the Sikh 'Bible,' the Adi-Granth which is also known as the Granth-Saheb or the Guru-Granth. He also went to the extent of incorporating the authentic poems of the fourteen bhaktas preceding Guru Nanak", calls this appendix "the most authentic anthology of the movement and a memorable collection of medieval devotional literature", and adds: "The Guru-Granth was completed at Amritsar in 1604" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 407, folio 383). The date string printed beside his name in Rizvi's text is damaged and cannot be read with confidence; the index gives "b. 1563 guru 1581-1606" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 466, folio 442). Rizvi also counts "more than a hundred s/okas [slokas] ascribed to Baba Farid Ganj-i Shakar in the Guru Garanth [Guru Granth], compiled by the fifth Sikh Guru, Arjan, in 1604" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328). Dhillon writes that Guru Nanak's Bani "was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 9, folio 9).

*A White Trail* names as a major contribution "the compilation into the Granth Sahib of the writings of all the previous Sikh Gurus and other non-Sikh saints" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 198, folio not stated); Baba Fareed's poetry, collected by Guru Nanak at Pak Pattan, "was later included in the Granth Sahib by Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated). Chishti says that he gathered Baba Nanak's words into the "گرنتھہ[OCR?] یعنی کتاب مذہب[OCR?] سکھوں کی" and fixed some rules for the Sikh community (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686).

*Walking with Nanak* follows the book's making. "Guru Arjan asked one of his followers to go to Lahore to bind the Adi Granth" — Bhai Bannu (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 39, folio 21). After the compilation he was summoned, through Prithi Chand, over its alleged "anti-Muslim and anti-Hindu content", and sent "Bhai Gurdas", who "clarified the misunderstanding" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 254, folio not stated). The Adi Granth "played a significant role in the development of a separate Sikh identity", one reason given being rumours that "Meherban, the son of Prithi Chand" was compiling his own (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 256, folio 230). Arjan "has the greatest number of hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289), a figure the book gives elsewhere as "2218 [OCR?]" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 256, folio 230), and in the Granth's naming "Arjan becomes the fourth Nanak" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 98, folio 80).

The same book credits him with "the completion of the Amrit Sar the tank of nectar that was started by his father at Ramdaspur", after which "the Harmandir Sahib was constructed there" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 257, folio not stated), and with "the daswandh", "10% of their earning to the cause of the Guru" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289), collected "one-tenth of their earnings" through the Masands, "a tradition that was started by Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 256–257, folio 230 / folio not stated). Dhillon adds that the Kartarpur near Jalandhar was founded "in 1594, by the fifth Guru, Arjan Dev, on land granted during the reign of the third Mughal Emperor, Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 175, folio "l92" [text-layer?] [192]).

## Disciples and an Emperor's Visit

Two of his followers are remembered at shrines Khalid visited. Iqbal Qaiser, the historian who guided Khalid, told him that the gurdwara at Mandi Mangat "was the house of Bhai Bannu, who was a devotee of the fifth Sikh guru, Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). "According to the Encyclopaedia of Sikh Literature", another shrine "is the shrine of Sahari Mal, a disciple of the fifth Sikh guru, Guru Arjan"; Khalid calls Sahari Mal "a Hindu (Sikhism as an institutionalized religion was not yet established)", while Haji Kamal, one of Khalid's informants, says "We know that Sahari Mal was a Sikh Jat but that doesn't matter to us" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated).

Bhandari's chronicle records an imperial halt at the Guru's lodging. Crossing the Beas, the emperor came "بمنزل گورو ارجن[OCR?] سجاده نشین بابا نانک که در معرفت الهی مشهور بود" — to the halting place of Guru Arjan, *sajjada-nishin* of Baba Nanak (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 164); the grammar leaves it open whether the words famed in the knowledge of God describe Arjan or Nanak. The emperor was pleased "از ملاقات او و اصغاۓ اشعار هندی تصنیف بابا نانک که در معرفت حق گفته از زبان او شنیده", by the meeting and by hearing from his lips the Hindi verses Baba Nanak had composed, and Guru Arjan, counting it an honour, made a fitting offering (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 164). He then petitioned for the peasants: while the imperial armies were in the Punjab grain had been dear and the revenue demand had been raised, but now grain had become cheap and "رعایا از عهده اداۓ جمع نمیتوانند برآمد"; at his request the *diwans* were ordered to lighten the demand on the peasants (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 164). The chronicle does not name the place of the meeting beyond the river.

## The Martyrdom of 1606

That very flourishing drew the suspicion of the Mughal state. The Emperor Jahangir, in his memoir the *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*, records his displeasure at the Guru's rising influence and at the many who were drawn to him, and complains further that Arjan had extended his blessing to the rebellious prince Khusrau, Jahangir's own son, then in flight through the Punjab. On these grounds the Guru was summoned to Lahore, and a heavy fine — or, failing it, punishment — was imposed.

Sikh tradition holds that the Guru refused to pay or to alter a word of the sacred scripture, and that, at the instigation of the Lahore financier Chandu Shah, he was subjected to days of torture: seated, it is recounted, upon a heated iron plate while burning sand was poured over him, and made to endure scalding water. Bearing these torments with serene equanimity, and declining every inducement to convert, Guru Arjan died in 1606 — his *shaheedi* (martyrdom) traditionally commemorated in the month of Jeth, in late May or early June. By tradition his body was given to the waters of the Ravi and was never recovered. He was the first Sikh Guru to be martyred, and his death is reckoned a watershed in Sikh history.

*Walking with Nanak* quotes the emperor's memoir: "In Goindwal which is on the river Beas, there was a Hindu named Arjan"; Khusro "happened to halt at a place where he was", and Arjan made "a finger-mark in saffron which the Indians call Qashga"; Jahangir had his property handed "to Murtaza Khan" and ordered that he be "dealt with the penal Laws of Yasa" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 252, folio 226). *A White Trail* quotes the same memoir, through Dalbir Singh Dhillon's *Sikhism: Origin and Development*: "this insignificant fellow (Guru Arjan) ... commanded that he should be put to death" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 198, folio not stated). In that book Khusrau, "Jahangir's rebellious son", "stopped over at the Langar of the Guru in Amritsar and sought blessings for his victory", and the *tilak* that was the blessing was "considered treason by the Emperor" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 199, folio not stated).

Chishti gives the meeting from a book whose name is uncertain in the printed text ("لیتی[OCR?] ر بلاس[OCR?]"): Khusrau, "شاہزادہ خلف حضرت جہانگیر بادشاہ", driven from Delhi, came to "ترن تاران" in the district of Amritsar, and Arjan kept him three days and gave him "مبلغ پانسو روپیہ نقد", five hundred rupees in cash (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509).

*Walking with Nanak* gives the Sikh explanation: "The Sikhs believe that he was assassinated due to the connivance of one Chandu Shah who wanted to marry his daughter to Guru Arjan's son, but was refused" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289). Elsewhere it names him "a Hindu Khatri called Chandu Lal", Diwan of Lahore, allied with Prithi Chand (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227), and observes that "Mughal sources and particularly the Tuzk-e-Ja hangiri [OCR?] [Tuzk-e-Jahangiri]" are "glaringly silent about the role of Chandu Lal", Jahangir stating that Arjan "was punished because of his sympathies for his rebel son Khusro" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 255, folio 229). He "was summoned to Lahore by Emperor Jahangir" over his role "during the rebellion of Prince Khusro", appointed "Hargobind as the sixth Guru" and "was subsequently martyred" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 234, folio 208).

Chishti, too, traces Chandu Lal's enmity to a proposed match of his daughter with Arjan's son: it was declined after Sikhs wrote against it, and Arjan married his son to "دو سکھوں کی لڑکیوں", the daughters of two Sikhs (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 500). When Jahangir came to Lahore and Arjan did not present himself, Chandu Lal reported him as "حاکم امرت سر[OCR?] ارجن"; a *farman* summoned him, and he came to Lahore "با پنج سکھہ نامدار[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509). Chishti names the Sikhs who came with him: "بھائی جیٹھا ۔ بھائی برانا[OCR?] ۔ بھائی لنگا[OCR?] ۔ بھائی تی[OCR?] ۔ بہی[OCR?] چند ۔ بھائی منج[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 501).

The accounts of the torture differ in place and length. *A White Trail* sets it "Outside the Alamgiri gate of the Lahore fort, the Guru was forced to sit in a cauldron of boiling water. Burning sand was poured on him" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* places it in the walled city: "there is a place near the Rang Mahal known as ... Khoi [OCR?] [Lal Khoi?], of the Red Well"; "It is believed that Arjan was kept in a room next to this well, which was the haveli of the Mughal Diwan of Lahore", and boiling sand (the word is damaged in the printed text) was poured on his head while he was "immersed in a cauldron" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227); "For five days the Guru was tortured" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 252, folio 226). In Chishti he had no audience; Chandu Lal took him to his *haveli* in "محلہ ہیرامنڈی", imprisoned him alone and tortured him for a month (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 501–502), while one of his Sikhs recited aloud the "بانی ... مصنفہ گورو ارجن صاحب", the Guru's own hymns (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 499).

"On the fifth day of the torture, the Guru requested a bath in the River Ravi, flowing next to the fort"; "Guru Arjan (1563-1606)" took a dip and did not emerge (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* gives the same as Sikh belief — he took "a dip in the waters of the Ravi" and "did not emerge from the water" — and also writes that "His body was then thrown into the river" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227). Kanhaiya Lal writes: "اگرچہ گرو ارجن دریا میں بوقت غسل مفقود ہو چکا تھا نعش اسکی جلائی نہیں گئی مگر یہ سمادہ یادگار کے طور پر بنائی گئی" — although Guru Arjan had disappeared in the river at the time of his bath and his corpse was not cremated, this *samadh* was built by way of a memorial; for the manner of his death he refers the reader to his own history of the Punjab (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). Chishti has him go with his Sikhs toward the "دریائے راوی", die, and be cremated by Sikh *khadims* "اسی مقام پر", at that very place, where a "مندر[OCR?] مڑھی[OCR?]" was raised as a marker (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 502–503).

Chishti dates the death "روز جمعہ یعنی چہارم ماہ جیٹھ سدی[OCR?] سمت[OCR?] اکہارہ[OCR?] سو[OCR?] [illegible] یکم[OCR?] ماہ جیٹھ مطابق سنہ[OCR?] [illegible] ہجری", a Friday in the month of Jeth, given in both the Samvat and the Hijri eras, with the years lost to illegible words (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 502); in another place he gives the year as "سولہ سو چ[OCR?] [illegible] عیسوی", sixteen hundred and something of the Christian era (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686). His table of the Gurus gives the place of death as "بمقام لاہور", at Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 515).

*Walking with Nanak* adds the place of the shrine to the story: "near Lahore Fort there is a small yellow structure which is now referred to [as] the samadhi" of Guru Arjan, and "It is believed that the Guru lost his life there" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227). *A White Trail* writes that he spent a lot of time in Lahore, "where he was assassinated and his remains interred" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).

In Chishti's account, Guru Hargobind later told Jahangir that Arjan's *mala*, "جو اس سے ہزار درجہ بالا تھی", was held by Chandu Lal, and a man in Lahore through whom Chandu Lal used to have something poured on the Guru's body, the word illegible in the printed text, later killed Chandu (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 513).

## The Gurdwara

Sikh tradition records that the Guru's son and successor, Guru Hargobind, raised a memorial platform at the site of the martyrdom in the years that followed. It was under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, however, in the early nineteenth century, that the present *gurdwara* took its handsome form, embellished in the manner of Sikh sacred architecture, with a gilded dome that answers, across the Hazuri Bagh, the domes of the Badshahi Mosque. The proximity of the shrine to Ranjit Singh's own *samadhi* — his memorial tomb — binds it into the great ensemble of monuments that crowns this quarter of Lahore. Within, the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the scripture that Guru Arjan himself first compiled, is enshrined and reverently read, and the shrine functions as a living house of worship.

Khalid gives the same history: "a small structure was raised at the spot by his son, Guru Hargobind to mark the samadhi of the Guru and it is still present there to this day", and "The present structure was first erected by Maharaja Ranjit Singh with further extensions made by the Sikh community in the early years of the twentieth century" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated). "After partition, the Gurdwara came under the control of the Pakistan Government" through the Evacuee Trust Property Board, and "the ETPB regularly undertakes renovation work here"; "In 1996, rooms were built in the complex" for pilgrims "from India and other parts of Pakistan", and "This new hostel was named after Mian Meer" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).

Khalid describes it from the street: "Facing the fort is a small yellow building with a golden dome. A thick yellow wall protects it", with street vendors at the base of the wall, the place "teeming with visitors on any given day", and the Badshahi Mosque beside it (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). Of the garden beside it: "This is where the Sikh ruler of Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, used to meet his subjects. A Mughal baradari (a pavilion with twelve pillars) stands in the middle of the garden"; "All of these three places are famous with the tourists"; and "A giant gateway leading into the yellow building from here facing the garden is permanently locked" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated).

Inside, after a last security check, the inner structure is the same yellow as the wall, and "A couple of rooms at the entrance have been taken over by the security officials" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). The Nishan Sahib "stands at the edge of the courtyard" on "a circular platform about five feet from the ground" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). The heart of the shrine is a small room "with windows on all sides, protected by iron bars"; in its centre "a small bulge which is covered by a velvet cloth ... This is the main attraction; the samadhi of Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 197–198, folio not stated). "A small door from the samadhi of Guru Arjan" leads to the Langar Hall, "divided into two sections", its mats laid "in four lines" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 201, folio not stated).

Chishti's section on the "Dera" of Guru Arjan survives only in fragments: a bazaar whose name is illegible, the word "روشنائی[OCR?]", the building "قلعہ کو باہر", outside the fort, and "دیوار بیرونی قلعہ سے صرف ایک سڑک", only a road from the outer wall of the fort; a door with "حسن طلا[OCR?]" and "منقش لکڑ[OCR?]", a "مسجد" facing it, and "ایک دروازہ کلاں[OCR?]"; a "تحریرِ سنت[OCR?]" naming the Guru and a *sahibzada*; and lines in Gurmukhi of which only "੧ਓ[OCR?]" and "ਸਤਿਗੁਰ[OCR?]" can be read (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 516). In his section "احوال مکان سمادہ گورو ارجن صاحب" he places the *samadh* past the "روشنای" gate, between the gate and the "قلعہ شاہ", to the west (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498). On the next page of the description a Gurmukhi line naming the Guru is printed, much of it uncertain: ਗੁਰੂ ਅਰਜਨ[OCR?] [illegible] ਸੰਮਤੁ[OCR?] ੧੮੭੧੮[OCR?] ਸਾਵਨ[OCR?] ਸੁਦੀ[OCR?] ੧੫[OCR?] (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 517); and "گورو ارجن [illegible]" is pictured in the niche of the *samadh* (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 520).

## Kanhaiya Lal's Samadh

Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* describes a *samadh* of Guru Arjan, "گرو ارجن پانچواں گرو قوم سکھہ کا تھا", the fifth Guru of the Sikh *qaum*, without naming it Dera Sahib and without a date of any kind for the Guru (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). Its position fits this site: "یہ سمادہ روشنائی دروازے شہر لاہور کے سامنے واقع ہے" — opposite the Roshnai Gate of Lahore — with the wall of the fort to its east, "بفاصلہ ایک رستہ[OCR?]", at the distance of one road, and to the west, at a distance lost in the printed text, the wall of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's *samadh* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 205–206, folios 208–209). But the same enclosure has a *baoli*, the feature of Lahore's other shrine of the Guru, Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, and the book never uses either name; whether his description belongs to Dera Sahib has not been settled (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).

He gives the building two phases: "پہلے یہ مختصر مکان تھا مہاراجہ رنجیت سنگہ کے وقت یہ عالیشان مکان بنایا گیا" — formerly a small building, and in Ranjit Singh's time the grand building was made — with no year for either (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). The enclosure was of fired brick and lime with a parapet; two of its doors were kept shut and all traffic passed through the great eastern door, over which letters are written "بخط گرمکھی", in Gurmukhi script, which the text calls "تصویر[OCR?] یہ بھی گرو ارجن کی تحریر ہے". To the south within the four walls stood the grand domed *samadh* building; to its north a three-bayed hall in whose middle bay "اسمیں گرنتہ صاحب بآداب تمام رکھا رہتا ہے", the Granth Sahib is kept with full reverence; and the *samadh*'s own platform, of brick and lime, where the description breaks off in an illegible passage (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).

In one corner outside the hall was a great well with a *baoli*, "چاہ کلان با دلی[OCR?] یعنی چاہ پختہ وار", its stair running from north to south down to the water, where a slab of red stone is set so that "وہان کھڑا ہوکر آدمی چاہ سے پانی لے سکتا ہے", a man standing there can draw water (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). In another corner stood four *samadhs* of a man's height, one of them "لچھمی سرکار زوجہ مہاراجہ رنجیت سنگہ کی والدہ کی", of the mother of Lachhmi Sarkar, wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh; and "شمال کی طرف بھی چند کوٹھریان سکھوں کے آرام کے واسطے بنی ہین", rooms on the north for the Sikhs' rest (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).

On the south was a lime-plastered building, "اس مکان کو سکھوں کی دیگ[OCR?] کہتے ہین", called the Sikhs' *deg* (the word uncertain in the printed text), because "اسمیں ایک کوڑہ[OCR?] پتھر کا زمین کے اندر گاڑا ہوا ہے اور ایک لکڑی موٹی جسکو ونڈ[OCR?] کہتے ہین بنگ گہوٹنے کیواسطے پاس رکھی ہے": a stone mortar is sunk in the ground and a thick wooden pestle called *wand* kept beside it for pounding *bhang*, which the Sikhs grind and drink there (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).

The same book records, in its notice of Guru Hargobind's house at Mozang, that "اب متعلق سمادہ گرو ارجن کے یہ مکان بھی ہے جو آمدنی اس جگہ کی وہی شخص لیتا ہے جو گرو ارجن کی سمادہ کا پجاری ہو" — that house is now attached to the *samadh* of Guru Arjan, and its income is taken by the *pujari* of Guru Arjan's *samadh* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 226, folio 229). The notice does not say where that *samadh* is, so it may or may not refer to this shrine.

## Devotion and Practice

Since the Partition of 1947 the shrine has been maintained within Pakistan under the Evacuee Trust Property Board, and it remains a solemn and much-visited station for the Sikh pilgrims who come to Lahore, above all upon the anniversary of the Guru's martyrdom, observed in the month of Jeth.

Khalid's chapter is a report of that anniversary on 6 June 2011. "About three hundred pilgrims from India have come to Lahore for this event, while several hundred have come from other parts of the country"; the Indians stay "for three days", after which some return "while others will visit sacred shrines in Nankana Sahib and Hassan Abdal" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated). Most pilgrims were Sikhs "bearing the 5 Ks", with a few clean-shaven "Nanak Panthi Sikhs" from "South Punjab and Sindh" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). The lawn became "a temporary camp for pilgrims who do not have rooms", "primarily Pathan-Sikh families who have come from Nankana Sahib, Hassan Abdal, Peshawar and the Tribal Areas", while Indian pilgrims and "other important guests" had rooms (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 201, folio not stated).

The courtyard was tented against "the intense heat of June" and carpeted, the congregation facing the Granthi, the recitation carried through "a small speaker" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). Men prayed to the Khanda on the Nishan Sahib, touched its base and kissed their hands or touched their eyes to the platform (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). In the *samadhi* room, whose "capacity [is] no more than five people", there were "About twenty attendees", and women recited from "pocket Granths" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 197–198, folio not stated). At the conclusion of the Akhand Path "bhog (community prayer) is performed"; "Waheguru"; "the entire community prostates [as printed] to the living Guru, the Granth Sahib", and Sikh boys served cold milk, juice and "freshly cut water melons" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 201, folio not stated). The *langar* was prepared by volunteers and employees, "an overwhelming majority of who seem to be low-caste Nanak Panthis from Southern Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 201, folio not stated).

For all its renown, Khalid found the approach closed. "Today, this place is deserted": the only road "is cordoned off by the police", behind a barricade "fortified with barbwire", and only people "carrying special cards, which have been made for them by the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB)" may pass; "Many local tourists return disappointed", and at the metal-detector door the sign reads 'Out' while the 'In' gate is shut (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated). On ordinary days "hundreds of local visitors" peek in, and the security men's answer is: "If you are a Muslim, you are not allowed." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated). Male and female police search the pilgrims, and bags pass "through an X-ray machine" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated).

Khalid met members of Pakistan's own Sikh community at the shrine. Kartar Singh Kartar was "temporarily residing at this Gurdwara for his education and being given free accommodation and food at the shrine", and joked "I am a langur (a species of monkey)" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated); he is "the most highly qualified Pakistani Sikh", hoping "to do my PhD in the Punjabi language" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 202, folio not stated). "32 year old Dr. Manoj Singh" is "the first MBBS doctor from the Pakistani Sikh community", "serving at the Ganga Ram Hospital" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 201–202, folio not stated). "25 year old Premjeet Singh, the first Pakistani Sikh to have been commissioned into the Pakistan Rangers", was allotted a room "because of his social standing", shared "with five other family members" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 202, folio not stated).

Kanhaiya Lal's account, if it is of this site, shows its nineteenth-century life: the Granth Sahib kept with full reverence in the hall, rooms for the Sikhs' rest, the well from which water was drawn, and the room where the Sikhs pounded and drank *bhang* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). It had a *pujari*, who also took the income of Guru Hargobind's house at Mozang (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 226, folio 229).

## Legends and Miracles

The books record the Guru's end as more than a death. "Legend has it that the Guru was lifted alive into the sky by God" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). In the Sikh belief that *Walking with Nanak* reports, when he took his dip in the Ravi and did not come out, "the Guru had performed a miracle and passed onto the other world" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227).

In the same Sikh account the Sufi Mian Mir asked leave "to bury alive his oppressors. The Guru refused" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227). *A White Trail* notes that "the friendship between Mian Meer and Guru Arjan is also the subject of several folk tales" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated), and the pilgrims' hostel built at the gurdwara in 1996 bears Mian Meer's name (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).

Chishti's account carries a story of the Guru's protection: when a *mir* sent to arrest him was killed on the road near Ambala, the rumour spread that it had happened "یہ برکت گورو ارجن صاحب", through the blessing of Guru Arjan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509).

## In Verse

The books carry little of Guru Arjan's own verse, and that only in Urdu script in Chishti's book, without an English version. Chishti prints the fourth *pauri* that, he says, Arjan composed at once when Guru Ram Das asked for it, on the day he was made Guru (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 505):

بھاگ ہویا گر سنت ملایا …
جن نانک داس تمہارے جی

The *pauri* composed by Guru Arjan when Guru Ram Das seated him on the *gaddi*: its opening and its closing words as Chishti prints them, with no translation given (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 505).

He also prints three of the Guru's verse letters, "گربانی یعنے خط منظومہ", written to Guru Ram Das, each with an Urdu gloss: one opening "میرا من لوچے گورو درشن تائین" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 503), one with the line "تیرا مکھ سہاوا جی", and one with the line "اک گھڑی نہ ملتے[OCR?] ... کلجگ[OCR?] ہوتا[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 504).

The Guru's compilation drew poets to it, at least in later report. Naveed Alam, translating the Sufi poet Shah Hussein, writes: "According to some sources, Shah Hussein travelled to Amritsar to get his poetry included in the Granth Sahib being compiled by Guru Arjun Dev (1563–1605). He offered this kafi for inclusion. Though the account is unverifiable, the thematic content of this kafi might have lent itself to the speculation." (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 186, folio 186). The poetry of Baba Farid, collected by Guru Nanak at Pak Pattan, "was later included in the Granth Sahib by Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).

## Setting

The books describe the quarter of Lahore around the shrine. Khalid's *A White Trail* writes that "The Roshani gate, one of the thirteen gateways that lead into the ancient walled city of Lahore, is between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque"; lamps "were lit all along the passageway ... hence the name Roshani gate, or the gate of lights" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). "Behind it is the Heera-Mandi bazaar", and the area is "also famous for the food street that runs parallel to the wall of the Badshahi Masjid" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). Chishti counts the gate, as "روشنای دروازہ", among the twelve gates of Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498).

The river beside which the Guru died has moved. The Ravi, which flowed next to the fort, "has changed its course, moving a few kilometres away" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). The city's Sikhs have thinned too: "it is now rare that one runs into a Sikh in this city, a city which was once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of their political strength" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated). Lahore holds more of the Gurus' memory than this shrine: Guru Ram Das "was also born in present day Pakistan, in the city of Lahore", and Guru Hargobind "also spent a lot of time here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* adds that Chandu Lal was "appointed as the Diwan of Lahore by the Mughal authorities" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227), and that Khusro "rebelled against his father and moved towards Lahore" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 255, folio 229).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The Guru's dates.** The site's account gives 1563–1606, and so does *A White Trail*, "Guru Arjan (1563-1606)" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated), and *Walking with Nanak*, with his guruship from 1581 (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289); Dhillon gives his guruship as 1581 to 1606 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 240, folio 265). Alam prints "(1563–1605)" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 186, folio 186). Rizvi's body text prints a damaged date string, and his index "b. 1563 guru 1581-1606" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 407, folio 383; p. 466, folio 442). Chishti's year is partly illegible, "سولہ سو چ[OCR?] [illegible] عیسوی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686). Bhandari gives no year, only that he died twenty-five years after succeeding his father (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Kanhaiya Lal gives no date of any kind (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).
- **The name of the Lahore official.** The site's account calls him Chandu Shah, "the Lahore financier", and so does one passage of *Walking with Nanak* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289). Another passage of the same book calls him Chandu Lal, a Khatri and Diwan of Lahore (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227), and Chishti calls him Chandu Lal (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509).
- **Who was to blame.** The site's account has Jahangir act on the Guru's influence and his blessing of Khusrau, with the torture at Chandu Shah's instigation. *Walking with Nanak* sets the Sikh explanation, Chandu Lal's connivance with Prithi Chand, against the Mughal sources, which are silent about Chandu Lal and give the Guru's sympathy for Khusro as the cause (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227; p. 255, folio 229). Chishti puts Prithi Chand's slanders and Chandu Lal's report behind the summons (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 499; p. 509).
- **Where and how Khusrau met the Guru.** The site's account says Jahangir complained that Arjan had blessed the prince. Jahangir, as *Walking with Nanak* quotes him, sets the meeting at Goindwal on the Beas and the blessing as a saffron finger-mark (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 252, folio 226). *A White Trail* has the prince stop at the Guru's *langar* in Amritsar and receive a *tilak* (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 199, folio not stated). Chishti has him come to Tarn Taran, stay three days and receive five hundred rupees (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 509).
- **The penalty.** The site's account has a heavy fine or, failing it, punishment. Jahangir, as *Walking with Nanak* quotes him, gave the Guru's property to Murtaza Khan and ordered him dealt with by the laws of Yasa (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 252, folio 226).
- **Where he was tortured, and for how long.** The site's account gives days of torture without a place. *A White Trail* sets it outside the Alamgiri gate of the fort, the Guru going to the river on the fifth day (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* sets it in the Mughal Diwan's *haveli* by the Red Well near the Rang Mahal, for five days (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227; p. 252, folio 226). Chishti sets it in Chandu Lal's *haveli* in Hira Mandi, for a month (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 501–502).
- **The manner of the torture.** The site's account has a heated iron plate, burning sand and scalding water. *A White Trail* has a cauldron of boiling water and burning sand (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated); *Walking with Nanak* has him immersed in a cauldron with boiling sand poured on his head (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227).
- **What became of his body.** The site's account has it given to the Ravi and never recovered. *Walking with Nanak* has it thrown into the river, and reports the Sikh belief that he went into the water and did not come out (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227); *A White Trail* has him take a dip and not emerge, records the legend that he was lifted alive into the sky (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated), and elsewhere says his remains were interred in Lahore (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal has him vanish in the river while bathing, his corpse never cremated (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). Chishti has him cremated by Sikh *khadims* at the spot (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 502–503).
- **The first memorial.** The site's account and *A White Trail* have Guru Hargobind raise it (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated). Chishti has the Sikh *khadims* who cremated the Guru raise a marker there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 502–503). Kanhaiya Lal says only that it was at first a small building (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209).
- **The present building.** The site's account and Kanhaiya Lal give it to Ranjit Singh's time (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 206, folio 209). Khalid has it first erected by Ranjit Singh, with extensions by the Sikh community in the early twentieth century (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).
- **Its colour.** The site's account calls the shrine white and gold. Khalid calls it "a small yellow building with a golden dome" behind a yellow wall (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated), and *Walking with Nanak* "a small yellow structure" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227).
- **Which Guru he was.** The site's account and the books make him the fifth Guru; *A White Trail* once calls him "the fourth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 168, folio not stated), against "fifth" on its other pages (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 162, folio not stated; p. 198, folio not stated).
- **Whether Kanhaiya Lal's samadh is this site.** Its place, opposite the Roshnai Gate between the fort and Ranjit Singh's *samadh*, fits Dera Sahib; its *baoli* could point to Gurdwara Baoli Sahib; the book names neither (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 205–206, folios 208–209; p. 206, folio 209).
- **The spelling of the name.** The site's account spells him Arjan; Alam prints "Guru Arjun Dev" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 186, folio 186).

## Legacy

The martyrdom of Guru Arjan altered the course of Sikh history. His son, Guru Hargobind, on assuming the Guruship, is remembered as having girded himself with two swords, symbolising *miri* and *piri* — temporal and spiritual authority — and as having built the Akal Takht at Amritsar, thus arming and organising the community for its own defence. The pacific movement of Guru Nanak's early followers began, from this point, to take on the resolve and martial spirit that would mark later Sikh history. Gurdwara Dera Sahib thus stands not merely as a memorial to a single death, but as the birthplace of an idea — that faith may be defended, and that the willing acceptance of martyrdom is itself a form of victory.

The books agree on the turn. Rizvi: "After the death of the Fifth Guru, Arjan, at the hands of the Mughal Jahangir, the Sikhs dropped their pacifist policy and adopted their famous martial spirit" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 419, folio 395). *Walking with Nanak* calls the Guru "Regarded as the first martryr [OCR?] [martyr] of Sikhism" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289), crushed "in the fight between the Mughal 'elephants'" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 255, folio 229); the assassination is "the Karbala of Sikh history" and "precipitated the development of the Khalsa" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 255–256, folios 229–230). "The martyrdom of Guru Arjan provided the Sikh community with a cohesive motivation", though militarisation had begun, following Grewal, "during the period of the fifth Sikh Guru" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 232, folio 206; p. 234, folio 208). "He was the last Guru in the line of the Gurus who focused solely on spiritual matters" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 256, folio 230), and his assassination "marks the beginning of a long conflict between Mughal authorities and Sikh Gurus" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289). Tegh Bahadur "was the first Guru since Guru Arjan to compose hymns" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 134, folio 116).

*A White Trail* calls him "the first Sikh martyr, assassinated by the fourth Mughal Emperor, Jahangir (1569-1627)" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 162, folio not stated), and writes that "Guru Arjan's martyrdom is a low point in Sikh history" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 206–207, folio not stated). The memory reaches far beyond Lahore: Operation Blue Star was launched "on a day when thousands of Sikhs from all over Punjab had gathered at the shrine to commemorate the death anniversary of the fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan", and "In a long list of martyrs who followed Guru Arjan", its victims "became the latest entry" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 162, folio not stated). His name is among those painted after Nanak's picture on the dome at Jhaman (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 51, folio 33).

## Bibliography

- Pashaura Singh, *The Life and Work of Guru Arjan* (Oxford University Press), on the fifth Guru, the compilation of the *Adi Granth*, and the martyrdom.
- The *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri* (memoirs of the Emperor Jahangir), a primary source for the imperial order against Guru Arjan.
- Khushwant Singh, *A History of the Sikhs*, and Max Arthur Macauliffe, *The Sikh Religion*, on Guru Arjan and its aftermath under Guru Hargobind.
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan*, on the shrine at Lahore and its setting among the city's monuments.
- Records of the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) and heritage documentation of the Lahore Fort and Badshahi Mosque ensemble.
- Haroon Khalid, *A White Trail: A journey into the heart of Pakistan's religious minorities* (westland ltd, 2013; first e-book edition 2013).
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).
- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).
- Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, Vol. I, *Early Sufism and its History in India to 1600 AD* (New Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers Pvt. Ltd.; first published 1978, copyright line 1975).
- Harish Dhillon, *Janamsakhis: Ageless Stories, Timeless Values* (Hay House India, 2015; paperback 2020).
- Sujan Rai Bhandari of Batala, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* (Persian; composed in regnal year 40 of Aurangzeb; 1918 Delhi lithograph edited by Zafar Hasan).
- Madho Lal Hussein; Naveed Alam (tr.), *Verses of a Lowly Fakir* (2015).

Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Ram Das stands in the Chuna Mandi quarter of the Walled City of Lahore, upon the site traditionally revered as the birthplace and childhood home of Guru Ram Das (1534–1581), the fourth of the ten Sikh Gurus and the founder of the city of Amritsar. Set along the old *Shahi Guzargah*, the "royal road" that ran from the Delhi Gate to the Lahore Fort, near the Fort itself and the Begum Shahi Mosque, the shrine joins Lahore's several great gurdwaras in binding the city to the early history of the Sikh faith.

Of the books consulted, one describes the gurdwara itself: Kanhaiya Lal's Urdu history of Lahore, *Tarikh-e Lahore*. He opens his account with the place: "جس مقام پر گورامداس صاحب مذہب سکہی کے جانشین چہارم کا جنم ہوا", the place where Guru Ram Das, the fourth successor of the Sikh religion, was born, "اور اسی جگہ پرورش پائی", and where he was reared as well (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). He calls the building "یہ عبادت گاہ سکہی مذہب سے متعلق ہی", a house of worship of the Sikh faith, and writes that Sikhs "اس متبرک مکان کا کمال ادب کرتے ہین", showing the blessed house the utmost reverence, while Hindus high and low also attend it and hold the place extremely pure (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).

The other books speak of the Guru, not of the gurdwara. Haroon Khalid writes in *A White Trail* that "Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru, was also born in present day Pakistan, in the city of Lahore" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated), and Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's Urdu *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* gives "لاہور" as his birthplace in a table (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 515); neither names the shrine. Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* gives the Guru a chapter of his own, and tells his life without mentioning the Lahore site. What these books say of the Guru is gathered below as his life, not as the history of this building.

## The Life of Guru Ram Das

Ram Das was born in the Chuna Mandi bazaar of Lahore in 1534, in a family of modest means, and was known in his boyhood as Bhai Jetha. Orphaned young, he came under the influence of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, whose daughter he married and whom he served with such devotion and humility that he was in time chosen to succeed him. As the fourth Guru he is remembered above all for founding the settlement that grew into Amritsar — first excavating the sacred pool, the *Amrit Sarovar*, from which the city takes its name — and for composing the *Lavan*, the four hymns that form the heart of the Sikh marriage rite and are sung at every *Anand Karaj* to this day. His verses occupy a cherished place in the *Guru Granth Sahib*, the Sikh scripture.

That the founder of Amritsar should himself have been born in Lahore gives this shrine its particular resonance, joining the two cities most closely associated with the early Gurus.

Khalid's list of the Gurus gives him as "4. Guru Ram Das (1534-1581, Guru from 1574 to 1581)", and adds: "Born in 1534 Guru Ram Das became the first Sodhi Guru"; the Gurudom thereafter "remained within the Sodhi family till Guru Gobind singh" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289). Harish Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis gives the same span of office, "Ram Das (Guru from 1574 to 1581)", naming him among the later Gurus whose stewardship Baba Budha witnessed (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 240, folio 265).

Chishti's table records the birth in the month of Kartik, "[illegible] کاتک سمت [illegible] بوقت چار گھڑی[OCR?] دن", at four *gharis* of the day; the day and the year are illegible in the printed text. The same table gives the birthplace as Lahore, the father as "ہرداس[OCR?]" and the mother as "[illegible] کنور[OCR?]", her first name lost (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 515). In his narrative Chishti names "ہر داس" and describes the family as "کھتری قوم سود ہی ساکن لاہور", Khatris of the Sodhi line and residents of Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498). Khalid, citing P. S. Grewal's "Nanak's Doctrine and the Feudalization of the Sikh Gurudom", calls Jetha "a Sodhi Khatri, an ancient caste of kings", and notes that "Amar Das himself belonged to the Khatri Bhalla caste" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 272, folio 246).

Kanhaiya Lal places the family's home on this spot: "خاص جائے سکونت گورامداس کے ماباپ کی اس جگہ پر تہی", the particular residence of Ram Das's mother and father was at this place. Then, "سبب انقلاب زمانہ", by a turn of the times, they left Lahore for "گوبندوال", Goindwal, and "وہان ہی شادی گورامداس کی امرداس کی لڑکی کے ساتہ ہو گئی", there his marriage with Amar Das's daughter took place (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). He gives no date for the birth, the departure or the marriage (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).

Khalid tells the boyhood differently. "Jetha's parents had died at a young age" and his grandmother raised him; as a child "he sold boiled grain and wheat in the village of Basarke near Amritsar", where Amar Das first saw him (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 272, folio 246). He followed Amar Das to "Khadur", where he looked after "the langar at the darbar of the Guru", and later followed him to "Goindwal" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 272–273, folio 246 / folio not stated). His own family complained of his "servile attitude" towards his in-laws (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 273, folio not stated). Chishti, too, has him serve "بارہ برس", twelve years, in the *langar*, and speaks of the "نعمت", the favour, that he received (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498).

## Marriage and Succession

In Khalid's telling, Guru Amar Das's wife recommended "the young man Jetha" as a husband for their younger daughter, "Bibi Bhani", and the Guru "was relieved" to learn that he was a Sodhi Khatri (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 272, folio 246). Chishti names the wife "بی بی بھانی", and records her request that the honour of the Guruship, "یہ شرف گورو ای[OCR?]", should stay in their offspring; he gives the couple three sons (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498). His account of the marriage itself is garbled in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498).

Khalid writes that Amar Das "put his two sons-in-law and his two sons through a few tests", and that "All Sikhs accepted the choice … except his eldest son Mohar [OCR?]" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248). In *A White Trail* he puts it plainly: "Guru Amar Dass selected his son-in-law, Guru Ram Das, as his successor" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated). Sujan Rai Bhandari, writing in Persian in the reign of Aurangzeb, records that at his death Amar Das seated "رامداس عرف سودهی داماد خود", Ramdas known as Sodhi, his own son-in-law, in his place, although he had children of his own, and that "او هفت سال سجده گاه مریدان بود", for seven years he was the object of his disciples' prostration (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).

Chishti names him in two forms. One passage reads "چوتہی گورو رام داس خلف گورو امرداس[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 680). The other names "گورو امر داس کا داماد", the son-in-law of Guru Amar Das, adding "اوسکی اولاد سوڈھی[OCR?] کہلاتی ہی", his descendants are called Sodhi; the place and the year given with it, "[illegible] پور" and "سولہ[OCR?] سو [illegible] عیسوی", are only partly legible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686).

"Guru Ram Das became the first Sodhi [Guru]" [OCR?], Khalid writes, and by the time of Gobind Singh it "was understood" that the Guruship would pass only within the Sodhi caste (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248). "After Ram Das, the succession of Guruhood became a family affair in which the son of the Guru was preferred over others" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 273, folio not stated).

## Ramdaspur and Amritsar

The site's account remembers the Guru as the founder of the settlement that grew into Amritsar. Khalid gives the story of the land. "When Amar Das appointed Ram Das as his successor over his sons, he too asked Ram Das to move to Ramdaspur" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 291, folio 265). In one passage, "Ram Das moved to K[…] [OCR?]", the name of the place cut off in the printed text, a "small town that he had founded on the land that was gifted [to] his wife by the Mughal Emperor Akbar when he met Guru Amar Das"; there "the Guru started the construction of the Amrit Sar", and to fund it "the Guru introduced the system o[f] Masand" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248). Elsewhere Akbar "allotted a huge tract of land to the daughter of Amar Das, Bibi Bhani, the wife of Guru Ram Das instead" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 292, folio 266).

In another place "Guru Ram Das had a jagir where he laid the foundation of the ... [Ramdaspur]", which "eventually became Amritsar", and he was "responsible for the establishment of the Masand system" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 254, folio not stated); it was he who started the tank at Ramdaspur (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 257, folio not stated). Khalid's list of the Gurus calls him "known for starting the construction of the Harminder Sahib". He appointed "his Masand or deputies in different regions" to spread the message and "collect offerings", and "the revenue of the seat of the Guru began to increase under him" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289).

Chishti, too, ties the Guru to the city. He places "چوتھی بادشاہی گورو رام داس کی امرتسر میں", the fourth *Padshahi*, that of Guru Ram Das, at Amritsar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 280); and of Amritsar he writes, in a phrase partly uncertain in the printed text, "گورو رام داس کی لگی[OCR?] مشہور" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 500); and he names "گورو رام داس[OCR?]" beside his son Arjan in his Amritsar passage (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686).

Khalid reads the grant of land as a turning point. "with this event also begins the process of feudalisatio[n] [of] Guruhood. All subsequent Gurus after Ram Das were huge land[owners]" [OCR?] (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248).

## The Choice of Guru Arjan

The Guru's own succession divided his sons. Khalid writes that he appointed his younger son, Arjan, rather than Prithi Chand (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25). In *A White Trail*, too, Ram Das appointed his son, Guru Arjan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated). Chishti calls Arjan the Guru's "فرزند خورد", his younger son, made "ولی عہد سجادہ نشین", heir and successor to the seat, to the anger of Prithi Chand (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 499). Chishti's account then turns to Arjan's letters, which were intercepted (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 503–504), and to "موضع گوبندوال جو متصل ضلع امرتسر ہے", the village of Goindwal near the district of Amritsar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 505).

Lahore has its part in the story. In Khalid's account the Guru sent Arjan to Lahore for a wedding and, on discovering Prithi Chand's deception, called him back and appointed him Guru (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 253–254, folio 227 / folio not stated). Sikh tradition, Khalid writes, traces the quarrel between the brothers to "Arja[n]'s trip to Lahore" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248). The conflict arose "between the Guru's two sons, Prithi Ch[and] and Arjan", over an "immense property", "essenti[ally] the entire city of Ramdaspur and the area around it" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248), and bypassing Prithi Chand began "a conflict that was to last for several generations after him" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289). Near Lahore, Khalid notes, "The Bedian road is the old route to Amritsar", and Prithi Chand's rival shrine would lie "on the route from Lahore to Amritsar" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 38, folio 20; p. 44, folio 26).

Chishti's table places the Guru's death at Goindwal in the district of Amritsar, "سمت [illegible] … گوئندوال[OCR?] ضلع امرتسر", the year illegible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 515). Dhillon and Khalid end his Guruship in 1581 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 240, folio 265; Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 315, folio 289).

## The Shrine and Maharaja Ranjit Singh

The Guru's childhood home is said to have survived on this spot until the era of the Sikh Empire. Tradition relates that Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the ruler of the Sikh state at Lahore, was asked to raise a fitting shrine at the site — according to the account, at the request of his wife Maharani Datar Kaur, during the celebrations that attended the birth of their son Kharak Singh in 1801. The Maharaja agreed, acquiring the surrounding plots and building the gurdwara that stands, much altered, today. Its situation within the dense fabric of the old city, hard by the Fort and the imperial mosque of the Mughals, speaks to the layered history of Lahore, where the monuments of Mughal, Sikh, and later ages stand shoulder to shoulder.

Kanhaiya Lal tells the founding in his own way. "پہلے اس جگہ چہوٹا سا مکان تہا", there was formerly a small house on the spot. Then, "مہاراجہ رنجیت سنگہ کی اخیر عملداری مین", in the last years of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's rule, the Guru's Sikhs turned their attention to it, and "مہاراجہ کے حکم سے محلہ سوداگران کے مکانات جو اس کے ساتہ ملحق تہے لے گئے": by the Maharaja's order the houses of Mohalla Saudagran adjoining it were taken. The land was enlarged, the foundation laid, and the building "ایک سال کے عرصے مین تیار ہو گیا", was ready within one year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). He says nothing of any payment for the houses, and gives no year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).

He places the gurdwara "بازار چوک متی[OCR?] کے جنوبی لین مین", in the southern lane of a bazaar whose name is uncertain in the printed text, with "سرِ بازار ایک عالیشان دروازہ پختہ", a lofty brick gateway on the bazaar, and a stair in the *deorhi*, the entrance hall (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). Within is an upper courtyard, with a well in its north-west corner and a *bel* tree; in the courtyard "ایک علم یعنی چہنڈا کہڑا کیا گیا ہی", a standard, that is a flag, has been raised; and on the east is a stepped jharokha of ornamented brick (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).

"یہ عالیشان عمارت دربار امرتسر کی قطع پر ہی ہوئی ہے", Kanhaiya Lal writes: the stately building is made on the pattern of the Darbar of Amritsar (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 101–102, folios 104–105). It has four doors on its four sides, and "بیچ مین اگرچہ گنبد نہین ہی", though there is no dome at its centre, it has four two-storeyed *shah-nashins* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

Writing of Lahore's Sikh buildings in general, and not of this one, Khalid reports Iqbal Qaiser's lecture on Sikh architecture in the city: "like the Sikh religion, which picks up from both Hinduism and Islam, Sikh architecture draws inspiration from both Hindu and Muslim architecture"; domes "initially part of the Muslim buildings" were made "smaller" by the Sikhs, and Sikh shrines carry "graphic depictions of Sikh Gurus and also sometimes Hindu deities (in older buildings)" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 309–310, folio not stated / folio 284).

Of the Maharaja's patronage across the province, Khalid writes: "When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras", and "attached vast tracts of land to these gurdwaras, so that the revenues from the lands could facilitate their functioning" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 34, folio 16). In *A White Trail* he says that Ranjit Singh renovated "many Gurdwaras all over Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 208, folio not stated). Neither passage names this gurdwara, and Kanhaiya Lal records no endowment, land or income for it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

## Worship in the Nineteenth Century

Kanhaiya Lal describes the gurdwara at worship. An elaborate floor covering stays spread, and "گرنتہہ صاحب کمال آداب سے رکہا رہتا ہی", the Granth Sahib is kept there with the greatest reverence. Sikhs come in numbers and perform "جبین سائی[OCR?]", prostration, and "دو وقت روز مرہ گرنتہہ پڑہا جاتا ہی", the Granth is read twice daily, before large gatherings (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

There is singing, and not only by Sikhs: "قوال موحدانہ کافیان گا کر لوگون کو محظوظ کرتے ہین", *qawwals* delight the people by singing monotheist *kafis* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105). A larger assembly comes round regularly: "آٹہوین روز انوار[OCR?] کے دن تیسرے پہر بڑا مجمع زن و مرد کا ہوتا ہی", on the eighth day, on the day the printed text gives as "انوار", in the third watch, a great gathering of men and women takes place. A selection from the Gurus' Granths is read and "شبد توحید آمیز گائے جاتے ہین", *shabads* imbued with the oneness of God are sung; "جلسہ لایق دید ہوتا ہی", the gathering is worth seeing (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

He records one dated occasion, though he does not give its year. "ابہی[OCR?] کے ہولیون کے دنون مین سنگہ سبہا کے ممبرون[OCR?] نے یہان بڑا جلسہ کیا تہا … تمام مندر اور بازار مین روشنی کی اور تمام رات شبد گاتے رہے تہے": recently, in the days of the Holi festival, members of the Singh Sabha held a great assembly here, lit up the whole temple and the bazaar, and sang *shabads* all night (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105). The reading of the opening word and of the members' title is uncertain in the printed text.

He names the custodians of his day: "فی الحال پجہاری اس گردوارے کا جیت سنگہ اور معتمد و معاون حلقہ کا ایک شخص کنہیا لال ہے", the *pujari* of the gurdwara at present is Jeet Singh, and the trusted agent of the circle is a man named Kanhiya Lal. His verdict on the two is lost in the printed text: "حقیقت مین یہ [illegible] شخص ہین" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105). He records no endowment, land, income or annual festival for the gurdwara (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

## Partition and Its Aftermath

The Partition of 1947 fell heavily upon the Sikh shrines of Lahore. Amid the communal violence that swept the city, some eighteen Sikhs are reported to have been killed within the premises of this gurdwara — one of many such tragedies that emptied the western Punjab of its Sikh population almost overnight. In the decades that followed, the shrine, like the other historic gurdwaras of Pakistan, passed into the care of the Evacuee Trust Property Board.

In recent years the gurdwara has been reopened to worship and to pilgrimage, and the birthday of Guru Ram Das draws Sikh visitors to the narrow lanes of Chuna Mandi to honour the Guru at the place of his birth. Its careful upkeep forms part of the wider, if uneven, effort to preserve and restore Pakistan's Sikh heritage.

The books consulted do not describe the gurdwara in 1947 or after. Khalid writes of the city's eve of Partition that "Tara Singh, a prominent Sikh leader at that time, took out his kirpan on the stairs of the Punjab Assembly in Lahore and said that the time to take revenge for the Gurus had come" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 199, folio not stated). Of Lahore today he writes that "it is now rare that one runs into a Sikh in this city, a city which was once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of their political strength" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated).

Of Sikh and Hindu sites after 1947, Khalid writes that without the care of one family the temple of Ram Thamman "would have also been taken over by the refugees and converted into a household, like the hundreds of temples and Gurdwaras all over Pakistani Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 58, folio not stated). In *In Search of Shiva* he adds: "I have seen several gurdwaras and temples being taken over and destroyed by the migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated). Neither passage names this gurdwara.

## Setting: The Gurus' Lahore

The city where Ram Das was born kept its hold on his line. Khalid writes that "Guru Arjan spent a lot of time in the same city, where he was assassinated and his remains interred", and that Guru Hargobind "also spent a lot of time here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). Arjan "was summoned to Lahore by Emperor Jahangir" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 234, folio 208) and died there; Chandu Lal, Khalid adds, had been "appointed as the Diwan of Lahore by the Mughal authorities" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227).

Lahore had drawn the Gurus before him. In Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis, Guru Nanak came to the city when Daulat Khan Lodhi governed it, and Duni Chand, the *amil*, the revenue collector, of Lahore, became his disciple and gave away his seven lakh rupees (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 124, folio 138; p. 134, folio 148). In Khalid's account Nanak and Mardana reached Lahore on their way home (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 163, folio 145). Later in the line, Guru Har Rai "along with his forces, reached Lahore" and met Dara Shikoh there after the prince's defeat by Aurangzeb (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 210–211, folios 184–185); Bhandari has the Guru leave Dara's camp at Lahore in the same way as others had slipped away (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 76).

Bhandari, writing under Aurangzeb, calls Lahore "شهریست بزرگ و مصریست سترگ", a great city and a mighty metropolis, where "درهر کوچه و بازار مساجد بسیار از بسیار است", there are mosques beyond counting in every lane and bazaar (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 524). Chishti counts "شہر لاہور کے بارہ دروازہ ہی[OCR?]", the twelve gates of the city of Lahore, the Delhi Gate, "دہلی دروازہ", among them (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498). Khalid writes that "The Roshani gate, one of the thirteen gateways that lead into the ancient walled city of Lahore, is between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated).

Ranjit Singh came to the city in 1799, Khalid writes, and "was greeted enthusiastically by a population sick of the lawlessness of that time"; he was crowned ruler of the Punjab in 1801 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal writes that "اس مہاراجہ نے چالیس سال تک پنجاب میں حکومت کی", the Maharaja ruled the Punjab for forty years (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 217, folio 220). Kharak Singh, the son whose birth the site's account ties to the gurdwara, followed him on the throne: "مہاراجہ رنجیت سنگہ کے مرنے کے بعد اُسکا حقیقی بیٹا مہاراجہ کہڑک سنگہ پنجاب کی حکومت کے تختہ پر بیٹھا", after Ranjit Singh's death his own son, Maharaja Kharak Singh, took the throne of the Punjab (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 221, folio 224). Chishti, too, has Kharak Singh sit on "کرسی حکومت پنجاب" at his father's death (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 586). The Sikh state ended with Dalip Singh, who, Chishti writes, left Lahore in December of a year printed as 1849, the reading uncertain and the day illegible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592).

## In Verse

None of the books consulted quotes the Guru's own hymns, the *Lavan* among them. Khalid notes that his poetry is in the *Guru Granth Sahib* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 317, folio 291), and Kanhaiya Lal records the verse that was sung at this gurdwara in his day, the *shabads* of the Gurus and the monotheist *kafis* of the *qawwals*, without quoting any of it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 102, folio 105).

The verse the books do carry speaks of the Punjab in the century before the Maharaja built here. It is given as context for the province, not as verse about the Guru or the site. Bulleh Shah, who died in 1758 (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 28, folio 8), lived through what Taufiq Rafat calls a time when "the Punjab was being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders"; "The full bitterness of Bulleh Shah's 'Punjab has gone to the dogs' will only come through against this backdrop" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 16, folio xvi). The lines, in Rafat's English, read:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 149, folio 129)

Christopher Shackle translates another lyric: *The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state.* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 52, folio 27). Shackle reads a verse in a third lyric as "Taken to be an allusion to the Sikhs, whose guerilla horsemen ultimately destroyed the Mughal authority in Panjab" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 193, folio 168).

Chishti's account of the end of the Sikh state carries a *qita* on Dalip Singh's departure from Lahore, which includes these lines:

چون شمع[OCR?] پنجاب از پنجاب رفت
نو گلی از گلشن پنجاب رفت

The lines are printed so in Chishti's book, the reading of one word uncertain; they are left untranslated here (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The bazaar.** The site's account places the gurdwara in Chuna Mandi. Kanhaiya Lal places it "بازار چوک متی[OCR?] کے جنوبی لین مین", in the southern lane of a bazaar whose name is uncertain in the printed text (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).
- **What stood on the spot.** The site's account says the Guru's childhood home survived on this spot until the era of the Sikh Empire. Kanhaiya Lal writes that his parents' residence was at this place, and that before the gurdwara was built "پہلے اس جگہ چہوٹا سا مکان تہا", there was a small house here; he does not say that it was the same house (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).
- **When the gurdwara was built, and at whose wish.** The site's account has Ranjit Singh build it at the request of Maharani Datar Kaur, during the celebrations for Kharak Singh's birth in 1801. Kanhaiya Lal sets the building "مہاراجہ رنجیت سنگہ کی اخیر عملداری مین", in the last years of the Maharaja's rule, when the Guru's Sikhs turned their attention to the spot, the work done by the Maharaja's order and finished within a year; he gives no year and does not name Datar Kaur (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).
- **How the land was obtained.** The site's account says the Maharaja acquired the surrounding plots. Kanhaiya Lal says that by his order the houses of Mohalla Saudagran adjoining the spot "لے گئے", were taken, and mentions no payment (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104).
- **Where the Guru grew up.** The site's account and Kanhaiya Lal have him born and reared at this place (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). Khalid has him raised by his grandmother after his parents' early death, and selling boiled grain as a child in the village of Basarke near Amritsar (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 272, folio 246).
- **His parents, and how he came to Amar Das.** The site's account calls him orphaned young, and Khalid writes that his parents died at a young age (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 272, folio 246). Kanhaiya Lal has his parents leave Lahore for Goindwal, where he was married to Amar Das's daughter (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 101, folio 104). Khalid has Amar Das first see him at Basarke, and Jetha follow the Guru to Khadur and then to Goindwal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 272–273, folio 246 / folio not stated).
- **His relation to Amar Das, in Chishti.** One of Chishti's lists styles him "خلف گورو امرداس[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 680); another calls him "گورو امر داس کا داماد", Amar Das's son-in-law (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 686). Bhandari and Khalid call him the son-in-law (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520; Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated).
- **How many sons.** Chishti gives the Guru and Bibi Bhani three sons (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498). Khalid speaks of the dispute "between the Guru's two sons, Prithi Ch[and] and Arjan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248).
- **Whose land Ramdaspur stood on.** The site's account has the Guru found the settlement. Khalid writes in one place that the town stood on land "gifted [to] his wife by the Mughal Emperor Akbar" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248), and in another that Akbar allotted the land to Bibi Bhani (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 292, folio 266); in a third, "Guru Ram Das had a jagir where he laid the foundation" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 254, folio not stated). Khalid also has Amar Das ask Ram Das to move to Ramdaspur on appointing him (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 291, folio 265), and elsewhere has Ram Das move to a small town that he had founded himself (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 274, folio 248).
- **The gates of the walled city.** Writing of the city, not of this site, Chishti counts twelve gates (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498), and *In Search of Shiva* calls Bhatti Gate "one of the twelve entry points" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated); *A White Trail* calls the Roshani Gate "one of the thirteen gateways" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated).

## Legacy

For the Sikh community, Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Ram Das is doubly precious: it marks the earthly beginning of the Guru who gave Sikhism its holiest city and its wedding liturgy, and it stands as a reminder that Lahore — for so long a great centre of Sikh power and devotion — was also his cradle. Amid the crowded bazaars of the Walled City, the shrine keeps alive the memory of a boy born here in 1534 whose life would reshape the faith and give the world Amritsar.

The Guru's image appears elsewhere too. Khalid finds his name among the figures on the frescoes of the dome at Jhaman (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 51, folio 33), and Chishti records him among the Gurus pictured in the niche of a *samadh* he describes (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 520). Khalid's *A White Trail* counts him among the "eclectic religious preachers" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 199, folio not stated), and *Walking with Nanak* gives the fourth Guru a chapter under his own name, "Guru Ram Das" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 11, folio not stated).
