Name: Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh
Events: Martyrdom commemoration (1 July)
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh, in the Naulakha bazaar quarter of the walled city of Lahore, marks one of the most harrowing and revered episodes in Sikh history: the martyrdom of *Bhai Taru Singh* (c. 1720–1745), the young cultivator who chose to have the skin of his scalp cut away rather than his sacred, uncut hair. His story stands at the heart of the eighteenth-century Sikh memory of persecution and steadfast faith, and the shrine that bears his name is a place of deep veneration for Sikhs across the world.

## The Life and Martyrdom of Bhai Taru Singh

Bhai Taru Singh was born around 1720 into a Sikh family of modest means and raised, after his father's early death, by his widowed mother alongside his sister, Bibi Tar Kaur. He took up farming at the village of Poola in the Kasur district of the Lahore region, growing crops and living simply. These were bitter years for the Sikhs of the Punjab: under the Mughal governor *Zakariya Khan*, a price was placed on Sikh heads and the community was driven into the forests and wastes, sustained by sympathisers in the villages. Bhai Taru Singh was one such sympathiser, quietly giving a share of his harvest to feed the Sikh bands who lived as fugitives.

He was denounced to the authorities — by tradition, betrayed by an informer — and arrested together with, in some accounts, his sister. Brought before Zakariya Khan at Lahore, he was offered the customary choice: embrace Islam, of which the outward sign would be the cutting of his *kesh* (the unshorn hair kept by observant Sikhs), or die. Bhai Taru Singh refused to cut his hair or renounce his faith. In an act of calculated cruelty, the governor is said to have ordered that his scalp be sliced from his skull with a blade, so that his hair could never be shorn nor grow again. This is believed to have taken place in the summer of 1745.

Sikh tradition relates that the martyr did not die at once, and that Zakariya Khan was soon afflicted by a torment of his own — an inability to pass water — that no physician could relieve. It was said he would find no ease until struck with the shoe of the man he had wronged; when Bhai Taru Singh's shoes were brought and struck against the governor's head, Zakariya Khan died in agony. Bhai Taru Singh, having outlived his persecutor, is said to have given up his life of his own will on 1 July 1745. His fortitude made him one of the great *shaheeds* (martyrs) of the Sikh Panth, remembered daily in the *Ardas*, the Sikh prayer that honours those who suffered for their faith.

## The Shrine

The gurdwara at Naulakha marks the place associated with his martyrdom, in the vicinity of the celebrated *Shahidganj* — the "treasury of martyrs" — where, through the eighteenth century, many Sikhs were put to death. The site has long been a focus of devotion and, in the colonial period, of legal and communal contest over its custody. Today the shrine preserves the memory of Bhai Taru Singh's sacrifice, and Sikh pilgrims visiting Lahore make their way to it to pay homage.

## Legacy

The martyrdom of Bhai Taru Singh has become one of the defining stories of Sikh identity — a parable of the *kesh* held dearer than life itself, and of faith unbroken by torture. His image, the young farmer whose scalp was taken rather than his principles, is invoked in sermon, art, and remembrance wherever Sikhs gather. The gurdwara in Lahore, standing on the soil where he suffered, is both a memorial to one man's courage and a monument to the endurance of a community through its darkest years.

Name: Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian
Sufi Saint: Sikh women & children martyrs (18th century, Mir Mannu era)
Events: Martyrdom commemoration; pilgrim visits
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian, in the Naulakha Bazaar quarter of the walled city of Lahore, is among the most solemn of Sikh memorials in Pakistan. Its name — *Shahid Ganj*, "treasury of martyrs", and *Singhnian*, "of the Sikh women" — commemorates the many Sikhs, and above all the women and children, who were tortured and killed here during the great persecutions of the mid-eighteenth century. It stands within the cluster of martyrdom sites at Naulakha, close to the shrine of Bhai Taru Singh, that together mark one of the darkest chapters of Sikh history.

None of the books consulted uses the full name with *Singhnian*. Two of them write of a place called Shahid Ganj outside Delhi Gate, and it is on the name, the place and the account of the killings that their passages are read here as concerning this gurdwara. Haroon Khalid's travelogue *Walking with Nanak* gives a long history of a "Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj" in Naulakha Bazaar, told to him by the historian Iqbal Qaiser in his own words, from a small mosque to a court battle lasting generations and a rebuilding finished in 2004 (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 76–77, folios 58–59; p. 78, folio 60). The name in his book lacks the word *Singhnian* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's nineteenth-century survey of Lahore, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, describes a mosque used by the Sikhs outside Delhi Gate and a Sikh *samadh*, each called Shahid Ganj, and sets the tomb of Mir Mannu in the same quarter (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121; p. 122). A third book, Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, has an entry under the same name for a quite different kind of place, a burial ground of Muslim martyrs, which nothing in the book ties to this gurdwara (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 264, folio 252).

## Mir Mannu and the Persecution

After the Mughal–Afghan struggles of the 1740s, *Muin-ul-Mulk* — the governor of Lahore from 1748, known to the Sikhs as *Mir Mannu* — set himself to the extermination of the Sikh community. Mobile columns hunted the Sikhs who had taken refuge in the forests and wastes, and captives were brought in numbers to Lahore. The men, refusing conversion, were put to death; the women and children were consigned to a prison where they were set to grinding heavy quotas of grain by hand, starved and brutalised. Sikh tradition preserves the memory of mothers made to watch the killing of their children, and of their steadfast refusal to abandon their faith in exchange for their lives. The traditional accounts speak of enormous numbers of dead; while such figures are impossible to verify and are best understood as expressions of collective memory, the historical reality of a sustained and savage persecution under Mir Mannu is well attested.

Iqbal Qaiser, telling Khalid the story, names the same governor: "Thousands of them, men, women and children alike were slaughtered and thrown into a well here on the orders of the Governor of Lahore, Moin-ul-Mulk also known as Meer Manu" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59). He adds that a room was built there to hold prisoners before their execution (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59).

Chishti, writing of the Shahid Ganj quarter, records that "علاقہ شہید گنج" holds the tomb of Mir Mannu, and that in his time there was a general order to seize and kill the Sikhs (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121). On the same page he places Mir Mannu's rule in the reign of the emperor Muhammad Shah: "بعہد محمد شاہ یہہ نواب لاہور مین حاکم تہا", in Muhammad Shah's time this nawab was ruler in Lahore; the order came, he explains, because the Sikhs had grown in number (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121). He knew a Panjabi saying about the governor, but its words are illegible in the printed text beyond its opening, "میر منو ساڈی[OCR?] [illegible] اسی[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121).

## The Martyrdom of the Singhnian

It is the constancy of the women — the *Singhnis* — that gives this gurdwara its name and its particular sanctity. In the retelling that every Sikh child learns, the women endured imprisonment, forced labour and the murder of their infants without renouncing the *Khalsa*, and their courage transformed a place of suffering into a place of honour. The site came to be venerated as a *shahid ganj*, and after the consolidation of Sikh power in the later eighteenth century a gurdwara was raised to enshrine the memory of the martyrs.

The ground itself, in Qaiser's telling, still held the dead. When the gurdwara was being rebuilt, "skeletons of children and adults would emerge", and Qaiser identifies them as the Sikhs killed on Meer Manu's orders (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60).

Chishti gives the naming of a Shahid Ganj in his own terms. He describes "ایک مکان کلاں سمادہ[OCR?] سکھو[OCR?] کی", a large building, a *samadh* of the Sikhs, raised because a governor whom the printed text names "میر[OCR?] مسعود[OCR?]", and calls "قاتل[OCR?] قوم سکہو[OCR?]", the killer of the Sikh people, had put Sikhs to death on that spot; and, he writes, "نام اس سمادہ[OCR?] کا شہید گنج رکہا", the *samadh* was given the name Shahid Ganj (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122). The reading of the governor's name is uncertain in the printed text.

## The Gurdwara and its Memory

The Naulakha martyrdom sites became, in the colonial and post-colonial periods, focal points of Sikh commemoration and, at times, of communal contest over ownership. The Shaheed Ganj Singhnian is maintained today under the Evacuee Trust Property Board and is visited by Sikh pilgrims to Lahore, who come to pay homage alongside the neighbouring shrine of Bhai Taru Singh. The gurdwara's austerity is fitting: it is less an architectural showpiece than a site of remembrance, where the recitation of the *Guru Granth Sahib* and the ardas (prayer) keep alive the names and the example of those who died.

## The Place and the Mosque

Qaiser first told Khalid the story "when we drove around the railway station" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58). He is emphatic about where it lies: "No, this is not the walled city of Lahore. This [is] outside Delhi gate. This area is known as Naulakha Bazaar" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58; p. 77, folio 59). Prince Dara Shikoh, he says, had his Naulakha palace there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58; p. 77, folio 59).

Qaiser describes the quarrel over the site as "an old issue that started about two centuries" before his telling, the last word of the phrase damaged in the printed text (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 76–77, folios 58–59). On a vacant plot there stood "a small mosque" from which "the Qazi would announce punishment to criminals"; "The mosque was small and was never used as a place of worship" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 76–77, folios 58–59). Under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, he says, the Sikhs "placed the Guru Granth Sahib inside it, converting it into a gurdwara. The Muslims could not do anything then" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 76–77, folios 58–59).

Chishti's survey describes a similar arrangement in his own day. Near "سرائی میاں محمد سلطان[OCR?]" outside Delhi Gate, he writes, stood two mosques; the Sikhs used one of them, the *Granth* ("گرنتھ[OCR?]") was read there, and the place was known by the name Shahid Ganj: "اس [illegible] نام شہید گنج[OCR?] مشہور[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122).

## The Courts and the Riots

The dispute that Qaiser recounts ran on from British rule into Pakistan's. In the British period, he says, the Muslims applied to the courts for the building's return. "The Lahore High Court" asked for a living witness who had seen it used as a mosque, found none, and "decided in favour of the Sikhs"; the Sikhs then razed the building, and there followed "rioting between Muslims and Sikhs", which Qaiser lays at the door of the British policy of divide and rule (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59). Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Allama Iqbal, he says, became involved, and he has seen a photograph of Jinnah addressing a crowd "at the Badshahi Mosque at the time of this riot"; in the end "the gurdwara remained a gurdwara" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59).

After Partition, with the creation of the Auqaf Department, the question came back to the Lahore High Court, which ruled, "Around 1957-58", that the building "would remain a gurdwara" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59; p. 78, folio 60). In the late 1980s petitioners sought a review "again"; the judge said he would convert the site if they could produce "even one person who had prayed at the mosque", and none was produced (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60).

## The Rebuilding of 2004

"In about 1994-95, the Kar Sewa Committee of England" sought permission to renovate the gurdwara, and the government agreed (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60). Avtar Singh Panghedha asked Qaiser to supervise the construction, and, Qaiser says, "all the money, the contracts ... went through me" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60). When the newspapers reported the work, "the Muslims tried once again to create an issue" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60).

The opposition was turned, in Qaiser's account, by an ironsmith named Rana, who persuaded the local traders that the gurdwara "would attract foreign pilgrims"; the traders of Naulakha Bazaar became stakeholders in the project, and "this gurdwara was eventually constructed in 2004" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60). It was during this construction that the skeletons of children and adults came to light (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 78, folio 60).

## Devotion and Practice

In the site's account, the recitation of the *Guru Granth Sahib* and the ardas keep the martyrs' memory alive at the gurdwara. Chishti, describing the Shahid Ganj of his day, records that the *Granth* was read there and that "بہنگ[OCR?] بکثرت خرچ ہوتی ہی", bhang was consumed in quantity; and he adds that formerly, "بعہد مہاراجہ صاحب", in the Maharaja's time, the place had been a "فیض عام", a source of open bounty to all (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 123).

Khalid's book offers a general frame for that earlier patronage, said of the province and not of this site: "When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras", and "attached vast tracts of land to these gurdwaras, so that the revenues from the lands could facilitate their functioning" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 34, folio 16).

## Another Shahid Ganj

Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, a tazkira of the saints of the Punjab completed in 1875, has an entry headed "مزار شہید گنج". It describes a mass grave of Muslim martyrs of the Ghaznavid period at "محلہ سادھواں", and its table of contents lists it, as entry 211, among the Punjab elders whose dates of death are not established (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 264, folio 252; p. 20, folio 8). The entry names no landmark beyond the mohalla, and whether this Shahid Ganj and the Sikh one at Naulakha are the same place cannot be settled from the book; it is noted here only because the two share a name.

Lahori's entry draws its history from the *Tuhfat al-Wasilin*: "جب سلطنت سلاطین غزنویہ کی پنجاب میں ہوگئی اور لاہور دار الحکومت قرار پایا", when the Ghaznavid sultans' rule was established in the Punjab and Lahore became its capital, it held for a long time, until strife among the Ghaznavids in the time of Shah Bahram left the government of the Punjab weak; Raja Anangpal then took Lahore, and there was Hindu rule until an army returned from Ghazni (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 264, folio 252). In a note on another entry, the modern editor of the *Hadiqat* calls that source "تحفۃ الواصلین ایک وضعی تذکرہ", a fabricated tazkira (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–192, folios 179–180).

## Setting: Lahore and the Punjab in Mir Mannu's Time

The books say a good deal about the governor and his years in general terms; none of what follows is said of this site. Lahori's modern editor dates the first assault of Ahmad Shah Abdali on the city: "احمد شاہ ابدالی کا لاہور پر پہلا حملہ (۱۱۶۱ھ) ۱۷۴۸ء کو ہوا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 214, folio 202). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* tells how Jani Khan, with his brother Mir Muin al-Mulk, defeated Ahmad Shah Durrani, who went back to Kabul, and how "اسکے جانے کے بعد پنجاب کا انتظام میر معین الملک نے اپنے طور پر کیا", after his going Mir Muin al-Mulk ran the Punjab in his own way (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 270, folio 273).

Khalid's *In Search of Shiva* gives a modern reading of the governor's war. "Moin-ul-Mulk, popularly known as Meer Manu" "was the governor of Punjab" and was "constantly pestered by the Sikh insurgent groups Misl, which had sprung up all over Punjab"; "The Sikh groups did not control much land but because of their anti-status quo politics the lower rungs of the society supported and protected them" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated). Meer Manu, Khalid argues, "cast the battle between the state and insurgents as a war between Muslims and Sikhs, even though there were several Muslims in the Sikh groups and many non-Muslim soldiers in the army of Meer Manu" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated). He writes that Abdali had "agreed an annual tax stipulation which the governor was responsible of paying to him, for the right of governing Punjab", and that "Before Ahmad Shah could reach Lahore, the prize possession of Punjab, Meer Manu met him at a place near the city of Gujrat"; on a later raid, which he dates as "the 1751 attack by Ahmad Shah Abdali", the Afghan bypassed the governor and laid siege to the city: "For months the citizens were trapped within the walls of their city" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated).

Chishti records what came after the governor's death: "جہان کسی سکہہ[OCR?] نے موقع پایا حاکم ہو بیٹہا", wherever a Sikh found the chance, he set himself up as ruler (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 719). The upheaval left its mark on the Muslim scholars of the province too: Lahori's editor writes of Ghulam Murtaza Qasuri that "آپ نے پنجاب میں سکھ گردی سے تنگ آکر پشاور ہجرت فرمائی", that, worn down by the Sikh disorders in the Punjab, he migrated to Peshawar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 152, folio 140).

Khaled Ahmad's introduction to Taufiq Rafat's translations of Bulleh Shah sketches the same decades from the side of the Punjab's peasantry: "Marauding Sikh bands formed themselves into robber baronies and imposed their own system of extortion on the Punjab farmer", and Abdali's "treatment of the Punjab weakened the government in Lahore and delivered the various doabs into the hands of the Sikh" confederacy (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 27, folio 7). "As Bulleh Shah lay dying in 1758 at the age of 78, the rape of the Punjab was proceeding apace" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 28, folio 8). In a passage that runs from Banda Bairagi through Abdul Samad Khan, Zakriya Khan and Nadir Shah, the same introduction names 'Shahidganj in 1746'; the passage as quoted does not say which Shahid Ganj is meant or what happened there (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, pp. 42–43, folios 22–23).

Bulleh Shah, who died in 1758, left verses on the state of the province that his translators read as a witness to the times. In Christopher Shackle's translation, one *kafi* speaks of 'The twelfth century' that 'has come with gaping mouth' (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 52, folio 27), the twelfth century of the Hijri era, which Shackle's note equates with the eighteenth century C.E. (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 165–166, folios 140–141). It goes on:

*"The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell."* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 52, folio 27)

And in Taufiq Rafat's:

*"Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell." … "This century cramps our style."* (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 149, folio 129)

Rafat's translator's note explains its force: "The full bitterness of Bulleh Shah's 'Punjab has gone to the dogs' will only come through against this backdrop", a Punjab "being persistently rent by petty chiefs and marauders" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 16, folio xvi). Shackle notes another of the poet's verses as "Taken to be an allusion to the Sikhs, whose guerilla horsemen ultimately destroyed the Mughal authority in Panjab" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 193, folio 168).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where the gurdwara stands.** The site's account places it in the Naulakha Bazaar quarter of the walled city of Lahore. Qaiser says "this is not the walled city of Lahore" but outside Delhi Gate, in the area known as Naulakha Bazaar (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58; p. 77, folio 59); Chishti places his Shahid Ganj outside Delhi Gate, near a sarai whose name is uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122).
- **The name.** The site's name is Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian, and its bibliography gives Shahid Ganj Singhnian. Khalid writes "Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59), and Chishti only Shahid Ganj (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122). Lahori uses the same name for a mass grave of Muslim martyrs of the Ghaznavid period, which may or may not be the same place (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 264, folio 252; p. 20, folio 8).
- **How the gurdwara began.** The site's account says a gurdwara was raised after the consolidation of Sikh power in the later eighteenth century to enshrine the memory of the martyrs. Qaiser says the building was a small mosque, never used for worship, into which the Sikhs placed the *Guru Granth Sahib* under Maharaja Ranjit Singh (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 76–77, folios 58–59). Chishti describes two mosques, one used by the Sikhs for reading the *Granth*, and separately a large Sikh *samadh* built where Sikhs had been killed and given the name Shahid Ganj (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122).
- **Who ordered the killings.** The site's account names *Muin-ul-Mulk*, known as *Mir Mannu*; Qaiser names "Moin-ul-Mulk also known as Meer Manu" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59); Kanhaiya Lal writes Mir Muin al-Mulk (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 270, folio 273). Chishti names Mir Mannu for the general order against the Sikhs and for the tomb in the Shahid Ganj quarter (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121), but in his account of the *samadh* the killer's name is printed as Mir Masud, the reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 122).
- **What was done there.** The site's account has the men put to death and the women and children imprisoned and set to grind grain. Qaiser has men, women and children alike slaughtered and thrown into a well, and a room built to hold prisoners before execution (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59).
- **When.** The site's account sets the persecution under Mir Mannu, governor from 1748. Khaled Ahmad's introduction names 'Shahidganj in 1746', without saying which Shahid Ganj is meant (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, pp. 42–43, folios 22–23). Chishti places Mir Mannu's rule in the reign of Muhammad Shah (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 121).
- **The building today.** The site's account calls the gurdwara austere, less an architectural showpiece than a site of remembrance. Qaiser says the old building was razed in the British period and the present gurdwara constructed in 2004 with the backing of the Kar Sewa Committee of England (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 77, folio 59; p. 78, folio 60).

## Legacy

In Sikh historical consciousness the martyrdoms at Lahore under Mir Mannu occupy a place beside the sacrifices of the Gurus themselves, invoked daily in the ardas that recalls "the Singhs and Singhnis who gave their heads but did not surrender their faith". Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Singh Singhnian is the physical anchor of that memory in the city where it happened. For the study of eighteenth-century Punjab it testifies to the ferocity of the state's campaign against the early Khalsa; for the Sikh community it remains sacred ground.

The rebuilding had consequences beyond Naulakha. Afterwards, Khalid writes, "the Government of Pakistan woke up to the potential of Sikh pilgrimage tourism" and invited the Sikh community abroad "to invest in the renovation of any Sikh gurdwara in the country" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 79, folio 61). The long quarrel also became a byword: at a place the book calls Sachkand, Khalid and Qaiser name it as the outcome to be feared: "we could have a situation similar to Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj here?" — "Precisely." (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58).

## Bibliography

- Hari Ram Gupta, *History of the Sikhs*, vol. II: *Evolution of Sikh Confederacies* (Munshiram Manoharlal).
- Khushwant Singh, *A History of the Sikhs*, vol. I (Oxford University Press).
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998).
- Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee and SikhiWiki, entries on Gurdwara Shahid Ganj Singhnian, Lahore.
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).
- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Persian, composed 1292 AH / 1875 CE; read in an Urdu edition annotated by محمد اقبال مجددی and issued by تصوّف فاؤنڈیشن).
- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).
- Taufiq Rafat (tr.), *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, with an introduction by Khaled Ahmad (Lahore: Vanguard Publications Ltd., 1982).

Description:
## Overview

The Gurdwara Singh Sabha in Quetta is the principal Sikh place of worship in the capital of Balochistan, serving a small community whose roots in the province run deep. Restored to the Sikhs only in 2020 after more than seven decades of other use, the *gurdwara* has become an emblem both of the long Sikh presence in Balochistan and of the community's patient struggle to recover its sacred places. It takes its name from the *Singh Sabha*, the reformist movement that shaped modern Sikh congregational life across the subcontinent.

## Sikhs in Balochistan

Sikhs have lived in Balochistan for a very long time — by some accounts for around three centuries — settling as traders and shopkeepers in Quetta and the towns of the province. Their numbers were once substantial: the census of 1941 recorded some twelve thousand Sikhs in the Baluchistan Agency, a little over one per cent of the population, with the largest concentration in the Quetta–Pishin district. The community's long roots were violently disrupted at the Partition of 1947, when, like the local Hindus, the Sikhs were attacked and largely forced to flee eastward, and their properties and places of worship passed into the charge of the Evacuee Trust Property Board. A tradition of the city, attached to the nearby Gurdwara Tilganji Sahib, even holds that Guru Nanak himself passed through Quetta during his travels, though such associations are matters of devotional memory rather than documented history.

## From Gurdwara to Girls' School

The Gurdwara Singh Sabha is said to be around two centuries old, dating to the early nineteenth century. After the departure of the Sikhs in 1947, the building was put to secular use, serving for decades as a government girls' high school run under the auspices of the All Pakistan Women's Association. For the Sikhs who remained or who later returned to Quetta, the *gurdwara* stood as a visible reminder of a heritage from which they had been separated, and its recovery became a long-cherished aim of the community.

## Restoration in 2020

After more than seventy years, the building was at last restored to the Sikh community in 2020, an event widely reported and warmly welcomed as the fulfilment of a decades-long wait. The return of the *gurdwara* allowed the *sangat*, the congregation, once more to install the *Guru Granth Sahib* and to hold worship in a historic house of the Gurus in the heart of Quetta. The restoration was seen as part of a broader, if halting, effort to return and rehabilitate Sikh and Hindu shrines across Pakistan.

## Legacy

For the roughly two thousand Sikh families of Balochistan, the Gurdwara Singh Sabha is more than a building: it is the recovered centre of their communal and religious life in the province, and a symbol of continuity across the rupture of Partition. Its restoration has affirmed the place of the Sikhs in the story of Quetta and offered a measure of hope to a minority community intent on preserving its faith and its heritage in the land where it has so long belonged.

## Bibliography

- *Bolan Voice*, "Historical background of the Sikh community in Balochistan province".
- World Gurudwaras, entry on Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, Quetta.
- Wikipedia, "Sikhism in Pakistan" (with cited sources).

Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Sri Kiara Sahib stands amid the fields on the eastern side of Nankana Sahib, the town in the Punjab that was the birthplace of *Guru Nanak Dev Ji*, founder of the Sikh faith. Its name comes from the Punjabi *kiara*, meaning a field or plot of cultivated ground, for the gurdwara marks the very field where one of the best-loved miracles of Guru Nanak's boyhood is remembered to have taken place. Set a little apart from the great shrines at the centre of the town, Kiara Sahib belongs to the intimate landscape of sites in and around Nankana Sahib that together preserve the memory of the Guru's early years.

Two of the books consulted name the gurdwara, both of them by Haroon Khalid. In his travelogue *Walking with Nanak*, where the name is spelt Kiari Sahib, the gurdwara is "said to mark the spot where Guru Nanak's buffaloes spoilt the fields of a local farmer who is reported to have complained to Nanak's father" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). In *A White Trail*, his book on Pakistan's religious minorities, "Gurdwara Kiara Sahib" at Nankana Sahib is the place "where his cattle destroyed the fields of a farmer while he slept" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). That is all the books say of this gurdwara itself. The others name no gurdwara at Nankana Sahib: Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's history names the town only as "the village of Talwandi later known as Nankana Sahib, about forty miles south-west of Lahore, now part of Pakistan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 407, folio 383); Harish Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis speaks of "Nanakana Sahib (earlier called Talwandi)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 175); and Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, of the town, records only that Baba Nanak was born at Talwandi Rai Bhoi and lived there in his grandfather's house (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). What these books say of the Guru's boyhood, of Talwandi and of the modern town is gathered below as context: it is said of the Guru and of the place, not of this gurdwara.

## The Miracle of the Field

The tradition attached to Kiara Sahib belongs to the cycle of *sakhis*, the accounts of Guru Nanak's life, that centre on his childhood at what was then the village of Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, later renamed Nankana Sahib in his honour. As a boy, Nanak was set to tend the family's cattle, and — as the stories tell — he would let the animals graze while he himself sat absorbed in meditation, heedless of the world about him. On one such day the buffaloes are said to have strayed into a neighbour's standing crop, and the aggrieved peasant hurried to *Rai Bular Bhatti*, the local landlord, to complain that young Nanak's herd had ruined his field.

When the field was inspected, however, the crop was found whole and unharmed, as though nothing had touched it. The onlookers took this for a miracle, and the plot was thereafter revered as *Kiara Sahib*, "the honoured field." For the Sikh tradition the episode is one of a series of signs by which Rai Bular, a Muslim landlord, came to recognise the extraordinary nature of the child in his village, and it is remembered less as a marvel of crops than as an early disclosure of the Guru's sanctity and of the divine favour that rested upon him.

Khalid's two books tell the story more briefly, and differently. In *Walking with Nanak* it is the buffaloes that "spoilt the fields of a local farmer", and the farmer is "reported to have complained to Nanak's father" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). In *A White Trail* the animals are cattle, they "destroyed the fields of a farmer", and the boy was asleep (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). Neither book says what was found when the field was inspected, and neither names the farmer.

The herding itself is told in the other retellings of the Guru's youth, though none of them ties it to this field. In Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis, at sixteen the boy herded cattle (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 23, folio 27). In *Walking with Nanak* Khalid also retells Nanak's youth as a novel, a part of the book he himself calls fictionalised (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 17, folio not stated); there Mehta Kalu calls the family "Bedis ... the ancient orators of the Vedas" and himself "an accountant", and the boy herds buffaloes, which once enter a field belonging to "Raj Kumar" [OCR?] (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 63, folio 45; p. 64, folio 46). In the same pages the boy is found hiding in a grove of *waan* trees outside the town by his father and "his employer and friend, Rai Bular" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 64, folio 46). Of this reconstruction Khalid writes that "my depiction of Nanak in this book is not an accurate version of Nanak" but what he wants Nanak "to be like" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 229–230, folio not stated / folio 204).

That the boy showed signs of sanctity is an old claim. Bhandari, writing in Persian under Aurangzeb, records that in his childhood signs of spiritual unveiling and of wonders appeared in him: "درخورد سالگی(۱) علامات کشف و کرامات و ایات خارق عادات از و بمنصه ظهور رسید"; the editor of the printed text gives the variant "ده سالگی", at the age of ten (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). In Dhillon's retelling, the village astrologer, Pandit Hardyal, foretold the child's greatness (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 18, folio 20), and at school the boy showed "a brilliance that had never before been seen in any child in Talwandi" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 18, folio 20).

## Rai Bular and the Village

The landlord of the story belongs to the family that rebuilt the village. Dhillon writes that Talwandi's last rebuilding "took place under the supervision of Rai Bhoe", a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 15–16, folios 17–18), and that Rai Bhoe's son was Rai Bular; Shiv Ram, head of a Bedi family, was accountant to Rai Bhoe and was succeeded by his son Kalyan Chand Das Bedi (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 17, folio 19), "or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called", the Guru's father, accountant of the Bhatti family under Rai Bular (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 17–18, folios 19–20). In Khalid's reconstruction Mehta Kalu keeps "the accounts of the ruler of Talwindi, Rai Bular Bhatti", his friend (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 22, folio 4), and is a Hindu of the 'warrior caste' (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 29, folio 11).

Dhillon's retelling returns to the family later. When Nanak and Mardana came back to Talwandi from the first of his journeys, Nanak spent time daily with Rai Bhoe, who "looked upon" him "as his Guru", and Mehta Kalu was "a little in awe of his son" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 123, folio 137; p. 124, folio 138). Later, after Pak Pattan, "Nanak travelled back to Talwandi"; the village "was now no longer an obscure little village but had become a place of pilgrimage", and Nanak sat by Rai Bular, who was sick and dying (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 172, folio 188).

## The Gurdwara

A shrine was raised in later times to mark the sacred field, and the present building is associated with the great works of gurdwara construction carried out in the decades before Partition. It was reconstructed by *Sant Gurmukh Singh* — remembered by the epithet *Sevavale*, "the one devoted to service," for his lifelong labour of building and restoring Sikh shrines — in the years leading up to 1947. The gurdwara comprises a square, domed sanctum set upon a raised plinth, with a circumambulatory verandah about it, in the characteristic idiom of Punjabi gurdwara architecture, and it stands amid open ground that still recalls the agricultural setting of the original miracle.

None of the books consulted describes the building, dates it or names its builder. Khalid places it. Of "a total of six gurdwaras associated with Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72), he puts Kiari Sahib with Malji Sahib as "the furthest from Gurdwara Janamsthan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). Writing of Rai Bhoi di Talwindi, "which later became Nankana Sahib", he says that it is the place "where there are several gurdwaras marking events from his childhood" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25).

Since the Partition of 1947, when the Sikh population of west Punjab migrated to India, Kiara Sahib — like the other shrines of Nankana Sahib — has stood in a land with few resident worshippers, cared for by the bodies responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan and visited chiefly by pilgrims who cross the border on the great anniversaries. On the *Gurpurab* marking Guru Nanak's birth, and on other occasions when *jathas* of pilgrims travel to Nankana Sahib, the gurdwara receives the devotions of the faithful who come to walk the ground of the Guru's childhood.

Elsewhere Khalid's books describe the gurdwaras of the town as a group. "There are seven Gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib, most of which are associated with incidents from the life of Baba Guru Nanak" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 192, folio not stated). "All year round most of them remain locked, only to be opened at the time of the festival. There are security guards employed at the entrance to all of them." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 227, folio not stated). The name of the Kar Seva is on yellow dustbins and other boards "placed in different Gurdwaras of the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). Kartar, one of Khalid's informants, remembered the years after Partition: "There was no Sikh left here after partition. Our Gurdwaras became barren and were in a bad state" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated). Giani Pratap, who in Kartar's account came with an Indian pilgrimage party "sometime in the sixties" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated), "After looking at the dilapidated condition of the shrines here he decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. That was the first time someone had taken the initiative to take care of the gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib after Partition" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72).

Of the province, Khalid writes that "When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras", and "attached vast tracts of land to these gurdwaras, so that the revenues from the lands could facilitate their functioning" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 34, folio 16); in *A White Trail* he says that Ranjit Singh renovated "many Gurdwaras all over Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 208, folio not stated). Of the years after 1947 he writes, of the country as a whole, "I have seen several gurdwaras and temples being taken over and destroyed by the migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

## Devotion and Practice

Khalid names Kiara Sahib in his chapter on Guru Nanak's birthday at Nankana Sahib, in a passage on the town's gurdwaras. "Originally called Rai-Bhoi-Di-Talwandi, this city was rechristened Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak"; because Nanak spent his early years here there are "several Gurdwaras in the city", all of which the pilgrims visit (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). The festival, which he also calls "Guru Nanak Jayanti or Gurpurab", is large: "According to official estimates, ten to fifteen thousand people come to Nankana Sahib for this festival every year, which is celebrated during the last days of November"; in 2011, "According to media reports, only three thousand people are attending", and "This year it began on the 8th of November and will conclude today, on the 10th of November" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).

The pilgrims from India, by Khalid's account, come by train from Delhi, Gujarat and Amritsar, cross at Wagah, where representatives of the Evacuee Trust Property Board and the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee receive them and a *langar* is laid on, and stay three days at Nankana (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 222–223, folio not stated). Three days of *Akhand Path* end in the *bhog*, and the *Nagar Kirtan* follows on the final day; the pilgrims then go on to other cities, richer pilgrims from Britain, America and Canada come by chartered plane and hire buses, and travel companies' posters promise "all" the gurdwaras in Pakistan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). Devotees walk barefoot (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 221–222, folio not stated), and there is "a heavy presence of police officials at all the entrances to the city. No car is permitted inside" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated). "The entire city looks like a mini-India during these few days" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 226, folio not stated).

The pilgrims come from abroad above all. Khalid counts "Guru Nanak's birthday at Nankana Sahib" among the events that foreign pilgrims kept alive after Partition (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 176, folio not stated), and Sikhs from abroad come to Pakistan for festivals "like Baisakhi and the birthday of Guru Nanak, which were attended by thousands of Indian pilgrims" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 214, folio not stated). Pilgrim tourists "come to Nankana Sahib and Hassan Abdal" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 79, folio 61). At Manora in Karachi, Jeeta Singh holds a small festival "every November when the festival of Guru Nanak is celebrated at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 228, folio 202).

The Sikhs who live in the town today are mostly newcomers. Khalid writes that they "are not indigenous people from the city, but recent migrants from Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) where there is a considerable Sikh population" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 235, folio not stated), and that "Most of the newcomers were incorporated within the Gurdwaras, in rooms which were generally reserved for pilgrims" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 176, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* "the Sikh community in Nankana Sahib, which amounts to about two hundred-odd households", has had Jatha Singh as its leader for several years (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69).

## Setting: Nankana Sahib

Talwandi, in Dhillon's retelling, was "the village of Talwandi, which lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi"; "Thirteen times was the village of Talwandi destroyed and thirteen times - like the fabled phoenix - it rose again from its ashes" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 15–16, folios 17–18). It "lay in the path of numerous mendicants, sadhus and holy men", who camped "in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 24, folio 28). Writing of the province in Nanak's century, Rizvi says that "In the fifteenth century, the Panjab enjoyed a peaceful period due to Afghan rule", the Afghans resettling the land and "founding many new towns and promoting trade and commerce" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 408, folio 384).

"The name of Rai Bhoi di Talwindi has been changed to Nankana Sahib in honour of the first Sikh Guru who was born there" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 31, folio 13). The mound of the old settlement "now rests" behind Gurdwara Janamsthan, "away from the hub of the new settlement" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). Iqbal Qaiser, Khalid's guide, told him that it "is an archaeological mound. The settlement there was destroyed after which Rai Bhoi di Talwindi was constructed within a boundary wall" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). It is a steep climb "with no proper path", "at least twenty metres from the ground", covered with shrubs of *karir*, with "shards of broken pottery and other mud utensils" underfoot (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 92, folio 74). A young Nanak, Khalid writes, "used to spend a lot of time in conversation with yogis, sadhus and dervish who would pass through Talwindi" there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). His route "back from Chuhrkhana to Nankana Sahib, which at that point in time was still known as Rai Bhoi di Talwindi", crossed "a vast jungle that existed then between Nankana and Chuhrkhana" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 86, folio 68).

The modern town, as Khalid saw it, has "one main road that runs through the entire city"; "The entire city needs a major uplift. The buildings are old and the road has pot holes"; "Most of the buildings are from the late British or the early Pakistan era" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 186, folio not stated). From a roof he saw the minarets of mosques, the "small white domes of the Gurdwaras", and the "remains of a few Hindu temples", "cone like structures rising from houses abandoned at the time of partition" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 225, folio not stated). "In 2005, Nankana Sahib was separated from Sheikhupura and made into an independent district, with this city becoming the district headquarters" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 226, folio not stated). It is "a city considered to be one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, as the founder of their religion, Nanak, was born here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 183, folio not stated). "Guru Nanak is celebrated all over Nankana Sahib. There is a Guru Nanak High School, a Guru Nanak grocery store and a Guru Nanak cloth shop, all run by Sikhs" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 172, folio not stated).

Khalid found the town's Muslims less warm to the Guru than those he met elsewhere. The regard for Nanak among Muslims at Gurdwara Sachkand, he writes, is not found among the Muslims of Nankana Sahib; Iqbal Qaiser explained that most of them migrated from the other side of the border after Partition, their attitudes "shaped by those experiences" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 76, folio 58). In a third book Khalid notes "a picture of Baba Farid accompanying the picture of Guru Nanak at the shrine of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib", without saying which of the town's gurdwaras he means (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

## Guru Nanak in the Wider Record

What the books say of Guru Nanak himself is said of the Guru, not of this site; it is gathered here because the gurdwara exists for his sake. Dhillon calls the Janamsakhis "cycles of tales purportedly drawn from the life of the first Guru of the Sikhs" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 9, folio 9), and the back cover of his book notes that "The earliest known janamsakhi" dates to 1658, nearly 120 years after the Guru's death (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 271, folio not stated). Khalid calls them "Sikh texts on Nanak's life, written by his devotees after his death", "the primary sources", in "different versions" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 17, folio not stated).

Dhillon has him born "On 14 April 1469" to Kalyan Chand Das Bedi (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 17–18, folios 19–20); the back matter of *Walking with Nanak* gives "Born Talwandi (now known as Nankana Sahib in Pakistan) on October 20, 1469" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 314, folio 288). Bhandari, introducing it with "گویند" (it is said), dates the birth "درسنه هزار و پانصد و بست و شش بکرماجیت مطابق هشتصد و هشتاد هجری درزمان سلطان بهلول لودی": in Samvat 1526, corresponding to 880 Hijri, in the reign of Sultan Bahlul Lodi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Khalid writes that the Janamsakhi writer Meherban "claims that Guru Nanak was born in Dera Chahal and not Rai Bhoi di Talwindi", while other Janamsakhi writers and Sikh scholars "are unanimous that Nanak was born in Rai Bhoi di Talwindi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25). Two stories of the birth point beyond the Sikh tradition. Citing Dhillon's *The First Sikh Spiritual Master*, Khalid writes that Mata Tripta "would regularly visit an ancient Hindu temple situated on top of a mound not very far from Rai Bhoi di Talwindi to pray for a child" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 30–31, folio 13), and a booklet of the Auqaf department states that "Guru Nanak was born after Baba Naulakha Hazari prayed for his mother" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 31, folio 13). Iqbal Qaiser told him: "The Sikhs don't accept it but the Muslim tradition is that Guru Nanak was born by the blessing of Baba Naulakh Hazari." (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated).

The years of the boyhood are the years of the field. In Dhillon's retelling, at thirteen Nanak refused the sacred thread, the *janeu*, in his father's courtyard, saying that "it is our actions and our actions alone" that give a man his position; Dhillon calls it "the beginning of a lifelong crusade against the performing of empty rites and rituals" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 19–21, folios 21–23). At sixteen he herded cattle (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 23, folio 27), and he "became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 24, folio 28). In Khalid's reconstruction the boy sits at dusk under a *waan* tree hung with cloths "tied as supplication", "about two furlongs" from home, hearing the *azaan* and the temple bells together (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 59, folio 41; p. 60, folio 42); he refuses the *janeu*, which "caused a furore", and "Respectable Hindus started to avoid the Bedi" family (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 61–62, folios 43–44); and his mentor is "Sayyed Hassan, a Muslim Sufi, who lived near his house" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 62, folio 44). The story of the *Sacha Sauda*, the true bargain, begins in Dhillon with goods to be sold in Talwandi (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 25, folio 29); in Khalid's version, "According to the legend, when Baba Guru Nanak turned eighteen, his father asked him to take up a trade. He gave him twenty rupees", and Nanak left "the city (present day Nankana Sahib)" with Bhai Mardana (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 182, folio not stated).

From Talwandi Nanak went to Sultanpur, "around 60 km from Talwandi", as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's stores (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 44, folio 49). Dhillon dates his marriage: "He got married on 24 September 1487" to Sulakhini, "daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of the town of Batala", and gives his sons as "Sri Chand (8 September 1494) and Lakhmi Das (12 February 1497)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 44, folio 49). At Sultanpur, in Dhillon's telling, he vanished in the stream for a week and came out saying, "There is only one God. There is no Hindu, no Mussalman." (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 45–46, folios 50–51). Dhillon sets out two schemes of the *udasis*, the Guru's journeys: "According to the Puratan Janamsakhi… he undertook five journeys" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 54–55, folios 60–61), while "More modern accounts" give four, spanning twenty-three years (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 55, folio 61); Dhillon himself holds to four (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 56, folio 62). Khalid gives the travels as "about twenty-four years", mostly on foot, east to Bengal, south to Sri Lanka, north to Kashmir, Nepal and Tibet, and west to Mecca (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 54, folio 36). "Whenever he would visit an area he would visit its religious shrines, Muslim, Hindu and of any other denomination" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 37, folio 19). At the end, settled at Kartarpur, Nanak sends to Talwandi for his family (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 296, folio 270).

Bhandari calls Baba Nanak "قافله سالار مسالک حقیقت و مشعله دار طریق طریقت", a caravan-leader on the paths of truth and torch-bearer of the mystic way (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). "دوازده کروهے بتاله برلب دریاے راوی مکان بابا نانک است که تا حال اولادش درانجا سکونت دارد": twelve *kos* from Batala on the bank of the Ravi is the place of Baba Nanak, where his descendants still live; and "عالم عالم خلایق از اطراف ممالک آمده مرید شدند", people came from every land to become his disciples (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). He died, Bhandari writes, "درعهد سلطنت سلیم شاه افغان درعمر مابین هفتاد و هشتاد سالگی", in the reign of Salim Shah Afghan, between the ages of seventy and eighty (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520); Dhillon gives the date of his death as 22 September 1539 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 259, folio 287). Bhandari writes that Nanak had a son, "لکهمیداس نام خلف رشید", but passed him over and made a Khatri named Lehna, with the title Guru Angad, his successor at the hour of death (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). "On his deathbed, he appointed not his son but his most loyal student as his spiritual successor", Khalid writes (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 16, folio not stated). Michel Boivin, writing of Sindh, names Sri Chand as "the eldest son of Guru Nanak who was not recognized as guru by the mainstream Sikh community", whose tradition the Udasis follow (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 53, folio 40).

His followers, in Bhandari's account, count service of the traveller, "درخدمت صادر و وارد", as "عبادت عظمی", the highest worship; whoever arrives at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name is treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 519). "It is believed that the tradition of Langar began with Guru Nanak", Khalid writes (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated). Dhillon's Nanak was "no unworldly mystic" but "a householder in every sense of the word" who "brought a message of peace and harmony to believers of the mutually hostile religions of Islam and Hinduism" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 12, folio not stated). "It is said" that, asked by his Hindu and Muslim companions which religion to adopt, he told them to be true Muslims or honest Hindus: "That would be Nanak's religion" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 219, folio not stated). Khalid, who once found Nanak "my own, being a Punjabi" yet "an alien, since he was a non-Muslim" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 15, folio not stated), writes that he "vehemently spoke against organised religion" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 16, folio not stated) and associated with "people of lowercastes, terming them people of God" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 82, folio 64). "Some scholars have argued that the beauty of Nanak's message is that through his own example, he glorified peasantry" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 303, folio 277).

Others tie him to the Sufis. Rizvi, against W.H. McLeod, argues that "all literate Panjabis, both Hindus and Muslims, at the time of Guru Nanak were conversant with" 'Attar, Rumi and Sa'di (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 420, folio 396). "Guru Nanak was a spiritual follower of Baba Fareed. He traveled to Pak Pattan where he met the spiritual descendants of Baba Fareed and collected the poetry of the saint" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated). Shemeem Burney Abbas writes that Baba Farid's "texts are revered among the Sikhs because he influenced the founder of their own religion, Baba Guru Nanak" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 87, folio not stated), and that "Reformers and mystics like Kabir" and Guru Nanak "were certainly influenced by Sufism" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 48, folio not stated). Robert Rozehnal reports that a twentieth-century Chishti Sabiri shaykh, in certain lectures, describes "non-Muslim spiritual luminaries—Krishna, Rama, Sita, Lachman, and Guru Nanak—as believers in the one true God and religious leaders with 'Divine connection' (nisbat)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 63, folio 53). Omar Kasmani, citing Boivin, notes that the trope of the flower in milk is told also of "Guru Nanak, the spiritual leader and founder of Sikhism" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 195, folio 178, ch. 5 n. 17).

His devotion reaches beyond the Sikhs. Khalid writes of Nanak Panthis, "Hindus who believe in the teachings of Guru Nanak, but not in the Khalsa", in whose temples in Sindh and southern Punjab "one will find portraits of Guru Nanak, along with Krishna, Kali Mata and other Hindu deities" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated), and that "many Muslims, acquainted with the teachings of Guru Nanak, are devoted to him too and visit his shrine" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated). Boivin notes "a growing similarity between the iconography of Guru Nanak and Jhulelal" in Sindh (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41). Jürgen Schaflechner records "the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak" in the valley of the goddess Hinglaj, and writes that "The hollowed-out footsteps of Guru Nanak connect Hinglaj to the Sikh and Nanak paṃth (Hin. sect) traditions" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 256, folio not stated; p. 257, folio not stated); "Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 80, folio not stated).

## Legends and Miracles

The field of Kiara Sahib is one miracle among many told of the Guru; the others below are told of him, not of this place. The best known is the Kaʿba that turned. "According to legend, Nanak once travelled to Mecca where he performed Hajj"; he slept with his feet towards the Kaaba, was rebuked, turned his feet, "and as he did so, the Kaaba miraculously turned towards his feet"; Khalid comments, "What is important in this story is Nanak's criticism of the concept of a 'sacred space'" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 82, folio 64). In Dhillon's telling Nanak's feet were said to point towards "a place where God does not reside", and the *qazi* conceded that "God lives everywhere" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 198–201, folios 218–221). Another legend, which Khalid gives in a footnote, turns on goods spoilt and restored: a trader told Nanak that his mules carried "Just some mud"; his "sugar and gur (jaggery) had turned into mud", and when he repented "his mud became Sugar and gur once again" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 71, folio 53).

Some writers set the miracles against the man. Dhillon writes of "Guru Nanak's clear and emphatic disavowal of the miraculous" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 11, folio 11), and in his retelling the Guru tells Karori, who calls his cure a miracle, that "there is no such thing as a miracle" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 190, folio 209). Khalid writes that Nanak "abhorred the concept of associating miracles with religious personalities", yet "his biography is nothing but a story of his miracles" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 16, folio not stated). Of the legends in which Nanak humbles a Muslim Sufi, at Sialkot and Pasrur, he writes that they are "pointless stories" and that "His genius lies in the poetic use of words and not in miracles"; Iqbal Qaiser's comment is, "That is to show that our saint is more powerful than yours" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 199, folio 173). For his method Qaiser advised: "read what Nanak wrote at these places and try to get into his mind" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 286, folio 260).

## In Verse

None of the verse the books quote is tied to Kiara Sahib or to Nankana Sahib; it is given here as the poetry of the Guru the gurdwara remembers. Dhillon notes that Nanak's *Bani* "was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 9, folio 9). Bhandari says that the Guru composed "اشعار هندی" on the truth of God, setting out divine unity "بعبارات واضحه و استعارات لایحه", in clear words and shining metaphors; that a singer named Mardana, "مردانه نام مطرب", sang his verses and drew people "در دام عقیدت", into the snare of devotion (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520); and that the worship of his followers is the reading of their master's verses, which they sing: "خلاصه عبادت اینطایفه مطالعه اشعار مرشد خویش است که بسرود و نغمه میگویند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 519).

Khalid, who "truly discovered Guru Nanak" through Iqbal Qaiser's recitation of the *Babur Bani*, in which Nanak "lays the blame of Babur's wrath at God's feet" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 15–16, folio not stated), quotes the Guru's verse throughout *Walking with Nanak* in published English translations. The *aarti*, which Qaiser reads as praising a God who resides "in nature", calling Nanak "a naturalist" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 55, folio 37; p. 56, folio 38), begins in one translation:

*The sky the salver, the sun and moon the lamps …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 55, folio 37)

and in another:

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 243–244, folios 217–218)

On the oneness of God:

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 60, folio 42)

*God is One, / The Path is One* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 144, folio 126)

The poem on the sacred thread, which in Khalid's reconstruction the boy refused at Talwandi:

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 61–62, folios 43–44)

On washing:

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 192, folio 166)

The song Nanak sings, in Khalid's reconstruction, to innkeepers who meant to rob him:

*The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 123–126, folios 105–108)

Other openings Khalid quotes: *O my merchant friend* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 56–58, folio 40); *Launch ye the boat of austere contemplation …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 148–149, folios 130–131); *As a beggar goes a-begging …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 158, folio 140); and *His goodness cannot be priced or traded …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 280, folio 254).

The Guru's language and forms are part of his legacy. "Nanak incorporated several words which were not part of the Punjabi of the time … which is why Nanak's contribution as a poet to Punjabi is immense" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 278–279, folios 252–253). Abbas writes of the *dohā*, a rhyming couplet in an old Prakrit and Hindi metre: "Poets such as Kabir and Nanak used it to write their mystical poetry" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 141, folio not stated); her glossary defines the *banī* by him: "Devotional verses such as those of Guru Nanak; verses of supplication, entreaty, humility, and reverence" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 179, folio not stated). Annemarie Schimmel, writing of the province, observes that Panjabi "was used almost exclusively by the Sikhs as their literary medium, whereas the Panjabi Muslims resorted to Urdu" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 427, folio 396).

The Guru's verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. Abbas quotes Abida Parvin: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 54, folio not stated). In Sindh, Boivin records, "Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the banis of Shri Guru Nanak and the kalams of the Sufis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55), and he reports Ajwani's judgement that "Guru Nanak was the greatest poet of the Bhakti" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 90, folio 77).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **To whom the farmer complained.** The site's account has the peasant hurry to Rai Bular Bhatti, the local landlord. *Walking with Nanak* says the farmer "is reported to have complained to Nanak's father" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). *A White Trail* does not say (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).
- **Whether the crop was harmed.** The site's account says the crop was found "whole and unharmed", and that this was taken for a miracle. *Walking with Nanak* has the buffaloes "spoilt the fields of a local farmer" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73); *A White Trail* has the cattle "destroyed the fields of a farmer" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). Neither book records an inspection or a restoration.
- **What the boy was doing.** The site's account has him "absorbed in meditation". *A White Trail* has the cattle destroy the fields "while he slept" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).
- **The animals.** The site's account speaks of the family's cattle and has buffaloes stray into the crop; *Walking with Nanak* names buffaloes (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73); *A White Trail* says cattle (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).
- **The name.** The site's account and *A White Trail* write Kiara Sahib (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated); *Walking with Nanak* writes Kiari Sahib (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73).
- **How Rai Bular is described.** The site's account calls him "the local landlord" and "a Muslim landlord". Khalid's reconstruction calls him "the ruler of Talwindi, Rai Bular Bhatti" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 22, folio 4). Dhillon makes him the son of Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajput who had converted to Islam and under whom Talwandi was rebuilt (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 15–16, folios 17–18; p. 17, folio 19).
- **How many gurdwaras Nankana has.** *A White Trail* counts seven (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 192, folio not stated); *Walking with Nanak* counts six associated with Guru Nanak (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72).
- **The date of birth.** Dhillon gives "On 14 April 1469" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 17–18, folios 19–20); the back matter of *Walking with Nanak* gives "October 20, 1469" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 314, folio 288); Bhandari, with a "گویند", gives Samvat 1526, corresponding to 880 Hijri, in the reign of Bahlul Lodi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).
- **The place of birth.** The site's account and every book place it at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib; Khalid reports that the Janamsakhi writer Meherban "claims that Guru Nanak was born in Dera Chahal and not Rai Bhoi di Talwindi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25).
- **The birth and a Muslim saint's prayer.** Khalid, citing Dhillon's *The First Sikh Spiritual Master*, has Mata Tripta pray for a child at an ancient Hindu temple on a mound near Talwandi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 30–31, folio 13); an Auqaf booklet says he was born after Baba Naulakha Hazari prayed for his mother (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 31, folio 13); Iqbal Qaiser calls this "the Muslim tradition", which "The Sikhs don't accept" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9, folio not stated).
- **The signs of childhood.** Bhandari's text dates the first signs of wonders to the Guru's childhood, "درخورد سالگی"; the editor's variant reads "ده سالگی", at the age of ten (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).
- **The Guru's wife and sons.** Dhillon has Sulakhini, daughter of Mul Chand and Chando Rani of Batala, married on 24 September 1487, and the sons Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 44, folio 49). Khalid's reconstruction has Sulakhni, "the daughter of Moolchand Khatri from the village of Pakhoke near Gurdaspur", and the sons Sri Chand and Lachman Das (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 67, folio 49; p. 68, folio 50). Bhandari names the son passed over as Lakhmidas (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).
- **How many journeys.** Dhillon reports five *udasis* in the Puratan Janamsakhi and four in more modern accounts, spanning twenty-three years, and holds to four himself (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 54–55, folios 60–61; p. 55, folio 61; p. 56, folio 62). Khalid gives the travels as about twenty-four years (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 54, folio 36).
- **The date of death.** Dhillon gives 22 September 1539 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 259, folio 287); Bhandari gives the reign of Salim Shah Afghan, at an age between seventy and eighty (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).
- **Who cared for the gurdwaras after Partition.** The site's account says the shrines of Nankana Sahib have been cared for by the bodies responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan. Kartar says that "There was no Sikh left here after partition" and that the gurdwaras "became barren and were in a bad state" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated); *Walking with Nanak* says that Giani Pratap's decision to stay was "the first time someone had taken the initiative to take care of the gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib after Partition" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72).

## Legacy

Kiara Sahib is one of the cluster of gurdwaras that make Nankana Sahib the holiest town of the Sikh world after Amritsar, each marking a remembered moment of the Guru's early life — his birth, his schooling, his play, and the miracles of his boyhood. The field of the untouched crop speaks to a theme dear to Sikh devotion: that the greatness of Guru Nanak was manifest from his earliest years, and that even a landlord of another faith was moved to acknowledge it. For the pilgrim, to stand at Kiara Sahib is to enter the pastoral world of the *sakhis*, where a boy lost in the remembrance of God let his cattle wander, and the very fields bore witness to his sanctity.

Khalid calls Nankana Sahib "one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, if not the holiest" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 221–222, folio not stated). Writing of Pakistan as a whole, he says that "Guru Nanak was born in a city now called Nankana Sahib, Pakistan. He passed away in a small village called Kartarpur also in present day Pakistan", and that "Gurdwaras that were built there later by the devotees still stand tall" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 168–169, folio not stated). When the festival is over, "Things in Nankana Sahib will soon calm down" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 232, folio not stated). Khalid's own book on the Guru, its blurb says, is "not merely a story about gurdwaras" but a retelling of "Nanak the son, the poet, the wanderer, the father, the friend" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 2, folio not stated), and he asks whether "Nanak's legacy in its true essence is also slowly disappearing" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 230, folio 204).

## Bibliography

Name: Gurdwara Sri Tilganji Sahib
Events: Daily worship; Sikh anniversaries
Description:
Gurdwara Sri Tilganji Sahib stands on Masjid Road in the heart of Quetta, the capital of Balochistan. By Sikh tradition the site marks a visit by Guru Nanak, the first Guru, during one of his great journeys, or udasis: it is said that the Guru honoured the assembled sangat by distributing til — sesame seeds — as parshad, the sanctified offering, and that from this the shrine took its name, Tilganji deriving from til (sesame) and ganj (treasury or store). The gurdwara is a substantial domed building whose main gateway is said to resemble that of a mosque; within its precincts, in a pattern common to many gurdwaras in Pakistan after 1947, a government school — the Government Sandeman School — has long functioned, occupying land belonging to the shrine. Quetta was almost entirely destroyed in the catastrophic earthquake of 1935, so that the present fabric of the building, like much of the city, is unlikely to be of great antiquity, even if the sanctity of the site is older. The gurdwara is one of the principal Sikh shrines of the city and is to be distinguished from the Gurdwara Singh Sabha of Quetta, recorded separately in this dataset. Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey of Sikh shrines in Pakistan records that, in addition to the Sandeman School already functioning within the shrine's precincts, a new government school building had by then been constructed on vacant land belonging to the gurdwara, and that the Sangat of Quetta had filed suit in the lower courts seeking to recover possession of the property.

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Lahore: Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 134.
