Name: Gurdwara Tambo Sahib
Events: Guru Nanak Gurpurab
Description:
## Overview

Gurdwara Tambu Sahib stands in Nankana Sahib, a short distance east of the central shrine of Janam Asthan that marks the birthplace of *Guru Nanak Dev Ji*, founder of the Sikh faith. Its name comes from the Punjabi *tambu*, a tent, for the gurdwara grew up around a great *van* tree whose spreading, low-hanging branches formed a natural canopy — a living tent — beneath which the young Nanak is remembered to have taken shelter. It is one of the cluster of shrines in and around the holy town that preserve, site by site, the episodes of the Guru's boyhood.

Of the books consulted, two name the gurdwara itself, both by Haroon Khalid. *Walking with Nanak* calls it "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib" and places it "in between Janamsthan and Kiari Sahib and Malji Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). *A White Trail* writes it both "Gurdwara Tamboo Sahib" and "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib", and puts it "a few hundred metres away from Gurdwara Janamasthan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated); it reports the festival of Lohri there in January 2011 and the birthday of Guru Nanak, and recalls the gathering of 1921 that began within its grounds. Harish Dhillon's retelling of the Janamsakhis tells the story of the bargain that the gurdwara remembers but names no gurdwara at Talwandi, the old name of the town. The other books speak only of Guru Nanak, of Nankana Sahib, or of the Punjab, not of this place, and what they say is given below as being about the Guru or the town.

## The True Bargain and the Tent-Tree

The tradition attached to Tambu Sahib is bound up with one of the most beloved of the *sakhis*, the story of the *sacha sauda* or "true bargain." Nanak's father, Mehta Kalu, anxious that his contemplative son should learn a trade, gave him a sum of money and sent him to the market town of Chuharkana to buy goods and turn a profit. On the way Nanak encountered a company of hungry holy men, and, judging that no bargain could be truer than the feeding of the poor and the servants of God, he spent the whole sum on food for them and returned home empty-handed but content. Fearing his father's anger, the boy is said to have stopped short of the village and seated himself beneath the great *van* tree, whose branches enclosed him like a tent, until he was found and brought home. The gurdwara raised on the spot preserves the memory of that refuge. (A separate, often-conflated Nankana Sahib legend — of a tree's shadow standing still while all others moved — properly belongs to the nearby Gurdwara Mal Ji Sahib, not this site.)

Khalid gives the legend in *A White Trail*. "According to the legend, when Baba Guru Nanak turned eighteen, his father asked him to take up a trade. He gave him twenty rupees", and Nanak left "the city (present day Nankana Sahib)" with Bhai Mardana (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 182, folio not stated). He fed starving *jogis* with the money, and on his way back "hid under this tree"; his family found him there. "Now there are two Gurdwaras to commemorate this event. One is this Gurdwara, Tamboo Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 182, folio not stated). Elsewhere in the book the gurdwara marks the place "where he hid after returning from the incident that came to be known as Sacha Sauda" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated).

In *Walking with Nanak* Khalid writes that Nanak, "after he had spent all his father's money on a good deed", "looked for sanctuary in a group of waan trees that existed outside the town. Those trees still exist and are held sacred by Sikh devotees" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 86, folio 68; p. 87, folio 69). The road home, he writes, ran "back from Chuhrkhana to Nankana Sahib, which at that point in time was still known as Rai Bhoi di Talwindi", across "a vast jungle that existed then between Nankana and Chuhrkhana" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 86, folio 68).

The same book retells Nanak's youth in a reconstruction that Khalid himself calls fictionalised (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 17, folio not stated). In it Mehta Kalu calls himself "an accountant" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 63, folio 45), and Nanak is found hiding "in the growe [OCR?] [grove] of wax [OCR?] [waan] trees outside town" by his father and "his employer and friend, Rai Bular" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 64, folio 46). An earlier scene of the reconstruction, which does not name the site, has the boy sitting at dusk under "this waan tree", with cloths "tied as supplication" on its branches, "about two furlongs" from his home, hearing the call to prayer and the temple bells together (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 59, folio 41; p. 60, folio 42).

Dhillon's retelling sends the boy out with goods to be sold in Talwandi (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 25, folio 29), and his chapter on the bargain ends in "the forest" and back in "Talwandi" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 38, folio 42). Of Talwandi he writes that it "lay in the path of numerous mendicants, sadhus and holy men", who camped "in a grove of trees on the outskirts of the village" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 24, folio 28).

## The Name

Both of Khalid's books derive the name from the tree. *Walking with Nanak* says it is "derived from the fambu [OCR?] [tambu] (tent) like trees under which Nanak hid" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). *A White Trail* says: "The word tamboo comes from the tent like cover of this tree. Tamboo means tent in Punjabi." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated). The tree itself, in that book, "is spread out like a tent", "an ancient tree, called Waan in Punjabi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated).

## The Gurdwara

A shrine was established beside the tree during the period of Sikh rule in the Punjab, about a furlong east of Janam Asthan, and its architecture echoes that of the other Nankana gurdwaras: a domed sanctum set within a square hall, decorated in the idiom of Sikh sacred building, though plainer in some of its detailing than its neighbours. It lies close to the gurdwaras of Mal Ji Sahib and of the fifth and sixth Gurus, so that the pilgrim moving among them traces a compact circuit of the Guru's early life. Within the sanctum the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed, and the site is maintained, like the other shrines of the town, by the authorities responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan.

Khalid describes the place in both books. In *Walking with Nanak*: "Next to the trees is a small gurdwara, a yellow single storied structure. Behind it are two large hostels used by Sikh pilgrims at the time of the largest Sikh festival in Pakistan—the birthday of Guru Nanak, celebrated in November every year" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). The gurdwara has a "blue gate" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73).

In *A White Trail* the tree is "protected by a boundary fence" with one gate, and shoes come off before entering (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated). Behind the tree stands "a small mango coloured building with a small dome on the top", with a board reading "Gurdwara Tamboo Sahib." and the saffron *Nishan Sahib* in the courtyard (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated). Describing the same building at the festival of Guru Nanak's birthday, he writes: "The shrine, which is a small yellow structure, stands in the middle of the ground with a white dome on the top" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). One of the book's photographs is captioned "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib at the time of sunset." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 107, folio not stated). Among the plates of *Walking with Nanak* is one captioned "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib", which names no town; the caption also names "Sacha Sauda", the episode (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 167, plate).

Inside is "the Thara Sahib (a wooden pavilion which hosts the Granth Sahib)", and two swords lie there in blue velvet sheaths (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 185, folio not stated).

The grounds are large. Khalid found a single-storey building used by farmers, a tractor, and "vast land laying vacant on both sides of the shrine which is used for agriculture"; "A tall barb-wired wall" ran on all sides, with one gate from the main market, a board by the road in "English, Shahmukhi ... and Gurmukhi", and a second, blue gate "kept permanently locked for security reasons" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 181–182, folio not stated). "The area belonging to Gurdwara Tambu Sahib is the second largest in the city, making it the second most popular destination after Janamasthan", the ground "big enough to host an international cricket match" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated).

## Custodians, Lands and Buildings

*Walking with Nanak* names the man in charge. Jatha Singh, "the self-appointed caretaker of the gurdwara", is "in-charge of the vast property associated with the gurdwara, which was allotted to it by the Sikh ruler of Punjab, Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the nineteenth century", and "receives millions of rupees in donations from Sikh expatriates residing in first world countries", to be spent "on the upliftment of the gurdwara and the Sikh community in Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). Writing of the province and not of this gurdwara, Khalid adds that "When Maharaja Ranjit Singh became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras", and "attached vast tracts of land to these gurdwaras, so that the revenues from the lands could facilitate their functioning" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 34, folio 16).

Jatha Singh kept his room "in one of the rooms of a hostel". When Khalid called on him he was arbitrating between two feuding Muslim families, and the guests were served "langar, vegetables along with lentils and hot rotts [OCR?] [rotis]" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). Of the town's Sikhs Khalid writes, in the same passage, of "the Sikh community in Nankana Sahib, which amounts to about two hundred-odd households", whom Jatha Singh "has for several years played the role of a leader" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69).

*A White Trail* describes the newer buildings. By the entrance stands a newly built triple-storey residential hall, with two larger residential buildings raised from devotees' donations and "a single storey Langar Hall" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). "Three hostel blocks have been constructed here with the help of donations from pilgrims coming from Britain, Canada and America"; "A large amount has been donated by Kar Seva, an England based non-profit organization" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated), and a yellow board on the Langar Hall reads: "This newly constructed building has been made by Kar Seva" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 224, folio not stated). "Shaheed Hall, next to the Langar Hall", also built from Kar Seva's donations and "Recently completed", is a "five storey building" whose roof is closed to pilgrims (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 224–225, folio not stated). "In the future, the Government of Pakistan plans to construct a Guru Nanak University in the vicinity of this complex", Khalid adds, a "persistent demand of the expat Sikh community" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 223–224, folio not stated).

## Devotion and Practice

The tree is the heart of the devotion. "Pilgrims tie pieces of cloth onto the branches of these stooping trees as a supplication", Khalid writes (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). In *A White Trail* he describes the custom at Lohri. Kartar Singh Kartar tore a saffron cloth from inside the gurdwara and each person tied a piece to the tree; his Muslim friends tied cloth too, but kept their hands at their sides (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated). According to Kartar, "by tying a cloth on the branches of this sacred tree, our wishes come true"; at Guru Nanak's birthday "People tie over each other's cloth" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 182, folio not stated). Candles were lit at the base of the *Nishan Sahib* (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated).

The prayer that followed, which Khalid's account places in the gurdwara of the compound, was "a Sikh-only affair", with the other three doors closed. Kartar prostrated before the Thara Sahib and offered "a ten rupee note", "the highest one being that of fifty" among the offerings (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 185, folio not stated). The room filled to "about fifty people", "as many men as there are women"; the donations "will be used for the renovation of the Gurdwara". A *Granthi* "in his mid-sixties" read for half an hour, then came a community prayer with "Waheguru", and *Prasad* of naan and a sweet made in *desi ghee* (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 185, folio not stated). Candles were "held up in a circle around the arti that carries lit incense", and people "place their hand on top of the fire and rub it on their faces" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 185–186, folio not stated). From there the procession went on to Janamasthan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 185, folio not stated).

Writing of the town's Lohri and not of this gurdwara alone, Khalid records that "Lohri like Vaisakhi or Basant, is an ancient festival of the Punjab that commemorates the change of season", celebrated "on the 13th of January" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 192–193, folio not stated). Kartar told him that Lohri and Guru Gobind Singh's birthday "have only begun in the last couple of years", made possible "by the increase in the Sikh population as a result of the migration from the tribal areas after the war"; "Earlier, there was only a prayer at the Gurdwara." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 193, folio not stated). "It is ironical though", Khalid writes, "that this Punjabi tradition shunned by Punjab is now being revived by a group of Pathan men residing in Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 194, folio not stated).

At the birthday of Guru Nanak the gurdwara fills. "Most of the pilgrims from the developed countries stay at Gurdwara Tambu Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated); Shaheed Hall is the "first choice of pilgrims from developed countries", though as their numbers have fallen it now houses many Indian pilgrims (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 224–225, folio not stated). Security is "lax" compared with Janamasthan: there are metal detectors and a few guards, but it is "fairly easy to walk in unnoticed" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). Food is served around the clock (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 229, folio not stated).

In the parking area stands a book stall of the "Dyal Singh Memorial Trust, a pre-partition trust based in Lahore", where Iqbal Qaiser, 58, sells his *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan*: "This is the only time in the year my book sells … somewhere between twenty to thirty copies" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 224, folio not stated). Police stand on the roofs of the Langar Hall and the residential buildings (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 224, folio not stated). Arshad Malik, a constable of 35 with "eighteen years" in the police, on a twelve-hour duty since eight in the morning, told Khalid that "the entire police force of the city has been deployed at the Gurdwaras for these three days" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 225, folio not stated). He would not eat from the *langar*: "We are Muslims. We don't eat with the Sikhs or Hindus" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 225–226, folio not stated).

Writing of the festival in the town as a whole, Khalid gives the official estimate that "ten to fifteen thousand people come to Nankana Sahib for this festival every year, which is celebrated during the last days of November"; in 2011, "According to media reports, only three thousand people are attending", and "This year it began on the 8th of November and will conclude today, on the 10th of November" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). It is called "Guru Nanak Jayanti or Gurpurab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). Of the town's gurdwaras generally he writes: "All year round most of them remain locked, only to be opened at the time of the festival. There are security guards employed at the entrance to all of them." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 227, folio not stated).

## The Gathering of 1921

*A White Trail* records one historical event at the gurdwara. On 20 February 1921 unarmed Sikhs from other districts "gathered at Gurdwara Tamboo Sahib", accused the *mahant*, and after a short prayer resolved to walk to Janamasthan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 189–190, folio not stated). Writing of the Punjab in general, Khalid explains the background: "As a result of sectarian divisions between the Sikh communities and the takeover of Punjab by the British, a large number of important Sikh Gurdwaras were being administered by Hindu mahants" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 189, folio not stated).

## Setting: Nankana Sahib

What follows is said of the town, not of this gurdwara. Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi places Guru Nanak's birth in "the village of Talwandi later known as Nankana Sahib, about forty miles south-west of Lahore, now part of Pakistan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 407, folio 383). Khalid writes that "The name of Rai Bhoi di Talwindi has been changed to Nankana Sahib in honour of the first Sikh Guru who was born there" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 31, folio 13), and that "Originally called Rai-Bhoi-Di-Talwandi, this city was rechristened Nankana Sahib in honour of Guru Nanak", so that Nanak's early years there account for "several Gurdwaras in the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 222, folio not stated). It is "a city considered to be one of the holiest cities in the world for the Sikhs, as the founder of their religion, Nanak, was born here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 183, folio not stated).

Bhandari's Persian history says that Baba Nanak "درمکان تلونڈی رائے بهوئه[OCR?] سعادت ولادت یافته همانجا درخانه جد ابادری می بود": that he was born at Talwandi Rai Bhoi, and lived there in his grandfather's house (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Dhillon describes Talwandi as "the village of Talwandi, which lay between the rivers Ravi and Chenab, directly in the path of the armies that had set their eyes on Delhi": "Thirteen times was the village of Talwandi destroyed and thirteen times - like the fabled phoenix - it rose again from its ashes", and "Its last rebirth took place under the supervision of Rai Bhoe, a Bhatti Rajpur [text-layer?] [Bhatti Rajput], who had converted to Islam" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 15–16, folios 17–18).

Behind Gurdwara Janamsthan rises an old mound. Iqbal Qaiser told Khalid that "The settlement there was destroyed after which Rai Bhoi di Talwindi was constructed within a boundary wall" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73). "It is believed that in the years between the incident of Sacha Sauda and his migration to Sultanpur, Nanak started to frequent this place", talking with the yogis, *sadhus* and dervishes who passed through: "That period of six to seven years" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73; p. 92, folio 74).

The books count the town's gurdwaras differently. *Walking with Nanak* says: "There are a total of six gurdwaras associated with Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72); *A White Trail* says: "There are seven Gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib, most of which are associated with incidents from the life of Baba Guru Nanak" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 192, folio not stated). "Gurdwaras that were built there later by the devotees still stand tall", Khalid writes of the places across the country where Nanak stayed (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 168–169, folio not stated), and Kar Seva's name appears on "yellow dustbins and other boards that have been placed in different Gurdwaras of the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated).

After Partition the town's gurdwaras stood empty. Khalid writes of Giani Pratap: "After looking at the dilapidated condition of the shrines here he decided to stay and look after these holy buildings. That was the first time someone had taken the initiative to take care of the gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib after Partition" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72). The informant Kartar told him: "There was no Sikh left here after partition. Our Gurdwaras became barren and were in a bad state" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 184, folio not stated). Most of the town's present Sikhs, Khalid writes, "are not indigenous people from the city, but recent migrants from Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) where there is a considerable Sikh population" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 235, folio not stated), and "Most of the newcomers were incorporated within the Gurdwaras, in rooms which were generally reserved for pilgrims" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 176, folio not stated). He gives the numbers in more than one way: "There were only about thirty to forty Sikh houses in Nankana ten years ago" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 174–175, folio not stated), and "In about ten years, the population in Nankana Sahib increased to about two hundred houses" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 175, folio not stated).

## Guru Nanak in the Wider Record

What the books say of Guru Nanak himself is said of the Guru, not of this site; it is gathered here because the gurdwara exists for his sake. Khalid gives his dates as 1469–1539, calling him "the founder of the Sikh religion" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated), and in *Walking with Nanak* has him "Born Talwandi (now known as Nankana Sahib in Pakistan) on October 20, 1469" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 314, folio 288). Dhillon calls the Janamsakhis "cycles of tales purportedly drawn from the life of the first Guru of the Sikhs" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 9, folio 9), and has him born "On 14 April 1469" to Kalyan Chand Das Bedi, "or Mehta Kalu as he was affectionately called", accountant to the Bhatti family under Rai Bular (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 17–18, folios 19–20); he gives the date of his death as 22 September 1539 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 259, folio 287). Bhandari reports, with a "گویند", a birth "درسنه هزار و پانصد و بست و شش بکرماجیت مطابق هشتصد و هشتاد هجری درزمان سلطان بهلول لودی", and a death "درعهد سلطنت سلیم شاه افغان درعمر مابین هفتاد و هشتاد سالگی" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Khalid records that one Janamsakhi writer, Meherban, "claims that Guru Nanak was born in Dera Chahal and not Rai Bhoi di Talwindi", while the other Janamsakhi writers and Sikh scholars "are unanimous that Nanak was born in Rai Bhoi di Talwindi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25).

In Dhillon's retelling, Nanak refused the sacred thread at thirteen, "the beginning of a lifelong crusade against the performing of empty rites and rituals" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 19–21, folios 21–23); at sixteen he herded cattle (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 23, folio 27) and "became well acquainted with the dervish Sayyad Hussain and gained an intimate knowledge of the Sufi line of thought" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 24, folio 28). In Khalid's reconstruction his mentor is "Sayyed Hassan, a Muslim Sufi, who lived near his house" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 62, folio 44). After the bargain, in Dhillon's telling, "Nanak moved to Sultanpur (around 60 km from Talwandi)" as keeper of Nawab Daulat Khan's stores (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 44, folio 49).

Bhandari calls him "قافله سالار مسالک حقیقت و مشعله دار طریق طریقت" and writes that the signs of his gift showed early, "درخورد سالگی(۱) علامات کشف و کرامات و ایات خارق عادات از و بمنصه ظهور رسید" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520), and that a singer named Mardana, "مردانه نام مطرب", sang the Guru's verses and drew people "در دام عقیدت" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Of the Guru's followers he writes that they count service of the traveller, "درخدمت صادر و وارد", as "عبادت عظمی", and that whoever arrives at midnight speaking Baba Nanak's name is treated as a brother and a friend and served, even a stranger, a thief or a highwayman (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 519). Khalid writes that "It is believed that the tradition of Langar began with Guru Nanak" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated).

Dhillon writes that Nanak "brought a message of peace and harmony to believers of the mutually hostile religions of Islam and Hinduism", that he taught that "all men and women were equal, irrespective of caste, creed, wealth, social standing and gender", and that a good life rested on honest labour, compassion, selfless service and prayer (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 12–13, folio not stated / 13). He also writes of "Guru Nanak's clear and emphatic disavowal of the miraculous" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 11, folio 11). Khalid writes that Nanak "abhorred the concept of associating miracles with religious personalities", yet "his biography is nothing but a story of his miracles" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 16, folio not stated).

Muslim writers and singers have claimed the Guru too. Khalid writes that "many Muslims, acquainted with the teachings of Guru Nanak, are devoted to him too and visit his shrine" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 220, folio not stated), and that "Guru Nanak was a spiritual follower of Baba Fareed" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated); in *In Search of Shiva* he notes that "There is a picture of Baba Farid accompanying the picture of Guru Nanak at the shrine of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib", without saying which gurdwara he means (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Shemeem Burney Abbas writes that Baba Farid's "texts are revered among the Sikhs because he influenced the founder of their own religion, Baba Guru Nanak" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 87, folio not stated). Robert Rozehnal reports that a twentieth-century Chishti Sabiri shaykh, in certain lectures, describes "non-Muslim spiritual luminaries—Krishna, Rama, Sita, Lachman, and Guru Nanak—as believers in the one true God and religious leaders with 'Divine connection' (nisbat)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 63, folio 53). Omar Kasmani, citing Michel Boivin, notes that the trope of the flower in milk is told also of "Guru Nanak, the spiritual leader and founder of Sikhism" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 195, folio 178, ch. 5 n. 17). At the shrine of the goddess Hinglaj, Jürgen Schaflechner records "the engraved footsteps of Guru Nanak" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 256, folio not stated).

## In Verse

None of the verse the books quote is tied to Tambu Sahib; it is given here as the poetry of the Guru the gurdwara remembers. Dhillon notes that Nanak's *Bani* "was compiled as part of the Adi Granth by Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, in 1604" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 9, folio 9). Bhandari says that the Guru composed "اشعار هندی" on the truth of God, setting out divine unity "بعبارات واضحه و استعارات لایحه" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520), and that the worship of his followers centres on reading their master's verses, which they sing: "خلاصه عبادت اینطایفه مطالعه اشعار مرشد خویش است که بسرود و نغمه میگویند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 519). Abbas's glossary defines the *banī* by him: "Devotional verses such as those of Guru Nanak; verses of supplication, entreaty, humility, and reverence" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 179, folio not stated).

Khalid quotes the Guru's verse throughout *Walking with Nanak*, in published English translations. Among them, fitting a gurdwara that remembers a bargain, is a poem he quotes under the opening 'O my merchant friend' (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 56–58, folio 40). The *aarti*, sung in praise of a God whom Qaiser reads as residing in nature, begins in one translation:

*The sky the salver, the sun and moon the lamps …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 55, folio 37)

and in another:

*In the salver of the firmament, / The sun and the moon shine as lamps* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 243–244, folios 217–218)

On the oneness of God:

*My Master is One / He is One, brother, the only One* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 60, folio 42)

*God is One, / The Path is One* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 144, folio 126)

The poem on the sacred thread, the *janeu*, which in Khalid's reconstruction the boy Nanak refused:

*From the cotton of compassion, / Spin the thread of contentment* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 61–62, folios 43–44)

On washing:

*As hands or feet besmirched with slime, / Water washes white* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 192, folio 166)

Other openings Khalid quotes: *As a beggar goes a-begging …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 158, folio 140); *Launch ye the boat of austere contemplation …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 148–149, folios 130–131); and *His goodness cannot be priced or traded …* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 280, folio 254).

The Guru's verse is sung outside the gurdwaras too. Abbas quotes Abida Parvin: "I sing Shah Hussain, Bulle Shah, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Hazrat Khawaja Ghulam Farid, Sacchal Sarmast, Baba Farid, and Guru Nanak" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 54, folio not stated). In Sindh, Boivin records, "Sain Vasan Shah became famous for reciting the banis of Shri Guru Nanak and the kalams of the Sufis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The spelling of the name.** The site's account writes Tambu Sahib, and the gurdwara is listed as Tambo Sahib. *Walking with Nanak* writes "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 91, folio 73); *A White Trail* writes both "Gurdwara Tamboo Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated) and "Gurdwara Tambu Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). The site's account names the tree *van*; Khalid writes "waan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 86, folio 68) and "Waan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated).
- **One tree or several.** The site's account speaks of "a great *van* tree", and *A White Trail* of "an ancient tree, called Waan in Punjabi", where Nanak "hid under this tree" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated; p. 182, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* speaks of "a group of waan trees" and of "these stooping trees" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 86, folio 68; p. 87, folio 69).
- **Its distance from Janam Asthan.** The site's account puts the gurdwara "a short distance east" of Janam Asthan, "about a furlong east". *A White Trail* puts it "a few hundred metres away from Gurdwara Janamasthan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated). In a reconstruction scene that does not name the site, *Walking with Nanak* puts a waan tree with cloths tied on its branches "about two furlongs" from Nanak's home (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 59, folio 41; p. 60, folio 42).
- **Who found the boy.** The site's account says he stayed under the tree "until he was found and brought home". *A White Trail* says his family found him there (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 182, folio not stated); Khalid's reconstruction in *Walking with Nanak* has his father and Rai Bular find him (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 64, folio 46).
- **The building.** The site's account describes "a domed sanctum set within a square hall". *Walking with Nanak* has "a yellow single storied structure" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). *A White Trail* has, on one visit, "a small mango coloured building with a small dome on the top" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 181, folio not stated) and, on another, "a small yellow structure" with "a white dome on the top" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated).
- **The hostels.** *Walking with Nanak* has "two large hostels" behind the gurdwara (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). *A White Trail* has "Three hostel blocks", besides a triple-storey residential hall, two larger residential buildings and the five-storey Shaheed Hall (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated; pp. 224–225, folio not stated).
- **Who keeps the gurdwara.** The site's account says it is maintained "by the authorities responsible for Sikh heritage in Pakistan". *Walking with Nanak* names Jatha Singh, "the self-appointed caretaker of the gurdwara", in charge of its property and its donations (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69).
- **The Sikhs of Nankana Sahib.** The site's account says that "Since Partition in 1947 the resident Sikh community of Nankana Sahib has been gone", and that the gurdwara is visited "chiefly by pilgrim *jathas*". *Walking with Nanak* speaks of "the Sikh community in Nankana Sahib, which amounts to about two hundred-odd households" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69). *A White Trail* describes resident Sikhs, most of them recent migrants from Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, keeping Lohri at the gurdwara, and gives their numbers as "only about thirty to forty Sikh houses in Nankana ten years ago" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 174–175, folio not stated) and "about two hundred houses" after about ten years (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 175, folio not stated).
- **The number of gurdwaras in the town.** *Walking with Nanak* counts "a total of six gurdwaras associated with Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 90, folio 72); *A White Trail* counts "seven Gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 192, folio not stated).
- **The Guru's birth.** Khalid gives "October 20, 1469" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 314, folio 288); Dhillon gives "14 April 1469" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 17–18, folios 19–20); Bhandari, with a "گویند", gives Samvat 1526, 880 Hijri, in the reign of Bahlul Lodi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520). Khalid reports that Meherban placed the birth at Dera Chahal, against the other Janamsakhi writers' Rai Bhoi di Talwindi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 43, folio 25).
- **The Guru's death.** Dhillon gives 22 September 1539 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 259, folio 287); Bhandari gives the reign of Salim Shah Afghan, at an age between seventy and eighty (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 520).

## Legacy

Since Partition in 1947 the resident Sikh community of Nankana Sahib has been gone, and Tambu Sahib, with the other shrines, is visited chiefly by pilgrim *jathas* who travel from India and the diaspora for the great anniversaries, above all the *Gurpurab* of Guru Nanak's birth, when the town fills with the faithful. The tent-tree of Tambu Sahib carries a lesson dear to the Sikh conscience — that the truest use of wealth is the service of others, the principle of *sacha sauda* — and the site endures as a gentle monument to the boy who thought the feeding of the hungry the best of all bargains.

Khalid's two books show the gurdwara as both of these things at once: a sacred tree that pilgrims and townspeople, Sikh and Muslim, hung with cloth, "held sacred by Sikh devotees" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 87, folio 69), and, with its grounds "the second largest in the city", "the second most popular destination after Janamasthan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 223, folio not stated), where the pilgrims of the Sikh diaspora sleep and the halls their donations built now stand.

Name: Guru Gurpat Mandir (DB-80 Sirey Ghat)
Location: DB-80 Sirey Ghat, Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 1931 (present darbar building); Baba Gurpat Sahib active in Hyderabad c. 1830-1877
Events: Community worship; langar-adjacent hospitality
Description:
## Overview

On a plot known as DB-80 in the Sirey Ghat quarter of Hyderabad, Sindh, stands the Guru Gurpat Mandir — also called the Darbar of Baba Gurpat Sahib — a Nanakpanthi shrine, registered with Pakistan's Evacuee Trust Property Board as a functional mandir, built around a Sant revered as a twelfth-generation descendant, in the Jagiasi lineage, of Guru Nanak. Unlike many of the small, poorly documented sant-shrines of upper and central Sindh, Baba Gurpat Sahib's life and the founding of his darbar are recorded with unusual specificity, principally through community memory preserved by his present-day trust and reported in recent press coverage.

None of the books consulted for this article mentions the mandir, Baba Gurpat Sahib or the Sirey Ghat quarter. Jürgen Schaflechner's study of the goddess Hinglaj, which reports an attack on "a temple in Hyderabad" in March 2014, does not name the temple it means (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 17, folio not stated). What the books do carry is context, and it is set out below as context: what they say of the path of Guru Nanak in Sindh, of the Sindhi *darbar*, of the city of Hyderabad, and of the province around it. None of it is said of this darbar.

## The Life of Baba Gurpat Sahib

According to the darbar's own tradition, Gurpat Sahib was born into the Jagiasi lineage of Nanakpanthi Sants — spiritual descendants of Guru Nanak through Baba Sri Chand's Udasi line — in Punjab, and travelled to Sindh in the early nineteenth century. He is said to have settled first at Khairpur during the reign of the Talpur ruler Mir Murad Ali Khan, carrying letters of introduction and support from the Sikh court of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, before moving on to Hyderabad around 1830.

Among the relics he is said to have carried and enshrined were hair said to be from Baba Sri Chand, a Nanak Shahi–era rupee, and a ring attributed to Guru Gobind Singh — objects still spoken of at the darbar today. In the course of his ministry he is credited with founding several Jagiasu *tikanas* (seats) beyond Hyderabad, including at Khairpur, Halani, and Kandyaro, before his death in 1877 at the age of about seventy.

None of the books consulted records Baba Gurpat Sahib, his lineage, his relics or his seats. Michel Boivin's study of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh notes, of the province rather than of the Sant, that after 1857 "many Kayasht migrated to work in the Princely States, including the Khairpur emirate in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 26, folio 13), and that under "the Talpur rule (1783–1843)" the Amils, the Hindu scribal class, "almost monopolized the function of kardar" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 44, folio 31).

## The Darbar and Its Trust

The present building at DB-80, Sirey Ghat is dated by community record to Vikram Samvat 1988 — 1931 in the Gregorian calendar — standing on a plot of some 595 square yards, and is maintained today as a registered charitable trust (*tikkano*) whose historic trusteeship is remembered under Bao Santokdas.

In addition to its worship hall, the darbar today also runs a modest vegetarian eatery and space for pilgrims to stay, with donors' names recorded on inscribed tiles — a continuation of the *langar*-adjacent hospitality long associated with Nanakpanthi and Sikh sant-shrines across Sindh.

## Community and Standing

The mandir forms part of a wider constellation of small Jagiasi and Nanakpanthi shrines scattered across the Dadu–Hyderabad belt of Sindh — the same milieu that produced the darbars of Sant Baba Bhagat Ram, Bhai Sant Thawan Das, and Gurdas Ram, all likewise registered with the Evacuee Trust Property Board. Its comparatively rich documentation — a named founder, a dated building, and a preserved lineage — makes it one of the better-attested sites in this cluster, even as the deeper historical record beyond community memory remains thin.

## The Path of Nanak in Sindh

The books say a good deal about the followers of Guru Nanak in Sindh, though nothing of this darbar. What follows is said of the province and its people.

**A dominant path.** "In nineteenth-century Sindh," Boivin writes, "the Nanakpanth, or 'the path of Nanak', was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 90, folio 77). Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups, he says, "two main cults were followed: the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth", the second "based on the deification of the Indus River" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). "In Sindh, many Nanakpanthis belonged to a subgroup known as the Udasis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 53, folio 40). An endnote adds that "The Udasis of Sindh are coined as being a heterodox Sikh tradition, in one of the very few, if not the sole, academic papers devoted to the Nanakpanth in Sindh (Jatt 2016)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 209, folio 196).

**Hindu or Sikh.** Schaflechner writes that "Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, somewhat obscuring their religious affiliation for the colonial officers. Hence, in the 1881 census, Lohanas from Shikarpur and Hyderabad were counted as Sikhs, while ten years later, in the 1891 census, they were classified as Hindus (Lari 1994, 211f.)" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 80, folio not stated). Today, he observes, "many middle- and upper-class Hindus in Sindh are followers of the Nanak paṃth" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 257, folio not stated), and "it is common to cover one's head before walking into a tikānā (Sin.), the temple containing the Guru Granth Sahib" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 286, folio not stated). Boivin describes the outcome of the Singh Sabha process: "The Sindhi Nanakpanthis were thus not included in the Sikh community, and they identified themselves as being a Hindu religious sect" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 200, folio 187). He adds that "Due to the spread of the Nanakpanth in Sindh, the Hindu Sufis were very familiar with Sikh terminology", and that "in Sindh, the groups of Sufis and Nanakpanthis did not have a central organization ruling an encompassing body of followers" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 202, folio 189).

**Nanak Panthis today.** Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* writes that the Nanak Panthi Sikhs "belong to the areas of South Punjab and Sindh", that their temples there hold portraits of Guru Nanak alongside Hindu deities, and that "They are found in very large numbers in the province of Sindh" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* he writes that the communities who refused the Khalsa and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak "still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Baptised Sikhs look down upon them"; at Manora he saw them "now merging into the larger groups of Sikhs" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 230, folio 204). He also records the tradition that "Nanak visited Uch Sharif on his way to Sindh, towards the end of his travels" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).

**Nanak and the Sufi poets.** Boivin reports Jotwani's description of Shah Abdul Latif and Sachal as "the late participaters in the Bhakti movement which had a major impact in Sindh through the spread of Guru Nanak's teaching" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 91, folio 78).

## The Darbar in Sindh

The word by which this site is also known has a history of its own in the province. "In Sindh, another Persian word was mostly used, that of darbar", Boivin writes, and "In Sindh, the darbar was the sacred territory in which the Sufi culture was at work"; it was a term "used by the Sikhs, the Muslims and the Hindus" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 37–38, folios 24–25). British colonization, he argues, brought "a renewal of religiosity in relation to the spread of a composite middle class. It was marked by the emergence of the darbars, spreading a darbar culture" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 64, folio 51).

The Nanakpanthi darbars belong to that story. The religious recomposition of colonial Sindh "is attested to by the creation and the development of several important Nanakpanthi darbars throughout Sindh", and "although some darbars had been created in the late eighteenth century, there was a renaissance of the Nanakpanthi darbars in the second half of the nineteenth century" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 53–54, folios 40–41). His conclusion restates it: "Sindh was submitted to a religious recomposition in the late nineteenth century and early twentieth century, as is attested by the building of many new Nanakpanthi darbars all over Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 199, folio 186).

After Partition, Boivin writes, "The darbars in Sindh were most of the time preserved with different arrangements regarding their management", often with Indian *gaddi nashins* or followers paying keepers, and "despite the fluctuant diplomatic relations between Pakistan and India, it was always possible to travel across the border" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55). The darbars that the migrants founded in India, he notes, "are not centred on tombs, unlike those of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 131, folio 118). In Sindh itself, Schaflechner records government funding seen "in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh within the past decade" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 16, folio not stated).

## Setting: Hyderabad

The books speak of Hyderabad as a city, and say nothing of Sirey Ghat or of this darbar. What follows is said of the city.

**The Talpur capital.** Boivin calls Hyderabad "the late capital of the independent Sindh before the British conquest" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 30, folio 17). Of a Hindu holy man of the city he writes that Dalpat Sufi "founded an astano, a place of residence for a renunciant, in Hyderabad, on the Sipahimalani Lane. He is said to have attracted many followers, Muslims and Hindus, and the Talpur mirs are said to have looked after it"; after his death it "became a pilgrimage centre under the guidance of his successor, Keshavram Sipahimalani. The place was known as Guru Sehwani's place" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 118, folio 105). His own note qualifies this: "Apparently, he used to stay in a place in Hyderabad which can be called a darbar" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 209, folio 196). "The Sipahimalanis were a well-known Amil family of Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 119, folio 106).

**The Amils of Hyderabad.** Several of Boivin's Hindu Sufis came from the city. Hiranand Advani "was born in Hyderabad in a family of Khudabadi Amils" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 103, folio 90); Molchand Kripalani was "born in Hyderabad in 1887 in a Krishnaite family (Kripalani 1986: 3)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 123, folio 110); Mulchand "studied up to class 6 at the Hiranand Academy in Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 59, folio 46); and "In 1901, aged 22, Rochaldas married and settled in Hyderabad to enrol as a student at the medical college of the city" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43). Boivin speaks of "the role played by the Hyderabadi Amils in the spread of the Sufi culture", while suggesting that the devotional centres of Sindh may have shifted north after the British conquest (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 60, folio 47). Brahmashankar Mishra spent years in Karachi and Hyderabad, yet "no formal relation between Sindh and the Hindu branch of the Naqshbandiyya has been found" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 26, folio 13).

**Theosophy.** Annie Besant, known in Sindh as Basanti Devi, "visited this city as well as Hyderabad, where she delivered a number of lectures", and "in Hyderabad, her speech was about Hindu religion (Sadhu Vaswani 2001: 31)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 46–47, folios 33–34). Of one of the figures he follows, Boivin writes that "the printing house he founded in Hyderabad was named Blavatsky Printing" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 48, folio 35).

**Sufi shrines of the city.** Boivin names "Tando Jahaniyya in Hyderabad" as one of three Sufi traditions among the Hindu Sufis (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 60, folio 47). Qutub Ali Shah "was a famous Sufi from Hyderabad… His dargah is located in Jahaniyya, a neighbourhood in Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 95, folio 82), and its *sajjada nashin* came "from Pakistan twice, in 1957 and in 1980" to perform the *dastarbandi* ceremony for two of the figures Boivin follows (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 167, folio 154). Shemeem Burney Abbas records of one community of musicians that "Their pir (spiritual mentor) is Qutb Din Darya, whose shrine is called Tando Jahana and is in the Civil Lines at Hyderabad" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 71, folio not stated). Annemarie Schimmel uses the city as a landmark: Shah Abdul Latif was born "in Hala, near present-day Hyderabad-Sind" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 421, folio 390), and Jhok is "not far from Hyderabad" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397).

**A city of music and print.** For Abbas, Hyderabad is the centre of Sindhi devotional music on the air. The singer Taj Mastani left Sehwan for it "because it is a large urban center", and "affirmed that in Hyderabad she can earn a living from the radio" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 34, 63, folios not stated). "within areas such as Hyderabad or Faisalabad the local recording companies have assisted women musicians in earning a living from recording their Sufi lyrics with music" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 35, folio not stated). At Radio Pakistan Hyderabad, its director Sikander Baloch and music director Naseer Mirza told her that "they no longer have to go to melās at the Sufi shrines to hunt for talent" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 80, folio not stated). "there are two gharānās in Hyderabad—the Indore gharānā and the Gawalior gharānā" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 61, folio not stated), and the singer Zeena Bai "is buried in the Hyderabad graveyard where all the great musicians of the city are buried" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 62, folio not stated). "The Institute of Sindhology in Hyderabad, Sind, is one such source" for the documentation of Sindhi Sufi music (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 175, folio not stated).

The city is also a place of Sindhi publishing. "The Shah Waliul-lah Academy in Hyderabad, Sind, under the presidency of Maulana Ghulam Mustafa Qasimi, has published a number of Wallullah's works, as well as studies about him." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 403, folio 372). Schimmel's *As Through a Veil* lists the Sindhi Adabi Board of Hyderabad as the publisher of five Baloch volumes of 1960–1962 (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 314, folio 296), and Hyderabad as the place of Lilaram Watanmal's 1889 biography of Shah Abdul Latif (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 308, folio 290). Kasmani writes that "Starting in the 1960s, the Sindhi-language newspaper Daily Ibrat (published in Hyderabad) started to report the ʿurs at Sehwan in great detail." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 189, folio 172, ch. 1 n. 29).

**Pilgrims and violence.** Schaflechner names Hyderabad as a source of *mīlād-al-nabī* and *ʿāśūrah* visitors to Hinglaj (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 272, folio not stated) and of *ʿīd* and *muḥarram* pilgrims (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 291, folio not stated). He reports the attack on an unnamed temple in Hyderabad on 28 March 2014 (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 17, folio not stated), and quotes K. R. Malkani, "a Sindhi in exile who, as a Hindu, left Hyderabad after Partition and settled in New Delhi" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 87, folio not stated). Boivin recalls "the railway line which formerly connected Hyderabad (Sindh) to Barmer and Jodhpur" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 189, folio 176).

## Setting: Sindh

The books' accounts of the province give the wider frame in which the darbar's tradition places its founder, a Sant who came from the Punjab to the Talpur courts of Sindh. They are said of the province, not of this site.

**Under the Talpurs.** Boivin asks, "How was the society of Sindh organized in 1843?" "Given the political domination of the Talpurs, the Baluchis were at the top of local society"; and "Before 1843, Muslims were divided between being Sunnis and Shiites. The Sunnis were in the majority, but the sovereigns, the Talpur, were themselves Shiites" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 38–41, folios 25–28). "In the Hindu society of Sindh", he writes, the Lohanas "represented half of the total Hindu population" and were divided into Amils and Bhaibands, and "The panchayat system prevailed among the Hindus of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 40–41, folios 27–28). Schaflechner quotes Burton that "a description of them [the Lohanas], therefore, will be a general portrait of the Sindh Hindoos" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 79, folio not stated). Schimmel records that the *hurr*, the disciples of the Pir Pagaro, were "gathered first to support Ahmad Brelwi's struggle against the Sikh (1829-31) and later actively joined in the struggle against the British" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 427, folio 396).

**Under the British.** "Sindhi continued to flourish after the British occupation in 1843", Schimmel writes, and "The country had always been proud of its mystical heritage. Did not Diwan Gidumal, the minister, give the invading Nadir Shah (1739) the most precious treasure Sind had to offer, some of the dust of its saints?" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 427, folio 396). Robert Rozehnal quotes Katherine Ewing that "British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sind, was to treat them in essentially the same way that landlords and tribal leaders were treated" — them being the hereditary saints (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 33, folio 23). Boivin reports Narsain's statement that "the integration of Sufism inside of the religious environment of the Hindu Sindhis dates back to the nineteenth century, and that the main actors involved were the Amils, the literary class" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 27, folio 14), and writes that "In the religiosity of Sindh, the devotional relationship of a follower with a spiritual Master was prevalent, rather than the focus being on affiliation to an institutionalized religion" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38).

**Partition.** "By early November of 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail. As of 1 January 1948, it was estimated that nearly 500,000 people had sought refuge in India." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49). Schaflechner writes that "The departure of the Hindu elite and the influx of Muslim refugees (“Muhajirs”) from India dramatically altered the local demography" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 87, folio not stated). After Partition, Boivin writes, "Molchand was worried that it was difficult for Hindu Sindhi Sufis to pay a visit to the Sufi places in Sindh, now in Pakistan" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 124, folio 111).

**The Hindus of Sindh today.** "Although a large majority of Hindus have migrated to India from 1947 onwards, Sindh is the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 176–177, folios not stated and 164). Schaflechner calls Sindh "home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Khalid writes that "The majority of the Hindu community is based in Sindh and Southern Punjab, where they have a proportionate representation from the lower and the upper castes" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 233, folio not stated). The formula *Sab ka malik ek hai*, Boivin observes, "has for some years been very popular among the Hindus of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173).

**The older Sindh.** Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, composed under Aurangzeb, describes the Mughal suba of Thatta. Its greatest river, it says, is the Indus, "بزرگ ترین دریائے سند است", by which merchants from Multan and Bhakkar ship goods to Thatta; it gives the suba's length "از بهکر تا کچ مکران" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 529), and records that "اکثر مدار بر کشتی است", most traffic going by boat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 530).

**A song of the province.** Abbas records Alan Faqir reciting a line that he read as a statement about Sindh; her note explains that "'Sind is not the amir' means that Sind is not in the position of leadership or amirship" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 210–211, folios not stated):

*Punnu is not in the Kec / Sind is not the amir* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 156, folio not stated)

Of his land he said in the same interview: "It has been looted—it has been plundered—it has been assaulted—but it goes on—it has not died—it will not die—it has existed for centuries and it shall exist—Sindhri is beaten—and yet Sindhri goes on" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 156–157, folios not stated); "Sindhri", her note explains, is "A name used for Sind in the poetic traditions" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 210–211, folios not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Hindu or Sikh.** The site's account calls the darbar a Nanakpanthi shrine registered as a mandir, and its Sant a spiritual descendant of Guru Nanak through Baba Sri Chand's Udasi line. Schaflechner records that Lohanas of Hyderabad who followed Nanak were counted as Sikhs in the census of 1881 and as Hindus in that of 1891 (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 80, folio not stated). Boivin writes that the Sindhi Nanakpanthis "identified themselves as being a Hindu religious sect" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 200, folio 187), and reports Jatt's description of the Udasis of Sindh as "a heterodox Sikh tradition" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 209, folio 196). Khalid calls the same communities Nanak Panthi Sikhs (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated), and writes that "Baptised Sikhs look down upon them" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 230, folio 204).
- **The name of the seat.** The site's account calls the Sant's seats *tikanas* and the trust a *tikkano*, and spells the lineage both Jagiasi and Jagiasu. Schaflechner writes *tikānā*, "the temple containing the Guru Granth Sahib" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 286, folio not stated). Boivin writes *darbar*, a term "used by the Sikhs, the Muslims and the Hindus" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 37–38, folios 24–25).
- **The Sufi shrine of Tando Jahaniyya.** Boivin places the dargah of Qutub Ali Shah "in Jahaniyya, a neighbourhood in Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 95, folio 82). Abbas names Qutb Din Darya as the pir "whose shrine is called Tando Jahana and is in the Civil Lines at Hyderabad" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 71, folio not stated). Neither book says whether the two are one shrine.
- **How many Hindus live in Pakistan.** Schaflechner puts Pakistan's Hindus at "between 6 and 10 million people—an estimate that varies widely according to the source" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "the Sindhi Hindus number several millions, with a majority of them belonging to the so-called scheduled castes" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 175, folio 162). Khalid gives no figure, citing the census of 1998 for the Hindus as the country's largest minority (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated).
- **How many Hindus left Sindh at Partition.** Boivin reckons the migrants "would have been closer to 0.8 million, if not less", while noting that "there is a kind of consensus that they numbered around 1 million" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48).
- **Caste in Sindh.** Boivin writes that "Frequently, the claim arises that there was no caste system in Sindh", and that "it is possible that Sindh hosted a specific social fabric", while the colonial power renewed that fabric (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 36–37, folio not stated / folio 24). Schaflechner quotes Thakur that the "[c]aste system is almost absent in Sind", and links that perception to Sindhi nationalist discourse, which Dalit organizations oppose (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 277–278, folio not stated).
- **Whether Sindh was free of communal strife.** Schaflechner calls the common notion of "the harmonious coexistence of the religions" in Sindh "merely a nationalist utopian ideal" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 90–91, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "even if it never reached the level of violence in Punjab, it is irrelevant to claim there was no communal violence in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49), while arguing that "the Sufi culture still pervades Sindhi society" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 177, folio 164).

## A Note on the Sources

Much of what is recorded here rests on the darbar's own community tradition as related in recent press coverage rather than independent archival verification. The identification of the ETPB-registered "Guru Gurpat Mandir, DB-80 Sirey Ghat" with the Baba Gurpat Sahib darbar described in that coverage is highly probable — same name, same locality — but not explicitly cross-confirmed in a single authoritative source. Dates and figures should be read with this in mind.

The books cited above do not close that gap. None of them names the mandir, its Sant or its quarter; what they offer is the history of the Nanakpanth and the darbar in Sindh, and of Hyderabad and the province, against which the darbar's own account can be read.
