Name: Jagannath Temple, Sialkot
Location: Paris Road, Mohallah Puran Nagar, Sialkot, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Community worship; no fixed festival documented
Description:
## Overview

On Paris Road, in the Mohallah Puran Nagar area of Sialkot's commercial quarter, stands a Hindu temple referred to locally as the Jagannath Temple — a considerably more recent structure than, and a separate building from, the ancient Shivala (Shawala) Teja Singh Temple in Sialkot's Mohallah Dharowal. The two are sometimes conflated in secondary sources — an English Wikipedia article titled "Jagannath Temple, Sialkot" redirects to the Teja Singh temple's page — but the facts recorded for each, location, founding circumstances, and history, do not overlap, and this entry treats them as distinct pending stronger evidence otherwise.

## Founding

Community and press accounts describe the Paris Road temple as built, or substantially re-established, in early 2007, with a grant of roughly Rs 200,000 from the Punjab provincial government under then-Chief Minister Chaudhry Pervaiz Elahi. The grant is reported to have been channelled through a minority-seat provincial legislator, Joseph Hakim Din, at the advocacy of Hakem Ratan Lal Bhagat of Sialkot's District Peace Committee, on behalf of the city's Hindu residents. A further renovation, funded by a roughly Rs 2,000,000 Punjab government grant, is reported for 2017.

## Community and Use

The temple serves Sialkot's small resident Hindu community as a place of worship in a city whose Hindu population, once substantial, was overwhelmingly displaced at Partition. Its modern, grant-funded origins make it emblematic of the more recent, state-assisted rebuilding of minority worship spaces in Punjab's cities, distinct from older survivors like Shivala Teja Singh that predate 1947.

## A Note on the Sources

Much of what is reported about this temple circulates through a small number of near-identical web accounts rather than independent documentation, and no primary institutional record — comparable to the Evacuee Trust Property Board's role at Shivala Teja Singh — has been located confirming its founding or administration. The dates and figures above should be treated as provisional until corroborated by a more authoritative source.

## Bibliography

- Community and press accounts of Hindu temple grants in Sialkot under the Pervaiz Elahi provincial government (2007) and subsequent renovation (2017).
- Odishabytes, "There's a Jagannath Temple in Pakistan (and Bangladesh) too."
- Wikipedia, "Shivala Teja Singh temple," for contrast; the redirect from "Jagannath Temple, Sialkot" reflects an unresolved identification, not a confirmed identity between the two sites.

Name: Jain Mandir, Lahore
Location: Lytton Road, Old Anarkali, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Reopened for active worship 2022; no fixed public festival calendar
Description:
On Lytton Road in Old Anarkali, directly opposite the Anarkali station of the Orange Line Metro Train, stands the Jain Mandir, one of the last physical reminders of Lahore's once-substantial Jain community. Built around 1940 to serve the city's Bhabra Jain merchant families — Punjab having historically been home to a significant Jain trading population — the temple follows a shikhara-style form typical of North Indian Jain architecture and was dedicated to the veneration of the Tirthankaras, the enlightened teacher-figures central to Jain belief and practice. Like much of Lahore's pre-Partition religious minority heritage, the temple fell into disuse after 1947, when the great majority of the city's Jain and Hindu population departed for India. Its most severe blow came in 1992, when it was heavily vandalised in retaliation for the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, India, leaving the building damaged and effectively abandoned for three decades. The turning point came in December 2021, when Pakistan's Supreme Court ordered its restoration, leading to an eight-month conservation effort. The temple reopened in June 2022, allowing religious use to resume after a hiatus of roughly thirty years — an unusual and widely reported instance in Pakistan of an active return to worship, rather than mere heritage preservation, at a minority religious site. Though Jainism has only a residual presence in contemporary Pakistan, the temple's revival has been framed in Pakistani and international press as a significant, if modest, gesture of religious pluralism, and the building today stands as a rare functioning Jain place of worship anywhere in the country, embedded within the dense, historically layered streetscape of Old Anarkali. Independent, established-press reporting adds further precision to this account: Dawn's Sheharyar Rizwan reports that the temple was "constructed by a woman with her own resources in 1940," though her name is not recorded in the surviving coverage, and that after the 1992 attack "the temple's canopy was the only piece of the original structure that survived"; its ruins then lay neglected for over two decades until, in 2016, the remaining site was enclosed behind a boundary wall and the land given away to the Orange Line Metro Train project. The Supreme Court's restoration order, issued in December 2021 by then Chief Justice Gulzar Ahmed, came a day before the nineteenth anniversary of the Babri Masjid's demolition and was reported by the Express Tribune to run alongside a parallel restoration case for Lahore's Neela Gumbad (Blue Tomb); of at least a dozen Jain temples once standing in the city, per Youlin Magazine, this is the sole survivor, and it is not listed among the Punjab Archaeology Department's own "Religious Monuments."

## Bibliography
- Sheharyar Rizwan, "Under-reconstruction Jain Mandir in Lahore all set to reopen," *Dawn*, 1 April 2022.
- "Pakistan set to reopen Lahore's famous Jain temple," *The Express Tribune*, 5 December 2021.
- Muhammad Asif Nawaz, "Story of the Jain Mandir," *Youlin Magazine*, 20 July 2022.
qa_note: Sources disagree slightly on the exact construction period: Dawn (1 April 2022) states the temple was built specifically "in 1940," while Youlin Magazine (20 July 2022) hedges that "it is safe to assume it came about in late 1930s or early 1940s"; neither source names the woman credited with funding its construction, and this is reported rather than resolved. Separately, Dawn's April 2022 report quotes ETPB's Faraz Abbas estimating restoration completion "in just over a month" (around May 2022) with "over 70pc" of work then done; no source verified in this research pass confirms whether that timeline held, so the June 2022 reopening date given elsewhere in this entry is not independently reconfirmed here.

Name: Jhollay Lal Mandir
Location: Darya Lal Street, Jodia Bazaar, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Cheti Chand
Description:
## Overview

On Darya Lal Street in Jodia Bazaar, in Karachi's old commercial quarter near Sarafa Bazaar, stands a modest Hindu temple known locally as the Jhulay Lal Mandir (or Jhollay Lal Mandir) — a shrine distinct from, though dedicated to the same venerated figure as, the larger and better-known Darya Lal Sankat Mochan Mandir near the Custom House and Native Jetty, several kilometres away in Saddar. Both temples honour Jhulelal (also called Darya Lal or Udero Lal), the Sindhi water-saint revered by Hindus as an incarnation of Varuna, but they are separate buildings on separate streets, serving separate congregations.

## A Lasi Community Shrine

The Jodia Bazaar temple has historically been maintained by Karachi's Lasi Hindu community — families whose origins lie in Lasbela district, Balochistan — distinct from the fisherfolk congregation of Mohalla Mahigir associated with the Custom House temple. It is a comparatively small, square structure housing a hall and devotional images, with a rooftop swing (*jhula*) from which the deity's popular name is drawn, evoking the swing on which the saint is depicted in devotional imagery.

## Rites and Observance

Like other Jhulelal shrines across Sindh and the Sindhi diaspora, the temple's principal occasion is Cheti Chand, the spring new-year festival marking Jhulelal's birth, when the Lasi community and other Sindhi Hindus gather for prayer, a procession, and veneration of the *baharana sahib*, the ritual water vessel.

## Distinguishing from the Custom House Temple

Because "Jhulelal," "Darya Lal," and "Udero Lal" are used interchangeably for the same venerated figure, and because Karachi's most heavily documented Jhulelal shrine is the Darya Lal Sankat Mochan Mandir near the Custom House, the Jodia Bazaar temple is easily overlooked or conflated with it. Field documentation of Karachi's Hindu temples, however, records them as two separate buildings on two separate streets, each with its own congregation.

## Present State

Documentation of the temple's founding date and building history is thin; what is recorded is its continued use by the Lasi community and its part, alongside the Custom House temple, in Karachi's Cheti Chand observances.

## Bibliography

- Udero Lal Research Project, field documentation of Karachi's Jhulelal temples — Jodia Bazaar and Custom House sites (2016).
- Wikipedia, "Darya Lal Mandir," for contrast with the Custom House site.
- General accounts of Sindhi Hindu Cheti Chand observance and the Jhulelal/Udero Lal tradition.

Name: Kalat Kali Temple
Founded/Opened: traditionally said to be about 1,500 years old (Sewa dynasty, pre-Islamic era); exact date unknown
Events: Annual three-day Kali festival (January)
Description:
## Overview

In the Shahi Bazaar of Kalat — the ancient hill-town of central Balochistan that was for centuries the seat of the Khanate of Kalat — stands a Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Kali. Local tradition holds the shrine to be of great antiquity, with some accounts tracing its origins to the pre-Islamic Sewa dynasty period and claiming an age of some 1,500 years; no dated inscription or independent historical record has been located to confirm so early a founding, and the claim is best treated as devotional tradition rather than settled fact.

## A Living Shrine in a Historic Bazaar

The temple's presence within the working fabric of Kalat's old bazaar reflects a resident Hindu trading community that has occupied the town's commercial life alongside its Baloch and Brahui neighbours, a pattern of minority presence in Balochistan's interior towns that predates the modern state and has persisted, in much reduced form, into the present.

## Festival and Pilgrimage

The temple's clearest claim to wider recognition is its annual three-day Kali festival, held each January, which draws Hindu pilgrims from across Pakistan and, on occasion, from India — a notable instance of cross-border devotional travel to a small provincial shrine.

Independent confirmation of the temple's antiquity comes from the colonial-era *Ethnographic Survey of Baluchistan* (1913), which records the Kalat shrine as "probably the oldest place of Hindu worship" in the region and describes a perpetual lamp, or *jōt*, kept burning day and night, its oil historically supplied by the state itself. Press coverage of the temple's 2023 festival reports that it houses the second-largest Kali statue in Asia, and a 2017 profile found its rites then led by a young priest, Maharaj Sain Shamgir, before a congregation of about 35 worshippers, with Kalat city's own Hindu population put at some 200 households — of an estimated 100 families who had migrated elsewhere, roughly 80 were reported to have since returned. That same 2017 account also recorded a local priest's tradition that the city of Kalat itself takes its name from a Hindu ruler he called "Kalat Seva" — a separate oral tradition, distinct from the Sewa-dynasty founding narrative above, and not independently corroborated.

Name: Kali Bari Mandir
Events: Durga Puja; daily worship
Description:
## Overview

The Kali Bari Mandir is a Hindu temple in the cantonment of Peshawar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, dedicated to the goddess *Kali*. Its name — literally the "house of Kali", in an idiom associated with the Bengali Hindu communities that once served in the garrisons and administrations of British India — points to the diverse origins of the Hindu population that gathered in the frontier city. Today it is one of a very small number of functioning Hindu temples in Peshawar, and among the few that remain in daily use.

## Kali Worship on the Frontier

*Kali*, the fierce and protective form of the great goddess, has long been venerated across the subcontinent, and her worship reached the north-western frontier through the merchants, soldiers and officials who settled in Peshawar. The temple's principal festival is *Durga Puja*, the autumn celebration of the goddess in her many aspects, which remains the high point of its devotional calendar. The precise date of the temple's foundation is not securely recorded; like many shrines of the cantonment, it is best understood as a creation of the colonial and pre-Partition era, when Peshawar sustained a substantial and varied Hindu community.

## A Surviving Temple of Peshawar

The Hindu heritage of Peshawar, once considerable, was gravely diminished by the upheavals of 1947 and the decades that followed, and many temples were abandoned, converted or lost. Against this background the Kali Bari Mandir has acquired particular importance as a survivor. It is generally counted, together with the *Dargah* of Pir Ratan Nath in Jhanda Bazaar, among the very few temples of Peshawar still in regular worship. Others of the city's historic shrines have fared less well: the ancient Gorakhnath temple at Gor Khatri, for instance, was for long closed and, following legal intervention, is opened chiefly once a year at *Diwali*. The Kali Bari's continued daily use therefore makes it a rare living centre of Hindu devotion in the provincial capital.

## Renovation and Revival

In recent years the community has worked to renew the temple. A programme of renovation begun in 2017 included the building of a *langar* hall for the communal meal, the replacement of the roof, the repair of the domes and the installation of a new *kalash*, the finial that crowns a Hindu shrine. These works, modest in scale but significant in meaning, reflect both the small size and the resilience of the Hindu population that maintains the temple, and the importance attached to keeping its worship alive.

## Legacy

The Kali Bari Mandir stands as a quiet emblem of continuity in a city where Hindu life has been much reduced. As one of the last temples of Peshawar in daily use, it preserves the worship of the goddess on the frontier and offers a gathering place for a community determined to sustain its traditions. For the study of the religious history of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa it is a valuable witness to the plural past of Peshawar and to the endurance of its Hindu heritage into the present day.

Name: Kalka Cave Temple (Asthan of Kalka Devi)
Events: First Monday of each month; major goddess festivals
Description:
## Overview

The Kalka Devi Cave Temple is one of the most venerated Hindu shrines of Sindh, set within a natural cavern in the limestone hills of the Rohri plateau, about a mile south of the ruins of ancient *Aror* (Alor), the pre-Islamic capital of Sindh, near Sukkur. Dedicated to the goddess *Kalka Devi* — a form of *Kali* — the cave draws pilgrims from across Pakistan and, when circumstances allow, from India, and is remarkable for the reverence it commands among local Muslims as well as Hindus.

## Aror and the Sacred Cave

The setting is steeped in antiquity. Aror was the seat of the Rai and Brahman dynasties of Sindh and the capital of Raja Dahir at the time of the Arab conquest in the early eighth century; the shifting of the Indus away from the city in the historic period left its ruins stranded on the edge of the Rohri limestone escarpment. Within these hills, a natural cave has long been held sacred to the goddess. The present temple complex — the shrine chamber deep in the cave together with the rooms, halls and lodgings built around and before it — is generally attributed to the 1920s and to the patronage of a devotee named Hemraj Kewalramani, though the sanctity of the site is understood by its devotees to be immeasurably older. The built fabric blends Hindu iconography with the arches and ornament of regional Islamic architecture, a hallmark of Sindhi sacred building.

## Mythology and the Hinglaj Connection

According to the legend cherished at the shrine, the goddess *Kalka Devi* halted here, or made her appearance, while journeying to the great *Shakti Peetha* of *Hinglaj Mata* in the mountains of Balochistan — binding this cave into the wider sacred geography of Devi worship that stretches across Sindh and Balochistan. The temple's caretakers relate that two tunnels within the cave are said to lead, by hidden ways, to Hinglaj itself; such traditions, common to cave shrines, are best understood as expressions of devotional imagination rather than literal topography. The association with Hinglaj places Kalka Devi within the same current of pilgrimage that culminates in the *Hinglaj Yatra*, one of the most important observances of Pakistan's Hindu community.

## Devotional Life

The rhythm of worship at Kalka Devi is marked above all by the gathering of devotees on the evening of the first Monday of each month, and by far larger crowds at the great festivals of the goddess, when many rooms built around the cave serve to lodge pilgrims who arrive in their thousands. That the shrine is frequented by Muslims as well as Hindus — indeed, local accounts hold that Muslim visitors are often in the majority — reflects the shared reverence for holy places that has long characterised the Indus valley, where a sacred site may transcend the boundaries of formal religion.

## Legacy

As a living shrine of undoubted antiquity, the Kalka Devi Cave Temple is among the most significant Hindu sites in northern Sindh, complementing the great riverine temple of Sadhu Bela at nearby Sukkur. It has in recent years faced threats from illegal quarrying and hill-cutting in the Rohri hills, prompting appeals for its protection as both a religious and a heritage site. For the Hindu community of Sindh it remains a place of pilgrimage and continuity; for historians it is a tangible link to the deep pre-Islamic past of Aror and the enduring worship of the goddess in the land of the Indus.

## Bibliography

- Endowment Fund Trust for Preservation of the Heritage of Sindh, "Heritage of Sindh" documentation.
- *The Friday Times* and *The Express Tribune*, features on the Kalka Devi Temple, Rohri.
- H. T. Lambrick, *Sindh: A General Introduction* (Sindhi Adabi Board), on Aror and the historical geography of the Rohri region.
- Wikipedia, "Kalka Cave Temple" and "Aror (Alor)" (with cited sources).

Name: Katas Raj Temples
Location: Choa Saidanshah, Chakwal District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Maha Shivratri; periodic cross-border pilgrimage
Description:
## Overview

The Katas Raj Temples (*Qila Katas*) form one of the most venerable Hindu sacred complexes in Pakistan, set amid the arid folds of the Salt Range in the Potohar Plateau, near the town of Choa Saidanshah in Chakwal District, Punjab. Perched at roughly 2,000 feet, the site clusters a group of ancient shrines around a spring-fed emerald pond, the *Katas kund*, whose waters Hindus revere as profoundly holy. A short distance to the south-west stands a second cluster known as the *Satghara*, or "seven temples", the architectural and ceremonial heart of the complex. Occupied across many centuries and many faiths, Katas Raj preserves layers of Buddhist, Hindu Shahi, Sikh and later occupation, making it at once a *tirtha* (place of pilgrimage), an archaeological palimpsest, and a poignant emblem of the subcontinent's shared heritage.

Three of the books consulted name the site itself. Haroon Khalid, who writes of it in two books, calls it 'Katas Raj or Killa Katas', or simply Katas, and gives a chapter to it under the title "Shivratri at Killa Katas" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 5, folio not stated; p. 45, folio not stated). He describes it as "a holy site for thousands of years" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated), and in *Walking with Nanak* he calls Katas Raj, in the voice of his reconstruction of Guru Nanak's time, "the holiest of holy temples in Punjab", "a collection of temples located around a sacred pond" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210). Harish Dhillon's retelling of the *Janamsakhis*, the traditional lives of Guru Nanak, names 'Katasraj' among the shrines Nanak and Mardana visited (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 224, folio 246). Khalid places the complex "Situated near the small town of Kalar Kahar" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated), and, in his later book, a few kilometres from Kallar Kahar on the Motorway (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219); the present account gives the nearby town as Choa Saidanshah, and both placings are set out below under the sources' disagreements.

Khalid's two visits frame most of what the books record. In *A White Trail* he reports the Shivratri of "2nd March 2011", when Hindu pilgrims from across Pakistan came to the pond (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 47, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* he returns years later, "driving back to Islamabad after a weekend in Lahore", to look for the place where Guru Nanak is remembered at Katas (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219).

## Mythology and the Tears of Shiva

The sanctity of Katas rests above all upon the sacred pond and the legend attached to it. According to Puranic tradition, when the goddess Sati immolated herself, her consort Shiva was plunged into such inconsolable grief that he wandered the earth weeping. His tears, it is said, fell to form two sacred pools: one at Pushkar in Rajasthan, and the other here at Katas. The very name is popularly derived from the Sanskrit *kataksha*, meaning "tearful eyes" or "raining eyes", a poetic echo of the god's sorrow. The pond is thus held to be filled with the grief of Shiva himself, and bathing in its waters is believed to cleanse the pilgrim of sin.

Khalid gives the legend as the pilgrims and guides tell it. In *Walking with Nanak* the pool, "constructed in the shape of an eye", "was created when Lord Shiva shed a tear after his wife Sati passed away, or so the story goes", and the tear "could wash away the gravest of sins" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210); earlier in the same book the pond is "considered to have been filled up by a tear drop of Lord Shiva" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3). On his last visit he writes of "The sacred pond, believed to be the tear of Lord Shiva" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).

In *A White Trail* the legend comes from Shakeel, a young guide at the site, who tells visitors that the Hindus believe the pond was formed from a tear Shiva shed at the death of Sati (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). Shakeel's version names a second pond, not at Pushkar but in India at Ajmer: the pond is "in the shape of an eye", from Shiva's tear, and "Another tear fall in Ajmer Sharif, India, where there is another ancient pond" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). He also warns: "No one knows how deep it is", and adds that "There are poisonous lizards and snakes living inside" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). He tells tourists, too, a story of Ganesh as "the son of the Hindu God, Shiva" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated).

Beside the myth Shakeel keeps what Khalid calls his own "truth": that the whole place was once "under the sea", and that the pond was formed when the land emerged. As evidence he points to a leaf fossil, and to a "fauna fossil" in a cave "across the road from the complex", a cave with stalactites (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). Elsewhere Khalid names Katas with Hinglaj as an ancient Hindu temple and place of pilgrimage around which "Such myths have developed" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated).

## The Pandavas and the Epic

Katas is also woven into the great epic tradition. According to legend, the region corresponds to the *Dvaitavana* of the *Mahabharata*, and the Satghara is traditionally identified as the place where the five Pandava brothers made their home during a portion of their twelve-year exile. It is here, tradition holds, that the celebrated dialogue of the *Yaksha Prashna* unfolded, when a *yaksha* guarding the waters posed a series of riddles to the Pandavas, testing the wisdom of Yudhishthira. Such associations gave the site enduring prestige among pilgrims across the subcontinent.

Khalid records the tradition in a different form: "It is believed that these temples were constructed by the Pandavs [OCR?] brothers when they were sent on a thirteen year exile", after the Kauravas had taken the throne, and "In the Mahabharata these temples are mentioned as sacred spaces" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210). In *A White Trail* the guide Shakeel dates the temples "from the time of the Mahabharata" and says the exiled Pandavas built them, a claim, Khalid writes, "confirmed by a blue board put up by the authorities here, noting the date of Mahabharata to be around 1500 BCE" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated).

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian history *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, in a passage about the Pandavas and not about Katas, carries the brothers through this part of the country at the end of their story. After Yudhishthira's abdication, at the coming of the age the book calls دور کلجگ, the five brothers and Draupadi went through Bengal, the Deccan, Gujarat and Dwarka, and then "سیر ولایت تهتهه[OCR?] و ملتان و پنجاب نموده", touring the lands of Thatta, Multan and Punjab, before going to the mountain of Badrinath (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 479). Bhandari says nothing more of these lands and names no temple in them.

## The Temple Complex and Architecture

The Satghara temples represent a distinctive regional building tradition, generally attributed to the Hindu Shahi (Odi Shahi) rulers who dominated the north-western subcontinent from roughly the seventh to the tenth centuries CE. The principal shrine, sometimes designated "Temple A" by surveyors, is dated to around the tenth century and executed in a Gandhara-influenced *Nagara* idiom, with squat proportions, trefoil-arched recesses and fluted decorative work characteristic of the Salt Range group. The temples are built of the local kanjur stone and were once richly plastered, some retaining traces of the fresco decoration that once enlivened their interiors.

The site's religious history reaches still deeper. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded a substantial Buddhist stupa in the vicinity, and the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham, who surveyed the complex as Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1872, likewise documented Buddhist remains alongside the Hindu shrines, confirming a long sequence of sacred occupation. A *baradari* (pillared pavilion) and other later structures cluster near the pond, and small residential quarters attest to the site's role as a living pilgrimage centre well into the modern era.

Khalid's first description of the complex is a list: "a natural pond, fossils dating back to millions of years, ancient caves, an unexcavated Buddhist stupa, Hindu temples said to be thousands of years old, and a university which attracted scholars from other parts of the world" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). There are "several small temples built around the pond, dedicated to the different Hindu deities"; "an iron fence protects the complex", with "only one entrance", though a visitor can also get in by "climbing the mound" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated).

The pond, in his account, is "turquoise" and "round". A rock divides off a small section of clear water "only three feet deep", and "Ancient buildings stand at the edge of the deeper end"; "The pond is clearly the lifeline of this complex. Numerous myths have developed around it" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). A photograph in the book carries the caption "The historical temple of Katas Raj with its emerald pool." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 106, folio not stated).

The Shiva shrine stands "next to the pool": "a small light brown building, with a small dome at the top", with "a wooden door, covered with floral decorations" and a marble floor, and at its centre "the Shivling"; it is "a small room, which can only accommodate about ten people" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 52, folio not stated). The temples themselves are "the three tall cone shaped structures" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated). Of their age Khalid sets two views side by side: the guide's, that they date "from the time of the Mahabharata", and his own, that "Experts say that these temples were constructed between the 7th and 10th century CE, when this area was under the influence of the Kashmiri kingdom" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* he calls them the Kashmiri temples dedicated to Shiva, "built in the seventh and eighth century" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).

The tallest building is a Sikh-period house: "the haveli of Hari Singh Nalwa, a general in the army of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1780-1839)", "the tallest here, standing like a cube with a small dome at the top". Inside, "The artwork has been recently renovated with depictions of Hindu deities on the walls", among them Ganesh and Krishna "playing the flute while he flirts with the maidens" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* the haveli of Hari Singh Nalwa stands in front, with the Shiva temples behind it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).

Next to the haveli is "a Buddhist stupa that has been partially excavated". Shakeel dates it "from the 3rd century BC, from the time of Taxila", and "More than half of the structure is still underground" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* Khalid writes of a "half excavated stupa" that is "at least four thousand years old", with "the temple dedicated to Ram" beside it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).

Across the road, on a mound, an "ancient staircase" leads up to "a newly constructed single storey rectangular structure" which Shakeel calls "the site of a world famous ancient Hindu university" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated). The building, put up "a few years ago", "acts as the Archaeology Department office" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* Khalid likewise places "the offices of the Archaeology Department" and "a small hotel" across the road from the pond (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).

## Al-Beruni and the Seat of Learning

The university on the mound carries one of the site's most repeated claims. According to Shakeel, "Al-Beruni, a Muslim scholar from the 11th century studied Hindu religion" there, and "calculated the radius of world" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated). Khalid takes up the story in his own voice: "Al-Beruni came to India during the first half of the 11th century, after the Muslim invader Shah Mahmood Ghaznvi attacked Punjab. Al-Beruni arrived at this temple, which was known as a seat of learning at that time. He spent several years here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated).

## Guru Nanak at Katas

Katas holds significance for Sikhs as well as Hindus. Tradition records that Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, visited the site, and a Gurdwara associated with his memory was later raised near the pond.

The books carry the visit in three forms. Dhillon's *Janamsakhis* has Nanak, on his return to the Punjab, visit with Mardana "the shrines of Tilla Balnath and Katasraj (both now in Pakistan)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 224, folio 246); on the same page the book has him take a south-eastern route back to the Punjab at the close of his fourth journey, around the time of Babur's third incursion into India (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 224, folio 246). Khalid, in *A White Trail*, writes that Guru Nanak "(1469-1539) also came here, as it was a popular destination for ascetics at that time", and cites for it Iqbal Qaiser's *Historical Sikh Shrines* (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* he writes that "historical records clearly state Nanak visited this sacred site" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219).

The third form is Khalid's own imagined scene, which he presents as reconstruction rather than record. He sets it at "the annual festival of Shivratri", on "a cold February night". Katas Raj, "Situated on the slope of the mountain", is a cluster of temples around the pond; the Shiva temple "at the edge of the pool" is "the most important temple here", and there are temples "dedicated to the goddesses Kali and Durga" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210). "Pilgrims from hundreds of kilometres away came here to purify their lives"; some devotees bathe the Shiva shrine "with milk" while others sing his praises, and offerings placed in the pond are carried off by a stream that runs into the mountains, a passage damaged in the printed text (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210). In "a small cave" sit "a few yogis, devotees of Lord Shiva", in meditation, while pilgrims climb to temples higher up (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 237, folio 211).

In that scene Nanak sits "inside the temple amongst the devotees", while Mardana waits on the neighbouring mountain, because "being a Muslim, Mardana would not have been allowed inside such a sacred Hindu space" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 237, folio 211). Khalid's reconstruction puts the temple "about fifty kos" from Talwandi, printed 'Talwindi' [OCR?], and has yogis whom Nanak had met there spend time at Katas (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 237, folio 211). Later in the same chapter he imagines Nanak at a Shiva temple that the book does not name or tie to Katas, where milk poured over the *lingam* runs out by "a small passageway" into a stream (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 240, folio not stated), the priest declares "Shiva has the power to destroy the world", Nanak calls it "one of the most sacred temples dedicated to Shiva" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 241, folio 215), and Nanak says: "My Shiva is the Supreme Creator" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 242, folio 216).

Katas enters Khalid's book once before Nanak himself. In his reconstruction of the lives of Nanak's parents, Tripta and her husband, on their way home from Tilla Jogian, "stopped at Katas Raj, where both of them took a dip in the holy pond" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3).

## The Search for Nanak's Gurdwara

Khalid's last visit is a search for the building that remembers Nanak. He had come "several times" before without seeing it. "A few years ago", when he came "to document the festival of Maha Shivratri", the local guide told him "there was no such building here"; yet, he writes, Iqbal Qaiser "had seen and photographed the place for his book" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219). This time, with his wife Anam, he stopped "to see Nanak's Gurdwara" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219).

Again a guide insisted: "There is no gurdwara here". Khalid telephoned Iqbal Qaiser, who told him, "It is next to the fort", and the only fort at Katas was one "built by Hari singh Nalwa" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221). The building he found "was at a little distance from the complex. It was not renovated as the rest of the complex was"; the path to it "had been neglected". It was "a big building, with several pillars that once supported a roof", but "The roof was now gone", and "a staircase leading nowhere" stood in it. It was "bigger than I had expected", and the guide told him: "We never knew what this building was" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221).

## Sikh Patronage

Under the Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century, the complex received renewed patronage, with repairs and plastering to the principal structures attributed to the noble Sardar Gulab Singh.

Khalid's books tie the Sikh period at Katas instead to Hari Singh Nalwa, Ranjit Singh's general, whose haveli is the tallest building in the complex (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated) and whose fort stands near the ruin of Nanak's gurdwara (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221). Of Ranjit Singh in general, and not of Katas, *Walking with Nanak* writes that when he "became the sovereign of Punjab at the end of the eighteenth century he spent large amounts of money on the renovation and expansion of many gurdwaras", and "attached vast tracts of land to these gurdwaras, so that the revenues from the lands could facilitate their functioning" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 34, folio 16). *A White Trail* calls him "the first Punjabi to rule Punjab", who renovated "many Gurdwaras all over Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 208, folio not stated).

## Partition, Neglect and Restoration

The Partition of 1947 severed the temples from their community of worshippers, and the site fell into prolonged neglect, its shrines decaying and its pond periodically depleted. In recent decades Katas has drawn renewed attention. In 2005 the Government of Pakistan undertook a programme of restoration, and cross-border pilgrimages by Hindu devotees from India have occasionally been permitted. Controversy has attended the site as well, notably concern over the alarming drop in the sacred pond's water level, attributed to industrial extraction by nearby cement factories, an issue that reached the country's Supreme Court.

Khalid tells the same history from the ground. Before Partition Katas was "a popular religious site for the Hindus", and "Thousands of pilgrims used to descend here from faraway places on the occasion of Shivratri" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). "This temple was abandoned as a result of partition", its buildings "falling into disrepair and the pond being polluted", and "a few cement factories opened in the surrounding area and started sucking the water out from here" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 45–46, folio not stated). No one guarded the place; "Several phone numbers and names are still engraved" on its walls, and the few Hindus who came did so "pretending to be tourists" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 46, folio not stated).

Prem Gupta, who first came in 2003, remembered: "There were boys jumping from the windows and alleys of temples into this sacred pond. They would leave juice boxes and chips wrappers in the water" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 46, folio not stated). "Things changed for the shrine in 2005, when the veteran Indian politician L.K Advani came here and expressed displeasure", and the Government of Pakistan began the work of renovation (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 46, folio not stated). "Major renovation work of the temple was undertaken by the Department in 2005": the pond was cleaned, the buildings "painted and restored", and "blue boards were raised" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). The Archaeology Department appointed Shakeel, "a 25 year old graduate" from Kalar Kahar, and a few others as guides when the site was renovated (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 42–43, folio not stated).

By the time of Khalid's later visit the pond "had recently been renovated" and was "brimming with water", free of the garbage he had seen "the last time", and "Muslim boys" were diving into it from the rooftops (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220). The water level "had started to fall" because "the cement factories around this area were sucking the groundwater"; after writers and journalists took it up, "the government woke from its slumber", and "The water level has now been restored" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220). The cement factories have changed the road as well: the National Highway Authority was widening the single-lane road to Katas, and "Cement factories dotting this area" had lobbied hard for it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219).

The restoration did not hold everywhere. In 2011 there was "a small building, the only restaurant in the area", and Khalid notes that "Just a few years ago, this place would have refused to serve these people", so that "untouchability, at least here, has receded"; the pilgrims had "the only washroom the pilgrims can use", which closed "at eleven in the night" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 48–49, folio not stated). "There is no electricity". Haroon Sarab Diyal, who led the pilgrims from Peshawar, told him: "The authorities have not paid the bill of this temple for the past three months", and "Ever since the Indians have stopped coming, they have become negligent again. The temple is falling into disrepair" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 49–50, folio not stated).

## Shivratri and Pilgrimage

The great festival of Katas is Shivratri, the night of Shiva. Khalid describes it, as a festival and not as this site's alone, as "a Hindu festival dedicated to the worship of Lord Shiva" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated), and writes: "The celebration of Shivratri, which literally means the 'the night of Shiva' includes the worship of Shiva throughout the night, as well as a symbolic marriage between him and his counterpart Parvati" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 51, folio not stated). Dhillon, writing of Maha Shivratri at Achal, near Batala in Gurdaspur, and not of Katas, calls it "the great night of Shiva" and the day "Shiva was married to Parvati" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, pp. 240–241, folio 265 / not stated).

After the restoration of 2005 the festival drew pilgrims from India. "In the subsequent year" the government invited Indian pilgrims for Shivratri: "About three hundred pilgrims came, which became national news". They stayed "for three days", with security, shelter and "free food", lodged "at the building at the site of the ancient university" in an area cordoned off. "This continued until 2008". After the Mumbai attacks of "between the 26th and 29th of November 2008", "Pilgrims didn't come to Katas for Shivratri in 2009" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 46, folio not stated). In 2010 Hindu organisations wrote to the Archaeology Department, the ETPB, the police and the Ministry of Minorities, and "did not receive any response"; even so, "About two thousand Hindus came to Katas from various cities of Pakistan unannounced, including Lahore, Rahim Yar Khan, Peshawar and Nowshera" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 46–47, folio not stated).

Khalid was at Katas for the Shivratri of 2011. In the afternoon pilgrims were preparing for the night, "for which about two thousand pilgrims would pour in from different parts of the country", and Hindu children "who have come from Gujranawala" were playing on the steps of the pond (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated). Prem Gupta's banner read "'Welcome Yatrees (pilgrims)'" and bore a picture of Lord Shiva, and a canopy had been raised inside the complex (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 47, folio not stated). On the banner, "A snake is coiled around his neck. A third eye, which he can use to destroy the world, is visible on his forehead. The moon is in his hair" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 47, folio not stated).

Only "five officials" of the police stood at the gate, which Khalid reads as "an indication of the scant importance that Hindu pilgrims are accorded" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 47, folio not stated). A professor and students from the NCA were turned back ("Muslims are not allowed inside today," a police official said), while Hindu boys went in wearing a "Maha Shivratri" tag (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 47–48, folio not stated). About a hundred pilgrims came from Peshawar "in two large buses", led by Haroon Sarab Diyal, and more from Nowshera, Rahim Yaar Khan and Bahawalpur (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated); once all the buses had come, "There are about a thousand people" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated). A DSP at first refused to open the department's hall, citing "the security conditions of the country", and then opened one hall for the women, the children and the old (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 50–51, folio not stated).

The next morning the Archaeology Department's officials "find their offices invaded and the temples full of sleeping pilgrims", and junior officials threw the pilgrims' luggage, their *langar* utensils and their rice onto the road (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 52–53, folio not stated). "It is too cold to take a bath", so the pilgrims poured the pond's water over their heads, as "a substitute to performing a ritual ablution or ashnan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 53, folio not stated).

The books record no festival at Katas other than Shivratri. Khalid's reconstruction of Guru Nanak's visit is also set at Shivratri (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210). The sources consulted give no verse, hymn or inscription about Katas itself.

## Shiva in the Books

Some of what the books say of Shiva is said of the god in general, and is given here as context for the shrine of the *lingam* at the pond, not as a description of this site. Khalid writes that the Shivling "represents the potent force of Lord Shiv" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 52, folio not stated). In *In Search of Shiva*, his study of folk religious practices in Pakistan, which names no site of the Salt Range, he writes: "In Hinduism, Shiva is depicted as a lingam which is a phallus. In Hindu temples, the lingam is placed inside a structure called yoni, signifying the vagina. Together they represent the divine power of procreation" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

The same book, citing Mahadev Chakravarti's *The Concept of Rudra Śiva Through the Ages*, says that in post-Vedic literature "Shiva is known as the god of procreation" and that "Shiva is also worshipped as the god of cultivation" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated). It reports the view of the archaeologist Mark Kenoyer that seals from Mohenjo-daro showing a figure seated in a yogic posture "could actually be a prototype of Lord Shiva, one of the most important Hindu deities", and notes that "In Hinduism, Shiva worship and worship of a snake go hand in hand" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated). Its thesis is that the shrine practices Khalid met, "Even though Islamic in its garb", had roots in "the different spiritual traditions that developed around the cult of Lord Shiva" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 6, Introduction, folio not stated).

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* names the god Mahadev (مهادیو). Every temple it ascribes to Mahadev lies outside Pakistan, in the parts of the empire the book treats as the subas of Kashmir, Gujarat and Berar, and none is in the Salt Range. Of one it writes "نوسر[OCR?] نام معبدیست منسوب بمهادیو", a temple ascribed to Mahadev whose name is printed نوسر[OCR?], where pilgrims hear a sound of worship, "و کس نداند که از کجاست", and no one knows where it comes from (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 507).

## Setting

The pilgrims Khalid met at Katas came from far away because the Hindus of Pakistan live, for the most part, far from the Salt Range. In *A White Trail* he writes, of the country and not of this site, that most of Pakistan's Hindus live "in the 'faraway' 'peripheral' regions of Southern Punjab, inner Sindh and Baluchistan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 12, folio not stated), and that "The majority of the Hindu community is based in Sindh and Southern Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 233, folio not stated). Of Central Punjab, where he did his research, he writes: "My perception is that the conditions under which members of the Hindu community live in Central Punjab are the harshest compared to the other regions" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 233, folio not stated). "A lot of Hindus in Punjab do this, passing off as Muslims or Christians by taking up non-Hindu names. This is a survival technique in a hostile environment" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 39, folio not stated).

Of the fate of other sacred buildings in the province after 1947, Khalid writes of "the hundreds of temples and Gurdwaras all over Pakistani Punjab" taken over by refugees and turned into houses (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 58, folio not stated), and in *In Search of Shiva*: "I have seen several gurdwaras and temples being taken over and destroyed by the migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The nearby town.** The site's account places the complex near the town of Choa Saidanshah in Chakwal District. Khalid places it "near the small town of Kalar Kahar" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated), and a few kilometres from Kallar Kahar on the Motorway (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 245, folio 219).
- **The age and builders of the temples.** The site's account attributes the Satghara temples to the Hindu Shahi (Odi Shahi) rulers of roughly the seventh to the tenth centuries CE, and dates the principal shrine to around the tenth century. Khalid gives the experts' dating as "between the 7th and 10th century CE, when this area was under the influence of the Kashmiri kingdom" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated), and elsewhere calls them Kashmiri temples "built in the seventh and eighth century" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220). The guide Shakeel dates them "from the time of the Mahabharata", with a board at the site giving "around 1500 BCE" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated).
- **The Pandavas at Katas.** The site's account has the Pandavas make their home at the Satghara during part of a twelve-year exile. Khalid reports the belief that the Pandavas built the temples, during "a thirteen year exile" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210); Shakeel too says the exiled Pandavas built them (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 44, folio not stated).
- **The second pond.** The site's account has Shiva's tears form two pools, one at Pushkar in Rajasthan and one at Katas. Shakeel puts the second tear at "Ajmer Sharif, India, where there is another ancient pond" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated). The site's account speaks of Shiva's tears; Khalid speaks of a single tear (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 236, folio 210; p. 21, folio 3).
- **The age of the stupa.** The site's account says that Xuanzang recorded a substantial Buddhist stupa in the vicinity in the seventh century, and gives it no date of building. Shakeel dates the stupa "from the 3rd century BC, from the time of Taxila" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated); *Walking with Nanak* calls it "at least four thousand years old" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).
- **Whether the stupa is excavated.** *A White Trail* calls it "a Buddhist stupa that has been partially excavated" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated), and two pages later lists "an unexcavated Buddhist stupa" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 45, folio not stated). *Walking with Nanak* calls it "half excavated" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 246, folio 220).
- **The Sikh-period builder.** The site's account attributes the Sikh-period repairs and plastering to Sardar Gulab Singh. Khalid's books name no Gulab Singh at Katas and tie the Sikh-period haveli and fort to Hari Singh Nalwa (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated; Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221).
- **Where Nanak's gurdwara stands.** The site's account places the gurdwara associated with Guru Nanak near the pond. Khalid found it "at a little distance from the complex", next to the fort, unrestored and roofless, after guides had told him there was no gurdwara at Katas at all (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221).
- **The numbers at Shivratri, 2011.** Khalid first reports that "about two thousand pilgrims would pour in" for the night (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated); once the buses had arrived he counts "about a thousand people" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 49, folio not stated).

## Legacy

Today the Katas Raj Temples stand as one of the most significant surviving monuments of Hindu civilisation in Pakistan, a place where myth, epic and archaeology converge. The complex embodies the deep antiquity of Hindu worship in the Salt Range and remains a treasured pilgrimage destination and heritage site, at once fragile and enduring, its weathered shrines still mirrored in the tears of Shiva.

The books add the shape of that survival. For Hindus of Pakistan it is still the place they come to at Shivratri, from Peshawar and Nowshera, Lahore, Bahawalpur and Rahim Yar Khan, even in years when no one answered their letters (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 46–47, folio not stated). For Khalid and his guide Iqbal Qaiser it keeps the memory of Guru Nanak's visit, in a ruined building that the site's own guides could not name (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 247, folio 221). And for its guides it remains a place of many stories at once, Shiva's tear beside an ancient sea, the Pandavas beside Al-Beruni, which, as Khalid writes of the pond, is "clearly the lifeline of this complex" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 43, folio not stated).

Name: Khatwari Darbar, Shikarpur
Location: Thekrati Bazar, old city, Shikarpur, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Bhai Gurdas Singh (Kanhiya Lal), disciple of Guru Gobind Singh
Events: Sikh and Nanakpanthi festivals
Description:
The Khatwari Darbar is among the most celebrated of the historic Sikh and Nanakpanthi shrines of Shikarpur, the north-Sindh town once known as the "Paris of Sindh" for the wealth of its merchant houses. It is traditionally held to have been founded by Bhai Gurdas Singh — also remembered by the name Kanhiya Lal — a disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who, after the Guru's death in 1708, is said to have travelled to Sindh and preached the Sikh teaching at Shikarpur. He is remembered as delivering his sermons seated upon a *khat* (a rope cot), from which the darbar took its name, "Khatwari". The building most likely dates to the second quarter of the eighteenth century and is one of the finest structures in the town: a two-storey *haveli*-style darbar noted for its fresco paintings and intricate woodwork, decoration rarely matched elsewhere in upper Sindh. Images of the ten Sikh Gurus adorn its walls, and three doorways open onto the main hall, where the *Guru Granth Sahib* is installed. The darbar belongs to the shared Nanakpanthi and *Udasi* devotional world of Sindh, in which Sindhi Hindus and Sikhs venerated the Gurus together. There are in fact three Khatwari Darbars in Shikarpur — the principal one, or Khatwari Dharamshala, in Thekrati Bazar — and the tradition of Bhai Gurdas is also remembered at Shahdadkot and at Gandava in Jhal Magsi.

Local tradition, as recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, adds a specific origin story: Guru Gobind Singh is said to have found Bhai Gurdas serving water to wounded Muslim and Sikh soldiers alike, and instructed him to carry the teaching to Shikarpur. The darbar's hall houses, alongside the *Guru Granth Sahib*, an image of Sri Chand — Guru Nanak's eldest son — and the *Jyot*, or sacred light, of Jhulelal, binding the shrine into Sindh's wider devotional world. The building was originally five storeys and is now reduced to two; its two entrances carry marble images of Durga and of Ganpati flanked by his two wives, and its central door bears ten carved panels of Sikh Gurus and saints, including Baba Sewa Das and Baba Kashi Das. By 2018 its mural paintings were reported in advanced decay and its ornate wooden doors sold off to dealers, and the darbar's once-extensive precinct has shrunk to a few buildings, with its former Vidyalaya now rebuilt as a charity hospital; a branch was also established in Mumbai after Partition. The darbar's continued existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib were independently confirmed in 2013, when it was named among Sindh shrines hit by a wave of reported desecrations.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," *Youlin Magazine*, 6 June 2024.
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Gurus in Shikarpur," *The Friday Times*, 12 January 2018.
- Staff Reporter, "Desecration of Guru Granth Sahib across Sindh cities slammed," *Dawn*, 28 August 2013.
qa_note: The addition above draws on two articles by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro (The Friday Times, 2018; Youlin Magazine, 2024) and an independent 2013 Dawn report confirming the darbar's existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib. Several points remain unresolved across the sources: Kalhoro's own two articles spell the founder's original name differently ("Kanhiya Lal" in 2024 vs "Kanya Lal" in 2018); the 2024 article records an alternative tradition that Bhai Gurdas first preached at Gandava in Balochistan, not Shikarpur; and a Wikipedia passage (not independently verified) describes the darbar as dedicated to Bhai Kanhaiya, the Sewapanthi founder, whose water-carrier story is similar to but distinct from the one told here of Bhai Gurdas — the relationship between the two figures could not be resolved in this research pass. The detailed architectural and biographical material rests substantially on Kalhoro's own scholarship; only the darbar's bare existence and its housing of the Guru Granth Sahib have independent corroboration.

Name: Krishna Mandir (Kabari Bazar)
Events: Holi; Diwali; Janmashtami
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Krishna Mandir of Rawalpindi, standing between the city's railway station and the Kabari Bazaar in the old cantonment quarter of Saddar, is the principal — and effectively the only fully functional — Hindu temple serving the Hindu population of Rawalpindi and neighbouring Islamabad. A compact double-storeyed building dedicated to *Lord Krishna*, it has become, by attrition of the region's other temples, the beating heart of Hindu religious life in the "twin cities".

## Foundation in Colonial Rawalpindi

The temple was built in 1897, during the later years of the British Raj, by two prosperous Hindu merchants of Saddar, the brothers *Kanji Mal* and *Ujagar Mal Ram Rachpal*, as a place of worship for the Hindu families of the surrounding bazaars. Rawalpindi in this period was a thriving garrison and commercial town with a substantial Hindu and Sikh mercantile community, and the Krishna Mandir was one of several temples that served it. The building occupies a very small plot — less than four *marlas*, little more than a hundred square metres — with a courtyard capable of holding around a hundred worshippers, a scale that speaks to its origins as a neighbourhood shrine rather than a grand civic temple.

## The Twin Cities' Hindu Centre

The Partition of 1947 and the decades that followed hollowed out the region's Hindu population and left most of its temples disused, damaged or repurposed. The Krishna Mandir survived, and today it carries a significance out of all proportion to its size: it is the one temple where the several thousand Hindus of Rawalpindi and Islamabad can gather for regular worship, the others in the district — such as the temples at Lal Kurti and the Valmik shrine in Gracy Lines — being largely non-functional. Managed under the umbrella of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, it serves as temple, community hall and gathering place all at once, hosting weddings and the life-cycle ceremonies of a small and close-knit community.

## Festivals and Devotional Life

The temple comes most fully alive at the great festivals of the Hindu year. *Holi*, the festival of colours, and *Diwali*, the festival of lights, are celebrated here with particular fervour, as is *Janmashtami*, the birthday of Krishna to whom the temple is dedicated. On these occasions the modest courtyard fills to capacity and beyond, and the temple becomes a rare and visible assertion of Hindu presence in a city where the community has grown accustomed to worshipping quietly. In recent years the temple has also drawn attention as a focus of debate over the maintenance and restoration of Pakistan's minority places of worship.

## Legacy

The Krishna Mandir of Rawalpindi is a poignant survivor: a small Victorian-era shrine that has outlasted the world of prosperous bazaar merchants who built it, and that now shoulders the devotional needs of an entire region's Hindus. Its continued function — and the periodic campaigns for its repair and protection — make it both a living temple and a symbol of the fortunes of Pakistan's Hindu minority. For the historian it preserves a fragment of colonial Rawalpindi's plural society; for the worshipper it remains simply the mandir, the one place where Krishna is served in the twin cities.

## Bibliography

- *Dawn* and *The Express Tribune*, features on the Krishna Temple, Rawalpindi, and the temples of the twin cities.
- Heritage surveys of Rawalpindi's colonial-era architecture.
- Records of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, Government of Pakistan.
- Wikipedia, "Krishna Temple, Rawalpindi" (with cited press sources).

Name: Krishna Mandir (Ravi Road)
Events: Janmashtami; Holi; Diwali
Description:
## Overview

The Krishna Mandir on Ravi Road, opposite the Timber Market in the northern part of Lahore, is one of only two functioning Hindu temples in a city that was, before 1947, dotted with them. Dedicated to *Lord Krishna*, this modest shrine has become — together with the Valmiki temple — the surviving remnant of Lahore's once-rich Hindu sacred landscape, and it has weathered decades of neglect, communal tension and rumour of demolition to remain in worship today.

## A Surviving Temple of Lahore

Lahore was historically home to numerous mandirs, from the Loh temple within the Fort to the great riverside shrines and the neighbourhood temples of Anarkali, Ravi Road and the walled city. The Partition of 1947 emptied most of them, and in the years since, the majority were demolished, encroached upon or converted to other uses. The Ravi Road Krishna Mandir endured, in part because a small community of Hindu families remained in the vicinity to maintain worship. Its precise date of foundation is not securely recorded and should be regarded as uncertain, though it belongs to the fabric of colonial-era Lahore; the temple is today administered, like other minority shrines, under the Evacuee Trust Property Board.

## The 1992 Attack and Rebuilding

The temple's modern history was marked by the violence that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya, in India, on 6 December 1992. In the reprisal riots that swept parts of Pakistan, the Krishna Mandir was badly damaged by mobs. When it was rebuilt, the reconstruction was deliberately restrained — designed to blend into the surrounding streetscape rather than to stand out — a defensive architectural choice that speaks eloquently to the vulnerability felt by the community. In 2006 the temple was again the subject of alarm when press reports claimed it was to be demolished; the reports proved to be mistaken, and the petition raised on its behalf was withdrawn once it was confirmed that the temple stood intact.

## Devotional Life Today

Despite its small size and turbulent recent past, the Ravi Road temple functions as an active place of worship for Lahore's remaining Hindus, hosting the observance of *Janmashtami*, *Holi* and *Diwali* and serving as a gathering point for a community that is otherwise largely invisible in the life of the city. Modest sums have periodically been allocated for its renovation and extension, and it features regularly in journalistic accounts of the fate of Lahore's religious minorities.

## Legacy

The Krishna Mandir on Ravi Road is significant less for its architecture than for its sheer survival. In a city that has lost almost all of its Hindu temples, its continued existence — and its careful, self-effacing rebuilding after 1992 — makes it a barometer of the condition of Pakistan's Hindu minority and of Lahore's transformation from a plural, cosmopolitan city to a far more homogeneous one. For scholars of Partition and its long aftermath, and for the worshippers who still light lamps before Krishna here, it is a place of memory and of stubborn continuity.

- Hindu American Foundation and other reports on the condition of Lahore's temples.
- Records of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, Government of Pakistan.

Name: Lal Kurti Temple (Balmiki Mandir), Rawalpindi
Location: Lalkurti, Rawalpindi Cantonment, Rawalpindi, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Diwali; Holi; Raksha Bandhan; daily worship
Description:
The Lal Kurti Temple — also called the *Balmiki* (Valmiki) Mandir — stands in the historic Lalkurti quarter of Rawalpindi Cantonment, a bazaar district whose name ("red shirt") recalls the red tunics of the British Indian Army soldiers who once shopped there and gave the old British Infantry Bazaar its popular name. Completed in 1905 in a Mughal-influenced idiom, the temple is dedicated to the sage-poet *Valmik* (Valmiki), revered as author of the *Ramayana* and venerated especially by the Balmiki community. It remained a focal point for local Hindus both before and after the Partition of 1947; while most of the quarter's Hindus left in 1947, a small community stayed on and kept the temple in worship, and its first post-Partition custodian, Kheera Lal, is buried within a side portion of the complex. As of 2025 it is reported to be the only Hindu place of worship still functioning in Lalkurti — a neighbourhood that once held shrines of several faiths — and it is counted as one of the three principal Hindu temples of Rawalpindi district, alongside the Krishna Mandir of Saddar and the Valmiki Swamiji Mandir of Gracy Lines. The temple hosts daily worship and the major festivals of *Diwali*, *Holi* and *Raksha Bandhan*, and its upkeep has been associated with the Pakistan Hindu Balmik Welfare Society and with the few dozen local families who continue to maintain it.

As of 2025, more than 60 Hindus were reported to live in the immediate Lal Kurti locality, within a wider Hindu population of the twin cities estimated at around 6,000. The temple's caretaker, Om Prakash Narain, 80 years old at the time, was also reported to serve as General Secretary of the Pakistan Hindu Balmik Welfare Society and as a member of the District Peace Committee and the Interfaith Harmony Committee. Press coverage is careful to distinguish this temple from a separate, unrelated structure of similar name — the ruined "Guru Balmik Swamiji's Mandir," a triple-storey temple built in 1880 in Rawalpindi's Purana Qila, stripped of its woodwork and now built over with shops — which should not be confused with the active Lal Kurti temple described here.

Name: Lal Shahbaz Qalandar
Events: Annual urs (Sha'ban); Thursday-evening dhamal and qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

At Sehwan Sharif, in Sindh, stands the great shrine of Hazrat Lal Shahbaz Qalandar (c. 1177–1274) — perhaps the most ecstatically beloved saint in all of Pakistan, and the object of one of its largest and most exuberant pilgrimages. A wandering *qalandar* — a mystic of the free, rapturous, rule-breaking kind — Lal Shahbaz drew Sindh into the world of Sufi devotion, and his memory is celebrated in the thunder of the *dhamal*, the trance-dance beaten out on the great drums of his shrine, and in the anthem *Dama Dam Mast Qalandar*, which has carried his name across the world. His golden-domed darbar is the heart of Sehwan, and its urs one of the defining festivals of the Sindhi year.

The books consulted bear out that fame from many sides. Omar Kasmani, whose book takes the saint as its whole subject, calls him "Pakistan's most beloved figure of devotion, whose tomb-shrine in Sehwan, a town of about a hundred thousand residents, draws millions each year" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 20, folio 3), and sums up the town in one sentence: "Sufi by renown, Shivaite in heritage, and increasingly Shiʿi in following, Sehwan is in many ways Pakistan at its complex best." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 20, folio 3). H. T. Sorley, in his study of Shah Abdul Latif, names him "the famous Lal Shahbaz, or Jivelal", the 'living Pir', "whose shrine at Sehwan attracts a great gathering of both Mussulmans and Hindus every year in a strange mixture of worship" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 257, folio 248). For Annemarie Schimmel, his settling at Sehwan is where the mystical history of Sindh begins: "From the day that Lal Shahbaz Qalandar settled in Sehwan in the 13th century … Sind had produced an immense number of mystics, whose shrines are scattered all through the Indus Valley" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 25, folio 21). Michel Boivin makes the town one of the three case studies of his chapter on shared shrines: "Sehwan Sharif, a main Sufi pilgrimage centre of Sindh, where the darbar of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar is located" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 179, folio 166).

Kasmani gives the measure of the figure in a few lines: "Saints, even if ubiquitous, are divisive figures in Pakistan, though none is more vexing than the saint in question" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 20, folio 3), and "Lal Shahbaz Qalandar is a plurivocal figure and a ubiquity hard to miss. He embodies a historical continuum and bridges multiple and oftentimes contradicting genealogies attributed to him" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, pp. 57–58, folios 40–41). "Lal and Sehwan are inseparable figures, always in narration." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 165, folio 148).

## The Life of the Saint

Sayyid Usman Marwandi — known to the world as Lal Shahbaz Qalandar — was born around 1177 at Marwand, in the Persian-speaking lands to the west (in the region of present-day Afghanistan/Iran), into a Sayyid family tracing descent from the Prophet through the Imams. Steeped from youth in learning and devotion, he took to the path of the wandering dervishes and travelled widely through the Muslim world — through Iraq, the Hejaz, and Central Asia — before coming to Sindh and settling at Sehwan, an ancient town with a deep pre-Islamic sacred history. There he lived as a *qalandar*, drawing crowds by his ecstatic sanctity, and there he died around 1274. He is called *Lal* (“the Red”) for the crimson robe of his order, and *Shahbaz* (“royal falcon”) for the soaring freedom of his spirit; and he is counted, in Sindhi and Punjabi tradition, among the “four friends” (*chaar yaar*) of the qalandari way, alongside such saints as Baba Farid and Bahauddin Zakariya, with whom legend links him in companionship.

The books stress, in their own words, how little of this life is documented. Kasmani writes that "historical references to Lal are few and far between, a patchwork at best of brief mentions found in other saints' biographical texts", and that "he evades hagiographical hold and historical record. Mystery suits him better than history" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45); elsewhere, "the history of the saint of Sehwan is at best a patchwork of brief references, some found in sparse historical accounts, some in other saints' hagiographies." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 165, folio 148). He sends readers to Michel Boivin for "a detailed biography of the saint (in French)" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 184, folio 167). Sorley notes that Jethmal Parsram gave "some account of him and his companions" in his book *Sind and its Sufis*, "but the facts are meagre" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 299, folio 290), and judges that between "the thirteenth century when Lal Shahbaz flourished and the eighteenth century" there is "very little that can be said to be securely established in the way of verified historical fact" about the Sufi poets of Sindh (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 299, folio 290).

Even his name is contested. Kasmani writes that "his followers cannot quite agree on his doctrinal persuasion, Sufi affiliations, not even his actual name, Sayyid Usman Marwandi. The saint is better known by the three-part epithet Lal Shahbaz Qalandar." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 35, folio 18), and that "matters like the saint's origin or real name… are actively debated in Sehwan" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45). In a note he records that "Custodian families in Sehwan take the position that the saint's actual name was most likely Shah Hasan and not Usman, the latter commonly associated with the Sunni", and that "The title Lal Shahbaz as reference to the saint is first recorded in late seventeenth-century textual sources" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 184, folio 167, intro n. 33). Sorley gives the personal name once, as Sayid Usman Marwandi, with the word 'Shah' printed before Marwandi in a damaged line, a man "who became famous as" Lal Shahbaz "with a popular shrine at Sehwan" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 298, folio 289); he also quotes Jethmal Parsram's form of the name, 'Kalandar Lal Marwandi' (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 299, folio 290). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes instead that "Lal Shahbaz's real name was Mir Saiyid 'Usman and he was a native of Sehwan in the Sind" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 328, folio 306), and gives no 'Marwandi'.

The two halves of the epithet are explained in more than one way. Rizvi: "Often he wore a red dress, hence his name lal (red). Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din Zakariyya gave him the title 'Shahbaz,' the noblest species of falcon." (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 328, folio 306). Kasmani: "Lal (red, dear one) or Laʿl (ruby, gem), though different words and both ascribed to the saint, are indistinguishable in Sehwan since there is no difference in pronunciation." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 182, folio not stated, intro n. 5). As one fakir learned it, Kasmani writes, "red was the color associated with Lal, whose variant Laʿl means ruby, or that Shah-baz (or royal falcon) referred to a miracle attributed to the saint." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 64, folio 47). Boivin records "Mast qalandar", the name of the song, used once as a name for the saint himself (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 141, folio 128).

Kasmani, following Boivin, writes that "he is most likely to have been born in Marwand, near Tabriz (in present-day Iran), and his lineage through Jafar al-Sadiq's son Ismaʿil makes him an important figure of the Ismaʿili line of the Shiʿi faith", adding: "This also means that he is a descendant of Ali and thus related to the Family of the Prophet (ahl-e bayt)" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45). Boivin's one biographical statement is a negative one: "Despite his fame, Lal Shahbaz was not Sindhi since he was born in Persia and his alleged diwan is composed in Persian." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 213, folio 200, Ch. 4 n. 4). Rizvi, as above, makes him a native of Sehwan.

Kasmani gives his death once, in his own voice, as "d. 1274 ce", and calls him "a thirteenth-century mystic known for his radical rejection of Islamic religious institutions, norms, and practices." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 20, folio 3); everywhere else he gives only the century. The Library of Congress cataloguing heading printed on his book's copyright page gives '1177–1274' (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 5, folio not stated); Kasmani himself never states a birth year. Schimmel's index to *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* prints his death as 1262 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 520, folio 489), and the index to *As Through a Veil* gives only '13th cent.' (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 357, folio 339). Sorley, Rizvi, Boivin, Abbas and Schaflechner give no year at all.

Sorley places him in a wave of migration: "From the thirteenth century onwards there was a great immigration into Sind of learned and religious-minded men from the centre of the Muslim world. Lal Shahbaz, who came with several companions, some of whom made names for themselves elsewhere in India, was a man of this kind." (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 302, folio 293). The companions are not named. Schimmel, in *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, sets him in "the same period during which" Muʿīnuddīn Chishtī and Bahāʾuddīn Zakariyā were preaching divine love and union, as the representative of "Another aspect of mystical life" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354).

The dates of his coming are given several ways, and Kasmani joins none of them. "Also unsettled is the year of his arrival in Sehwan, of which 1272 ce is considered to be more reliable" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45); a note adds only "The other date is 1251" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 13). Following Boivin, Kasmani writes that "he is likely to have first arrived in Multan in 1263", and that he stopped at Makran, Lahut-lamakan, Panjgur and Pasni in Balochistan and at Naing, Lake Manchhar and Sehwan in Sindh (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 14). "He later settled in Sehwan for the last year or two of his life" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45), and the stories of his burial place it "a year after he arrived in town" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 163, folio 146). Of the town he came to, Kasmani writes that "Sehwan at this time was also under the influence of the Ismaʿilis", which might explain his arrival or his choice to settle there (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 16), and that "Sehwan at the time of the saint's arrival was dominated by followers of Shiva as well as Daryapanthis, who divinized the Indus River" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 195, folio 178, ch. 5 n. 8).

The books do not agree on his spiritual descent. Rizvi introduces him in a run of qalandars "Among the Suhrawardiyyas" and makes him an exception to his master's rule: "Shaikh Baha'u'd-Din disliked qalandars intensely and certainly never encouraged their unwelcome visits. Lal Shahbaz was an exception and was adopted as his disciple." (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 328, folio 306). Kasmani reports that "Lal bears at least three genealogies — Sufi, Shiʿi, and Shivaite", and that "Lal's Shiʿi descent through the Ismaʿili line is well established; however, he is also claimed through Suhrawardi and Qadiri Sufi registers." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 35, folio 18). "In Sufi terms, Lal is claimed by both Suhrawardi and Qadiri orders and is popularly regarded as one of a quartet of mystics, chahar-yar or 'four friends.'" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45). "For many fakirs in Sehwan, Lal is an original thirteenth-century qalandar, who they believe was initiated at the hands of the order's founding figure, Jamal al-Din Savi of Damascus." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45); yet "historical sources do not confirm that Lal observed chahar-zarb or the fourfold shave typical of the early qalandars" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 62, folio 45).
