Description:
## Overview

At Kot Mithan (Mithankot), in the Rajanpur district on the edge of the Cholistan desert, lies the shrine of Khwaja Ghulam Farid (1845–1901) — the supreme poet of the Seraiki language and one of the last great masters of the classical Sufi *kafi*. A Chishti saint of the Kot Mithan line, Ghulam Farid poured the mysticism of *wahdat al-wujud* into verses of extraordinary tenderness, sung in the sweet Seraiki of the southern Punjab and steeped in the landscape of the Rohi, the great desert he loved. His shrine is the spiritual centre of the Seraiki belt, and his kafis are sung across it to this day.

The books bear out the poet more fully than the place. Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence call him "another great nineteenth-century Chishti" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 146, folio 134), and Robert Rozehnal "the nineteenth-century Chishti master Ghulam Farid" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 223, folio 215). Annemarie Schimmel describes Khwaja Farid as "a popular Siraiki poet of the late nineteenth century" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 286, folio 268); Michel Boivin as "a Siraiki-speaking author" whose verse is quoted in the devotions of Sindhis as well (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 91, folio 78); and Shemeem Burney Abbas follows his *kafis* into the concert repertoire of Abida Parvin (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 136, folio not stated). His discourses survive as a Persian *malfuzat*, compiled between 1893 and 1901 and translated into Urdu in 1979 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230). Of the shrine itself, the books consulted say very little: one names him "of Kot Mithan Sharif" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 392), and another knows Kot Mithan a century before him as a town of learning (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 123, folio 111).

## The Life of the Poet-Saint

Ghulam Farid was born in 1845 at Chachran, near Kot Mithan, into a Sayyid Koreja family of the Chishti Sufi tradition; his father and, after him, his elder brother were the spiritual guides (*sajjada-nashins*) of their line, and on his brother’s death Ghulam Farid succeeded to the seat. Learned in Arabic and Persian and in the religious sciences, he was nonetheless a poet and mystic to the core, and he is famous for the years he spent in the wilderness of the Rohi (Cholistan), whose dunes, herders, and camel-caravans fill his poetry with an unmistakable local beauty. He was a contemporary and, in matters of the spirit, a critic of the Nawabs of Bahawalpur — remembered for counselling the ruler in the interest of the people. He died in 1901 at Chachran and was buried at Kot Mithan.

The scholarly books give his dates more than one way. Rozehnal prints "(1844–1901)" in his text (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 223, folio 215) and "(d. 1901)" in his bibliography (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 263, folio not stated). Ernst and Lawrence head their bibliography entry 'Ghulam Farid, Khwaja (d. 1319/1901)' (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230), but in their text write "Ghulam Farid (d. 1911)" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 146, folio 134). The index of Schimmel's *As Through a Veil* gives him "(d. 1901)" as well (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 353, folio 335). Both Ernst and Lawrence and Rozehnal call him a Chishti; none of these books names his pir, his birthplace, his place of death or his tomb.

He also took disciples. In the life of Khwaja Hasan Nizami, Ernst and Lawrence record that "at sixteen his brother made him a murid of Khwaja Ghulam Farid" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 127, folio 114).

The books spell his name in several ways. Ernst and Lawrence write Khwaja Ghulam Farid (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 127, folio 114), Ghulam Farid (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 146, folio 134), Khwaja Farid (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 225, folio 214) and Khawaja Farid (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 230, folio 219); Abbas writes Khawaja Ghulam Farid and Khawaja Farid (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 136, folio not stated; p. 149, folio not stated); Boivin and Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah give the bare 'Ghulam Farid', with no honorific, no date and no place (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 171, folio 158; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 236, folio 216). He should not be confused with a namesake in Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's tazkira of the Punjab saints, "مولوی غلام فرید لاہوری", who died in 1216 AH and is buried in the Miani graveyard at Lahore, a century earlier and in another city (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 222, folio 210).

## The Poetry

Khwaja Ghulam Farid’s fame rests on his *Diwan* of Seraiki *kafis* — hundreds of short mystical lyrics, cast (like those of Shah Hussain and Bulleh Shah before him) largely in the longing voice of a woman for her absent beloved, in which the Beloved is God and the desert of Rohi the very landscape of the soul. His verse unites the boldest metaphysics of the unity of being with the sweetest folk-idiom of the southern Punjab, and its refrains are known by heart across the Seraiki country. Most famous of all is his declaration that the Beloved is everything, the only reality:

میڈا عشق وی توں، میڈا یار وی توں

*You are my love, and You are my beloved; You alone are all.*

His kafis are sung to this day by the folk-singers and qawwals of the Seraiki belt, and he is honoured as the poet who gave that language its highest literary and spiritual expression.

Abbas, who studies the *kafis* as women sing them, sets the same woman's voice at the centre of his work: "The kāfis that are investigated here are the creation of the Siraiki Sufi poet Khawaja Ghulam Farid. The female narrator in the kāfīs mourns her separation from her beloved, who has gone to a distant land" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 148, folio not stated). That voice is borrowed from the romance of the Punjab: "Khawaja Farid additionally uses Hir's voice for that ultimate spiritual union or iśq-e haqīqī through the imagery of iśq-e majāzī (earthly love)" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 149, folio not stated). Schimmel, writing of the mystical poetry of the region at large and not of Ghulam Farid, observes that "In the province of Sind, as well as in Punjab, a special aspect of mystical appreciation of women can be observed that is rarely encountered in other parts of the Muslim world, i.e., the representation of the longing soul in the form of a woman", and that "The tragic heroines of the Sindhi and Panjabi folk tales—like Hir, Sassui, Sohni, and many others—represent the human soul in search of the beloved" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 465, folio 434).

One of his lyrics, as Abbas heard it sung, takes up the lovers Layla and Majnun. Abida Parvin sang a song of a black Layla at her Open University concert and "attributes the poetry to the Sufi poet Khawaja Ghulam Farid, who wrote in Siraiki" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 136, folio not stated). Abbas gives the burden of the poem in prose: "When folks asked Majnun about his black Layla, he retorted with an example from the Quran. He questioned them: If the pages from the Quran can be white but the ink be black, then what is so wrong for him to love a woman of color" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 137, folio not stated). "In fact, it is the poet Ghulam Farid who asks this question on behalf of Qays or Majnun" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 137, folio not stated).

The poet names himself in the lyric. Abbas prints his signature in the Siraiki twice, in roman letters and without a translation: *Vo la- akhe Ghulām Farīd-ā* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 136, folio not stated), and the fuller line *Ākhe Ghulām Farīd-ā O jeh nāl dil aṛ pave O gorī hove yā kālī* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 137, folio not stated).

Schimmel singles out a further theme of his work. In a note to *As Through a Veil* she directs the reader, "For the combination of exercise and interior pilgrimage in the work of Khwaja Farid, a popular Siraiki poet of the late nineteenth century", to Christopher Shackle's essay "The Pilgrimage and the Extension of Sacred Geography in the Poetry of Khwaja Ghulam Farid." (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, pp. 286–287, folios 268–269), which appeared in a volume edited by Attar Singh, *Socio-cultural Impact of Islam on India*, at Chandigarh in 1976 (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 339, folio 321). Pilgrimage and the sacred geography of the poems are named there as a subject; the book does not describe them further.

Of the *kafi* as a form, Naveed Alam, the translator of Shah Hussain, writes in general terms that "Kafis, the stanzaic poems couched in folkloric themes and techniques, were easy to understand and memorize, and thus served as the ideal means to disseminate the mystical teachings among the illiterate masses dependent on the oral transmission of knowledge. Even to this day, most Punjabis and Sindhis are more likely to have heard a kafi than read one" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 15, folio 15).

## The Discourses

Beside the poetry stands a book of his conversations. In their Persian bibliography Ernst and Lawrence list 'Isharat-i Faridi or Maqabis al-majalis', with references to Monzavi and one manuscript; they add that it was translated into Urdu by Wahid Bakhsh Siyal (Lahore: Islamic Book Foundation, 1399/1979), and that the discourses were compiled between 1893 and 1901 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230). Rozehnal lists the same work under 'Farid, Khwaja Ghulam (d. 1901)', compiled 1893–1901 and translated from the Persian by Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani (Lahore: al-Faisal, 1979/1993) (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 263, folio not stated), and renders its title in English: "the shaykh's lengthy introduction to the discourses (malfuzat) of the nineteenth-century Chishti master Ghulam Farid (1844–1901) titled Maqabis al-majalis [The Lessons of the Spiritual Assemblies]" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 223, folio 215).

The translator was a twentieth-century shaykh, and his introduction became a work in its own right. Ernst and Lawrence write: "In the lengthy Urdu introduction to his translation of the discourses (malfuzat) of another great nineteenth-century Chishti, Ghulam Farid (d. 1911), Capt. Wahid Bakhsh devotes more than a third of 225 pages to the exposition and defense of" *samaʿ* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 146, folio 134). They draw on that introduction three times in their notes, once where it cites Ashraf 'Ali's *Khumkhana-i batin* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 217, folio 206). Rozehnal, too, points the reader to "Wahid Bakhsh's introduction to Khwaja Ghulam Farid (compiled 1893–1901), Maqabis al-majalis", and names a chapter of the same work, 'The Taste of Sama'' (*Zauq-i sama'*), though that note gives the author's surname as 'Faridi' (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 261, folio 254).

An English rendering of the discourses also exists: Ernst and Lawrence list Christopher Shackle's *The Teachings of Khwaja Farid* (Multan, 1978) among the translations of Chishti *malfuzat* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 225, folio 214).

## The Shrine

Khwaja Ghulam Farid’s shrine at Kot Mithan is the chief centre of pilgrimage of the Seraiki region, kept by his descendants and drawing devotees throughout the year for prayer, blessing, and the singing of his verse. The annual urs gathers great crowds for days of kafi-singing, qawwali, and *langar*, and the town of Kot Mithan is known above all as the resting place of the poet. His memory is inseparable from the cultural identity of the Seraiki people.

The books consulted add nothing about the tomb itself. Of all of them, only one ties the poet's name to the town, and that in a publisher's list printed at the end of Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib's tazkira, which advertises "کلام خواجہ غلام فرید", *Kalam-e Khwaja Ghulam Farid*, by "خواجہ غلام فرید کوٹ مٹھن شریف", Khwaja Ghulam Farid of Kot Mithan Sharif (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 392). Ernst and Lawrence, Rozehnal, Schimmel, Boivin and Abbas name no tomb for him and set him neither at Mithankot nor in Rajanpur; none records the date of the building, its builder, the *ʿurs* or its custodians, which rest on the site's own account alone.

## Devotion and Practice

His verse is sung far beyond the town. In Abbas's account of women's performance of Sufi poetry, Abida Parvin's repertoire includes him (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 54, folio not stated), and he is among the spirits invoked at the outset of performances (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 99, folio not stated). Abida Parvin's improvised performance at Islamabad drew "references from Shah Abdul Latif's poetry and Khawaja Ghulam Farid's texts" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 151, folio not stated), and he holds two separate items, both in Siraiki, on the programme of that concert (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 101, folio not stated).

Abbas records, too, how a singer of his verse spoke of her gift: "Surraiya Multanikar, a Siraiki singer of Sufi poetry, in particular that of Khawaja Ghulam Farid, also confirmed in her interview with me that she is specially blessed by her pir, a Gilani Syed. She said that, because of his prayer, there is much sūr (melody) in her voice" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 199, folio not stated). His name stands in the title of a recording, *A Tribute to Great Mystics: … Khawaja Farid* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 205, 212, 216, folios not stated). Elsewhere Abbas writes that "The singer invoked the Sufi poet Farid to create the mystical frame", with the refrain 'Yā-ā-r Farīd' (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 118, folio not stated); she does not say which Farid is meant, the setting is Siraiki, and she names Baba Farid of Pakpattan a few pages later, so the invocation may belong to either poet.

The qawwals sing him as well. Rozehnal names him, in the same clause as Mehr 'Ali Shah, among the poets of the qawwals' repertoire (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 229, folio 221).

His verse also crosses into the devotions of another community. Boivin, describing the Sindhi Hindu Sufis, writes that "Sometimes, Sufi poetry authored by non-Sindhis also played a liturgical role during the performances", and that "One can quote Bulhe Shah or Ghulam Farid, the latter being a Siraiki-speaking author, this being a language in which many Sindhis also composed poetry." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 91, folio 78). Elsewhere he notes that "Non-Sindhi poets are also quoted, including Bullhe Shah, Shah Bahu and Ghulam Farid" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 171, folio 158).

## Setting: Kot Mithan and the Siraiki Country

Kot Mithan was a place of teaching a century before Ghulam Farid. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, in its entry on Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, writes that "ابتدائے حال میں قصبہ کوٹ مٹھن میں قاضی محمد عاقل کی خدمت میں حاضر ہو کر علم ظاہری حاصل کیا": in his early days he attended Qazi Muhammad Aqil in the *qasba* of Kot Mithan and acquired the outward sciences there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 123, folio 111). The book's modern editor identifies the teacher as Khwaja Muhammad Aqil, of the Faruqi family, whose father was Muhammad Sharif and whose family title was Koreja, and who died on 14 Rajab 1229 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). The same editor gives Taunsvi's birth as 1184 AH and his death as 1267 AH, and writes that "پنجاب میں سلسلہ چشتیہ نظامیہ فخریہ کی زیادہ اشاعت حضرت خواجہ سلیمان تونسوی کے ذریعہ ہوئی": the Chishti Nizami Fakhri line spread most widely in the Punjab through him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). The book's index sends Mithankot, Taunsa and Dera Ghazi Khan to the same page (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 336, folio 324). It says nothing of a shrine at Kot Mithan or of Ghulam Farid, and gives no detail that would set this Kot Mithan apart from any other place of the name.

Sharib's tazkira likewise places the *madrasa* of "قاضی محمد عاقل" at Kot Mithan and Khwaja Muhammad Sulaiman's studies there, again without a word of a shrine (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 363). Ernst and Lawrence, writing of the order in the southern Punjab and without naming Kot Mithan, name a Muhammad 'Aqil (d. 1814) and his disciple Gul Muhammad Ahmadpuri (d. 1827), "both of whom founded religious schools in the southern Punjab that provided free instruction and lodging to hundreds of students" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, pp. 121–122, folios 108–109); the books do not say whether this is the same man.

The town's name appears once more, in the title of an early nineteenth-century river journey: Rozehnal cites the "Journal of Captain C.M. Wade's Voyage from Lodiana to Mithankot by the River Satlaj on His Mission to Lahore and Bahawalpur in 1832–1833" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 241, folio 234).

Of the language of the poems, the books speak in general terms. Boivin writes that "The Siraiki language is mainly spoken in Southern Punjab, with Multan as capital. Interestingly, this area was a part of Sindh during the Middle Ages" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 216, folio 203), and defines Siraiki as "a language spoken in Northern Sindh and Southern Punjab" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 220, folio 207). Haroon Khalid, travelling south, writes that "The boundary between Sindh and Punjab becomes a blur as we drive through Bahawalpur", that "This is where the cultures of Punjab and Sindh merge", and that Siraiki is "an amalgamation of the two languages"; his companion Iqbal Qaiser adds: "The Siraiki spoken in Multan is closer to Punjabi, while here it is more like Sindhi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). Schimmel, comparing the poets of Sind and the Punjab, writes that Siraiki "forms the transition to Panjabi; thus, the imagery of both, or rather all three, linguistic areas is very closely related" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 154, folio 154), and Abbas that the Sohni legend "is sung in Sufi poetry in all the regions of the Sind, the Siraiki-speaking area of the Panjab" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 126–127, folios not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his birth.** The site's account gives 1845. Rozehnal gives 1844, in the dates "(1844–1901)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 223, folio 215). No other book consulted gives a birth year.
- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives 1901, and so do Rozehnal (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 263, folio not stated) and the index of Schimmel's *As Through a Veil* (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 353, folio 335). Ernst and Lawrence print it two ways: 'd. 1319/1901' in their bibliography (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230) and "Ghulam Farid (d. 1911)" in their text (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 146, folio 134).
- **The language of his verse.** The site's account calls him the supreme poet of Seraiki. Schimmel, Boivin and Abbas call him a Siraiki poet (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 286, folio 268; Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 91, folio 78; Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 136, folio not stated), and Ernst and Lawrence list his *Fifty Poems* under Siraiki (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 230, folio 219). Rafat's selection reports Asaf Khan's view, which "relates the diction of all the great Punjabi poets to Central Punjabi but accepts variations of vocabulary in Shah Husain, Ghulam Farid, etc." (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 236, folio 216), and Rozehnal names him as a Punjabi poet in the qawwals' repertoire (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 229, folio 221).
- **The Koreja name.** The site's account places Ghulam Farid in a Sayyid Koreja family. Lahori's editor gives Koreja as the family title of Khwaja Muhammad Aqil of Kot Mithan, whom he places in the Faruqi family (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). The book does not connect Muhammad Aqil with Ghulam Farid.
- **The Urdu translation of his discourses.** Ernst and Lawrence give the translator as Wahid Bakhsh Siyal and the imprint as Lahore: Islamic Book Foundation, 1399/1979, and give the work a second title, *Isharat-i Faridi* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230). Rozehnal gives the translator as Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani and the imprint as Lahore: al-Faisal, 1979/1993 (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 263, folio not stated), and in one note cites the work under the surname 'Faridi' (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 261, folio 254).

## Legacy

Khwaja Ghulam Farid is to Seraiki what Bhittai is to Sindhi and Bulleh Shah to Punjabi — the poet who raised his mother-tongue to the summit of mystical expression and made of its desert landscape an image of the soul’s love for God. His kafis remain among the most cherished poetry of the southern Punjab, and his shrine at Kot Mithan endures as the spiritual and cultural heart of the Seraiki belt.

His work has been carried into print and into English largely from Multan. Ernst and Lawrence list two English translations by Christopher Shackle, *The Teachings of Khwaja Farid* (Multan, 1978) and *Fifty Poems of Khawaja Farid* (Multan, 1983) (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 225, folio 214; p. 230, folio 219). Abbas cites *Kalām-e Farid*, edited by Kefi Jampuri (Multan: Bazm-e Saqafat) (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 209, 222, folios not stated); *Naghmā-e Sehrā*, translated by Kashafi Multani (Multan: Bazm-e Saqafat) (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 222, folio not stated); Shackle's *Fifty Poems of Khawaja Farid* (Multan: Bazm-e Saqafat) (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 207, 232, folios not stated); and M. Abdul Wasi's *Divān-e Farid Ma Dhorājāt* (Multan: Qadimi Kutab Khana, n.d.) (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 235, folio not stated).

His discourses kept a living Chishti readership through their translator. Rozehnal, writing of Wahid Bakhsh's own mission, reports that the will of his master Shahidullah Faridi says Wahid Bakhsh "has initiated halqa zikr and guidance in Bahawalpur" and "should spread the silsila in this place only", and reads it so: "Here Shahidullah effectively delineates the southern Punjab as Wahid Bakhsh's personal spiritual domain (wilayat)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 90, folio 80).

Name: Mohra Sharif (Khanqah)
Location: Mohra Sharif village, Murree Tehsil, Rawalpindi District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs
Description:
Mohra Sharif is a celebrated *khanqah* — a Sufi lodge and spiritual centre — set in a small village in the Murree hills of the Punjab, some distance above Islamabad and Rawalpindi. It is the home of the *Naqshbandi Mujaddidi Qasimiya* order, and takes its name (the "holy village") from its sanctity. The centre was established by *Khwaja Muhammad Qasim Sadiq*, born about 1846 (1263 AH), whose forebears are said to have migrated from Iran and settled in the Rawalpindi district. According to the traditions of the order, he journeyed on foot to the shrine of his spiritual guide, *Khwaja Nizamuddin Aulia* of Kahiyan Sharif in the Neelam Valley of Kashmir, and there received *khilafat* with the instruction to settle at Mohra Sharif. He is said to have undertaken a *chilla* — a forty-day retreat of unbroken devotion — and the stone slab on which he sat throughout is preserved at the shrine as a relic (*tabarruk*). On his death the spiritual seat passed to his son Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, remembered as the first *sajjada nashin* (custodian) of Mohra Sharif, and thence down a line of successors. The khanqah remains an active centre of Naqshbandi devotion, drawing pilgrims especially at its annual *urs*, and is counted among the important Sufi shrines of the northern Punjab.

The khanqah's own historical account names the specific line of succession only broadly gestured at above: Khwaja Pir Muhammad Zahid Khan, the founder's third son and first *sajjada nashin*, is recorded as having died on 9 December 1993; he was followed by Hazrat Khawaja Pir Badshah Sahib, who died on 13 August 2008; and then by Pir Auliya Badshah Farooq Sahib as the third *Sajjada Nasheen*. In January 2026, the German Ambassador to Pakistan, Ina Lepel, visited the khanqah — described in press coverage as a "200-year-old Sufi centre" — and met with its custodian, named in that report as Pir Mujtaba Farooq Gull; a second report of the same visit notes that she spent considerable time at the khanqah's attached madrassa, observing classes and discussing curriculum with students.

Name: Nagarparkar Jain Temples (Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape)
Location: Karoonjhar Mountains region, Nagarparkar, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: None - abandoned; heritage visitation
Description:
## Overview

Scattered across the pink-granite folds of the *Karoonjhar* mountains and the plains around Nagarparkar, in the far south-east of Sindh, stand the abandoned Jain temples that give this remote corner of Pakistan its most celebrated monuments. Built between roughly the twelfth and fifteenth centuries by a prosperous local Jain community, the temples — grouped by the Government of Pakistan under the title *Nagarparkar Cultural Landscape* — were placed on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites in 2016. Though the dataset files them, for convenience, among Hindu temples, they belong properly to the *Śvetāmbara* Jain tradition, and together they represent one of the high points of Jain architectural achievement in the subcontinent.

## The Jain Community and the Port of Parinagar

Nagarparkar lies in a zone of transition, where the salt-flats and marshes of the Rann of Kutch give way to stabilised sand dunes and the ancient granite of the Karoonjhar hills. For several centuries this was a flourishing centre of Jainism. The Jains of the region were maritime merchants and financiers who served as advisers to the Rajput chiefs, the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, and who dominated the trade of the area through the nearby port of *Parinagar*, believed by tradition to have been founded many centuries before the common era. The wealth generated by this commerce was poured into pious building, and the hills around Nagarparkar became a place of pilgrimage known as *Sardhara*, where Jain ascetics established themselves and where temple after temple rose in honour of the *Tirthankaras*.

## The Temples and their Architecture

The surviving monuments are dispersed across several locations — among them the temple in Nagarparkar town itself, the cluster at *Bhodesar*, the shrines at *Viravah* near the old site of Parinagar, and, most famously, the *Gori* temple between Islamkot and Nagarparkar. They are built in the *Māru-Gurjara* idiom of western India, distinguished by finely carved stone, richly ornamented ceilings, clustered subsidiary shrines and stepped tanks. The Gori temple, dated to 1375–76, is especially prized: its interior frescoes are held to be the oldest surviving Jain wall-paintings in the northern part of the subcontinent. So powerful was the local architectural language that even the fifteenth-century mosque at Bhodesar was raised in a style visibly indebted to the temples around it — an eloquent testament to the shared craft traditions of the region.

## Decline and Abandonment

The prosperity that raised the temples proved impermanent. As silt carried by the Indus gradually filled the Rann of Kutch, the Arabian Sea retreated from the centres of Jain commerce, and the trade on which the community depended withered. A large-scale movement of the Jain population away from the area took place in the nineteenth century, and those who remained departed at the Partition of British India in 1947. The temples were left empty, their sanctuaries silent, and over time they passed into the care of the state as protected monuments and popular heritage sites rather than as living places of worship.

## Significance Today

The Nagarparkar temples endure as among the most important pre-Islamic monuments in Pakistan and as the principal surviving witnesses to the once-thriving Jain civilisation of the lower Indus. They draw travellers, scholars and heritage enthusiasts to a landscape of striking beauty, where the rose-coloured Karoonjhar hills frame the carved stone of the shrines. Their inclusion on the UNESCO tentative list has focused attention on the need for their conservation, even as quarrying and neglect threaten parts of the wider landscape. For the study of religion in the region they are invaluable: a reminder that the sacred geography of Sindh has embraced Jain, Hindu and Muslim devotion alike, and that this arid frontier was once a centre of learning, art and pilgrimage.

- Endowment Fund Trust for Preservation of the Heritage of Sindh, documentation on the Nagarparkar temples.
- *The Friday Times*, "Jain Legacy of Nagarparkar" (2019).
- Wikipedia, "Nagarparkar Jain temples" and "Nagarparkar" (with cited sources).
- Ahmad Nabi Khan, *Islamic Architecture of Pakistan* (for the Bhodesar mosque and regional context).

Name: Panj Tirath
Events: Historically Kartik bathing; not currently observed
Description:
## Overview

Panj Tirath — the "five bathing places" — is one of the most ancient sacred sites of Peshawar, a Hindu pilgrimage complex whose name records the five pools of water that lay at its heart. Set in the Hashtnagri quarter of the old city, it belongs to a stratum of the region's religious history far older than the Islamic and Sikh monuments that surround it, reaching back through the Hindu and Buddhist antiquity of the Peshawar valley. Long neglected and much reduced, it was declared a protected national heritage site in 2019, an acknowledgement of a sanctity that local memory traces to the age of legend.

## Antiquity and Legend

The site takes its name and its holiness from its five *tirthas*, the pools in which pilgrims bathed. Local tradition, recorded by Munshi Gopal Das in his *Tareekh-e-Peshawar* of 1874 and repeated by the Hindu community, connects Panj Tirath with the five sons of *Pandu* — the *Pandava* heroes of the *Mahabharata* — and holds that the site was hallowed by their presence, so that its origins are woven into the great epic geography of the subcontinent. Alongside this Hindu memory runs a Buddhist one: the celebrated archaeologists Sir Alexander Cunningham and Alfred Foucher identified Panj Tirath and its environs with places associated in ancient accounts with the Buddha, including the relic of his begging-bowl, which was long kept at Peshawar (the ancient *Purushapura*). The site thus stands at the confluence of the two great faiths that shaped the valley before Islam, and its sanctity is best understood as very old and layered, rather than fixed to any single founder.

## History

Like so many of the region's shrines, Panj Tirath passed through cycles of destruction and revival. It is recorded to have been damaged during the turbulence of the Durrani period in the eighteenth century, around 1747, and then rebuilt by the Hindus of Peshawar in 1834, in the years of Sikh ascendancy in the north-west, when worship was restored at the pools. Through the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it remained an active centre of pilgrimage, its waters visited especially during the month of *Kartik* — the season, falling between late October and late November, when bathing at sacred *tirthas* carries particular merit in the Hindu calendar.

## Decline and Protection

The Partition of 1947 and the departure of most of Peshawar's Hindu population left Panj Tirath without a resident community to maintain it, and in the decades that followed the site was encroached upon and largely built over: much of its ground was absorbed into a public park, and its structures — two temples and a gateway among them — fell into dilapidation, some pressed into use as storerooms. In January 2019 the Directorate of Archaeology, acting under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Antiquities Act of 2016, declared Panj Tirath a protected national heritage site, a step welcomed by heritage advocates and the Hindu community alike, though the physical fabric of the complex remains fragile and in urgent need of conservation.

## Legacy

Panj Tirath is a witness to the deep and plural past of Peshawar — a city that has been in turn a Buddhist metropolis, a Hindu centre, a Mughal and Durrani stronghold, and a Sikh and British garrison. Its five pools, and the memory of the Pandavas and the Buddha that clings to them, connect the modern city to an antiquity measured in millennia. That the site survives at all, and now enjoys a measure of legal protection, offers some hope for the preservation of a heritage that belongs not to one community but to the long history of the region as a whole.

## Bibliography

- Munshi Gopal Das, *Tareekh-e-Peshawar* (1874), for the tradition linking the site to the sons of Pandu.
- A. Cunningham, *The Ancient Geography of India*, and A. Foucher's studies, on the Buddhist associations of Peshawar (*Purushapura*).
- Reporting in *The Friday Times* and *Dawn* on the 2019 heritage listing and the condition of Panj Tirath.
- Directorate of Archaeology, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, notifications under the KP Antiquities Act 2016.

Name: Parnami Mandir
Events: Historically an annual mela in Chaitra; not currently observed
Description:
## Overview

At Malka Hans, a historic village of the Pakpattan district in southern Punjab, stands the crumbling but still imposing *Parnami* (or *Pranami*) temple, one of the most significant surviving monuments of a distinctive Hindu devotional tradition in Pakistan. Once a central *ashram* of the Pranami faith west of the present border, the multi-storeyed building enshrined the *samadhi* of a revered teacher remembered locally as *Dya Ram*, and it drew large gatherings of devotees before the Partition of 1947. Today it survives chiefly as a heritage landmark in a village otherwise famous for its association with the Punjabi poet Waris Shah, who is said to have composed his celebrated *Heer* in a nearby mosque.

## The Pranami Tradition

The Pranami *sampradaya* — also called *Dhami* or *Nijananda* — is a Vaishnava tradition within Hinduism centred on the worship of *Krishna*. It emerged in western India in the seventeenth century from the teachings of the *bhakti* saint Devchandra Maharaj and, above all, of his foremost disciple Mehraj Thakur, better known as *Mahamati Prannath*, from whose name the tradition takes its own. Its adherents "bow" (*pranam*) in devotion — hence the name Pranami — and its teaching, gathered in a scripture called the *Tartam Sagar*, is notable for a strongly monotheistic emphasis and for language that sought common ground between Hindu and Islamic conceptions of the divine. The tradition spread across northern and western India and into Sindh and the Punjab, establishing temples and *dhams* that became centres of pilgrimage; the movement is also remembered for its historical links to the ruler Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand.

## The Temple at Malka Hans

Local accounts describe the Malka Hans temple as a tall building of several storeys, richly conceived, whose main chamber housed the *samadhi* of Dya Ram, honoured as the teacher associated with the establishment of the shrine. Precisely who Dya Ram was, and exactly when the temple was raised, are matters on which the surviving evidence is thin: heritage writers variously place its construction two centuries or more ago, while the Pranami tradition to which it belongs reaches back to the seventeenth century, and these datings should be treated with caution rather than as false precision. What is consistently reported is that the site functioned as an important Pranami centre, that a large annual *mela* was held here in the spring month of *Chaitra*, and that several further *samadhis* stand on the outskirts of the village, marking it as a place of sustained religious activity. The temple's height and prominence made it a notable feature of the local landscape.

## Decline and the Present Day

With the Partition of 1947 the Hindu population of this part of the Punjab migrated to India, and the temple, deprived of its congregation, fell silent. In the decades since it has suffered the familiar fate of abandoned sacred buildings — weathering, encroachment and the slow accumulation of decay — even as its scale continues to impress visitors. It has attracted the attention of heritage enthusiasts, photographers and journalists who document Pakistan's vanishing Hindu monuments, and it features in accounts of Malka Hans alongside the village's literary associations. Whether the structure will be conserved remains uncertain, and its condition has been a recurring subject of concern.

## Legacy

The Parnami temple of Malka Hans is a reminder that the religious map of the Punjab was once far more varied than it now appears, embracing not only the major Hindu, Muslim and Sikh traditions but also smaller reforming movements such as the Pranami faith, with its ecumenical cast and its Krishna-centred devotion. As one of the few tangible remains of that tradition on the Pakistani side of the border, the temple has a value for the history of religion in the region that far exceeds its present ruinous state, and it stands as a quiet monument to a community and a devotional world that have almost entirely passed from the local scene.

## Bibliography

- Wikipedia, "Pranami" (Pranami Sampradaya) and "Mahamati Prannath", with cited sources.
- Documentation of the Malka Hans temple by heritage writers on Pakistan's Hindu monuments (e.g. the *lahOre and mOre* and Ali Usman Baig field accounts).
- Haroon Khalid, writings on the folk and minority religious heritage of the Pakistani Punjab.
- General literature on the *bhakti* movements of western India and their spread into Sindh and the Punjab.

Name: Prahladpuri Temple
Location: Fort of Multan (near Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya), Multan, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: None - destroyed 1992
Description:
## Overview

The Prahladpuri Temple stood upon a raised platform at the southern tip of the great fort of Multan, immediately beside the shrine of the Sufi saint Bahauddin Zakariya — an eloquent juxtaposition of Multan's Hindu and Muslim sacred pasts on the same commanding mound. Dedicated to the deity *Narasimha*, the man-lion incarnation of Vishnu, and named for the devotee-prince *Prahlada*, it was among the most storied Hindu temples of the Indus plain, and in popular tradition it is remembered as a place from which the festival of *Holi* took its origin. Today the temple survives only as a ruin, its destruction in the late twentieth century having severed a line of worship that legend traced back to the beginnings of the world's ages.

Two books by Haroon Khalid describe the temple, though neither uses the name Prahladpuri. In *Walking with Nanak* it is "The temple of Prahlad Bhagat", "one of the most important Hindu temples" of Multan, with the shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya "located beside the temple" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 123, folio 105). In *A White Trail*, whose chapter "Holi at Multan" is given to the city and its Hindus (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 5, folio not stated), it is the temple built "in the memory of Prahlad" and "the historical Prahlad Temple" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated; p. 24, folio not stated). Both books identify it by its place beside Bahauddin Zakariya's shrine and by Prahlada's name; neither names Narasimha, the deity to whom the temple is dedicated. The other books consulted speak of Multan, of its Hindus, or of the Narasimha myth, but not of this temple; what they say is given below as the setting of the temple, not as an account of it.

## Mythology and Origins

The temple belongs to the great cycle of the *Narasimha* legend, one of the best-known narratives of Vaishnava devotion. As the story is told, the *asura* king *Hiranyakashipu* had won a boon that made him all but invincible and demanded to be worshipped as a god, but his own son *Prahlada* remained steadfastly devoted to Vishnu. Enraged, the king sought to destroy the boy, whose faith was at last vindicated when Vishnu burst forth from a pillar in the royal court in the form of *Narasimha*, half-man and half-lion, to slay the tyrant at a threshold that was neither inside nor out, at a twilight that was neither day nor night — circumventing every term of the boon. According to local tradition it was Prahlada himself who raised the temple at Multan in thanksgiving, enshrining an image of Narasimha upon the spot.

Khalid's account of the temple's beginning differs. In *A White Trail* he writes: "His devotees built a temple in the memory of Prahlad at the spot where he supposedly killed his father – on a mound outside the city, which later became a popular spiritual site with mystics and saints" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated). Hiranyakashipu, in his telling, is "the tyrant who is believed to have ruled the city of Multan thousands of years ago" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 19, folio not stated), and the city "continues to move forward unaware of its ancient past and the mythical association that it has with the story of Hiranyakashipu and Prahlad Bhagat" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 20–21, folio not stated). A photograph in the same book carries the caption "Celebrating Holi in the city of Hiranyakashipu and Prahlad Bhagat." (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 108, folio not stated).

The man-lion himself appears elsewhere in Khalid's book, far from Multan: in the Sri Valmiki shrine at Bahawalnagar he saw "a picture of Narasimha, tearing Hiranyakashipu apart" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 36, folio not stated). Jürgen Schaflechner, writing on the goddess Hinglaj, names the myth only in passing, as "the famous myth of Narasimha, canonized in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 229, folio not stated), and of another story he writes that it is one "which is clearly a reference to the legend of Narasimha in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 230, folio not stated). Neither passage concerns Multan or this temple.

Bound to this is the tradition that connects Multan with the origins of *Holi*. The bonfire of *Holika* — the demoness sister of Hiranyakashipu, who sought to burn the child Prahlada but was herself consumed while he emerged unharmed — is remembered in the spring festival of colour and fire, and Multan's temple was long held to be the very stage of that deliverance. Whatever weight one gives to these legends as history, they made Prahladpuri a site of unusual resonance in the sacred geography of the subcontinent.

## The Temple and the Mound

Khalid makes the temple the reason the mound became holy. Because the mound was linked with the temple, he writes, "the area came to be considered holy", and it drew Muslim mystics, among them Bahauddin Zakariya, "whose shrine came to be situated next to the temple" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* he sets the two side by side in a city that was, in Guru Nanak's day, "one of the biggest cities of Punjab and was known for the religious shrines of Muslim saints, and Jain and Hindu temples. It was a sacred space for people of all religious denominations" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 123, folio 105).

The order of the two sites has since reversed. The temple, Khalid writes, "now lies in obscurity under the shadow of this massive shrine" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated), and he calls it, "even though in shambles now", "an anomaly next to the shrine, an unacceptable act of treason in 'Muslim' Pakistan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).

## History and Destruction

For centuries the temple was a living centre of worship, repaired and rebuilt across the vicissitudes of Multan's turbulent history. During the siege of Multan in 1848, in the campaigns that preceded the British annexation of the Punjab, a shell struck a powder magazine within the fort and the ensuing explosion is said to have carried away the temple's roof; in the aftermath the East India Company held the fort directly for some years before restoring the shrines to their communities around 1852. The building suffered again amid communal violence in 1881, when it was set alight, only to be renovated once more by Multan's Hindu community.

Its end came in December 1992. In the wave of reprisals across Pakistan that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya in India, a mob attacked and destroyed the Prahladpuri Temple and its adjoining *dharamshala*, reducing the historic structure to rubble. The site of the temple is now held by the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the state body that administers the properties of communities displaced at Partition, and proposals for its restoration have been discussed from time to time without a full rebuilding having been achieved.

Khalid gives the temple's recent history in other terms. "The temple stands even today, a worn down building with several cracks in its walls. It has remained abandoned ever since partition, occasionally becoming victim to the passion of fanatic mobs like the one in 1992" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated). Of the days after the demolition of the Babri Mosque, dated in his book to the "6th of December 1992", he writes more generally that "Well-known Hindus living in the cities of Punjab had to hide for several months after the incident" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 22, folio not stated). One of his informants in Multan, Parvati Devi, "a 44 year old classically trained professional singer from Multan, who is also a social activist", recalls a mob in those days that had "destroyed the Valmiki temple" near her house and wanted to burn her alive (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 17, 21, folio not stated); afterwards she "took up a Muslim name, Shaila Bibi" and stopped appearing on radio and television (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 21, folio not stated). Her account names the Valmiki temple, not the Prahlad temple.

## The Temple Today

Khalid's informants describe who holds the temple and what has been built on its ground. According to Parvati Devi, the temple "comes under the jurisdiction of the Awqaf department (a government institution that looks after all the historical Muslim shrines and mosques of the country)", and she says: "It is our demand that the temple be restored and given to the Hindus of the city who are its real owners" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated). She recalls that "in 2006 and 2008" the authorities of Bahauddin Zakariya's shrine "extended the shrine into the premises of the historical Prahlad Temple by constructing a place for ablutions first and then a Langar Hall" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated).

The matter reached the courts. Khalid records that "25 year old Usman Chaudary, President of the RAS (Organisation for Religious and Sexual Minorities) society filed a petition in the High Court", that "the Court passed a stay order against any further construction on the premises of the temple", and that the RAS Society "has petitioned that the temple be handed back to the Hindu community in the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated). The book does not say how the petition ended.

## Holi at Multan

Khalid's chapter on Holi follows the festival that tradition ties to this temple into the Multan of his own day; the celebrations he describes are held in a Hindu locality and before the city's press club, not at the temple. The "thirty odd women" who burned the Holika, he writes, "are now the only link that the city has with that story"; these Hindus "lived here before Multan became a part of Pakistan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 21, folio not stated). The locality where he watched the festival, "situated next to the Railway station, is one of several areas where the Hindu community of the city is located"; the community numbers "little more than a thousand", and "there isn't a centralized celebration"; the settlement has "about a hundred houses", "only about ten to twelve belonging to Hindu families" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 23, folio not stated). According to Parvati Devi, "There were several historical temples in Multan from the pre-partition days. All of them have become ruins now", and the community has turned other spaces "into make-shift temples" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated).

The public festival, in Khalid's account, had lapsed and returned. "As recently as 2010" festivals including Holi "were not celebrated in the city"; that year Usman organised "a token celebration of Holi in front of the Multan Press Club" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 24–25, folio not stated). Holi, "even though on a small scale is now celebrated every year in Multan" and is "regularly featured in the local media"; Usman has been alleged to be "an Indian agent", and "More than once he along with his friends has been physically attacked" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 25, folio not stated).

## Setting: Multan

The books' accounts of Multan speak of the city, not of the temple, but they show the place in which it stood. Harish Dhillon, retelling the Janamsakhis of Guru Nanak, calls Multan one of the oldest cities in South-East Asia, a city where three rivers merge before the Indus and "a commercial hub for national and international trade, including with Persia, Central Asia and the Arab world" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 165, folio 181). He writes that "During the time of the Mahabharata, it was the capital of the Tuganta kingdom", that legend has Alexander struck by an arrow there, that "For the next thousand years, Multan was ruled by Hindu and" Buddhist kings, and that the Chinese traveller Heun Tsang, as the book spells him, visited it in A.D. 641; he calls it the city of gold, its Suraj temple "Claimed to be by far the biggest temple in the subcontinent" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 165, folio 181). In the eleventh century, he writes, Mahmud of Ghazni damaged the Suraj temple and destroyed "the giant idol", and in time the town became studded with mosques as it had once been with Hindu temples (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 166, folio 182). By the time Nanak came to Multan, "the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 167, folio 183).

Annemarie Schimmel gives 711 as the year in which "the Arabs conquered Sind and the adjacent provinces northward up to Multan" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 375, folio 344). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes that "Multan had become a dependency of the Fatimids of Egypt", that "by the middle of the eleventh century, sufism had penetrated into the areas surrounding Multan", and that "in 1175 Mu‘izzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized Multan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 128, folio 110). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, under the heading "صوبه دار الامان ملتان", says of the city: "از شهرهاے پاستان است و قلعه خشتین دارد", that is, it is one of the ancient cities and has a fort of brick; he adds that besides the saints he names, "بسیاری از اولیاے دران شهر سعادت بهر اسوده اند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528).

The nineteenth-century wars that the temple's own history records touched the city as a whole. Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence note that Hafiz Muhammad Jamal (d. 1811), a successor of Nur Muhammad, "is also said to have taken part in resistance to Sikh attacks on Multan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* records the Sikh conquest of Multan in a year written out as "سن اٹھارہ سوا اٹھارہ", with Kharak Singh sent against the city (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 580); when Ranjit Singh conquered Multan, he writes, Nawab Muzaffar Khan was killed, and others of the family, Sarfraz Khan among them by an uncertain reading, were captured with their households and came to Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 130). In a year printed uncertainly as 1848, "دیوان مولراج پسر ساون مل ناظم ملتان" raised a disturbance and had "اگنیو[OCR?] صاحب بہادر" with another sahib, and "کاہن[OCR?] سنگھ ناظم جدید ملتان[OCR?]", the new governor of Multan, killed; the readings of both names are uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592). Chishti traces the troubles of that year from Multan through Hazara and four hard battles to a date printed, uncertainly, as 29 March 1849, when, as he puts it, "تمام ملک سلطنت انگریزی مین داخل ہو گیا", and he closes with a *qitʿa* on the departure of Maharaja Dalip Singh, whose lines include "چون شمع[OCR?] پنجاب از پنجاب رفت" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592).

Multan also enters the verse of the region, though never this temple. In Naveed Alam's translation of a kafi of Madho Lal Hussein, the city is named as the place where one item of a bride's trousseau was bought:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 51, folio 51).

Schimmel writes of the vernacular poets of Pakistan that for them "Mecca and Medina (and for the Sindhi and Panjabi, also Multan) are inside the heart" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 178, folio 160).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Who built the temple.** The site's account gives the local tradition that "it was Prahlada himself who raised the temple at Multan in thanksgiving". Khalid writes that "His devotees built a temple in the memory of Prahlad" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **What happened on the spot.** The site's account tells that Vishnu, as Narasimha, slew Hiranyakashipu, and that Prahlada raised the temple in thanksgiving "upon the spot". Khalid places the temple "at the spot where he supposedly killed his father", the "he" being Prahlad (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **Where the mound lay.** The site's account sets the temple "at the southern tip of the great fort of Multan". Khalid sets it "on a mound outside the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **To whom the temple belongs.** The site's account dedicates the temple to Narasimha and names it for Prahlada. Khalid calls it "The temple of Prahlad Bhagat" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 123, folio 105) and the temple "in the memory of Prahlad" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated), and does not name Narasimha in connection with it.
- **When worship ceased.** The site's account has the temple as "a living centre of worship" for centuries, renovated by Multan's Hindu community after 1881, until its destruction in December 1992 "severed a line of worship". Khalid writes that it "has remained abandoned ever since partition" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **Whether the building still stands.** The site's account says the 1992 mob reduced "the historic structure to rubble" and that the temple "survives only as a ruin". Khalid writes that "The temple stands even today, a worn down building with several cracks in its walls", the 1992 mob being one of those to which it has "occasionally" fallen victim (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 20, folio not stated).
- **Who holds the site.** The site's account says the temple's site "is now held by the Evacuee Trust Property Board". Khalid's informant Parvati Devi says the temple "comes under the jurisdiction of the Awqaf department" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated).

## Legacy

The ruins of Prahladpuri remain among the most poignant of Pakistan's lost Hindu monuments, a fragment of the deep Hindu antiquity of Multan — a city whose very name is bound in classical sources to a famed sun-temple, and whose fort mound has borne temples and shrines in almost unbroken succession for millennia. That the remains of the Narasimha temple and the tomb of a great Muslim saint share the same eminence is itself a lesson in the layered religious history of the Indus valley. For the Hindu communities of Pakistan and for pilgrims and scholars abroad, Prahladpuri endures as a place of memory: a temple whose legend gave the subcontinent one of its most joyous festivals, and whose fate records one of the harder chapters of the region's recent past.

For Khalid the temple's legacy is its claim on the city's memory, and the claim of the city's Hindus on the temple. Multan, he writes, goes on "unaware of its ancient past" and of its tie to the story of Hiranyakashipu and Prahlad Bhagat (Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 20–21, folio not stated); the demand his informant puts to him is that the temple "be restored and given to the Hindus of the city who are its real owners" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 24, folio not stated).

Name: Purana Bhalwal
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Purana Bhalwal, the old settlement that gives its name to the modern town of Bhalwal in Sargodha District, stands the shrine of *Hazrat Shah Sulaiman Nuri*, a sixteenth-century Sufi of the *Qadiriyya* order who is remembered locally with the affectionate title *Sakhi Badshah*, 'the generous king'. The dargah is the spiritual heart of an otherwise unassuming corner of central Punjab, drawing devotees from the surrounding villages of the Chaj Doab, the fertile tract between the Jhelum and the Chenab.

None of the books consulted describes the shrine at Purana Bhalwal itself. Its tomb, its courtyard and its yearly gatherings are known here only from the site's own account; what the books record is the saint. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, composed in 1292 AH, 1875 CE, as an account of the saints of Punjab, gives him an entry of his own, numbered 26 and headed "شاہ سلیمان قادری", Shah Sulaiman Qadri, and calls him a *khalifa* of Shah Maruf Chishti (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55). The book's modern editor corrects its author three times in that one entry: on the name of the place, on the saint's family and on the year of his death (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55). It is the editor's correction of the place name, not the author's own text, that makes the place Bhalwal (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55, حاشیہ 3). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names him once, as "شاہ سلیمان نوری", Shah Sulaiman Nuri, in a spiritual pedigree that runs from Shah Maruf Chishti through him to Naushah Ganj Bakhsh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).

## The Life of Shah Sulaiman Nuri

Shah Sulaiman Nuri is traditionally said to have lived a remarkably long life, from the early sixteenth century until 1604. According to the accounts preserved by his devotees, he was a scholar and ascetic trained in the *Qadiri* path, and his spiritual guide (*pir*) was Shah Maroof Khushabi of the nearby town of Khushab. It is related that his teacher, recognising his disciple's attainment, directed him to settle at Purana Bhalwal and to make it the centre of his teaching and service. There he is said to have spent the remainder of his life in devotion, instruction and the feeding of travellers and the poor — the quality of open-handed hospitality from which his epithet *Sakhi Badshah* is popularly derived.

As with many saints of this period, the details of his biography survive largely through oral tradition and later hagiography rather than contemporary record, and precise dates should be treated as traditional. He is said to have died at a great age on the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan, one of the most sacred nights of the Muslim calendar, a detail that has only deepened the reverence in which he is held.

## Family and Birthplace

Lahori's entry opens with the saint's father and his village. The author writes: "ان کا باپ منگو قوم موچی موضع بھیلووال [OCR?] میں رہتا تھا": his father, Mangu, of the Mochi caste, lived in the village of Bhelowal, a name whose reading is uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55).

The editor's footnotes correct both halves of that sentence. Of the place he writes "بھیلووال کی بجائے بھلوال ہونا چاہیے": instead of Bhelowal it should be Bhalwal (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55, حاشیہ 3). Of the family he writes that the saint's father was Shaikh Abdullah, known as Mian Mangu, of the Qureshi caste, and that "آپ موچی نہیں تھے", he was not a Mochi; for the Qureshi genealogy he cites Sharafat Naushahi's *Sharif al-Tawarikh*, volume 1, page 865, and Umar Bakhsh Rasulnagri's *Manaqibat-e Naushahi* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55, حاشیہ 2). The book thus carries two accounts side by side: the author's Mochi father named Mangu, and the editor's Qureshi father, Shaikh Abdullah, called Mian Mangu.

## His Master and His Disciple

The site's account makes Shah Maroof Khushabi his *pir*. Lahori calls him a *khalifa* of Shah Maruf Chishti (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55), and in another passage speaks of "شاہ معروف چشتی و قادری", Shah Maruf, Chishti and Qadiri, the subject of his twelfth entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 50, folio 38). Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* records that Maruf Chishti held authority to initiate in two orders, "قادریہ و چشتیہ", the Qadiriyya and the Chishtiyya (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).

Lahori records that Shah Maruf marked Sulaiman out while he was still a child (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55). The site's account, for its part, relates that his teacher, recognising his disciple's attainment, sent him to settle at Purana Bhalwal.

The disciple who carried the line on was, in Lahori's account, Haji Muhammad Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, who was brought to Shah Sulaiman by Mulla Karim al-Din (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 70–71, folios 58–59). Lahori's own entry on that disciple is headed "شیخ حاجی محمد قادری المشہور بحضرت نوشہ گنج بخش", and says that the Naushahi way began with him: "طریقہ نوشاہیہ جس کے فقیر پنجاب میں ہزاروں ہیں۔ ان سے شروع ہوا", the thousands of its *faqirs* in Punjab being those of the author's own day (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58).

The same chain appears in *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, in the second *shajra*, or spiritual pedigree, of one Bhage Shah: "… حضرت حاجی محمود شاہ نوشاہ گنج بخش اونکو[OCR?] شاہ سلیمان نوری اونکی حضرت معروف چشتی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467). Here Shah Sulaiman Nuri stands between Naushah Ganj Bakhsh and Hazrat Maruf Chishti, and the disciple is named Haji Mahmud Shah rather than Haji Muhammad.

Of the spread of the Naushahi order Lahori also writes, in a passage on the lifetime of Shah Maruf, "انہیں کی ذات بابرکات سے پنجاب میں سلسلہ نوشاہیہ نے فروغ پایا": the Naushahi order spread in Punjab through him. The sentence names Sayyid Mubarak Haqqani just before, and the text does not settle whether 'his' means Shah Maruf or Sayyid Mubarak (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 50, folio 38).

## Teaching, Listening and Ecstasy

Lahori's entry describes the saint's way of devotion. He listened to *sama*, and in *wajd* he would fall so senseless "کہ مرگ کی حالت تک پہنچ جاتے", that he reached the condition of death (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55). Thousands, the book says, entered his *bai'at* and reached high degrees, and his whole life was spent guiding students (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55).

## His Death

The site's account gives his death as 1604, on the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan. Lahori's author gives the year in words, "سال ایک ہزار پینسٹھ", with ۱۰۶۵ in the margin: 1065 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55, حاشیہ 1). The editor rejects it: "آپ ۲۷ رمضان ۱۰۱۲ھ میں فوت ہوئے (عمر بخش: مناقبات نوشاہی قلمی)، ۱۰۶۵ھ غلط ہے", he died on 27 Ramadan 1012 AH, citing Umar Bakhsh's *Manaqibat-e Naushahi*, and 1065 AH is wrong (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55, حاشیہ 1). The editor's 1012 AH is the Hijri year in which 1604 falls; the author's 1065 AH is not.

## The Name in the Books

The names the site uses are not all in the books. Lahori's entry heads him Shah Sulaiman Qadri and gives neither 'Nuri' nor 'Sakhi Badshah'; *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* calls him Shah Sulaiman Nuri (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467). The index of *Hadiqat al-Awliya* lists a "سلیمان بھلوالی", Sulaiman of Bhalwal, and on a separate line a "سلیمان قادری لاہوری شاہ"; the first carries the place and the second the order, and neither line carries both, so which of them leads to this entry is not settled (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 319, folio 307). The same index keeps several other Sulaimans apart from these two (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 319, folio 307).

## The Shrine and its Devotional Life

The shrine at Purana Bhalwal follows the familiar pattern of Punjab's smaller Sufi dargahs: a whitewashed tomb chamber sheltering the grave, enclosed within a courtyard where devotees gather to offer *Fatiha*, tie threads of intention, and distribute food. The saint's *urs* — the annual commemoration of his death anniversary, understood in Sufi thought as the soul's union with the Divine — is the principal event of the devotional year, when *qawwals* perform devotional song and *langar* (the free communal meal) is served to all who come.

The books say nothing of the shrine's building, its founding, its custodians or the date of its *urs*. They do speak of the traditions the gathering draws on. Regula Burckhardt Qureshi, writing of *qawwali* in general and not of this shrine, distinguishes the tunes of its two principal regions, Uttar Pradesh and a Panjab she does not divide between India and Pakistan: "A predominantly quantitative emphasis characterizes tunes from Uttar Pradesh, while Panjabi tunes tend to be rhythmically organized according to 'quality' or stress", the drum's articulation of the metre being "more strongly accentual than in Uttar Pradesh" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 73, folio 53). Annemarie Schimmel, writing of the mystical literature of Sind and Punjab, notes that "Both provinces have also produced hymns extolling the great masters of the mystical orders", particularly ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani, in imagery that "could easily be understood by everybody in the village" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 417, folio 386).

Bhalwal itself grew as an agricultural market town under the canal colonies of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and the shrine anchored the older village of Purana ("old") Bhalwal as the newer town expanded around the railway. For the cultivators of the district the saint remains a figure of intercession and blessing, invoked at times of illness, harvest and family need, in the manner characteristic of the living shrine culture of rural Punjab.

## Setting

The books that describe the country around Bhalwal speak of the province, not of the town. Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, describing the Mughal suba of Lahore, divides it into five *doabs*, the tracts between its rivers, and names the doab between the Chenab and the Bihat "چنتهه[OCR?]", the reading uncertain in the printed text, with "چونهت" for Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 511; p. 515). In that suba, he writes, "اکثر مدار اب یاری[OCR?] چاه است": irrigation depended mostly on wells, each worked by a wheel of "سیصد و شصت چوب" and more than a hundred small pots turned by a pair of oxen, while the *kharif* and *rabi* harvests and the cheapness of grain depended on the rain (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 510).

The canal colonies came later. Haroon Khalid writes of the province as a whole that "the British connected the five rivers of Punjab with each other through canals, turning several acres of jungle land into agricultural land", that "thousands of new villages, referred to as chaks were established, and farming families from all over Punjab were invited to settle", and that its former inhabitants "were primarily nomads", unable "to prove ownership over land": "Their land was snatched away and allotted to these migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

Of the order the site names, Lahori writes that the first of the Qadiri line to come to Punjab was "حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی", who came by way of Khurasan to Multan and settled at Uch, after his ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan; the book gives no year, and the editor's footnote adds, on the authority of Ali Asghar Gilani, that he entered Uch in 887 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28).

*Hadiqat al-Awliya*, the book that keeps the fullest record of Shah Sulaiman, closes with chronograms for its own completion. One, by Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, whom the book calls the author's "خلف", sets out its scope in Punjab:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram couplet on the book's scope, the saints of Punjab; the closing chronograms read ۱۲۹۲ھ, 1292 AH* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 282, folio 270).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives 1604, on the night of the twenty-seventh of Ramadan. Lahori's author gives 1065 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55, حاشیہ 1). His editor gives 27 Ramadan 1012 AH, citing Umar Bakhsh's *Manaqibat-e Naushahi*, and calls 1065 AH wrong (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 67, folio 55, حاشیہ 1).
- **His father and caste.** Lahori's author names the father Mangu, of the Mochi caste (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55). His editor names him Shaikh Abdullah, known as Mian Mangu, of the Qureshi caste, and says he was not a Mochi, citing *Sharif al-Tawarikh* and *Manaqibat-e Naushahi* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55, حاشیہ 2). The site's account does not name his father.
- **The name of the place.** The site's account gives Purana Bhalwal. Lahori's author writes "بھیلووال [OCR?]", Bhelowal; his editor says it should be Bhalwal (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55, حاشیہ 3).
- **The saint's name and title.** The site's account calls him Hazrat Shah Sulaiman Nuri and Sakhi Badshah. Lahori heads his entry "شاہ سلیمان قادری" and gives neither Nuri nor Sakhi Badshah (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55). *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* calls him "شاہ سلیمان نوری" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).
- **His master and his order.** The site's account names his *pir* as Shah Maroof Khushabi of Khushab and places him in the Qadiri path. Lahori calls him a *khalifa* of Shah Maruf Chishti (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55), and elsewhere calls Shah Maruf "چشتی و قادری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 50, folio 38). *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names him "حضرت معروف چشتی", with authority in both the Qadiriyya and the Chishtiyya (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).
- **The name of his disciple.** Lahori names the disciple Haji Muhammad Naushah Ganj Bakhsh (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 70–71, folios 58–59), and heads his entry "شیخ حاجی محمد قادری المشہور بحضرت نوشہ گنج بخش" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58). *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names him "حضرت حاجی محمود شاہ نوشاہ گنج بخش" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).

## Legacy

Shah Sulaiman Nuri belongs to the dense network of Qadiri and Chishti saints whose shrines dot the Chaj and Rechna Doabs, forming a sacred geography that shaped the religious life of Punjab long before modern boundaries were drawn. While he never attained the trans-regional fame of a Data Ganj Bakhsh or a Baba Farid, his dargah illustrates how Sufi devotion took root at the local level, giving small communities their own centre of blessing and continuity. The shrine remains in active use today, cared for by the descendants and devotees of the saint and, like many such sites, falling under the general oversight of the provincial Auqaf administration.

The books place him at a turning in the history of the orders of Punjab. In Lahori's account he is the link between Shah Maruf Chishti and Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, from whom the Naushahi way began (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 66–67, folios 54–55; pp. 70–71, folios 58–59; p. 70, folio 58), and *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* keeps him in the same place in Bhage Shah's pedigree (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).

Of the hereditary saints of the province in general, not of this shrine, Robert Rozehnal quotes Katherine Ewing's *Arguing Sainthood*: "British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sind, was to treat them in essentially the same way that landlords and tribal leaders were treated", the hereditary saints being those who "were seen primarily in terms of their economic power", and the policy one of securing "the loyalty of the pirs, landlords, and chiefs by reinforcing their economic positions and educating them in the British tradition" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 33, folio 23).
