Name: Rahman Baba Mausoleum (Rehman Baba Shrine)
Location: Hazarkhwani (Ring Road), Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs with mushaira (poetic assembly); rabab recitals
Description:
## Overview

At Hazarkhwani, on the edge of Peshawar, stands the mausoleum of Rahman Baba (Abdur Rahman Mohmand, c. 1653–1711) — the most beloved poet of the Pashto language and the great mystic voice of the Pashtuns. For three centuries his *Diwan* has been the book most cherished after the Qur’an in countless Pashtun homes, its verses of love, humility, and the vanity of the world quoted as proverbs and sung by musicians from Peshawar to Kandahar. His shrine is the spiritual and literary heart of the Pashto-speaking world, and a traditional gathering place of poets and singers.

The books consulted say little of him, and of the mausoleum itself only one sentence. Haroon Khalid, writing of Pakistan's folk religious practices, records that "In March 2009 the popular shrine of Rahman Baba was attacked in Peshawar resulting in the death of over 100 people" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). No book consulted names Hazarkhwani, describes the tomb's building, or records its *ʿurs*. Annemarie Schimmel writes of the poet, not the tomb: Abdur Rahman, "lovingly called Rahman Baba", was a mystic of the Chishti order, one "who lived during the Aurangzeb period (d. 1709) and is usually regarded as the best mystical poet in Pashto." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399). Her death year differs from the one given above, and the two are set side by side below.

## The Life of the Poet-Saint

Abdur Rahman was born around 1653 near Peshawar, into the Mohmand tribe of the Pashtuns; he is remembered as a man of humble means and retiring temperament, a dervish who shunned the powerful and lived in poverty and prayer. Little of his outward life is documented — he was no courtier and left no chronicle of himself — but his verse reveals a soul of deep Sufi devotion, gentle, self-effacing, and wholly turned toward God. He belonged to the broad Sufi current of his time and place, and by tradition performed the Hajj; he died around 1711 and was buried at Hazarkhwani, where his shrine arose.

Schimmel names his order, calling him a mystic of the Chishti order (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399). She places him in the reign of Aurangzeb and gives his death as 1709, in her running text and again in her index, where he stands as Abdur Rahman (Rahman Baba), d. 1709 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399; p. 510, folio 479). She gives the retiring life as legend, and in so many words: "As legend has it, he led a life of withdrawal and seclusion, and his poetry reflects a sadness and ascetic feeling that are not too frequent in the mystical poets of this period." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399).

She names a second Pashto poet of his order: "a remarkable poet tried to express mystical teachings in Pashto. This poet was Khwaja Muhammad Bangash", who was, like Abdur Rahman, a member of the Chishti order (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 432, folio 401). She gives no tomb, no Peshawar and no Hazarkhwani for Rahman Baba.

## The Poetry

Rahman Baba’s fame rests entirely on his *Diwan* — a body of Pashto verse of unmatched sweetness and moral depth. His great themes are the love of God, the transience of the world, humility, tolerance, and the dignity of the poor; he preaches, again and again, that one should return kindness for cruelty and sow good rather than harm. One of his most quoted teachings runs, in sense:

[“Sow flowers, that your garden may bloom about you; the thorns you plant will wound your own feet.”]

His poetry is at once popular and profound — simple enough for the unlettered to carry in memory, deep enough to nourish the mystic — and it has done more than any other book to shape the moral imagination of the Pashtuns. His verses are sung to the *rabab* and recited in gatherings, and his name is spoken with an affection given to no other Pashto poet.

Schimmel adds a note of her own on the verse's mood, in the words of the legend quoted above: "his poetry reflects a sadness and ascetic feeling that are not too frequent in the mystical poets of this period." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399). The books consulted quote none of his lines, in Pashto or in English.

His verse has reached readers abroad in selection. In a note on Pashto mystical poetry in another of her books, Schimmel writes that "Good examples are found in H . G . Raverty, Selections from the Poetry of the Afghans; James Darmesteter, Chants populaires des Afghans, and Jens Enevoldsen, Selections from Rahman Baba" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 278, folio 260). Her bibliography dates Enevoldsen's volume to 1977, from the publisher Paul Kristensen; the place of publication is damaged in the printed text (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 319, folio 301). That book says nothing else of him, and nothing of his tomb.

## The Shrine

Rahman Baba’s mausoleum at Hazarkhwani has long been a centre of pilgrimage and of Pashto literary life, where poets and singers gather and an annual urs is held in his honour with music and *mushaira* (poetic assembly) alongside the rites of devotion. The shrine was severely damaged by a bombing in 2009 — an attack on the tolerant, musical devotion it represents — but it was subsequently rebuilt, and pilgrims and lovers of his poetry returned. It remains the great shrine of the Pashto-speaking world.

Khalid gives the attack its month and its toll: "In March 2009 the popular shrine of Rahman Baba was attacked in Peshawar resulting in the death of over 100 people" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). It is the one sentence on the shrine in the books consulted; none of them records who built the mausoleum, when, or how it was rebuilt, and none gives the date of the *ʿurs*.

## Setting

The books say more of Peshawar and its country than of the poet's tomb, and what follows is about the place, not the shrine.

Sujan Rai Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, a Persian history composed in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, writes that "پشاور شهر قدیم است که در کتب متقدمین پرشاور و فرشاور نیز نویسند", that Peshawar is an old city which the earlier books also write as Parshawar and Farshawar (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 503). It describes the district "مشهور به پشاور" as having grapes, peaches and melons like those of Turan, heat, cold, seasons and rain like those of Hindustan, rice better than Bengal's, and crops and grain in plenty (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 504). Of its people it says that "تمام[OCR?] این تومان بنگاه افغانان مهمند و غیر ذلک است", that the whole district is the home of the Mohmand Afghans and others; the Mohmand are the tribe into which, in the current account, Rahman Baba was born (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 504–503). The same history records three roads from Peshawar to Kabul: by Nikshab, hard and long; by a road joining the highway at Jalalabad, with narrow defiles, little water and Afghan raids; and by Ali Masjid and the Khyber, easier than the others and used by armies and caravans (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 502–501).

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes of the city's religious past long before the poet that "From the eleventh century the Nath yogis began to spread throughout northern India, and from their centre at Peshawar moved to all parts of Central Asia and Iran, at the same time influencing both qalandars and sufis" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 355, folio 333). Rizvi does not name Rahman Baba.

Of the frontier's shrines in general, Robert Rozehnal quotes a woman disciple from Peshawar, contrasting her home with Pakpattan: "In the frontier, we have so many shrines where you can walk into the saint’s shrines. Women can go inside, we can touch the graves. At many places there is a separate side for the women. It is not like this at Pakpattan Sharif" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 219, folio 211). She names no Peshawar shrine. And in Schimmel's paraphrase of the boldest mystical verse of the Panjabi and Sindhi poets, Peshawar stands among the identities the Sufi leaves behind: "the Sufi is no longer Arab, Hindu, Turk, or Peshawari; eventually Hallaj and the judge who condemned him, the lover and the theologian, are seen as nothing but different manifestations of the one divine reality." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 417, folio 386).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- The year of his death. The current account gives it as around 1711; Schimmel gives 1709, in her running text and in her index alike (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399; p. 510, folio 479).
- His retiring life. The current account gives his humble, retiring temperament as how he is remembered; Schimmel gives his life of withdrawal and seclusion as legend: "As legend has it" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399).
- His Sufi affiliation. The current account places him in the broad Sufi current of his time and place, naming no order; Schimmel calls him a mystic of the Chishti order (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399; p. 432, folio 401).
- The 2009 attack. The current account speaks of a bombing that severely damaged the shrine; Khalid speaks of an attack in March 2009 resulting in the death of over 100 people (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

## Legacy

Rahman Baba stands to Pashto as Bhittai to Sindhi and Bulleh Shah to Punjabi: the poet who gave his people’s language its deepest and most beloved voice. His gospel of love, humility, tolerance, and the emptiness of worldly pride has been for three centuries a moral compass for the Pashtuns, and his *Diwan* a household treasure. His shrine at Peshawar — rebuilt after violence — endures as the hearth of Pashto poetry and the resting place of a saint whose verse still teaches a gentler way.

Schimmel's judgement, that he "is usually regarded as the best mystical poet in Pashto", is the books' own measure of that standing (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 430, folio 399).

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- Rahman Baba, *Diwan* (his Pashto poetry; the quoted teaching given here in English translation only).
- General established histories of Pashto literature and Sufism.
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *As Through a Veil: Mystical Poetry in Islam* (New York: Columbia University Press, 1982; Lectures on the History of Religions, New Series 12).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).
- Sujan Rai Bhandari of Batala, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* (Persian; composed in regnal year 40 of Aurangzeb; 1918 Delhi lithograph edited by Zafar Hasan).
- Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, Vol. I: Early Sufism and its History in India to 1600 AD (New Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers Pvt. Ltd., first published 1978).
- Robert Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound: Politics and Piety in Twenty-First Century Pakistan* (2007).

Name: Ram Mandir, Saidpur (Ram Kund Mandir)
Location: Saidpur Village, Margalla Hills, Islamabad Capital Territory, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 16th century (traditionally attributed to Raja Man Singh I)
Events: Heritage/tourist site; regular worship discontinued
Description:
## Overview

The Ram Mandir at Saidpur — also known as the Ram Kund Mandir — stands in the historic village of Saidpur, set in a fold of the Margalla Hills on the northern edge of Islamabad. A Hindu temple dedicated to *Lord Rama*, it is traditionally dated to the sixteenth century and attributed by some accounts to Raja Man Singh I, the Rajput general of the Mughal emperor Akbar.

None of the books consulted for this article describes the temple, and none mentions this Saidpur or its Ram Kund. What they offer concerns Rama himself. Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* traces the line of Raja Ramchandar and gives a list of its kings (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 795–796); translations of Bulleh Shah and of Waris Shah gloss the story of the *Ramayana* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175; Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13); Jürgen Schaflechner follows Rama along the pilgrimage route to the goddess Hinglaj (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 119, folio not stated); Haroon Khalid writes of his festivals (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated); and the verse of Bulleh Shah and Madho Lal Hussein, and a song sung at Sehwan, carry his name into Sufi poetry (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 116, folio 91; Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 181, folio 181; Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 57, folio 40). That material is set out below as context about Rama and the epic, not as the history of this temple; the books' few passing words on Islamabad and the Margalla Hills are gathered under Setting.

## The Temple

Before Partition, Saidpur was a place of notable interfaith coexistence, home to Muslims, Hindus, and Sikhs together, its skyline holding a mosque, this Hindu temple, and — from the early twentieth century — a Sikh *gurdwara*. The books consulted add nothing to this account: none names the temple's builder, gives the year of its building, or records a custodian or an endowment.

After 1947 the temple ceased to function as a place of worship; it was used for a time as a girls' school, and in the 2000s the Capital Development Authority restored Saidpur as a heritage and arts village, conserving the temple's fabric while its idols were removed and its images painted over.

*Dawn*'s 2016 reporting adds that in 2006 the Capital Development Authority had the by-then-vacated building formally cleared and preserved as a tourist attraction, and that visitors have since documented restaurants operating within the complex serving meat dishes, a practice criticised by Hindu commentators as an affront to the site's sanctity.

The building survives as a protected monument and a popular destination for visitors to Islamabad, though the local Hindu community has not been permitted to resume regular rituals there — a source of continuing appeal by Hindu representatives. A 2020 report independently corroborated the temple's sixteenth-century dating and confirmed that regular Hindu worship remains barred there.

The books speak of Rama's images and temples elsewhere, never of this one. Haroon Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* describes tiles of 'Ram and Sita' at a temple at Manora, their faces wiped clean (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 229, folio not stated). His *A White Trail* finds "depictions of ... Ram and Sita" among the faded frescoes of the Ranjit Singh samadhi (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 209, folio not stated), and reports that the rationale of those who demolished the Babri Mosque "was that the mosque had been built ... on the site of a Hindu Temple, birth site of the mythological Hindu King, Ram" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 21, folio not stated).

## Worship and Festivals

According to *Dawn*'s 2016 reporting, local memory also ties the site to the adjoining Ram Kund pond, where — per the 1893-94 Rawalpindi Gazetteer as cited by that report — an annual fair once drew Hindus from across the district.

The books consulted describe no worship at Saidpur and give no date for the fair. What they record of the festivals of Rama is said of those festivals in general, and is given here as context.

The annotator of Charles Frederick Usborne's translation of Waris Shah writes that the victory over Ravana "is celebrated every year at the Hindu festival of the Dushera when Ravana's effigy is ceremonially burnt" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13). In Amog Lila's account of Navratri, as Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* gives it, Sita prayed for nine nights while "Ravan and Rama (Sita's husband)" fought; "On the tenth day, the goddess heard her plea and Ram was able to kill Ravana and thus won the war. The burning of Dushera (on the tenth day) is a remembrance of that victory" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 40, folio not stated). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, too, speaks of Dussehra as a commemoration, in a passage whose reading is uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 794).

In *In Search of Shiva*, Khalid quotes William Henry Sleeman's *Rambles and Recollections of an Indian Official*: "When Ram set out with his army for Ceylon, he is supposed to have worshipped the little tree called 'cheonkul', which stood near his capital of Ajodhya". Sleeman says he saw "a procession of more than seventy thousands persons" attend their prince to worship the tree "on the festival of the Dashara" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 9, ch. 3, folio not stated).

The same book argues that Eid Milad-Un-Nabi "was originally inspired by a Hindu festival called Ram Navami. The festival celebrates the birth of Ram, a popular deity"; Khalid writes that "Streets are lit and the entire community takes part", and that "Hindus have been celebrating Ram Navami for centuries" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

## Rama and the Legend of the Site

The site's sanctity is bound to the belief that Rama, with Sita and Lakshmana, passed through this country during the years of exile recounted in the *Ramayana*: the natural springs of the village, fed by the hill streams, were revered as sacred pools, and four of them are traditionally named for Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and Hanuman.

None of the books consulted tells this legend, and none sets Rama, Sita, Lakshmana or Hanuman at Saidpur. What they say of the four is said of the epic at large.

Christopher Shackle, glossing the names in his translation of Bulleh Shah, defines "Ram (Skt. Rāma) Hindu name of God, the divine hero of the Ramayana who killed Ravan." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175).

Sita he glosses separately: "sita (Sītā) the wife of Ram." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175). Chishti makes her the daughter of Raja Janak (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 796–797) and tells of her banishment, 'بنواس یعنی دیس نکالا' (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 794). In Khalid's *A White Trail*, Sita bore "the twin sons of Ram, Luv and Kush" at Valmiki's ashram "after she had been banished by Ram", and she is "the perfect woman, the wife of Ram" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 71, folio not stated).

Lakshmana appears in the books as Lachhman in Shackle, as لچہمن in Chishti, as Lachman in Robert Rozehnal and as Laxman in Michel Boivin (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 155, folio 130; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 792; Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 63, folio 53; Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94). Shackle has Ravan's capital of Lanka "under attack by Ram and Lachhman" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 155, folio 130).

Hanuman, in *A White Trail*, "was a follower of Ram and played a central role in the battle between Ram and Ravana" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated). Taufiq Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah speaks of "the Rama-Sita story of the 'Ramayana' in which Ravana and Hanuman figure as two poles of mystical knowledge." (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 40, folio 20).

Of Ravana, Shackle writes "ravan (Skt. Rāvaṇa) the ten-headed demon king of Lanka who abducted Ram's wife, Sita." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175), and of his realm "Lanka the kingdom of Ravan." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 199, folio 174). The annotator of Usborne's Waris Shah explains that "Ravana is the legendary king of Ceylon, who figures as the chief adversary of Rama in the Ramayana epic"; Ravana carried off Sita, Rama's wife, "whose rescue is the main theme of the poem", and was killed in battle by Rama (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13).

## The Line of Raja Ramchandar

Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* writes of Rama as Raja Ramchandar, and itself ties 'راجہ رامچندر' to the 'راما' of the Ramayana (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 797). Like the other books, it says nothing of the Saidpur temple.

The line, in Chishti's account, runs from 'اچہواک[OCR?]', Ichhwak, of 'اجودہیا پوری' to 'دسرتہہ', whose four sons were 'رامچندر اور لچہمن اور بہرتہ اور سترگہن[OCR?]', the last name uncertain in the printed text; the history, he says, is in the 'کتاب راماین' (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 792–794). Lachhman was 'حقیقی بہائی راجہ رامچندر', Raja Ramchandar's own brother, and 'سورج بنسی', of the Suraj Bansi (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 792). Of Chandrat the book says that it was 'خاص جائی نشست لچہمن جی برادر راجہ رامچندر[OCR?] کا', the particular seat of Lachhman Ji, brother of Raja Ramchandar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 791).

By the belief of the Hindus, 'حسب عقیدہ اہل ہنود', Chishti writes, Ramchandar was an 'اوتار' in 'ترپتا' (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 794). Raja Ramchandar is to him 'خاندان سورج بنسی کا چشم و چراغ', the eye and lamp of the Suraj Bansi family, and his account of the epic runs through the 'بن باس', Ravan, 'راجہ سنگلدیپ', and the bridge from the Deccan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 796–797).

A list of kings follows (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 795–796). Ramchandar's two sons, it says, were Kushu and Lohu (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 795), and 'رامچندر کی اولاد مین برابر پانسو برس راج رہا', the rule remained among Ramchandar's descendants for a full five hundred years (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 796). From Ichhwak to Ramchandar it counts 'ستاون [OCR?]', fifty-seven, holders of the *gaddi*, the reading of the number uncertain in the printed text, and it names the 'ترپتا جگ' (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 796). At an earlier place the book says 'راجہ رام چند کے[OCR?] بیٹے[OCR?] تین تھے[OCR?]', that Raja Ram Chand had three sons, the reading uncertain at three words (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 661).

On the dating, Chishti reports what English historians say. Ichhwak came, by their reckoning, 'سن عیسوی سے دو ہزار یا دو ہزار دو سو برس پہلے', two thousand or two thousand two hundred years before the Christian era (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 796). Of Ramchandar he writes 'راجہ رامچندر بارہ سو برس پہلے سن عیسوی سے ہوا ہے', that he lived twelve hundred years before the Christian era, because 'مسٹر بنٹلی [OCR?] صاحب', a Mr Bentley if the reading is sound, studied the horoscope by 'دال میکہ [OCR?]' and placed it '[OCR?] نو سو اکسٹہہ [OCR?] برس پہلی', some nine hundred and sixty-one years before, the figure uncertain at both ends in the printed text; the two figures stand side by side as printed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 796–797).

The English historians, Chishti reports, hold that the saying 'کہ راما دیوتا تہا اور راکہشون سے لڑا', that Rama was a devta and fought the rakhshas, is poetic: brave rajas were called devtas, and their enemies rakhshas (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 797).

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* is briefer still. It names a 'راجه رام چند', whom it does not identify further, only as the father of 'لو', to whom the founding of Lahore is attributed (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525). Among the books its author read it lists 'ترجمه رامائن که متضمن بر احوال سری رام چند از کتب مشهور است', a translation of the Ramayan, which contains the life of Sri Ram Chand and is counted among the famous books, rendered 'از سنسکرت بفارسی', from Sanskrit into Persian, by 'جماعه مذکور', the group already named, whose names the text does not repeat there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 583). Neither passage names a site.

## Rama on the Road to Hinglaj

Jürgen Schaflechner's study of the Hindu temple of Hinglaj Devi never connects Rama to Saidpur, to Islamabad or to any temple of his own, but Rama runs through its account of the pilgrimage to the goddess: "no figure was ever as present in the representations of the traditional pilgrimage to Hinglaj as Rama, the seventh incarnation of the God Vishnu." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 119, folio not stated). What follows is told of that pilgrimage, not of Saidpur.

The legend, as Schaflechner records it, tells of Rama's *brahm hatyā* and of the sentence of pilgrimage (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 120, folio not stated). He is defeated by the Goddess's army at the Ungakhera Bherum Luk pass and fights a twelve-year battle (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 120–121, folios not stated); a condition is set that he come as a simple pilgrim from Ram Bagh (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated); the Devi makes a promise to his excluded men (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated); Hanuman, Lakshmana and Sita work miracles of water (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated); and Rama carves a sun and a moon on the mountain opposite the temple (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 121, 132, 142, 257, folios not stated).

His ninety-six Brahmins, Schaflechner writes, accepted Hinglaj as their clan Goddess (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 76, folio not stated). The Saraswat Brahmins have a *ṭīkā* which, Schaflechner writes, citing Burton (1851), "according to legend—they had gotten from Ramacandra. Rama was in need of a priest and since he could not find any in Balochistan he simply applied a ṭīkā on a mlecch's (Hin. barbarian) forehead." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 100, folio not stated). Lalu Jasraj is "the aguā of Ramacandra's party and the first Kapri" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 181, folio not stated).

The *pūjā* places named for him on the route include "the resting place of Rama (Sin. rām jharoku)" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 256, folio not stated), and "Khari Nadi, where people take a bath in the ocean and worship Rama", with "the Rama pūjā" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 203, 204, folios not stated). Schaflechner writes, too, of "the mytho-historic journey of Rama and his entourage", now largely destroyed, he says, by Karachi's growth (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 322, folio not stated).

## Rama in Verse

None of the verse in the books consulted speaks of Saidpur. What they carry is verse in which Rama's name or story appears, quoted here in the books' own English.

Bulleh Shah's lyrics, in Christopher Shackle's translation, appeal to Ram:

*When I realized this, I appealed to Ram: you and I are one, there is no one else in this house in the city of love* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 116, folio 91)

Elsewhere in the lyrics:

*Sometimes you utter appeals to Ram, sometimes you put the tilak on your forehead.* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 59, folio 34)

The epic enters the lyrics too. One line says to its addressee, 'you had Lanka plundered by Ram' (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 141, folio 116), and a passage recalls Kumbhakaran, Ravan and Lachhman:

*When Kumbhakaran goes back the way he came, the mystery of Lanka is created. Now that Ravan the ten-headed is destroyed and Lachhman remains, the unstruck music sounds.* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 31, folio 6)

Shackle explains one such reference: "This reference to the story of the Rāmāyaṇa describes a reversal of the arrival of Kumbhakaran to assist his brother Ravan, when his capital of Lanka was under attack by Ram and Lachhman." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 155, folio 130). Another of his notes reads "The capital of Ravan's kingdom, attacked by Ram." (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 168, folio 143).

Waris Shah's romance of Hir and Ranjha, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, invokes the epic in a single question:

*Did not a woman kill Ravana?* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 3, folio 2)

Its annotator glosses the line with the story of Ravana and Rama (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13). Later the epic returns as a courtroom analogy, "This swindler took her away as Ravan ran away with Sita." (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 53, folio 52), which the annotator reads as a tactic: "This reference to the Ravan-Sita episode, which is the subject of the 'Ramayana, is intended to curry favour with the Raja, who is a Hindu." (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 54, folio 53).

In *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, Naveed Alam's translation of Madho Lal Hussein, Ram is one of the two or three names the poet uses in place of Allah, and he uses it often: "If not Sain, then it is Rab, Maula, Ram. Actually, he uses Ram quite often (see kafis 68, 80, 81, 89)" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 181, folio 181); "Mostly Sain, Ram, Rab and Maula have been used" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 185–186, folios 185–186). In the verse it is the name to be recited and sung:

*Time to invoke, girl, let's rise and praise Ram* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 28, folio 28, kafi 7)

*What's the joy of life / without the constant evocation of Ram?* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 160, folio 160)

Other lines run "Praise Ram, I pranced all the way to the groom" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 90, folio 90), "Sometimes rise and recite Ram in the morning" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 103, folio 103), "You lose if you don't sing of Ram" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 104, folio 104) and "Come, girl, let's praise Ram" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 112, folio 112). One kafi addresses him directly, and so does its Variation:

*The whole world begs your favours, O Ram* — and, in the Variation, *You are the great giver, O Rama* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 172, folio 172)

Taufiq Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah sets the name Ram beside the name Allah in a two-line poem headed NAMES, an argument about divine labels. The reading of the printed text is uncertain at two points, and the readings proposed there stand in square brackets:

*Having understood, why heed the storm over such. [OCR?] [such] names as Allah.and [OCR?] [Allah and] Ram.* (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 147, folio 127)

Mai Dhadli's Urdu song at a fakir dwelling in Sehwan, in the English of Omar Kasmani's *Queer Companions*, runs:

*Muhammad in one place, Ali in another, and yet elsewhere, Qalandar is Ram.* (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 57, folio 40)

Kasmani adds that the saint's memory is said to span "Muhammad, Ali, or Ram" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, pp. 57–58, folios 40–41).

## Rama Among the Sufis

Several of the books trace Rama's name through Sufi teaching and Hindu devotion at large; none of them speaks of this temple.

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes of the deity "adored in the form of two of his ten incarnations, Rama and Krishna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354), and of "devotion to the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of Rama, and of his consort Sita" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 379, folio 357). He notes that "A Hindi scholar identified Pitambar Pir with the Hindu god, Rama", and sets Kabir's 'Nirguna Rama' against 'Ram Chandar' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 398, 401; folios 374, 377). He records the view that "Ram and Rahim were the same Being" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 412, folio 388), and counts Rama among the "traditional terms used by Hindus and Muslims to invoke God, such as Allah, Khuda, Sahib, Hari and Rama"; in Guru Nanak's usage, as Rizvi presents it, Hari and Rama are names for a single formless God, not the deities of cult sites (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 415, folio 391).

Michel Boivin writes that "Sachal mentions different Hindu gods, such as Ram, Hanuman, Sita and especially Krishna", and that "Sachal also refers to this episode of the Ramayana", in a passage on Diwali and Ram's return to Ayodhya (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 106, folio 93). "Qutub Ali Shah gives the names of Laxman and Sita, Ram and Krishna" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94), and, citing Paniker, Boivin reports that "Murad stated that the jogis are fascinated by Rama" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 108, folio 95).

Robert Rozehnal, reporting the lectures of the Sufi shaykh Zauqi Shah, writes: "In certain lectures the shaykh describes non-Muslim spiritual luminaries—Krishna, Rama, Sita, Lachman, and Guru Nanak—as believers in the one true God and religious leaders with 'Divine connection' (nisbat)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 63, folio 53).

## Setting

The books speak of Islamabad and of the Margalla Hills only in passing, and never of Saidpur. Werbner and Basu's *Embodying Charisma* names "Pakistan's capital city, Islamabad", on whose outskirts stand the village of Nurpur Shahan and Barri Imam's shrine (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 151, folio 140). Haroon Khalid writes that "Rawalpindi happens to be the twin city of Islamabad, the federal capital of the country" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 265, folio 239).

In *In Search of Shiva*, the travel writer Salman Rashid tells Khalid, "I have heard of a bodhi tree in Islamabad and one near Jhelum" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 9, ch. 3, folio not stated). Khalid places Taxila's Dharmarajika "in the heart of Margalla hills, where the federal capital of Pakistan is", and describes it as "a stupa around which are the remains of a monastery and giant sculptures of Lord Buddha and Bodhisattva, dating back to the third century BCE", "believed to have been constructed by the great Mauryan emperor, Ashoka" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 11, ch. 5, folio not stated). What he says there is said of Taxila, not of Saidpur.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Who Rama was.** The site's account calls him *Lord Rama*. Shackle has "Hindu name of God, the divine hero of the Ramayana who killed Ravan" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175); Schaflechner, "the seventh incarnation of the God Vishnu" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 119, folio not stated); Rizvi, "the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of Rama" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 379, folio 357), while he sets Kabir's 'Nirguna Rama' against 'Ram Chandar' (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 398, 401; folios 374, 377); Khalid, "a popular deity" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Chishti calls him Raja Ramchandar, an 'اوتار' by the belief of the Hindus (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 794), and reports the English historians' view that to call Rama a devta who fought the rakhshas is poetic, brave rajas having been called devtas (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 797).
- **When Rama lived.** Chishti gives 'راجہ رامچندر بارہ سو برس پہلے سن عیسوی سے ہوا ہے', twelve hundred years before the Christian era, and in the same passage the figure '[OCR?] نو سو اکسٹہہ [OCR?] برس پہلی', nine hundred and sixty-one years before, uncertain at both ends, from the reading of the horoscope he reports; the two stand as printed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 796–797). For Ichhwak, at the head of the line, the English historians he cites give two thousand or two thousand two hundred years before the Christian era (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 796).
- **Rama's sons.** Chishti says in one place 'راجہ رام چند کے[OCR?] بیٹے[OCR?] تین تھے[OCR?]', that Raja Ram Chand had three sons, the reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 661), and in another names two sons, Kushu and Lohu (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 795). Khalid speaks of "the twin sons of Ram, Luv and Kush" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 71, folio not stated). Bhandari names a 'راجه رام چند', whom he does not identify further, as the father of 'لو' (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525).
- **Ravana's kingdom.** Shackle makes Ravan "the ten-headed demon king of Lanka" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175). Usborne's annotator calls Ravana "the legendary king of Ceylon" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13), and Sleeman, as Khalid quotes him, has Ram set out "with his army for Ceylon" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 9, ch. 3, folio not stated). Chishti calls Ravan 'راجہ سنگلدیپ' (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 796–797).
- **Who killed Ravana.** Waris Shah's poem, in Usborne's English, asks "Did not a woman kill Ravana?" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 3, folio 2); its annotator writes that Ravana was killed in battle by Rama (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 4, folio 3, note 13). Shackle's Ram is the hero "who killed Ravan" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 200, folio 175). In Amog Lila's account, as Khalid gives it, "the goddess heard her plea and Ram was able to kill Ravana" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 40, folio not stated).
