Name: Ramapir Temple, Tando Allahyar
Location: Tando Allahyar, Tando Allahyar District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Ramapir Mela (1 Bhadva, three days)
Description:
## Overview

The Ramapir Temple at Tando Allahyar, in the Sindh, is a Hindu shrine dedicated to *Ramdev Pir* — also called Ramapir or Baba Ramdev — a fifteenth-century saint of Rajasthan venerated across western India and Sindh as a worker of miracles and a champion of the poor and the low-caste. The temple is the focus of the annual *Ramapir Mela*, which is widely reckoned the second largest Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan after the *yatra* to Hinglaj, and it is celebrated above all for the way its devotion reaches across the boundaries of community, drawing Muslims as well as Hindus into its festival.

Of the books consulted, only one names the temple, and only in a single sentence. Jürgen Schaflechner, writing of the Hindus of Pakistan, notes that "Many—especially in the rural areas—follow the teachings of local Sufi pīrs (Urd. spiritual guide) or adhere to the teachings of the fourteenth-century saint Ramdevji, whose main temple is located in the Sindhi city of Thando Allah Yar." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). He says nothing more of the temple or the saint. Schaflechner spells the town Thando Allah Yar and the saint Ramdevji; this article keeps Tando Allahyar and Ramdev Pir except in quotation. Michel Boivin's *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia* knows the saint as Rama Pir, Ramdeo and Ramdeo Pir and describes his cult in Sindh, but it never names Tando Allahyar and never names any temple of his; what it says is about the saint and his devotees, not about this temple. The other books consulted speak only of Sindh at large, and appear below as the setting of the cult.

## Ramdev Pir and the Legend of the Temple

Ramdev Pir is remembered in tradition as a ruler-saint of medieval Rajasthan, held by his devotees to have been an incarnation of Krishna, who used his powers to defend the humble and to dissolve the barriers of caste; his principal shrine stands at Ramdevra (Runicha) in the Jaisalmer region of Rajasthan, where he is said to have taken *samadhi* in the year 1459. His cult spread widely among both Hindus and the Muslim communities of the desert borderlands, so that he is honoured as a *pir* — a Sufi title — as readily as a Hindu saint.

According to the legend attached to the Tando Allahyar temple, a devotee carried an earthen lamp from the original shrine at Ramdevra, some four hundred and sixty kilometres to the north-east, across what is now the India–Pakistan frontier, and enshrined its flame here, founding the temple in his master's honour. The building itself dates from the British colonial period, traditionally placed in the mid-nineteenth century, around 1859.

## Rama Pir in the Books

Boivin places the saint among the folk heroes of the poor. Writing of the untouchable castes of Sindh, he says: "The untouchables venerated Devi as well as a specific category of divinities that Christopher Fuller described as 'divinized heroes' (Fuller 1992: 49–50). In Sindh, the most popular deified heroes were Rama Pir (Ramdeo or Ramdev), Pithoro Pir, Pabuji and Guga Pir." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 43, folio 30). He gives the three spellings in that order and gives the saint no dates, no place of burial and no temple.

He returns to the saint in discussing Pithoro Pir, and there gives the fullest account the books hold of Ramdev Pir's standing in Sindh: "Pithoro Pir is most of the time associated with soteriological figures. In this category, the saint most venerated is Ramdeo Pir, still known in Sindh as Rama Pir. Ramdeo Pir is also the object of widespread worship in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Although he is very present for the untouchable ones, he is also venerated by the Nathpanthis of Gujarat. In Sindh, he is today integrated into the temples dedicated to the pan-Indian divinities." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).

The two cults, in Boivin's account, overlap without being equal: "The worship is not exclusive: the majority of Meghwars who venerate Pithoro Pir also venerate Ramdeo Pir. On the other hand, the reverse is less sure. The pir of Pithoro does not mention Ramdeo Pir among the companions with whom Pithoro Pir travelled." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). What joins them, he suggests, is an ideal of holiness that can be seen in their images: "A most interesting point is the convergence of certain elements within these methods of worship, starting with the iconography. The figures of the two saints seem to draw with them a common model of holiness based on the renouncement." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).

Boivin gives one example of the saint's place in a temple of Sindh, and it is in Karachi, not Tando Allahyar: "In Karachi, for example, a painting of Ramdeo Pir stands in the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). Schaflechner, too, attests devotion to the saint in Karachi, mentioning "the local Ram Pir temple" in the city's Narayanpur neighbourhood (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 163, folio not stated); that temple is a different place from the temple at Tando Allahyar.

Boivin's bibliography includes the study that heads this article's own list of sources, Dominique-Sila Khan's *Conversions and Shifting Identities: Ramdev Pir and the Ismailis in Rajasthan*, which it gives as published at Delhi by Manohar in 1997 (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 235, folio 222).

## The Temple

Beyond Schaflechner's sentence calling it the saint's "main temple" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated), the books consulted say nothing of the temple at Tando Allahyar: they do not describe its building, name its founder or its custodians, or mention the Ramapir Mela. Schaflechner gives the saint no death year, no lineage and no festival (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). What is known of the temple's founding, its fair and its rites comes from the site's own account, given here as it stands.

## The Ramapir Mela

The temple's fame rests chiefly upon its great fair. Held on the first day of the month of *Bhadva* (falling in August or September), the Ramapir Mela is a pilgrimage of three days that draws thousands of the faithful from across Sindh and beyond. Its rites unfold in a rhythm of dawn flag-hoistings, barefoot processions, the singing of *bhajans*, offerings of coconuts and lengths of cloth, and the communal *langar*, or free kitchen, that feeds all comers without distinction.

What most strikes observers of the mela is its shared character. Although Hindu ritual predominates — the *aarti*, the offerings, the devotional song — the festival's appeal has never been confined to a single community. Muslim devotees, too, come to the shrine, offering *chadars* — the embroidered sheets laid upon the tombs of Sufi saints — and joining the processions, in a fusion of Hindu temple worship and the idiom of the Sufi *dargah* that is characteristic of the folk religion of Sindh. In a country where the Hindu minority is small and often anxious, the Ramapir Mela stands out as a rare and vivid expression of a devotional culture that both faiths can share.

## Devotional Life

Beyond the days of the mela, the temple serves the settled Hindu population of Tando Allahyar and the surrounding district, a community with deep roots in the agrarian society of lower Sindh. The cult of Ramdev Pir, with its emphasis on the dignity of the poor and the irrelevance of caste before the divine, has long held a special appeal for communities at the margins, and the temple remains a place where that message is renewed in song and ritual.

The books describe that constituency in Sindh at large. Boivin, as quoted above, finds the saint "very present for the untouchable ones" and venerated by the majority of the Meghwars (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). Schaflechner names the teachings of Ramdevji beside those of the local Sufi *pirs* as what many follow, 'especially in the rural areas' (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated).

## Setting

The books consulted describe the Hindu population of Sindh among whom the saint's cult lives; what follows is about the province, not the temple. Schaflechner calls Sindh "home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus", whom he numbers at "between 6 and 10 million people—an estimate that varies widely according to the source", and he writes that "over 90 percent—belong to the underprivileged Hindu tribes or sub-castes, such as the Meghvar, the Bhil, and the Kohli, who frequently work as manual laborers for the powerful landowning elite in Sindh" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin agrees in substance: "In Pakistan, despite the mass migration, the Sindhi Hindus number several millions, with a majority of them belonging to the so-called scheduled castes, mostly Menghwars, Bhils and Kohlis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 175, folio 162). "Since partition, the majority of the Pakistani Hindus of Sindh have belonged to the low castes. They are Dalits, as they are named by some, and some even claim they are not Hindu", he writes, and adds that "the Sufi legacy is still alive among the Dalits of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 194, folio 181); among the Hindus of the province, he notes, "there is a debate among the Hindus to determine if the term 'Dalit' is relevant" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174). Haroon Khalid places most of the country's remaining non-Muslims among "Hindus living in the 'faraway' 'peripheral' regions of Southern Punjab, inner Sindh and Baluchistan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 12, folio not stated).

Several of these communities look east, across the present border, toward the Rajasthan of Ramdev Pir's own legend. Boivin writes that "Contrary to popular belief, there were many untouchables in Sindh", among them the "Bhils or Kohlis" and "the Menghwar, mostly settled around Umerkot", and that "The first census reports that many would have migrated from Gujarat or Rajasthan between 1843 and 1872" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 40, folio 27). Shemeem Burney Abbas, writing of the region's music, calls the Kolhis "the indigenous peasant communities of Sind who are sometimes migratory", adding that "together with the Bhils they are the native inhabitants of the Sind-Rajasthan continuum" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 46, folio not stated). "There is evidence of roving minstrels in the Sind-Rajasthan area," she writes (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 77, folio not stated), and her glossary describes the Manganhar as "Hereditary professional musicians in the Sind and Rajasthan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 184, folio not stated).

The books also describe the common ground between Hindu and Muslim devotion in Sindh on which the site's account of the mela draws. Boivin recalls that "As Richard Burton noted as early as 1851, it is indeed the worship of the intercessors that constitutes the common religious idiom of Hindus and Muslims" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38), and that "In Sindh, we already know that a number of sacred figures have a dual religious identity, Muslim and Hindu. The Muslim identity is always related to Sufism, while the Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174). He writes that "the Hindus of Sindh are coming to the Sufi mausoleums since the nineteenth century" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 183, folio 170), and asks what that means: "The large majority of the Hindus used to pay a visit to the Sufi shrines, but does it mean they are Sufi? Of course not. It does mean that, for them, the Sufis are a part of their religious legacy" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 192–193, folios 179–180). He explains the province's openness by its position: "It is a fact that Sindh, because of its geographical location both as an isolated and a buffer zone, has hosted many unorthodox versions of normative religions, especially Hinduism and Islam." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 29, folio 16). Annemarie Schimmel finds Hindu participation in the Muslim mystical orders "more visible in Sind than in the Punjab", and notes that "Hindu writers wrote mystical poems in which they used the imagery of the Muslims" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387). Schaflechner writes that "The south of Pakistan, and especially Sindh, offers a whole range of salvific spaces that are frequently visited by different religious communities and form a network of pilgrimage routes or ritual journeys." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 107, folio not stated).

Both authors also qualify that picture. Schaflechner writes of "the common notion among Sindhis today that in the history of Sindh, there is no religious tension between the two communities—Muslims and Hindus. This notion of the harmonious coexistence of the religions, however, is merely a nationalist utopian ideal, as Aggarwal (2013) has shown" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 90–91, folio not stated). Boivin suggests that "the Hindu population of Pakistan, including Sindh, is more and more under the threat of the radical Muslims of the country" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 127, folio 114), and Khalid records that after the demolition of the Babri Mosque on 6 December 1992 "Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 22, folio not stated). Against this Schaflechner sets government funding for minority places of worship, which "is seen in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh within the past decade"; "While in Sindh, I visited many temples that were renovated within the past decade, coinciding with changes in the political landscape" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 16, folio not stated). He does not say whether the temple at Tando Allahyar was among them.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **When Ramdev Pir lived.** The site's account calls him a fifteenth-century saint who is said to have taken *samadhi* at Ramdevra in 1459. Schaflechner calls him "the fourteenth-century saint Ramdevji" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin gives him no dates (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 43, folio 30; p. 192, folio 179).
- **Where his main temple is.** The site's account places his principal shrine at Ramdevra (Runicha) in the Jaisalmer region of Rajasthan, from which the flame of the Tando Allahyar temple is said to have been carried. Schaflechner writes that his "main temple is located in the Sindhi city of Thando Allah Yar" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated).
- **How he is worshipped in Sindh.** The site's account describes a temple dedicated to him, with its own fair. Boivin writes that "In Sindh, he is today integrated into the temples dedicated to the pan-Indian divinities", and gives as his example a painting of the saint in the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan at Karachi (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).
- **What kind of holy figure he is.** The site's account makes him a ruler-saint, held by his devotees to be an incarnation of Krishna, and honoured as a *pir* as readily as a Hindu saint. Boivin counts "Rama Pir (Ramdeo or Ramdev)" among the "deified heroes" of Sindh, a category of divinities venerated by the untouchables (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 43, folio 30), and elsewhere calls him a saint among the "soteriological figures", whose model of holiness is "based on the renouncement" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).
- **His name, and the town's.** The site's account calls him Ramdev Pir, Ramapir or Baba Ramdev, and the town Tando Allahyar. Boivin prints Rama Pir, Ramdeo, Ramdev and Ramdeo Pir (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 43, folio 30; p. 192, folio 179). Schaflechner prints Ramdevji, and spells the town Thando Allah Yar (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated).
- **How harmonious Sindh's shared devotion has been.** The site's account calls the temple "a living emblem of Sindh's syncretic religious temperament" and speaks of "the older, more porous boundaries of devotion in the Indus lands". Writing of the province, not of this temple, Schaflechner calls the notion that Sindh's history knew no religious tension between Muslims and Hindus "merely a nationalist utopian ideal" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 90–91, folio not stated).

## Legacy

The Ramapir Temple at Tando Allahyar is at once a major centre of Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan and a living emblem of Sindh's syncretic religious temperament. In the flame said to have been carried from Ramdevra, in the pilgrims who walk barefoot to its doors, and in the Muslim chadars laid alongside Hindu offerings, it preserves a vision of shared sanctity that has become increasingly precious. Second only to Hinglaj among the Hindu pilgrimages of the country, it testifies to the endurance of the faith and to the older, more porous boundaries of devotion in the Indus lands.

## Bibliography

- Dominique-Sila Khan, *Conversions and Shifting Identities: Ramdev Pir and the Ismailis in Rajasthan* (Manohar).
- Michel Boivin, studies of the shared religious culture and shrines of Sindh.
- Contemporary press coverage of the annual Ramapir Mela (Dawn, The Express Tribune).
- Reports of the Pakistan Hindu Council on the temples and festivals of Sindh.
- Regional gazetteer material on the cult of Ramdev Pir and Ramdevra.
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2018; print line 2017).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, 2011).
- Haroon Khalid, *A White Trail: A journey into the heart of Pakistan's religious minorities* (westland ltd, 2013; first e-book edition).

Name: Ranmal Sharif
Events: Annual urs; qawwali and naat; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Ranmal Sharif, near Phalia in the Mandi Bahauddin region of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Syed Muhammad Noushah Ganj Bakhsh (1552–1654) — the founder of the Naushahia branch of the Qadiri Sufi order. A saint of long life and wide influence, Noushah Qadiri established a spiritual line that spread across the Punjab and beyond and endures to this day, and his darbar at Ranmal Sharif remains an important centre of pilgrimage.

None of the books consulted here names Ranmal Sharif or Phalia as the place of the saint's tomb. What they offer is the saint himself, his order and his disciples. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, a tazkira of the saints of the Punjab composed in 1875 and read here in a modern annotated Urdu edition, gives him a full entry headed "شیخ حاجی محمد قادری المشہور بحضرت نوشہ گنج بخش" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 70–72, folios 58–60), with his parents, his training, his pir, a Persian chronogram on his death and a circle of disciples; and the book's modern editor states that "آپ کا مزار شریف اس وقت ساہنپال شریف ضلع گجرات پنجاب میں ہے", that his holy mazar is at present at Sahnpal Sharif, district Gujrat, Punjab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* carries a chapter headed "حال حضرت نوشہ صاحب رحمتہ اللہ علیہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 483), whose damaged passage on his burial names district Shahpur and Sahn Pal in district Gujrat (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 483–484). Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore names "نو شاہ گنج بخش" only at the head of a Naushahi spiritual pedigree, and says nothing of the site (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 304, folio 307). Everything below drawn from the books is therefore said of the saint, his order or the town, not of the shrine at Ranmal Sharif.

## The Life of the Saint

Muhammad Noushah — honoured as *Ganj Bakhsh*, “the bestower of treasure,” and *Noushah*, “the bridegroom” — was born in 1552. He took the Sufi path in the Qadiri order and, attaining a high spiritual station, founded his own branch, the *Naushahia*, which he propagated with great energy across the Punjab. He lived through a full century of the Mughal age, guiding a vast body of disciples and establishing a network of successors, and he is remembered both as a saint of powerful blessing and as an organiser of an enduring order. He died in 1654, full of years, and was buried at Ranmal Sharif, which became the seat of his line.

Lahori's book lists him in its contents as "حضرت نوشہ گنج بخش", entry no. 30 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3), and its persons index gives his personal name as Haji Muhammad: "نوشاہ گنج بخش (حاجی محمد)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 332, folio 320). Elsewhere the book names him in full honorific as "حضرت حاجی محمد نوشہ گنج بخش" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 272, folio 260). Lahori calls him a wali from birth and the khalifa of Shah Sulaiman Qadri; states of *jazb* and *sukr*, of love and longing, dominated him, and he was unequalled in asceticism, piety and *karamat* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58).

**His parents.** Lahori names both on one page. His father, Haji Ala al-Din, was himself a great elder who performed the Hajj seven times and was honoured with a vision of the Prophet; his mother, Bibi Jiwani, was also a great worshipper and ascetic (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58). The book's indexes list them as "جیونی بی بی (والدہ نوشاہ گنج بخش)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 316, folio 304) and "علاؤ الدین (والد نوشاہ گنج بخش)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 323, folio 311). Chishti, citing a work he calls "مناقب نوشاہیہ", gives the family's old home as "موضع کہلیانوالی[OCR?]", the father as "شیخ علاء الدین" and the mother as "ملا بی جیون[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 486).

**His birth and boyhood, as Chishti tells them.** The father left three months into the pregnancy, saying "پہلوان دین ہوگا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 486), and returned "سفر مکہ سے", from the journey to Mecca, when the child was four (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 487). "حضرت شاہ سلیمان صاحب", the "قطب وقت", foretold the birth (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 486–487) and advised the family (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 487–488). Chishti names a brother, "شیخ اسمعیل" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 488). At twelve the boy was taken for "بائیس[OCR?] برس" in age, so strong was he, and he fought in "اکثر لڑائیون" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 488–489). He then withdrew into a "لق و دق" wilderness, "دائم الصوم", and was fed with milk each night (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 489–490); he studied at "موضع حاکوثارہ[OCR?]" near "نوشہرہ" and memorised the Quran in a single night, where the printed text breaks off (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 490).

**His training and initiation, as Lahori tells them.** Up to the age of seventeen he completed the exoteric sciences; then he renounced the world and stayed in zikr in the reed-bed of "ساندل بار", Sandal Bar, "مگر والدین نے ان کو وہاں نہ چھوڑا". Coming away, he was brought by Mulla Karim al-Din to Shah Sulaiman, took *bai'at*, and in a few years reached completion (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 70–71, folios 58–59). The book's editor corrects the place: "ساندل بار کی بجائے گوندل بار ہونا چاہیے", instead of Sandal Bar it should be Gondal Bar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58, حاشیہ 2).

**The founding of the order.** Lahori states it plainly: "طریقہ نوشاہیہ جس کے فقیر پنجاب میں ہزاروں ہیں۔ ان سے شروع ہوا", the Naushahia path, whose faqirs in the Punjab number in the thousands, began with him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58). The same book names the order "نوشاہیہ قادریہ خاندان" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 272, folio 260). In another entry, however, it ascribes the order's rise in the Punjab to another figure (see below, under the disagreements).

**His death.** The current account gives 1654. Lahori himself gives 1103 AH, with the chronogram "پیر فیاض" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59). His modern editor rejects that year in a footnote: "حضرت نوشہ رح کا سال ولادت ۹۵۹ھ بمطابق یکم رمضان ہے" — his birth fell on 1 Ramadan 959 AH — and "آپ کا صحیح سال وفات ۱۲ ربیع الاول ۱۰۶۴ھ ہے۔ ۱۱۰۳ھ غلط ہے۔ سید شرافت نوشاہی نے تحقیق سے ثابت کیا ہے": his correct year of death is 12 Rabi al-Awwal 1064 AH, 1103 AH is wrong, as Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi has proved by research in his *Sharif al-Tawarikh* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ 2). The same editor's own list of his publications gives yet another date, describing the collected verse as that of "حضرت حاجی محمد نوشہ گنج بخش قادری ف ۱۶۵۳ء", who died in 1653 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 307, folio 295). Lahori also records a *bai'at* the saint accepted when he was ill and one day remained before his death, without giving the year (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229).

**A family wedding.** Chishti tells the story of the marriage of Hazrat Naushah's daughter, in which the bride's side demanded "ایک سو روپیہ لاگون کا", a hundred rupees of *lagan*, "حسب دستور مسلمانان پنجاب", after the custom of the Muslims of the Punjab (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 484).

## The Shrine and the Naushahia Order

The shrine of Noushah Ganj Bakhsh at Ranmal Sharif is the mother-shrine of the Naushahia Qadiri order, kept by his descendants and successors, and a busy centre of pilgrimage. It maintains the customary devotions — prayer, qawwali and *naat*, and the free kitchen — and its annual urs draws great crowds of the order’s followers and of the wider devout. The Naushahia order he founded remains active across the Punjab and among the Punjabi diaspora, so that his shrine is the head of a living and widespread spiritual family.

The books consulted record nothing of the village of Ranmal, its urs, its custodians or its fabric. The place they give for the saint's tomb is another. Lahori's modern editor writes "آپ کا مزار شریف اس وقت ساہنپال شریف ضلع گجرات پنجاب میں ہے", that the mazar is at present at Sahnpal Sharif in district Gujrat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ); the same editor describes the author of the order's chronicle *Tazkira-e Naushahi* as Hafiz Sayyid Muhammad Hayat Rabbani Naushahi Sahnpalvi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ 1). Chishti's passage on the burial is damaged in the printed text: "مزار مقام [illegible] ضلع شاہ پور مین اور انکے مزار بمقام سہن پال[OCR?] بہ [illegible] شیر شاہ[OCR?] بہ رسول نگر[OCR?] [illegible] ضلع گجرات مین". It names a mazar in district Shahpur and a mazar at Sahn Pal in district Gujrat, near names read as Sher Shah and Rasul Nagar, and whose mazar each clause names is not clear (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 483–484).

Lahori's index names a holder of the order's *sajjada*: "پیر محمد سجادہ نوشاہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 315, folio 303). In the editor's time the manuscripts of the order were mostly held in a private Naushahi library at Sahanpal, Gujrat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 292–295, folios 280–283; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 243, folio 231).

## Devotion and Practice

The current account records prayer, qawwali and *naat*, the free kitchen and the annual urs at Ranmal Sharif. The books speak of the order's devotions, not of this site's.

**The *sama* of the order.** Writing in his own present, in the 1870s, Lahori describes the ecstatic *sama* of the order under the entry for Abdul Rahman Pak Naushahi, whom he calls "بڑے خلیفہ حضرت حاجی محمد نوشہ گنج بخش", the great khalifa of Noushah Ganj Bakhsh (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 80, folio 68 [marker 78]):

"پوشیدہ نہ رہے کہ فرقہ نوشاہیہ عالیہ میں سب لوگ صاحب وجد و سماع و شوق و ذوق و مستی ہیں۔ مگر فقرائے سلسلہ پاک رحمان کے سماع کے وقت سب سے زیادہ مست ہو جاتے ہیں۔ جب تک ان کے پاؤں میں رسہ ڈال کر الٹا نہ لٹکائیں اور وہ ساعت دو ساعت اسی حالت میں رقص نہ کریں سرد نہیں ہوتے اور اگر اس عمل سے ہوش میں نہ آئیں تو اسی حالت میں ان کو زمین پر کھینچتے ہیں۔ جب تک وہ ہوش میں آ جائیں رسن ان کے پاؤں سے کھولا نہیں جاتا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 81, folio 69 [marker 79]).

All in the order, he says, are possessed of ecstasy and *sama*, but the faqirs of the Pak Rahman line become the most intoxicated at *sama*: they do not cool until a rope is put round their feet and they are hung upside down and dance so for an hour or two; failing that they are dragged along the ground, and the rope is not untied until they come to themselves (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 81, folio 69 [marker 79]). Chishti, too, speaks of the Naushahi followers, "نوشاہی" and "نوشاہیان", and of their qawwali and their "حال" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 466).

**Grain at his door.** A party of "فقرائے ہنود", Hindu faqirs, among whom the apostate Hafiz Tahir had joined, passed his house: "ایک روز ان کا گذر حضرت نوشاہ کے دولت خانے پر ہوا۔ حضرت نے حکم دیا کہ ہر ایک شخص کو غلہ گندم دے دو۔ چنانچہ سب کو مل گیا۔ مگر حافظ طاہر کو کچھ نہ ملا کہ غلہ ختم ہو چکا تھا". The saint ordered wheat to be given to every one of them; all received it except Hafiz Tahir, for the grain had run out (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230).

**A deathbed initiation and a teaching.** Of Shah Abdullah, whom the book describes as "منصبدار ہفت [OCR?] ہزاری دربار عالمگیری", Lahori writes: "وہ خدمت شیخ حاجی محمد نوشاہ کے حاضر ہوا۔ اس وقت حاجی محمد بیمار تھے اور ایک روز ان کی وفات میں باقی تھا حضرت نے اس کی بیعت قبول کی اور ذکر و شغل کی اجازت دی" — he came when Haji Muhammad was ill, with one day left before his death, and the saint accepted his *bai'at* and gave him leave for *zikr* and spiritual practice (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229). When Shah Abdullah insisted on becoming a *majzub*, the saint answered in words the book preserves: "تعلق میں بے تعلق رہنا مردوں کا کام ہے۔ مجذوب ہونا آسان ہے" — to remain detached amid attachments is the work of men; becoming a *majzub* is easy. He gave way only when Shah Abdullah "خدا کا واسطہ درمیان لایا", invoked God between them (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229).

## The Saint's Circle

**His khalifas.** Chishti names "دو خلیفہ نامی", two renowned khalifas: "فقیر عبد الرحمن", called "پاک رحمن", and "پیر محمد سچیار[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 484). Lahori says of Abdul Rahman Pak Naushahi that his pir's favour to him "کسی پر نہ تھی", was shown to no one else (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 80, folio 68 [marker 78]), and that his "مزار پر انوار موضع بھڑی [OCR?] زیارت گاہ خلق ہے", his radiant mazar at the village of Bharri is a place of pilgrimage. The author gives his death as 1153 AH; the editor, from three family manuscripts, *Lataif-e Gul Shahi*, *Bayaz-e Qadri* and *Kitab al-Fawaid*, gives 4 Muharram ۱۱۱۵ھ [OCR?], "جو معتبر ہے", and his birth as 995 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 81, folio 69 [marker 79], حاشیہ 1).

**A chain of succession.** Under entry ۲۳۱ Lahori sets out a five-step Naushahi Qadiri chain that ends in the saint: "نوشاہیہ قادریہ خاندان میں بیعت اس بزرگ کی بخدمت رحمان شاہ کے اور اس کی بخدمت محمد صدیق کے اور اس کی بخدمت شاہ فرید لاہوری کے اور اس کی بخدمت پیر محمد سچیار کے اور اس کی بخدمت حضرت حاجی محمد نوشاہ گنج بخش کے تھی" — Fazl Shah, from Rahman Shah, from Muhammad Siddiq, from Shah Farid Lahori, from Pir Muhammad Sachyar, from Haji Muhammad Naushah Ganj Bakhsh (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 272, folio 260). Beside it stand "حضرت شاہ کنٹھہ [OCR?] نوشاہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 272–273) and "حضرت شاہ فرید نوشاہی", a murid of the same "شیخ پیر محمد سچیار" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 274, folio 262). Of this line Lahori says "اس خاندان کے مرید بھی اکثر لوگ شہر میں ہیں", that most of the family's murids are in the city of Lahore, and that it was materially supported by the Sikh state through Raja Dina Nath (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 273, folio 261). Chishti gives the same Fazl Shah line — Rahman Shah, Muhammad Siddiq, "شہ[OCR?] فرید[OCR?]", "حضرت بجیبار[OCR?]" — ending "اور اونکی پیر روشن ضمیر حضرت نوشہ گنج بخش" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 337). He also closes Shah Kamaita's spiritual pedigree with "… اور یہ حضرت نوشہ صاحب کا فقط" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 349), and sets Bhage Shah's second pedigree directly below Shah Sulaiman Nuri (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 467).

**Four God-absorbed disciples.** The sixth section of Lahori's book, "چھٹا چمن / مجانین و مجاذیب کے ذکر میں", on the madmen and the God-absorbed, opens at p. 236 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 236, folio 224), and four of its *majzubs* were Noushah Ganj Bakhsh's disciples, each carrying the *nisba* "نوشاہی". The book introduces them in turn as "شیخ مٹھا مجذوب نوشاہی … یہ بزرگ حضرت حاجی محمد نوشاہ گنج بخش کا مرید تھا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 240, folio 228); "سید شاہ عبد اللہ مجذوب نوشاہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229); "نانو مجذوب نوشاہی … حاجی محمد نوشاہ گنج بخش کا مرید تھا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230); and "حافظ طاہر مجذوب نوشاہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230).

Of Shaikh Mittha the book says: "حالت جذب و استغراق اس پر ایسی غالب ہوئی کہ ہمیشہ ویرانے جنگل میں پھرا کرتا اور وحش و طیور سے ہم کلام ہوتا اور جس شخص پر توجہ کرتا۔ وہ بھی مجذوب ہو جاتا" — absorption so mastered him that he wandered the wilderness, spoke with beasts and birds, and whoever he turned his attention upon became a *majzub* too (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 240, folio 228). Of Nanu, whose real name, the editor says, was Namak — "نانو مجذوب کا اصل نام نامک تھا۔ عوام میں نانو معروف ہو گئے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, حاشیہ 1) — the book tells that, hearing that on the Day of Judgement all men save the Prophet would be beardless, "اس نے موچنا خریدا اور تمام ریش و بروت کے بال اکھاڑ ڈالے", he bought tweezers and plucked out every hair of beard and moustache (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230). After his pir's death he left for the wilderness: "بعد وفات پیر روشن ضمیر کے یہ شخص جنگل کو نکل گیا اور آبادی کا رہنا ترک کیا۔ وہاں اس شخص کو قطاع الطریقون نے سال ایک ہزار ایک سو پینتیس میں شہید کیا", and there highway robbers killed him in 1135 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230). The editor gives his grave: "شیخ نانو مجذوب کا مدفن موضع کلاسکے [OCR?] چیمہ ضلع گجرات پاکستان ہے", the name of the village uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230, حاشیہ 2).

## Legends and Miracles

Lahori says his *karamat* "کا انتہا نہیں ہے", have no end, and that they are set out in detail in the *Tazkira-e Naushahi* of Muhammad Hayat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59). He relates two of them through his disciples.

**The worn shirt.** When Shah Abdullah would not be dissuaded from the way of the *majzub*, "ناچار حضرت نے ایک کرتہ جس کو آپ چند روز پہن چکے تھے۔ اس کو دیا اور کہا کہ اس کو پہن لے۔ بمجرد پہننے کے عالم ملکوت اس پر منکشف ہوگیا" — the saint, left no choice, gave him a shirt he had worn for some days and told him to put it on, and as soon as he wore it the angelic realm was disclosed to him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229).

**Hafiz Tahir at the door.** When the party of Hindu faqirs came for grain, the saint called the stranger by name, "حافظ طاہر ہمارے پاس آ۔ کہ حصہ تیرا ہمارے پاس ہے", Hafiz Tahir, come to us, your share is with us; he ordered his servant "اس کا کرتہ اتار کر اس کے گلے میں جو زنار ہے توڑ دے", to take off his shirt and break the sacred thread at his neck; "من بعد مجدداً مسلمان ہوا اور ایک نظر فیض اثر سے اس کو واصل بحق کیا" — after which Hafiz Tahir became a Muslim anew, and with a single look the saint brought him to God (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 243, folio 231).

## In Verse

Lahori closes his entry with a Persian chronogram on the saint's passing:

حضرت حاجی محمد پیر نوشہ گنج بخش
آنکہ شد مشہور در اہل جہاں اجلال او
کرد چوں آخر عروج از فرش بر عرش بریں
پیر فیاض است ہم اہل سخاوت سال او

The book gives no translation of the chronogram; its final line carries "پیر فیاض", the phrase in which the author reads the year 1103 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 72, folio 60; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59).

Lahori's editor records that his Urdu and Punjabi verse was selected and edited by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi as "گنج شریف" and published by Dar al-Mu'arrikhin, Lahore, in 1975 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59). The editor's own list of publications gives it as "گنج شریف (کلیات نظم اردو حضرت حاجی محمد نوشہ گنج بخش قادری ف ۱۶۵۳ء) جامع سید شرافت نوشاہی۔ تقدیم محمد اقبال مجددی", with his foreword, beside a 64-page "احوال و آثار سید شرافت نوشاہی۔ لاہور ۱۹۷۱ء" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 307, folio 295). The books consulted quote none of the saint's own lines.

## The Order's Own Record

The Naushahi family's manuscripts were the order's archive, and Lahori's editor draws on them throughout. He lists nine sources for the Naushahia line (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59): Razi al-Din Qazi Ganjahi, *Risala Tuhfa-e Razwiya*, within Mirza Ahmad Beg Lahori's *Risala al-Ijaz*; Ahmad Beg Mirza Lahori, *Risala al-Ijaz*, 1107 AH; Sadaqat Muhammad Mah Ganjahi, *Thawaqib al-Manaqib*, 1126 AH; Hafiz Muhammad Hayat, *Tazkira-e Naushahi*, 1146 AH; Pir Kamal b. Shaikh Usman Lahori, *Sahaif-e Qudsiya*, 1186 AH; Imam Bakhsh Barqandazi Jalandhari, *Mirat al-Ghafuri*, 1186 AH; Muhammad Ashraf Manjri, *Kanz al-Rahmat*, 1220 AH, printed at Lahore in 1330 AH; Ghulam Muhi al-Din Faqir Lahori, *Tashrif al-Fuqara*, about 1248 AH [OCR?]; and Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi's own *Sharif al-Tawarikh*, 1355–1394, "سہ جلد سات ہزار صفحات", three volumes of seven thousand pages, in manuscript in its author's possession. All but the last two, the editor says, are owned by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi.

The *Tazkira-e Naushahi*, by Hafiz Sayyid Muhammad Hayat Rabbani Naushahi Sahnpalvi (d. 1173 AH), was composed in 1146 AH and "اصل میں رسالہ الاعجاز مولفہ مرزا احمد بیگ لاہوری کی مشروح نقل ہے", an annotated copy of the *Risala al-Ijaz* with additions, holding only the affairs of the Naushahia elders; four manuscripts are in Sharafat Naushahi's library and two in the Punjab University Library (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ 1). The author himself cites it, "کتاب تذکرہ نوشاہی میں لکھا ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230), and the editor cites a copy as "محمد حیات نوشاہی : تذکرہ نوشاہی قلمی ملکہ سید شرافت نوشاہی گجرات" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 243, folio 231). The edition's bibliography adds the *Risala al-Ijaz*, "(حالات مشائخ سلسلہ نوشاہیہ) ۱۱۰۷ھ مملوکہ مولانا سید شرافت نوشاہی، ساہن پال گجرات" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 292, folio 280), and Naushahi works such as "عمر بخش رسول نگری : مناقبات نوشاہی", by Umar Bakhsh Rasulnagri, "غلام قادر نوشاہی : بیاض قادری", by Ghulam Qadir Naushahi, and "گل محمد نوشاہی : لطائف گل شاہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 294, folio 282). Which of these treat Noushah Ganj Bakhsh himself the book does not say.

## Setting: Phalia

Haroon Khalid, writing of the town and not of the shrine, records the story he had heard that Phalia "was named after Alexander's legendary horse Bucephalus— Phalus became Phalia", and that the horse's grave was there (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). His companion Salman Rashid disputed it: "The horse is not buried here ... He was buried near Jalalpur on the other side of the river's bank where his grave was swept by the flood only a few months after"; "Coins dating back to the Indo-Greek era were discovered from the pahari of the city of Phalia, giving birth to the rumour"; and "This version became popular during the colonial era when British officers roamed all over the country collecting oral history" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). The old mound, Rashid said, now has "a government office there along with a school", and Iqbal Qaiser relayed an old shopkeeper's report: "That pahari has been sold by the department for nine crore rupees. Now there will be a shiny, new shopping plaza there" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where the saint is buried.** The current account places his shrine at Ranmal Sharif, near Phalia. Lahori's editor writes that his mazar is at present at Sahnpal Sharif, district Gujrat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ). Chishti's damaged passage names a mazar in district Shahpur and a mazar at "سہن پال[OCR?]" in district Gujrat, without making clear whose each is (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 483–484).
- **The year of his death.** The current account gives 1654. Lahori gives 1103 AH, with the chronogram "پیر فیاض" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59). His editor's footnote gives 12 Rabi al-Awwal 1064 AH and calls 1103 AH wrong (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ 2). The editor's own list of publications gives 1653 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 307, folio 295).
- **His birth.** The current account gives 1552. Lahori's editor gives 1 Ramadan 959 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 71, folio 59, حاشیہ 2).
- **His name.** The current account calls him Syed Muhammad Noushah Ganj Bakhsh. Lahori heads his entry "شیخ حاجی محمد قادری المشہور بحضرت نوشہ گنج بخش" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 70–72, folios 58–60), and the index gives his personal name as Haji Muhammad (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 332, folio 320).
- **Who began the order.** The current account and Lahori's entry on him make him its founder: the Naushahia path "ان سے شروع ہوا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58). In his entry on Shah Maruf Chishti wa Qadri, Lahori writes "انہیں کی ذات بابرکات سے پنجاب میں سلسلہ نوشاہیہ نے فروغ پایا", that through his blessed person the Naushahia line flourished in the Punjab; the pronoun may refer to Shah Maruf or to Sayyid Mubarak Haqqani, named just before (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 50, folio 38).
- **Where he withdrew as a young man.** Lahori writes Sandal Bar; his editor says it should be Gondal Bar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58, حاشیہ 2). Chishti speaks of a "لق و دق" wilderness and of study at "موضع حاکوثارہ[OCR?]" near "نوشہرہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 489–490; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 490).
- **His mother's name.** Lahori gives Bibi Jiwani, "جیونی بی بی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 316, folio 304); Chishti "ملا بی جیون[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 486).
- **The chain through Pir Muhammad Sachyar.** Lahori names the link above the saint "پیر محمد سچیار" and the link below him "شاہ فرید لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 272, folio 260); Chishti's version of the same chain reads "حضرت بجیبار[OCR?]" and "شہ[OCR?] فرید[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 337), while his list of khalifas has "پیر محمد سچیار[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 484).
- **Shaikh Mittha's death and name.** The author gives 1115 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 240–241). The editor writes "شیخ مطا [OCR?] مجذوب نوشاہی کا سالِ وفات ۱۱۱۵ ھ غلط ہے۔ بلکہ ۱۰۷۶ ھ خاندانی روایات کے مطابق صحیح ہے", that 1115 is wrong and 1076 is right by the family traditions, spelling the name differently from the author's "شیخ مٹھا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229, حاشیہ 1).
- **Shah Abdullah's death.** The author gives "۱۱۳۱ ھ ایک ہزار ایک سو اکتیس ہجری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241). The editor: "خاندانی مآخذ کے مطابق ۱۰۹۲ ھ درست ہے۔ اس لیے مفتی صاحب کا مندرجہ سال وفات ۱۱۳۱ ھ غلط ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 241, folio 229, حاشیہ 2).
- **Nanu's death.** The author gives 1135 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242). The editor notes that the *Khazinat al-Asfiya* gives 1132, calls both years wrong, and gives the year of his martyrdom in the family sources as "۱۰۹۴ ھ [OCR?]" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 242, folio 230, حاشیہ 2).
- **Hafiz Tahir's death.** The author gives 1136 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 243). The editor: "حافظ طاہر نوشاہی کا سال وفات بھی ۱۱۳۶ ھ غلط ہے۔ جناب سید شرافت نوشاہی کی تحقیق کے مطابق صحیح سال وفات ۱۰۹۷ ھ [OCR?] ہونا چاہیے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 243, folio 231, حاشیہ 1).
- **Pak Rahman's death.** The author gives 1153 AH; the editor gives 4 Muharram ۱۱۱۵ھ [OCR?] from three family manuscripts (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 81, folio 69 [marker 79], حاشیہ 1).

## Legacy

Syed Muhammad Noushah Ganj Bakhsh is remembered as the founder of the Naushahia Qadiri order — one of the enduring Sufi lines of the Punjab — a saint whose long life and organising genius planted a spiritual family that has lasted nearly four centuries. His shrine at Ranmal Sharif remains its living heart and a major centre of Qadiri devotion in the region.

Already in the 1870s Lahori counted the faqirs of the Naushahia path in the Punjab in the thousands (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58), and he found the order's murids numerous in Lahore (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 273, folio 261). Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore, which speaks of a Lahore tomb and not of this site, carries the order's spiritual pedigree up to the saint through the custodian of Shah Kanhh[OCR?]'s tomb outside Mochi Gate: "جواہر شاہ خادم آلہی شاہ او وہ گامی شاہ کا او وہ محمد زبان[OCR?] کا او وہ شاہ عصمت المند[OCR?] کا او وہ شیخ عبد الرحمن المعروف پاک رحمان کا او وہ نو شاہ گنج بخش کا" — Jawahar Shah, *khadim* of Alahi Shah, he of Gami Shah, he of Muhammad Zaban[OCR?], he of Shah Ismat al-Mand[OCR?], he of Shaikh Abdul Rahman known as Pak Rahman, he of Nau Shah Ganj Bakhsh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 304, folio 307). At that tomb, Kanhaiya Lal records, Jawahar Shah "سنہ ۱۲۹۴[OCR?] ہجری مین" rebuilt the tomb anew and made the mosque *pakka*; "جواہر شاہ سجادہ نشین بنا ہے", Jawahar Shah has become *sajjada nashin*; and a dalan, a kothri and a well "فقرا کے آرام کے لئے", for the faqirs' comfort, stand within the enclosure (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 304, folio 307).

Name: Sadh Belo (Sadh Belo Island Temple)
Location: Sadh Belo Island, near Sukkur/Rohri, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual festival (boat pilgrimage to the island)
Description:
## Overview

Sadh Belo is a serene temple complex occupying a wooded island in the River Indus, set between the twin cities of Sukkur and Rohri in Sindh. One of the most important living centres of Hindu worship in the province, it is intimately bound to the *Udasi* tradition, the ascetic order that traces its lineage to Sri Chand, elder son of Guru Nanak, and so stands at a confluence of Hindu and Sikh devotion. Spread across two interconnected islets, the complex encompasses temples, shrines, *samadhis* (memorial tombs of holy men), gardens, a communal kitchen and living quarters, all of it founded in the early nineteenth century amid the palms and greenery that give the island its name.

Two of the books consulted name the site, both under the spelling Sadh Bela. Michel Boivin, in his study of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh and their migration to India, counts "Sadh Bela, on another island" among the remarkable sanctuaries of the Rohri–Sukkur–Shikarpur country and calls it "the famous Udasi temple in Sadh Bela", created "thanks to a gift of land" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18). Jürgen Schaflechner, in his study of the goddess Hinglaj, describes it as "a tīrtha, as he is told, in the city of Sukkur on an island in the River Indus", and records the hospitality of its abbot to a pilgrim on the road to Hinglaj (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated). Neither book names Baba Bankhandi Maharaj, gives a foundation date, or describes the buildings; what the other books consulted say of Sukkur, Rohri, the Nanakpanthi and *Udasi* communities and the province of Sindh is set out below as context, and is said of those places and communities, not of this island.

## History and the Coming of Baba Bankhandi

The founding of Sadh Belo is attributed to the *Udasi* saint Baba Bankhandi Maharaj, born Balchand Sharma, whose origins are variously traced, according to differing accounts, to Kero Khetar near Delhi or to Nepal. As a young spiritual seeker, still in his teens, he is said to have arrived in Sukkur, then a flourishing trading hub of the subcontinent, in the year 1823. Drawn to the tranquil, forested island in the Indus, he settled there and made it a place of meditation and worship, and it came to be known as *Sadhu Belo*, meaning "the woods of the sage". Under Baba Bankhandi and the succession of *gaddi nashin* (spiritual successors) who followed him, the island grew into a substantial religious establishment.

The complex enshrines a broad and characteristically syncretic array of devotion. Baba Bankhandi is credited with establishing places of worship dedicated to Hindu deities including Annapurna, Hanuman, Ganesh and Shiv Shankar, while also making provision for the veneration of the *Guru Granth Sahib* and the *Bhagavad Gita* side by side, an expression of the inclusive *Udasi* ethos. Much of the architecture visible today, including the principal temple, was raised somewhat later; the main shrine is generally dated to the closing years of the nineteenth century, built under an eighth successor in the lineage, Sant Harnam Das, and further embellished in subsequent decades.

Boivin's one statement on the temple's origin sets it among the works of princely patrons. Writing of the amirs of Khairpur, he observes that "the amirs of Khairpur were themselves staunch Shia Muslims, and they built beautiful imambaras in the nineteenth century, but it did not prevent them from being generous patrons for all of the religious buildings as, for instance, the famous Udasi temple in Sadh Bela which was created thanks to a gift of land" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18). He gives no year for the gift, no extent of land and no name for the giver or the receiver.

## The Udasi Tradition and the Island Complex

The distinctive character of Sadh Belo flows from its rootedness in the *Udasipanth*. This religious and ascetic movement grew from the teachings of Sri Chand, the elder son of Guru Nanak, and blended devotional streams in a manner that resists neat sectarian classification, honouring Sikh scripture and Hindu deities alike, and cultivating a tradition of renunciation, pilgrimage and hospitality. Sadh Belo became one of the pre-eminent seats of *Udasi* religious life in Sindh.

The island itself is arranged to serve both worship and community. The principal island, Sadh Belo, houses the temples, verandahs and the *langar*-style kitchen that fed pilgrims and residents, while the adjoining island, sometimes called Deen Belo, contains *samadhis*, a park and the Rishi Nol *mandir*. Reached by boat across the Indus, the complex offered pilgrims a self-contained sacred world amid the river, its white temples and shaded courtyards forming a striking contrast to the surrounding waters.

Boivin places the island twice. In his survey of the shrines of northern Sindh, speaking of the country on "both sides of the Indus River", he writes: "It suffices to quote some remarkable sanctuaries such as Khwaja Khizr, on an island, Sadh Bela, on another island, and the dargah of Sachal Sarmast" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18). Later he speaks of "the Sadh Belo settled in the island in the Indus River, in Sukkur" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 69, folio 56). His index carries the site under both spellings, one after the other, as "Sadh Bela (sanctuary)" and "Sadh Belo" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 248, folio 235). Schaflechner, too, sets it "in the city of Sukkur on an island in the River Indus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated).

## The Nanakpanth and the Udasis in Sindh

What the books say of the *Udasis* and of the wider Nanakpanth in Sindh is said of the province and its communities, not of this island, but it is the world to which the temple belongs. Boivin writes that "In Sindh, many Nanakpanthis belonged to a subgroup known as the Udasis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 53, folio 40), and that "In nineteenth-century Sindh, the Nanakpanth, or 'the path of Nanak', was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 90, folio 77). Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups, he says, "two main cults were followed: the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30).

He describes a religious recomposition of the province in the colonial period, attested "by the creation and the development of several important Nanakpanthi darbars throughout Sindh", and adds that "although some darbars had been created in the late eighteenth century, there was a renaissance of the Nanakpanthi darbars in the second half of the nineteenth century" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 53–54, folios 40–41). The word *darbar* itself, he notes, was "used by the Sikhs, the Muslims and the Hindus" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 37–38, folios 24–25). After the Singh Sabha process, "The Sindhi Nanakpanthis were thus not included in the Sikh community, and they identified themselves as being a Hindu religious sect" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 200, folio 187). In an endnote he records that "The Udasis of Sindh are coined as being a heterodox Sikh tradition, in one of the very few, if not the sole, academic papers devoted to the Nanakpanth in Sindh (Jatt 2016)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 209, folio 196).

Schaflechner writes that "Many Lohanas in Sindh follow the teachings of Nanak, somewhat obscuring their religious affiliation for the colonial officers. Hence, in the 1881 census, Lohanas from Shikarpur and Hyderabad were counted as Sikhs, while ten years later, in the 1891 census, they were classified as Hindus (Lari 1994, 211f.)" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 80, folio not stated). He adds that "many middle- and upper-class Hindus in Sindh are followers of the Nanak paṃth" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 257, folio not stated), and that "it is common to cover one's head before walking into a tikānā (Sin.), the temple containing the Guru Granth Sahib" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 286, folio not stated).

Haroon Khalid found the Nanak Panthi temples of Sindh and southern Punjab holding portraits of Guru Nanak alongside Hindu deities, and writes that these communities "are found in very large numbers in the province of Sindh" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 197, folio not stated). In a later book he writes that the communities who refused the Khalsa and called themselves followers of Guru Nanak "still exist in Sindh and in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Baptised Sikhs look down upon them" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 230, folio 204).

## Devotion and Practice

The island remains the focus of an annual festival that gathers Hindus from across Sindh and beyond, when boats ferry pilgrims to the island for days of worship, music and communal meals, and its kitchen has long fed pilgrims and residents alike.

Boivin's account of the riots at Sukkur in the colonial period preserves the river crossing as the pilgrims' way to the island: "the local Hindus opposed this rehabilitation since it was located in the harbour on the Indus River, from which the pilgrims reached the sacred site of Sadh Belo" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48). He gives no date for any festival and names no custodian.

Schaflechner records the one act of the temple's life that his study carries: its hospitality to a pilgrim bound for the goddess Hinglaj. The pilgrim, Shastri, whose own account Schaflechner cites, "uses the time to go to Sadh Bela, a tīrtha, as he is told, in the city of Sukkur on an island in the River Indus". "There the mahaṃt (Hin. superior of a monastery, abbot) of Sadh Bela grows very fond of Shastri and provides him with supplies and advice for his pilgrimage." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated) The advice was practical: "The abbot instructs him to keep many onions in case of a drinking-water shortage; he advises that the onion's juice would help stave off nausea and dizziness as well as provide liquid (Shastri 1977, 8)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated) A note pairs the same onion advice with a second pilgrim's account, "Abadhut (1964, 79)" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 148, folio not stated). The abbot is not named, and the visit is not dated beyond Shastri's journey.

## Partition, Survival and Pilgrimage

The Partition of 1947 dispersed much of Sindh's Hindu population and cast uncertainty over its many shrines, yet Sadh Belo endured as one of the most significant functioning Hindu sites in Pakistan. It has continued to be maintained by its custodians and to draw devotees, and its survival has made it a cherished anchor for the Hindu community of the region and a rare instance of continuity across the rupture of Partition.

Of the province at large, Boivin writes that "By early November of 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail. As of 1 January 1948, it was estimated that nearly 500,000 people had sought refuge in India" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49), and that the Hindu Sindhis "started leaving Sindh especially after the Karachi riots in January 1948" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 66, folio not stated). Of the shrines they left behind, he says that "The darbars in Sindh were most of the time preserved with different arrangements regarding their management", often with Indian *gaddi nashins* or followers paying keepers, and that "despite the fluctuant diplomatic relations between Pakistan and India, it was always possible to travel across the border" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55).

The island's name also crossed into India. Writing of the Sindhi darbars there, Boivin names "Sadh Belo – which was transferred from Sukkur to Mumbai (Maharashtra)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55), and he observes the break in built form between the two: "In the Mumbai Sadh Belo, for example, it is difficult to see any architectural continuity with the Sadh Belo settled in the island in the Indus River, in Sukkur" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 69, folio 56).

On the Pakistani side, Schaflechner writes of Sindh as "home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated), and of government funding for the places of minority communities, seen "in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh within the past decade" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 16, folio not stated). He does not say whether Sadh Bela was among them.

## Setting

Sukkur and Rohri appear in several of the books, though none of these passages speaks of the island. Boivin treats them, with Shikarpur, as corners of a triangle of northern Sindh rich in sanctuaries (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18). He dates the "Sukkur riots" to "between December of 1939 and February of 1940", and notes that they "occurred beyond the city, in other cities such as Rohri, and also in other parts of Sindh, such as in Lakki" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48). Elsewhere he contrasts Sehwan with Sukkur: "Contrary to other cities in Northern Sindh – for instance, Sukkur, following the Manzilgah riots – no communal violence had ever been registered" there (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 71, folio 58).

Rohri, in Boivin's pages, is the birthplace of two Sufis: Rochaldas, "born in 1879 in Rohri, in the north of Sindh, to a family that his hagiographers call modest" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 55, folio 42), and the poet Bedil, "a Sufi born in Rohri" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 97–98, folios 84–85). Annemarie Schimmel writes that "Among them Bedil of Rohri (d. 1872) should be mentioned as a prolific, though not very outstanding, writer in five languages" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 427, folio 306 as printed), and names "the SuhrawardI mystic Janullah of Rohri, one of the outstanding Persian poets of Sind from the second half of the eighteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 428, folio 397). Shemeem Burney Abbas reports that the singer Alan Faqir "is reported to have sung on the buses and trains between Rohri and Sehwan Sharif in his youth" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 78, folio not stated).

The Janamsakhi traditions, in Harish Dhillon's retelling, bring Guru Nanak from Multan "to Sukkur from where he turned southwards along the river Indus" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 194, folio 214). And Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, composed in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, records Sukkur as a halt in the pursuit of Dara Shikoh: news reached the pursuing armies that Dara "از بهکر گذشته بست و پنجم محرم در سکهر نزول نمود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 51). The Mughal commanders who crossed "بجانب سکهر" lost many beasts to what the chronicle calls "کثرت بیشه و تراکم اشجار خاردار و مراحل دشوارگذار"; the baggage did not come up, and on the sixth of Safar they reached Sukkur (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 51). Shaikh Mir stayed a day at Sukkur, where the zamindars told him "از بست و پنج کروسے سکهر راهی بجانب قندهار جدا می شود", a road towards Qandahar; and a faujdar of Sukkur was appointed (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 50).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The name.** The site's account gives Sadh Belo, and *Sadhu Belo*, "the woods of the sage". Schaflechner spells it Sadh Bela throughout (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated). Boivin uses both: "Sadh Bela" where he names it among the sanctuaries and the patrons' temples (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18), and "Sadh Belo" when he writes of the pilgrims, the riots and the transfer to Mumbai (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48; p. 68, folio 55); his index prints the two spellings as separate entries (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 248, folio 235).
- **Where the island stands.** The site's account sets it between the twin cities of Sukkur and Rohri. Boivin writes of "the island in the Indus River, in Sukkur" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 69, folio 56), and Schaflechner of "the city of Sukkur on an island in the River Indus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated).
- **How the temple came to be.** The site's account has Baba Bankhandi Maharaj arrive in 1823, settle on the island and found the place of worship, with the main temple raised under his eighth successor, Sant Harnam Das, at the close of the nineteenth century. Boivin, who names neither man, gives the temple as an example of the patronage of the Shia amirs of Khairpur, "created thanks to a gift of land" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18), without a date or the giver's name.
- **What kind of place it is.** The site's account calls it a Hindu temple complex of the *Udasi* tradition. Boivin calls it an "Udasi temple" and, in his index, a "sanctuary" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 31, folio 18; p. 248, folio 235); Schaflechner calls it a "tīrtha" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated).
- **The head of the house.** The site's account speaks of a line of *gaddi nashin* who succeeded Baba Bankhandi. Schaflechner's account of the pilgrim's visit names its head by the office of *mahaṃt*, which he glosses as "superior of a monastery, abbot", and gives no name (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 138, folio not stated).
- **Sadh Belo after 1947.** The site's account presents the island as having endured in Pakistan, maintained by its custodians, a rare instance of continuity across Partition. Boivin writes that Sadh Belo "was transferred from Sukkur to Mumbai (Maharashtra)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55), and finds no architectural continuity between the Mumbai Sadh Belo and the island (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 69, folio 56).

## Legacy

Sadh Belo stands as a testament to Sindh's plural religious heritage and to the enduring vitality of the *Udasi* tradition on the banks of the Indus. As both a place of active pilgrimage and a monument to the syncretic devotion of Baba Bankhandi and his successors, the island temple remains one of the most beloved and evocative sacred sites of Hindu Sindh, its shrines rising from the river much as they have for two centuries. Its name now stands in two places: on the island in the Indus at Sukkur and in the Sadh Belo of Mumbai, to which, as Boivin records, it was transferred (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55; p. 69, folio 56).

Name: Sain Vali Vilayat Rai Darbar, Kambar
Location: Shivalo mohalla, Kambar (Qambar) town, Qambar–Shahdadkot District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Commemoration of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai; Nanakpanthi worship
Description:
The darbar of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai stands in the *Shivalo* quarter of Kambar (Qambar), the headquarters town of the Qambar–Shahdadkot District of upper Sindh, and is described by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro as the largest Nanakpanthi *darbar* in the district. Its founder, Vali Vilayat Rai, was born in 1825 into a prosperous Hindu family of Old Hala; his father, Pratab Rai, had served as a *munshi* (secretary) to the Talpur Mirs of Hyderabad. Vali Vilayat Rai settled first at Larkana and later moved to Kambar, where he chose the then-unpopulated Shivalo locality — remembered as a resort of *yogis*, *sants* and *sadhus* drawn from Kambar, Shahdadkot, Larkana and the surrounding towns — and there established his darbar, raising a great hall in which the *Guru Granth Sahib* was installed. Like the wider body of Sindhi Nanakpanthis, his followers venerate the Hindu deities together with Baba Guru Nanak, his son Baba Sri Chand, and the other Sikh Gurus, so that the darbar belongs at once to Hindu and to Sikh devotional worlds; it is entered here under "Hindu Temple" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, following the convention used for the other Sindhi *sant* darbars in this collection. The darbar and the *samadhi* (memorial shrine) of Vali Vilayat Rai remain at Kambar, and the lineage retains a devotional following, though — as with most Sindhi Hindu shrines — much of the community associated with it now lives in India. The saint is counted among a constellation of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Nanakpanthi masters of the Larkana country, among them Swami Dharmdas of Larkana and Bhai Waliram of Digano Mahesar.

According to a hagiographic account recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, Vali Vilayat Rai's turn to spiritual life followed his time as a *tapedar* (village accountant) under British rule: irregularities found in his accounts led to imprisonment, during which he is said to have received a vision of Guru Nanak revealing his own previous incarnation as a yogi; thereafter he is remembered as making an annual pilgrimage to the Sufi shrines of Rohri, Sehwan, and Jhok. The present darbar building, a three-storey structure with ornately carved doors and windows in a colonial idiom, is believed to have been erected in 1887. Leadership passed after his death to Sain Jiwat Singh, who ran a free dispensary for the poor of Kambar until his own death in 1899, and then to Jiwat Singh's chief disciple, Vishandas; a branch of the darbar was later established at Kandivali, Bombay (now Mumbai), in 1960, reflecting the wider migration of Sindhi Hindus after Partition.
