## Legends and Miracles

Kanhaiya Lal explains the two smallest samadhs on the platform: the pigeons "بوقت داغ[OCR?] دینے نعش کے چتا کے اندر اُڑتے ہوئے آ پڑے تھے اور مہاراجہ کی نعش کے ساتھہ بھی جل گئے تھے" — at the burning of the body they came flying and fell into the pyre, and were burned with the Maharaja's corpse (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 219, folio 222). He reports it flatly, the two samadhs standing as its evidence; Khalid, too, counts the two pigeons among those who burned in the pyre (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 210, folio not stated).

Chishti tells a story of the Maharaja at the tomb of Mian Mir. He came to strip the tomb, his horse "لیلی" bolted, and he fell and hurt his "جبڑوں[OCR?]"; "اب ہمکو سزا[OCR?] بےادبی[OCR?] کی ملی", he said, gave "پانسو روپیہ نذرانہ", ordered the tomb whitewashed, and remained a devotee of the saint and respectful of the *mujawirs* (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 296–297). He also records the prayers of Subah Shah for the Maharaja (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 86).

The deathbed of Lahori's tazkira belongs here as well as to the history: the faqir who tells the ailing king to send for sandalwood, and the king who dies as the faqir walks out of the fort (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 245, folio 233), and the same faqir's prophecy of nine years (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 244, folio 232).

## Setting: Hazuri Bagh and the Roshnai Gate

The material in this section is about the place around the samadhi, not about the samadhi.

Khalid sets the scene: "The Hazuri Bagh is situated in the middle of these monuments, with a single storey pavilion placed symmetrically at the center of the garden while four lanes lead towards it" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). "The Roshani gate, one of the thirteen gateways that lead into the ancient walled city of Lahore, is between the Alamgiri Gate and the Royal Mosque"; lamps "were lit all along the passageway ... hence the name Roshani gate, or the gate of lights" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). The gate "was once reserved for the prince and the princess, who would go from the Fort to the city through this entrance" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). Behind it lies the Heera Mandi bazaar, "still one of the largest markets for traditional instruments in the city" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated).

Kanhaiya Lal names Hazuri Bagh as "چہوٹا سا میدان جسکو اب حضوری باغ کہتے ہین", without mentioning the samadhi (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 138, folio 141). In his long description of the garden and its *baradari* he says that Ranjit Singh laid out the garden and sat at darbar on the *baradari*'s *shah-nashin*, again without mentioning the samadh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 339–342, folios 346–349). Of the *baradari* in the garden, Chishti writes that Zeb-un-Nisa's marble tomb was taken down to build it, "اب تک وہ بارہ دری حضوری باغ میں یادگار[OCR?] [illegible] مہاراج صاحب [illegible] موجود ہے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 637), while Khalid reports it as said that "The pavilion, which now stands in the middle of the ground, was part of the structure of Emperor Jahangir's tomb" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated).

"For the city that the Maharaja once ruled", Khalid writes of the Lahore of 2011, "he is an alien, his memory kept alive not by people of the land he once ruled but by people from the other side of the border" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 206, folio not stated); it is now rare, he adds, "that one runs into a Sikh in this city, a city which was once ruled by a Sikh and the seat of their political strength" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The date of death.** The site's account gives 27 June 1839, and Khalid gives his years as 1780–1839 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 42, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal gives the year as "۱۸۹۶[OCR?]" with no era and an uncertain month (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 217, folio 220), and elsewhere as "سن ۱۸۹۶ بکرمی" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 113, folio 116); he also gives 1896 Bikrami as the year of a severe illness (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 112, folio 115). Lahori's tazkira gives no year.
- **The day of the anniversary.** The site's account gives the death as 27 June and has pilgrims gather around the death anniversary. Khalid attended the death anniversary on "29th June 2011" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 206, folio not stated), and calls it twelve days after the Guru Arjan commemoration, which he dates to "6th June 2011" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 196, folio not stated).
- **The taking of Lahore.** The site's account has him found and rule the empire from 1801. Chishti has Shah Zaman give him leave to take Lahore in "سترہ سو اٹھانویں", and he took it (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 579). Khalid has him march into Lahore in 1799 and be crowned in 1801 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated).
- **Who died on the pyre.** The site's account has four queens and seven attendants. Kanhaiya Lal has eleven *ranis* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 219, folio 222). Khalid has "eleven women", "his wives and concubines" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 210, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal and Khalid add two pigeons.
- **What marks his remains.** The site's account has a lotus-shaped marble urn holding the ashes. Kanhaiya Lal has a stone samadh, "سمادہ سنگین", at the centre (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 219, folio 222). Chishti has a square memorial under a covering beneath the gilded dome (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 573). Khalid has a palanquin on a raised platform that marks the spot where the last remains "were buried" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 209, folio not stated).
- **Where he was cremated.** The site's account and Kanhaiya Lal put the samadhi on the spot of the cremation (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 217, folio 220). Khalid writes that "His cremation took place in the ground accompanying the building" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 209, folio not stated).
- **The images at the door.** The site's account has red sandstone doorways carved with Ganesha, Devi and Brahma. Kanhaiya Lal has three stone images over the door, of Shiv ji, Ganesh ji and a third whose name is uncertain in the printed text (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 217, folio 220). Chishti has a marble "مورت گنین[OCR?]" on the east, Hanuman in the southern niche and a marble Devi within (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 570; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 572). Khalid sees Krishna, Ganesh, Ram and Sita among the paintings (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 209, folio not stated).
- **The pavilion and its dome.** The site's account has a marble pavilion inlaid with pietra dura. Kanhaiya Lal's marble bungalow has marble columns "مگر اوپر کا گنبد خشتی ہے", a brick dome (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 219, folio 222). Khalid's palanquin has pillars of white marble (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 206, folio not stated).
- **The great dome.** The site's account has gilded fluted domes. Kanhaiya Lal has the great dome's ceiling worked with mirrors and gilding (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 219–220, folios 222–223); Chishti a gilded dome set with mirrors (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 573); Khalid a dome "decorated with coloured glass" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 209, folio not stated).
- **How many storeys.** Chishti calls the brick building "دو منزلہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 572). Kanhaiya Lal describes a second storey, a roofed terrace and a further *baradari* above the great dome (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 220, folio 223; Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 221, folio 224). Khalid's building "stands four floors from the ground" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated).
- **Where it stands beside Dera Sahib.** Khalid has the samadhi facing Dera Sahib across a lawn (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 201, folio not stated), and four pages later "Just behind the samadhi of Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 205, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal puts its wall to the west of Guru Arjan's samadh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 205–206, folios 208–209).
- **The Hazuri Bagh pavilion.** Chishti says it was built from the marble of Zeb-un-Nisa's tomb (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 637). Khalid reports it as said that it was part of the structure of Jahangir's tomb (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated).
- **Spellings.** Chishti prints it "رنجیت سنگھ" and, in several places, in forms uncertain in the printed text such as "مہاراجہ رحمت[OCR?] سکہ[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 585) and "مہارا حد رنجیت سنگہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 646). Lahori's tazkira prints his mother-in-law both "سدا کور" and "سدا کنور" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 258).
- **His temper toward other faiths.** Khalid calls him, "Like the third Mughal Emperor Akbar", a secular ruler (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 207, folio not stated). Chishti attributes his stripping of Mughal tombs to religious zeal, "بباعث تعصب مذہبی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 855), and praises the Wazir Khan endowment "با وجود دیگر[OCR?] انکے تعصب[OCR?] مذہبی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 747–748). Kanhaiya Lal both blames the Sikhs for the city's ruin, "سکھوں نے لوٹ کر [illegible] برباد کر دیا" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 22, folio 17), and makes Ranjit Singh the restorer whose accession woke the city's fortune (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 32, folio 35).

## Legacy

The samadhi is one of the most visited symbols of Sikh heritage remaining in Pakistan, and the monument is listed by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology among the province's protected religious monuments of the Sikh period.

The books consulted leave a double portrait of the man it commemorates. To Kanhaiya Lal he was the ruler under whom Lahore revived (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 32, folio 35), though the same book holds the Sikhs responsible for the city's earlier ruin (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 22, folio 17). To Chishti he was at once the patron of Muslim shrines and the man who carried the marble of Mughal tombs to Amritsar. Lahori's tazkira remembers him through the faqirs he could not buy: the majzub who refused his thousands, the majzuba who abused him and whom he would not leave, and the faqir who told him to send for sandalwood. Khalid found his memory kept on his anniversary by pilgrims from across the border, at a samadhi where the Akhand Path is read in his honour and the *langar* served afterwards (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 206, folio not stated; Khalid, *A White Trail*, pp. 210–211, folio not stated).

Name: Sant Baba Asudaram Darbar (Panno Aqil)
Location: Panno Aqil (Pano Akil), Sukkur District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual death anniversary (Anant Chaturdashi); continuous sadavrat
Description: The Darbar of Sant Baba Asudaram at Panno Aqil (Pano Akil), a town of the Sukkur District some forty kilometres north of Sukkur city, is among the surviving *sant* shrines of the Sindhi Hindu (Nanakpanthi) tradition. Asudaram (1895–1960), remembered by the honorific *Sakhi Baba*, "the generous master," was born on 3 April 1895 in the village of Jatoin near Panno Aqil, the son of Bhai Ludhrodmal and Chaini Bai. As a boy he came under the influence of Sant Shiromani Satramdas of Raharki (whose *Devri Sahib* is a separate entry in this dataset), and he later served at the Raharki *darbar* under the martyr-saint Bhagat Kanwar Ram (also recorded separately here), who is said to have given him the name *Shiv Swaroop*. On his Guru's instruction he returned to Panno Aqil in 1940 and there established his own *Darbar Sahib*. Around it grew a network of social works for which he became renowned — schools (*pathshalas*), a dispensary, and homes for the elderly and destitute — sustained by a *sadavrat* said to serve food and sweet water around the clock without distinction of caste or creed. He died on 4 September 1960, on the day of *Anant Chaturdashi*, and was succeeded by his son Sai Chanduram, whose activity later shifted to Lucknow in India. The darbar at Panno Aqil endures as the principal shrine of his lineage in Pakistan.

Name: Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir
Events: Not documented
Description:
## Overview

The Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir stands in the Shahi Bazar of Dadu, a district town on the right bank of the Indus in central Sindh. It is one of a number of functioning Hindu shrines in the province administered under the *Evacuee Trust Property Board*, and it belongs to a characteristically Sindhi form of religious site — the *darbar mandir*, in which the seat or memorial of a locally revered *sant* is joined to a temple of ordinary image-worship. Named for the saint Bhagat Ram, the shrine serves the Hindu families who remain in Dadu and preserves a strand of the region's devotional heritage. It should be noted at the outset that this is a modest local site on which scholarly documentation is sparse, and much of what follows is offered with due caution.

## Sant Baba Bhagat Ram and the Daduvansi Tradition

Local tradition associates the shrine with a *sant* named Bhagat Ram, remembered as one of a line of Hindu holy men active in and around Dadu, sometimes described as belonging to a *Daduvansi* lineage — literally the "line" or descendants of a saintly founder. Writers on the town's history mention such figures, among them a Dayo Ram Daduvansi said to have lived in the nineteenth century (dates variously given as 1836–1906), and it has even been suggested, though this is no more than a local hypothesis, that the name of the town of Dadu is itself connected to this saintly line. The historical detail behind these names is thin, and the biography, dates and teachings of Bhagat Ram himself are not securely recorded in accessible sources; the safest statement is that he was a locally venerated holy man whose memory the shrine keeps alive. Such *sant* devotion in Sindh characteristically drew on a blend of Vaishnava *bhakti*, Nanak-panthi and *Udasi* currents, in which the veneration of a living or departed teacher sat comfortably alongside the worship of images.

## The Darbar Mandir

The designation *darbar mandir* points to the dual character of the site. The *darbar* is the "court" or seat of the saint — often a *gaddi*, *samadhi* or memorial *takht* — before which devotees pay their respects, while the *mandir* houses the images and observances of temple worship. This pattern, in which a personal cult of a holy man is embedded within a temple, is widespread in the Sindhi Hindu landscape and reflects the province's distinctive religious culture, shaped by centuries of coexistence with Sufi Islam and by the shared idiom of saint-veneration. The shrine's location in the Shahi Bazar, the old commercial spine of Dadu, is typical of such urban community temples, which grew up amid the shops and homes of Hindu traders.

## Community and Custodianship

The Partition of 1947 and subsequent migrations greatly reduced the Hindu population of central Sindh, and shrines such as this passed, in the main, into the custody of the Evacuee Trust Property Board, the body that administers the religious properties of those who left. Where a resident community remained, sites like the Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir continued in worship, sustained by local families and by the wider networks of Sindhi Hindu devotion that persist in the province. The shrine's survival, and its continued identification with a named local saint, make it a small but genuine witness to the endurance of Hindu religious life in the towns of the Indus valley.

## Bibliography

- *Sindh Courier*, "Dadu: Exploring the Historical Background".
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, writings on the Hindu shrines and saint-cults of Sindh (e.g. "Sindh: A Place of Sadhus, Sanyasis, Sants, Udasis, Bairagis and Sufis").
- Evacuee Trust Property Board listings of functioning temples in Sindh.
- Wikipedia, "Hinduism in Sindh" and "Dadu, Sindh", with cited sources.

Name: Sant Bhagat Kanwar Ram Temple (Chak)
Events: Annual commemoration (2 November)
Description:
This temple at Chak, a town in Shikarpur district, is dedicated to the memory of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (1885–1939), one of the best-loved Sindhi Hindu saint-singers of the twentieth century. Born in the village of Jarwar in the Sukkur region, he became renowned for his rendition of the *Sur Prabhati*, sung in the early morning; the gramophone company HMV is said to have preserved a number of his devotional songs on record, spreading his fame across Sindh. Revered by Hindus and Muslims alike as a figure of piety and communal harmony, he was assassinated at Ruk railway station in the Sukkur area in November 1939 and is remembered as a martyr. The temple at Chak was raised in his name after his death and was rebuilt in 2006; its main hall holds canopies bearing images of Bhagat Kanwar Ram and of Sant Satram Das, the saint of the *Sacho Satram* tradition with whom his memory is closely linked. In a syncretic touch characteristic of Sindhi devotion, the *Guru Granth Sahib* is also installed within, so that the darbar is honoured by Hindu and Sikh worshippers together. Every year on 2 November his followers gather to mark the anniversary of his martyrdom, both at this shrine and at Ruk station where he was killed.

The temple stands specifically in the Lakhi Ghulam Shah taluka of Shikarpur district, roughly 24 km east of Lakhi Ghulam Shah town. Kanwar Ram — born 13 April 1885 at Tarachand's house in Jarwar, then part of Mirpur Mathelo tehsil, and a disciple of Sant Satram Das (1866-1910) — was also remembered for singing the verses of Sufi poets including Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Sachal Sarmast, Sami, and Kabir alongside his own devotional compositions. The Chak temple was first managed by Ladak Mal and his family and, following its 2006 rebuilding, has been maintained by Bal Chand Esrani, Tara Chand Thawani, and Prakash Lal Devani. A separate commemoration, distinct from both the Chak temple and the Ruk station gathering, has also been held at the Institute of Sindhology in Hyderabad, where in 2008 the university's vice-chancellor marked Kanwar Ram's 69th death anniversary by announcing a dedicated Bhagat Kanwar Ram Memorial Corner.

- Shaikh Abdul Rasheed, "Remembering Bhagat Kanwar Ram," *The News on Sunday*, 26 April 2020.

Name: Sant Satram Dham, Raharki (Sacho Satram / Devri Sahib)
Location: Raharki (Raherki Sahib), Daharki Taluka, Ghotki District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Annual birth-anniversary celebrations (October)
Description:
The town of Raharki (Raherki Sahib) in Ghotki district, in upper Sindh close to the Punjab border, is home to the *Sant Satram Dham* — also known as *Devri Sahib*, and, after the devotional movement it anchors, as *Sacho Satram* — reckoned among the largest and most frequented Hindu shrines in present-day Pakistan. It marks the birthplace of *Satguru* Swami Sai Satramdas Sahib, the revered Sindhi saint born here, according to the tradition, on 25 October 1866. He gave his life to spiritual teaching in the syncretic Sindhi devotional mould, preaching love, humility and service to the destitute, and drawing followers from across Sindh who came to him for blessing and healing; the tradition records that he "left the mortal body" on 25 January 1910. After his passing the *Devri* (shrine) at Raharki grew into the principal seat of his lineage, whose devotees revere a holy text recited at the shrine known as the *Dhuni Sahib*. Today thousands of pilgrims — Sindhi Hindus from Pakistan, India and the diaspora — gather at Raharki, especially each October to mark the saint's birth anniversary, and the site is locally described as one of the biggest temples in the country. A succession of *sants* has continued to lead the community, and the darbar sustains traditions of communal hospitality and worship; the town itself is noted as one where Muslims and Hindus have long lived together. His memory is closely linked with that of Bhagat Kanwar Ram (also recorded in this dataset), with whom the *Sacho Satram* tradition is associated.

According to *Dawn*'s 2012 reporting, the darbar forms a sprawling, multi-acre complex a few kilometres from the Bharchundi Sharif shrine, with an enormous pilgrim hostel under construction and a causeway, funded by the federal government, easing access to the site; caretakers there described a mid-April festival marking the death anniversary of Bhagat Kanwar Ram that draws tens of thousands of visitors, including from Dubai and India. A satellite Sant Satram Dham was separately established in Shikarpur town on 9 October 2000, its own displays acknowledging the Raharki complex as the "principal" *Devri Sahib*. In September 2019 the temple — also referred to in press coverage as the SSD Dham Mandir — was attacked during communal unrest in Ghotki; government and civil-society delegations investigating the violence met community leaders on-site and concluded the attack had been planned the night before, and PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari visited the ransacked temple in its aftermath.

Name: Sevapanthi Darbar (Bhai Gurdas), Gandava
Location: Heart of Gandava (Gandawah) town, Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Bhai Gurdas (Sevapanthi tradition); veneration of Guru Nanak
Events: No regular events documented
Description:
In the heart of Gandava — the old headquarters town of the Jhal Magsi District on the Kachhi (Kach Gandava) plain of Balochistan — stands a *darbar* of the *Sevapanthi* tradition, the order of devotees descended from Bhai Gurdas, the disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who is said to have carried the Nanakpanthi teaching into Sindh and Balochistan in the eighteenth century. According to the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, who has surveyed the Hindu and Sikh heritage of the region, the Gandava darbar was founded by one of Bhai Gurdas's disciples; the *Sevapanthis* (also written Sewapanthis, "those of the path of service") established such darbars and *dharamshalas* in many towns of Sindh and Balochistan, joining the veneration of Guru Nanak to a discipline of charitable hospitality. The Gandava darbar is celebrated above all for its woodwork: an intricately carved wooden frame decorating the main façade depicts Baba Guru Nanak flanked by his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, together with the Hindu deities Ganesha (*Ganpati*) and Krishna — a vivid emblem of the syncretic Nanakpanthi devotion in which Sikh and Hindu figures share a single sacred idiom. The carving belongs to the same tradition of craftsmanship that produced the famed woodwork of the Khatwari Darbar at Shikarpur (a separate entry in this dataset), and the wider district is noted for such carvings of Krishna, Ganpati and Guru Nanak with his minstrel companions. Filed here under "Sikh Gurdwara" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, the darbar is more precisely a Nanakpanthi–Sevapanthi shrine of the kind once common among the Hindu mercantile communities of the Sindh–Balochistan borderland. Its exact date of foundation is not securely recorded, and — like many such darbars whose congregations dispersed after 1947 — the details of its present custody and use are uncertain, though the building and its carved façade were reported still standing when documented in recent years. Kalhoro's account also gives Bhai Gurdas's personal history: born Bhai Kanya Lal, he is remembered as a Khalsa saint who received the blessing of Guru Gobind Singh himself before carrying that teaching into the towns of Sindh and Balochistan. Independent confirmation that Gandava possesses a Hindu temple comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage sites, which lists "a Hindu temple" alongside the tombs of Syed Noor Shah Hussaini and Mian Saleh among the settlement's notable structures — though this piece does not itself identify the temple with the Sevapanthi darbar described above, so it stands as corroboration only that such a building exists in the town, not as confirmation of the specific Bhai Gurdas attribution.

Name: Shah Noorani Shrine (Syed Bilawal Shah Noorani)
Location: Lahoot Lamakan valley, Khuzdar District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs; evening dhamal; qawwali and langar
Description:
## Overview

Deep in the mountains of the Khuzdar district of Balochistan, in the remote valley of Lahut Lamakan, stands the shrine of Shah Noorani (Syed Bilawal Shah Noorani), one of the most venerated and most inaccessible Sufi shrines in Pakistan. Set amid a landscape long held sacred and reached by a hard journey through the hills, the darbar draws pilgrims from across Sindh and Balochistan, who come in great numbers for its *dhamal* and its blessing, undeterred by its remoteness.

Jürgen Schaflechner, in his study of the goddess Hinglaj and her pilgrimage, describes the valley as "the abode of the saint Shah Noorani in the Khuzdar district in Balochistan", a saint "who is said to have lived in this valley" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated). He writes the place as Lahoot la Makan, Lahoot or Lāhūt (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated). Omar Kasmani, writing of the fakirs of Sehwan, calls it Lahut, "a revered site in Balochistan" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97). Neither book gives the saint the names Syed Bilawal, and neither records his dates, his lineage, his spiritual order or an annual *ʿurs*; Kasmani names no saint, tomb or custodian at Lahut at all (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97).

## The Saint and the Sacred Valley

Shah Noorani is remembered as a Sufi saint of the medieval centuries who settled in the wild valley of Lahut Lamakan, a place whose very name (*la-hut la-makan*, “the placeless place of the divine”) marks it as a landscape of ancient sanctity, associated in legend with the mystic quest and revered across religious traditions. His life is known more through devotion and legend than through documented history, but his sanctity is held in the highest regard, and his shrine has for centuries been a goal of arduous pilgrimage. The setting, with its mountains, caves and springs held holy, gives the shrine an aura unlike any other.

Schaflechner's account bears out the valley's landscape. Comparing it with the valley of the goddess Hinglaj, he writes: "There are fascinating similarities between the two valleys. Both are small oases with natural springs (Urd. chaśmah) and caves in confined valleys." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) Of the saint himself he says only that he "is said to have lived in this valley" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).

The valley's sanctity, in the books, is older than the saint and wider than Islam. Schaflechner reports that "Abro suggests that Lahoot was once an important place for Hindu worship (Abro 1991), which is consistent with the history of other Hindu sites in the area that were converted to Sufi centers over time (Boivin 2007)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) The valley's name also appears in his book in the titles of two works in the region's own languages: Badar Abro's *Hinglāj ai Lāhūt* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 94, folio not stated) and an Urdu book by Nazamani, *Lāhūṭ lā Makān* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).

Two other saints pass through the valley in these books. Schaflechner lists "Lahoot (Khuzdar)" among the places of Shah Abdul Latif's wandering (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 95, folio not stated). Kasmani, in a note on the journey of the saint he calls Lal, lists Lahut-lamakan among the places where he stopped, with Makran, Panjgur and Pasni in Balochistan and Naing, Lake Manchhar and Sehwan in Sindh (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 14). What these passages say is said of the valley and of those saints, not of Shah Noorani or his shrine.

## The Shrine

The heart of the site, in Schaflechner's description, is a cave: "The main attraction in Lahoot is the cave of the saint Shah Noorani, who is said to have lived in this valley." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) He visited it himself in 2010 (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).

Inside the cave is a stone. "Inside the cave, one finds a curiously shaped stone that is allegedly the image of Ali's camel. Some authors claim that this image used to be worshipped as a śiva liṅga before the place became associated with the Sufi saint (Khatri 1973), and indeed, the shape of the stone would support this idea, as I could see during a visit in 2010." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated)

The sources consulted describe no tomb and record no date of building, no builder or patron, no custodian and no endowment for the shrine.

## Devotion and Pilgrimage

Despite its remoteness, Shah Noorani's shrine is a place of intense devotion, famous above all for the *dhamal*, the ecstatic drum-driven trance-dance performed by crowds of pilgrims, and for the *langar* and qawwali that mark its gatherings. Pilgrims undertake the difficult journey to seek healing, fulfil vows, and share in the charged atmosphere of the sacred valley.

Both books place the valley on a pilgrimage route that runs from Sehwan. Schaflechner writes that "Lal Shahbaz is also the starting point for the pilgrimage to Lahoot la Makan" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated). Kasmani's fakirs "proceed to Lahut, a revered site in Balochistan, as do many fakirs upon the culmination of the three-day annual fair of" Sehwan (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97). In one of Kasmani's narratives, Lahut is a possible end of a woman's journey, and her husband, searching for her, wonders: "And if she was indeed in Lahut, would she trace her journey back to Sehwan or would she rather follow other fakirs and proceed to shrines in Karachi?" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97)

The route once ran further, to the goddess of Hinglaj. "This pilgrimage route was once connected to the Makran Coast and the abode of 'Nani Hinglaj'… Today, however, this path seems to have been widely forgotten." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) Schaflechner finds a trace of it in Nazamani's Urdu book: "A vestige of this now obsolete pilgrimage route can be found at the end of the Urdu book Lāhūṭ lā Makān by Nazamani, which provides a description of the way from Lahoot to Hinglaj (Nazamani 2009, 26)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) In 2010 he met at Lahoot la Makan a Punjabi pilgrim who had come from Sehwan Sharif and who "confirmed that this side of the pilgrimage route is still frequented; however, he mentioned that the longer path to Hinglaj is no longer used due to the dangerous political situation in the area." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 147, folio not stated)

Schaflechner also records a recent change in the journey itself: "Interestingly, and similar to Hinglaj, Lahoot is currently experiencing a new wave of interest mainly due to a newly constructed road leading to the shrine thus making the journey through the mountainous area easier." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated)

The sources consulted give no date for an *ʿurs* at the shrine.

## The Attack of 2016

The shrine's fame and its throngs also made it a target. In November 2016 a suicide bombing during the evening *dhamal* killed and injured many worshippers, one of the deadliest attacks on a Pakistani shrine; yet, as at other darbars struck by such violence, the devotion of the pilgrims endured and the shrine continued to draw them.

Schaflechner, setting the attack against the new road and the new interest it had brought, writes: "However, a terrible bomb blast in November 2016, killing more than fifty people, has curbed the growing influx of visitors and has created a volatile situation for Balochistan's shrines." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated) He names no attacker.

## Legends

The one legend the books record at the site belongs to the stone in the cave, which, Schaflechner reports, is "allegedly the image of Ali's camel" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated). Beside it he sets the claim of other authors that the same stone was once worshipped as a *śiva liṅga* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).

A possible further mention of the saint stands in the same book, and its reference is uncertain. Raj Kumar, a pilgrim whose words Schaflechner reports, says: "Again we are climbing the mountains for Noorani" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 160, folio not stated). The book does not say which Noorani is meant, and its index carries "Noorani" and "Noorani, Shah" as two separate headings (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 354, folio not stated). Another saint of Balochistan, Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani of Jhal Magsi District, bears the same name, so the words may not refer to Shah Noorani of Lahut Lamakan at all.

## Setting

The books say a good deal about Balochistan in general, and some of it frames the shrine's world. None of what follows is said of Shah Noorani or his valley.

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi dates the first Muslim advance through the region: "In 710 Muhammad bin Qasim al-Saqafi began his advance through Makran and Baluchistan with the conquest of Sind between 711 and 712" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 127, folio 109). After that conquest, writes Shemeem Burney Abbas, "a long line of Sufi mystics came to the region through Baluchistan, Mekran, Multan, and Sind itself" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 50, folio not stated). Annemarie Schimmel finds the popularity of Gilani in the region in its names: "Proper names like Ghauth Bakhsh, 'gift of the help,' in Sind and Balochistan point to his [Gilani's] popularity" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 279, folio 248).

Abbas writes of a shared devotional world: "The mystical lore of the region that includes Sind, Baluchistan, and the coastal belt of Iran shares myths, melodies, and linguistic codes" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 47–48, folios not stated), and the "Mast Qalandar" *dhun* is "reported to be sung all along the Rajasthan, Sind, Baluchistan, and Iran continuum" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 57, folio not stated). Of the *dhamal* she writes: "Many times, families will bring women who are emotionally disturbed to participate in the dhammāl, which devotees claim has healing powers. In Baluchistan, such healing ceremonies are called guāṭi" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 66, folio not stated). Her glossary defines the same word as "A ritual for making vows at Sufi shrines in Baluchistan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 182, folio not stated). She describes the *mugarmān* drum as "held sacred by the Sidi communities in Sind, Baluchistan, Rajasthan, and Gujrat who use them in their shrines and for rituals" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 185, folio not stated).

The region's poetry and legend are held in common with Sindh. Abbas writes that the Sassi myth is "told in the lands of Sind and Baluchistan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 118, folio not stated), and Schimmel counts "the hill slopes of Balochistan" within the geography of Sind's folk tales (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 161, folio 161). H. T. Sorley, in his study of Shah Abdul Latif, writes that the poetry of Sind and that of Baluchistan have certain elements in common (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 256, folio 247); quoting Longworth Dames, he describes the Baluchis' poetry as "wholly oral", "sung by professional minstrels called Doms or Dombs who sing the songs in the gatherings of the clans" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 255, folio 246).

For pilgrims from India, Schaflechner writes, the province is hard to reach: they "must obtain an additional visa allowing travel to Balochistan, a province that has been in a state of a latent insurgency since the establishment of Pakistan (Axmann 2012)" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 169, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The name of the valley.** The site's account writes Lahut Lamakan, glossing it as “the placeless place of the divine”; the location given for the shrine is Lahoot Lamakan. Schaflechner writes Lahoot la Makan, Lahoot and Lāhūt, and gives the Urdu title *Lāhūṭ lā Makān* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated). Kasmani writes Lahut and Lahut-lamakan (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97; p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 14).
- **The attack of November 2016.** The site's account calls it a suicide bombing during the evening *dhamal* that killed and injured many worshippers. Schaflechner calls it "a terrible bomb blast in November 2016, killing more than fifty people", and does not say when in the day it struck or who carried it out (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).
- **The pilgrims after 2016.** The site's account says that the devotion of the pilgrims endured and the shrine continued to draw them. Schaflechner writes that the blast "has curbed the growing influx of visitors" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).
- **The journey.** The site's account calls the shrine one of the most inaccessible in Pakistan, reached by a hard journey through the hills. Schaflechner reports "a newly constructed road leading to the shrine thus making the journey through the mountainous area easier" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).
- **What guāṭi means.** Abbas, in her text, calls the healing ceremonies of the *dhamal* in Baluchistan guāṭi (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 66, folio not stated); her glossary defines the word as "A ritual for making vows at Sufi shrines in Baluchistan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 182, folio not stated). She says this of Baluchistan, not of this shrine.

## Legacy

Shah Noorani stands among the great shrines of Balochistan and lower Sindh: a saint of the sacred mountain valley of Lahut Lamakan whose darbar, for all its remoteness, remains a powerful centre of ecstatic devotion. Its *dhamal*, its legends and its holy landscape make it one of the most singular pilgrimage places in Pakistan, and its endurance after the tragedy of 2016 a testament to the tenacity of popular faith.

In the books, the valley's place is that of a station on a long road of devotion: a goal for the fakirs who leave Sehwan when its fair is over (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97), once a stage on the way to the goddess of Hinglaj (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated), and a valley whose cave and stone carry the memory of more than one faith (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 108, folio not stated).

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- General established accounts of the Shah Noorani shrine and the Lahut Lamakan valley.
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2018; print line 2017).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series, published with the Center for Middle Eastern Studies, University of Texas at Austin).
- Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, Vol. I, *Early Sufism and its History in India to 1600 AD* (New Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers Pvt. Ltd.; first published 1978, copyright line 1975).

Name: Shah Yousuf
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

A shrine locally known as Darbar Hazrat Shah Yousuf stands in the Shah Yousaf locality of Shahpur tehsil, Sargodha District, Punjab — a modest, little-documented Sufi shrine that should not be confused with the far more famous shrine of Shah Yusuf Gardezi in Multan, a twelfth-century saint of an entirely different lineage and city, some 150 kilometres to the south. The Shahpur shrine is officially recognised in its own right: it appears on the notified-shrines list maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department under its Sargodha zone, alongside other local dargahs of the district.

## A Locally Rooted, Thinly Documented Figure

Beyond its official listing, and the place-name it has given to its own locality — a government secondary school in the area is registered as "GHS Shah Yousaf, Shahpur" — almost nothing about the saint's life, lineage, or era survives in accessible written sources. The fifteenth-century founding date sometimes attached to the site could not be corroborated in gazetteers or published local histories and should be treated as provisional pending a district gazetteer or Auqaf departmental record. Notably, the neighbouring town of Shahpur itself is documented to take its own name from a different, later Sufi figure — Syed Shams Shah Shirazi, said to have arrived around 1606 and to have converted the formerly Hindu-majority settlement then known as Rampur — so the naming of this shrine rests on local memory rather than a firm documentary trail distinct from that town history.

## Distinguishing from Shah Yusuf Gardezi

Because the honorific "Shah Yousuf/Yusuf" recurs among Punjabi Sufi figures, this Shahpur shrine is easily conflated with the much larger, better-documented shrine of Shah Yusuf Gardezi in Multan, a twelfth-century saint of the Gardezi Sayyid lineage. The two are unrelated: different centuries, different cities, and no source treats them as the same figure. This entry describes only the local Shahpur site.

## Present State

Practically nothing has been published on the shrine's current physical form, custodianship, or the rites practised there. What can be said with confidence is that it remains an active, Auqaf-administered site of local pilgrimage in the Sargodha countryside.

## Bibliography

- Punjab Auqaf & Religious Affairs Department, list of notified shrines, Sargodha zone.
- District school directories, Sargodha (locality confirmation: "GHS Shah Yousaf, Shahpur").
- Local histories of Shahpur town, for contrast with its separately documented founding figure, Syed Shams Shah Shirazi.

Name: Shahwala Teja Singh Mandir
Events: Maha Shivratri
Description:
## Overview

The Shivala (or Shawala) Teja Singh Temple stands in the Dharowal quarter of the old city of Sialkot, in the Punjab, a historic Hindu temple dedicated to *Shiva* whose soaring shikhara long dominated the surrounding rooftops. Named for Teja Singh, who is remembered as its builder or patron, the temple is counted among the oldest surviving Hindu shrines of the Pakistani Punjab, and its recent restoration and reopening — after more than seven decades of closure — made it a symbol of the fragile revival of Hindu heritage in the region.

## Antiquity and Tradition

Heritage accounts hold the site to be very ancient; some traditions reckon it nine hundred to a thousand years old, which would place its origins among the oldest Hindu places of worship in this part of the Punjab. Such figures should be treated with caution, for they rest largely on local memory and devotional tradition rather than firm documentary record; what is clear is that the temple served for centuries as a living centre of worship for the Hindu community of Sialkot, a city that before 1947 possessed a substantial Hindu and Sikh population. Dedicated to Shiva, it would have drawn its greatest crowds at *Maha Shivratri*, the night sacred to the god.

## Architecture

The temple is built in the characteristic north Indian *nagara* idiom, its sanctum crowned by a tall, curvilinear tower rising in tiers above the shrine — a form designed to be seen from afar and to mark the sacred centre against the skyline of the crowded old city. For much of the twentieth century, standing sealed and neglected, it survived as one of the most conspicuous relics of Sialkot's pre-Partition religious landscape, its weathered tower a landmark even in disuse.

## Closure, Damage, and Restoration

Like most Hindu temples in the western Punjab, the Shivala Teja Singh Temple was abandoned at the Partition of 1947, when Sialkot's Hindus departed for India, and it was thereafter sealed. In 1992 it suffered further damage during the unrest that followed the demolition of the Babri Masjid in India, when a number of temples across Pakistan were attacked. For decades it stood shuttered and decaying, and by the 2010s Hindu leaders were publicly urging the authorities to arrest its ruin.

The turn came at the end of the decade. Under the Evacuee Trust Property Board, and with the help of the Lahore-based Sir Ganga Ram Heritage Foundation, the temple was renovated, and in 2019 it was formally reopened and handed over for the use of pilgrims — the first time in some seventy-two years that Hindu worship was again possible there. The reopening was widely reported as a gesture towards Pakistan's religious minorities and towards the preservation of the country's diverse heritage.

## Legacy

The Shivala Teja Singh Temple endures as one of the most evocative Hindu monuments of the Pakistani Punjab: a shrine of great, if imprecisely known, antiquity, damaged by the passions of the twentieth century and partly restored in the twenty-first. Its reopening did not conjure back the vanished Hindu community of Sialkot, but it returned to that community's descendants and to the wider public a place of worship and a piece of the city's layered past. As both a functioning temple and a heritage site, it stands as a reminder of the plural religious life that once flourished in Sialkot.

## Bibliography

- Reeta Grewal and others on the urban and religious history of the colonial and pre-colonial Punjab.
- Reports of the Evacuee Trust Property Board (Pakistan) and the Sir Ganga Ram Heritage Foundation on temple conservation.
- Contemporary press coverage of the 2019 restoration (Dawn, The Express Tribune, and international agencies).
- Prakash Tandon, *Punjabi Century* (for the texture of Hindu life in pre-Partition Punjab).
- George Michell, *The Hindu Temple: An Introduction to Its Meaning and Forms* (on the *nagara* tradition).
