Name: Sharada Peeth
Founded/Opened: Active c. 6th–12th c. CE; likely commissioned c. 724–760 CE
Events: None - ruin; access restricted near the Line of Control
Description:
## Overview

Sharada Peeth is the ruined but hallowed remnant of what was once among the most illustrious temples and centres of learning in the Indian subcontinent, standing beside the Neelum River in the village of Sharda, in the Neelum Valley of Azad Kashmir. Set at nearly 2,000 metres in the shadow of Mount Harmukh, revered by Kashmiri Pandits as an abode of Shiva, the site was dedicated to the goddess Sharada, the Kashmiri form of *Saraswati*, deity of learning, and gave her name both to the celebrated *Sharada* script and to Kashmir itself, long known as *Sharada Desh*, the "Land of Sharada". Simultaneously a temple, a fabled university, and one of the great *Shakti Peethas*, Sharada Peeth occupies a singular place in the cultural and religious memory of Kashmir.

Of the books consulted for this article, none names Sharada Peeth. Two of them, both by Haroon Khalid, speak of the goddess Saraswati, with whom Sharada is identified, and nothing more: one describes an image of her painted on the wall of a Valmiki temple, the other mentions her in a remark about peacocks. What they say, set out below, is said of the goddess in general, not of this temple, its ruins or its history.

## The Shakti Peetha and the Goddess of Learning

Sharada Peeth is counted among the *Shakti Peethas*, and by Kashmiri tradition it is enumerated among the eighteen *Maha Shakti Peethas*. According to the legend common to all these seats, the shrine marks a place where a part of the body of the goddess Sati fell to earth after Vishnu dismembered her corpse with his discus to end Shiva's grief-stricken dance; at Sharada, tradition holds, it was the goddess's right hand that descended, and here she is worshipped in her form as Sharada. The site's association with Saraswati fused devotion and scholarship in a manner rare among the Peethas, so that the goddess was venerated as the very source of knowledge, letters and wisdom. Its renown was such that the great teacher Adi Shankara, in his hymnic enumeration of the eighteen seats of the Goddess, named Sharada in Kashmir alongside Kamakshi at Kanchipuram and Vishalakshi at Varanasi.

## The Temple University and the Sharada Script

Between roughly the sixth and twelfth centuries CE, Sharada Peeth flourished as one of the foremost temple universities of the subcontinent, a rival in reputation to the great monastic seats of learning elsewhere in India. Tradition and later accounts describe a renowned library that drew scholars from great distances, and the site is associated in memory with luminaries such as the philosopher Adi Shankara, the historian Kalhana, author of the *Rajatarangini*, and the scholar Vairotsana. It was, above all, a pre-eminent centre of Sanskrit scholarship, where numerous important manuscripts were composed and copied.

The most enduring legacy of this learning is the *Sharada* script itself, which developed and spread from this centre and was named in the shrine's honour. For centuries the *Sharada* script was the principal medium for writing Sanskrit and Kashmiri in the region, and it remains sacred to Kashmiri Pandits, used in ritual and in the writing of horoscopes. So intimately was the goddess bound to the intellectual life of Kashmir that to be admitted to the shrine's precincts came to symbolise scholarly attainment.

## Decline, Partition and the Present

Sharada Peeth's decline unfolded over many centuries, its academic pre-eminence fading after the twelfth century amid the political upheavals that swept Kashmir. Earthquakes, neglect and the passage of time reduced the once-great complex to the massive stone shell that survives today, its walls of large ashlar blocks standing roofless within a walled enclosure. The Partition of 1947 and the ensuing division of Kashmir placed the shrine within Pakistan-administered territory, close to the Line of Control, and effectively cut it off from the Kashmiri Pandit community for whom it remained a spiritual lodestar.

In recent years the site has become a focus of renewed attention and appeals for conservation. Kashmiri Pandit organisations have campaigned for access and preservation, and there have been proposals for a pilgrimage corridor comparable to that opened at Kartarpur; on the Indian side of the Line of Control, a new Sharada temple was consecrated in Kupwara in 2023, seeking to rekindle the devotional link to the ancient seat.

## Saraswati in the Books Consulted

Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail*, a journey among Pakistan's religious minorities, describes the goddess as she is pictured on the wall of a Valmiki temple: "the female deity of knowledge, music, arts and science, clad in a white sari standing with her sitar" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 80, folio not stated). The passage concerns that painting alone; the book does not mention Sharada Peeth.

In another of his books, *In Search of Shiva*, a study of folk religious practice in Pakistan, Khalid names the goddess, whom he spells Sarasvati, only in passing, in a remark about peacocks: "In Hindu tradition, peacocks acquire a special status because of their association with the deities Krishna and Sarasvati", and "A peacock is depicted as Goddess Sarasvati's ride" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Nothing in the book concerns the site, and the remark is given here only because it speaks of the goddess to whom the site was dedicated.

Neither book records anything of Sharada Peeth's foundation, its fabric, its pilgrimage or its decline, and neither quotes a verse about the goddess or the site; the account of those matters given above rests on the works listed in the bibliography.

## Legacy

Sharada Peeth endures as one of the most poignant and evocative sacred sites of the subcontinent, a ruin that once embodied the highest achievements of Kashmiri learning and piety. As the namesake of a script, a goddess and a land, and as a *Shakti Peetha* revered across generations, it remains a powerful emblem of Kashmir's ancient identity as the "Land of Sharada", even as its weathered stones await the care their history so richly merits.

## Bibliography

- Kalhana, *Rajatarangini* (the twelfth-century chronicle of Kashmir), for the shrine's medieval renown.
- Aurel Stein, *Kalhana's Rajatarangini: A Chronicle of the Kings of Kashmir* (translation and topographical notes locating Sharada).
- Studies on the development of the *Sharada* script and Sanskrit manuscript culture in Kashmir.
- Adi Shankara's hymns enumerating the eighteen *Maha Shakti Peethas*.
- Contemporary heritage and press coverage of conservation appeals and the Sharada corridor initiative (Kashmir press; Indian and Pakistani media).
- Haroon Khalid, *A White Trail: A journey into the heart of Pakistan's religious minorities* (westland ltd, 2013; first e-book edition 2013).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).

Name: Shergarh
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

At Shergarh, in the Okara district of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Daud Bandagi Kirmani (1513–1575), a revered Qadiri saint of the sixteenth century who did much to spread the Qadiri order in the Punjab. A contemporary of the Mughal emperors Humayun and Akbar and of the great Lahori saints of his age, Daud Bandagi made Shergarh a centre of devotion, and his darbar remains a place of pilgrimage in central Punjab.

Several of the books name the tomb at the town. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, writing in 1875, says that "مزار گوہر بار بمقام شیر گڈھ زیارت گاہ خلق اللہ ہے اور ہر سال بڑا ہجوم حضرت کے مزار پر ہوتا ہے", that his pearl-scattering mazar at the place Sher Garh is a place of pilgrimage for God's creatures, and that every year a great crowd gathers at his mazar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti speaks of a Hazrat Daud Bandagi "جنکا مزار شیر گڑھ میں ہے", whose mazar is at Shergarh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 179). Haroon Khalid, travelling in the Punjab, writes: "One of the places we stopped at was Shergarh, about an hour from Lahore, where we witnessed the festivities at the annual festival of Daud Bandagi Kirmani" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

The older books do not all call him by the name the shrine bears today. Lahori never prints "Bandagi"; he calls him Shaikh Daud Kirmani of Shergarh and gives his toponymic name in two forms. Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib calls him simply Hazrat Shaikh Daud of Shergarh, and Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore Khwaja Daud of Sher Garh. They agree that he was a master at Shergarh from whom later masters took their path: Shah Abul Muali of Lahore in the accounts of Lahori, Sharib and Chishti, and Shah Abu Ishaq in those of Kanhaiya Lal and Chishti. Lahori dates his death to 982 AH. These differences are set out side by side below.

## The Life of the Saint

Daud, honoured with the title *Bandagi* ("servitude," marking his devotion) and the epithet *Kirmani* for his family's origins, was born in 1513. He gave himself to religious learning and the Sufi path, and became a shaykh of the Qadiri order (the line of Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad) at a time when that order was taking firm root in the subcontinent. From his base at Shergarh he taught, guided disciples, and spread the Qadiri way across the Punjab, living through the turbulent early Mughal decades. He was among the notable saints of the generation of Shah Hussain of Lahore, part of the flowering of Punjabi Sufism in the sixteenth century. He died in 1575 and was buried at Shergarh.

Lahori gives him a full notice, the ninth in the Qadiri chapter of his *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 48–49, folios 36–37). His table of contents names him "شیخ داؤد جہنی وال شیر گڈھی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3), while the heading of the notice itself reads "شیخ داؤد چونی وال شیر گڈھی [OCR?]", the reading of that word uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48). Elsewhere the book calls him simply "شیخ داؤد کرمانی شیر گڈھی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 58, folio 46, حاشیہ 1) and "شیخ داؤد کرمانی شیر گڑھی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 293, folio 281).

Lahori traces his descent as a Kirmani sayyid. On the authority of the *Shajarat al-Anwar* he carries the line to Imam Musa Kazim: Sayyid Daud, son of Sayyid Fath Allah Kirmani, son of Sayyid Mubarak, son of a Sayyid whose name is printed as سید قمیص اللہ [OCR?], son of Safi al-Din Adam Kirmani, son of Sayyid Taqi al-Din Ahmad, and so on to Musa Mubarqa, son of Imam Musa Raza (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 48–49, folios 36–37). He then records a correction from another genealogy, which runs through Sayyid Muhammad Aaraji, son of Sayyid Musa Mubarqa, son of Imam Muhammad Taqi, son of Imam Ali Musa Raza, "کیونکہ سید مبرقع کوئی صاحبزادہ حضرت امام رضا کا نہ تھا", because Musa Mubarqa was no son of Imam Raza (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).

The family's coming to the Punjab is told, on the authority of Dara Shikoh's *Safinat al-Auliya*, as a story of two stages. His father, Sayyid Fath Allah, came first from Arabia to Hind and settled at Haibatpur Patti, and then moved to the *qasba* of Chunian, "قصبہ چونیاں". When the father died, Sayyid Daud was born four months after his death. He took a full share of the exoteric sciences from Maulana Ismail Lahori, and then turned to the inner sciences (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).

In Lahori's account he was famous among the Qadiri elders of the Punjab as a master of *hal* and *qal*, of *shariat* and *tariqat*. He was at worship from evening to morning and never slept the whole night, passing it now standing, now prostrate, now bowing, now seated. From the abundance of his austerity a special *nisbat* with Ghaus al-Azam arose in him, and by Ghaus al-Azam's inner permission he presented himself to Sayyid Hamid Ganj Bakhsh, reached completion, and took the *khirqa* of *khilafat* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48, folio 36). He was one of the two "کاملین خلفا", the perfect *khalifas*, of Sayyid Hamid Ganj Bakhsh, the other being Sayyid Sher Shah Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48, folio 36). Chishti's chain of Shah Bilawal likewise runs from Hazrat Daud Bandagi back through a Sayyid Hamid to Ghaus al-Azam (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 179).

Lahori gives his death in 982 AH, with two chronograms for it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37), set out under "In Verse" below. Sharib dates his death only relatively, in his account of the disciple: Shah Abul Muali came to Lahore "اپنے پیر دستگیر کے وصال کے بعد", after the passing of his pir, in a year printed as "1110ھ[OCR?]", a reading the printed text leaves in doubt (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 257, folio 253).

## His Disciples and Successors

The disciple through whom he is best remembered is Shah Abul Muali of Lahore. Lahori makes Abul Muali his nephew and *murid*, who spent thirty-two years with him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 57, folio 45), and in a note names the saint of Shergarh as Abul Muali's uncle, father-in-law and pir, and as the subject of Abul Muali's *Naghmat-e Daudi* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 58, folio 46, حاشیہ 1).

Sharib tells the story from the disciple's side. Abul Muali's father had already settled the family at Shergarh, "شیر گڑھ", and Abul Muali was born there (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 255, folio 251). He went "دہلی سے شیر گڑھ", from Delhi to Shergarh, and presented himself "حضرت شیخ داؤد کی خدمت میں", in the service of Hazrat Shaikh Daud (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252). "آپ حضرت شیخ داؤد کے مرید اور ممتاز خلیفہ ہیں": he was the *murid* and distinguished *khalifa* of Hazrat Shaikh Daud (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252). The condition of his training was that he live always with his pir: "ہمیشہ میرے پاس رہو، تاکہ تم کو وہ حاصل ہو، جو دوسری جگہ ساری عمر میں بھی حاصل نہ ہو" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252). In the same pages a *majzub*'s Persian names the master as "شیخ داؤدی" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252).

Chishti, in his account of Shah Abul Maali, calls the murshid at Sher Garh "حضرت شیخ داؤد[OCR?]", from whom the disciple set out, and says that at his halts on the road the disciple faced towards Sher Garh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 479–480).

A second line of succession runs through Shah Abu Ishaq. Kanhaiya Lal writes that "شاہ ابو اسحاق قادریہ سلسلہ مین خواجہ داؤد شیر گڑہ [OCR?] کہ بہی کا مرید و خلیفہ تہا", that Shah Abu Ishaq was, in the Qadiriya silsila, the *murid* and *khalifa* of Khwaja Daud of Sher Garh; the place-name is uncertain in the printed text, and the words between it and "کا" cannot be recovered (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 283, folio 286). Chishti gives the same link in the chain of Shah Bilawal: Shaikh Shams-ud-Din, then Shah Abu Ishaq, "وہ مریدِ حضرت داود[OCR?] بندگی[OCR?] کے جنکا مزار شیر گڑھ میں ہے", the disciple of Hazrat Daud Bandagi, whose mazar is at Shergarh, then Sayyid Hamid, and so back to Ghaus al-Azam (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 179).

## The Shrine

The shrine of Daud Bandagi Kirmani at Shergarh is a centre of pilgrimage kept by his successors, where devotees come to recite the Fatiha and seek the saint's blessing. The place takes its sacred identity from the darbar of the saint who made it a seat of the Qadiri order.

Lahori's "مزار گوہر بار", the pearl-scattering mazar at Sher Garh, is a place of pilgrimage for God's creatures (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37). Chishti speaks of "مقبرہ عالیشان حضرت داود بندگی[OCR?] کا", the lofty tomb of Hazrat Daud Bandagi, in a passage that also names the tombs of Shah Abul Maali and Pir Dastgir, and of "مزار شیر گڑھ[OCR?]"; the same passage names "مزار سید جلال الدین [illegible] کوٹھال[OCR?]" with a "سید رحمت اللہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 124). How these tombs stand to one another the passage, as it survives, does not make clear.

Khalid saw "the footprints of the saint engraved on a small marble platform" beside the grave (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

Sharib's account names Shergarh only as a place of residence, birth and initiation, never as the site of a shrine (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 255–256, folios 251–252). The sources consulted do not record who built the tomb, when, or what endowments it held.

## Devotion and Practice

The shrine maintains the customary devotions (prayer, qawwali, and the free kitchen), and its annual urs gathers the faithful of the region. Lahori, in the nineteenth century, records that every year a great crowd gathers at the mazar, though he gives the gathering no name and no date (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37). In our own day Khalid witnessed "the festivities at the annual festival of Daud Bandagi Kirmani" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated); the year of his visit is not stated.

Khalid's account dwells on a *malang* he watched there. "Halting at the threshold of the shrine, he said a silent prayer. He touched the base of the entrance and entered". His eyes were "smeared in kohl"; he wore "a vertical mark on his forehead", "a glass earring on his right ear", "thin black clothes" and "a thick bangle on his right ankle", with his head shaved and no facial hair (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). "Circling around the grave of the saint Daud Bandagi, the malang stopped at a spot where he kissed the footprints of the saint engraved on a small marble platform" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

Khalid's guide, the historian Iqbal Qaiser, explained that *malangs* "only drape a shawl when they are in public ... When they are with other malangs they wear nothing but a small lungi" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). Of the footprints he said: "If you go to Jain temples there are footmarks of their prominent priests which become objects of veneration. This is exactly like that", and "There has to be some sort of an inspiration from that particular Jain sect as well" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). Khalid himself asked "They are Nanghe sadhus, aren't they?", and wrote that the *malang* "looks like a Digamabar Jain monk" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

Leaving the town, Khalid met more ascetics: "Driving out of Shergarh towards Tibba Haji Deen, we drove past a small group of ascetics walking barefoot on the road". The eldest wore "a black shawl", "a green turban", and "a belt of bells ... around his waist" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated).

## Legends and Miracles

Sharib relates that the master read his disciple's state by *kashf* and consoled him with the words "معالی! امروز یا فردا ترا بجانب جناب مقدس معلی حاضری می کنم۔ منتظر ساعد[OCR?] و وقت باش" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252).

A note in Lahori's book, sourcing the family of Hujra, relates an anecdote from the *Maqamat-e Daudi* of عبدالباقی حجی [OCR?], a manuscript owned by Muhammad Iqbal Mujaddidi: during Hazrat Daud Kirmani's period of *i'tikaf* Hazrat Baha al-Din Hajrawi came to meet him, and because of the *i'tikaf* the meeting could not take place (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 47, folio 35, حاشیہ 4). The note names him only as Hazrat Daud Kirmani, with no place, date or order.

## In Verse

The sources consulted carry no verse of his own. What survives in verse is his death, in the two chronograms Lahori gives for the year 982 AH. The first is the phrase from which, he says, the date of the death appears:

پیر حق پرست

A chronogram on the saint's death, given by Lahori (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).

The second is the chronogram recorded in Abdul Haq's *Akhbar al-Akhyar*:

مشتاق منان

A second chronogram on the same death, which Lahori takes from the *Akhbar al-Akhyar* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).

His disciple Shah Abul Muali wrote of him in the *Naghmat-e Daudi* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 58, folio 46, حاشیہ 1); the sources consulted quote none of it.

## Setting

Lahori's history of the Qadiri order in the Punjab, which speaks of the order and the province and not of Shergarh, holds that of the Qadiri line "حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی اول پنجاب میں آئے", Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus of Uch was the first to come to the Punjab, coming by way of Khurasan to Multan and settling at Uch; the editor's note, not the author, gives the year of his entry into Uch as 887 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28).

Khalid places Shergarh "about an hour from Lahore", on the road to Tibba Haji Deen (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). Sharib, in his account of Shah Abul Muali, gives in a footnote a migration in stages across four generations that ends at this town: from Kirman to Hindustan in 796ھ, then to Uch, "اوچہ", then to a place printed as "داؤد جال[OCR?]" near Multan, then to one printed as "سنگھڑہ[OCR?]", and at last to Shergarh, the readings of both names uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 255, folio 251, حاشیہ 1).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His name.** The shrine's account calls him Daud Bandagi Kirmani, as do Khalid (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated) and, for "Bandagi", Chishti, whose reading of the word is uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 179). Lahori never prints "Bandagi" and calls him Shaikh Daud Kirmani of Shergarh (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 293, folio 281). Sharib never gives him "Bandagi" or "Kirmani" and calls him Hazrat Shaikh Daud (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252). Kanhaiya Lal calls him Khwaja Daud (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 283, folio 286).
- **His toponymic name.** Lahori's table of contents reads "جہنی وال" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3); the heading of his notice reads "چونی وال", its reading uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48). The same notice has his father move to "قصبہ چونیاں" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).
- **The year of his death.** The shrine's account gives 1575. Lahori gives 982 AH, with two chronograms (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37). Sharib dates it only as before Abul Muali's coming to Lahore in a year printed as "1110ھ[OCR?]", a reading the printed text leaves in doubt (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 257, folio 253).
- **His descent.** The *Shajarat al-Anwar*, as Lahori reports it, carries the line through Musa Mubarqa as a son of Imam Musa Raza; the other genealogy Lahori follows makes Musa Mubarqa a son of Imam Muhammad Taqi, "کیونکہ سید مبرقع کوئی صاحبزادہ حضرت امام رضا کا نہ تھا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 48–49, folios 36–37).
- **How the family reached the Punjab.** Lahori, after the *Safinat al-Auliya*, has his father come from Arabia to Hind, settle at Haibatpur Patti and move on to Chunian (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37). The footnote in Sharib's account of Shah Abul Muali has a migration from Kirman to Hindustan in 796ھ, by way of Uch and the Multan country, ending at Shergarh after four generations (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 255, folio 251, حاشیہ 1).
- **His title in the order.** Lahori and Sharib call him Shaikh (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 58, folio 46, حاشیہ 1; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 256, folio 252); Kanhaiya Lal calls him Khwaja (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 283, folio 286); Lahori's genealogy calls him Sayyid (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 48–49, folios 36–37).
- **The footprints.** Iqbal Qaiser likens the footprints at the grave to the venerated footmarks of Jain priests and looks for a Jain inspiration (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). No other source consulted mentions them.

## Legacy

Daud Bandagi Kirmani is remembered as one of the saints who firmly planted the Qadiri order in the sixteenth-century Punjab, a devout shaykh of the age of Akbar whose shrine at Shergarh has kept his memory for four and a half centuries. He belongs to the great generation of Punjabi Sufism, and his darbar remains a living centre of the devotion he inspired.

His memory was kept in writing early. The modern edition of Lahori's book lists, as item ۲۳ of its sources, "عبدالباقی حجی قادری : مقامات داؤدی (احوال شیخ داؤد کرمانی شیر گڑھی) ۱۰۵۶ھ مملوکہ محمد اقبال مجددی", an account of the saint dated 1056 AH and owned by the editor himself (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 293, folio 281). Lahori's notice names seven works on him: Abul Muali Shah Lahori's *Naghmat-e Daudi*; Abdul Baqi b. Jan Muhammad Haji Qadri's *Maqamat-e Daudi*, of 1056 AH, copied in 1201 AH, in a manuscript owned by Muhammad Iqbal Mujaddidi; Abdul Qadir Badayuni's *Muntakhab al-Tawarikh*, Nawal Kishore edition, at 287–291; Nizam al-Din Ahmad's *Tabaqat-e Akbari*, at ۱۱ [OCR?]; Abdul Haq's *Akhbar al-Akhyar*, at 193–195; Ghausi's *Azkar-e Abrar*, or *Gulzar-e Abrar*, at 207; and Dara Shikoh's *Safinat al-Auliya*, at 193 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 49, folio 37).

Through his disciples his name runs on in the chains of later masters: through Shah Abul Muali, who spent thirty-two years at his side (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 57, folio 45), and through Shah Abu Ishaq, Shaikh Shams-ud-Din and Shah Bilawal (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 179; Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 283, folio 286).

## Bibliography

- General established histories of the Qadiri order in the Punjab.
- Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Persian, composed 1292 AH / 1875 CE; read in an Urdu edition annotated by محمد اقبال مجددی and issued by تصوّف فاؤنڈیشن).
- Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* (dated 1867 for the original, the date unconfirmed).
- Kanhaiya Lal Hindi, *Tarikh-e Lahore* (1884 original).
- Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind* (تذکرہ اولیائے پاک و ہند, *Khum Khana-e Tasawwuf*; first edition October 1999, preface signed 4 April 1965 at Ajmer Sharif; Progressive Books, Lahore).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).

Name: Shiv Mandir Chiti Ghati
Location: Ghandian, Mansehra District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Events: Maha Shivratri (late winter)
Description:
## Overview

The Shiv Mandir at Chitti Gatti, some fifteen kilometres from the town of Mansehra in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is among the oldest surviving Hindu temples in Pakistan and one of the very few active shrines of *Shiva* in the country's north. Set in the green hills of the Hazara region, the temple enshrines an ancient *lingam* of Shiva that its devotees hold to be of immense antiquity, and it remains a place of living pilgrimage, drawing worshippers from across Pakistan and from abroad to its annual celebration of *Shivratri*.

## The Ancient Lingam

The temple's fame rests above all upon its *lingam*, the aniconic emblem of Shiva enshrined within. Tradition and popular report hold the stone to be some two to three thousand years old, and it is spoken of as the oldest such object of worship in Pakistan; according to legend the *lingam* emerged of its own accord from the ground in the remote past and has remained ever since. Archaeological opinion suggests that a place of Hindu worship existed on the site long before the present building, marking Chitti Gatti as a sacred spot of great age. Such claims of extreme antiquity are, of course, difficult to verify and are best received as the cherished belief of the shrine's community; what is not in doubt is that the site preserves a very old and deeply venerated focus of Shaiva devotion.

## The Temple of the Jammu Raja

The structure that stands today is of more recent date. It is generally attributed to a Raja of Jammu, who is said to have had the temple built in the 1830s as an act of devotion, raising a fitting shrine over the ancient *lingam*. In its architecture and setting the temple reflects the Hindu building traditions of the mountainous Hazara country, a region that before 1947 sustained a notable Hindu and Sikh presence; indeed a Sikh *gurdwara* associated with the Gurus also stands in the neighbourhood of Chitti Gatti, a reminder of the plural religious life of the area.

## Partition, Closure and Reopening

The temple's history in the twentieth century mirrors the fate of much of the region's Hindu heritage. In the turmoil of 1947–48 it was seized and sealed, and for some six decades thereafter it stood abandoned and inaccessible, closed to the community that had once gathered there. Only in recent years has it been partly restored and reopened for worship, allowing the ancient rites to resume at the shrine. The reopening has been welcomed as a significant moment for Pakistan's Hindu community and for the cause of protecting the country's non-Muslim places of worship.

## Legacy

The Shiv Mandir of Chitti Gatti holds a special place among the Hindu shrines of Pakistan: a temple of great reputed antiquity, restored to life after long silence, and once again the goal of pilgrims at *Shivratri*, which falls in the late winter. Its ancient *lingam* and its dramatic mountain setting make it a site of both religious and historical importance, a living link to the deep Hindu past of the Hazara hills and a symbol of the endurance of that heritage into the present.

## Bibliography

- *The Friday Times*, "Mansehra's Shiv temple".
- Wikipedia, "Mansehra Shiva Temple" and "Chitti Gatti" (with cited sources).
- Reports in *Dawn* and *The Express Tribune* on the reopening and restoration of the temple.
- Reema Abbasi, *Historic Temples in Pakistan: A Call to Conscience* (Niyogi Books).

Name: Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple, Karachi
Location: Near Clifton Beach / Jehangir Kothari Parade area, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Maha Shivratri (principal festival)
Description:
## Overview

The Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple is a historic cave shrine of *Shiva* near Clifton Beach in Karachi, celebrated as one of the oldest and most atmospheric Hindu sites in the city. Dedicated to Mahadev — the "Great God" Shiva — and said to be more than three centuries old, the temple is renowned for its subterranean setting beside the promenade known as the Jehangir Kothari Parade, and for the great gathering of pilgrims that it draws each year at the festival of *Shivratri*.

## A Cave by the Sea

In earlier times, according to the traditions of the shrine, the sea reached to the very walls of the temple, and the sanctuary was a cave set some thirty or forty feet into the water, with a spring of fresh water rising within it — a natural marvel of the kind that has long been held sacred in the Hindu imagination. The gradual retreat of the shoreline and the growth of the city have since left the cave inland, but the sense of a hidden, water-blessed sanctuary has remained central to its appeal. The adjoining Jehangir Kothari Parade, the seaside promenade built on land given to the city in 1919 by the Parsi philanthropist Jehangir Hormasji Kothari, today frames the approach to the temple.

## The Underground Temple

The shrine is described as an underground complex reached by staircases near the Kothari Parade, descending through several levels to the sanctuary below. Devotees speak of a marble courtyard on one of the lower floors and, on a level deeper still, of a tunnel said to lead towards the Mohatta Palace — a tradition of the sort common to old cave temples, and best regarded as an expression of devotional lore rather than of surveyed fact. Whatever the precise form of its chambers, the temple's descent into the earth, and its association with a subterranean spring, lend it an air of antiquity and mystery that few urban shrines can match.

## Shivratri and Devotional Life

The great occasion of the temple's year is *Shivratri*, the night sacred to Shiva, when many thousands of worshippers — by local reckoning as many as twenty-five thousand — throng to the shrine from across Karachi and beyond. On this and other festivals the underground sanctuary becomes the focus of the city's Shaiva devotion, with offerings, vigils and the chanting of the god's praises. Through the rest of the year it remains a quiet place of worship for the Hindu families of the Clifton neighbourhood.

## Preservation Struggles

The temple's survival has not been untroubled. In 2014, under a scheme to improve traffic at Clifton, the construction of underpasses and a flyover began near the shrine, and cracks appeared in the fabric of the cave. The Pakistan Hindu Panchayat brought the matter before the Supreme Court, which ordered the restoration of the temple — a further instance of the community's recourse to the law to protect its endangered heritage.

## Legacy

The Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple stands among the most evocative of Karachi's surviving Hindu monuments: a cave sanctuary of Shiva that has kept its sanctity through the transformation of a fishing coast into a great metropolis. For the city's Hindus it is a living centre of pilgrimage and festival; for the wider public it is a reminder of the deep and continuing presence of Hindu devotion in the fabric of Karachi.

## Bibliography

- *Dawn* and *The Express Tribune*, reports on the Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple and the 2014 Supreme Court order.
- Habib University Ethnography Lab, field documentation of the Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple.
- Wikipedia, "Shree Ratneshwar Mahadev Temple, Karachi" and "Jehangir Kothari Parade" (with cited sources).
- Reema Abbasi, *Historic Temples in Pakistan: A Call to Conscience* (Niyogi Books).

Name: Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir (Native Jetty Bridge)
Location: Under Native Jetty Bridge, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Ganesh Chaturthi; Holi; Raksha Bandhan; asthi visarjan rites
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir is a Hindu temple in Karachi remarkable for its situation: it stands beneath the Native Jetty Bridge, on the banks of the Chinna Creek, the only temple in the city set directly upon the tidal waters that open onto the Arabian Sea. Reputed to be some two hundred years old, it is dedicated to *Lakshmi* and *Narayan* — the goddess of fortune and the preserving god *Vishnu* — and it is among the oldest continually operating temples of Karachi, cherished above all for the seaside rites that its unique location makes possible.

Of the books consulted for this article, one appears to name the temple, and only in a single sentence. Michel Boivin's study of the Hindu Sufis of Sindh, discussing the deified hero Ramdeo Pir, writes: "In Karachi, for example, a painting of Ramdeo Pir stands in the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). He gives no address, no custodian, no date and no description beyond the painting, and the sentence is taken to refer to this temple only because it names a temple of Lakshmi-Narayan in Karachi; if Boivin meant another Karachi temple of that dedication, the passage is not about this one. No book names the Native Jetty Bridge or the Chinna Creek, describes the temple's rites by the water, or records its festivals or the court case that saved it. What the other books carry is set out below as it stands: what they say of the goddess Lakshmi, and, under Setting, what they say of Karachi and of the Hindus of Sindh. None of that is said of this temple.

## Lakshmi-Narayan and Worship by the Sea

The pairing of Lakshmi and Narayan is one of the most beloved in the Hindu tradition, expressing the union of prosperity and divine sustenance. At Karachi the temple's devotion has been shaped by its place at the water's edge. Overlooking the creek where it meets the sea, the shrine is a favoured site for those rituals that require flowing or tidal water — most importantly the immersion of the ashes of the dead, the *asthi visarjan* by which Hindus commit the remains of the departed to sacred waters. For a community far from the great river-*ghats* and coastal *tirthas* of India, the temple on the Chinna Creek has offered an irreplaceable link to the wider ritual geography of the faith. Within the sanctuary, alongside the principal images, devotees also honour *Hanuman* and *Sai Baba* of Shirdi.

## The Painting of Ramdeo Pir

The one detail of the temple's interior that a book records is a painting. Boivin mentions it as an example: "In Karachi, for example, a painting of Ramdeo Pir stands in the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). He spells the goddess's name Lakhshmi. He says nothing of where in the temple the painting hangs, how old it is, or who placed it there.

The sentence belongs to Boivin's account of the deified heroes whom the Hindus of Sindh shared with their Muslim neighbours. "In Sindh, the most popular deified heroes were Rama Pir (Ramdeo or Ramdev), Pithoro Pir, Pabuji and Guga Pir" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). On the same page as the Karachi painting he writes that Ramdeo Pir is "still known in Sindh as Rama Pir … In Sindh, he is today integrated into the temples dedicated to the pan-Indian divinities" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179); the painting in the Karachi temple of Lakshmi-Narayan is his instance of that. The case of Pithoro Pir, discussed on the same page, shows in his words "the variety of the negotiations between Sufism and Hinduism in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).

Boivin frames such figures within a wider pattern. "In Sindh, we already know that a number of sacred figures have a dual religious identity, Muslim and Hindu. The Muslim identity is always related to Sufism, while the Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174). He sorts the ways in which the Hindus of Sindh are related to Sufism into three: "the most common", a Sufi tomb "visited both by Muslims and Hindus"; the "also relatively common" saint with "a double identity, Muslim and Hindu"; and "a Sufi darbar … managed by the Hindus" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 177–178, folios 164–165). "The large majority of the Hindus used to pay a visit to the Sufi shrines, but does it mean they are Sufi? Of course not. It does mean that, for them, the Sufis are a part of their religious legacy" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 192–193, folios 179–180).

A painted image in a Hindu temple of Sindh has a further context in Boivin's notes. An endnote records that wall paintings of Krishna in Hindu temples "could mean there was a kind of Krishnaite revival in the nineteenth century among the Sindhi Hindus (Kalhoro 2014: 238–44)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 213, folio 200). None of this is said of the Karachi temple.

## Lakshmi in the Books

The books that name the goddess speak of her in other places, never of this temple, and none of them names her consort Narayan with her. Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* describes, on the wall of a Valmiki temple, "Laxmi, the spouse of Lord Vishnu", pictured "resting on a lotus flower" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 80, folio not stated). His *Walking with Nanak*, in a scene the author reconstructs, has Tripta visit "the Laxmi temple" in Talwindi at sunrise (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3). In Saidpur, the same book records, every shop kept idols, and "Laxmi" was the most popular (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 103, folio 85).

Boivin writes that "the Muslim Sufis of Sindh were mostly attracted by the Vishnuite school of Hinduism" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94). Among the Hindus themselves, "Krishna's worship had already developed in late-nineteenth-century Sindh among the Amils", and "the Vallabhachari sect was accepted by some members of the Amil community" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 135, folio 122). "A number of Sufis from nineteenth-century Sindh, such as Sachal, Qutub Ali Shah and Bedil, themselves include Krishna in their Sufi poetry … despite the fact that Sindh was Muslim dominated, the Krishnaite Bhakti was influential among wujudi Sufis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 198, folio 185).

## The Temple by the Creek

The temple's setting is at once its glory and its vulnerability. Tucked beneath the approaches of the Native Jetty Bridge, it looks out across the water, and the sea has long lapped close to its precincts. Its festivals mark the turning of the devotional year: *Ganesh Chaturthi*, the birthday of Ganesha, is celebrated here, together with the spring festival of *Holi* and *Raksha Bandhan*, the observance of the bond between brothers and sisters. On these days the modest shrine fills with the Hindu families of Karachi, for whom it is a place of gathering as much as of worship.

The books consulted record none of these festivals at this temple, and none describes its building, its priests or its rites by the water. The nearest they come to the worship of water in Sindh is Boivin's account of the province's Hindu trading castes: "Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups, two main cults were followed: the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth". The Daryapanth "is in all probability the oldest of the two. It is based on the deification of the Indus River", and it was served by "a priestly caste, the Thakurs" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). "In nineteenth-century Sindh, the Nanakpanth, or 'the path of Nanak', was probably the dominant religious path among the Hindu Sindhis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 90, folio 77). An endnote adds that "The Thakurs were the priests of Jhulelal. In Sindh, they were settled in different cities but they migrated to India from 1947 onwards" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 211, folio 198).

## Under Threat

The very features that make the temple precious have placed it in jeopardy. The development of the port and the construction that has crowded the shoreline near the site have threatened both its access to the seawater essential for its rituals and the integrity of the structure itself. In September 2012, after a petition brought by the local Hindu community, the Sindh High Court issued an order restraining the Karachi Port Trust from demolishing the temple. The episode drew wide attention to the fragility of the city's surviving Hindu heritage and to the community's determination to defend it.

The books do not mention the 2012 order, but they describe both the restoration of Hindu places in the province and the pressures on its Hindus. Jürgen Schaflechner, writing of Sindh, records that government funding for minority community places "is seen in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh within the past decade", and that "While in Sindh, I visited many temples that were renovated within the past decade, coinciding with changes in the political landscape" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 16, folio not stated). In his book Karachi is, among much else, a city of violence against Hindus (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 18, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "the Hindu population of Pakistan, including Sindh, is more and more under the threat of the radical Muslims of the country" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 127, folio 114), and Khalid that after the demolition of the Babri Mosque in December 1992 "Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 22, folio not stated).

## Setting

The books say a good deal about Karachi and about the Hindus of Sindh, and nothing about the Native Jetty Bridge or this temple. What follows is said of the city and the province.

**Temples of Karachi.** Haroon Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* describes a visit to the city's old temples; the book identifies none of them with this one. At Ram Bagh, he found, the area was now called Aram Bagh, the added letter, as he put it, neutralising its religious sense (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 222, folio not stated). The temple had a painted Krishna "with his maidens" under its roof and "a peacock guarding the entrance"; an old man told him "This temple is one hundred and fifty years old", and Khalid remarked that "Hundred and fifty seemed to be the standard age of all temples here". The temple was "much more elaborately decorated", and its community "much larger", than in Lahore (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 223, folio 197). An officer said: "I don't know exactly how old this temple is but it is old… existed before Partition" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 223–224, folios 197–198). Along with the temple at Clifton, Khalid concluded, it "must have been a historical Hindu temple" in Guru Nanak's time (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 224, folio 198), and he cites Iqbal Qaiser's identification of the Clifton temple as "the temple which Nanak had visited on his tour of Sindh" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 217, folio 191).

At a temple within the Port Grand complex he found "a newly constructed mosque for tourists" built right on top of it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 224, folio 198). He describes separate entrances for women and men, food being prepared, "probably… an offering from a rich Hindu", stairs leading into water "blackened by all the industrial waste", fishermen's boats, pigeons fed with rice, rooms "reserved for different deities", and a mural of "a male deity sitting [on] top of a giant fish", Jhule Lal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199). The book does not name the deity of that temple.

**The port city.** "At the time of Partition, Karachi was a minor port city", Khalid writes, which migrants from India made "the largest city of Pakistan"; the port itself was "a modest structure, a minor tower… A clock is placed within the tower", a symbol of "colonial rule" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200). Its Hindu fisherfolk "lived here before Kolachi became Karachi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199), and "these Hindu fisherfolk are now the only connection" between the city and the old village of Kolachi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200). A legend told to him explains the name: an old woman known as Mai Kolachi, whose son "was killed [by] a fish", "tore apart the fish and retrieved" him, and the place came to be known as Kolachi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199). In a collection of essays on Sufi devotion, the quay of "Karachi port" is where a disciple about to sail to Iraq saw his master's face in the water (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 154, folio 143).

**Hindu Karachi.** Khalid's *A White Trail* finds Karachi the supplier of Hindu worship elsewhere in Pakistan. Boys from Bahawalnagar "bought an idol of Durga from Karachi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 31, folio not stated); a vendor's idols "have been brought from Karachi, where there are still a reasonable number of Hindus living or from India through illegal channels", and Navratri pilgrims come "from as far as Karachi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 33, folio not stated). In Schaflechner's *Hinglaj Devi*, Karachi is the seat of the Nagnath and Jagnath *akhāṛās* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 127, 138, 159, 207, 292–294, folios not stated), the staging city for Indian pilgrims (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 175, 180, 181, 183, folios not stated), the home of the Devipujak-Vagri community (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 306–312, 322, folios not stated), and the start of the road to the goddess Hinglaj, "about 240 kilometers long" from Narayanpur (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 158, folio not stated). The city's growth swallowed the old pilgrim road: "The ongoing growth of Karachi and the corresponding urbanization of the areas where the early stops occurred caused all but a few of the resting places to completely disappear." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated).

**Colonial Karachi.** Boivin writes of "the growth of new emporium in Sindh, especially Karachi", after which the Lohanas invested in land and "became powerful landowners, locally known as zamindars, at the end of the nineteenth century" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 43–44, folios 30–31). Sir Charles Napier, "the conqueror and first governor of Sindh", built "a Masonic lodge in 1843 in Karachi", and "In Karachi, the Theosophical Society was founded in 1896" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 46, folio 33); its founders were "Dhunjishaw, Jamshed Nusserwanji and Dayaram Jethmal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 46, folio 33). "In Sindh, a printing press was brought to Karachi in the 1850s, but the main event in relation to Sufism came with the printing in 1866 of the Shah jo Risalo" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 47–48, folios 34–35).

**Partition.** Boivin estimates that "In 1941, the Hindus made up about 21 per cent of the total population of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48), and that "By early November of 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49). The Hindu Sindhis "started leaving Sindh especially after the Karachi riots in January 1948" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 66, folio not stated). The narrative of the Hindu Sufi Rochaldas, he writes, alludes to violence spread through Sindh that was "not perpetrated by the Muslim Sindhis, but by the Mohajirs who clearly wanted to take over the houses of the Hindus, at least in Karachi" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 70–71, folios 57–58). Schaflechner writes that "The departure of the Hindu elite and the influx of Muslim refugees (“Muhajirs”) from India dramatically altered the local demography" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 87, folio not stated). After 1947, Boivin records, "The darbars in Sindh were most of the time preserved with different arrangements regarding their management" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 68, folio 55).

**The Hindus of Sindh today.** Sindh, in Schaflechner's account, is "home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin writes: "Although a large majority of Hindus have migrated to India from 1947 onwards, Sindh is the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 176–177, folios not stated and 164). Khalid writes that by the census of 1998 "the Hindu minority is the largest minority in the country" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated), and that "The majority of the Hindu community is based in Sindh and Southern Punjab" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 233, folio not stated). Schaflechner notes that "many middle- and upper-class Hindus in Sindh are followers of the Nanak paṃth" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 257, folio not stated), and Boivin that the formula *Sab ka malik ek hai* "has for some years been very popular among the Hindus of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173).

**The older province.** Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian history, composed under Aurangzeb, describes the Mughal province of Thatta: its greatest river is the Sind, "بزرگ ترین دریائے سند است", by which merchants of Multan and Bhakkar ship their goods down to Thatta (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 529); its southern bound is "دریائے شور", the salt sea (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 529); and its life turns on boats, "اکثر مدار بر کشتی است", of which, small and great, there would be forty thousand (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 530). Its diet rests on rice, curds and fish (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 530).

**Sind in song.** Shemeem Burney Abbas records the singer Alan Faqir's words about the province: "It has been looted—it has been plundered—it has been assaulted—but it goes on—it has not died—it will not die—it has existed for centuries and it shall exist—Sindhri is beaten—and yet Sindhri goes on" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 156–157, folios not stated). "Sindhri", her note explains, is "A name used for Sind in the poetic traditions" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 210–211, folios not stated). Among the lines he recited:

*Punnu is not in the Kec / Sind is not the amir* (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 156, folio not stated)

Her notes explain that "'Sind is not the amir' means that Sind is not in the position of leadership or amirship", and that "These are all Alan Faqir's political interpretations of the female myths" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 210–211, folios not stated).

**Sufi Karachi.** Regula Burckhardt Qureshi counts the city, with Hyderabad in India, among "two important urban centres of Sufism", where members of the Qawwal Bachche lineage "actively maintain their special Qawwali heritage" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 33, folio 13). Robert Rozehnal writes that "In Karachi, the order's current teaching shaykh, Siraj 'Ali Muhammad, leads weekly halqa (communal zikr sessions) on Thursday evenings." (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 165, folio 157). Abbas records the Sidi congregation held in April "in Karachi at Manghopir" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 70–71, folios not stated), and Annemarie Schimmel the alligator miracle "(as happened in Mango Pir near Karachi)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 238, folio 207). Schimmel writes that the Hindu share in the Muslim orders is "more visible in Sind than in the Punjab": "Hindu writers wrote mystical poems in which they used the imagery of the Muslims; they composed poems in honor of the Prophet" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The goddess's name.** The site's account writes Laxmi Narayan and Lakshmi and Narayan. Boivin prints "the temple of Lakhshmi Narayan" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). Khalid writes "Laxmi" alone, without Narayan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 80, folio not stated; Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3).
- **How many Hindus live in Pakistan and Sindh.** Schaflechner puts Pakistan's Hindus at "between 6 and 10 million people—an estimate that varies widely according to the source", of whom "over 90 percent" belong to the underprivileged tribes and sub-castes (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "the Sindhi Hindus number several millions, with a majority of them belonging to the so-called scheduled castes" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 175, folio 162). Khalid gives no figure, but cites the census of 1998 for the Hindus as the country's largest minority (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated).
- **How many Hindus left Sindh at Partition.** Boivin reckons the Hindus of 1941 at "exactly 0.9 million", and the migrants at "closer to 0.8 million, if not less", while noting "a kind of consensus that they numbered around 1 million" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48).
- **Whether Sindh knew caste.** Schaflechner quotes Thakur that the "[c]aste system is almost absent in Sind", a perception he links to the Lohanas and to nationalist portrayals of Sindh as "a place of religious harmony and tolerance" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 277–278, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "Frequently, the claim arises that there was no caste system in Sindh", and that "Contrary to popular belief, there were many untouchables in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 36–37, folio not stated / folio 24; Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 40, folio 27).
- **Whether Sindh was a land without communal strife.** Verkaaik, as Schaflechner quotes him, writes that "both Sindhi Hindus and Muslims were influenced by mysticism and religious tolerance. This was the Sindhi essence that both Hindus and Muslims shared" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 89, folio not stated). Schaflechner himself calls the notion of "the harmonious coexistence of the religions" in Sindh "merely a nationalist utopian ideal" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 90–91, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "even if it never reached the level of violence in Punjab, it is irrelevant to claim there was no communal violence in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49).
- **The Lohanas' share of Sindh's Hindus.** Boivin writes that the Lohanas "represented half of the total Hindu population" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 40–41, folios 27–28). Schaflechner quotes McMurdo that "The Lowannas or Lohannas compose the great body of Hindus in Sindh", and Thakur that they form "the general body of the Sind Hindus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 79, folio not stated; Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 80, folio not stated).

## Legacy

The Shri Laxmi Narayan Mandir endures as a small but singular monument: a living temple that has kept its place on the Karachi waterfront through two centuries of change, and that continues to serve the ritual needs of a community whose presence in the city long predates the creation of Pakistan. Its survival, secured in part through the courts, stands as a testament to the resilience of Karachi's Hindus and to the enduring importance of the sea in their devotional life.

In the scholarship, the temple's one appearance is as a witness to the shared religious culture of Sindh: a painting of Ramdeo Pir, one of the deified heroes of Sindh, standing in a Karachi temple of Lakshmi-Narayan (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179).
