Name: Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir (Karachi)
Location: Soldier Bazaar, Karachi East, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Hanuman Jayanti; Holi; Diwali
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir, in the Soldier Bazaar quarter of Karachi, is one of the most remarkable and most ancient Hindu temples in Pakistan, famed for its extraordinary *panchmukhi* ("five-faced") image of the monkey-god *Hanuman*, which devotees hold to be *svayambhu*, self-manifested rather than made by human hands. Believed by tradition to be many centuries old, the temple was declared a protected site of national heritage under the Sindh Cultural Heritage (Preservation) Act of 1994, and it remains a busy centre of worship for Karachi's Hindu community.

None of the books consulted for this article describes the temple. None names Soldier Bazaar, and none speaks of the five-faced form of the god. Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail*, a book about Pakistan's religious minorities, speaks of "the monkey deity, Hanuman" but never names the Karachi temple (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated); Jürgen Schaflechner's study of the Hindu temple of Hinglaj Devi writes of Hanuman only on the pilgrimage road to that goddess, in another place altogether (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 279–280, folio not stated). What the books do carry is set out below as it stands: what they say of Hanuman himself, in prose and in verse, and, under Setting, what they say of Karachi and of the Hindus of Sindh. None of it is said of this temple.

## The Five-Faced Image

Hanuman, the devoted servant of Rama and one of the most beloved deities of popular Hinduism, is here venerated in his rare *Panchamukha* form, bearing five faces that in the classical iconography represent Hanuman himself together with *Narasimha* (the man-lion), *Garuda* (the eagle), *Varaha* (the boar), and *Hayagriva* (the horse-headed form), each face turned to a direction and each embodying a divine power. What sets the Karachi image apart, in the belief of its devotees, is that it is a "natural" statue: not carved by any sculptor but revealed from the earth, which the faithful hold to make it unique among shrines of Hanuman.

Pilgrims come to offer worship before it, and the temple is especially thronged at *Hanuman Jayanti*, the deity's birth anniversary, as well as at *Holi* and *Diwali*. The books consulted record none of these festivals at this temple, and none describes its image, its priests or its rites.

## Antiquity and Tradition

The temple's origins are wreathed in legend and great antiquity. Devotional tradition holds that *Rama* himself passed this way during his years of exile, and that long afterwards the image of Hanuman was uncovered at the spot, whereupon a shrine was built to house it. The site is popularly said to be at least fifteen hundred years old, with some accounts reaching back further still; such datings are traditional and cannot be verified, but they express the deep sense of sanctity and age that the temple carries for its worshippers.

The books consulted neither confirm nor dispute these traditions. None gives a date for the temple, names a founder, or tells the story of the image's uncovering.

## Rediscovery and Renewal

In modern times the temple has passed through periods of difficulty, including the loss of part of its land, but it has also seen renewal. A programme of renovation was undertaken in 2012, supported by donations from local Hindus. In 2019, during construction and restoration work, a number of further images and artefacts were unearthed, reported to include several statues of Hanuman together with other sacred figures, a discovery that drew the interest of archaeologists and museum authorities and renewed public attention to the temple's long history. These finds, and the temple's protected status, have strengthened its standing as a heritage site of national importance.

The renovation belongs to a wider pattern that Schaflechner observed in the province, though he does not name this temple. Government funding for the places of minority communities, he writes, "is seen in a wave of restorations of temples across Sindh within the past decade", and "While in Sindh, I visited many temples that were renovated within the past decade, coinciding with changes in the political landscape" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 16, folio not stated).

## Hanuman in the Books

The books that name Hanuman speak of the god, never of this temple, and most of them only in passing.

Christopher Shackle, in the glossary to his translation of Bulleh Shah, lists the god among the legendary figures of the poems, as "Hanuman (Skt.,P. Hanūvant)", giving the Sanskrit and the Punjabi forms of the name (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173). Michel Boivin's index enters him as 'Hanuman (god)' (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 243, folio 230). Haroon Khalid calls him "the monkey deity, Hanuman", and writes that he is "depicted as a mighty warrior, the Indian version of Hercules" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated).

Schaflechner names him as "Rama's close ally" in the stories of the pilgrimage to Hinglaj (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 119, 121, 122, folios not stated). Taufiq Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah speaks, beside the poet's references to the Kurus and Pandus of the Mahabharata (a word imperfectly printed in the book), of "the Rama-Sita story of the 'Ramayana' in which Ravana and Hanuman figure as two poles of mystical knowledge." (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 40, folio 20).

Images of the god appear in the books at other sites, none of them in Karachi. Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's Urdu *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, describing the *samadh* of Ranjit Singh, records 'طاقچہ جنوبی میں مورت ہنومان سنگ مرمر کی': in the southern niche, an image of Hanuman in marble (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 570). At Chandrat, the same book lists him among the pictures on the walls, beside 'گنیش', Ganesh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 792). Khalid's *A White Trail* describes him painted on the wall of a Valmiki temple, "carrying an entire mountain on his hand while flying back to Lanka" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 80, folio not stated).

Boivin records Ramakrishna's absorption "in other incarnations such as Hanuman, Sita and Krishna" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 104, folio 91). Annemarie Schimmel's *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* carries the god's name only in its index, as a single headword with one locator and no context (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 516, folio 485).

## Legends of Hanuman

The books tell two legends in which Hanuman makes water flow, neither set in Karachi and neither connected with this temple.

On the pilgrimage road to Hinglaj, Schaflechner records that "The Bahur River, for example, is said to have been created by Hanuman's attempt to get water for Sita." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 119, 121, 122, folios not stated). Further along the same road, a *paṛāv*, a halting place in the Hinglaj valley, is contested in its dedication, and pilgrims, he reports, "even put a small Hanuman statue there!" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 279–280, folio not stated).

Khalid's *A White Trail* gives a second legend in the words of an informant. According to Advit's aunt, the Ram Thamman pool "was first dug by the monkey deity, Hanuman": he "created this ancient pool, digging with a shovel only two and a half times" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated).

## Hanuman in Verse

The books carry Hanuman's name in the poetry of the Sufis, never in verse about this temple. The fullest line is Bulleh Shah's, in Christopher Shackle's English, where the poet recalls the epic of Rama:

*When Ravan the ten-headed abducted poor Sita, Hanuman burned Lanka. Ravan was completely humiliated, and finally you killed him* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 141, folio 116)

In Shackle's notes the god appears under both his Sanskrit and his Punjabi names, Hanuman and Hanūvant (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173).

Annemarie Schimmel's *As Through a Veil*, paraphrasing a Muslim poet's folk verse in which all categories collapse, sets Hanuman in a list of paired opposites: "finally Hallaj and his judge, Shams-i Tabriz and the molla, and Abu Hanifa and Hanuman are one and the same, and there is no longer Turk, Hindu, or Peshawari." (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 176, folio 158). The name stands there as one term in the list, not as the subject of the poem.

Michel Boivin counts Sachal and Qutub Ali Shah among the "Sufis from nineteenth-century Sindh" who brought Krishna into their poetry (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 198, folio 185), and they named Hanuman's circle as well: "In his poetry, Sachal mentions different Hindu gods, such as Ram, Hanuman", Sita and especially Krishna (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 106, folio 93), and "Sachal mentions Hanuman while Qutub Ali Shah gives the names of Laxman and Sita, Ram and Krishna" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 107, folio 94).

## Setting

The books say a good deal about Karachi and about the Hindus of Sindh, and nothing about Soldier Bazaar or this temple. What follows is said of the city and the province.

**Hindu Karachi.** Haroon Khalid's *Walking with Nanak* describes a visit to Karachi's old temples. At Ram Bagh, he found, the area was now called Aram Bagh, the added letter, as he put it, neutralising its religious sense (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 222, folio not stated). The temple there had a painted Krishna "with his maidens" under its roof and "a peacock guarding the entrance"; most of the quarters behind it held Hindu households, and the temple was "much more elaborately decorated" and its community "much larger" than in Lahore (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 223, folio 197). An old man told him "This temple is one hundred and fifty years old", and Khalid remarked that "Hundred and fifty seemed to be the standard age of all temples here" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 223, folio 197). An officer said: "I don't know exactly how old this temple is but it is old… existed before Partition" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 223–224, folios 197–198). Along with the temple at Clifton, Khalid concluded, it "must have been a historical Hindu temple" in Guru Nanak's time (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 224, folio 198), and he cites Iqbal Qaiser's identification of the Clifton temple as "the temple which Nanak had visited on his tour of Sindh" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 217, folio 191).

At the Port Grand temple he found "a newly constructed mosque for tourists" built on top of it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 224, folio 198), rooms "reserved for different deities", and a mural of "a male deity sitting [on] top of a giant fish", Jhule Lal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199). "At the time of Partition, Karachi was a minor port city", he writes, which migrants from India made "the largest city of Pakistan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200). Its Hindu fisherfolk "lived here before Kolachi became Karachi", and "these Hindu fisherfolk are now the only connection" between the city and the old village of Kolachi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199; *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200). A legend told to him explains the name: an old woman known as Mai Kolachi, whose son was killed by a fish, tore the fish apart and retrieved him, and the place came to be known as Kolachi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199).

Khalid's *A White Trail* finds Karachi the supplier of Hindu worship elsewhere in Pakistan. Boys from Bahawalnagar "bought an idol of Durga from Karachi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 31, folio not stated); a vendor's idols "have been brought from Karachi, where there are still a reasonable number of Hindus living or from India through illegal channels", and Navratri pilgrims come "from as far as Karachi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 33, folio not stated). Hinglaj lies "about two hundred and fifty kilometres from the coastal city of Karachi" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 32, folio not stated).

In Schaflechner's *Hinglaj Devi*, Karachi is a city of violence against Hindus (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 18, folio not stated), the seat of the Nagnath and Jagnath *akhāṛās* (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 127, 138, 159, 207, 292–294, folios not stated), the staging city for Indian pilgrims (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 175, 180, 181, 183, folios not stated), the home of the Devipujak-Vagri community (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 306–312, 322, folios not stated), and the start of the road to the goddess, "about 240 kilometers long" from Narayanpur (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 158, folio not stated). The city's spread swallowed the old pilgrim road: "The ongoing growth of Karachi and the corresponding urbanization of the areas where the early stops occurred caused all but a few of the resting places to completely disappear." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated).

**Colonial Karachi.** Michel Boivin writes of "the growth of new emporium in Sindh, especially Karachi", in the late nineteenth century (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 44, folio 31). Sir Charles Napier, "the conqueror and first governor of Sindh", built a Masonic lodge in Karachi in 1843, and "In Karachi, the Theosophical Society was founded in 1896" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 46, folio 33); "a printing press was brought to Karachi in the 1850s" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 48, folio 35).

**Partition.** Boivin estimates that in 1941 the Hindus "made up about 21 per cent of the total population of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48), and that "By early November of 1947, 246,000 Hindus had already left Sindh by sea, air or rail." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49). The Hindu Sindhis "started leaving Sindh especially after the Karachi riots in January 1948" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 66, folio not stated). The narrative of Rochaldas, he writes, alludes to violence spread through Sindh that was "not perpetrated by the Muslim Sindhis, but by the Mohajirs who clearly wanted to take over the houses of the Hindus, at least in Karachi" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 70–71, folios 57–58). Schaflechner likewise describes the departure of the Hindu elite and the influx of Muslim refugees from India as having dramatically altered the province's demography (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 87, folio not stated).

**The Hindus of Sindh today.** Sindh, in Schaflechner's account, is "home to the majority of Pakistan's Hindus" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "Sindh is the province of Pakistan with the most significant Hindu population" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 176–177, folios not stated and 164), and that Ramdeo Pir, known in Sindh as Rama Pir, is "today integrated into the temples dedicated to the pan-Indian divinities" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 192, folio 179). Khalid writes that by the census of 1998 "the Hindu minority is the largest minority in the country" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated), and that after the demolition of the Babri Mosque in December 1992 "Hindu communities in Sindh and Quetta were attacked" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 22, folio not stated).

**Hindus and the older Sindh.** Richard M. Eaton writes that in 711 Muslim navies "conquered and occupied the densely-populated Hindu—Buddhist society of Sind" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 30, folio 18). H. T. Sorley records, of the centuries after the mass conversions to Islam, "Hindus visiting Mussulman shrines and making votive offerings" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 175, folio 166), and observes that "Most of the musicians in Sind have been Hindus and not Mussulmans" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 231, folio 222). Shah Abdul Latif's stories, he argues, "are all Hindu in origin" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 269, folio 260). Christopher Shackle's notes to the *Risalo* describe the long sea voyages "undertaken by the Hindu traders of Sindh to locations like Aden, Gujarat, or Lanka" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 16, folio not stated), the custom of their wives of making offerings to the water deity for their husbands' safe return, and "The Hindu festival of lamps celebrated in the autumn, which marked the beginning of the trading season" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 324, folio not stated).

The *Risalo*'s best-known prayer is for the province itself. Shah Abdul Latif's rain-song, the Sarang, catalogues the places the rains reach, among them Umarkot, of which the verse says "Some have passed over Umarkot and have made the ground green", and closes, in Shackle's English, by asking God to make Sindh flourish forever:

*Dear friend and sweet beloved, make the whole world prosperous* (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 265, folio not stated)

Shackle's note calls that final invocation of God's blessings on Sindh "one of the most often quoted verses of the Risālo" (Shackle, *Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif*, p. 338, folio not stated).

**Sufi Karachi.** Several of the books speak of the city's Sufi life. Regula Burckhardt Qureshi counts it, with Hyderabad in India, among "two important urban centres of Sufism", where the Qawwal Bachche lineage keeps its heritage (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 33, folio 13). Robert Rozehnal describes the Chishti order's teaching shaykh, who "leads weekly halqa (communal zikr sessions) on Thursday evenings" in Karachi (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 165, folio 157); Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence record that the Chishti master Zauqi Shah "was therefore present at the first meeting of the Muslim League in Karachi in 1907" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 96, folio 82). Omar Kasmani writes that after the annual fair at Sehwan, fakirs "follow other fakirs and proceed to shrines in Karachi" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97). Shemeem Burney Abbas records a Sidi congregation at Manghopir (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 70–71, folios not stated), and Annemarie Schimmel the alligator miracle "(as happened in Mango Pir near Karachi)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 238, folio 207). Scott Kugle notes that Hajji Imdadullah went "from Karachi into exile in Mecca" after the uprising of 1857 (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 280, folio 259).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Hanuman's standing beside Rama.** The site's account calls him "the devoted servant of Rama". Schaflechner calls him "Rama's close ally" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 119, 121, 122, folios not stated). Khalid has him "depicted as a mighty warrior, the Indian version of Hercules" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated). Rafat's selection sets him with Ravana as "two poles of mystical knowledge" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 40, folio 20), and Schimmel's paraphrase of the mystical folk poets makes "Abu Hanifa and Hanuman" one and the same (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 176, folio 158).
- **The god's name.** The site's account and most of the books write Hanuman, and the site's account calls him the monkey-god; Khalid writes "the monkey deity, Hanuman" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 64, folio not stated); Shackle gives the Punjabi form Hanūvant beside the Sanskrit (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173).
- **How many Hindus live in Pakistan and Sindh.** Schaflechner puts Pakistan's Hindus at "between 6 and 10 million people—an estimate that varies widely according to the source", of whom "over 90 percent" belong to the underprivileged tribes and sub-castes (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 13, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "the Sindhi Hindus number several millions, with a majority of them belonging to the so-called scheduled castes" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 175, folio 162). Khalid gives no figure, but cites the census of 1998 for the Hindus as the country's largest minority (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 87, folio not stated).
- **How many Hindus left Sindh at Partition.** Boivin reckons the Hindus of 1941 at "exactly 0.9 million", and the migrants at "closer to 0.8 million, if not less", while noting "a kind of consensus that they numbered around 1 million" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 61, folio 48).
- **Whether Sindh was a land without communal strife.** Sorley finds in Sindh "a kind of rapprochement between the deeper mystical" ideas of Muslim and Hindu thought (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 225, folio 216). Schaflechner calls the common notion of "the harmonious coexistence of the religions" in Sindh "merely a nationalist utopian ideal" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 90–91, folio not stated). Boivin writes that "even if it never reached the level of violence in Punjab, it is irrelevant to claim there was no communal violence in Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 62, folio 49).

## Legacy

The Shri Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir occupies a singular place among the Hindu shrines of Pakistan: a temple whose central image is held to be self-born, whose traditions reach back to the age of the *Ramayana*, and whose soil has yielded up sacred figures buried for generations. For the Hindus of Karachi it is a cherished house of worship and a point of continuity with a distant past; for the wider heritage of the city it is a monument that binds legend, devotion, and archaeology into a single enduring landmark.

Name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Karachi
Location: M. A. Jinnah Road, Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: Janmashtami; Holi; Diwali
Description:
## Overview

The Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, rising behind its long frontage on M. A. Jinnah Road in the heart of Karachi, is the principal Hindu temple of Pakistan's largest city and the only surviving temple of the *Swaminarayan Sampradaya* — the devotional tradition founded in early nineteenth-century Gujarat — in the country. Spread across a walled compound of some thirty-two thousand square yards, it has for well over a century been both a place of worship and a refuge, and its story is woven into the history of Karachi itself.

## The Swaminarayan Tradition

The Swaminarayan movement takes its name from *Swaminarayan* (Sahajanand Swami, 1781–1830), the reformer and teacher who gathered a large following across Gujarat and Kutch and preached a disciplined, devotional Hinduism centred on the worship of Narayana, ethical conduct, and service. His followers spread with the trading networks of the Gujarati mercantile castes, and it was these communities — the *Lohana* and *Bhatia* merchants of Kutch and Kathiawar who had settled in the port of Karachi — who raised the temple to serve their spiritual needs. The temple is generally held to have been established around the middle of the nineteenth century, in the decades after Karachi passed under British rule and grew rapidly as a commercial port.

## The Temple and Its Life

Within its spacious precincts the mandir houses shrines to Swaminarayan and the deities of the tradition, together with halls, lodgings, and open courtyards that can accommodate large gatherings. It has long been the focal point of Hindu festival life in Karachi, most notably at *Janmashtami*, the celebration of Krishna's birth, and *Holi* and *Diwali*, when the compound fills with worshippers. The temple's ample grounds have also served secular and civic purposes over the years, hosting community functions and, at times, providing shelter in the crowded life of the city.

## Partition and the Refuge of 1947

The most poignant chapter in the temple's history came with the Partition of the subcontinent in 1947. As communal violence convulsed the region and hundreds of thousands of Hindus and Sikhs sought to leave the newly created Pakistan, the spacious compound of the Swaminarayan Mandir became a transit camp for refugees awaiting passage by ship from Karachi's port to India. Tradition records that *Muhammad Ali Jinnah*, the founder of Pakistan, visited the temple during this period and is said to have offered reassurance to those sheltering there. The episode is remembered as a moment when the great temple stood as a place of sanctuary amid the upheaval that reshaped the subcontinent.

## Legacy

Today the Shri Swaminarayan Mandir remains an active and well-attended temple, serving Karachi's Hindu minority and standing as one of the most visible symbols of the community's long presence in the city. Its survival — as the last Swaminarayan temple in Pakistan and one of the country's largest functioning Hindu shrines — makes it a landmark of both religious devotion and shared history, a reminder that the great port of Karachi has always been home to many faiths.

## Bibliography

- Williams, Raymond Brady. *An Introduction to Swaminarayan Hinduism*. Cambridge University Press.
- Markovits, Claude. *The Global World of Indian Merchants, 1750–1947*. Cambridge University Press.
- Government of Pakistan / Evacuee Trust Property Board records on functioning Hindu temples.
- Contemporary press reporting (Dawn, The Express Tribune) on Karachi's Hindu heritage and festivals.
- Studies of Partition migration through the port of Karachi.

Name: Shri Varun Dev Mandir
Location: Manora Island (Manora Beach), Karachi, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: None - derelict; conservation appeals ongoing
Description:
## Overview

On the low, wind-scoured island of *Manora*, guarding the mouth of Karachi harbour, stands the Shri Varun Dev Mandir — a temple dedicated to *Varuna*, the ancient Vedic lord of the waters and the sea. It is believed to be the only temple to Varuna in Pakistan, and its weathered stonework, set almost within reach of the waves, makes it one of the most atmospheric and least-known of the country's Hindu shrines. For the Hindus of Sindh, and especially for seafaring and mercantile communities, it has long been a place to honour the deity who rules the ocean on which their fortunes depended.

## Varuna, Lord of the Waters

In the oldest stratum of Hindu tradition, Varuna is among the most exalted of the gods — guardian of cosmic order (*rita*), sovereign of the celestial ocean, and in later devotion the presiding deity of the seas, rivers, and rain. In the religious life of coastal and riverine Sindh, reverence for the water-god blended with the veneration of *Jhulelal*, the beloved Sindhi Hindu deity likewise associated with the waters of the Indus, so that the temple at Manora belongs to a distinctly Sindhi tradition of devotion to the divine in its aquatic form.

## History and Antiquity

The precise age of the temple is uncertain, and tradition claims for it a very great antiquity, with some accounts holding the site sacred for many centuries. According to one local tradition, Manora Island was purchased in earlier times by a wealthy sailor — remembered as *Bhojomal Nenshi Bhatia* — whose family is said to have commissioned a temple upon it. The structure that survives today is generally dated to the early twentieth century, with records pointing to construction or major rebuilding around 1917–18 and further embellishment, including its tilework, in the years around 1937–40. It is prudent to treat the temple's more ancient origins as traditional rather than documented, while its present fabric belongs to the last century or so.

## Decline and Preservation

For many decades the temple stood neglected and exposed to the elements. The salt-laden sea winds of Manora have eaten into its masonry and eroded the fine carvings that once adorned its walls, and by the early twenty-first century it had fallen into a dilapidated condition. Its plight has drawn the attention of heritage advocates and of Hindu community organisations in Pakistan, and there have been calls and efforts to conserve and restore the shrine as an important relic of Sindh's religious and architectural heritage.

## Legacy

The Shri Varun Dev Mandir is a rare and poignant survival — a temple to the god of the ocean standing on an island at the edge of the sea, its stones slowly yielding to the salt air that is itself the element of the deity it honours. As the only known temple of Varuna in Pakistan, and as a monument to the maritime and mercantile Hindu communities of old Karachi and Sindh, it holds a singular place among the sacred sites of the country, and its preservation is a matter of concern to all who value that shared heritage.

## Bibliography

- Cousens, Henry. *The Antiquities of Sindh, with Historical Outline*. Archaeological Survey of India.
- Boivin, Michel. *Historical Dictionary of the Sufi Culture of Sindh* and related studies on Sindhi religion.
- Contemporary press reporting (Dawn, Youlin Magazine, The Express Tribune) on Manora and its temple.
- Studies of the cult of Jhulelal and water-veneration among Sindhi Hindus.
- Heritage documentation of Manora Island and Karachi's endangered monuments.

Name: Shrine at Odero Lal (Udero Lal Teerath Asthan)
Location: Odero Lal Village (near Tando Adam), Matiari District, Sindh, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Sheikh Tahir (also revered as Udero Lal/Jhulelal)
Events: Cheti Chand; shared Hindu and Muslim observance year-round
Description:
## Overview

The shrine at Odero Lal — also spelt Udero Lal — in the village of the same name near Tando Adam in Sindh, is among the most remarkable sacred places in Pakistan: a single sanctuary revered and used in common by both Hindus and Muslims, where a Hindu temple and a Muslim tomb stand together under one roof and are tended by caretakers of both faiths. To the Sindhi Hindus the saint of the shrine is *Jhulelal*, understood as an incarnation of *Varuna*, the ancient deity of the waters; to the Muslims he is a holy man whom they call *Sheikh Tahir*, or simply, in a name both communities honour, *Zinda Pir* — "the living saint." The shrine is one of the great living symbols of the shared religious culture of Sindh, and of the reverence, common to both traditions there, for the life-giving waters of the Indus.

Of the books consulted, Michel Boivin's *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia* is the one that describes the site itself. He calls it "the darbar of Udero Lal", "the main darbar devoted to Jhulelal" and "the huge sanctuary close to Hyderabad where Hindus and Muslims worship a dual figure: Jhulelal/Shaykh Tahir" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 184, folio 171), and he writes that "the main centre of the Daryapanth is in Udero Lal, the name given to the village which houses a vast sanctuary dating back to the seventeenth century" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). For him the darbar is the best example of a sacred place where "the saint has a double identity, Muslim and Hindu" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165). Boivin spells the Muslim saint's name Shaykh Tahir; this article keeps Sheikh Tahir except in quotation.

Annemarie Schimmel knows the figure but names no place for him. In *Pain and Grace* she calls him "Shaikh Tahir, called by the Hindus Lal Udero" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 28, folio 24), and in *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* her index sends the reader from "Tahir, Sheikh" to "Lal Udero" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 526, folio 495), so that both her books join the two names that the shrine joins; neither describes a shrine, a village or a festival. H. T. Sorley, writing of Sindh in the eighteenth century, uses the name Udero Lal only once, and then of a different saint at a different place: "the shrine of the Kalandar Shah Lal Baz (or Udero Lal) at Sehwan" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 168, folio 159). That identification is his alone; it is set out below among the points on which the sources disagree.

## The Legend of Jhulelal

The story that gives the shrine its meaning is set in a time of persecution. According to Sindhi Hindu tradition, a tyrannical ruler — remembered as *Mirkh Shah* of Thatta — commanded the Hindus of Sindh to abandon their faith and accept Islam. In their fear the Hindus gathered on the banks of the Indus and prayed to *Varuna*, the lord of the river, for deliverance; and the god answered that he would be born among them as a child, at *Nasarpur*, to save them. The saviour so promised is *Jhulelal*, whose birth the Sindhi Hindus still celebrate at *Cheti Chand*, the festival that marks the Sindhi new year and is kept as his birthday. In the devotion of Sindh, Jhulelal is the protector of his people and the spirit of the river itself, and Odero Lal is honoured as the centre of his cult.

Boivin gives the tradition in a shorter and somewhat different form: "According to tradition, Udero Lal emerged from the river to help the Hindus persecuted by a Muslim ruler in the mid-tenth century." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 42, folio 29). He does not name the ruler. Tradition also has an end for the story at the shrine itself: Jhulelal "is said to have disappeared in a well set up in the darbar of Udero Lal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173), and Boivin reads the presence of a well in another Sindhi shrine as "strongly reminiscent of Jhulelal" for that reason (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173).

## Jhulelal, Udero Lal and Sheikh Tahir

The figure of the shrine carries many names, and the books trace them in different ways. Boivin is cautious about the Hindu figure's origins: "Jhulelal was probably a modern figure of the Vedic god Varun, the god of the Indus River. He is briefly mentioned in historical sources" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41). He does not say which sources. Of the darbar he writes that "The Hindus worship Jhulelal, who they claim to be an avatar of the Vedic God Varun." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165), and in the colonial period he places "an attempt made to create a centralized path devoted to Jhulelal, then known as Amar Lal or Udero Lal, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41).

Omar Kasmani, citing Boivin, gathers the names of the river cult in a single note: "According to Boivin (2012b, 43), the Indus was worshipped under the name Udero Lal, depicted as an incarnation of Varuna, the Vedic deity of waters. Other references include Amar Lal, Darya Shah, Darya Nath, Zinda pir, Shaykh Tahir, and the Quranic figure (Khwaja) Khizr." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 185, folio 168, intro n. 37). He adds that "In most historical accounts, it is the figure of Udero Lal who is conflated with Khizr in Sindh" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 195, folio 178, ch. 5 n. 9).

The Muslim tradition of the site tells that the saint interred here was born a Hindu named Odero Lal and embraced Islam, becoming known as Sheikh Tahir; some identify the figure with *Khwaja Khizr*, the deathless guide associated in Islamic lore with the waters. Boivin records two further Muslim accounts. One gives the saint a Sufi lineage: "a Sufi genealogy has been built – if in an unknown period", in that "a tazkira refers to him as a disciple of the same Bahauddin Zakariyya already mentioned" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38); Boivin does not name the *tazkira*. The other concerns his order: "The Muslims venerate a Sufi, Shaykh Tahir, who could have been a Sohrawardi." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165). The hedge is Boivin's own.

Schimmel speaks of Sheikh Tahir as a mystic rather than as a god of the river. In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* she writes: "A strange fact—more visible in Sind than in the Punjab—is the way Hindus shared in the Muslim orders. Some saints were claimed by both communities, like Sheikh Tahir," whom the Hindus, she goes on, called Lal Udero (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387). "This sixteenth-century mystic was one of the most ardent defenders of the unity of being", she continues, and he saw God 'even in a camel' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387); her index, however, places him in the seventeenth century (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 520, folio 489). Her source for the identification is Mir ʿAli Shir Qaniʿ's *Tuhfat al-kiram*, in its Hyderabad (Sind) edition of 1957 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387). In *Pain and Grace* she makes him her named case of the shared saint: "The most famous case is that of Shaikh Tahir, called by the Hindus Lal Udero, who is venerated by members of both communities, and about whose ecstatic 'states' strange legends are told" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 28, folio 24). She does not tell the legends there.

## Legends and Miracles

Beside the Hindu legend of the river's deliverer, one story of Sheikh Tahir himself reaches the books, and it is the same story in both of Schimmel's: that he saw God in a camel. In *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* it is the measure of his devotion to the unity of being (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387). In *Pain and Grace*, at the far end of the book, she treats it with open irony: "when Shaikh Tahir saw God even in a camel behind which he started running we reach the border between the lofty and the ridiculous" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 251, folio 251). The judgement is Schimmel's, not the tradition's; her footnote there again names Qani‘'s *Tuhfat ul-kiram*, in a Sindhi translation, as the source (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 251, folio 251).

## The Sanctuary

Boivin dates the sanctuary to the seventeenth century and calls it "vast" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). He notes that "Although there are several temples dedicated to Udero Lal", the village of Udero Lal is the main centre of the cult (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30); the other temples are not named. He locates the darbar "about 50 kilometres north of Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41).

Of its fabric he records one fact, in a note on the domes of Sindhi temples: "the pre-partition temples devoted to Jhulelal in Sindh were built with a dome, as were some Sikh samadhis. The main site known as the darbar of Udero Lal hosts many domes (Boivin and Rajpal 2018)." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 210, folio 197, Ch. 2 n. 5). He does not count the domes. Within the darbar is the well into which Jhulelal is said to have disappeared (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173).

The plan of the sanctuary answers to its two communities. "In Udero Lal, for example, to which I shall return, the Hindus venerate Udero Lal in a chapel of the sanctuary, and the Muslims worship Shaykh Tahir in another chapel of the same sanctuary (Boivin and Rajpal 2018)." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38). Boivin's general description fits it: "although there is a single sanctuary, the Hindus worship the saint with a specific name and in a specific chapel, while the Muslims give him another name and worship him in another chapel" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 50–51, folios 37–38). Elsewhere he describes the type more fully: "It is a sacred place hosting one or two tombs and catafalques, and the saint has a double identity, Muslim and Hindu. The best example is the darbar of Udero Lal." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165).

## A Shared Sanctuary

A beloved legend accounts for the shrine's dual character: when Hindus and Muslims disputed over the saint, a voice is said to have come from the heavens commanding that the shrine be made acceptable to both — one part a temple, the other a *dargah* — for the saint belonged to all.

And so it remains. Within the complex, Hindus perform *puja* and *aarti* while Muslims offer their prayers at the tomb; an ever-burning lamp and the veneration of the nearby Indus are shared by both, and the custodianship of the shrine is divided between the two communities. Few places express so directly the interwoven devotional life of Sindh.

Boivin describes the division in its offices and its festival: "The annual fair is performed separately, and there is a gaddi nashin for the Hindus and a sajjada nashin for the Muslims." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165). He names neither incumbent. He also cautions against too easy a picture: "Such a scenario should not be idealized since the groups interact very little, and many disputes arise regularly." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165). The sharing, in his account, runs one way: "In this case, this is a shared space, but only the Hindus pay a visit to Shaykh Tahir's tomb. The Muslims do not go to the space devoted to Jhulelal." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165).

Boivin dates one fair: "In this darbar, during the annual fair in April of 2016, there was a huge poster staging Shah Abd al-Latif and Jhulelal, with the epigram: Sab ka malik ek hai." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173). He writes that the formula "has for some years been very popular among the Hindus of Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173). It was in the same month that he began "a new research project on the darbar of Udero Lal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 184, folio 171), and with a team "toured in Southern Sindh to map out the different shrines devoted to Jhulelal in Southern Sindh" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 184, folio 171).

## Devotion and Practice

In Boivin's account the darbar is the main centre of the Daryapanth, the river cult which he places among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups. "It is based on the deification of the Indus River. … The Daryapanth was managed by a priestly caste, the Thakurs. Most of the rituals were related to changes in the level of the Indus during a given year." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 42, folio 29). He judges that "The Daryapanth is in all probability the oldest of the two" cults, the other being the Nanakpanth (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 42, folio 29).

The Thakurs, he writes, were the priests of Jhulelal in general, not of this shrine alone: "The Thakurs were the priests of Jhulelal. In Sindh, they were settled in different cities but they migrated to India from 1947 onwards. Here, the Thakurs came from Sehwan Sharif." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 210, folio 197, Ch. 2 n. 6). He is careful over the name: "In Sindhi, the Rajut Thakur is written with a long 'a', while the Jhulelal Thakur is written with a short 'a'." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 217, folio 204, Ch. 7 n. 7). In Sehwan itself the Thakurs ran "Jhulelal's temple in the northwestern part of the town" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 71, folio 58).

In the colonial period the darbar was a meeting place for the Hindu community of Sindh. Boivin records "a meeting organized by several Hindu panchayats of Sindh at Udero Lal, in the main darbar devoted to Jhulelal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41), which he dates only to the last decade of the nineteenth century and sets beside the attempt to centralise the Daryapanth (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41). He gives neither its year nor its outcome.

Two devotional formulas of Jhulelal appear in Boivin's book: the inscription "Jhulelal bera par (May Jhulelal safely guide our nave)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 186, folio 173), and the devotional songs to Jhulelal called *panjro*, which fill "the last four pages" of a devotional book he examines (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 158, folio 145). That book "starts with Guru Nanak and Jhulelal, here named Darya Shah (and Zinda Pir in the caption of the image)" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 156, folio 143). Boivin also notes "a growing similarity between the iconography of Guru Nanak and Jhulelal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41).

## Setting

The books set the shrine's double devotion within a wider pattern in Sindh. Boivin sorts the ways the Hindus of Sindh are bound to Sufism into three kinds of site, each with its example: a Sufi tomb "visited both by Muslims and Hindus" (Bhit Shah), a saint with "a double identity, Muslim and Hindu" (Udero Lal), and "a Sufi darbar … managed by the Hindus" (Pithoro Pir) (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 177–178, folios 164–165). "In Sindh, we already know that a number of sacred figures have a dual religious identity, Muslim and Hindu. The Muslim identity is always related to Sufism, while the Hindu side usually belongs to the Nathpanth." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 187, folio 174). He recalls that "As Richard Burton noted as early as 1851, it is indeed the worship of the intercessors that constitutes the common religious idiom of Hindus and Muslims" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38). Among the Lohanas and related mercantile groups, he writes, "two main cults were followed: the Nanakpanth and the Daryapanth" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30).

Sorley, writing of the province in the eighteenth century, records the river's place in the common religion of Sindh. The cult of Khwajo Khizr was "linked up with the worship of the river Indus and supported by Muslim and Hindu alike", and Khizr is "called in Sind Zinda Pir" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 177, folio 168). Quoting Longworth Dames, he adds: "In Sind under the name of Khwajo Khizr this saint has always exercised a great power and has in popular superstition become somehow identified with the spirit of the waters and … with the deity of the river Indus", and "The Daryapanthis of Sind are believers in the sanctity of the River God or the God of Waters, and the belief affects Hindu and Muslim alike" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 301, folio 292). Sorley also notes, of the province at large, "Hindus visiting Mussulman shrines and making votive offerings" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 175, folio 166). Kasmani observes that "Offerings to the Indus River can still be documented in the wider region of Sindh" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 195, folio 178, ch. 5 n. 11).

The name Jhule Lal reaches beyond this shrine. Kasmani, whose book names no temple of the figure and describes no site outside Sehwan, writes that "Jhule Lal, the modern chant directed at the saint, was once a call to the river deity of the Indus worshipped by the Hindu Daryapanthis." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 36, folio 19), and that "in the figure of Lal, the Quranic river saint Khizr meets an Indic fish god." (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 162, folio 145). A pilgrim train carried the name: "special trains like the Jhule Lal Express" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 70, folio 53). Haroon Khalid describes a temple mural at Port Grand of "a male deity sitting [on] top of a giant fish", with water beneath, whom he names as "the famous Hindu deity also revered in certain Muslim traditions—Jhule Lal" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199); the temple he describes is not this shrine.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where Udero Lal is venerated.** The site's account and Boivin place the cult of Udero Lal at the village of that name; Boivin calls it "the main centre of the Daryapanth" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, pp. 42–43, folios 29–30). Sorley gives Udero Lal as another name for the Qalandar of Sehwan: "the shrine of the Kalandar Shah Lal Baz (or Udero Lal) at Sehwan" (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 168, folio 159), and his index repeats the equation (Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit*, p. 441). He describes no separate shrine of Udero Lal.
- **Where the shrine lies.** The site's account places it near Tando Adam; Boivin places it "about 50 kilometres north of Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41) and calls it "the huge sanctuary close to Hyderabad" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 184, folio 171).
- **The deliverance legend.** The site's account names the persecutor as Mirkh Shah of Thatta and has Varuna promise to be born as a child at Nasarpur. Boivin's tradition has Udero Lal emerge "from the river to help the Hindus persecuted by a Muslim ruler in the mid-tenth century", naming no ruler and no birthplace (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 42, folio 29).
- **Who the saint was.** In the site's Muslim tradition he was born a Hindu named Odero Lal who embraced Islam and became Sheikh Tahir, and some identify him with Khwaja Khizr. Boivin reports a *tazkira* making Udero Lal a disciple of Bahauddin Zakariyya (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 51, folio 38) and calls Shaykh Tahir a Sufi who "could have been a Sohrawardi" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165), while judging Jhulelal "probably a modern figure of the Vedic god Varun" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 54, folio 41). Kasmani, after Boivin, makes Udero Lal the name under which the Indus itself was worshipped (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 185, folio 168, intro n. 37). Schimmel calls Sheikh Tahir a mystic of the unity of being whom the Hindus called Lal Udero (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387).
- **When Sheikh Tahir lived.** Schimmel's text calls him a "sixteenth-century mystic" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387); her index places him in the seventeenth century (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 520, folio 489). Boivin's tradition sets Udero Lal's emergence from the river in the mid-tenth century (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 42, folio 29).
- **How far the sanctuary is shared.** The site's account has both communities venerating the lamp and the river together, the boundary between them dissolving in shared reverence. Boivin writes that only the Hindus visit Shaykh Tahir's tomb, that the Muslims do not go to the space devoted to Jhulelal, that the annual fair is performed separately, and that "the groups interact very little, and many disputes arise regularly" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 178, folio 165).
- **The camel story.** Schimmel gives the same anecdote two readings: in *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* it shows Sheikh Tahir as "one of the most ardent defenders of the unity of being" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 418, folio 387); in *Pain and Grace* it marks "the border between the lofty and the ridiculous" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 251, folio 251).

## Legacy

The shrine at Odero Lal has endured as a symbol of tolerance and common humanity, a place where the boundary between Hindu and Muslim dissolves in shared reverence for a single saint and a single sacred river. In a subcontinent whose modern history has too often been marked by communal division, Udero Lal stands as testimony to an older and more generous pattern of coexistence, and it continues to draw pilgrims of both faiths — Sindhi Hindus above all, for whom it is a spiritual homeland, and Muslims who honour the *Zinda Pir*. Its festivals, and especially the celebration of Cheti Chand, keep alive a devotion that has bound the peoples of Sindh together for centuries.

After Partition the cult of Jhulelal travelled with the Sindhi Hindus to India, and Boivin follows it there. Jhulelal became "the isht devta of the Hindu Sindhis of India" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 70, folio 57) and "the Sindhi god of India par excellence" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 174, folio 161); Boivin speaks of "the consecration of Jhulelal as isht devta, or community God, of the Hindu Sindhis of India" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 156, folio 143) and of "Jhulelal as the embodiment of the Sindhi culture in India" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 157, folio 144). Before Partition, he notes, "Jhulelal was already worshipped by some segments among the Hindus of Sindh, but as we saw before, they were in majority Nanakpanthis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 158, folio 145). The change had a cost: the turn to Jhulelal's worship "can be seen as a kind of soft hinduization of the Sindhi legacy in India" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 159, folio 146), and "With the spread of the Jhulelal's apotheosis, room for the Sufi legacy was reduced among the Hindu Sindhis" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 201, folio 188). In Ulhasnagar a temple of Jhulelal "had recently been built by Sehwani Thakurs" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 83, folio 70). Boivin's own work with Bhavna Rajpal traces the same path in its title, "From Udero Lal in Sindh to Ulhasnagar in Maharashtra: Partition and Memories across Borders in the Tradition of Jhulelal" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 233, folio 220).

## Bibliography

- "Shrine at Odero Lal," in reference encyclopaedias, for the dual Hindu-Muslim character of the site.
- Studies of the Jhulelal / Zinda Pir cult and Cheti Chand among Sindhi Hindus.
- Reporting in *Dawn* and *Daily Times* on Udero Lal as a site of interfaith harmony.
- Academic work on shared sacred spaces and river veneration in Sindh.
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, 2019).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Pain and Grace: A Study of Two Mystical Writers of Eighteenth-Century Muslim India* (1976; 1997 edition).
- H. T. Sorley, *Shah Abdul Latif of Bhit: His Poetry, Life and Times — A Study of Literary, Social and Economic Conditions in Eighteenth Century Sind* (Lahore / Karachi / Dacca: Pakistan Branch, Oxford University Press; first published 1940, reprinted 1966).
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).

Name: Shrine of Abdullah Shah Ghazi
Events: Annual urs; Thursday-evening qawwali and dhamal
Description:
## Overview

On a low hill in Clifton, overlooking the Arabian Sea in the heart of Karachi, stands the shrine of Hazrat Abdullah Shah Ghazi, the patron saint of the city, whose green-domed darbar is among the most visited and most beloved sacred places in Pakistan’s largest metropolis. Tradition places him in the eighth century and holds him to be a descendant of the Prophet through the line of Imam Hasan. For the people of Karachi he is the guardian of the city, believed to shield it from storm and calamity, and his shrine is a ceaseless resort of pilgrims of every kind.

The books consulted here say little about the saint himself. None of them gives his dates, his lineage or an account of his life, and none describes the building. What they record is the shrine in recent times: Haroon Khalid calls it "the most famous shrine in the city" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated), records the attack on it in 2010 (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated), and names it among the Sufi shrines of Pakistan that have come under attack (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252). Omar Kasmani's study of the fakirs of Sehwan quotes a woman who petitioned at "Abdullah Shah [a shrine in Karachi]", which may be this shrine; the book gives no "Ghazi" and no Clifton, and its words do not exclude another Karachi shrine of the same short name (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102).

## The Life of the Saint

The historical record of Abdullah Shah Ghazi is thin and wrapped in legend, but the tradition is strong and old. He is remembered as a Sayyid of the family of the Prophet, by the usual account a descendant of Imam Hasan, who came to Sindh in the early Islamic centuries: the eighth century, in the age when Islam was first spreading in the region through Muhammad bin Qasim and after. He came, the tradition holds, as a merchant, a warrior (*ghazi*) and a preacher.

He is said to have settled by the sea near what became Karachi, and to have died there, some traditions holding that he was martyred. His grave on the Clifton hill became a place of blessing, and over the centuries grew into the great shrine that now bears his name.

The books consulted here record no year of birth or death for him, no teacher and no Sufi order, and none of them tells the story of his coming to Sindh. Kasmani's book prints no "Ghazi", no Clifton, no dates, no order, no custodian and nothing about the fabric of the shrine (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102).

## The Patron Saint of Karachi

Abdullah Shah Ghazi is woven into the very identity of Karachi. It is widely believed that his presence protects the coastal city from cyclones and disaster, and that the sea has never brought ruin upon Karachi because the saint keeps watch over it from his hill. Khalid calls it "the most famous shrine in the city" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated).

## Devotion and Practice

His shrine draws an immense and continuous cross-section of the city, rich and poor, of every sect and background, who come to recite the Fatiha, tie vows, distribute food, and share in the qawwali and the *dhamal* that fill its evenings, above all on Thursdays and at the annual *ʿurs*. The books consulted here give no date for the *ʿurs*.

Kasmani quotes a woman, Zaheda, who may have brought her petitions here. Her family had moved to Karachi in the early 2000s, when her husband found work in the army, and it was there that she "got acquainted with the shrines of the Sindh region" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102). She tells of going from shrine to shrine without the answer she sought: "It may have been possible perhaps that someone else would give me something; that I would go to another shrine and he [that saint] would have given me something. I have wandered through numerous saints' places. I have also tried two or three times at Abdullah Shah [a shrine in Karachi]. I even broke down into tears" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102). The words in square brackets are the book's own. The book's words name only "Abdullah Shah" in Karachi; the link to this shrine rests on that name, and the book does not exclude another Karachi shrine called by it (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102).

Khalid recalls a news broadcast from "sometime ago", giving no date, in which "the anchor, a self-proclaimed vigilante, entered the shrine of Abdullah Shah Ghazi in Karachi ... and secretly filmed people consuming hashish", and then "began harassing the caretaker of the shrine for allowing such a practice" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Khalid found "the apologetic response of the caretaker" a disappointment: "under pressure, in front of the camera, the caretaker failed to explain the cultural context of the shrine and promised to monitor the situation better in the future" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). That is Khalid's own judgement of the episode; he gives neither the channel nor the caretaker's name.

## The Attack of 2010

Like other great shrines, it has been a target of violence: a suicide bombing struck it in 2010. Khalid gives the date and the toll: "On 6 October 2010 the shrine of Abdullah Shah Ghazi in Karachi was attacked killing eight people" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). In another book he names "Abdullah Shah Ghazi's in Karachi" among the Sufi shrines that have "come under attack" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).

The devotion of Karachi has never faltered, and the shrine, since rebuilt and expanded with its landmark green dome, remains thronged. The books consulted here do not describe the rebuilding or say who carried it out.

## Setting

The books' wider accounts of Karachi and of Sindh speak of the city and the province, not of this shrine, but they help to place it.

The current account of the saint sets his coming in the age of Muhammad bin Qasim. Rizvi dates that conquest, writing that "In 710 Muhammad bin Qasim al-Saqafi began his advance through Makran and Baluchistan with the conquest of Sind between 711 and 712" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India, vol. 1*, p. 127, folio 109). He adds that of the early Arab period "no such developments in Sind are recorded" as the spread of Sufism seen further north and west, and that "Early Arab conquerors settled their families in large numbers in the various towns of Sind" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India, vol. 1*, p. 127, folio 109). Shemeem Burney Abbas writes that "The Sufi mystical traditions came to the subcontinent of Pakistan and India through the Sind province", and that after Muhammad bin Qasim's conquest "a long line of Sufi mystics came to the region through Baluchistan, Mekran, Multan, and Sind itself" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 50, folio not stated).

Of the place itself, Khalid notes that "A large part of Clifton is constructed on reclaimed land" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 217, folio 191). He also gives a legend of the city's name, told to him by a companion: the area was "known as the area of [Mai] Kolachi", after an old woman "known as Mai Kolachi" whose son "was killed [by] a fish"; she "tore apart the fish and retrieved" him, and the city "came to be known as Kolachi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199). "At the time of Partition", he writes, "Karachi was a minor port city", and migrants from India made it "the largest city of Pakistan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200).

The devotions described in the current account have their context in the books' accounts of the city and the province. Regula Burckhardt Qureshi names Karachi as one of "two important urban centres of Sufism", with Hyderabad in India, "where members of the same Qawwal Bachche lineage actively maintain their special Qawwali heritage" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 33, folio 13). Abbas defines the *dhammal* as "The vigorous ritual dance performed at Sufi shrines in Panjab and Sind" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 180, folio not stated). Kasmani describes Karachi's shrines as a stage in the fakirs' round: after the three-day annual fair of Sehwan, fakirs "follow other fakirs and proceed to shrines in Karachi" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97). Of the Karachi shrines, the only one his book names is "Abdullah Shah" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The saint's name.** The site's account and Khalid call him Abdullah Shah Ghazi (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Kasmani's informant names only "Abdullah Shah [a shrine in Karachi]", with no "Ghazi" and no Clifton, and the book does not exclude another Karachi shrine of the same short name (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 119, folio 102).
- **The attack of 2010.** The site's account speaks of a suicide bombing in 2010 and gives no date or toll. Khalid writes that "On 6 October 2010 the shrine of Abdullah Shah Ghazi in Karachi was attacked killing eight people", and does not say how it was attacked (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

## Legacy

Abdullah Shah Ghazi is the spiritual guardian of Karachi: a saint of the earliest Islamic centuries whose shrine on the Clifton hill has become the sacred heart of a modern megacity of many millions. In him a coastal metropolis of migrants and strangers finds a common patron and a place of refuge, and his darbar remains one of the most vibrant centres of popular devotion in Pakistan.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- General established histories and traditions of Karachi's patron saint.
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India, vol. 1: Early Sufism and its History in India to 1600 AD* (1978; Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers Pvt. Ltd., New Delhi; the copyright line reads 1975).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series, published with the Center for Middle Eastern Studies, University of Texas at Austin).
- Regula Burckhardt Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan: Sound, Context and Meaning in Qawwali* (1986; 1995 edition).

Name: Shrine of Abul Faiz Qalander Ali Suharwardi
Events: Annual urs (11-12 Rabi al-Awwal); weekly Sunday milad; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

On the Multan Road at Hanjarwal, on the south-western edge of Lahore, stands the shrine of Hazrat Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Gilani Suhrawardi — a rare instance of a great Sufi shrine that belongs not to the distant past but to living memory. Abul Faiz Qalandar (died 1958) was at once a scholar, orator, author, and spiritual master: a distinguished pupil of the celebrated Ala Hazrat Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly, an heir to the Qadiri-Gilani and Suhrawardi orders, and the guide of thousands of disciples in twentieth-century Punjab. His darbar, kept by his own descendants beside the Jamia Masjid Suhrawardia, is a busy centre of devotion and learning, and it shows how the ancient traditions of Sufi Lahore continued to put out new life into the modern age. To understand the shrine is to follow the life of a man who joined the learning of the seminary to the ecstasy of the *qalandar*.

## The Life of the Saint

Abul Faiz Qalandar was born into a learned Gilani sayyid family of the Sialkot district in the last decades of the nineteenth century — by one careful account on Monday, 18 November 1885, at Kotli Loharan, and by another — the account kept by the shrine's own custodians — on 4 January 1895. Devotional tradition holds that his birth was foretold: a saint is said to have brought his grandfather, Jamal-ud-Din Gilani, the glad tidings that a grandson would be born in his house who should be named Abul Faiz Qalandar, and who would win great fame, serve the faith, and reach a lofty spiritual station — and so the grandfather named him. His father, Rasool Bakhsh Gilani, was himself a man of much learning, but the boy was able to keep him only some eight years before his father died; from him he had his first schooling, and thereafter he set out into the world of knowledge alone, often withdrawing for many days at a time into the wilderness.

In 1910 he came to Lahore, and for four years pursued the religious sciences at the Madrasa Shah Al-Maali. There, and in the years that followed, he mastered both the outward learning of the scholar and the inward knowledge of the mystic, until — in the phrase his devotees use — “his knowledge began to speak.” At the Jamia Shah Al-Maali he served as imam and preacher (khatib) and taught the memorisation and recitation of the Qur’an, and it was from this base of sober learning that he grew into one of the notable Sufi masters of his age. He died on 9 September 1958, and was buried at Hanjarwal, where his shrine now stands.

## Teachers and the Chain of Transmission

Abul Faiz Qalandar’s spiritual formation passed through the hands of several of the greatest figures of the age. He presented himself before Ala Hazrat Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly — the towering scholar of the Barelvi tradition — and, deeply impressed, took the oath of allegiance (bai‘at) at his hand, becoming counted among his special pupils; he would later write a commentary on the famous *Qasida Ghausiya*. He also received knowledge from Pir Mian Sher Muhammad of Sharaqpur, and drew great light from Hazrat Pir Meher Ali Shah of Golra Sharif. It was Meher Ali Shah, tradition says, who told him that his true portion lay in the Suhrawardi order, with Hazrat Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi, and bade him take allegiance there — which he did.

His lineage was thus doubly rich: his family descent as a Gilani sayyid is traced, through some twenty-three links, to Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad, and his Sufi allegiance, through some nineteen links, to Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar Suhrawardi, the great systematiser of the Suhrawardi way. Though he carried both the Gilani-Qadiri and the Suhrawardi inheritances, it was the Gilani-Suhrawardi path that he made his own. A cherished story tells that his master Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi once summoned him and said that his own murshid, Baba Jango Pir Shah Suhrawardi, had appeared to him in a dream, foretelling the coming of a young man who should be cared for, “for his manifestation will come about through my name.” Returning to Lahore, Abul Faiz kept his first spiritual retreat (chilla) at the shrine of Shaikh Hassan, known as Sohteli Suhrawardi; and when at last he met his master again, Ghulam Muhammad Suhrawardi told him, “You have made me happy; go, I am pleased with you.” To the end, Abul Faiz would say that whatever he was, he was fulfilling the word of Baba Jango Pir Suhrawardi — as though, he said, the saint were working within him.

## The Scholar and Author

Unusually among the qalandars, Abul Faiz was first and foremost a man of the pen. A recognised scholar of the Ahl-e-Sunnat tradition and a pupil of Ala Hazrat, he is listed among the notable disciples of Ahmad Raza Khan in the biographical compendia of the school, and he devoted much of his life to writing. His books — among them *Jamal-e-Rasool* (“The Beauty of the Messenger”), *Jamal-e-Ilahi* (“The Divine Beauty”), his commentary on the *Qasida Ghausiya*, and many other treatises, tracts, and poems — are steeped in the love of God and of the Prophet, and are still read with esteem. *Jamal-e-Rasool*, dedicated directly to the Prophet and composed in the memory of his own murshid, is a scholarly work saturated in *ishq-e-Rasool*, the passionate love of the Messenger that lay at the heart of his devotion, and he was known too for his devotional verse (naat) in the Prophet’s praise. In an age of religious controversy he wielded both the sermon and the book, and his learning was regarded by his followers as itself a kind of miracle.

## Teaching and Reform

Abul Faiz Qalandar is remembered above all as a reformer of souls — a master of *islah*, the correction of character — whose method was gentleness and example rather than censure. In a gathering, reproving those quick to condemn the faults of others, he is said to have taught: “Keep your own shirt clean and do not point at another’s dirty shirt; seeing your clean shirt, the man with the soiled one will mend himself of his own accord.” And again: “The time you would spend reforming others, spend it on reforming yourself.” He held that his knowledge was a trust to be spent in the service of others — “this is my duty, that I benefit people through what I know” — and his door was famously open: he used to say that whoever came to it never went away empty-handed, and that God does not turn away the prayer of one who comes to this threshold. It was for this union of learning, humility, and generosity that the great scholars of his day sought his company and, having met him, came to love him.

## Miracles

As with every saint, a body of miracle-stories (karamat) gathered about him, and they are still told at the shrine. Once, standing in the mosque as the rain began, he stretched his blessed hands out into it and, wetting them, remarked that he would be no true friend of God who could not number the drops that fall upon the earth. On a journey by train with his students, all the travellers stepped down at the end with their clothes soiled and their faces streaked with grime — all, that is, but the saint, whose face alone was clean; and when they asked how, he answered, “The dirt is subject to us; we are not subject to the dirt.” His students marvelled, too, that in writing his books he would cite other works of the scholars and the saints though those books were nowhere at hand; asked how this could be, he explained that when he began to write, all those books opened themselves before him. He was believed to know the outward and the inward alike, and to answer the need of those who came to him before ever they voiced it.

## A Life in a Changing Country

Abul Faiz Qalandar’s life ran through the last decades of British India and the birth of Pakistan, and he did not stand apart from the affairs of his people. He is remembered as having played a part in the politics of the age and in the Pakistan Movement, and, at the time of the First World War, as having roused a spirit of courage and steadfastness among the people. He belonged to that long line of Indian Sufis — reaching back to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, whose Suhrawardi order he inherited — who joined the inward path to an active concern for the community, and he laboured, as his followers put it, day and night for the faith through the middle of the twentieth century.

## The Suhrawardi Way

The order into which Abul Faiz Qalandar was ultimately drawn is one of the oldest and most influential in Islam. The Suhrawardiyya takes its name from Abu Najib al-Suhrawardi and, above all, from his nephew Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi of Baghdad, whose manual *‘Awarif al-Ma‘arif* became one of the classic guides of the Sufi path. In contrast to some of the more antinomian and ecstatic movements, the Suhrawardi way was known for its sobriety, its insistence on the outward law and on refined manners (*adab*), and its readiness to engage with rulers and society for the good of the community — a temper well suited to a scholar-saint. The order was carried into the Indian subcontinent in the thirteenth century, most famously by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, whose great shrine remains one of the anchors of Sufism in Pakistan, and it put down deep roots across the Punjab and Sindh. In taking allegiance in this line, Abul Faiz Qalandar joined a chain of transmission seven centuries deep — even as he bore, in his Gilani descent, the blood and the blessing of the Qadiri order of Abd al-Qadir Jilani. His life thus gathered up two of the great rivers of Islamic spirituality, the Qadiri and the Suhrawardi, and carried them into twentieth-century Lahore.

## The Shrine

Abul Faiz Qalandar died on 9 September 1958, and his resting place at Hanjarwal Mor, on the Multan Road in Lahore, was raised into a shrine that his family has tended ever since. It stands within a wider sacred ground — beside the Hanjarwal graveyard and the shrine of Baba Pir Hanjar Wali Sarkar, where other holy men of the region also lie. Around the tomb has grown a small religious complex that reflects the saint’s own character as a scholar-Sufi: the Jamia Masjid Suhrawardia, where the five daily prayers are offered in congregation, together with a Madrasa Suhrawardia and a library at which students still read. Buried alongside the saint are his four sons; of one of them, Ejaz Ahmad Gilani Suhrawardi, who had gone into the film world, it is remembered that his father, disowning that path in his lifetime, said he could do no more for him than pray for his hereafter — yet at his death he too was laid to rest here. The shrine is not a government-managed darbar but private property, held and maintained by the Gilani-Suhrawardi family.

## The Living Lineage

What most distinguishes this shrine is that the spiritual line it commemorates is unbroken and still living. After Abul Faiz Qalandar, the seat (gaddi) passed to his successor Miraj-ud-Din Gilani Suhrawardi, who guided and initiated many disciples and who is buried beside his master; after him to Rasool Shah Gilani Suhrawardi, likewise buried at the shrine; and it is now held by the latter’s son, Shahid Rasool Shah Gilani Suhrawardi, who oversees the darbar and continues to accept the allegiance of new disciples. Pilgrims come not only to honour a saint of the past but to enter a living chain of guidance — to take *bai‘at* at the hand of the present successor and to be counted, as tens of thousands before them have been, among the disciples of the Suhrawardi way as it has been kept at Hanjarwal.

## Devotion and Events

The shrine draws a steady daily stream of visitors — up to some two thousand on an ordinary day — who come to recite the Fatiha, to seek the saint’s intercession (waseela), and to lay their needs before God at a threshold famed for never sending anyone away empty. Every Sunday the darbar holds gatherings and *milad* assemblies in honour of the Prophet, well attended, at which disciples also present themselves to the living successor. The great occasion of the year is the annual urs, held on the 11th and 12th of Rabi-ul-Awwal, when the shrine fills with as many as two hundred thousand devotees for days of qawwali and *dhol*, *langar* (the free distribution of food), the ceremonial washing (*ghusl*) of the tomb and the changing of its cloth (*chadar*). The adjoining mosque, madrasa, and library mean that the life of the shrine is one of learning and prayer as much as of festival, in keeping with the character of the scholar-saint it honours.

## Legacy

Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Gilani Suhrawardi stands as a bridge between the classical world of the Punjabi Sufi orders and the modern age. In him the disciplined learning of Ala Hazrat’s school met the ecstatic freedom of the qalandar and the ordered devotion of the Suhrawardi silsila; he wrote and preached and reformed, and gathered thousands into a chain of guidance that his descendants carry still. His shrine at Hanjarwal — mosque, madrasa, library, and tomb together — is at once a place of pilgrimage, a seat of a living Sufi order, and a reminder that the sacred history of Lahore did not close with the great saints of the past but continued into the century just gone.

## Bibliography

- Sayyid Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Suhrawardi, *Jamal-e-Rasool* (Lahore: Oriental Publications) — the saint’s own devotional work in praise of the Prophet.
- Professor Dilawar Khan, *Talzeem-e-Ala Hazrat: Hazrat Abul Faiz kī ‘Ilmī Khidmāt kā Mutāla‘a* — a study of the saint’s scholarship as a pupil of Ahmad Raza Khan.
- *Darbar Abul Faiz Qalandari Gilani Soharwardi* — Urdu account of the shrine and lineage.
- Shrines Project field survey, Darbar Abul Faiz Qalandari responses (surveyor: Saifullah), 2026.
