## Disciples and Succession

Rizvi calls Nizamuddin Auliya "Baba Farid's most outstanding khalifa" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150), and dates his discipleship closely: "In 655/1257-58 Nizamu'd-Din left Delhi for Ajodhan"; "Nizamu'd-Din was immediately initiated and his head shaved"; he made three visits in all, and "In Jumada I 663/February 1265, the Shaikh made his third and final visit to the Baba" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156); "He received his khilafat-nama from Baba Farid on 13 Ramazan 663/29 June 1265" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Baba Farid "offered him a bed in the jama'at-khana" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156). Schimmel writes that "After his third visit to Pakpattan, he was appointed khalifa in Delhi", and that Nizamuddin was Farid's outstanding khalifa, "whom he met in 1257" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Bhandari writes that Nizamuddin "در بست سالگی بقصبه اجودهن رسیده از شیخ فرید الدین گنجشکر ارادت گرفت", and that having obtained "کلید گنجینه معنوی" he was given leave for Delhi to guide the people (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 556). Kugle: "Near the end of his life, Shaykh Farid al-Din delegated his authority to a young follower", Nizam al-Din; "Farid al-Din charged him to become the embodiment of love, through whom the comforting shade of divine mercy would pour forth in the capital city of Delhi, infusing all corners of the Islamic empire in India" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Regula Burckhardt Qureshi's study of qawwali calls Baba Farid, in her glossary, "spiritual guide of Nizamuddin Auliya" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 262, folio 242).

The training was severe. "The method by which Baba Farid trained Shaikh Nizamu'd-Din Auliya' to take up his position as successor in the order became engraved in the latter's memory" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157), and Baba Farid justified it: "the pir is the mashshata (hairdresser) of the murids (disciples)" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 176, folio 158). His parting words, in Rizvi: "'You will be a tree under whose shadow the people will find rest… you should strengthen your spirits by devotion…I have handed over all these things to you for at the time of my death you will not be present.'" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Lahori tells that after eating the cowpeas Nizam al-Din had bought by pawning his turban, he blessed the disciple's kitchen: "ہم نے خدا سے مانگا ہے کہ تیرے مہمان خانے میں ہر روز تہتر من نمک خرچ ہوا کرے" — seventy-three maunds of salt a day (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 95, folio 83 [marker 93]). Nizamuddin later found himself unable to abolish prostration before the pir, because of "the traditions followed by Shaikh Qutbu'd-Din Bakhtiyar Kaki and Shaikh Faridu'd-Din, who had both permitted prostration" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 239, folio 219). He drew up his own disciples' diplomas "according to a strict procedure that Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar employed" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 194, folio 182).

How the tokens of succession reached Nizamuddin is told several ways. Kugle: "Upon his death in 1265, Farid al-Din sent his staff, sandals, and other tokens of his authority to Nizam al-Din in Delhi" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Sharib: "آپ کی وفات کے بعد حضرت نظام الدین اولیاء اجودھن آئے تو آپ کے داماد حضرت بدر الدین اسحق نے آپ کی وصیت کے مطابق جامہ ان کو دیا" — when Nizam al-Din Auliya came to Ajodhan after his death, his son-in-law Badr al-Din Ishaq gave him the robe in accordance with his will (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). Ernst and Lawrence's translation tells that "When Nizam ad-Din was laid in his grave, they covered his body with the cloak that he had received from Farid ad-Din and they put under his blessed head the prayer mat of the Shaykh" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 176, folio 164).

His khalifas are counted differently. Rizvi: "Later authorities give a long list of the khalifas of Baba Farid, but Amir Khwurd lists only seven. According to Baba himself, the khalifas were chosen in three different ways. The most outstanding were those whom God inspired the Shaikh to select. These were the Rahmani khalifas. The second category were those personally chosen by the Shaikh because of their own merits. The third group consisted of those disciples whom the Shaikh accepted as successors on the recommendation of others" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150). Schimmel: "Fariduddin invested seven khalifas with spiritual power; among his disciples, Jamal Hanswi and Nizamuddin must be counted as his special friends" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Sharib: "بعض نے لکھا ہے کہ آپ کے خلفاء پچاس ہزار سے زیادہ تھے" — some have written that his khalifas numbered more than fifty thousand (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).

His deputies carried signed documents, countersealed at Hansi. Lahori: "حضرت فرید الدین گنج شکر کا یہ دستور تھا کہ جس خلیفہ کو کسی ملک کو روانہ کرتے۔ فرمان اپنے دستخط سے لکھ کر اس کو دیتے اور فرماتے کہ خواجہ جمال الدین ہانسویؒ کے پاس جا کر اس کی مہر کرا لو" — every khalifa sent to a country carried a *farman* over Farid's own signature, to be sealed by Khwaja Jamal al-Din Hansvi at Hansi before he set out (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]). Sharib, in a chapter that places Baba Farid at Ajodhan and citing *Siyar al-Auliya*, has the same rule: if Shaikh Jamal sealed the *khilafat-nama* it was reckoned "مستند", authentic, and if he did not, Baba Sahib would not accept it either, saying "پارہ کردۂ جمال را نتوانیم دوخت", what Jamal has torn we cannot stitch (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 84, folio 80). Rizvi explains the rule by a forgery threat: "The Baba took care that his khilafat-namas were quite accurate and not forged as a disciple whom he considered unworthy of receiving a khilafat-nama threatened the Baba that he would prepare a similar document and use it for enlisting his own disciples" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 166–167, folios 148–149); "Maulana Badru'd-Din Ishaq who prepared copies of the khilafat-nama was required to sign them, and they were later endorsed by the Baba's senior disciple, Shaikh Jamalu'd-Din, who lived at Hansi" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149). Badr al-Din Ishaq was also "the steward of his jama'at-khana" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 170, folio 152). Jamal al-Din had a copy of the *'Awarifu'l-Ma'arif* "from Baba Farid at the time of receiving his khilafat-nama", which passed down to his grandson through Nizamuddin (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 196, folio 178). In Jamal al-Din's house, Sharib relates, there was a *kaniz*, "وہ پاک دامن خاتون تھیں", whom Baba Farid addressed as "مادر مومناں"; asked "مادر مومناں! جمال ماچہ می کند", she said that since meeting Baba Sahib he had wholly abandoned village, means, estate and the occupation of preaching, girding himself to starvation and labour, and Baba Sahib, delighted, said "الحمدللہ' خوش می باشد" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 84–85, folios 80–81). To Jamal al-Din's minor son Burhan al-Din Sufi he "ان کو خرقہ خلافت' مصلا اور عصا عنایت فرمایا", gave the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, the *musalla* and the staff (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 85, folio 81). Bhandari records at Hansi the "مزار شیخ جمال الدین خلیفه شیخ فرید الدین گنجشکر" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 554).

Sabir is told of in conflicting ways. In Lahori, Ala al-Din Ali Ahmad was given the title Sabir for twelve years' service in the kitchen without eating an unpermitted morsel, "اور دہلی کا قطب بنا کر فرمان لکھ دیا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]); when Jamal al-Din tore up the first *farman*, Farid said "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواند دوخت", and later wrote Sabir a "فرمان تولیت", a *farman* of custodianship, for Kaliyar in his own hand (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 91, folio 79 [marker 89]). Sharib's chapter on Sabir, which places Baba Farid at Ajodhan, says that "حضرت بابا فرید الدین گنج شکر رحمۃ اللہ علیہ نے لنگر تقسیم کرنے کی خدمت آپ کے سپرد فرمائی", he entrusted Sabir with distributing the *langar*; that "آپ نے 12 سال کے عرصہ میں کچھ نہیں کھایا", over twelve years he ate nothing of it; and that when Baba Farid learned this he said "علاؤ الدین احمد صابر ہیں", and the title stuck (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Sabir had come to Ajodhan with his mother and lived with his *mamun*, his maternal uncle, Baba Farid (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Entrusted with the *wilayat* of Delhi, with the instruction to have his certificate sealed at Hansi first (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74), Sabir rode into Jamal al-Din's *khanqah* at Hansi still mounted on his palanquin (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 78–79, folios 74–75); Jamal al-Din "حضرت جمال الدین ہانسوی نے آپ کا خلافت نامہ پھاڑ دیا۔ خلافت نامہ پر مہر نہیں لگائی", tore the certificate up and did not seal it (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 79, folio 75); at Ajodhan Baba Farid said "پارہ کردہ جمال را فرید نتواں دوخت", and then "حضرت بابا صاحب نے آپ کو کلیر کی ولایت سپرد فرمائی' آپ کی مثال پر اپنے دستخط کئے اور اس مرتبہ آپ کو حضرت جمال الدین ہانسوی کے پاس جانے کی تاکید نہیں فرمائی" — he entrusted him with the *wilayat* of Kaliyar, signed the deed himself, and this time did not send him to Jamal al-Din (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 79–80, folios 75–76). Kugle tells it otherwise: Sabir's "ability to channel this force into performing miracles was so audacious that Shaykh Farid al-Din was wary of granting him leadership of the community and exposing the wider public to his spiritual heat. Instead, he sent the young Shaykh Sabir out to the wilderness" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). He calls Sabir "a follower and nephew of Shaykh Farid al-Din 'Ganj-i Shakar'" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 259, folio 238), and reports that Sabir's followers "regarded him as the true inheritor of Shaykh Farid al-Din's saintly authority and the only one of his followers to adhere closely to the saint's rigorous concentration on bodily control" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 261, folio 240). Rizvi writes that in later sources "the sufi whose khilafat-nama, Shaikh Jamalu'd-Din had torn was Sabir, and he was also depicted as the nephew of Baba Farid", and calls these stories legendary (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 172, folio 154). Ernst and Lawrence report that Shaykh 'Ali ibn Ahmad Sabir "is said to have been the Shaykh 'Ali Sabir who is briefly mentioned in Siyar al-awliya' as a disciple of Shaykh Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar. No less an authority than Shaykh 'Abd al-Haqq, however, questions the conflation of the two names and persons" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 74, folio 60).

Through these two the order divided. "The centuries-old division between the two branches stems from the time of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar, and it is his two disciples 'Ala' ad-Din 'Ali Sabir and Nizam ad-Din Awliya', after whom these two branches are named" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 131, folio 118); "Both the major sublineages of the Chishtis derive from him" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Kugle: "not all Chishtis were followers of Nizam al-Din, even if the majority were, for Nizam al-Din was not the only follower of the passionate and ascetic Shaykh Farid al-Din" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). In Qureshi's table of the Chishti hierarchy, Baba Farid stands below Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar-e-Kaki and above the pair Ala'uddin Sabir and Nizamuddin Auliya (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 101, folio 81); in the Chishti Sabiri *shajara* that Rozehnal prints, "19. Farid ad-Din Mas'ud Ganj-i Shakkar (d. 1265)" is followed by 'Ala ad-Din 'Ali Ahmad Sabir, "eponymous founder of the Chishti Sabiri order" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 15, folio 4). Ernst and Lawrence count him the third of "the five human pillars on whom the Indian extension of the Chishti order was built" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 80, folio 66), one of "the three Chishti giants, Farid ad-Din, Nizam ad-Din, and Nasir ad-Din, who complete the first cycle of the Chishtiyya" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 183, folio 171), and write that "Shaykh Farid was in the first generation of Indian-born masters of the Chishti order" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 111, folio 98).

Other disciples pass through the books. Shams al-Din Turk was told at his leave-taking "کہ پانی پت میں مستقل سکونت اختیار کریں' کیوں کہ پانی پت کی ولایت ان کے سپرد کی گئی ہے", to settle at Panipat because its *wilayat* had been entrusted to him; and Baba Farid declared his own *khilafat* insufficient for him, "حصول نعمت و کمال تو موقوف بر مرشد دیگر است", and sent him to Sabir at Kaliyar (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 92, folio 88). Sabir sent away the qawwal حسن قوال with a few gular figs, which he brought to Baba Sahib at Ajodhan; "حضرت بابا صاحب نے وہ گولر حاضرین کو تقسیم فرمائے", and whoever ate of them "اس کی کثافت دور ہوئی' اس کو نور باطن حاصل ہوا" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 82–83, folios 78–79). Lahori records that a grandson, Shaikh Ala al-Din, received the Hindu Sohan Majzub "اجودھنی پاک پٹنی" into Islam (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 236, folio 224), and that Shah Kaku Chishti of Lahore was "حضرت خواجہ فرید الدین گنج شکر کی اولاد سے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 99–100, folios 87–88 [markers 97–98]). Generations later, Burhan ad-Din Gharib asked of Nizam ad-Din "the gift of being under the direct spiritual observation (nazar) of Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 192, folio 180).

## Teaching and Poetry

Baba Farid’s teaching was the pure Chishti gospel of love: of God to be sought through humility, poverty (*faqr*), patient endurance, and above all a boundless compassion that returned kindness for cruelty. He is remembered for counselling his disciples to answer harshness with gentleness — to give those who bring thorns the softest of replies. What sets him apart in the history of the Punjab is that he expressed this vision not only in the Persian of the learned but in the language of the common people, and he is honoured as one of the earliest and greatest poets of Punjabi. His *shlokas* (couplets) have such authority that the Sikh Gurus included a body of them in the Guru Granth Sahib. Their tone is unmistakable — the ache of the soul for God, and the memory of death that makes the world small:

کاگا سب تن کھائیو، چُن چُن کھائیو ماس
دوے نیناں مت کھائیو، مینوں پِیا ملن دی آس

*"O crow, eat all my flesh, pick and eat it piece by piece — but do not eat these two eyes, for I still long to see my Beloved."*

فریدا جے تُوں عقل لطیف ہیں، کالے لِکھ نہ لیکھ
آپنڑے گریوان مہ سِر نیواں کر ویکھ

*"Farid, if you are of subtle wit, write not against another’s account; bow your head into your own collar, and look there instead."*

Rizvi gives the teaching in his own summary: "To Baba Farid, sufism was a strenuous exercise leading one to a pious life within the society in which one lived. It demanded humility, modesty, patience, fortitude and a cleansing of the heart from all conceit. Self-abnegation involved careful concern for any offence to another, and in the event of such a situation, sincere and copious apologies were demanded" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). "Five hundred aphorisms of Baba Farid were collected", and Rizvi prints sixty of those Amir Khwurd selected, which "give some insight into the Baba's broadly based, humanitarian teachings" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). Among them is a parable of renunciation: "The zakat of Sharia'a [OCR?] [Shari'a] was five dirhams out of 200, the zakat of Tariga [Tariqa] involved the payment of 195 dirhams out of 200 and the retention of only five dirhams and the zakat of Hagiqa [Haqiqa] entailed the payment of everything, while retaining nothing" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). "He encouraged education in his disciples and considered the 'ulama' to be nobler than the common people, though he disliked their self-satisfied indifference to others"; the *faqirs*, he asserted, were superior to the *'ulama'* "and occupied the same place among them as the full moon amongst a constellation of stars" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* quotes the saying in Arabic, "العلماء اشرف الناس والفقراء اشرف الاشراف والفقیر من العلماء کالبدر فی الکواکب", together with "الآفتہ فی التدبیر والسلامت فی التسلیم" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233). "Fasting was the first half of the way along the sufi path, said the Baba, and prayers and pilgrimages the other" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156).

Asked whether to give up study for prayer, he answered, in Rizvi's paraphrase, that the disciple should "continue both, as the two were necessary for the life of a dervish and he would then see which would emerge as the most dominant" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 174, folio 156); in Ernst and Lawrence's translation, "Do both till one predominates" — though they warn at once that "This anecdote is not found in Fawa'id al-fu'ad. It may or may not be true" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 87, folio 73). Sharib sets out his teachings at length: six kinds of *tauba*, of heart and tongue, eye, ear, hand, foot and *nafs*; that a dervish who seeks the eminence of this base world "درویش نہیں ہے' درویشوں کا نام بد نام کرنے والا ہے اور مرتد طریقت ہے' کیونکہ فقراء کو دنیا سے اعراض ہے", is no dervish but one who defames dervishes and an apostate from the *tariqa*; "محبت کے ساتھ سو مقام ہیں", love has a hundred stations, the first being patience under affliction from the Friend; that the *kulah* may not be worn until one guards the four worlds of eye, ear, tongue, and hand and foot; and four questions "چار چیزوں کے متعلق سات سو پیران طریقت سے پوچھا گیا' سب نے ایک سا جواب دیا", put to seven hundred pirs of the *tariqa*, all of whom answered alike — the wisest is he who abandons sins, the most alert he whom nothing troubles, the richest the contented, the neediest he who abandons contentment (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 64–65, folios 60–61). Among his sayings Sharib prints "تصوف مولیٰ کی صفا دوستی[OCR?] کا نام ہے" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 65, folio 61), and calls his teachings "آپ کی تعلیمات تصوف کا بیش بہا خزانہ ہیں", a priceless treasury of *tasawwuf* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 64, folio 60).

His prayers became remedies. Sharib gives *aurad* and *waza'if* in his name: Sura Baqara recited between the *sunnats* and *farz* of the dawn prayer for three days fulfils a purpose; Sura An'am recited seventy times fulfils a need; "لا الہ الا انت سبحانک انی کنت من الظالمین" frees one from grief and worry; and "حسب ذیل دعا اکثر پڑھنے سے معاش میں تنگی دور ہوتی ہے" — frequent recitation of the following prayer removes straitness in livelihood — "بسم اللّٰہ الرحمٰن یا دائم العز والملک والبقاء یا ذو الجلال و الجود والفضل والعطاء یا و دود ذو العرش المجید یا فعال ما یرید" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 66, folio 62). Ernst and Lawrence write that "Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar is the source of specific zikr formulas, including some in Indian languages" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 45, folio 31), and quote one, from Awrangabadi: "Say *wuhi hi* upwards, *hi hi* to the left side of the breast, *hin hi* toward the heart." These phrases, they add, "belong to a long tradition of adapting" hatha yoga mantras to Islamic themes and Sufi practices (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 47, folio 33). Nizamuddin traced his own amulet-writing to him, recalling "the fact that Shaikh Faridu'd-Din once gave me a pot of ink and ordered me to write amulets for the people" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 193, folio 175), and Farid had himself asked his master about amulets, receiving the answer that "the fulfilment of desires belonged to no-one; the amulets contained God's name and His words, and could be given to the people" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 154–155, folios 136–137).

He loved *sama'*. Sharib: "آپ کو سماع کا بہت شوق تھا", he was very fond of *sama'* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 62–63, folios 58–59), and his saying "سماع راحت دل ہے اور اہل محبت کو جنبش دینے والا ہے' جو بحر محبت میں شناوری کرتا ہے" — *sama'* is the heart's ease and sets the people of love in motion (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 65, folio 61). Asked about its lawfulness, "a topic disputed among the 'ulama", he replied, in Ernst and Lawrence's translation, "Praise be to God!" and then: "One group has been burnt to ashes, while the other is still arguing" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 170, folio 158). Ashraf Jahangir Simnani counted him among the Indian shaykhs who favoured music and "experienced empathetic ecstasy and danced" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 57, folio 43). Once, Rizvi writes, "the Baba wished to partake of sama' although no musician was present", and had the letters of Qazi Hamidu'd-Din Nagauri read to him instead, falling at once into an ecstatic swoon (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 216, folio 198). Usborne's annotator to Waris Shah writes that "The Chishtiyya sect of Sufis, which counts Fariduddin Shakarganj among its leaders, regards music (Sama) as a permissible means of experiencing spiritual exaltation" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 19, folio 18, note 1 to Ch. 12).

Whether he wrote books is disputed. Sharib calls "فوائد السالکین" his famous book, in which he collected his pir's *malfuzat*, and says of the *risalas* "موجود وجود", "گفتار" and "الٰہی نامہ" that they, in its words, "بھی آپ کی تصانیف بتائی جاتی ہیں", are also said to be his (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). Lahori's editor declares *Fawaid al-Salikin*, *Asrar al-Auliya* and *Rahat al-Qulub* — the first the malfuzat of Qutb al-Din Bakhtiar Kaki said to be compiled by Baba Sahib, the second compiled by Shaikh Badr al-Din Ishaq, the third by Khwaja Nizam al-Din Auliya — "یہ تمام مجموعے محض وضعی اور منسوب ہیں", all merely fabricated and falsely attributed (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]). Rizvi lists the same three among works "embroidered by anonymous authors who were bereft of either a feeling for history or a first-hand knowledge of the lives of their heroes" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 18, folio 4). Ernst and Lawrence translate Nizam ad-Din's testimony that neither Farid ad-Din nor Qutb ad-Din nor any Chishti saint before them wrote a book (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 178, folio 166), record that "Some of the sayings [malfuzat] of Shaykh Farid ad-Din Ganj-i Shakar have been recorded by Shaykh Nizam ad-Din Awliya in a letter" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157), and list two works only attributed to him, the *Ganj-i asrar* and the *Risala-i 'irfani* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 241, folio 231). Rizvi says Nizamuddin had tried to write down what he heard from Baba Farid and had found himself unable to write a word (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 19, folio 5).

Most of the books call him a poet, though in which tongues, and how surely, is argued. Sharib: "آپ شاعر بھی تھے", he was also a poet (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). Rizvi: "Baba Farid was himself a scholar and wrote excellent poetry in Arabic, Persian and the local Hindawi dialect. He recited the Qur'an perfectly, popularized the study of the" *'Awarifu'l-Ma'arif* and lectured on the *Lawa'ih* of Qazi Hamidu'd-Din Nagauri (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146). "Most of the Hindawi songs recited at sama' gatherings held during this period have been lost, but a few verses that have survived have been ascribed to Shaikh Hamidu'd-Din Nagauri and Baba Farid" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 349, folio 327); "The Siyaru'l-Auliya' quotes a verse composed by Baba Farid in the Multani dialect whose precise meaning is difficult to decipher" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328). Haroon Khalid writes that "Baba Farid is considered to be the first poet of the Punjabi language", who "wrote for the people in a language that they could understand" when the elite used Persian and Arabic, and who "first uses the symbolism of a wife being abandoned by her husband" for devotee and deity (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135); and, again, "Perhaps the greatest contribution of Baba Farid is not in religion but in literature. He is believed to be the first poet of Punjabi" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Rafat calls him "The 12th century poet Baba Farid, the first of the Punjabi language extant" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 47, folio 27), and writes that "Baba Farid's slokes are called kafis" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 49, folio 29). Dhillon quotes the judgement that "Farid laid the basis for a vernacular Punjabi literature" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 172, folio 188). Shemeem Burney Abbas reports that he "is said to be the creator of the kāfī form in which the human soul is treated as a female and contextualized in the imagery of the medieval institution of marriage" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 148, folio not stated). Schimmel is more careful: "In the Panjab, popular mystical poetry may have emerged as early as in the days of Fariduddin Shakarganj, the Chishti saint of Pakpattan" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 16, folio 12); "Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar of Pakpattan is credited with having used a kind of Old Panjabi for his mystical songs" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 415, folio 384); and "It is possible that Fariduddin composed a few lines of poetry in the local dialect, which would place him in the chain of those mystics who helped disseminate Sufi teachings in popular songs, thus influencing the population, particularly the women, who used to sing these simple verses while doing their daily work" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348).

Rizvi gives the sense of two of his *dohas*, preserved with a Persian rendering in Mir 'Abdu'l-Wahid Bilgarami's *Saba'-Sanabil*; both attack false initiation and outward asceticism (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328):

*You give a cap as a mark of initiation, and this indicates that you are presumptuous* (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328)

*You shave your head but what you should do is to cut lust from the heart* (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328)

Of the *shlokas* in the Guru Granth Sahib the sources tell different histories. Rafat writes that he "would have been without trace had not the Sikh saint Guru Nanak taken his slokes from a descendant of the poet two centuries later. Farid is a poet of the Granth and has survived with the sacred book of the Sikh religion" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 47, folio 27); and, in a note: "Guru Nanak (1469-1538) collected the great first poet's work from his heirs and wrote it down in his note-books", and "Guru Arjun (1553-1606) put together the first copy of the Holy Granth out of these notebooks and thus secured Baba Farid from obscurity. Today he is the most important poet of the Granth, with more slokes than any other selected poet" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). In Dhillon's retelling Nanak "spent many days there holding discussions with him", and "Later, he personally included 134 hymns composed by Baba Farid in the Adi Granth" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187). Khalid writes that the scribe of Sheikh Ibrahim, Farid's descendant, compiled "all the poems of Baba Farid" and handed them to Nanak, and that "It was through this channel that the poems of Baba Farid found their place in the Guru Granth Sahib" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 149, folio 131); in *A White Trail* he has Nanak go "to Pak Pattan, the city of Baba Fareed, to collect his poetry from his descendants", the poems later included in the Granth by Guru Arjan (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated). Abbas writes that "To this day some of Shaikh Fariduddin Ganj-e Shakar's" best Panjabi poetry is preserved in the Gurmukhi script in the sacred texts of Sikhism (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 49, folio not stated). Rizvi doubts the authorship itself: "Controversy surrounds more than a hundred" *slokas* ascribed to Baba Farid Ganj-i Shakar in the Guru Granth, compiled by the fifth Sikh Guru, Arjan, in 1604 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328); "Some scholars assert they were composed by Baba Farid himself but the language indicates they were the work of his successors who may have rewritten some of Baba Farid's original slokas into a more intelligible Multani. Some of these slokas are even ascribed to Kabir" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 350–351, folios 328–329); and his own conclusion is that "A careful analysis of Baba Farid's slokas in the Guru Granth would tend to suggest they were not composed by one individual. Therefore it is wrong to ascribe them either to Shaikh Ibrahim or another of Baba Farid's descendants, known as Farid Sani. They represent the teachings of Baba Farid through the years from his own time to the fifteenth century and were therefore composed by a number of different descendants, all using Farid as their nom de plume" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 351, folio 329).

His voice lives on in later poets. Rafat writes that "The tradition already existed in relation to Baba Farid and a number of Sikh gurus wrote poetry using 'Farida' as vocative" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220), and that "Bulleh Shah does not mention either Rumi or Baba Farid, classics in whose technical and intellectual traditions he was steeped. Two of his Kafis are exact quotations from their work" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 37, folio 17). He finds in Farid and Bulleh Shah the same confessional vein, "so pronounced in Baba Farid and Bulleh Shah" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 30, folio 10), and notes that East Punjab's Sikh scholars passed over Bulleh Shah "in favour of Baba Farid and Hashim Shah, both integrally related to their religion and politics" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 51, folio 31). Rozehnal heard his own Persian verse sung at the *'urs*: "The three hour evening sama' session was filled with ancient Hindi songs of Amir Khusrau and the Persian songs of Hazrat Baba Farid himself" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 232, folio 224). In a scene Khalid reconstructs, qawwals sing what he calls "Sheikh Farid's most popular qawwali" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 138, folio 120):

*I did not sleep with my love tonight / And every bit of my body aches* (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 138, folio 120)

## The Shrine

Baba Farid’s tomb at Pakpattan grew, over the centuries, into a great shrine that has been honoured by every power to rule the Punjab — sultans, Mughals, and later rulers alike — and it remains among the most visited darbars in Pakistan. Its custodianship passed to a line of hereditary keepers, the Diwans of Pakpattan, descended from the saint’s family.

The older Urdu and Persian books name the tomb in a line. Lahori: "روضہ منورہ بمقام پاک پٹن زیارت گاہ خلق ہے" — his illuminated *rauza* at Pak Pattan is a place of pilgrimage; a Persian chronogram follows, both of its couplets ending "فردے یگانہ فرید" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]). Sharib: "مزار پر انوار پاک پٹن میں فیوض و برکات کا سرچشمہ ہے" — his radiant mazar at Pak Pattan is a fountainhead of graces and blessings (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). Bhandari: "درشهر پتن عرف اجودهن سرکار دیپالپور خاور رویه ملتان خوابگاه شیخ فرید الدین گنجشکر", the tomb in the city of Patan alias Ajodhan, sarkar Dipalpur, east of Multan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*: "مزار پر انو[OCR?] حضرت کی پاک پٹن میں موجود ہے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233). Qureshi's table of the Chishti order gives him "d. 1266, Pakpattan" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 101, folio 81), and Usborne's annotator to Waris Shah writes that "Shakarganj is the saint of Pakpattan" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 57, folio 56) and that Baba Farid "honoured it by making it his home and his place of burial" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 2, folio 1). Ernst and Lawrence name the town of the tomb seven times, as "Ajodhan (modern Pakpattan)" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 105, folio 92) and as "Pakpattan/Ajodhan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 99, folio 86), but describe no building.

Eaton dates the complex from the death. "In 1265 Baba Farid died, and with his death began the career of the vast shrine complex based on his tomb, in time encompassing a mosque, a welfare kitchen", the *langar khana*, and a number of related buildings (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 218). When the saint came, Eaton writes, "a Jami mosque had already been established there", with a resident qadi and a Muslim governor at nearby Dipalpur (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 217), and the mosque, "now part of the shrine complex", by its large size "attests to the presence of a substantial Muslim population at that time" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 223). The grandest building is not the saint's own: "soon after 'Ala' ad-Din's death in 1335", the grandson's, "Sultan Muhammad commissioned two engineers to construct what proved to be one of the finest examples of Tughluq architecture in the subcontinent. It is also the most imposing structure in the entire shrine complex, dwarfing by far Baba Farid's own tomb" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 221); its date "comes from an inscription on the tomb itself—Safar, 737, which corresponds to Sept./Oct., A.D. 1336" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 221, n. 19). In his second essay Eaton describes the shrine itself as "a magnificent marble edifice constructed in the fourteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 239), and the colonial court at Montgomery as some 25 miles down a dusty road "from the hallowed marble domes of Pakpattan" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 257); he does not reconcile the two descriptions.

Nur Ahmad Chishti, who had himself been there — "عرصہ بیس[OCR?] سال کا گذرا[OCR?] کہ راقم الحروف بہی وہان حاضر ہوا تہا" — describes the building as "میانہ[OCR?] اوسط", lower than the ground of the town, with two doors (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233). One door, "اب سرور سی[OCR?] یہ دروازہ کہلاتا ہی", he explains by a dream of Nizam-ud-Din's in which the Prophet said "وَ مَنْ دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِنًا"; "لاکہہ در لاکہہ آدمی وہاں حاضر ہوتی میں", as the author saw for himself, and the crowd was kept in order by beating; devotees came from "تمام ملک ہندوستان و پنجاب وغیرہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 234).

Haroon Khalid's two books describe the shrine as he saw it. "The shrine of Baba Farid is located on the top of a mound that overlooks the entire city"; "The madrassah of Baba Farid was located on the mound where he is buried"; "It seems as if the entire city of Pakpattan has developed around this shrine. All roads lead here. The name of every other shop or business entity either includes Baba Farid or his title Ganj Shakar" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Stairs lead up to "an open courtyard with a new mosque on one side and the shrine of Baba Farid in front", with "a huge line of men" waiting; "This was a modest building". "Behind the shrine is a splendid structure rising several metres higher. This is where the progeny of Baba Farid is buried. The graves of his female family members are covered with purdah. Here too women are not allowed". "Facing the shrine is an ancient Karir tree", and "Behind the qawwals was the langar hall, offering free food to all" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). In *Walking with Nanak* the shrine is the highest point of the area; it was "an abandoned mound, probably carrying within it the secrets of an ancient city, when Farid moved here with his students. Now it is a shrine spread over a vast tract of land", and the shops on the approach are named after Baba Farid or "his title Shakarganj" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 154, folio not stated); "the shrine of Sheikh Farid at Pakpattan, one of the biggest centres of the Sufi Chistiyan school of thought in all of South Asia" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 143, folio 125). In his reconstruction of the town in Nanak's day the shrine "was in one corner" of a courtyard, beside a tomb "which contained the graves of the descendants of the saint" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 142, folio 124). Khalid reads the modest tomb and the grander building of the progeny as showing "the transition that occurred after the death of Baba Farid" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

Rozehnal describes "The regional shrine complex in the small pilgrimage town of Pakpattan—120 miles southwest of Lahore", which "has for centuries served as a central marker in the regional history of Punjab" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 35, folio 25); "Since the thirteenth century, the tomb of the saint, Baba Farid, has linked the local population to a wider universe of Islamic piety and Chishti Sufi spiritual hierarchy" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 35, folio 25). He names "the narrow stairwell at the extreme north end of the shrine, a passageway typically reserved for the Diwan and his personal guests" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, pp. 36–37, folios 26–27), "the northern gate" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 38, folio 28), "a large stage in the center of the courtyard" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, pp. 37–38, folios 27–28) and "the inner sanctum of the tomb" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 219, folio 211). "This is especially true at Pakpattan where thousands of pilgrims are pressed into an extremely cramped area. As a result, murids generally avoid lingering in the shrine for extended periods of time" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 217, folio 209). Books are sold "in the myriad bookstalls that flank the country's major Sufi shrines, most prominently in the narrow lanes surrounding the tomb complex of Baba Farid, the Chishti saint, in Pakpattan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 130, folio 121).

Around the shrine there grew a family of others. Eaton: "small memorial shrines to Baba Farid began appearing, scattered throughout the countryside of central Punjab", and "what is significant is that they were built not by the Tughluq sultans as were the main structures of the Ajudhan complex, but by the common people themselves" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 222). Amir Khurd, a contemporary of the grandson 'Ala' ad-Din, wrote that "in the countryside around Ajudhan, Dipalpur, and in the hills toward Kashmir, the people out of love and belief have built structures and tombs in the name of his shrine…and they go to these villages for alms and devotions" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 222, n. 25). The devotees saw the shrine as "occupying one in a network of sacred wilayats, or territories under the spiritual authority of one or another pir (saint), which dot all of North India", these shrines being "related to each other in terms of a ranked hierarchy, with the shrine of Baba Farid being the supreme shrine of the Punjab, to which others were subordinate" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 241–242); "this ranked hierarchy was ritually acted out according to an unwritten etiquette governing the attendance of shrine rituals by the sajjada-nishins of other shrines" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 242). One sajjada-nishin listed among its subordinates the shrines of Shaikh Jamal al-Din of Hansi, of Nizam al-Din Auliya' in Delhi, Piran Kaler, Golra Sharif, Taunsa Sharif, Uch Sharif, Kasur and Panipat, among others — a single witness's claim (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 241–242, n. 12). "Although one shrine located in the nearby town of Dipalpur had been given land by an earlier Diwan of Pakpattan and for this reason saw itself as subordinate to Baba Farid's shrine, most of the 'daughter' shrines of Baba Farid in the Punjab were founded by family descendants of Baba Farid, and hence they looked upon the shrine at Pakpattan as their spiritual superior" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 242, n. 13). Among such shrines in Pakpattan itself is that of Baba Farid's son-in-law, Badr al-Din Ishaq, which the Diwan visited at its own *'urs* (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 255).

The shrine has known violence and the hand of the state. "A couple of years prior to our visit there was a blast at the entrance of the shrine killing six people", Khalid writes; women were searched by female police officials; and of all such shrines he notes that photography was strictly prohibited, and that "Earlier these shrines would remain open throughout the night providing shelter to all, but now they are shut at midnight on the order of the government" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). He names "Baba Farid's at Pakpattan" among the Sufi shrines that have "come under attack" in "a wave of Islamic purism" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).
