## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his birth.** The site's account gives c. 1173. Lahori's text gives 583 AH; its editor rejects 582 AH, notes 569 AH from *Sair al-Auliya*, and chooses 571 AH from *Fawaid al-Fawad* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]). Sharib gives 575 AH, and 569 AH as what some have written (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52). Rizvi gives "569/1173-74 or 571/1175-76" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Rafat gives 1175 twice (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 25, folio not stated; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 29, folio not stated) and 1173 twice (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 30, folio 10; Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). Khalid gives 1173 CE (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132), and Dhillon 1173 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187).
- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives 1266, as do Qureshi (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 101, folio 81), Omar Kasmani (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17) and Dhillon (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187). Lahori gives 5 Muharram 664 AH, and his editor affirms it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]). Rizvi gives "5 Muharram 664/17 October 1265" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* gives "سنہ ۶۶۳[OCR?] ہجری" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 234). Bhandari gives Saturday 5 Muharram 667 AH, at Patan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526). Sharib gives 5 Muharram 670 AH, and 664 AH as what some have written (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58). Ernst and Lawrence print "d. 664/1265" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 159, folio 147), 1265 elsewhere (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 17, folio 2), and "5 Muharram 634 A.H." (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157). Eaton (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 218), Kugle (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239), Schimmel (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 8, folio 4; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346; Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 353, folio 335) and Rafat (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222) give 1265. Rozehnal gives 1265 in his text (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 29, folio not stated) and 1295 in his index (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 276, folio 270).
- **His age at death.** Ernst and Lawrence give 95 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 169, folio 157); Eaton ninety (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241); Lahori's editor cites *Fawaid al-Fawad* for 93 years (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]).
- **His century.** Qureshi calls him a "major thirteenth-century saint of the Chishti order in India" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 263, folio 243), and Rozehnal "his renowned thirteenth-century predecessor" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 175, folio 167); Rafat calls him "The 12th century poet" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 47, folio 27), and Khalid calls him a mystic "from the twelfth century" in one book (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated) and "a Muslim Saint from the twelfth century" in another (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated), while also writing that he settled at Ajodhan "in the thirteenth century" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The name of his birthplace.** The site's account gives Kothewal. Lahori's book prints کھوتوال (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]), کتہوال [OCR?] (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75), and کہتوال corrected to کوٹھے وال (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 345, folio 333). Sharib and Rizvi have Kahtwal (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139); Bhandari کهوتوال (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526); Khalid Tibba Haji Deen, formerly Kothewal (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 150, folio 132).
- **Who came from Kabul, and who was Qazi Shuaib.** The site's account says his grandfather came from Kabul. Lahori's author has his father, Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, come from Kabul to Lahore, his grandfather having been martyred (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 88, folio 76 [marker 86]); Lahori's editor has Qazi Shuaib come to Hindustan in 552 AH / 1157 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75 [marker 85]). Sharib makes Qazi Shuaib his grandfather and the qazi of Kahtwal (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52); Lahori's editor makes Jamal al-Din Sulaiman, after Qazi Shuaib's death, the qazi there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75); Rizvi makes Qazi Shu'aib his father and the qazi of Kahtwal (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139).
- **His father's name.** Lahori and Sharib give Jamal al-Din Sulaiman (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 86–87, folios 74–75 [markers 84–85]; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52); Bhandari prints "جلال الدین سلیمان" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527); Rizvi names the father Qazi Shu'aib (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139).
- **His mother's name, and who Bibi Sharifa was.** Lahori and Sharib name his mother Qursum Khatun (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 250, folio 238; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 56, folio 52), and Lahori's editor says her father is named by no contemporary writer (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 87, folio 75). In Thanvi's account as Ernst and Lawrence give it, his mother is Bibi Sharifa, of whom "Her son, Baba Farid" said that she would have been worthy of *khilafat* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122). Rizvi leaves his mother unnamed and makes Bibi Sharifa his daughter, of whom "Her father" said the same (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150); Sharib also lists a daughter بی بی شریفہ (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58).
- **His age, and the place, of his initiation.** Sharib has him come to Multan at fifteen (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54) and take *bai'at* in 590 AH, aged fifteen (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55); Rizvi has him settle in Multan at eighteen, reports Jamali's account of initiation at Multan, and thinks it "more likely" that he was initiated at Delhi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139). Bhandari has him meet the Khwaja at Multan and become his disciple at Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526).
- **Whether he followed his master to Delhi at once.** The site's account says that after meeting Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki at Multan he followed him to Delhi. Sharib says the Khwaja refused him leave to follow and ordered him to go on with his studies, that he went to Qandahar for five years, and that he came to Delhi in 595 AH (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 58–59, folios 54–55; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 58, folio 54; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 59, folio 55). Rizvi reports Jamali's account of a visit to Qandahar and thinks it "more likely" that he reached Delhi shortly after the Khwaja (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 157, folio 139); Bhandari has him go with the Khwaja to Delhi, and reports that some say he first studied at Qandahar and Sistan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526).
- **Who succeeded Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki.** The site's account says that on his master's death Farid became the head of the order, and Schimmel calls him Bakhtiyar Kaki's successor (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Rizvi says the relics implied he was the Khwaja's successor in Delhi, yet "His successor in Delhi was Shaikh Badru'd-Din, who came from Ghazna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 156, folio 138; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140).
- **Where he performed the inverted *chilla*.** Rizvi places it in a lonely mosque at Uch (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140), and Ernst and Lawrence's translation in the well of the Hajj mosque of Ucch (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156). Khalid reports the tradition that "he hung himself inside a well not far from the shrine" at Tibba Haji Deen, and a shrine official's denial: "Baba Farid did not hang inside the well, as it is believed" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 17, ch. 11, folio not stated). Schimmel says that he performed it (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Ernst and Lawrence, through Thanvi, that he "was reputed to have practiced" it (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 135, folio 122). The timing differs too: Rizvi has him suspended "for forty days and nights" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140); Ernst and Lawrence's translation has him suspended "every night" and pulled out at daybreak (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156); Kugle describes the practice as "remaining in an inverted state of contemplation from daybreak to sunset" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239).
- **How he came by the name Ganjshakar.** The site's account: a pebble or a morsel turned to sugar in his mouth during his fasts. Sharib gives two reasons, mud turned to sugar and a merchant's sugar turned to salt and back, and chooses neither (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 57, folio 53). Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140) and Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, pp. 377–378, folios 346–347) give the pebbles; Ernst and Lawrence the pebbles and the merchant (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156); Bhandari earth turned to sugar under his gaze (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 526); Khalid a myth that he was "extremely soft-spoken" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The renaming of Ajodhan and its meaning.** The site's account gives Pakpattan as "the Holy Ferry"; Eaton "('the holy ferry')", the name dating "by the sixteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228); Schimmel "the ferry of the pure", the name in use "ever since" his time (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); Khalid has the name changed after Baba Farid settled there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 141, folio 123).
- **Where Pakpattan lies.** The site's account puts it on the old bank of the Sutlej in southern Punjab, and Eaton halfway between Ferozepore and Bahawalpur (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 216–217); Dhillon calls Pak Pattan "a town near Sirhind" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187).
- **How long he lived at Ajodhan.** Eaton, citing *Siyar al-auliya'*, says "only sixteen or twenty-four years" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228, n. 43); Rizvi has him there "from about 1236 until his death" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140).
- **Who offered him villages.** Rizvi says Ulugh Khan offered a *farman* of four villages (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144); Sharib that Sultan Nasir al-Din, having visited him, sent a *farman* for villages whose number is uncertain in the printed text (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57). Rizvi also says that Ulugh Khan prevented Sultan Nasiru'd-Din from seeing him in 650/1252-53 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144).
- **The marriage to Balban's daughter.** Sharib states that Balban married his daughter to him, and names her first of four wives (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 61, folio 57); Rizvi calls the story "hardly historical as the Shaikh died before Ulugh Khan became Sultan Balban" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 162, folio 144).
- **His wives and children.** Sharib names four wives (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 61–62, folios 57–58); Rizvi says "two or three wives" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 167, folio 149). Rizvi and Sharib give five sons and three daughters, Sharib adding a further son, شیخ عبد اللہ; Schimmel says eight children survived (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 378, folio 347).
- **The tokens that passed to Nizamuddin.** Kugle: sent "Upon his death in 1265" to Delhi (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239). Rizvi: handed over in his lifetime, "for at the time of my death you will not be present" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 175, folio 157). Sharib: the robe given at Ajodhan after his death by his son-in-law, under his will (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).
- **The number of his khalifas.** Seven according to Amir Khwurd, as Rizvi reports (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 168, folio 150), and to Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348); more than fifty thousand according to what "some have written", as Sharib reports (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 62, folio 58).
- **Sabir.** Lahori says Farid made him *qutb* of Delhi and later gave him a *farman* for Kaliyar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 90, folio 78 [marker 88]; Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 91, folio 79 [marker 89]), and Sharib that he gave him the *wilayat* of Kaliyar, and makes Baba Farid his maternal uncle (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 79–80, folios 75–76; Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 78, folio 74). Kugle says Farid was wary of granting him leadership and sent him to the wilderness, and calls him a nephew (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 260, folio 239; Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 259, folio 238). Rizvi calls the torn certificate and the nephew stories legendary (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 172, folio 154), and Ernst and Lawrence report Shaykh 'Abd al-Haqq's doubt that Sabir is the disciple named in *Siyar al-awliya'* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 74, folio 60).
- **His writings.** Sharib calls *Fawaid al-Salikin* his famous book and lists three *risalas* said to be his (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 63, folio 59). Lahori's editor (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 89, folio 77 [marker 87]) and Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 18, folio 4) call *Fawaid al-Salikin*, *Asrar al-Auliya* and *Rahat al-Qulub* spurious; Ernst and Lawrence give Nizam ad-Din's testimony that he wrote no book and list two works only attributed to him (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 178, folio 166; Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 241, folio 231).
- **Whether he composed in Punjabi.** The site's account calls him one of the earliest and greatest poets of Punjabi, and Khalid "the first poet of the Punjabi language" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135). Schimmel writes that "It is possible that Fariduddin composed a few lines of poetry in the local dialect" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 379, folio 348). Rizvi credits him with poetry in Arabic, Persian and Hindawi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 164, folio 146).
- **The *shlokas* in the Guru Granth Sahib.** The site's account calls them his, and Rafat calls him "the most important poet of the Granth" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). Rizvi concludes that they "were not composed by one individual" but by "a number of different descendants, all using Farid as their nom de plume" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 351, folio 329). Rafat (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222), Khalid (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated) and Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328) have Guru Arjan compile them into the Granth, Rizvi in 1604; Dhillon has Guru Nanak "personally" include "134 hymns composed by Baba Farid in the Adi Granth" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 171, folio 187). Rizvi counts "more than a hundred" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 350, folio 328).
- **The building and the ground.** Nur Ahmad Chishti describes the tomb as lower than the ground of the town (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 233); Khalid as "located on the top of a mound that overlooks the entire city" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated) and as the highest point of the area (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 154, folio not stated).
- **Which building is the great one.** Eaton calls the grandson 'Ala' ad-Din's tomb "the most imposing structure in the entire shrine complex, dwarfing by far Baba Farid's own tomb" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 221), and elsewhere calls the shrine itself "a magnificent marble edifice constructed in the fourteenth century" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 239). Khalid calls the saint's shrine "a modest building" and the burial place of his progeny behind it "a splendid structure" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **Whether every power honoured the shrine.** The site's account says the shrine has been honoured by every power to rule the Punjab. Eaton writes that the Khalji sultans "do not seem to have been interested in the shrine" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 220), and that in 1810 its holdings "were seized by Ranjit Singh" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 231); of the saint himself Eaton writes that he "assiduously avoided contact with the mundane world of the court and its ministers" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 219).
- **The name of the Gate.** The site's account calls it the *Bahishti Darwaza*, a silver-plated door. Eaton calls it "the southern door (shisha darwaza)" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 219, n. 11), the "Gate of Paradise" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 236) and the "Bahishti Gate" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 254); Rozehnal "the narrow Gate of Heaven (bihishti darwaza)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 36, folio 26). The *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* gives the door a name of its own, "اب سرور سی[OCR?] یہ دروازہ کہلاتا ہی", the reading uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 234).
- **Where the Chilla of Baba Farid in Delhi stands.** Qureshi places it "near the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 132, folio 112) and, in her glossary, attached to Humayun's tomb (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 262, folio 242).
- **Ibn Battuta's visit.** Eaton dates it to 1334 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 221–222); Ernst and Lawrence to "around the year 1340" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 105, folio 92).
- **Who comes to the shrine now.** Khalid writes that "Every year, hundreds of Sikhs and Hindus travel to Pakpattan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135), and also that Sikhs have petitioned for visas to attend the *'urs* "but in vain" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated); Rozehnal that "the shrine is now marked as exclusively Muslim space" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, pp. 35–36, folios 25–26).
- **Women at the qawwali.** Abbas calls qawwali at the Chishtiyya shrines, this one among them, "an exclusively male domain" where "women's presence at such performances is rare" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 84, folio not stated); Khalid, at the qawwali in the courtyard, writes "Here women and men sat together" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).
- **The court case of the 1930s.** Eaton's introduction calls it "a 1938 court dispute" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 16); his essay runs it from 6 April 1935 to 2 December 1938 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 238), with the appeal record dated 1939 (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 239, n. 3). The colonial assessment report he quotes is "An 1897 British Assessment Report" in his text and dated 1896 in his note (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 230, n. 52).
- **The dead of 2001.** Rozehnal gives "more than one hundred" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 29, folio not stated); the newspapers, as Tahir Jehangir reports them, "over forty" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 37, folio 27). The state blamed the Diwan's four-hour delay over the Awqaf annuity (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 39, folio 29); the Diwan's family blamed crowd control, the tragedy coming "some two hours after the Diwan's arrival" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 39, folio 29).
- **Conversion.** Eaton reports that "the vast majority" of the Jat and Rajput groups that became Muslim in the medieval period "claim to have been converted either by Baba Farid or by his contemporary, Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya (d. 1263)" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 227), and Schimmel that "A number of Punjabi tribes still claim to have been converted by Fariduddin Ganj-i Shakar" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 381, folio 350). Eaton doubts the claim, among his grounds the shortness of the saint's stay (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228); Rizvi rejects the view that he went to Ajodhan to convert "'backward Hindu tribes'" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 159, folio 141) and calls mass conversion "quite contrary to the Chishti mission" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 27, folio 13).

## Legacy

For the people of the Punjab, Baba Farid is not a remote historical figure but a living presence — "Farid" is a household name, his sayings are proverbs, and his verses are sung by qawwals and folk-singers alike. Through his disciple Nizamuddin Auliya and the generations that followed, the Chishti order he helped root in India became the most widespread of all the Sufi paths of the subcontinent; through his Punjabi poetry he became a father of the language’s literature and a shared inheritance of Muslims and Sikhs; and through his shrine at Pakpattan he gave the Punjab one of its enduring centres of pilgrimage. Compassion, poverty, and the sweetness that gave him his name remain the marks of his memory.

Eaton places the tomb among the first holy places of Muslim India: the tombs "of Mu'in ad-Din Chishti at Ajmer, Nizam ad-Din Auliya' at Delhi, and Baba Farid at Pakpattan—became the first Muslim holy places within India", which meant "that South Asian Muslims were no longer compelled to look exclusively to the Middle East for spiritual inspiration" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 236). Pakpattan is one of the three "enormous cults", beside Ajmer and Delhi, on which the order's wealth and power centred (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 265). For the devotees "The shrine was Baba Farid": "many murids referred to the saint and his shrine in the same terms, sometimes defining themselves as murids of Baba Farid, and sometimes referring to themselves as murids of the gaddi, or shrine" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241). "The shrine, on the other hand, has been there all along, sustaining the powerful baraka of the saint through its line of diwans" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 228). A landholder of Ferozepore District told the court, "As the Sajjada Nashin in office is a representative of Baba Farid, the same sanctity and reverence is shown to the Gaddi Nashin as is shown to Baba Farid" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 247, n. 32). In Eaton's words, "this saint has remained for many centuries an immensely popular 'invisible friend' among millions of villagers inhabiting the southwestern Punjab" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 238), and Rozehnal quotes Eaton's judgement that "The shrine of Baba Farid in Pakpattan provides a striking example of how Islam, the religion par excellence 'of the Book,' has been in one instance mediated among common villagers most of whom were illiterate" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 35, folio 25).

Many clans claim him as the one who made them Muslim. Witnesses before the court named "the Wattu, the Siyal, the Dogar, the Kathia, the Bhatti, and the Tiwana" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 9). A cultivator of Lyallpur said, "Our Tiwana tribe was converted by Baba Farid" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 10); another, "Baba Farid converted us Bhattis into Islam. Since that time we are the followers of the gaddi and respect the gaddinashin [i.e., sajjada-nishin, or Diwan] in office" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 241, n. 11); and a Wattu villager, "Khewa, one of my ancestors, was converted into Islam by Baba Farid, and since that time we have been following the gaddi in dispute" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 248, n. 35). His cult went with Punjabis far from home: the Mughal officer Mirza Nathan in Bengal was a "faithful disciple" of Farid al-Din Shakarganj, "probably because the writer's ancestors had come from the Punjab where Baba Farid's cult was especially prominent" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 265, n. 10).

He belongs to more than one faith. "The same Shaykh Farid ad-Din is so highly respected by Sikhs that they have incorporated his Punjabi verses for their holy scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 18, folio 3). Abbas: "Although Baba Farid" was "a Muslim Sufi saint who wrote devotional poetry in Panjabi, his texts are revered among the Sikhs because he influenced the founder of their own religion" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 87, folio not stated); "Thus, he is a revered Sufi among the Sikhs as well as among his Muslim devotees" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 89, folio not stated). "Being part of the Granth, Baba Fareed is also given a special status in the Sikh religion and revered like the Gurus" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 188, folio not stated). Khalid writes that Nanak "like Farid, also chose Punjabi as his medium of expression" and was "impressed by the fact that Baba Farid lived a life of simplicity and shunned violence" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 153, folio 135), and that "There is a picture of Baba Farid accompanying the picture of Guru Nanak at the shrine of Guru Nanak at Nankana Sahib" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated). Rizvi explains the Janamsakhis' meeting of Nanak and Farid by "the sufi and Nath belief that great saints did not die but remained accessible to important mystics in later ages through spiritual conversation" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389), and rejects the suggestion that Nanak met a namesake descendant as "far-fetched" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 413, folio 389). Khalid asks "why our heroes cannot be people like Baba Farid, Waris Shah and Bulleh Shah, who spread the message of peace and brought several religious communities together instead of shedding blood" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 14, ch. 8, folio not stated).

His line reaches far. Shaykh Salim Chishti of Fatehpur Sikri belongs to "the Faridi line" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 111, folio 98), and Hazrat Inayat Khan was "from the lineage of Farid ad-Din and Nizam ad-Din" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 18, folio 3). Kugle finds him the only South Asian saint in the ascension oath that Khidr teaches Muhammad Ghawth, sworn "by the Intimacy of Farid al-Din [Ganj-i Shakar] Ajhodani" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 159, folio 138). For the Chishti Sabiri order of today, "the contemporary silsila places the tomb of Shaykh Baba Farid ad-Din Mas'ud Ganj-i Shakkar in Pakpattan at the center of Sufi sacred geography in Pakistan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 206, folio 198); one of its shaykhs, Shahidullah Faridi, took the name Faridi "to mark his special relationship with the saint in Pakpattan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 77, folio 67), and its murids contemplate him daily (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 206, folio 198). "Sufi shrines such as Pakpattan serve as vital centers of popular piety—nodal points of local identity and culture." (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 47, folio 37). Ernst and Lawrence's headnote calls him "an extraordinary ascetic, noted for his controlled ecstasy; yet unlike Qutb ad-Din, he was also a loyal father and husband", whose life yields "the three characteristics of pious Chishtis: eschewing all stable income, engaging in meditation, often abetted by music, and training worthy disciples" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 167, folio 155). Schimmel quotes the judgement that "no saint excelled him in his devotions and penances." (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 378, folio 347).

He has drawn a long literature. Lahori's editor lists seventeen sources on him, among them *Fawaid al-Fawad*, Amir Khurd's *Sair al-Auliya*, *Akhbar al-Akhyar*, K. A. Nizami's *Life and Times of Sh. Farid-u-Din* (Aligarh, 1955) and Muslim Nizami's *Anwar al-Faridiya*, printed at Pak Pattan in 1965 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 89–90, folios 77–78 [markers 87–88]). Ernst and Lawrence give him twelve entries in their European-language bibliography, the earliest an account by Munshi Mohana Lala in the *Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal* of 1836 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 223, folio 212), and list Miles Irving's article on the shrine in the *Journal of the Panjab Historical Society* of 1911–12 beside Eaton's essay on its authority (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 227, folio 216). Khaliq Ahmad Nizami's biography of the saint is listed by Schimmel (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 293, folio 293), by Rizvi in its Aligarh edition of 1955 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 454, folio 430) and by Rozehnal in its Delhi edition of 1973 (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 241, folio 234). Shackle lists Gurbachan Singh Talib's *Baba Sheikh Farid Shakar Ganj* (New Delhi: National Book Trust, 1974) (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 204, folio 179), and Rafat cites Muhammad Asaf Khan's study of the provenance of his poetry, published by the Pakistan Punjabi Adabi Board, Lahore, in 1978 (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 242, folio 222). For the Chishti Sabiri order the book about him is Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani's *Maqam-i Ganj-i Shakkar* (Lahore: al-Faisal Publishers, 1994), in which Rabbani translated "the discourses of Farid al-Din Ganj-i Shakkar" into Urdu (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 111, folio 102; Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 250, folio 243).

Name: Shrine of Ganj e Inayat Sarkar
Events: Annual urs (27-28 Sha'ban); weekly Saturday gathering; langar
Description:
## Overview

In the busy heart of modern Lahore, at Firdous Market in Gulberg — a quarter once known by the older name of Kabutar Pura — stands the shrine of Hazrat Allama Maulana Pir Muhammad Inayat Ahmad Naqshbandi Mujaddidi, known to his devotees as *Huzoor Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar*, “the Treasure of Grace.” Unlike the ancient darbars of the city, this is a shrine of living memory: the saint died only in 2011, and the tomb was raised at his burial, on the very ground where he had lived, preached, and guided disciples for more than four decades. A Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi scholar-saint, orator, and author, Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar drew thousands into his spiritual fold, and his line continues unbroken under his son and successor. His shrine shows how the deep tradition of Punjabi Sufism has carried on into the twenty-first century, at the centre of a great contemporary city.

## The Name "Ganj-e-Inayat"

The honorific by which the saint is known — *Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar* — carries its own meaning and sets him within an old Punjabi tradition. *Ganj* is the Persian word for “treasure,” long bestowed upon the most beloved saints of Lahore and its region: Ali Hujwiri is *Data Ganj Bakhsh*, “the Bestower of the Treasure,” and Baba Farid of Pakpattan is *Ganj-e-Shakar*, “the Treasure of Sugar.” To call Pir Muhammad Inayat Ahmad “Ganj-e-Inayat” is thus to place him, in the affection of his devotees, in that same company — and the title turns gracefully on his own name, for *inayat* means “grace” or “divine favour.” *Ganj-e-Inayat* may be read as “the Treasure of Grace”: a saint understood as a store of blessing on which the needy may draw, and from whose door, it is said, no one returns empty-handed.

## The Life of the Saint

Muhammad Inayat Ahmad was born on 18 November 1937 at Kalisaah, a village of the Kashmir valley, into a household known for both learning and piety. His father, Hazrat Mian Sohbat Ali, was himself a man of religion and a spiritual disciple in the line of Batala Sharif, and his parents — simple and devout — raised their son with care. So marked was the child from the first that, when news of his birth reached the saint Hazrat Syed Wilayat Ali Shah, he is said to have come to the house, laid his hand upon the infant in affection, and blessed him. Inayat Ahmad received his first instruction, and his knowledge of the Qur’an, at home.

In search of deeper learning he left Kashmir and travelled to Gujrat, in the Punjab, and the villages around it, studying under a number of the noted religious teachers of the age — among them Hazrat Abu al-Barakat Syed Muhammad Ahmad, Hazrat Syedna Tahir Alauddin Qadiri Gilani, and the renowned orator Maulana Ghulam Ali Okarvi. It was at the seminary Ashraf-ul-Madaris in Gujrat that he found his own spiritual master: he took the oath of allegiance (bai‘at) at the hand of Hazrat Pir Syed Ismail Shah Bukhari — famous as *Karman Wali Sarkar* — and studied and served under his mentorship, receiving from him both learning and the promise, often repeated, that one day he would become a *wali-ullah*, a friend of God. From this master he received his authorisation (khilafat) in the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi order, becoming a *khalifa-e-mujaz* of Karman Wali Sharif. He lived to the age of seventy-four, dying in 2011.

## His Order, Learning, and Teaching

Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar belonged to the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi order — the branch of the Naqshbandi way renewed by the great reformer Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani), long noted for its strict adherence to the Sharia and its sober, God-centred discipline. This temper marked the saint through and through. His life was famously simple; he lived in a plain house and was remembered as a man of striking beauty and sincerity, such that (his devotees say) people would look on him and lose themselves in another world. He was rigorous in prayer, fasting, and the giving of *zakat*, and above all uncompromising in the doctrine of God’s oneness (*tauhid*): he counted the association of partners with God (*shirk*) as unbelief, and taught his followers to keep far from it. At the same time he held firmly to the Sufi conviction that the seeker needs a guide, and would say that until a person takes shelter with a *pir* he cannot come onto the straight path, and that to be joined to a true spiritual lineage (*nisbat*) is a means of a person’s salvation in this world and the next. He was a teacher and an author as well as a guide: among his works is the *Kitab-us-Salat*, a book on the blessings of prayer, of the *durood* (blessings on the Prophet), and of the Sufi path, written especially for the young — a sign of a saint who joined the pen and the pulpit to the practice of the heart.

## The Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi Way

The order to which Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar belonged is among the most influential in the Muslim world, and its character helps explain his own. The Naqshbandiyya takes its name from Khwaja Baha-ud-Din Naqshband of Bukhara (d. 1389), and is distinguished among the Sufi paths by its preference for the silent, hidden remembrance of God (*dhikr-e-khafi*) over audible or ecstatic forms, and by its insistence that the mystical life be lived in strict conformity with the Sharia and in the midst of society rather than in withdrawal from it — expressed in the famous Naqshbandi principle of “solitude within the crowd.” The order was carried into India around 1600 by Khwaja Baqi Billah, and it was his disciple Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi — revered as the *Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani*, the “Renewer of the Second Millennium” — who reshaped it into the Mujaddidi branch, laying a powerful stress on the purification of belief, the reaffirmation of God’s absolute oneness, and the reform of practice in accordance with the Prophet’s example. From Sirhindi’s Sirhind the Mujaddidi way spread across the subcontinent and beyond, becoming one of the great engines of Islamic renewal in South Asia.

It is this inheritance that one hears in Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar’s own emphases: his rigor in prayer and fasting, his uncompromising insistence on *tauhid* and his warnings against *shirk*, his union of sober scholarship with the guidance of a living master. In him the centuries-old Mujaddidi concern to wed the inward path to the outward law found a twentieth-century voice, and through his silsila — reaching back through his master Karman Wali Sarkar to the founders of the order, and forward now through his son — that chain of transmission continues in the Lahore of today.

## Lahore and the Making of the Shrine

In 1969 Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar came to Lahore and settled at Firdous Market in Gulberg 3, in the quarter formerly called Kabutar Pura. That same year a mosque was raised at the spot that would become the heart of his darbar, and from it he taught, led prayer, and gathered a following. There he remained for some forty-two years — the whole second half of his life — preaching the faith and drawing disciples from near and far, until his death in 2011. Because he had lived and laboured on that ground for so long and had bound so many to himself as their spiritual guide, it was there that he was buried, and the shrine (darbar) was founded over his grave at the time of his burial. Beside it lies a graveyard in which, it is said, many sayyid families are laid to rest, for burial near the saint is counted a blessing.

## Miracles and Healing

Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar was, in the eyes of his followers, a saint of evident spiritual power, and many stories of his grace are told at the shrine. It was said that one need not even speak one’s trouble to him: that on meeting him, people found their difficulties, their anxieties, and their spiritual afflictions (*bandish*) simply lifted, and that he would give to those who came before they had asked. Many recount healing (*shifa*) received at his hand or, after his death, at his shrine. One disciple related that he had suffered from the vomiting of blood, but that after coming to the saint and presenting himself in his presence he was never troubled by it again — healed, he believed, by the saint’s very gaze (*nazar*) — and that he bound himself to that door for life. It is such accounts, more than anything, that draw people to the shrine and keep them faithful to it.

## The Living Succession

What most distinguishes this shrine, like other recent darbars, is that the spiritual line it commemorates is living and directly continued. As his end drew near, Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar is said to have transferred his spiritual succession openly and unmistakably: before a great gathering of his disciples he placed his blessed saliva (*luab*) into the mouth of his eldest son, Sahibzada Muhammad Umar Naqshbandi, and announced to the thousands present that he was leaving all that was his to his son. Sahibzada Muhammad Umar Naqshbandi is today the *sajjada-nashin*, the keeper of the shrine and heir to its spiritual authority. It is he who now takes the seat of guidance, and pilgrims come not only to honour the departed saint but to enter a living chain — to take the oath of allegiance at the hand of the successor and to receive the blessing (*faiz*) of the line.

## The Shrine and Its Devotions

The darbar stands within a small religious complex at Gulberg: the tomb, the mosque built in 1969 where the five daily prayers are offered in congregation, and the adjoining graveyard. It is not a government-administered shrine but private property, cared for by the saint’s own family and disciples. Each week, on Saturday, Sahibzada Muhammad Umar Naqshbandi holds his gathering at the shrine — presiding over assemblies of *naat* (devotional poetry in praise of the Prophet), distributing *langar* (free food), meeting the general public and his disciples, and admitting new followers to the oath of allegiance. The great occasion of the year is the annual urs, held on the 27th and 28th of Shaban, when the shrine takes on a heightened and vivid spiritual atmosphere: the blessed cloth (*chadar*) over the grave is ceremonially changed, the tomb is washed (*ghusl*) with rose-water and perfumes, gatherings of naat and *sama* fill the nights, and *langar* is distributed continuously to the crowds who come from far and wide. On an ordinary day the shrine receives some one to one-and-a-half thousand visitors, amounting to around thirty thousand in a month, while at the annual urs the number swells to fifty or sixty thousand who gather to share in the blessings.

## Legacy

The shrine of Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar is a reminder that the making of saints and shrines is not only a matter of the distant past. Here is a holy man of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries — a Kashmir-born scholar of the Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi way, trained under the great teachers of his age, austere in doctrine yet warm in his care for the troubled — whose tomb, barely more than a decade old, has already become a fixed point of devotion in the heart of Lahore. In his simple life, his insistence on prayer and the oneness of God, his reputation for healing, and above all in the living succession he passed to his son, the darbar carries the ancient pattern of Punjabi Sufism forward into the present, gathering a new city’s hopes at a new saint’s door. In a metropolis of many millions, far from the quiet of the medieval khanqah, the darbar of Ganj-e-Inayat Sarkar stands as proof that the Punjab still makes its saints, and still knows how to gather at their thresholds.

Description:
## Overview

The shrine of *Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani* is among the most historically important Sufi mausolea of Multan, the "city of saints", and marks the resting place of the man traditionally credited with establishing the *Chishti* order firmly in the city. Born at Multan around 1747 (1160 AH) and dying in 1811, Hafiz Jamal was a disciple of *Khwaja Noor Muhammad Maharvi*, a leading Chishti master of the region, and became a renowned teacher and poet in his own right, composing in Arabic, Persian and Siraiki; his *Siharfi*, an acrostic poem of the Punjabi–Siraiki tradition, is his best-known literary work. His tomb stands near the Aam Khas Bagh outside the historic Daulat Gate, a fine piece of late-Mughal funerary architecture that still preserves original Mughal-era wall paintings. It remains an active centre of devotion, with an annual *urs*, and it forms part of the dense sacred geography of Multan alongside the great shrines of Bahauddin Zakariya, Shah Rukn-e-Alam and Shah Shams Sabzwari.

None of the books consulted here mentions the shrine itself: none describes the tomb, its paintings, its *urs* or its keepers. What they offer concerns the saint and his city. Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, in their history of the Chishti order, give him one sentence: "Another successor of Nur Muhammad, Sulayman Taunsawi's contemporary Hafiz Muhammad Jamal (d. 1811), is also said to have taken part in resistance to Sikh attacks on Multan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). The phrase 'is also said to have' is theirs: they report the tradition and do not vouch for it. The modern Urdu edition of Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* has an entry headed with the names "خواجہ محمد جمال / حافظ محمد جمال ملتانی" that appears to concern this saint, and its editor's footnote credits a Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani with the flourishing of the Chishti order in Multan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108); what that footnote says is set out below, with its uncertainties.

## The Life of the Saint

By the account the site has long carried, Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani was born at Multan around 1747 (1160 AH) and died in 1811. He was a disciple of Khwaja Noor Muhammad Maharvi, a leading Chishti master of the region, and became a renowned teacher and a poet in his own right, writing in Arabic, Persian and Siraiki.

Ernst and Lawrence count him among Nur Muhammad's successors: he is "Another successor of Nur Muhammad" and "Sulayman Taunsawi's contemporary", and they give his death as 1811 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). The same sentence records, as something said of him rather than as established fact, that he "is also said to have taken part in resistance to Sikh attacks on Multan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). On the same page they write of Shaykh Sulayman Taunsawi, his contemporary, that he "urged his followers to participate in resistance against Sikh aggression in the Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). Beyond that sentence the book names no tomb, no *urs* and no lineage for him other than the succession from Nur Muhammad.

The *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, composed in Persian in 1875 and read here in a modern Urdu edition, has an entry, no. 72, under the names "خواجہ محمد جمال / حافظ محمد جمال ملتانی", Khwaja Muhammad Jamal or Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). What the book is known here to say of him comes from the modern editor's footnote on that page, not from the author's own text. The footnote names him the third of the four chief *khalifas* of Khwaja Nur Muhammad Maharvi, called "صاحب قرب", those of nearness (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). It gives him a death year in the hijri reckoning, 1226 AH, in a sentence that is the editor's judgement of his place in the history of the order: "ملتان میں سلسلہ چشتیہ کو حضرت حافظ محمد جمال ملتانی ف ۱۲۲۶ھ کی بدولت فروغ ہوا", in Multan the Chishtiya silsila flourished thanks to Hazrat Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani, d. 1226 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). The date is the editor's, not the author's.

How firmly that entry belongs to this saint is not settled. The book's index lists the name as "محمد جمال ملتانی", without the title Hafiz, against the page of the entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 328, folio 316), and Multan has had more than one Muhammad Jamal. The same index, against the same page, lists Nur Muhammad Maharvi, his father Hindal, a Qazi Muhammad Aqil, and the places Bahadurpur, Parhar, Maharan and Narawal (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 332, folio 320; p. 328; pp. 333–336); the index thus puts him on the same page as Nur Muhammad Maharvi and his circle, but does not itself say who Muhammad Jamal was.

## His Sayings Collected

The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* names three collections of the saint's *malfuzat*, his recorded sayings: *Gulzar-e Jamaliya* by Allama Abd al-Aziz Parharvi, *Anwar-e Jamaliya* by Ghulam Hasan, and *Asrar al-Kamaliya* by Zahid Shah, "آپ کے ملفوظات کے مجموعے ہیں", these are collections of his *malfuzat* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). For further reading the same footnote points to *Manaqib al-Mahbubin* and to Khaliq Ahmad Nizami's *Tarikh-e Mashaikh-e Chisht* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5).

The bibliography at the end of *Sufi Martyrs of Love* lists works under a "Jamal al-Din Multani". One entry pairs "Jamal al-Din Multani and his disciple Khuda Bakhsh Multani" with Ghulam Husayn Multani, whose death it gives as 1265/1849, and the title *Anwar-i jamaliyya* (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 238, folio 228). Another lists *Anwar-i jamaliyya* again, compiled by 'Abd al-'Aziz Parharawi, with an edition from Multan (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230). A third, under Khuda Bakhsh Multani, notes: "It is noted here that the author studied with Wali Allah as well as with Jamal Multani", and dates Jamal Multani's death 1226/1811 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 244, folio 234). The book itself never says that this Jamal al-Din Multani is the Hafiz Muhammad Jamal of its narrative; the shared death year and the shared title *Anwar-i jamaliyya* are the only ties between them.

## The Shrine

The tomb stands near the Aam Khas Bagh, outside the historic Daulat Gate of Multan. It is a fine piece of late-Mughal funerary architecture: a square chamber rising to a twelve-sided drum and a hemispherical dome. It is especially valued because it preserves original Mughal-era wall paintings, a rarity, since the murals of most such monuments have been lost to whitewash and renovation. Alam Faqri's compendium of the saints of Pakistan confirms that his shrine is in the city.

The books consulted here do not describe the tomb. None of them records who built it or when, its paintings, its custodians or any endowment.

## Devotion and Practice

The shrine remains an active centre of devotion, with an annual *urs* commemorating the saint and continuous visitation by those seeking blessing. The books consulted here give no date for the *urs* and describe no rite at this tomb.

What they say of shrine music in the city is said of Multan at large. Shemeem Burney Abbas, writing of the performers she studied, says that "They additionally sing around shrines in Multan and Sahiwal to earn a living", naming no shrine (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 199, folio not stated). Ernst and Lawrence tell of an earlier singer from the city: "One time a qawwal, Abu Bakr by name, came from Multan to visit Nizam ad-Din's teacher" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 171, folio 159).

## The Chishti Order in Multan

The claim for which Hafiz Jamal is chiefly remembered is that he established the Chishti order firmly in Multan. Alam Faqri's general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints states plainly that Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani was "the first elder to lay the foundation of the Chishtia order" in Multan. The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* says that in Multan the Chishtiya silsila flourished thanks to him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5).

The same footnote credits the wider spread of the Chishtiya Nizamiya Fakhriya in the Punjab to his contemporary Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi: "پنجاب میں سلسلہ چشتیہ نظامیہ فخریہ کی زیادہ اشاعت حضرت خواجہ سلیمان تونسوی کے ذریعہ ہوئی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). Lahori's own text, opening its section on the Chishti masters, traces the spread of the order in Hind and the Punjab to Khwaja Mu'in al-Din Hasan Sijzi: "یہ سلسلہ ہند اور پنجاب میں حضرت خواجہ معین الدین حسن سجزی سے شائع ہوا" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 85, folio 73).

Ernst and Lawrence set the generation of Nur Muhammad's successors in a longer story. "The Nizami Chishtis came to prominence in the eighteenth century, principally in Delhi, the Deccan, and Punjab, through masters who were related to but in tension with local political leaders" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 119, folio 106). They also record a far older Chishti moment in the city: the visit of Qutb ad-Din to Multan, "a strategic commercial center in the Punjab", was the occasion on which Farid ad-Din pledged allegiance to the Chishti master (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 80, folio 66). Sujan Rai Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* likewise names Multan as the place where Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, coming from Baghdad, met Shaikh Baha al-Din Zakariya (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 556). These passages speak of the order and the city, not of Hafiz Jamal or his tomb.

## In Verse

Hafiz Jamal is remembered as a poet in Arabic, Persian and Siraiki, and above all for his *Siharfi*, an acrostic poem of the Punjabi–Siraiki tradition. None of the books consulted here quotes a line of his verse or names his *Siharfi*; the poetry they do carry speaks of his city and his province.

Schimmel, writing of Punjabi poetry in general and not of Hafiz Jamal, places its flowering in his own age: "The golden age of Muslim Panjabi poetry is the late 17th and the 18th century, e.g., the time when the province was invaded one time after the other by Mahrattas, Sikhs, and, in between, by the liberating Muslim armies" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 17, folio 13). She suggests that it may be older: "In the Panjab, popular mystical poetry may have emerged as early as in the days of Fariduddin Shakarganj" (Schimmel, *Pain and Grace*, p. 16, folio 12). Abbas, writing of the Siraiki region, speaks of "the Siraiki belt around the Multan, Bahawalpur, Mianwali, and northern Sind areas" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 148, folio not stated).

For the vernacular mystical poets, Schimmel writes, the holy cities lie within: "Mecca and Medina (and for the Sindhi and Panjabi, also Multan) are inside the heart" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 178, folio 160). She reads a poem of Sachal as speaking "of Shams-i Tabriz, Maulana Rumi's spiritual beloved who, according to the Indian tradition, was flayed alive by the mollas in Multan where his shrine is still venerated" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 175, folio 157). And of Fakhruddin 'Iraqi, who in Multan attached himself to Baha'uddin Zakariya (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 383, folio 352), she writes: "The tender and intoxicating love poems that the Persian poet composed are still being sung by Pakistani musicians at the door of the master's tomb in Multan" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 384, folio 353).

The Punjabi kafis of Madho Lal Hussein, in Naveed Alam's English, name the city once, as the source of a bride's finery:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 51, folio 51, kafi 29)

The *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, whose editor names Hafiz Jamal among Nur Muhammad's *khalifas*, closes with a chronogram by the author's son, Mufti Ghulam Safdar, encoding the year 1292 AH; its subject is the book's own, the saints of the Punjab:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

A chronogram on the saints of the Punjab whose lives the book records (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 282, folio 270).

## Setting: The City of Saints

The books' accounts of Multan speak of the city, not of this shrine, but they show the sacred landscape in which it stands. Bhandari, writing in Aurangzeb's reign, lists the saints buried in the city and adds that many more rest there: "بسیاری از اولیاے دران شهر سعادت بهر اسوده اند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). He also records a sultan who, coming to Multan, made the round of the tombs of its shaikhs, "در سنه ۸۳۵[OCR?] سلطان بملتان رسیده مزارات مشایخ را طواف نموده", the reading of the year uncertain in the printed text and no shaikh named (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 324).

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes that "by the middle of the eleventh century, sufism had penetrated into the areas surrounding Multan" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 128, folio 110). Richard Eaton notes that many Muslim clans of the Punjab claim conversion by Baba Farid or by "his contemporary, Baha' al-Haqq Zakariya (d. 1263), whose tomb is in Multan city" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 227, folio 215). Schimmel writes that "Multan is the resting place of the great Suhrawardi saint Baha'uddin Zakariya (d. 1267)" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 286, folio 268). Haroon Khalid, describing the city in Guru Nanak's day, writes: "At that time Multan was one of the biggest cities of Punjab and was known for the religious shrines of Muslim saints, and Jain and Hindu temples. It was a sacred space for people of all religious denominations" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 123, folio 105). Harish Dhillon writes that "By the time Nanak came to Multan, the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 167, folio 183).

The Sikh attacks on Multan that Ernst and Lawrence connect with Hafiz Jamal's name belong to a longer conflict over the city, which the books record only in general terms. Haroon Khalid writes of the Sikh period that "uprisings led by Muslim leaders began in Kasur and Multan", and that the rebellion "was given a religious colour against the infidel Ranjit Singh" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 210, folio not stated). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* records the fall of the city to Ranjit Singh: when he conquered Multan, Nawab Muzaffar Khan, "یہ[OCR?] نواب صاحبان والی ملتان", was killed, and members of his house were taken with their families to Lahore, where they lived in the author's day (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 130). Another passage of the same book, dated in words, tells of Kharak Singh sent with an army to conquer Multan, and of Multan conquered: "کھڑک سنگھ فتح ملتان پر بھیجا کی ملتان فتح ہوا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 580). The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* counts it among the book's merits that its author recorded as an eyewitness what the notables of the Punjab and the tombs of its shaikhs suffered under the Sikhs, "مشائخ کے مقابر کی تباہی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 33, folio 21). None of these passages names Hafiz Jamal or his shrine.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His death year.** The site's account and Ernst and Lawrence give 1811 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives 1226 AH, in the hijri reckoning only (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). The bibliography of *Sufi Martyrs of Love* gives 1226/1811 for a "Jamal Multani" whom the book does not equate with its Hafiz Muhammad Jamal (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 244, folio 234).
- **His name.** The site's account calls him Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani, as do Ernst and Lawrence in their narrative (Hafiz Muhammad Jamal) (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). The *Hadiqat al-Awliya* heads its entry with two forms, "خواجہ محمد جمال / حافظ محمد جمال ملتانی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108), and indexes him as "محمد جمال ملتانی", without the title Hafiz (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 328, folio 316). The bibliography of *Sufi Martyrs of Love* has "Jamal al-Din Multani" and "Jamal Multani" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 238, folio 228; p. 244, folio 234).
- **His master's name.** The site's account names Khwaja Noor Muhammad Maharvi, and the *Hadiqat al-Awliya*'s footnote on Hafiz Jamal has Nur Muhammad Maharvi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). In the same book's entry on Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, the same master's *nisba* is printed Majheel[OCR?], a reading uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 123, folio 111). Ernst and Lawrence call him simply Nur Muhammad (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108).
- **The Chishti order in Multan.** The site's account credits Hafiz Jamal with establishing the order firmly in the city, and Alam Faqri calls him "the first elder to lay the foundation of the Chishtia order" in Multan. The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* says that the order flourished in Multan thanks to him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). Ernst and Lawrence set an earlier Chishti event in the city, Farid ad-Din's pledge of allegiance to the Chishti master on Qutb ad-Din's visit to Multan (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 80, folio 66), and Bhandari has Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki meeting Baha al-Din Zakariya there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 556).
- **The *Anwar-e Jamaliya* and its compiler.** The editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya* names *Anwar-e Jamaliya* as the work of Ghulam Hasan and Abd al-Aziz Parharvi as the author of a different collection, *Gulzar-e Jamaliya* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). The bibliography of *Sufi Martyrs of Love* lists *Anwar-i jamaliyya* as compiled by 'Abd al-'Aziz Parharawi (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 240, folio 230), and elsewhere sets the same title beside Ghulam Husayn Multani (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 238, folio 228); its subject there is "Jamal al-Din Multani", whom the book does not equate with Hafiz Muhammad Jamal.

## Legacy

Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani is remembered as the master through whom the Chishti order took firm root in Multan,. His tomb, with its rare surviving Mughal-era paintings, remains an active centre of devotion and part of the dense sacred geography of Multan alongside the great shrines of Bahauddin Zakariya, Shah Rukn-e-Alam and Shah Shams Sabzwari.

The books add two strands to that memory. Collections of his sayings are named by the editor of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya*: *Gulzar-e Jamaliya*, *Anwar-e Jamaliya* and *Asrar al-Kamaliya* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108, حاشیہ 5). And in the history of the order he is remembered alongside Sulayman Taunsawi as one of Nur Muhammad's successors, who "is also said to have taken part in resistance to Sikh attacks on Multan" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108).
