Name: Shrine of Hazrat Madho Lal Hussain (Shah Hussain Darbar)
Location: Baghbanpura (near Shalimar Gardens), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Mela Chiraghan / annual urs (9-11 Shawwal); Thursday-evening lamp-lighting, dhamal and qawwali
Description:
## Overview

In Baghbanpura, close by the Shalimar Gardens on the eastern edge of Lahore, stands the shrine of Hazrat Madho Lal Hussain — the joint name of two men, and the sign of one of the most extraordinary bonds in the spiritual history of the Punjab. Within it rest Shah Hussain (1538–1599), the great Malamati Sufi and father of the Punjabi *kafi*, and Madho Lal, the Hindu youth he loved and whose name he joined for ever to his own. Around the darbar has grown one of the largest festivals in the region, the Mela Chiraghan or “Festival of Lamps,” and from it has flowed a body of Punjabi mystical verse that ordinary people still sing four centuries on. The shrine is at once a place of ecstatic devotion, a monument of Punjabi language and poetry, and a beloved emblem of love that overleaps the boundaries of caste and creed. To understand it, one must begin with the strange and luminous life of Shah Hussain.

The books consulted know him by many spellings, and one of them knows him as two men. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives the saint and his beloved two separately numbered entries: no. 17, headed "شیخ حسین المشہور بہ لال حسین لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 54–57, folios 42–45), and no. 24, listed as "شیخ مادھو لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 15, folio 3). The joint name occurs there only inside the parenthesis of an index line, "حسین لاہوری شاہ (مادھو لال حسین)" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 317, folio 305), and in the title of the editor's own encyclopaedia article, "مادھو لال حسین" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 303, folio 291). The book's link between the two men is a footnote in Husain's entry sending the reader to Madho's account, and the naming of "پہلے دیوان حضرت کے معشوق و محبوب شیخ مادھو", the first *Diwan* being Shaykh Madho, the Hazrat's beloved (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 55, folio 43).

Naveed Alam, who translates his verse as *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, writes "Shah Hussein" and "Madho Lal Hussein" throughout, and begins with "The portrait of Shah Hussein (1538–99), popularly known as Madho Lal Hussein" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). "Weaver, mystic, fakir, Shah Hussein continues to command great reverence in Punjab as a poet–saint more than 400 years after his death," he writes (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6), and: "His urs, or death anniversary, is still celebrated at his shrine in Baghbanpura, Lahore. In the inner sanctum of the shrine, buried right next to Hussein, is his young beloved and disciple, Madho (pronounced Madh-oh) Lal" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). Scott Kugle, whose fourth chapter in *Sufis and Saints' Bodies* is called 'The Lips of Shah Hussayn' (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 8, folio not stated), writes "Shah Hussayn" and calls him "a Sufi who will become one of Lahore's patron saints" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 204, folio 183). Annemarie Schimmel writes "Madho Lal Husain" and records that he "is buried together with his Hindu beloved in a modest tomb near the Shalimar gardens in Lahore" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, pp. 170–171, folios 152–153).

## The Life of Shah Hussain

Hussain was born in Lahore in 1538 into a family of weavers — his father, by tradition, a craftsman who stitched uniforms for the army of the Emperor Humayun. He was a child of unusual gifts and piety: he is said to have committed the Qur’an to memory by the age of seven, and at fifteen to have begun teaching recitation (tajweed) and preaching, leading the congregational prayers and the long Taraweeh prayers of Ramadan. For some twenty years he lived the life of an exact and disciplined scholar of the outward law, his devotion so evident that learned men sought his company and came away loving him. In his spiritual training he is remembered as a disciple of the Sufi master Bahlol (Bahlol Daryai) and as a devoted frequenter of the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh; there, the accounts say, he withdrew into a long spiritual retreat, keeping *chilla* by the darbar of Lahore’s patron saint for some twelve years, absorbed in the discipline of divine love (*ishq-e-haqiqi*), while those who came to sit with him took to calling him, simply, “Baba.”

The books agree that he was born in Lahore and differ over the year. Zahur ul-Hasan Sharib writes "آپ 945ھ میں لاہور میں پیدا ہوئے", that he was born in 945 AH in Lahore (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 249, folio 245), and Lahori's author gives the same year in words, "سال نوسو پینتالیس" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 55–56, folios 43–44). Alam gives 1538 (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). Kugle writes "He was born around 1539 C.E." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185, ch. 4 n. 7); Taufiq Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah gives "Shah Husain (1539-1593 A.D.)" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 24, folio not stated), and Schimmel's *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* gives 1539–93 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 415, folio 384). Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* records the birth only in a chronogram by Pir Muhammad, part of whose line cannot be read (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 45), and in a verse of the author's own, "بسال مولودش از سروش آل[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 46); no year can be read from either. Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* places him simply as a *salik* living in Lahore in Akbar's era (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 233, folio 236).

For his family the books give several accounts. Lahori's author writes that his grandfather, کلجس رائے [OCR?], was a Hindu who accepted Islam in the time of Firoz Shah Tughlaq; that his son Usman was a religious man who earned lawful sustenance "جولاہوں کے کام سے", by the work of weavers; and that Shaykh Husain was born in his house (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 54, folio 42). Kanhaiya Lal gives his caste as "ڈہو بند[OCR?] بافندہ", a weaver, and says that among his forebears one "کمس[OCR?] راے[OCR?]" was a Hindu who became Muslim in the پونی[OCR?] era, and "اُسکا پوتا یہ حسین تہا", that this Husain was his grandson (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 233, folio 236). Sharib writes "آپ کے آباؤ اجداد کائستہ [OCR?] تھے", that his forebears were Kayasth [OCR?], and makes the convert his father, کلسن رائے [OCR?], who "سلطان فیروز شاہ کے عہد میں اسلام قبول کیا", accepted Islam in the reign of Sultan Firoz Shah, was named "شیخ عثمان", and "وہ کپڑا بنتے تھے", wove cloth; he gives no date for the conversion and does not name the mother (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 249, folio 245). Chishti gives the name by which the saint is known as "حضرت کا نام مشہورہ ڈھاڈا[OCR?] حسین ہے[OCR?]", and sets beside ڈھاڈا[OCR?] the words "راجپوتوں میں ایک ذات"; he traces the paternal descent to "کلشتر[OCR?]", an ancestor who became Muslim and was titled "شیخ الاسلام", names the father in "حضرت کے والد کا نام مشہور عثمان[OCR?] تھا[OCR?]" and gives his trade as "پیشہ بافندگی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 45).

Alam writes that "Hussein's father, a Rajput from the Kalsrai clan, converted to Islam during the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and took on the Muslim name of Sheikh Usman" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6), and takes the mother's side from Dara Shikoh, who "calls him Hussein Dadha, using Hussein's matrilineal family name (his mother belonged to the Dadha clan of Rajputs)" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 8, folio 8); "Sheikh, the scholar, is also the family name of Hussein" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 181, folio 181). Kugle rejects the Rajput descent. "Hussayn belonged to a community of weavers, who had as a caste converted to Islam only a few generations before" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 228, folio 207, ch. 4 n. 52); "His family had joined Islam only a few generations before without claiming any Persian ancestry or educational ties." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 218, folio 197). Biographers like Ramakrishna, he writes, have made him a Rajput or Kayasth on the strength of later Urdu sources that put his family in the Dahda Rajput clan, but "these castes did not engage in weaving", and "The castes of weavers who converted to Islam in the medieval centuries had most likely been Shudras." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 329, folio 308, ch. 4 n. 52). He concludes: "The stories of Hussayn's 'noble' lineage are later accretions to make his image more acceptable to society, as are the stories of Madho's 'conversion' to Islam." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 329, folio 308, ch. 4 n. 52). Alam, for his part, says that the hagiographers "are not concerned with Hussein, the poet, or Hussein, the self-proclaimed weaver, but remain fixated on Hussein, the saint" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 8, folio 8).

The poems name the trade too. In Alam's English the weaver is addressed by name:

*O Hussein, the weaver! He earned no profit* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 176, folio 176)

On the same page comes the poems' one run of biographical negatives:

*Never got engaged, never got married / Never fixed a date, never held a wedding / Neither a householder nor a traveller / Neither a man of faith nor an infidel / He is what he is* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 176, folio 176)

Kugle quotes, from Shuja Alhaq's *Forgotten Vision*:

*O Friend, Hussayn is a weaver, no profit accrues to him / Neither was he betrothed nor married / Nor was any matrimony ceremony held for him* (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 328, folio 307, ch. 4 n. 26)

Of his schooling the accounts agree on a mosque and a teacher named Abu Bakr, and differ over his age. Lahori's author writes that at the age of seven, while he was reading the Quran with a learned man named Abu Bakr, Shaykh Bahlul happened to pass through that mosque, and his glance so fell on Husain that he became a perfect *wali* while still a child; the editor adds in a footnote that *Haqiqat al-Fuqara* instead has him become the pupil of Hafiz Abu Bakr at the age of ten, in 955 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 54, folio 42). Chishti has "حضرت لال حسین دہ سالہ تھی[OCR?]" when Bahlul came, memorising with Maulvi Abu Bakr and with the seventh *sipara* done, and puts his *maktab* in "وہ محلہ [illegible] دروازہ ٹکسالی[OCR?] لاہور متصل[OCR?] [illegible] دریا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 50). Elsewhere he locates outside "دروازہ ٹکسالی [OCR?]", where the Takia of Sher Ali Shah now is, a mohalla that held in the time of "بابر بادشاہ و اکبر بادشاہ" the house "حضرت حسین کی والدہ کا دولتخانہ", and in its mosque "حضرت حسین مرحوم مولوی [illegible] ابو بکر [OCR?] کے پاس سبق قرآن شریف [illegible] کا پڑھا کرتے تھے" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 101). Sharib sends him to the *maktab* at seven, where he memorised six *paras* from "حافظ ابوبکر" and read part of the "تفسیر مدارک" with "شیخ سعد اللہ"; but "آپ تعلیم زیادہ دن جاری نہ رکھ سکے", he could not keep his schooling up long (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 249, folio 245). Alam writes: "As a boy, Hussein joined the local mosque which also functioned as a madrasa, where memorizing the Quran by rote was the main method of learning" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). For Kugle, his study as a youth "consisted of memorizing the Qur'an, learning Arabic, and studying scriptural and legal interpretation" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185).

How the boy came to finish the Quran is told as a wonder. Sharib relates that Bahlol announced he would recite the Quran that Ramadan, and the boy objected "یہ کیسے ممکن ہے! مجھے تو صرف چھ پارے حفظ ہیں"; sent to the river, he met an elder, unnamed in the book, who had him pour water over his hands and "خوش ہو کر آپ کے منہ پر پانی کے چھینٹے مارے", and "اس کی برکت سے آپ نے اس سال رمضان المبارک میں پورا قرآن شریف سنایا" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246). After the Ramadan recitation "حضرت شیخ بہلول نے آپ کو امام بنایا", Bahlol made him *imam* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246). In Chishti's telling a *majzub* had ordered Bahlul "یہاں سے براہ لاہور کو جاؤ اور [OCR?] حسین کو راہ ہدایت[OCR?] دکھلاؤ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 49); the boy had recited all he knew by the seventh day of the *tarawih*, and the river water and a prayer that he be made "فقیر عارف" followed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 50), and he completed the Quran that Ramadan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 51–52). Chishti dates Bahlul's coming, after "حضرت پیر محمد صاحب حقیقت الفقر[OCR?]", with the line "سال پنجاہ و پنج و نہ صد بود", which names no era (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 52). Kugle gives another source of the gift: "Shah Hussayn himself is reported to have met the perennial spiritual guide Khidr in his boyhood. Khidr poured out some water from his jug into his own palm, and Hussayn drank from his hand. This transmission of spiritual blessing allowed him to finish memorizing the Qur'an with ease and eventually pushed him toward sainthood in his adult life." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 216, folio 195, ch. 4 n. 23).

Of his master the books say much. Lahori calls him the *khalifa* of Shaykh Bahlul Daryai, famous as a man of *hal*, *jazb*, longing, taste, *wajd* and *sama* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 54, folio 42), and in another entry records that "شیخ لال حسین لاہوری بسبب پیر بھائی ہونے کے ان کا کمال ادب کرتے تھے", that Lal Husain showed Shaykh Musa Khokhar the utmost respect because they were pir-brothers (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 273, folio 261). Kanhaiya Lal writes "شیخ بہلول قادری کا مرید ہوا", that he became the *murid* of Shaykh Bahlol Qadri (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 233, folio 236). Sharib calls his pir "حضرت شیخ بہلول", the "قطب زمان" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 249, folio 245), and writes "حضرت شیخ بہلول نے آپ کو مرید کیا اور خرقہ خلافت سے سرفراز فرمایا", that Bahlol made him a *murid* and honoured him with the *khirqa* of *khilafat*, then took his leave (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246). Chishti carries the chain of *bai'at* from Lal Husain to "حضرت بہلول", and on to "حضرت شہ[OCR?] لطیف بری[OCR?]", then "شاہ محمد مقیم[OCR?]" and "حضرت حیات المیر[OCR?] قادری[OCR?]", the "نبیرہ حضرت غوث الاعظم" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 46–47), and elsewhere names "حضرت [illegible] مادھو لال حسین صاحب [OCR?]" second among the *khalifas* of "حضرت بلاول دریائی [OCR?]", after "حضرت موسی کہوکر [OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 417). Alam writes of "Sheikh Bahlol Dariai, who took him under his wing", a dervish who "had travelled across the wide expanse of the fifteenth-century Islamic world, including Arabia, Mesopotamia, Persia and Afghanistan" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 6–7, folios 6–7). Haroon Khalid reports his guide Iqbal Qaiser's view that Behlol, whose shrine is at 'Tiba Shah Behlol', "was the spiritual master of Shah Hussain" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 16, ch. 10, folio not stated).

The years by Data Ganj Bakhsh are, in Sharib's account, an order from that master. Before leaving, Bahlol instructed him "کہ حضرت داتا گنج بخش رحمۃ اللہ علیہ کے مزار پر انوار پر پابندی سے حاضر ہوا کریں", to present himself at the luminous *mazar* regularly (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246), and he "بارہ برس تک نہایت پابندی سے حضرت داتا گنج بخش رحمۃ اللہ علیہ کے مزار پر حاضری دی آخر اس کا صلہ آپ کو مل ہی گیا", gave attendance for twelve years, and in the end the recompense came to him (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 251, folio 247). Chishti too has him at dawn and *ishraq* at Hujwiri's khanqah and *mazar*, "بارہ برس" there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 53). Kugle writes: "For the first half of his life, he lived as a mendicant student, wandering in the empty lands outside the city walls by day and returning at night to stay in the shrine of Lahore's patron saint", ʿAli Hujwiri, known as Data Ganj Bakhsh (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185).

The discipline of those years the books describe hour by hour. Sharib gives twenty-six years in worship, *riyazat* and *mujahida*, with a whole Quran completed daily (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 250, folio 246), and a timetable: nights in recitation; stillness at the riverbank and at Data Ganj Bakhsh's *mazar*; after the dawn prayer to the *maktab* for the *tafsir* lesson until Asr; *zikr* after Asr; *nafl* between Maghrib and Isha; and no variation even in illness (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 250–251, folios 246–247). Chishti calls him "دائم الصوم اور قایم اللیل" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 53), and later has him reciting the Quran until *chasht*, taking the *qailula*, teaching *tafsir* until Asr, and spending the night in the river (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 54). Kugle's portrait of the ascetic before the change: "He used to stand up to his waist in the Ravi River, lips blue from cold, while reciting the Qur'an all day." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 221, folio 200).

Then, around the age of thirty-two, everything changed. The scrupulous scholar became a *malang* — a wandering, dishevelled ecstatic. He set aside the robes and the reputation of a preacher, and took up instead the crimson dress by which he is remembered as “Lal” (the Red) Hussain, dancing the *dhamal* and carrying a flask in his hand that the scandalised took for wine. What had happened, in the language of the Sufis, was that the outward path of the *Shariat* had opened, for Hussain, onto the burning inward path of love — and he chose to walk it in the most confronting way he could.

The books tell the change as the work of one verse of the Quran. Lahori's editor, following *Haqiqat al-Fuqara*, writes that Husain, at first an orthodox Muslim, was reading the *Tafsir-e Madarik* with his teacher Shaykh Saad Allah Lahori, who died in 999 AH / 1590 CE, when the teacher explained "وما الحیوٰۃ الدنیا الا لہو ولعب", and Shah Husain understood the world to be mere play; he told his teacher "مجھے حال درکار ہے قال نہیں", that he needed *hal*, not *qal*, abandoned the student's life and took to the Malamati way (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44). The editor adds that Saad Allah himself often voiced the Malamati school, and quotes Nizam al-Din Ahmad's *Tabaqat-e Akbari* on him: "بروش ملامتیہ سلوک می نمود" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44). Chishti has the *tafsir* with "شیخ سعد اللہ", "تفسیر مدارک[OCR?] و نسفی[OCR?]", the verse of "لہو و لعب", dancing and a dispute (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 54–55); he left the madrasa dancing (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 55), and "اس روز سے آپ نے طریقہ ملامتیہ اختیار کر لیا تا لوگ اوسے نفرت کریں" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 56). In Sharib, after Shaykh Sa'dullah's exposition that the life of this world is "لہو و لعب", a "وجدانی کیفیت" came over him; he began to dance, threw his books into a well, was rid of beard and moustache, went about the lanes and bazaars intoxicated with a cup in his hand, frequented "طوائفوں", and in sum "ملامتیہ[OCR?] طریقہ اختیار کر لیا تھا" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 251, folio 247).

The English books put the turn later. Alam sets it "at the age of thirty-six, while studying with another respected scholar of the time, Sheikh Sa'ad Ullah" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 7, folio 7), cites the passages as Sura Al-Hadid 57:20 and Sura Ash-Sharh 94:1–4, and writes: "The words resonated so deeply with Hussein that he broke into a spontaneous dance of self-liberation"; and again, "In the middle of the prayer, Hussein broke into laughter and ran away when he recited these Quranic verses" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 7, folio 7). Kugle writes: "It was at the age of 36 that he experienced a dramatic spiritual opening", when the verse "The life of the world is nothing but play and pleasurable distraction" was recited (Q 6:32, echoed in 29:64 and 47:36), after which he resolved "to throw off constraints of ascetic piety, legal rectitude, and rational seriousness; he would instead lead his life as a child at play" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185). Sa'dullah, Kugle adds, "argued with him not to take literally" the verse, insisting that its tone was sarcastic (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 232, folio 211).

The master came to see for himself. In Sharib's chapter, headed for the episode "امتحان", the test, Bahlol heard at Chiniot that Husain drank, stayed intoxicated and had strayed from the *shariat*; he came to Lahore, "آپ کو دیکھا اور مطمئن ہو کر واپس تشریف لے گئے" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, pp. 251–252, folios 247–248). Kugle's Shaykh Bahlul "rushed to Lahore, ready to join Sa'dullah in urging him to return to 'the straight path'", but on seeing "Hussayn in ripped red clothes, dancing and drinking wine", he "realized that this was his personal path to religious sincerity. The Shaykh blessed him and returned to his home." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 232, folio 211). Chishti has Bahlul satisfied that "حضرت حسین باحق واصل ہیں" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 56); after Bahlul's death, he writes, Husain "بدستور لاہور میں مرجع خلق عام رہے[OCR?]", danced to the *chang* and *rabab* "واسطے اخفائے[OCR?] حال", and recited the Quran every night in the first watch (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 57).

## The Way of Blame

Hussain belonged, in spirit, to the *Malamatiyya* — the Sufis of the “path of blame,” who deliberately drew the censure of respectable society upon themselves in order to kill the ego’s hunger for esteem, hiding their inner sanctity beneath an outward show of impropriety. To dance and sing and carry a flask through the streets of Mughal Lahore was, for such a mystic, not a fall from grace but a discipline of self-effacement, a refusal of the world’s praise. Inevitably it drew fatwas and denunciations, and at last complaints reached the imperial court: some demanded that this man who seemed to mock the outward forms of religion be put to death.

The most famous story of his life belongs to this moment. Summoned before the ruler — the accounts name the Emperor Jahangir — and challenged over the wine he was said to carry, Hussain is said to have poured out his flask into the cups set before the court: and the liquid ran, in the first cup, as milk; in the second, as honey; and in the third, as the sacred water of Zamzam. The king and his courtiers, astonished, understood that they stood before no ordinary man. “Let him be,” they said; “he belongs to another world — let no one trouble him after this day.” The saint went his way, and the tale has been told ever since as a sign that what the world condemns in the friends of God it does not understand.

The red dress gave him his name, and the books say so in nearly the same words. Lahori writes "طریق ان کا ملامتیہ تھا۔ پوشاک سرخ رکھتے تھے۔ اس لیے لال حسین مشہور ہوئے", that his path was *Malamati*, he wore red dress, and so became famous as Lal Husain; his editor glosses the Malamatiyya as the name of a silsila of free-spirited sufis (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 54, folio 42). Kanhaiya Lal writes "چونکہ یہ بزرگ سرخ پوشاک رکھتا تہا اس سبب سے لال حسین خطاب پایا", that because he wore red clothing he received the title Lal Husain (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 233, folio 236). Kugle calls 'Lal Hussayn' the saint's own nickname, "alluding to his penchant for wearing only red clothing" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 328, folio 307, ch. 4 n. 24). Alam pictures "a rebel fakir dressed in all red, bearing a wine flask in one hand and an earthen bowl in another" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 7, folio 7), notes that "Shah Hussein is known to wander around in a red dress" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 180, folio 180), and reads the red into the poetry as "the colour of passion: lal (red)" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 13, folio 13).

*Malamati* is Alam's word for his path, and he glosses it more than once: "the promising young student turned malamati—one who seeks disgrace and censure—leading his pack of revellers through the town" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 7, folio 7); "as the prescribed norm of a malamati mystic" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 9, folio 9); "For a malamati, the ignominy ensures the grace" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 10, folio 10); and, in his notes to the poems, "Shah Hussein's humility cuts like an axe", "for he's a malamati, blameworthy, an outcast, a rebel, a transgressor of the bogus conventions of love, the one who breaks free" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 180, folio 180). "Hussein's malamati-style self-humiliation reaches its apogee in the line: I'm the bitch at your doorstep" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 11, folio 11). Haroon Khalid writes of "a wandering malamati Sufi in Lahore known by the name of Shah Hussain, a spectacular Punjabi poet" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 16, ch. 10, folio not stated), and the introduction to Rafat's selection of Bulleh Shah hears in that later poet "The malamatia overtones, reminiscent of his great predecessor Shah Husain" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 24, folio not stated). Sharib joins the blame to a second word: "آپ نے ملامتیہ طریقہ اختیار کیا تھا، آپ کا مشرب قلندرانہ تھا", he had adopted the Malamati way and his *mashrab* was *qalandarana* (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 254, folio 250). Chishti has "طریقہ حضرت لال حسین کا مخذ[OCR?] و بانہ[OCR?] قلندرانہ تھا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 610).

Two of the English books give him an order other than the Malamati. Kugle calls him "a Sufi of the Qadiri community and a Punjabi poet" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 202, folio not stated), writes that "He also joined the Qadiri Sufi lineage at a young age, in which he learned the value of poetic eloquence and ascetic rigor" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185, ch. 4 n. 7), and says that Shaykh Bahlul Darya'i initiated him into the Qadiri lineage at Chiniot, a village outside Lahore, when he was about ten years old; the Qadiris, he adds, had a reputation for being 'orthodox', but in Shah Hussayn's day they also included freethinking and antinomian characters (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 326, folio 305, ch. 4 n. 7). Kugle never calls him Malamati. He calls him a Qalandar, as a mode of life: "Shah Hussayn was one of these recklessly bold Sufis known by the label 'Qalandar,' whom we know as antinomian" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 203, folio 182); "Shah Hussayn's red clothes and his face shaved of facial hair marked him as a Qalandar." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 220, folio 199); "Shah Hussayn represents a long tradition in Sufism of Qalandar rebelliousness and homoerotic sensuality" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 229, folio 208). Schimmel calls him "the ecstatic mystic of the Qadiri order" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, pp. 170–171, folios 152–153), and Kanhaiya Lal, as above, gives a pir, Bahlol Qadri, rather than an order (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 233, folio 236).

What the blame looked like in the streets the books describe in lists. Kugle: "a widely known romance with another man, and he combined them with public forms of abandon: singing, drumming, dancing, wine drinking, shaving off all facial hair, trespassing divisions of social class, voluntary poverty. He displayed these practices in public to draw out from others their hypocrisy." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, pp. 231–232, folios 210–211). "He took to drinking wine" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 207, folio 186); "In addition to drinking wine in public, Shah Hussayn took to singing and playing musical instruments while dancing in the streets with his band of devoted friends and followers" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 207, folio 186), all "on very public display in the streets of sixteenth-century Lahore" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 206, folio 185). His reputation as a libertine, *laund*, and a drunk, *rind*, Kugle writes, was widely known (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 232, folio 211). Kugle also quotes a hagiographic description: "He wears red clothes, drinks wine openly, sings and plays music, and is surrounded by smooth-faced young men as beautiful as the moon. He dances with them in the street in front of his home. He shaves his beard off but lets his mustache grow long." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212, ch. 4 n. 57). In Alam's portrait "drunkenly he roams the streets of Lahore in the company of fellow carousers" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). Sharib writes "آپ کو ناچ گانے کا بہت شوق تھا", that he had a great fondness for dance and song, and "آپ لباس فقر میں اپنے آپ کو چھپائے رکھتے تھے", that he kept himself hidden in the dress of *faqr*; "روزانہ صبح کو قرآن مجید کی تلاوت کرتے تھے، رات ہنسنے اور رونے میں گزار دیتے تھے، آپ نشیلی چیزوں کا استعمال بھی کرتے تھے", daily recitation in the morning, nights passed in laughter and weeping, and the use of intoxicating things as well (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 254, folio 250).

Chishti preserves his sayings on the word فقر, letter by letter: ف for فقر و فاقہ و فنا, ق for قناعت and قرب حق, ر for ریاضت and رضا; and he records that the *sajjada nashin* holds a بیاض "بدست خط خاص اونکے", in the saint's own hand, on the five letters of درویش, such as د for درد دل and ش for شکر حق and شرم (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 46).

Lahori's editor gives the life a different close. It is a fact, he writes, citing Abdullah Khweshgi Qasuri's *Maarij al-Wilayat*, that in his last years Shah Husain repented of all acts contrary to the *shariah*, became regular in fasting and prayer, and died in that state (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44). He quotes Shaykh Muhammad Tahir Lahori, who died in 1040 AH, an extremely *shariah*-bound *khalifa* of the Mujaddid Alf-e Sani: "اگر مجھے علمائے ظاہر کے طعنوں کا خدشہ نہ ہوتا تو میں اکثر شیخ حسین کے مزار پر جا کر استمداد کرتا", "If I did not fear the taunts of the exoteric ulama, I would often go to Shaikh Husain's mazar and seek help", and takes it both as confirmation of the repentance and as "بین ثبوت", clear proof, that Shah Husain was an orthodox Muslim whose *wilayat* was accepted (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 56, folio 44).

## Before the Police Chief, the Judge and the Emperor

Kugle tells the confrontation with authority as a story in three trials. "These actions inevitably brought Shah Hussayn in conflict with the authorities of Lahore: the police chief, the chief judge, and finally the emperor himself." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212). It opens in "a large public square" before the high walls of the Red Fort in Lahore, where crowds come to see the execution of "rebels against the Mughal emperor, highway robbers, and tax evaders"; "Suddenly, a very different sort of man is brought forward in chains" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 203, folio 182). "He wears ragged scarlet clothes. His head is shaved, and his beard is shaved clean. He walks into the public square, laughing without fear" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 204, folio 183). Kugle does not date the scene, and does not say that the sentence was carried out (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 204, folio 183).

The police chief of Lahore, the *kotwal* whom Kugle names Malik Ali (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 239, folio 218), had been asked to keep a watch on Hussayn's misdeeds (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212). He was administering a public punishment in the market when Hussayn, by the side of the road, was caught in flirtatious eye contact with a handsome young man who proved to be the police chief's own son, and the chief "arrested him and had him chained up, charging him with being a heretical innovator in religious matters" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212). He threatened Hussayn with impaling, "a gruesome pantomime of anal rape" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 204, folio 183). In the verse Kugle quotes, the threat runs:

*yours will be a disgraceful death, driven through with a spike / A spike that will go into you from behind / so that your soul will leave you from behind* (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 234, folio 213, ch. 4 n. 58)

Hussayn, "laughing like a woman", answered in verse:

*For what reason do you treat me like this / what sin have I committed, you stupid ass?* (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212)

*I may be a sinner in respect to the religious law / but how have I injured you or the king who sent you? / If my actions are a sin, then I sin against God / but I commit no crime against anyone, you or your king!* (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212)

His poetry, Kugle writes elsewhere, sounded "as laughter in the face of distress through which he confronted the police chief and other critics" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 225, folio 204). The hagiographic sources, he says, picture Shah Hussayn confronting the police chief with a miracle: "the chains kept falling from his ankles no matter how the police chief struggled to secure them." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 239, folio 218). The end of the story belongs to the same sources: "In the end, the police chief himself is impaled to death upon the command of the emperor for having failed him in some unrelated matter." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 239, folio 218). In the opening scene, too, drawn from "a biographical poem on the Sufi's life", "As the police drag him into the square, the chains keep falling off his wrists and ankles" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 204, folio 183).

The second trial was a judge's. "His case came before the Shaykh al-Islam, or chief religious scholar and jurist of the realm, Abd al-Nabi Sultanpuri. The judge approached Shah Hussayn as a 'heretic' rather than for sexual improprieties and questioned him about the pillars of Islam." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 239, folio 218). The answer, in Kugle's English: the first, belief in one God, both men keep; "The second and third are prayer and fasting, which I ignore openly"; the fourth and fifth, "pilgrimage and alms, which you ignore in secret!" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 239, folio 218, ch. 4 n. 66). The counter-charges against the judge were his ruling "that the hajj to Mecca was no longer obligatory for all Muslims" and the allegation that he avoided paying the *zakat* due on the wealth he had accumulated (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 240, folio 219).

Sharib tells the same answer of the *qazi* of Lahore, who saw him dancing to a drum and wished to reprimand him: "پہلا کلمہ توحید اور رسالت… اس میں تو ہم دونوں شریک ہیں۔ دوسرا نماز اور تیسرا روزہ۔ ان دونوں کو میں نے ترک کیا۔ چوتھا زکوٰۃ، پانچواں حج، ان دونوں کو تم نے ترک کیا", the first we share; prayer and fasting I have abandoned; *zakat* and *hajj*, you have abandoned (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 252, folio 248). On the next page, among the closing pages of the chapter, "قاضی صاحب یہ سن کر مسکرائے اور چلے گئے", the *qazi* smiled at the answer and went away (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 253, folio 249).

The third trial was the emperor's, and the books that name him name Akbar. Sharib writes that Akbar summoned him to court after complaints of his "قلندرانہ مشرب", questioned him, and dismissed him "عزت و احترام سے" (Sharib, *Tazkirah Awliya-e Pak o Hind*, p. 253, folio 249). For Kugle, "The emperor called him to court, upon accusations of trickery and rebellion." "The royal inquisition centered on whether Shah Hussayn drank wine in public and whether he was miraculously able to turn wine into milk, water, tea, or punch." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 240, folio 219). According to the hagiographic record, he says, the saint was granted a miracle that turned the emperor's goblet of wine into water and other beverages, and the emperor was convinced (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 240, folio 219). "Akbar acknowledged Hussayn as a great saint and one of the pillars of Lahore's spiritual well-being" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 241, folio 220). Alam gives the legend another turn: "According to legend, the emperor was unimpressed by the wine-to-non-alcoholic-drinks miracle performed by Hussein when he was brought before Akbar for interrogation, and sent him to prison. While Hussein was in the dock, his likeness showed up in the harem attended upon by the royal ladies. Mystified by the miraculous feat, Akbar acknowledged Hussein's credentials as a saint, and set him free." (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 7–8, folios 7–8). His composite portrait from traditional sources has the saint who "breaks off the chains when officials approach to arrest him, baffles Akbar, the reigning emperor of the time, by appearing in his private chambers when he's supposed to be locked up", and who "turns wine into water, sherbet, milk, tea, vinegar and back to wine again" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 6, folio 6). "According to Muhammad Pir's Haqiqat al-Fuqra, when Emperor Akbar asked Hussein for any wish to be granted, Hussein requested he never be summoned to the royal court again" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 181, folio 181), which Alam offers as evidence of a 'note of anti-establishment'.

Chishti, citing *Haqiqat al-Fuqara*, gives the charge laid before Akbar: "داڑہی منڈا کر لباس لال سرح[OCR?] پہنتا ہی اور شراب پی کر رقص کنان[OCR?] [illegible] پہر تا ہی[OCR?]", and "اور دعوے ولایت کرنا ہو" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 63). He names among the saint's devotees "شاہزادہ سلیم", with "خواجہ دولت خاں", "خاں خاناں[OCR?]" and "ابو الفضل[OCR?]" among others, says that "آپ کسی کی طرف کوئی التجا نہ لاتے تہے", and that Akbar "دل جان سی آپ کا خادم ہوا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 65); at the head of the miracles he sets "حضرت نور الدیں جہانگیر بادشاہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 59). Alam notes the silence of the court's own records: "There is no account of Hussein in the annals of Akbar, though the Mughals were known for their meticulous record-keeping", and "No mention of Hussein is made even in Tuzk-i-Jehangiri" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 8, folio 8).

A Mughal noble's errand is told three ways. Kugle: "As one of Akbar's chief nobles, Abd al-Rahim Khan-i Khanan, was traveling with an army toward Sindh, he stopped in Lahore to receive the blessing of Shah Hussayn. The Mughal armies successfully conquered Thatta in Sindh, and Hussayn's reputation spread." "The admiration of Mughal nobles protects him from local censure, and reciprocally, he becomes a saint who protects Mughal rule." (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 241, folio 220). Chishti writes that the country of Thatta was granted to the Khan-e Khanan "حسب الدعا[OCR?] مے[OCR?] حضرت حسین لاہوری" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 68). Alam sets one of the poems against the story: "According to some hagiographers, Hussein gave the blessing of a military victory to Khan-e-Khana when he came as a supplicant to the saint; however, this kafi points out something different: a caveat of mortality to the powerful" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 184, folio 184).

The rebel of the current account appears in Alam too. "Even hagiographers like Muhammad Pir and Chisti admit that Hussein kept eluding Akbar's police till he was finally nabbed at the hanging of 'Dullah Bhatti, though they make it sound as if he was attending the event as a mere spectator" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 15, folio 15). Writing of the Punjab in the saint's times, he points to "the relevant historical account of a rebellion brewing in Punjab led by Abdullah Bhatti, commonly known as 'Dullah Bhatti, who was captured and hanged in public on Akbar's orders" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 14, folio 14).
