Name: Shrine of Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari
Location: Gandawah (Gandava), Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Annual urs
Description:
The shrine of Hazrat Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari is one of the principal Sufi dargahs of the Jhal Magsi district of Balochistan, situated at Gandawah (Gandava), the historic administrative town of the Kachhi plain. Its saint bore the *Bukhari* lineage, marking descent from the influential family of Sayyids who traced their origins to Bukhara and whose forebears — most famously Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif — spread the *Suhrawardi* devotional tradition across Sindh and the southern Punjab. The tomb is locally admired as one of the finest examples of shrine architecture in the district, and it stands among a cluster of Sufi graves in the Gandawah area that together form an important sacred landscape for the surrounding Baloch and Brahui communities. Devotees from across the district and beyond visit to seek blessing and intercession, and the saint's *urs* is observed as the chief event of the devotional year, drawing pilgrims, *qawwali* and the distribution of food. As with many shrines of interior Balochistan, the documented history of the saint is thin and his dates uncertain, so his biography is best treated as living tradition rather than established record; the *Bukhari* attribution and the shrine's standing as a regional pilgrimage centre are, however, well attested locally. It should not be confused with the separate and larger Dargah of Fateh Pur Sharif (Pir Rakhail Shah), also in the Jhal Magsi district. Independent confirmation of the tomb's standing among Gandava's principal monuments comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage, which names "the tombs of Ayub Shah Bukhari, Murad Kaleri, and Meeri of Khan-e-Qalat" together with the Jamia Mosque of Gandava among "the best examples of Islamic architecture in the area," though the article gives no further individual detail — no dates or architectural description — specific to this tomb.

Name: Shrine of Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar (Shah Ali Akbar Shamsi)
Events: Annual urs
Description:
The Shrine of Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar Shamsi stands in the historic neighbourhood of Suraj Miani in Multan, the celebrated "city of saints", and is counted among the oldest and most beautiful mausoleums of the city. Shah Ali Akbar is remembered as a descendant — by tradition of the eighth generation — of the great Sufi Shah Shams Sabzwari of Multan, and it is said that after the death of his father he settled permanently in the city. His tomb, built of brick in the octagonal, tiered form so characteristic of Multan, is often likened to a smaller version of the famous shrine of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, and it belongs to the classic tradition of Multani funerary architecture with its glazed tilework and tapering silhouette. According to inscriptions and local tradition, construction of the mausoleum began in 993 AH (about 1585 CE) and took some fifteen years to complete; it is said to have been raised by the saint's grandson, who is himself buried within the complex, and the work is attributed to the builders Ibrahim and Rajab, sons of the noted architect Musa Lahori. Despite its remarkable beauty and its importance to the architectural history of Multan, the shrine has often been described as one of the city's more neglected monuments. It remains a place of *ziyarat* and hosts an annual *urs* in the saint's honour. Also known by the alternate name Kabuli Mohallah, the shrine's compound is registered as a protected monument under the Antiquity Act of 1975 by the Directorate General of Archaeology, Punjab, whose own listing describes the building's brick construction as embellished with panels of glazed tiles, three arched panels on each side surmounted by a series of merlons set on bold moldings, its lower walls plastered in lime, and an interior decorated with panels of fresco painting — though the same listing notes this fresco work and lime plaster have been considerably damaged by the smoke of mustard-oil lamps and votive candles over the years. In 2019 the Punjab Archaeology Department proposed a Rs 30 million conservation and restoration project for the mausoleum, and by November of that year a related tender for a Rs 27.104 million project was opened for bids, though press reporting does not clarify whether this represents the same project re-costed or a later phase of the work.

- "Govt approves Rs30m to restore historic Multan site," *The Express Tribune*, 21 May 2019.
- Directorate General of Archaeology, Government of Punjab, "Tomb of Shah Ali Akbar & His Mother, Multan," https://archaeology.punjab.gov.pk/tomb_shahaliakbar, accessed 16 August 2026.

Name: Shrine of Hazrat Shah Daula Daryai
Events: Annual three-day urs (Auqaf-administered); langar
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of *Hazrat Shah Daula Daryai* stands in the city of Gujrat, in the fertile plain between the Chenab and Jhelum rivers in the Punjab. It commemorates a Sufi saint of the Mughal period, remembered above all as a builder of bridges, wells and *sarais* (rest-houses) and as a benefactor of the poor, the traveller and the afflicted. His epithet *Daryai* — from *darya*, "river" — is traditionally explained by his works of construction across the region's torrential streams. For nearly four centuries the *darbar* has been a focus of popular devotion in central Punjab; it is also, more painfully, the site around which one of South Asia's most persistent and troubling folk traditions grew up — that of the so-called "Shah Daula's mice" (*chuhas*), children affected by microcephaly who were historically associated with the shrine. The account below treats the saint first, and then addresses that tradition factually and with the medical understanding it requires.

Three books speak of the saint and his tomb directly, each from a different century and a different vantage. Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* describes him, in its account of the suba of Lahore and the town of Gujrat, as once the slave of a man of Sialkot who became the town's great builder and benefactor, and records that near that city ("درنزدیکی ان شهر") his tomb is a place of visitation for people of every class, "بزرگوار زیارتگاه طبقات خلایق است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514). Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, a nineteenth-century register of the saints of the Punjab, gives him entry no. 124 under the name "شاہ دولا دریائی گجراتی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), with a spiritual chain, a death date in a chronogram, and a picture of his household in his lifetime. And Jamal Malik's chapter in Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu's *Embodying Charisma* prefaces its reading of Ahmad Nadîm Qâsimî's Urdu story 'Bain' ('Dirge'), which is set at this shrine, with a historical sketch of the saint and his cult drawn from colonial and *malfûzât* sources; the volume also carries a photograph captioned "The shrine of Shâh Daulah" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 8, folio not stated).

The three books spell the name in their own ways. Bhandari writes شاه دولا; Lahori's entry writes "دولا", while the editor's source list and index in the same edition write "دولہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 317, folio 305); Malik writes "Shâh Daulah", and inside Qâsimî's story the saint is "Sân'în Daule Shâh" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

## The Life of the Saint

Reliable dates for Shah Daula are difficult to fix, and the sources differ; he is traditionally said to have lived roughly between 1581 and 1675, and to have settled in Gujrat in the early seventeenth century — some accounts placing this in the reign of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, others in that of Akbar. He is said to have travelled in his youth to the neighbourhood of Sialkot, where he became the disciple of a Suhrawardi *faqir* remembered as Shah Saidan Sarmast, serving at his master's *khanqah* with great devotion before being entrusted with its care. He later established his own *khanqah* at Gujrat, at the place formerly known as Garhi Shah Daula.

## Descent and Early Years

Malik gives the saint a birth name: "Shâh Daulah—whose birth name was Qâsim —lived in Mughal times and died at an advanced age around AH 1676 in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). His descent, Malik writes, is contested: "His ancestors were Afghans, but it is also claimed that he was a Sayyid (descendant of the Prophet)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). Of his youth he writes: "After a turbulent childhood he became supervisor of the treasury of a local official, and also worked as a mendicant and an ordinary labourer for some time" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

Bhandari's account, which he introduces with "گویند" (it is said), begins differently. At first, he writes, Shah Daula was the slave ("غلام") of a resident of Sialkot whose name is printed "کهابدهره[OCR?]", the reading uncertain in the printed text. He loved the faqirs and served "حضرت میان سیدنا(۱)" devotedly; the editor's footnote gives the variant "سیدنام[OCR?]" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

## The Master and the Turning

In Bhandari's telling, the change in Shah Daula came at his master's deathbed. When Mian Sayyidna was about to die, he cast "نظر فیض اثر" on Shah Daula; Shah Daula's state changed and "بانوار عرفان شبستان باطن روشن گشت". He then left Sialkot and settled in Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Bhandari adds: "از بس که روشن دل بود خزاین غیب نمودار مے گشت": because his heart was so illumined, treasures of the unseen became manifest to him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

Malik's sketch gives a longer apprenticeship and a quarrel: "He then spent twelve years at the feet of a Suhrawardi Sufi, but it is recorded too that he was initiated into the Qadiri order" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). "Due to some disputes with the local people of Sialkot, he migrated from there and, after some years, moved to Gujrat", Malik continues, 'in obedience to divine instructions' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## The Spiritual Chain

Lahori sets the saint at the end of a long chain that runs back, through Rajan Qattal of Uch, to Baha al-Din Multani. Shah Daula, he writes, was the disciple and *khalifa* of Shaikh Sina Sarmast; he of Shah Monga; he of Shah Kabir; he of Shaikh Shahr Allah, a name whose reading is uncertain in the printed text; he of Shaikh Yusuf; he of Pir Burhan; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din; he of Shaikh Badr al-Din; he of Shaikh Ismail Qureshi; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din Rajan Qattal Uchi; he of Shaikh Rukn al-Din Abu al-Fath Multani; he of Shaikh Sadr al-Din Arif; and he of Shaikh Baha al-Din Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). He adds that the saint also received grace from the Chishti line: "خاندان چشت اہل بہشت سے بھی ان کو فیض کامل حاصل ہوا", complete *faiz* from the Chishti family too (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

Lahori counts him "پنجاب کے مشہور بزرگوں میں سے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186), a man of lofty stations and marvels, of *jazb*, *ishq*, *zuhd* and *riyazat*, and "جامع فتوحات ظاہری و باطنی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

## The Saint's Household

Lahori pictures the saint's establishment in his lifetime as a royal one: "ان کی سرکار بادشاہوں کی سرکار کے مانند تھی۔ ہزاروں نوکر چاکر گھوڑا پالکی دروازہ پر حاضر رہتے تھے" — a court like the court of kings, with thousands of servants, horses and palanquins waiting at his door (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). And "اہل حاجت کا ہجوم ہر وقت رہتا تھا": the crowd of those in need was there at every hour (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

Bhandari describes the same throng and the saint's open hand. In his lifetime "عالم عالم خلایق" came from every quarter for *ziyarat* and offered "از نقد و جنس فراوان نذورات"; he gave visitors and petitioners more than they had brought, a generosity such that "سخاوت تمام عمر حاتم عشر عشیر ان نشود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik, from his sources, records the breadth of the saint's following and a refusal: he was popular among "Muslims as well as Hindus, became famous for his miracles and received large gifts" in kind, "but refused to accept land grants" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## The Death of the Saint

The books give the year of his death in several ways. Lahori writes: "وفات حضرت کی سال ایک ہزار پچھتر میں واقع ہوئی اور مادہ تاریخ لفظ خدا دوست ہے" — he died in the year 1075 AH, and the chronogram of his death is the phrase "خدا دوست" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). The edition's modern editor, in a footnote on the same entry, gives instead "۱۰۸۷ھ [OCR?] / ۱۶۷۶ع [OCR?] میں انتقال کیا", with both figures uncertain in the printed text, citing Mushtaq Ram Gujrati's *Karamat Nama*, owned by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184, folio 182). Bhandari dates the death by the reign of Alamgir: "بالآخر درسنه هفدهم[OCR?] عالمگیری بعالم بقا رحلت فرمود", in the seventeenth regnal year of Alamgir, the ordinal uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik's sketch says he "died at an advanced age around AH 1676 in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). The site's own account gives 1675.

## The Builder of Bridges

What is most consistently remembered of him is not doctrine but works of public benefit. He is credited with constructing bridges over seasonal watercourses — including, by tradition, a bridge over the Nala Dek — together with wells, mosques and rest-houses along the routes of travel, at a time when such infrastructure eased both trade and pilgrimage across the Punjab. He is also remembered for his *langar*, his charity to the destitute, and his care for animals and for people living with disabilities. In this he embodies a distinctively practical, service-oriented sanctity: a saint honoured less for miracles than for the tangible relief of hardship.

Bhandari makes this the heart of his account. Shah Daula settled in the *qasba* of Gujrat ("دران قصبه استقامت اختیار کرده"), built tanks, wells and mosques ("تالاب ها و چاهها و مساجد احداث نموده"), and bridged ("قنطره بست") the Chenab, which came down from the hills and used to damage the town (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). He raised buildings and bridges in many places, above all a bridge on the highway ("درشاهراه") over the river Deg, five *kos* from Eminabad in the direction of Lahore ("پنجگروهی امن اباد جانب لاهور"), a work so solid "که از احدی صاحب دولتان چنین عمارت متین نشود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). The bridge became a landmark: in his description of the Deg's course, Bhandari has the river pass "پایان پل شاه دولا که برشاهراه واقع است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516).

Bhandari credits the saint with the making of the town itself. Gujrat, he writes, "از ابتدا این قصبه چندان رونق نداشت" until Shah Daula settled there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515), and his settling "موجب ازدیاد ابادی و افزونی رونق گشت" — made the town grow in people and prosperity (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).

Malik reads the saint's two titles through the same works. During his life, he writes, the saint devoted himself to "works of public utility" and to the construction of religious buildings, and this is why he was called *Daulah*, which Malik glosses 'wealth'; his building of bridges, especially, earned him the second title, glossed 'one affiliated to water' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). At that point in the text the printed form of the second title is uncertain; elsewhere in the chapter it is *Daryâ'î*.

## The Shrine

His tomb, surmounted by a dome and set beside a spacious mosque, dates in its essentials from the seventeenth century, though the structure was substantially rebuilt in the late nineteenth century (traditionally 1898) and has been repaired and extended since. Since the mid-twentieth century the shrine has been administered by the Punjab Auqaf (Religious Affairs) Department, which now organises the annual three-day *urs* with arrangements for *langar*, sanitation and security, and with gatherings devoted to the saint's life and teaching.

Lahori, writing in the 1870s, calls the tomb a living place of pilgrimage: "مزار گوہر بار شہر پنجاب گجرات میں زیارت گاہ خلق ہے" — his mazar in the city of Gujrat, Punjab, is a place of pilgrimage for the people (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). Bhandari had placed it "درنزدیکی ان شهر", near the town, as a place of visitation for people of every class (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514).

Malik gives the reconstruction one date: the shrine "had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). It is the only date for the building in his chapter, which names no founder, no *sajjada nashin* and no custodian family.

## Endowment and Administration

The shrine, Malik writes, held no land: "the lack of regular income at the dargâh, since no land was attached to it, resulted in the holy men's total dependence on the alms and offering of the followers", and colonial authors also suspected the followers of trafficking in women, a suspicion Malik reports from Ibbetson and Maclagan (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He quotes the editor of the *Indian Antiquary* on "the absence of landed property in possession of the band, or any recognized right to succession to the leadership, and the entire dependence on the earnings" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Of the modern administration he writes of "this Sufi tomb, which was taken over by the Pakistan Auqaf Department in the 1960s" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193). The takeover, in his reading, did not displace the older authority on the spot: "even the nationalisation policy of the Auqaf Department since the 1960s could not totally change the perceptions deeply rooted in the minds of the rural population and the authority exercised by the shrine administrator, the mujâwir, who ideally represents state power" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

## Fertility, Justice and Punishment

Malik sums up the shrine's reputation in a phrase: "The sanctuary of Shâh Daulah thus has a particular reputation—fertility, justice and punishment" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He observes too that "the dargâh is a female domain, at least in quantitative terms—in contrast to mosques, which are frequented by men" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 208, folio 197), while adding elsewhere that "the power in shrines is usually held by men" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 214, folio 203).

## Devotion and Practice

The site's account describes an annual three-day *urs* under Auqaf administration, with *langar*. The books consulted give no date, month or duration for the *urs*.

Malik, writing of the shrine's older practice, describes the vow of a child. "The custom used to be to leave the child, as soon as it was weaned, at Shah Daulah's khanqah [Sufi lodge], as an offering to him"; after the saint's death, devotees "would make a vow either to present the child when born or make an offering to the shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). He analyses the exchange at the tomb as "a kind of a bargain between the parents and the mujâwir, like the mahr (bridewealth): the parents are declared dwellers of paradise (jannatî—without intercession of any authority) by the shrine administrator. In response they leave the child—the present (ni‘mat) —as a trust (amânat) at the dargâh" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 211, folio 200).

## The "Chuhas" of Shah Daula: Folklore and the Medical Reality

No account of this shrine can avoid the tradition of the *chuhas* — a word meaning "mice" or "rats" in Punjabi — the name long given to microcephalic children associated with the *darbar*. This tradition must be approached with care, both because it concerns vulnerable and disabled human beings and because it has frequently been sensationalised. The essential facts, as documented by observers and scholars since the nineteenth century, are these.

Microcephaly is a medical condition in which the head and brain are abnormally small, typically accompanied by intellectual disability; it has recognised genetic and environmental causes and occurs in populations everywhere. At Gujrat, individuals with this condition came to be linked with Shah Daula's shrine through a folk belief — first recorded in print in January 1839 by the observer Shahamat Ali — that childless women who prayed for offspring at the *darbar* would be granted a child, the first of whom must, according to the legend, be dedicated to the shrine and would be born with the characteristic small head. Such dedicated children were called *chuhas* and were often maintained at, or associated with, the shrine.

From the mid-nineteenth century onward the phenomenon attracted European medical and ethnographic attention, and with it arose the sensational speculation that the small heads were produced deliberately, by binding or by fitting clamps or vessels to the skulls of infants. This claim has never been substantiated: no such instrument has ever been found, no such procedure has ever been witnessed, and medical authorities regard the intentional production of microcephaly in this manner as implausible without causing fatal injury. The modern consensus is that the *chuhas* were, and are, individuals with naturally occurring microcephaly whose condition was interpreted through the lens of local religious belief and who were, in effect, drawn into the economy of the shrine — historically, in some periods, being sent out as itinerant beggars. It should be stressed that the folk belief linking the condition to the saint's blessing or curse has no basis in fact and is not endorsed here; it is recorded only as a documented social phenomenon.

Malik's chapter, drawing on colonial sources, records the same tradition in the words of its time. The shrine, he writes, "is particularly known for its Chûhâs or Rat-children, who are without understanding or the power of speech. After some initial training they are passed on to a faqîr (religious mendicant) and made to beg in the name of Shâh Daulah" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). A further passage describes a band or order of faqirs living off these children and "the convenient existence of an important shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). Malik reports, without endorsing it, the colonial suspicion that the children were "artificially produced after their birth as ordinary infants", citing Ibbetson and Maclagan (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195). He also reports a physiological explanation from Sharif Kunjahi's modern life of the saint: "the bad conscience of parents, particularly mothers, set free certain chemical reactions that caused this peculiarity" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Malik argues that the cult is late. Because it is absent from "contemporary and even later malfûzât and biographical accounts" of the saint, he concludes: "It therefore seems likely that this cult arose only later, by the end of the nineteenth century—after the shrine had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).

Reform came in the twentieth century. When the Auqaf Department assumed control of the shrine in the mid-twentieth century, it acted to forbid both the abandonment of such children to the *darbar* and the alleged deforming practices, and the population of *chuhas* associated with the site steadily declined. By the early twenty-first century observers reported that only one or two remained. The episode endures chiefly as a cautionary study for historians of medicine, disability and popular religion, in which a genuine medical condition, human vulnerability, exploitation and folk piety became tragically entangled.

## Legends and Miracles

The legend behind the *chuhas*, as Malik quotes it from colonial sources, runs: "Shah Daulah, like other saints, could procure the birth of a child for a couple desiring one, but the first child born in response to his intercession would be a Chuha—brainless, small-headed, long-eared and rat-faced" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). "After the saint's death the miracle continued, but in a modified way": where a promised gift was withheld, "the spirit of the offended saint so worked on the parents that the next child was born a Chuha, and all subsequent children as well, until the original vow was fulfilled" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). These are the words of the legend as the colonial sources recorded it, not a description of any person.

Malik attributes to the same colonial sources a second miracle: "through his charismatic or miraculous powers (karâmât) Shâh Daulah was able to control female infanticide, which was widespread in Jammu State at the time" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

Bhandari's single marvel is an inward one: because the saint's heart was so illumined, treasures of the unseen became manifest to him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Lahori calls him a man of marvels and of *jazb*, ecstatic attraction (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184).

## The Shrine in Fiction: Qâsimî's 'Bain'

Ahmad Nadîm Qâsimî's Urdu story 'Bain' ('Dirge'), as Malik reads it, "deals with the activities in and around the dargâh (court, shrine) of Shâh Daulah Daryâ'î in Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193), although the story does not mention the *chuha* cult, to "which Nadîm's story does not, however, refer directly" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 204, folio 193). What follows is the story's world, not a report of the shrine.

In the story the shrine "had become an institution of justice, symbolised by the holy hand of Shâh Daulah, which, in order to judge, would rise from the grave" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 207, folio 196). Malik gives the passage in full: "The upper part [sar bâne kî taraf se] of the holy grave opened and the Pîr stretched out his holy hand [dast-e mubârak]. The culprit then was drawn to the shrine [mazâr sharîf] from wherever he was, laid his neck into the holy hand of the Sân'înjî [the pîr] and died on the spot [dher honâ]" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199). "Therefore, nobody dared to neglect Sân'în Daule Shâh's orders" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

The *mujâwir* rules through a dream. He demands that the girl Rano recite at the *dargâh* for three days, which "Shâh Daulah had ordered in a dream" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 207, folio 196); otherwise, the villagers are warned, "Sân'în Daule Shâhjî would put all villagers to fire and ash" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 209, folio 198).

The *urs* frames the story's crisis: "the girl's maturity or sexualisation and the marriage proposal coincide with the anniversary of the holy man's death, ‘urs, the unification of the pîr with God" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 209, folio 198), and "During the ‘urs the girl falls victim to the corrupted society" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 211, folio 200). The shrine's kitchen and bath-house become the scene of defiance: Rano flings the skirt her parents bring "into the burning coals of the public kitchen (langar)", and her father later throws the *mujâwir*'s shroud "into the burning coals of the fire heating the water for the great ablution (ghusl)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 212, folio 201).

Malik's verdict on what the story shows is severe: "It shows that the shrine cult has become a falsehood void of any mysticism, or, in other words, an expression of corrupt political power" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 208, folio 197), and "fear is the prime motivational force inducing the villagers and adepts to be loyal to the moral authority emanating from the shrine" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 210, folio 199).

## In Verse

The books carry little verse on Shah Daula. What they hold is a chronogram. Lahori's entry closes the saint's life with a two-word *tarikh*, "خدا دوست", which he gives as encoding the year of death, 1075 AH; in his words, "مادہ تاریخ لفظ خدا دوست ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186).

The same book closes with a verse chronogram of its own, by Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, which gives the year 1292 AH. It speaks of the scope of the whole book, the saints of the Punjab, and not of this saint:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

*A chronogram on the book's own subject, the saints of the Punjab; the book gives no English.* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 282, folio 270)

## The Saint in Writing

The books point to a small literature on the saint. The *Hadiqat al-Awliya*'s editor catalogues, as his source for the death date, item no. 64, "مشتاق رام گجراتی : کرامت نامہ ۱۱۳۲ھ (حالات شاہ دولہ دریائی گجراتی) مملوکہ سید شرافت نوشاہی", a *Karamat Nama* of 1132 AH on the life of Shah Daula, by Mushtaq Ram Gujrati, owned by Sayyid Sharafat Naushahi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 296, folio 284). The same list has item no. 235, "نسیم ایم ایس : تذکرہ شاہ دولہ گجراتی۔ لاہور ۱۹۷۰ء" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 304, folio 292).

Malik names his own sources as "historical and biographical accounts as well as on malfûzât literature (namely, the imputed speeches and utterances of holy men)", among them Ibbetson's *Glossary* and the work of Sharîf Kunjâhî (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). Kunjâhî's book, *Hadrat Shâh Daulah Daryâ'î Gujrâtî: Hayât o ta'lîmât*, was published in Lahore in 1985 by the Punjab Auqaf Department's imprint, Markaz Ma'ârif Awliyâ Mahkamah Awqâf Punjâb (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 217, folio 206). It is in this title alone that Malik's chapter calls the saint *Gujrâtî*.

## Setting: Gujrat

The books that describe the town of Gujrat speak of the place, not of the shrine.

Bhandari places it in the Chaj doab between the Chenab and the Bihat: "در دوابه چونهت گجرات قصبه ایست". It was settled ("اباد شده") under the emperor Akbar, and villages were taken out of the pargana of Sialkot to make it a pargana of its own (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Under the heading "در بیان مقرر گردیدن پرگنہ گجرات و امن آباد" he tells how the pargana was made: "این تمام سرزمین داخل سیالکوت بود و قوم جت ورائچ[OCR?] متسلط بودند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 177). In the regnal year 37 or, by another account, 42, as the emperor was travelling from Lahore to Kashmir, a body of Gujars came to him after the Chenab crossing to complain of oppression by the Jats and the Raich, a name uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 176–177). The villages of their *zamindari* were separated off as "پرگنہ موسوم بگجرات[OCR?]", and a small fort and a town were founded, "قلعچہ و قصبہ احداث نموده" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 176). Bhandari does not name Shah Daula in this passage.

The town in Bhandari's own day was a market of the province: "انقصبه پیشگاه هرگونه مردم و جامع اجناس هر دیار و اشیاے نادره روزگار است". Rare swords and *jamdhars* were made there, and "کار چکن زیاده از سیالکوت می شود"; the district bred Iraqi horses, some worth up to "ده هزار روپیه" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Bhandari also sets an imperial episode in the neighbourhood. When the prince Khusrau rebelled and was turned back at the Chenab, he was seen at the ford at dawn, and "میر ابوالقاسم خان و هلال خان خواجه سرا که در حدود گجرات بودند" seized him and carried him to Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 146–145). He says nothing there of the saint or the shrine.

Usborne's annotator to Waris Shah ties the town's name to a tribe: "The Gujars are a famous tribe of the old Punjab who keep animals and sell their milk. They also engage in agriculture on a large scale. A number of Punjab towns, such as Gujranwala, Gujrat and Gujar Khan are named after the Gujar tribe" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 19, folio 18, note 3). Haroon Khalid's informant Iqbal Qaiser dates the town's rise to Akbar: "Gujrat became an important city during the tenure of Akbar. Before that it was a small village. One of Akbar's wives is also buried here" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Khalid's account of the Punjab after the Mughals also has the governor Meer Manu waiting 'near the city of Gujrat' (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 15, ch. 9).

Gujrat has other saints. Khalid writes of a crow saint who "seemed to have quite a following in this historic city", and of the city's major shrines put "on high alert" after a blast in Sindh (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). A poster reproduced in *Embodying Charisma* names a 'Sain Kanwan Wali (Gujrat)' (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 160, folio 149).

The Chenab country around the town is the land of Punjabi romance. Shemeem Burney Abbas begins the tale of Sohni with a potter "who lived in the Gujrat district of the Panjab" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 125, folio not stated), and places Ranjha's clan at Takht Hazara, "now Gujrat District of Pakistan" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 122, folio not stated). Usborne's annotator likewise has Sohni belong to Gujrat, "on the river Chenab", the town's name garbled in the printed edition (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 12, folio 11, note 5).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of death.** The site's account gives 1675, with a birth year of 1581. Lahori gives 1075 AH, with the chronogram "خدا دوست" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). His modern editor gives 1087 AH / 1676, both figures uncertain in the printed text, citing Mushtaq Ram Gujrati's *Karamat Nama* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184, folio 182). Bhandari gives the seventeenth regnal year of Alamgir, the ordinal uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik gives "around AH 1676" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His master's name.** The site's account names Shah Saidan Sarmast. Lahori names Shaikh Sina Sarmast (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). Bhandari names "حضرت میان سیدنا(۱)", with the editor's variant "سیدنام[OCR?]" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik names no master, speaking of twelve years "at the feet of a Suhrawardi Sufi" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His order.** The site's account makes his master a Suhrawardi *faqir*. Lahori traces his chain to Baha al-Din Multani through Rajan Qattal of Uch, and adds complete *faiz* from the Chishti line (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 184). Malik gives a Suhrawardi teacher but records "too that he was initiated into the Qadiri order" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His early life.** The site's account has him travel in his youth to the neighbourhood of Sialkot to become a disciple. Bhandari says he was first the slave of a resident of Sialkot (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik says he became supervisor of a local official's treasury and worked as a mendicant and labourer (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **Why he left Sialkot.** The site's account has him entrusted with his master's *khanqah* before establishing his own at Gujrat. Bhandari has him leave Sialkot after his dying master's glance transformed him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). Malik has him leave "Due to some disputes with the local people of Sialkot", moving to Gujrat after some years in obedience to divine instructions (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **His descent.** Malik gives both accounts himself: Afghan ancestors, and the claim that he was a Sayyid (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).
- **The great bridge.** The site's account names, by tradition, a bridge over the Nala Dek. Bhandari names a bridge over the river Deg on the highway five *kos* from Eminabad toward Lahore, and a bridge on the Chenab at Gujrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515).
- **Where the tomb stands.** The site's account and Lahori place it in the city of Gujrat (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). Bhandari places it "درنزدیکی ان شهر", near the town (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 515–514).
- **When the chuha tradition began.** The site's account says the folk belief was first recorded in print in January 1839 by Shahamat Ali. Malik, from its absence in the early lives of the saint, judges that the cult "arose only later, by the end of the nineteenth century—after the shrine had been reconstructed (1898)" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **The cause of the children's condition.** The site's account holds that they had naturally occurring microcephaly and that deliberate deformation was never substantiated. Malik reports the colonial suspicion that they were "artificially produced after their birth as ordinary infants", and Kunjahi's explanation that the bad conscience of parents set free "certain chemical reactions that caused this peculiarity" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **What the Auqaf takeover changed.** The site's account dates the takeover to the mid-twentieth century and says the Department forbade the abandonment of children, after which their number declined. Malik dates it to the 1960s and writes that it "could not totally change the perceptions deeply rooted in the minds of the rural population and the authority exercised by the shrine administrator" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195).
- **The spelling of the name.** Lahori's entry writes "دولا" and his editor's lists "دولہ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 317, folio 305); Bhandari writes شاه دولا (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515); Malik writes "Daulah", and in one sentence the second title's printed form is uncertain where elsewhere it is *Daryâ'î* (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194).

## Legacy

Shah Daula Daryai is remembered in the Punjab as a saint of works and mercy, whose bridges and wells served the living and whose shrine remains a busy centre of devotion in Gujrat. The disquieting tradition of the *chuhas* that attached itself to his name in later centuries belongs to the social history that grew up around the shrine rather than to the saint himself, and is best understood today through the twin lenses of medical fact and compassion for those who were affected. The *darbar* continues to draw pilgrims, to feed the poor at its *langar*, and to hold its annual *urs* under Auqaf administration.

The books add three witnesses across three centuries. For Bhandari, writing in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, the saint was the man who made Gujrat grow in people and prosperity, the builder of a famous bridge on the Lahore highway, and the saint whose tomb drew people of every class (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515). For Lahori in the 1870s he was a saint of the Punjab whose tomb was a place of pilgrimage and whose death was remembered in a chronogram (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 186). For Malik, writing on Qâsimî's story in a volume of 1998, his shrine had a particular reputation for "fertility, justice and punishment" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 206, folio 195), and had become the setting of one of Urdu fiction's critiques of shrine power.

Name: Shrine of Imam Ali-ul-Haq
Events: Annual urs; devotional music and langar
Description:
## Overview

The shrine of *Hazrat Imam Ali-ul-Haq* — known to the people of Sialkot simply and affectionately as *Imam Sahib* — stands in the heart of the old city of Sialkot in the Punjab, at the spot where the saint is traditionally believed to have died. He is venerated as a warrior-saint and martyr (*shahid*), one of the missionary holy men credited by local tradition with the coming of Islam to this corner of the upper Punjab, and his *darbar* is among the most important devotional sites of the city. It is essential at the outset to distinguish him clearly from the celebrated *Bari Imam* (Syed Abdul Latif Shah Kazmi) of Nurpur Shahan near Islamabad, with whom the similar honorific "Imam" sometimes causes confusion: the figure venerated at Sialkot is a separate personage belonging to the local history of that city. It must also be said plainly that the historical identity of the Sialkot saint is genuinely uncertain, and that the sources concerning him are thin and mutually contradictory; what follows therefore reports the traditions as traditions, and does not attempt to resolve them into a single confident biography.

Three older books in Persian and Urdu add their own testimony. Sujan Rai Bhandari of Batala, writing in Persian in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, writes that in the region of Sialkot lies "خوابگاه امام علی الحق", the resting place of Imam Ali al-Haq, and that his tomb is now a place of visitation (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names him as a companion of the Zanjanis whose tomb in Sialkot is a place of pilgrimage (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269). Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* indexes him as "علی الحق سیالکوٹی", Ali al-Haq of Sialkot (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 324, folio 312), and the bibliography of its modern edition lists a *Waqa'i Sialkot* on his martyrdom (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 299, folio 287). None of the three describes the buildings of the shrine or records an *ʿurs*. Where they differ from one another and from the traditions current at Sialkot, the differences are set out side by side below.

## The Saint and the Tradition

Two broad traditions circulate about Imam Ali-ul-Haq, and they cannot easily be reconciled. According to the more commonly repeated local account, he lived in the medieval period — often placed in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, and sometimes associated with the reign of the Delhi sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq — and came as a preacher and holy warrior who is said to have brought a large part of the surrounding population to Islam, so transforming Sialkot into a predominantly Muslim town. In this telling he was ultimately martyred by an unbeliever; one version relates that he was struck down while at prayer in a mosque, another that he fell in battle against the local Hindu ruler.

A quite different and considerably older dating derives from a single source: the nineteenth-century Persian chronicle *Chār Bāgh-i-Panjāb* of Ganesh Das Wadhera. This account maintains that "Imam Ali al-Haq" led an army from Arabia to Sialkot around 970–971 CE, where he was killed in a battle with a local raja named Sahan Pal (who is said to have taken the title Salbahan), and that many of his companions perished with him; it further connects his death with a subsequent invasion of the Punjab by Sultan Sabuktigin of Ghazni. It is important to note that this tenth-century account rests on Ganesh Das alone and is corroborated by no other historical work, so it cannot be treated as established fact. Taken together, these divergent traditions — differing by some three or four centuries — mean that the saint's true dates, origins and circumstances remain unresolved. What is consistent across the accounts, and what matters most for the shrine's devotional life, is the memory of a holy man who came from afar, who is credited with the Islamisation of Sialkot, and who died a martyr on the spot now marked by his tomb.

## The Saint in the Older Books

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, written in the reign of Aurangzeb, gives the saint a few lines within its description of Sialkot. It names him "امام علی الحق خلف امام زین العابدین", Imam Ali al-Haq, "son of Imam Zain al-Abidin", as the book prints it, and says that in that pleasant region his resting place is found: "دران خطه دل کشا خوابگاه امام علی الحق خلف امام زین العابدین است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Bhandari tells the story of his coming as hearsay, introducing it with "گویند", "it is said". He came to Hindustan "از عرب", from Arabia, with many Muslims, "بقصد جهاد", with the intention of holy war; by chance they reached Sialkot, the name printed "بسیالکوت[OCR?]" with its reading uncertain in the printed text; there they fought the Hindus, and "درجه شهادت یافتند", they attained the rank of martyrdom (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). The verb is plural: in Bhandari's telling the martyrdom belongs to the whole band, not to the Imam alone.

Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* places him in a different company. It counts him as the fourth companion of the Zanjanis, "جنکا مزار برابر[OCR?] انوار[OCR?] سیالکوٹ[OCR?] میں زیارت گاہ خلق اللہ ہے": one whose tomb in Sialkot is a place of pilgrimage for God's people, the words describing the tomb uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269). On the next page the book explains his name. Something, the words naming it lost in the printed text, "befell" (لاحق ہوئی), and "... کو لاحق ہوئی اس سے[OCR?] نام ہی[OCR?] انکا امام علی لاحق مشہور[OCR?] ہو گیا": from this, it says, he became famous by the name Imam Ali Lahiq (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270). What it was that befell, and so the story behind the name, cannot be read.

Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, composed in Persian in 1875 and read in a modern Urdu edition, names him in its index, which carries the entry "علی الحق سیالکوٹی | ۱۸۷", the *nisba* tying him to Sialkot (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 324, folio 312). The same number, 187, is given in that index for "بی بیاں پاک دامن", "حسین زنجانی", "حاج بی بی" and "خضر خان" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 324, folio 312). A separate index entry, "علی الحق شاہ | ۲۲۳", is not cross-referenced to the Sialkot saint (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 324, folio 312).

The same edition's list of sources names a dated account of his martyrdom: item 141, "محمد مقیم : وقائع سیالکوٹ ۱۰۷۱ھ (احوال شہادت امام علی الحق سیالکوٹی) مرتبہ ڈاکٹر عبداللہ چغتائی۔ لاہور ۱۹۷۷ء" — a *Waqa'i Sialkot* by Muhammad Muqim, dated 1071 AH, on the martyrdom of Imam Ali al-Haq of Sialkot, edited by Dr Abdullah Chaghatai and published at Lahore in 1977 (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 299, folio 287). Lahori's editor cites the same *Waqa'i Sialkot* of 1071 AH as his documentary evidence for the date 600 AH that he gives for Husain Zanjani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 199). The book does not say what the *Waqa'i* itself reports of the Imam's dates.

## The Shrine and its Devotional Life

The *darbar* of Imam Sahib is not a single monumental tomb but a dense and atmospheric complex in the old city, described by visitors as a maze of narrow corridors and stairways opening onto several graves — those, by tradition, of unnamed companions who fell with the saint, together with the resting-places of later *pirs* and holy men who chose to be buried in his shadow. The tomb of the saint himself is approached through a mirrored gateway ornamented with Qur'anic inscriptions and geometric tilework, in the idiom of Punjabi shrine decoration, and the passages leading to it are often lined with prostrating and praying pilgrims.

As a martyr's shrine, the site carries the particular charisma that Punjabi popular religion attaches to the *shahid* — the martyr who is believed to be present and living, and whose intercession and *baraka* are sought by the faithful. Devotees come throughout the year to offer prayers, tie votive threads and seek blessings, and the shrine, administered like many of the province's major *darbars* under the auspices of the Punjab Auqaf Department, is the focus of an annual *urs* commemorating the saint. On such occasions the surrounding lanes fill with pilgrims, and the customary features of a Punjabi shrine festival — devotional music, the recitation of poetry, and the distribution of *langar* — accompany the gathering. Because Imam Sahib is regarded as the spiritual founder of Muslim Sialkot, his memory is woven into the civic and religious identity of the city itself, and local commemorations periodically recall his role in its history.

The older books bear witness to the tomb as a place of pilgrimage long before the present day. Bhandari, in the reign of Aurangzeb, writes "اکنون مزار مظهر انوار ایشان زیارتگاه صغار و کبار است": now his tomb, a place where divine lights are made manifest, is visited by small and great alike (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Chishti calls it a "زیارت گاہ خلق اللہ", a place of visitation for God's people (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269). Neither book describes the building, its custodians or its endowments, and none of the books consulted gives the date of an *ʿurs*.

## Setting: Sialkot

The passages below speak of the city of Sialkot, not of the shrine; none of them mentions the Imam.

Bhandari places the city in the Rachna doab: "در دوابه رچنا شهر متقدمین سیالکوت است" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). It was once called "شلکوت", and its founding is attributed to "راجه شل[OCR?] طغائ[OCR?] پاندوان", a raja of the Pandavas' time named in the Mahabharata, "که از تصنیف ان قریب پنجهزار سال میگذرد", composed some five thousand years before (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). It is also called "سالکوت" and attributed to "راجه سالباهن", of whom "قلعه پخته از و یادگار است": a fort of fired brick is his memorial (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). "درزمان سابق دار الحکومت ولایت پنجاب بود و دو سه کروه آبادی داشت": in former times it was the seat of government of the Punjab, its habitation stretching two or three *kos*; and in Bhandari's day "از جمیع قصبات اینصوبه درابادی افزون است", it surpassed every other town of the suba in population (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). When Lahore lay in ruins in early times, "دار الحکومت این ولایت شهر سیالکوت گردید", until Sultan Mahmud's conquest and Malik Ayaz's rebuilding of Lahore (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 525).

Harish Dhillon, retelling the Janamsakhis of Guru Nanak, describes Sialkot as "a bustling city that was situated in the foothills of the Himalayas". Legend, he writes, has it founded by "Raja Sela, the uncle of the Pandavas", and rebuilt by "Raja Satya Vachan, when it became part of the kingdom of Kashmir"; "The earliest recorded mention of the city is found in ancient Greek texts going as far back as 322 B.C., where it is referred to as Sagala", and it was "famous for its silk" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 136, folio 151). Haroon Khalid's reconstruction of the city's past begins with another king: "Puran Bhagat was the son of the King of Sialkot, Raja Salivahan"; "It is believed that Sialkot was founded by this king"; "The well of Puran Bhagat was at a little distance from the city of Sialkot", and devotees raised a temple around it, "the most important temple in the ancient city of Sialkot" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 184, folio 158). Chishti, too, tells the Puran legend: Raja Salwan, the name uncertain in the printed text, held "راجہ [illegible] سیالکوٹ[OCR?] کی گدی[OCR?]", the seat of Sialkot (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 553); the well into which Puran was thrown, his hands and feet cut off, is still to be seen there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 554); and when Puran came to Sialkot a dried-up garden revived on his arrival (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 557). The name Salbahan, which the site's account gives as the title of the raja who fought the saint, thus recurs in the books' stories of the city's founding king (Bhandari's "راجه سالباهن", Khalid's Raja Salivahan); none of these books connects that king with the Imam.

Of the coming of Muslim rule and of the Sufis to the city, Dhillon writes that "Sialkot became a part of the Muslim Sultanate when Shahabuddin Muhammad Ghori captured Punjab in 1192", and that a garrison was left there (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 136, folio 151). Many Sufi missionaries, he adds, settled in the region, making it predominantly Muslim and "giving it a rich Sufi tradition", and the city was an important post on the trade route between West Asia and Delhi (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 137, folio 152). Bhandari tells of the same conqueror at the fort: Shihab al-Din of Ghur, failing at Lahore "درسنه پانصد و هشتاد(۲) هجری", came to Sialkot, repaired the old fort and left his army there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517); in another passage he restored the fort, "که بناۓ آن از قدیم است", whose foundation was ancient, and Khusraw Malik with the Khokhars besieged it for a time without success (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404). Under Akbar, "راجه مانسنگه اکبرشاهی", faujdar of Jammu and jagirdar of Sialkot, repaired the fort and improved the city; then "صفدرخان جهانگیری" rebuilt the fort and its tower, and most later governors made repairs too (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517).

The site's account ties the saint's death to an invasion of the Punjab by Sultan Sabuktigin of Ghazni. The books consulted do not mention the saint in that connection, but two of them speak of Sabuktigin and the province. Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore writes that "سلطان محمود و سبکتگین غزنوی نے پنجاب پر حملہ کیا" when Raja Jaipal ruled the Punjab from Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 14, folio 9). Richard Eaton writes that "The pattern commenced in 986, when the Ghaznavid Sultan Sabuktigin (r. 977-97) attacked and defeated the Hindu Shahi raja who controlled the region between Kabul and northwest Punjab" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 110, folio 98). Of the city's countryside, Eaton notes that Babur "described Jat pastoralist groups in the Sind Sagar doab and Sialkot regions" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, pp. 224–225, folios 212–213).

The Sialkot of Bhandari's day was a city of crafts and learning. Its paper, "کاغذ مانسنگهی و هم حریری و خاصه جهانگیری", was white and durable and sent to other regions; its *karchikan* embroidery in silk and *kalabatun* went all over the world, and its *jamdhar*, *katari* and *barchhi* were well made (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). Gardens surrounded it, among them "باغ نظر محمد بهوته[OCR?]" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). A stream rising in the hills of Jammu flowed below the city, and when it flooded in the rains "جمیع مردم سیالکوت از اکابر و اصاغر", great and small, played in the water, naked but for a loincloth and carrying leather water-skins; anyone from the city who was far away, Bhandari writes, remembered this with pleasure (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 517–516). The buildings of the qanungos and of some others were, he writes, "بغایت مطبوع و دل کشا", most pleasing and delightful (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517).

The city was, in Bhandari's words, "دار العلوم و جامع علما و معدن فضل و مسکن فضلاست", a seat of learning and a gathering-place of scholars (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Under Akbar, "مولاناے کمال الدین حسین" left Kashmir and came to Sialkot "درسنه نهصد و هفتاد و یک هجری", in the year 971 Hijri, and established teaching there; under Shah Jahan "مولوی عبدالحکیم" spread the sciences, wrote glosses, and drew students to his "مدرسه متبرکه"; his son "مولوی عبدالله" ran the madrasa after him and was called "امام وقت" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Annemarie Schimmel likewise calls Sialkot "one of the centers of Islamic scholarship during the Mogul period", where Ahmad Sirhindi studied (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 398, folio 367).

Other holy men of the city appear in the books. Shah Daula's first master lived in Sialkot (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 515), and in the volume edited by Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu, Shah Daulah himself is said to have left it: "Due to some disputes with the local people of Sialkot, he migrated from there and, after some years, moved to Gujrat" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 205, folio 194). Dhillon and Khalid both tell of the faqir Hamza Ghaus, whose curse was pronounced in "the centre of the market square" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 150, folio 165), and of whom Sialkot "was gripped by fear" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 197–198, folios 171–172).

Khalid found a modern city. "Sialkot has become one of the most important cities in Pakistan"; its business community "financed its own airport, which now handles international flights", and the highway, and on the way in he saw "several factories" and "a lot of mounds", "probably archaeological ruins, converted into graveyards" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 191, folio 165). "Sialkot is located right on the border", he writes, and "Historically, Sialkot provided Punjab with a connection to Kashmir" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 193, folio 167).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His dates.** The local account places him in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, sometimes in the reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq; Ganesh Das Wadhera's *Chār Bāgh-i-Panjāb*, as the site's account reports it, has him killed around 970–971 CE. Bhandari gives no date (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Chishti counts him a companion of the Zanjanis (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269). The *Waqa'i Sialkot* on his martyrdom is dated 1071 AH in the list of sources of Lahori's modern edition (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 299, folio 287).
- **Who he was.** The site's account calls him a missionary holy man and warrior-saint, in Ganesh Das's version the leader of an army from Arabia. Bhandari calls him "son of Imam Zain al-Abidin" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516). Chishti calls him the fourth companion of the Zanjanis (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269).
- **How he came to Sialkot.** Ganesh Das, as the site's account gives him, has him lead an army from Arabia to Sialkot; the local account has him come as a preacher and holy warrior. Bhandari has him come to Hindustan from Arabia with many Muslims for holy war and reach Sialkot by chance (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516).
- **How he died.** One local version has him struck down by an unbeliever while at prayer in a mosque; another, that he fell in battle against the local Hindu ruler; Ganesh Das, that he was killed in battle with Raja Sahan Pal, and many of his companions with him. Bhandari says that the whole band fought the Hindus and attained martyrdom, the verb plural (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516).
- **His name.** The site gives Imam Ali-ul-Haq, and Ganesh Das "Imam Ali al-Haq". Bhandari writes "امام علی الحق" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516), and Lahori's edition "علی الحق سیالکوٹی" in its index and "امام علی الحق سیالکوٹی" in its list of sources (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 324, folio 312; p. 299, folio 287). Chishti gives the name as "امام علی لاحق" and explains it from something that befell (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270).
- **Who founded Sialkot** (of the city, not the shrine). Bhandari attributes it to "راجه شل[OCR?] طغائ[OCR?] پاندوان" and, under its other name, to "راجه سالباهن" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). Dhillon gives the legend of "Raja Sela, the uncle of the Pandavas", the city rebuilt by Raja Satya Vachan (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 136, folio 151). Khalid writes that it is believed to have been founded by Raja Salivahan (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 184, folio 158).
- **Babur and Sialkot** (of the city, not the shrine). Bhandari records Babur's order "حکم شد که سیالکوت را خراب کرده ساکنان آن جا را در بهلول پور آباد گردانند": that Sialkot be laid waste and its people resettled at Bahlulpur (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 304). Dhillon writes that during "the Mughal Emperor Babur's third incursion into India", "Sialkot had offered no resistance and had been spared the usual bloody massacre and plunder" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 224, folio 246).

## Legacy

Imam Ali-ul-Haq occupies a place in Sialkot comparable to that of a patron saint: the figure to whom the city's Muslim character is popularly traced, and whose martyrdom sanctifies its very ground. That the details of his life are historically obscure — the sources disagreeing even on the century in which he lived — has done nothing to diminish his standing in local devotion, and may indeed be characteristic of the earliest layer of Punjabi Muslim sacred history, in which the memory of the warrior-saint who "opened" a region to Islam is preserved more in cult and story than in dated record. His shrine remains a living centre of pilgrimage and one of the defining landmarks of old Sialkot.

The older books show how long that memory has been written down. A *Waqa'i Sialkot* on his martyrdom is dated 1071 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 299, folio 287); Bhandari, in Aurangzeb's reign, found his tomb visited by small and great (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 516); and Chishti called it a place of pilgrimage for God's people (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269).
