## Death and the Building of the Shrine

Mian Mir died in 1635, and though he had expressly forbidden any tomb over his grave, a mausoleum of red sandstone was raised at his resting place in Baghbanpura in the years that followed, during the lifetime of Dara Shikoh, who could not bear that his master should lie unmarked. It grew into a dignified monument in the Mughal manner, its chambers finished in fine stone, and around it, in time, were gathered the graves of others of the imperial circle who had loved him — Dara Shikoh himself, executed in 1659, and his wife Nadira Begum among them. Thus the barefoot dervish who owned nothing and had asked for nothing came to rest at the centre of a small city of tombs, his wish overruled by the devotion of a prince.

Kanhaiya Lal tells the building twice. In one passage, when the governorship of the Punjab was entrusted to Dara Shikoh in Shah Jahan's reign, "اُس نے عمارتین بہت کین پہلے چوک بنوایا پہر عالیشان عمارت اپنے دادا مرشد میان میر بالاپیر کے روضہ کی تعمیر کی": he raised many buildings, first a chowk, then the lofty building of the rauza of his *dada murshid* Mian Mir Bala Pir; and then "پہر ملا شاہ قادری اپنے مرشد کا روضہ بنوایا جسکے حاطہ مین اب موضع میانمیر ایک گاؤن آبا دہی", the rauza of Mullah Shah Qadri, his own murshid, in whose enclosure, as the sentence runs, the village of Mauza Mian Mir now stands, though the village bears Mian Mir's name (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142). In the other, Dara Shikoh gathered much stone and building material and first built his own pir's rauza, "جسکی چار دیواری میں اب موضع میان میر آباد ہے", within whose walls the village of Mian Mir is now settled (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245). Neither passage dates the rauza. Chishti, too, says that Dara Shikoh built the "روضہ عالیہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 289): "حضرت کا روضہ[OCR?] بھی اوسی نے بنوایا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 291).

Lahori, in his entry for Mullah Shah Badakhshi, writes "ان کا روضہ دارا شکوہ نے کئی لاکھ روپے خرچ کر کے بنوایا تھا جس کے پتھر تمام و کمال رنجیت سنگھ اتروا کر امرت سر لے گیا": Dara Shikoh had the rauza built at a cost of several lakh rupees, and Ranjit Singh had its stones taken down entirely and carried off to Amritsar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 69, folio 57); his editor gives Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore as the authority (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 69, folio 57, حاشیہ 3). Because the sentence stands in Mullah Shah's entry, its "ان کا روضہ" may mean Mullah Shah's rauza rather than Mian Mir's; the wording does not settle whose tomb was stripped.

Dara Shikoh's devotion, Kanhaiya Lal writes, reached further: "اُسکا ارادہ تہا کہ چوک ودارا شاہ[OCR?] سے میان میر کے مقبرہ تاک ایک سٹرک سنگ سرخ کی ایسی مصفا وپاکیزہ بنوائے کہ روز سلام کیواسطے پا برہنہ وہان جایا آیا کرے اور اُس سٹرک پر سوے شہزادہ کے اور کوئی آمد ورفت نکرے". He meant to build, from the chowk of "دارا شاہ[OCR?]" to Mian Mir's maqbara, a road of red stone so clean and pure that he could go and come barefoot every day to pay his *salam*, and that none but the prince should travel on it. The plan was cut short when "عالمگیر اورنگ زیب نے باپ پر غالب آکر اُسکو قید کر لیا اور دارا شکوہ اپنے بہائی کو قتل کرا دیا", when Alamgir Aurangzeb overcame his father and imprisoned him and had his brother Dara Shikoh killed (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142). Chishti speaks of a red-stone road "حضرت کے روضہ مقدس سے تا قلعہ لاہور", from the holy rauza to the fort of Lahore, walked "پا برہنہ", barefoot (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 291).

Kanhaiya Lal adds that at the completion of the building much stone was left over, "اس عمارت کے اختتام پر پتہر بہت بڑہ رہا تہا", and that Aurangzeb "حکم دیا کہ موجود ہ پتہر کی ایک جامع مسجد بنائی جائے", ordered that a Jami Masjid be built from the stone on hand (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142).

Of the prince's household, Rafat's note says that Dara Shikoh's "wife lies buried near his mausoleum" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220). Chishti's register places the tomb of "نادراں بیگم [OCR?]" on the east, "روبرو طرف مشرق", and of that tomb says, in a damaged sentence that speaks of Mian Mir's own lifetime, "یہ مقبرہ [OCR?] عین حیات حضرت میاں میر کے [illegible]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 324).

## The Tomb in Kanhaiya Lal's Description

The fullest description of the building is Kanhaiya Lal's, and it is given here as his account; whether all of it belongs to this shrine is not beyond doubt. His table of contents gives the nearest tomb as "مقبرہ میاں منیر[OCR?]", Munir rather than Mir, a reading uncertain in the printed text (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3), while the account itself prints "شیخ محمد میر المشہور میان میر بالا پیر لاہوری" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245); and elsewhere in the book "Mian Mir" is only the name of the cantonment, with no saint, grave, mazar, urs or custodian named there.

In Kanhaiya Lal's measurement the enclosure is *pukhta*, of *chuna-gach*, with *qalbuti* arches in all four walls; its height, a reading uncertain in the printed text, is "پانچ گز کم[OCR?] نہیں", and its door is on the south. The rauza stands on a grand *chabutra*, "مربع ۱۹ ۔ ۱۹ ذرعہ طول و عرض کا", nineteen by nineteen *zar'a*, with a marble stair on the south, marble slabs set into its four faces (the word uncertain in the printed text) and stone paving on top. The tomb itself is "قدآدم بلند سنگ مرمر کی"; its door panel is of marble and its frame of red stone; inside, a marble floor is inlaid with black "سنگ موسی[OCR?]"; three *qalbuti* arches have stone frames (the word again uncertain), and the door stands in the fourth, the southern one. The interior marble work, he writes, "عمارت دارا شکوہ کے عہد میں بنائی گئی تہی", was built in Dara Shikoh's time. Glass-work in a vine pattern and a large mirror adorn the flanks of the northern arch and the ceiling of the dome. The grave stands on a marble *chabutra* a foot high, its *ta'wiz* of marble, "جسپر ہمیشہ غلاف قیمتی کپڑون کا پڑا رہتا ہے", on which a cover of costly cloths always lies; and the finial of the dome, the "کلس", is of marble too (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 243–245, folios 246–248).

The shrine's offices are built into its fabric. On the west of the enclosure "ایک عالیشان دالان … مجاورین کی نشستگاہ بنا ہے", a grand *dalan* is built as the seat of the *mujawirs*, and beside it stands a further building with a *bukharcha* (the word uncertain in the printed text) in which "نشست خاص سجادہ نشین کی ہوتی ہے", the special seat of the sajjada-nashin (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 243, folio 246). Because there was no well within the walls, "چونکہ اس چار دیواری کے اندر کوئی چاہ نہ تہا نور محمد ایاں والہ[OCR?] نے بمرور عرصہ پچاس برس کے یہ چاہ تیار کرایا تہا", a Nur Muhammad, his second name uncertain in the printed text, had one made over the course of fifty years, with a bathhouse beside it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 243, folio 246).

The mosque, too, was built across two reigns: "اس مسجد کی کرسی دارا شکوہ کے وقت بنی تہی جسپر پتہر لگا ہے و باقیماندہ تعمیر عالمگیر کے وقت ہوئی تہی", its stone-faced base was laid in Dara Shikoh's time and the rest was built under Alamgir (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 243, folio 246). The war of succession stopped the work — Shah Jahan imprisoned, Dara Shikoh killed, "اس سبب سے عمارت اسکی چند سال بند رہی" — and only on a petition to Alamgir by "متو سلطان[OCR?] اسی خاندان[OCR?]" was the building taken up again and finished, though not to the finish Dara Shikoh had intended: "اُس قسم کی تیاری کا مکان نہ بنا جس صورت سے دارا شکوہ چاہتا تہا" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 242–243, folios 245–246). Even the glass-work belongs to a later age: "یہ شیشہ کا کام اب ایک انگریز نے بنوایا تہا جسکا نام بیل[OCR?] صاحب اور گنبد[OCR?] صاحب سوداگر کا نوکر تہا باہر کی سفیدی بھی اس نے کرائی تہی" — an Englishman in a merchant's service, his name uncertain in the printed text, had it made, and had the outside whitewashed as well (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 245, folio 248).

## The Precinct and Its Graves

Lahori's appendix sites several graves by reference to Mian Mir's. His own stands at "میاں میر نزد [illegible] ریلوے سٹیشن", Mian Mir, near a railway station whose name is illegible in the printed text; Khwaja Bihari's lies "متصل روضہ میاں میر", adjoining Mian Mir's rauza, and is found today at "قصبہ میاں میر۔ بالمقابل مقبرہ حضرت میاں میر", opposite his maqbara; and Mullah Shah Qadiri's lies "بیرون مزار میاں میر بالا پیر", outside Mian Mir Bala Pir's mazar, and is found today "اندرون موضع میاں میر" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 287–288, folios 275–276). The locality itself thus bears his name, as قصبہ or موضع میاں میر. In the body of the book, too, Khwaja Bihari's mazar is "متصل روضہ میاں میر رح کے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 66, folio 54), and Mullah Shah's "مزار گوہر بار لاہور میں بیرون مزار میاں میر بالا پیر ہے", outside Mian Mir Bala Pir's mazar; "اب ان کے مزار کے احاطہ میں موضع میاں میر آباد ہے", the book continues as a fact of its own day: the village of Mian Mir Abad now stands within the enclosure of his mazar (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 69, folio 57).

Chishti's register of graves places them by the rauza and its walls, "سامنے روضہ حضرت میاں میر صاحب" and "بطرف مغربی [OCR?] چار دیواری حضرت میاں میر" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325). It names khadims of the shrine, "ملاں جان محمد گوجر [OCR?]" and "حضرت ابراہیم روسے [OCR?]", with years read as 1048 and 1040 (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325), and "حافظ اللہ یار [OCR?]" and "سائیں میر شاہ [OCR?]", "خادموں [OCR?] میں سے", with years read as 1265 and 1259 (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 324), every figure uncertain in the printed text. Three of his murids are buried by the rauza: "حاجی سلیمان", with a year read as 1031; "شیخ ابو الکارم [OCR?]", with 1021; and "شیخ ابو الخیر", with 1018, every year again uncertain; and the register says of them "یہ حضرات سب کاملین [OCR?] مریدان حضرت میاں میر [illegible]", that all were accomplished murids of Hazrat Mian Mir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325). It records a burial ground of Muhammad Sharif's kin, "گورستان اقربا [OCR?] محمد شریف [illegible] مرحوم", its graves of "تواریخ مختلفہ", various dates, "متصل خانقاہ و مقبرہ خواجہ بہار صاحب", adjoining the khanqah and tomb of Khwaja Bahar, "مگر نام کے معلوم نہیں", their names unknown. Of Mullah Shah's garden, against a year read as 1078, it says "یہ باغ و مقبرہ حضرت ملا شاہ ممدوح [OCR?] دارا شکوہ نے بنوا کر [illegible] حضرت محمد شریف سجادہ نشین [illegible] کیا", that Dara Shikoh built this garden and tomb of Mullah Shah, the rest of the sentence, partly illegible, naming Hazrat Muhammad Sharif, the sajjada-nashin; that "اب اس باغ میں [OCR?] زمینداران سکونت رکھتے ہیں", zamindars now live in the garden; and "تمام موضع میاں میر موسوم [OCR?]", that the whole village is called Mian Mir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325).

## The Chilla in Anarkali

Chishti gives a separate account, "احوال مکان چلہ حضرت میاں میر", to a house in Anarkali known as Mian Mir's chilla (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 254), and his table of contents lists, besides it and an account of the saint's house, a heading for the mazars connected with him, "نقشہ[OCR?] مزارات متعلق میاں میر[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 2). The house, "یہ مکان صدر بازار انارکلی میں", stands in Sadr Bazaar Anarkali, beside a merchant's kothi and shops; "کرایہ اسکا وہی فقیر لیتی[OCR?] ہیں", its rent goes to those same faqirs; and it has a running well, "چاہ روان[OCR?]", an arched way, a structure "لطور[OCR?] مسجد", a *tah khana* that is an old building, "قدیمی عمارت", trees, and a well (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 254). "یہاں ہر روز ایک سے دو چراغ روشن ہوتے ہیں": here one or two lamps are lit every day. "یہاں حضرت میاں میر صاحب بحیں[OCR?] حیات[OCR?] خود معتکف رہتو[OCR?] تھی[OCR?]": here, in his lifetime, Hazrat Mian Mir would stay in retreat. And Chishti reports what he learned from the mouth of the saint's sajjada-nashin, "زبانی سجادہ نشین میاں میر کی معلوم ہوا": that the saint spent nights here, that "یہہ مکان ایک باغ تھا", the house was once a garden, and that his death, "وفات", took place "اسی حکمہ[OCR?]", at this very place (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 255). Elsewhere he has Qazi Muhammad Afzal, "فضل گدا", visit the saint at "مقام انارکلی[OCR?] کہ جہاں اب چلہ حضرت میاں میر کا ہے", the place in Anarkali where his chilla now is (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 701).

## The Shrine Through the Centuries

The tomb passed through the turbulence of later ages. In the Sikh period much of its valuable stone was carried off under the builders of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who prized the material, and — by tradition — stone from the wider complex had earlier been drawn upon for imperial building under Aurangzeb; yet through every change of rule the shrine endured as a place of devotion. Under British rule it came under the care of the department of ancient monuments, and in 1985 it was formally declared a protected site by the Punjab Auqaf Department, which administers it to this day together with the shrine’s traditional sajjada-nashins, the hereditary custodians. The mausoleum stands in the Dharampura (Hashimpura) area of Lahore, its dome and gateway a familiar landmark, with an attached mosque and open courtyards to receive the crowds who gather there. Successive generations have repaired and adorned it, so that the austere saint who wished only for a ruined and level grave is honoured, instead, by one of the enduring monuments of the city.

Chishti returns, in other pages, to Ranjit Singh's stripping and to the Maharaja's repentance (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 296–297, 313).

Shemeem Burney Abbas, who visited the shrine in her fieldwork, found there the feature she had seen at Data Darbar, the extension and renovation of the shrine into a mosque with Friday congregational prayer (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 20–21, folios not stated): "I noticed the same feature at the Hazrat Mian Mir" … "shrine in Lahore, which I visited this summer". "The shrine had fallen to pieces almost a decade ago. It has been recently restored and is also used as a mosque" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 21, folio not stated).

## Devotion Today

The shrine of Mian Mir remains a living centre of popular piety. On ordinary days it draws on the order of one to three thousand visitors, who come to recite the Fatiha, tie vows, and seek the saint’s intercession for healing, for children, and for relief from hardship; many speak of the peace they feel within its walls and of prayers answered there. Qawwali is sung on Thursday evenings, the five daily prayers are held in the shrine mosque, and langar — free food — is distributed to visitors, sometimes twice a day. The shrine’s great annual occasion is the urs, held on 7 February, which marks the saint’s union with the Divine; the courtyards then fill with hundreds of thousands of devotees for days of qawwali, prayer, and communal feasting. Across the centuries — under Mughal, Sikh, and British rule, and in the Pakistan of today — the shrine has served as a shared space of devotion, remembered by writers from Dara Shikoh to Khushwant Singh as a place where the boundaries of community grew soft.

Kanhaiya Lal knew a fuller calendar: "اس مزار پر سال بہر میں پانچ میلے ہوتے ہیں میں ایک عرس سالیتہ[OCR?] ہوتا ہے اُس روز دو دون اور دو رات ہجوم خلقت اللہ کا رہتا ہے اور چار میلے برسات کے موسم میں ہوتی ہیں یعنی چار چہار شنبے جو ماہ ساون میں آتے ہیں". Five melas were held at the mazar each year: one the annual urs, the word read with uncertainty, when the crowd stayed two days and two nights, and four in the rains, on the four Wednesdays of the month of Sawan. "اگرچہ سکھون کے وقت بھی یہان بڑا میلہ ہوتا تہا مگر اب میانہ میں رونق زیادہ ہوتی ہے کیونکہ لاہور خاص و چہاوُنی میان میر و دیہات کی خلقت میلے کے روز بکثرت جمع ہو جاتی ہے اور آمدنی چڑہاوے کی بہت آتی ہے": a big mela was held there in the time of the Sikhs too, but in his day the gathering was the more prosperous, because the people of Lahore proper, of the Mian Mir cantonment and of the villages gathered in great numbers on the day of the mela, and much income came from the offerings (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 245, folio 248).

Pilgrims and seekers of many kinds have come to the tomb. Khalid writes of a shrine that "now attracts thousands of devotees in Lahore" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). Shah Muhammad Ghaus spent his first night in Lahore there and received his *shughl* in a dream (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 78, folio 66 [marker: 76]; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 177), and Fazl Shah, as far as a badly damaged line can be read, often went to the mazar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 336). Kugle finds the Qalandars of Lahore still associated with the saint (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 326, folio 305, ch. 4 n. 7).

## Setting: Mian Mir in the Map of Lahore

The saint's name runs through the topography of Lahore. Lahori places one tomb "لاہور کے باہر میاں میر کی سڑک کے پاس", outside Lahore near Mian Mir's road (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 44, folio 32), and another "لاہور کے باہر لب سڑک جو میاں میر کو انارکلی سے جاتی ہے", on the edge of the road that runs from Anarkali to Mian Mir (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 267, folio 255). Chishti, too, speaks of a road running from Lahore to Mian Mir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 360).

In Kanhaiya Lal's Lahore the name belongs above all to the cantonment. He records that the Anarkali cantonment was given up and the cantonment set in the plain of Mian Mir, "انار کلی کی چہاؤنی موقوف ہوکر میان میر کے میدان مین چہاؤنی قرار پائی" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 286–287, folios 289–290); that it was founded "بنظر و سعت زمین کے میانمیر [OCR?] کے میدان میں", in the plain of Mian Mir, for the breadth of its land, with a "صدر بازار میانمیر [OCR?]", great barracks and countless kothis costing lakhs (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 34, folio 37); and his contents list "چھاونی میاں میر کا گرجا", the church of the Mian Mir cantonment (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 5, folio 4). At none of these places does the book name a saint, a grave or a custodian, and it nowhere says there that the place is named after anyone. He sets other tombs by the cantonment and the road: Miskin Shah Amri's lies "چہاونی میان میر کی غربی سمت کو", on the west side of the Mian Mir cantonment (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 263, folio 266), and Sayyid Jan Muhammad Huzuri's adjoins "میان میر کی سڑک", the Mian Mir road, on the west (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 265, folio 268).

Writers on the city at large give the wider setting, and what follows speaks of Lahore, not of the shrine. Kugle calls Lahore "a seasonal capital city and home of the Mughal court during its perennial rotation" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 233, folio 212), and describes "Baghabanpur on the outskirts of Lahore (the neighborhood is now within the expanding city just next to the Shalimar gardens)" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 215, folio 194); he writes of the neighbourhood, not of Mian Mir. Abbas calls the Shalimar Gardens "Gardens built by Shah Jehan, the Mughal emperor" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 188, folio not stated). Chishti's own survey was commissioned: the commissioner ordered him "کہ حالاتِ عمارات و مزارات و مقابر و مساجد نواحِ لاہور مفصل تحریر کروں", to write a detailed account of the buildings, mazars, tombs and mosques of Lahore's environs (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 28). Of a site at Hashim Pura, in his account of the city's former extent, he writes "لاہور یہان تک تہا", that Lahore once reached that far (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 298). He records that in Ranjit Singh's time red, black and marble stones were torn down around Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 296), and that when the cantonments of Ranjit Singh's armies were built the bricks of old tombs and houses were pulled out, so that "ہزار ہا مقابر و گنبد و مساجد و باغات و حویلیہائے[OCR?] قدیمہ جو یادگار امرائے سلف تھیں گم گشتیں[OCR?]", thousands of old tombs, domes, mosques, gardens and havelis that were the memorials of the nobles of the past were lost (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 431).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **His name.** The site's account calls him Hazrat Mian Mir, Mir Mohammad of Sindh. Lahori heads his entry "شیخ محمد میر المشہور بہ میاں میر قادری لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 60–62, folios 48–50), and his editor gives Mir Muhammad, with the titles Mian Mir and Shah Mir (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 61, folio 49, حاشیہ). Kanhaiya Lal's account prints "شیخ محمد میر المشہور میان میر بالا پیر لاہوری" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245), but his table of contents "مقبرہ میاں منیر[OCR?]", with Munir for Mir (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3).
- **Where he was born.** The site's account gives Sehwan (Sivastan) in Sindh, between Thatta and Bhakkar. Lahori has "سیوستان میں آپ پیدا ہوئے", Sewistan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 60, folio 48); Chishti "مولد انکا شہر سیستان", the city of Sistan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284); Rafat "Sehwan Sharif in Sind" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220); Schimmel only Sind (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 392, folio 361). Kanhaiya Lal gives no birthplace and calls him Lahori (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245).
- **When he was born.** The site's account says the sixteenth century. Lahori gives 960 on the authority of the *Safīnat al-Auliyā* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 61–62, folios 49–50); his editor, on Dara Shikoh's authority, 957 AH / 1550 CE (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 61, folio 49, حاشیہ); Chishti nine hundred and fifty-seven of the hijra, the reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284); Khalid 1550 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated).
- **How long he lived.** The site's account says by tradition some eighty-eight years. Lahori says eighty-seven (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 61–62, folios 49–50); Chishti "اٹھانوے[OCR?] سال", ninety-eight, the reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284).
- **When he died.** The site's account gives 1635 (1045 AH), "the date held by the Auqaf Department and the great majority of sources, though a few place his death in 1645", and holds the urs on 7 February. Lahori gives 1045 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 61–62, folios 49–50); Kanhaiya Lal 1045, the figure uncertain, in the reign of Shah Jahan, with a chronogram over the tomb door that yields the year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245; p. 244, folio 247); Rafat, Ernst and Lawrence, and Schimmel's index 1635 (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220; Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 65, folio 51; Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 521); Khalid 1635 (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated). Chishti gives the Zuhr prayer on 7 Rabi al-Awwal, the year illegible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284).
- **Who initiated him.** The site's account has him leave home at about twelve with his widowed mother's blessing and receive initiation at the hands of the master whom the shrine's tradition remembers as Shaikh Siyustani. Lahori has him take *bay'a* in the Qadiri silsila at twelve at his own mother's hand, and only later go, with her permission, to Shaikh Khizr Sistani for its completion (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 61, folio 49). Chishti and Kanhaiya Lal make him murid and khalifa of Shaikh Khizr Sistani (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284; Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245). Ernst and Lawrence trace the line Dara Shikoh acknowledged to him through 'Abd al-Qadir II and 'Abd Allah Bhiti (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 65, folio 51).
- **His brothers.** Lahori names four more brothers, Mian Qazi, Qazi Usman, Qazi Tahir and Qazi Muhammad (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 62, folio 50); Chishti names "قاضی توکل[OCR?]", "قاضی عثمان" and "قاضی طاہر" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 284).
- **His breath.** The site's account has him hold the discipline of the breath from the Isha prayer until dawn. Lahori says that a whole night passed in a single breath (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 61, folio 49); Chishti, that a night passed in one or two breaths, and later in four (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 285).
- **Where he died.** The site's account has him die in the small cell where he had spent some sixty years. Chishti reports from the shrine's sajjada-nashin that his death took place at the Anarkali house known as his chilla, once a garden (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 255).
- **Where he kept his chilla.** The site's account speaks of a forty-day retreat at the khanqah of Data Ganj Bakhsh. Chishti describes a house in Sadr Bazaar Anarkali known as the chilla of Hazrat Mian Mir, where he stayed in retreat in his lifetime (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 254; p. 255; p. 701).
- **Dara Shikoh's relation to him.** The site's account calls the prince his most devoted disciple at court, with Mullah Shah as the prince's spiritual guide. Rafat counts Dara among his disciples (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220); Abbas calls him "a devotee of Hazrat Mian Mir" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 197, folio not stated); Schimmel makes Mian Mir the prince's first mystical guide, to whom Mullah Shah introduced him (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 464, folio 433; p. 392, folio 361). Kanhaiya Lal makes him the prince's "دادا مرشد" in one passage (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142) and the prince his "پوتا خلیہ[OCR?]" in another (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245); Chishti makes Dara a murid of Mullah Shah with "ارادت کاملہ" toward Mian Mir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 289, 291); Ernst and Lawrence name Mullah Shah as Dara's "own preceptor" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 65, folio 51).
- **Jahanara's guide.** The site's account makes the princess a disciple of Mullah Shah, reached through Dara Shikoh. Schimmel calls Mian Mir "Jihanara's and Dara's first mystical guide" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 464, folio 433), and Mullah Shah her master (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 394, folio 363).
- **Guru Arjan Dev and the foundation stone.** The site's account calls Mian Mir the Guru's close friend, gives the foundation stone as Sikh tradition, sets out the doubts of Madanjit Kaur and others, and holds that the objection does not really hold. Rafat writes that "Guru Arjun was a follower of the great Qadiriya mystic and had got him to lay the foundation stone of the Hariman-dir temple at Amritsar" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, pp. 41–42, folios 21–22); Khalid, that Mian Meer "laid the foundation" of the Golden Temple (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 167, folio not stated), and that he was "a close associate of Guru Arjan" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).
- **The offer against the Guru's oppressors.** In *Walking with Nanak* Mian Mir asks "permission to bury alive his oppressors" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 253, folio 227); in *A White Trail* he asks whether he should destroy them (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 195, folio not stated).
- **The order of Dara Shikoh's buildings.** The site's account has the mausoleum raised in the years after 1635, during Dara Shikoh's lifetime. Kanhaiya Lal, in one passage, has the prince, as governor of the Punjab, build first a chowk, then Mian Mir's rauza, then Mullah Shah's (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142); in the other, he first builds his own pir's rauza (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245). Neither passage gives a date.
- **What the tomb is made of.** The site's account calls it a mausoleum of red sandstone. Kanhaiya Lal describes a tomb of marble, its door frame of red stone and its interior marble work built in Dara Shikoh's time (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 243–245, folios 246–248).
- **The red-stone road.** Kanhaiya Lal has Dara Shikoh intend a red-stone road from the chowk of "دارا شاہ[OCR?]" to the maqbara, a plan cut short by Aurangzeb's victory (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142). Chishti speaks of a red-stone road from the rauza to the fort of Lahore, walked barefoot (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 291).
- **Whose enclosure holds the village.** Kanhaiya Lal, in one passage, puts the village of Mauza Mian Mir in the enclosure of Mullah Shah Qadri's rauza (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142); in the other, within the walls of the rauza of the prince's own pir (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 242, folio 245). Lahori, in Mullah Shah's entry, puts Mian Mir Abad within the enclosure of "ان کے مزار" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 69, folio 57). Chishti has zamindars living in Mullah Shah's garden and the whole village called Mian Mir (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325).
- **The stone and the great mosque.** The site's account gives as tradition that Aurangzeb drew upon stone from the complex for the Badshahi Mosque. Kanhaiya Lal writes that much stone was left over at the completion of the building, and that Aurangzeb ordered a Jami Masjid built from the stone on hand (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142).
- **The Sikh-period stripping.** The site's account says that much of the tomb's valuable stone was carried off under Ranjit Singh's builders. Lahori writes that Ranjit Singh had the stones of "ان کا روضہ" taken down "تمام و کمال", entirely, and carried to Amritsar, in a sentence that stands in Mullah Shah's entry and may mean Mullah Shah's rauza (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 69, folio 57).
- **Where the shrine stands.** The site's account sets it in Dharampura (Hashimpura), once the suburb of Baghbanpura, also recorded as Khanpura. Lahori's appendix places Mian Mir's grave at "میاں میر نزد [illegible] ریلوے سٹیشن", in a locality called قصبہ or موضع میاں میر (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 287–288, folios 275–276); his editor's table puts Bibi Jamal Khatun's grave, in its column for 1875, inside the enclosure of Mian Mir's khanqah, and in its column for 1974 between the Karachi railway line and Miani Sahib village (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 291, folio 279). Kanhaiya Lal's account of the two rauzas gives no quarter for either (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 139, folio 142).
- **The urs.** The site's account holds the urs on 7 February, with hundreds of thousands of devotees and days of qawwali. Kanhaiya Lal records five melas a year: the urs, when the crowd stayed two days and two nights, and four on the Wednesdays of Sawan (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 245, folio 248).
- **The state of the building.** The site's account has the shrine endure through every change of rule, repaired and adorned by successive generations. Abbas writes that "The shrine had fallen to pieces almost a decade ago" and had been recently restored and put to use as a mosque (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 21, folio not stated).
- **Nadira Begum's tomb.** The site's account has the prince and his wife laid to rest close to Mian Mir after the war of succession. Rafat says only that his wife "lies buried near his mausoleum" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220). Chishti's register places her tomb on the east, in a damaged sentence that speaks of Mian Mir's own lifetime (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 324).
- **When Bibi Jamal Khatun died.** Lahori gives 1000 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 255, folio 243); his editor, quoting Dara Shikoh, 27 Rabi al-Awwal 1057 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 255, folio 243, حاشیہ 1); Chishti's register a year read as 1055 (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325); Schimmel 1639 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 464, folio 433).
- **Where Bibi Jamal Khatun lies.** Lahori places her inside a khanqah in Lahore whose name is illegible (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 255, folio 243); his editor's quotation from Dara Shikoh has her living in Sehwan and never leaving it (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 255, folio 243, حاشیہ 1); the editor's table, in its column for 1875, inside the enclosure of Mian Mir's khanqah (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 291, folio 279); Chishti's register enters her mazar at the shrine, and a second grave, formerly *pakka*, since razed (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 325).

## Legacy

Mian Mir stands in memory as the very type of the Sufi ideal: a man who owned nothing and was sought by emperors; who wrote not a single verse and yet was praised in verse by a prince; who, rooted absolutely in his own faith, made his threshold a meeting-place for people of every religion. His disciples shaped the spiritual life of the Mughal court; his friendship with the Sikh Gurus became a legend of tolerance that Punjab still cherishes; his forty-day retreat at Data Darbar bound him to the patron saint of Lahore; and his tomb remains one of the anchors of the city’s sacred landscape. In honouring Mian Mir, Lahore remembers not only a saint of extraordinary austerity and learning, but a vision of holiness generous enough to hold an entire, plural world.

The books carry that memory forward in their own ways. For Lahori he is the root of a Qadiri line that ran on in Lahore through Mullah Shah and his successors (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 221–222, folios 209–210). For Rafat, after Khushwant Singh, he was "extremely popular with people of all religions" (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 240, folio 220). For Khalid, his friendship with Guru Arjan Dev lives on in folk tales, and a pilgrims' hostel built at Dera Sahib in 1996 "was named after Mian Meer" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 200, folio not stated).

Name: Shrine of Mian Umar Baba (Chamkani)
Events: Annual urs (first Wednesday and Thursday of Rajab); langar
Description:
The shrine of Mian Muhammad Umar Baba lies at Chamkani, a village on the eastern outskirts of Peshawar about seven kilometres from the old city. Mian Umar (traditionally 1671-1776) was a Sufi of the Naqshbandi order — a scholar, poet, social reformer, and historian who is counted, together with Akhund Darweza Baba and the warrior-poet Khushal Khan Khattak, among the great literary and spiritual figures of the Mughal-era Pashtun frontier. Said to have been born near Lahore and to have lived to a great age, he attracted disciples from every rank of society; tradition holds that even Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), the founder of the Afghan kingdom, visited him and became his devotee. Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* gives a specific account of his death — in the month of Rajab, 1119 AH (approximately 1707-1708 CE) — and records his burial at the village of Chamkani, three miles from Peshawar, consistent with the shrine's location as given above; that date, however, falls roughly seven decades earlier than the 1776 death year given elsewhere in this entry, and the discrepancy is left unresolved here, with both figures reported rather than reconciled. His tomb at Chamkani grew into a shrine and khanqah that remains a place of resort for the surrounding population, drawing its largest crowds at the annual urs, held over the first Wednesday and Thursday of the Islamic month of Rajab, when devotees gather for sermons, collective dhikr, and na'at, and the langar (free kitchen) is served. Like a number of Sufi shrines in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the site was targeted in militant attacks during the years of insurgency in the region, but it endures as an active centre of devotion. It complements the nearby shrine of the saint's contemporary Akhund Darweza Baba, also recorded in this dataset.

Name: Shrine of Miran Hussain Zanjani (Zanjani Sahib)
Events: Annual urs (autumn)
Description:
## Overview

In the old riverside locality of Chah Miran, named directly in his honour, stands the tomb of Syed Miran Hussain Zanjani, one of the earliest Muslim missionary figures associated with Lahore. The tomb, unusually for a site of such antiquity, rests on a simple raised platform without a dome, standing within what was once a dedicated garden named for the saint. It is formally recognised and maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, continues to host an annual *urs* drawing local devotees, and serves as the namesake and spiritual anchor of the surrounding Chah Miran neighbourhood on the historic bank of the River Ravi near the old walled city.

The books bear witness to the grave from several sides. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, in its modern annotated edition, places the burial of Shaikh Husain Zanjani at Chah Miran, "مدفون چاہ میراں", and its appendix gives the present location as Miran Husain Park, Chah Miran (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196; p. 289, folio 277). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi writes that "Zinjani was buried in Chah Miran, which is now a suburb of Lahore" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Two nineteenth-century surveys of Lahore's shrines, Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* and Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore*, describe the enclosure, the well and the yearly gathering at the grave, and set it in the village they call Khoi Miran (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403; p. 705; Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278).

The same books disagree, sharply, about who lies there and when he lived. The site's account gives his death as 1042 CE; Lahori gives 600 AH; Kanhaiya Lal prints a year 604 with no era; Rizvi dates his death only by the arrival of Ali Hujwiri at Lahore, about 1035. Lahori's modern editor goes further and argues that two different men of the same name have been run together. These accounts are set out below, each in its own words, and gathered side by side under *Where the Sources Disagree*.

## The Life of the Saint

According to the site's account he was a Hussaini Syed, born in 958 CE in Zanjan, in present-day Iran. He travelled to Lahore around 998 CE on the instruction of his spiritual master, Sheikh Abu al-Fazal Khatil, and is remembered to have preached in the city for some thirty-six years, converting large numbers of its inhabitants to Islam well before the Ghaznavid and later Mughal periods reshaped the region's religious landscape. He died in 1042 CE and was buried alongside his brother, Hazrat Musa Hussain Zanjani, whose own shrine lies nearby.

A substantial chapter devoted to the saint in Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* traces his family's descent from Imam Musa Kazim through the Zanjan line. The tazkira casts Zanjani as the elder of the two missionary saints credited with Lahore's early Islamization, his death preceding the arrival of the more widely celebrated Data Ganj Bakhsh.

Rizvi, who calls him "Shaikh Husain Zinjani", "Shaikh Husain Zanjani", and, in his report of Abu'l-Fazl, "Shaikh Husaini Zanjani", prints neither "Syed" nor "Miran" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112; p. 139, folio 121). He sets the saint's coming in the wake of the Ghaznavid conquest: "the annexation of the Panjab by Mahmud of Ghazna and its incorporation into his empire prompted many sufis to settle in the area", and Khattali "ordered his disciple, Shaikh Husain Zinjani to move to the Panjab", later sending Hujwiri after him (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112).

Lahori's own entry on him, headed "سید حسین زنجانی لاہوری", is four sentences long (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, folio 186). It counts him among the ancient elders, a man of guidance, austerity, piety, nobility and sayyid descent. His chain, it says, meets Junaid of Baghdad: "شجرہ ان کا حضرت جنیدؒ بغدادی کے ساتھ ملتا ہے". He came to Lahore together with Sayyid Yaqub Zanjani, "سید یعقوب زنجانی کے ساتھ یہ لاہور میں آئے", spent his whole life guiding the people, and died in the year 600 AH: "آخر سال چھ سو ہجری میں وفات کی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198).

Kanhaiya Lal tells the saint's coming differently. In the time of the Ghurid sultans, he writes, the saint came from the city of Zanjan to travel in Hind, toured the whole realm, and on his way back came to Lahore, settled, and died there: "سلاطین غوریہ کے وقت یہ شہر زنجان سے ہند کی سیر کو آیا اور تمام کشور ہند کی سیر کی واپسی کے وقت لاہور آ کر قیام پذیر ہوا اور یہان ہی فوت ہوا" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). He names no spiritual chain. His year of death is printed as "سال وفات اسکا سنہ ۶۰۴ [OCR?] ہے", the reading of the numeral uncertain in the printed text and no era given with it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278).

Chishti, citing Dara Shikoh's *Safinat al-Awliya*, has a party of saints come "ولایت سے ملک ہند میں", the first of them "شیخ المشایخ سید حسین زنجانی جنکی مزار [illegible] ہے کہ وہی [illegible] نواح لاہور میں موجود ہے", that is, the master of masters whose grave is in the environs of Lahore; he promises a separate account of him, "اوسکا[OCR?] حال انکا علاحدہ تحریر یہ ہوگا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269). All of them, he says, reached Lahore "پانچویں[OCR?] صدی[OCR?] ہجری میں", in the fifth century of the hijra, the reading uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270). In the separate account he has the saint come to Lahore with "حضرت صدر دیوان صاحب", in a year whose numerals cannot be read; of his death he can say only "تاریخ وفات انکی سنہ [illegible: year in numerals] ہجری", the year again unreadable, and that further particulars are "نامعلوم", unknown (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).

## The Pir-Brother of Data Ganj Bakhsh

The best-known story about the saint ties him to Ali Hujwiri, Data Ganj Bakhsh. In the form the *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves it, as one of Lahore's best-known early Sufi foundation stories, Ali Hujwiri was instructed by his own pir to travel to Lahore and preach, and replied that his senior "pir-brother," Hazrat Shaikh Hussain Zanjani, was already established in the city — only to arrive and find Zanjani's funeral procession already under way.

Chishti tells it the same way: Zanjani was Data Ganj Bakhsh's "پیر بہا ہی", already in Lahore, and Data joined his "جنازہ" and saw to "تکفین و تدفین", the shrouding and the burial (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163). Rizvi gives the morning of the funeral: "In the morning Shaikh Husain Zinjani's coffin was carried out for burial—he had died during the night. Zinjani was buried in Chah Miran, which is now a suburb of Lahore" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Rizvi dates the saint's death by this arrival alone, Hujwiri reaching Lahore "in c. 1035, while Sultan Mas'ud I (1031-41) reigned in Ghazna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112).

Lahori's modern editor reports the Mufti's telling of the same story in his other book, *Khazinat al-Asfiya*, on the authority of *Fawaid al-Fuad*: ordered to Lahore, Data objected, "وہاں تو میرے برادر طریقت حسین زنجانی موجود ہیں۔ میری کیا ضرورت ہے", that his brother in the path was already there; his murshid repeated the order; and on reaching Lahore Data saw Husain Zanjani's bier going past and understood his murshid's far-seeing eye (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).

## Two Men of One Name

It is that story which leads Lahori's editor to divide the saint in two. The Mufti, he writes, appears quite tangled over him: "شیخ حسین زنجانی لاہوریؒ کے حالات کے سلسلہ میں مفتی صاحب خاصے الجھے ہوئے معلوم ہوتے ہیں" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1). Hujwiri's death falls after 400 AH, the editor observes, so that on the bier story Husain Zanjani had died long before: "حضرت علی ہجویری کا سال وفات با ختلاف روایت بعد ۴۰۰ھ ہے۔ گویا اس مندرجہ روایت کے مطابق شیخ حسین زنجانی کا انتقال ۴۰۰ھ سے بہت پہلے ہو چکا تھا". Yet the Mufti himself, in *Khazinat al-Asfiya* and in this very book, gives 600 AH without any reference at all: "اب مفتی صاحب خود ہی خزینۃ الاصفیا (۲۵۰/۲) اور حدیقۃ الاولیاء میں شیخ حسین زنجانی کا سال وفات بغیر کسی حوالے کے ۶۰۰ھ لکھ دیتے ہیں" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).

The editor's resolution is that the man of this entry is a different person from the Shaikh Husain Zanjani of *Fawaid al-Fuad*: "حقیقت یہ ہے کہ زیر بحث شخصیت فوائد الفواد میں مذکور شیخ حسین زنجانی سے مختلف ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1). In his note on Data Ganj Bakhsh he names the later man as the one buried at this site: "معروف شیخ حسین زنجانی ف ۶۰۰ [OCR?] ہجری (مدفون چاہ میراں)", the well-known Shaikh Husain Zanjani, died 600 AH, the reading of the year uncertain in the printed text, buried at Chah Miran (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196). The editor thus separates the two as different persons (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 196–197, folios 184–185).

He supports the later date with two arguments. The first is a meeting. When Khwaja Muin al-Din Chishti came to Lahore around 585 AH, he writes, he had meeting and company with Shaikh Husain Zanjani: "حضرت خواجہ معین الدین چشتی اجمیریؒ جب قریباً ۵۸۵ھ (تاریخ السلف ۷، ۹) میں لاہور تشریف لائے تو شیخ حسین زنجانی سے ملاقات و صحبت رہی"; for the meeting he cites the *Ain-e Akbari*, Jamali's *Siyar al-Arifin*, Ghausi's *Gulzar-e Abrar*, Muhammad Salih Kanbo's *Amal-e Salih* and Dara Shikoh's *Safinat al-Awliya* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).

The second is a dated document. From *Waqai-e Sialkot*, written in 1071 AH by Muhammad Muqim, the editor quotes a Persian passage that mentions, in 758 AH, Khizr Khan, a grandson (نواسہ) of Sayyid Husain, with the words "برادر … سید یعقوب صدر شاہ زنجانی کہ مرقد مقدس ایشاں در لاہور گذر سنجا [OCR?] زیارت گاہ خاص و عام است", and places Khizr Khan "در مقربان عالی شان و امیران … فیروز شاہی", among the high intimates and amirs of Firoz Shah (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 199, بقیہ حاشیہ 1). His conclusion: in 758 AH the grandson was alive, and therefore the stated 600 AH is close to correct, "اس اقتباس سے تصریح ہوتا ہے کہ ۷۵۸ھ میں شیخ حسین زنجانی کے نواسے بقید حیات تھے۔ اس لیے شیخ حسین زنجانی کا مذکورہ سال وفات ۶۰۰ھ قرین صحت ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 199, بقیہ حاشیہ 1). The place-name in the passage, گذر سنجا, is uncertain in the printed text, and since the words about the holy grave follow Sayyid Yaqub's name, it is not clear whose grave the passage locates there (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 199).

## Khwaja Muin al-Din at the Tomb

Whether the founder of the Chishtiyya in India met Zanjani alive, or prayed at his grave, is itself an old question. Rizvi writes that Khwaja Muʿinuʾd-Din "stayed near the tombs of Shaikh Husain Zanjani and Shaikh ‘Ali Hujwiri" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121). In a footnote on the same page he sets out the earlier authorities. Jamali says that Hujwiri died in the year the Khwaja reached Lahore "but that Shaikh Husain Zanjani was still alive"; the *Fawaʿidu'l-Fuʾad* says that "Hujwiri reached Lahore in the year Shaikh Husain Zanjani died"; "According to Abu'l-Fazl, Khwaja Mu'inu'd-Din lived with Shaikh Husaini Zanjani"; and Firishta "simply mentions that after leaving Ghazna, the Khwaja stayed at Lahore" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121, footnote 3). Rizvi's own judgement: "Fawaidu'l Fu‘ad's statement appears to be correct and it is likely that the Khwaja stayed near the two tombs" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121, footnote 3).

Chishti, following Dara Shikoh, says that Muin al-Din "اوران حضرات سے ملاقاتیں کیں", met with these saints, after they had reached Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270). Lahori's editor, as above, gives the meeting and company around 585 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).

## The Shrine

The site's account describes a modest architectural footprint that belies its historical significance as one of Lahore's oldest surviving Islamic devotional sites, predating by centuries the grander Mughal-era shrines for which the city is more widely known: a simple raised platform without a dome, within what was once a garden named for the saint.

Lahori's entry on the saint gives no grave at all; the burial is stated in the editor's note on Data Ganj Bakhsh, "مدفون چاہ میراں" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196). The edition's appendix lists him as "سید حسین زنجانی قدس سرہ", with no address from the Mufti's text and a present location of "میراں حسین پارک چاہ میراں", Miran Husain Park, Chah Miran (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277).

Kanhaiya Lal, writing of the shrines outside the walled city, places it in a village east of the city: "یہ متبرک مزار موضع کہوئی میران بیرون شہر لاہور بجانب شرق بفاصلہ ایک میل کے واقع ہے", this blessed mazar lies in mauza Khoi Miran, outside the city of Lahore to the east, at a distance of one mile (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). The mazar stands inside a brick enclosure a man's height, "قد آدم بلند چار دیواری خشتی"; the grave itself is of brick; pakka houses have been built for faqirs to live in, "مکانات پختہ فقرا کی سکونت کے لئے"; and a Persian-wheel well is running, "چاہ چرخی دار جاری" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). His verdict on the place: "اگرچہ عمارت مختصر ہے مگر مکان قدیم ہے اور صاحب مزار قدما ئے بزرگان شہر لاہور سے ہے", though the building is small the place is ancient, and the one buried there is among the earliest elders of the city of Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). In his table of contents the shrine stands under the name "شاہ حسین زنجانی", Shah Husain Zanjani, with no place or date given there (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3).

Chishti describes the shrine twice. In the first account, headed in his contents "حال مزار شاہ حسین زنجانی[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 6), the "خانقاہ حضرت سید [OCR?] حسین زنجانی" lies "جنوب رویہ", on the south side, of Khoi Miran. It has a *chardiwari* with a door on the east "معہ طاق [OCR?] پختہ [OCR?]"; the mazar stands on a *chabutra* with a lamp-stand of brick, "خشتی [OCR?]"; north of the door is "ایک سہ درہ [OCR?]"; and there are a *dalan*, a well and a *charkhi*. But the place, he adds, is now forsaken: "مگر اب یہ مکان آوارہ [OCR?] … کوئی [OCR?] فقیر مکاندار [OCR?] یہاں نہیں بیٹھتا", no resident faqir sits here (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403).

In the second, fuller account he again sets it to the south of the village, "جنوب رویہ موضع میران دی کھوئی[OCR?] واقع ہے": a brick enclosure taller than a man with its entrance on the north, a niche with wooden shutters, a second enclosure with a "چراغدان", a three-arched *dalan*, a "چاہ چرخی دار", a few graves and a *kotha* (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).

The site's account says the shrine is now recognised and maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department. Chishti, in his day, names its holder: "مگر نامہم[OCR?] اوس مزار پر قبضہ کرم علی شاہ گدی نشین صدر دیوان صاحب کا ہی", the mazar being in the possession of Karam Ali Shah, *gaddi nashin* of Sadr Diwan Sahib; the faqirs there are few, and he mentions its income, "آمدنی[OCR?]" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705). Kanhaiya Lal records no offerings, custodian or endowment (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278).

## Devotion and Practice

The site's account records an annual *urs* that still draws local devotees. Chishti, too, writes that an *urs* is held once every year, "ہر سال ہمیشہ[OCR?] ایک دفعہ عرس ہوتا ہی" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705). In his first account he says that the *sajjada nashin* of Sadr Diwan has the *fatiha* said there year by year, "سجادہ نشین صدر دیوان [OCR?] سال بسال [OCR?] فاتحہ کرا دیتا ہی", in a sentence that opens on the well, "جب [OCR?] چاہ [OCR?] یہاں کا کم ہو گیا", its sense uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403).

Kanhaiya Lal remembers a larger gathering in decline: "سکہون کے وقت اس مزار پہ بڑا میلہ سالانہ ہوتا تہا مگر اب رفتہ رفتہ رونق میلے کی جاتی رہی ہے", in the Sikhs' time a great annual *mela* was held at this mazar, but now the mela's liveliness has gradually gone (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). He gives no date for the *urs* (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). On the same run of pages he notes the same fall in attendance after the Sikh state at the mazar of Fateh Shah Mast (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 274, folio 277).

## Legends and Miracles

Chishti writes that the saint's miracles are famous by the thousand, "کرامات انکی ہزار ہا مشہور ہیں", but he relates none of them (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705). The one story the books carry is that of Data Ganj Bakhsh and the bier, told above; in the Mufti's telling as his editor reports it, Data understood on seeing the bier his murshid's far-seeing eye (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).

## Companions and Namesakes

The site's account names his brother, Hazrat Musa Hussain Zanjani, buried nearby. The books name another Zanjani as his companion. Lahori has the saint come to Lahore with Sayyid Yaqub Zanjani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198), and the edition's appendix lists that saint on a separate line, "سید یعقوب المخاطب صدر دیوان زنجانی لاہوری قدس سرہ", at Hospital Road, Lahore, "ہسپتال روڈ لاہور" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277). Chishti has him come with "حضرت صدر دیوان صاحب" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705), and it is the line of Sadr Diwan whose *sajjada nashin* held the *fatiha* and the possession of the mazar in his day (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403; p. 705). The *Waqai-e Sialkot* passage quoted by Lahori's editor names "سید یعقوب صدر شاہ زنجانی" beside Sayyid Husain with the word "برادر" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 199, بقیہ حاشیہ 1).

Kanhaiya Lal places Shah Yaqub Zanjani, known as Sadr Diwan, outside Shah Alami Gate, and says he came from Zanjan in "سنہ ۵۳۵[OCR?] ہجری" and died in "سنہ ۵۵۶[OCR?] ہجری", the readings of both years uncertain in the printed text; the clause in which he names "سید حسین زنجانی" is damaged, "یہ سید حسین زنجانی کے لاہور میں آ کر سکونت پذیر ہوا", and does not show what relation, if any, he meant between the two (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 301, folio 304). The same book names a third Zanjani, "شیخ احمد زنجانی", author of the treatise *Tuhfat al-Wasilin*, whom it does not connect with the saint (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 14, folio 9).

## Setting

The books' wider remarks on Lahore and the Punjab speak of the city and the province, not of this grave. Rizvi ties the coming of Sufis to the Punjab to Mahmud of Ghazna's annexation, which "prompted many sufis to settle in the area" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112), and of eleventh-century Lahore he writes that "a number of mystics and scholars who had settled in Lahore were strongly hostile to the views of its author" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 131, folio 113).

Lahori's text gives the title of first caller to Islam in Lahore to another man, Shaikh Muhammad Ismail Muhaddith Lahori, a Bukhari sayyid who taught hadith and *tafsir* there and through whom, it says, "اور دین اسلام ان کے طفیل سے پنجاب میں شائع ہوا", the faith spread in the Punjab; it gives his death as 448 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 191, folio 179). Its modern editor rejects the source of that account and the date: "شیخ اسمٰعیل محدث لاہوری کا صحیح سال وفات ۹۸۰ ھ ہے نہ کہ ۴۴۸ ھ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 191–192, folios 179–180).

Of the neighbourhood, Kanhaiya Lal records a second shrine in the same village, the mazar of Faqir Sain Qutb Shah Qadri, lying "موضع کہوئی میران کے مشرق کی سمت", to the east of mauza Khoi Miran (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 271, folio 274). The arrangement he describes at the grave, faqirs' pakka quarters and a working Persian-wheel well, he records a page earlier at the mazar of Shah Gada Lahori (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 274, folio 277).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives 1042 CE. Lahori's text gives 600 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198), and its editor, in a note, "ف ۶۰۰ [OCR?] ہجری", the reading uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196). Kanhaiya Lal prints "سال وفات اسکا سنہ ۶۰۴ [OCR?] ہے", with no era (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). Rizvi dates the death only by Hujwiri's arrival at Lahore, "in c. 1035" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Chishti's year cannot be read, and he calls the particulars "نامعلوم" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).
- **When he came to Lahore.** The site's account has him born in 958 CE and arriving around 998 CE, on the instruction of Sheikh Abu al-Fazal Khatil. Rizvi has Khattali order him to the Punjab after Mahmud of Ghazna's annexation, before Hujwiri (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Kanhaiya Lal has him come from Zanjan "سلاطین غوریہ کے وقت", in the time of the Ghurid sultans (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). Chishti, following Dara Shikoh, has him reach Lahore in the fifth century of the hijra, the reading uncertain in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270). Lahori's editor argues that this saint lived around 585–600 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).
- **One man or two.** The site's account, after the *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, makes the saint of this tomb the senior pir-brother whose funeral Data Ganj Bakhsh met; Chishti agrees (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 163), and Rizvi has the man of the funeral buried in Chah Miran (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Lahori's editor holds that the Husain Zanjani buried at Chah Miran, died 600 AH, is a different person from the Husain Zanjani of *Fawaid al-Fuad* whose bier Data met (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196; p. 198, حاشیہ 1).
- **The Mufti against himself.** As his editor reports, the Mufti tells the bier story in *Khazinat al-Asfiya*, which would put the death well before 400 AH, and gives the death as 600 AH both there and in *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1).
- **Whether Khwaja Muin al-Din found him alive.** Jamali says he was "still alive" when the Khwaja reached Lahore; Abu'l-Fazl that the Khwaja "lived with" him; the *Fawaʿidu'l-Fuʾad* that he died in the year Hujwiri arrived; Firishta mentions only the Khwaja's stay at Lahore (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121, footnote 3). Lahori's editor gives a meeting and company around 585 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, حاشیہ 1), and Chishti, after Dara Shikoh, says Muin al-Din met these saints (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 270). Rizvi judges that the Khwaja "stayed near the two tombs" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121, footnote 3).
- **His name.** The site's account calls him Syed Miran Hussain Zanjani, and the *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* Hazrat Shaikh Hussain Zanjani. Lahori heads his entry "سید حسین زنجانی لاہوری" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198, folio 186). Kanhaiya Lal's contents and Chishti's contents print Shah Husain Zanjani (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3; Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 6). Rizvi prints Shaikh Husain Zinjani, Shaikh Husain Zanjani and Shaikh Husaini Zanjani, and neither Syed nor Miran (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112; p. 139, folio 121). The site's account names his master Sheikh Abu al-Fazal Khatil; Rizvi calls him Khattali (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112).
- **His spiritual chain.** Lahori says his chain meets Junaid of Baghdad (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198); Rizvi makes him a disciple of Khattali (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112); Kanhaiya Lal names no chain (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278).
- **His companion.** The site's account has him buried alongside his brother, Hazrat Musa Hussain Zanjani. Lahori has him come to Lahore with Sayyid Yaqub Zanjani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 198), whose own grave the edition's appendix places on Hospital Road (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 289, folio 277); Chishti has him come with Hazrat Sadr Diwan Sahib (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).
- **Where the grave stands.** The site's account places it in the riverside locality of Chah Miran, on the historic bank of the Ravi near the old walled city. Lahori's editor and Rizvi name Chah Miran (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 196; Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112). Kanhaiya Lal puts it in mauza Khoi Miran, a mile east of the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278). Chishti sets it to the south of Khoi Miran (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403; p. 705).
- **The doorway, in Chishti's two accounts.** One gives the enclosure a door on the east (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403); the other gives its entrance on the north (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).
- **Who keeps the shrine.** The site's account says it is maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department. Chishti, in his day, has it in the possession of Karam Ali Shah, *gaddi nashin* of Sadr Diwan Sahib (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705); in his other account no faqir sits there (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 403), and in this one the faqirs are few (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705).
- **The yearly gathering.** The site's account and Chishti record an annual *urs* (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 705). Kanhaiya Lal records a great annual *mela* in the Sikh period whose liveliness has since gone (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278).

## Legacy

As one of the earliest attested Sufi graves in the Lahore region, the shrine offers valuable testimony to the gradual, missionary-led spread of Islam in Punjab in the centuries before the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal empire. The nineteenth-century surveys already counted it among the city's oldest: Kanhaiya Lal calls the place ancient and its occupant one of the earliest elders of Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 275, folio 278), and Chishti, after Dara Shikoh, names him first among the saints who came from abroad to Lahore, "شیخ المشایخ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 269).

His name has also travelled with the story of Data Ganj Bakhsh, whose arrival in Lahore the books measure by Zanjani's funeral, and with that of Khwaja Muin al-Din Chishti, who is said to have kept company with him or to have stayed near his tomb. Whether one man or two lie behind that name, the locality of Chah Miran around the grave is named in his honour.
