Name: Shrine of Peer Makki
Location: Bhati Gate area (near Data Darbar), Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini (Peer Makki)
Events: Annual urs (9-11 Rabi al-Awwal); Thursday-night gatherings; dhamal and qawwali
Description:
## Overview

Standing close to the great mausoleum of Data Ganj Bakhsh, in the Walled City's Bhati Gate quarter, the shrine of Peer Makki commemorates Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini, a scholar-mystic born in Baghdad — the son of Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah, of a Hasani-Hussaini family of religious scholars that counted Junaid Baghdadi, Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal and Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani among its kin. He is said to have migrated to Mecca in 562 AH, at about the age of thirty, and to have spent twelve years there in ascetic seclusion — hence his popular title "Makki" — before journeying overland to India. Hagiographical accounts hold that he arrived in Lahore in 575 AH (around 1178 CE) by what tradition describes as divine instruction, and remained for some thirty-six years as a teacher of both the exoteric sciences of Islamic law and the esoteric path of the Junaidi Sufi lineage, tracing back to the classical Baghdad master Junayd. He is said to have died in 612 AH (1215 CE).

The shrine complex includes an adjoining mosque, the Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid, and is formally administered, like Data Darbar itself, by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department; its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat. Despite its proximity to one of Pakistan's most visited shrines, Peer Makki's own tomb receives markedly fewer pilgrims, giving it a more intimate, contemplative atmosphere.

Three of the books consulted name the shrine itself. Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, in its modern Urdu edition, gives him an entry of his own as "سید شیخ عزیز الدین مکی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), places his death in 612 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 201, folio 189), and lists his tomb among those still standing, on Ravi Road, in Pir Makki Street (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 290, folio 278). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, a survey of the tombs and buildings of Lahore, describes the grave, its wells and its keeper, and records an *ʿurs* and a land grant; but Chishti found no account of the saint in any book and proposes, only tentatively, who he may have been (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674; p. 675). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* lists "مزار پیر مکی" in its table of contents among the Muslim sites outside the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 5, folio 4). The books disagree with the site's account, and with one another, on where the tomb stands, on when the saint died, and on who he was; those differences are set out below.

## The Life of the Saint

His father, Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah, was himself a saint and a scholar who taught in Baghdad, and Peer Makki had his first education from him — memorising the Qur'an, then learning what is reported as the knowledge of the soul and of the sect, seated in the same row as everyone else in his father's circle. Having taken the outward sciences as far as they went, he judged that he must go looking for the hidden knowledge, and in 562 AH, at thirty, he left Baghdad for Mecca. He spent twelve years there, hearing the pleas of those who came to him, helping them, keeping his nights in the Haram in the remembrance of God, and — it is reported — receiving the blessing of the Prophet many times. He began to know what was to come, and did not show it.

The migration to India, it is reported, was not his own idea. Worshipping in the Haram, he received the Prophet's command to go to Hind, where the people had fallen into associating partners with God, and to bring them back to the Sunna and to the oneness of God. He did not wish to leave the House of God, but the command was the command: he made his last Hajj, took some companions with him, and turned first to Baghdad, to tell his family and to say the Fatiha at his father's grave, before setting out. Two roads led to India, one through the dry desert and one by sea; the journey was long and dangerous and there was little to eat or drink, but he preached along the way, and people were moved enough to join his caravan. Something close to a year later he reached India and gave thanks. He came to Lahore in 575 AH and settled in the mosque that today carries his name beside his shrine, leading the prayers, teaching the Qur'an, and calling people away from polytheism.

Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves the same broad outline — his given name Azizuddin, his Baghdad origin, and the twelve years spent in seclusion at Mecca that earned him the epithet "Makki" — and adds that on first reaching Lahore he went directly to the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh before settling at the site that became his own; the detail reinforces, without resolving, the chronological tension between the two saints' conventional dates that is set out below.

The political part of his life is reported at length. Lahore was held by Khusrau Malik — reportedly the last of Mahmud of Ghazni's line, and the son of King Khusrau — who is described as pleasure-seeking and unjust; Muhammad Shahab-ud-Din Ghori was advancing on the city, having already taken Multan and Sialkot. When Khusrau Malik came to ask how long his rule would last, the saint told him plainly that it would end soon, that what God has written must come, and that he should turn to God and deal justly with his people. When Ghori's army arrived, the people and the king both ran to him; he told them to be patient and to repent, and said the danger would pass and return in six years. Ghori withdrew, and the saint's name went round the city — but the people soon returned to their old habits, and exactly six years later Ghori came again. Again the saint promised a respite, and said it was the last; again the army turned back, and this time people called him a liar, saying the old man only ever said such things and that Ghori left out of fear. When Ghori finally took Lahore, Khusrau Malik's men were killed or went over to him, and the king himself was taken prisoner and later killed. Ghori, it is reported, came to the saint's door and told him he had known he was there, and that everything he had said had been true.

He preached in Lahore for thirty-six years after that, and died in 612 AH; the quarter took his name from him, as the title Makki had come from his years in Mecca.

## The Saint in the Books

Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, composed in 1875, gives the saint an entry with a date. Its table of contents lists him as entry 136, "سید شیخ عزیز الدین مکی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 18, folio 6), and the author's text gives his death as 612 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 201, folio 189). The book's index files him as "عزیز الدین مکی", so that both elements of his name here, Azizuddin and Makki, stand in the index's own words; the same index lists three other men named Aziz al-Din, none of them called Makki (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 323, folio 311). The index also cites him on a second page, inside the book's run of Suhrawardi saints of Multan, and does not say why (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 323, folio 311).

It is the edition's modern editor who ties the book's Shaikh Aziz al-Din to the popular name. He writes that he has prepared a detailed article on him, titled with the name by which Lahore knows him, for an encyclopaedia of the Subcontinent published in Tehran: "شیخ عزیز الدین مکی لاہوری پر ''پیر مکی'' کے عنوان سے ہم نے ایک مفصل مقالہ دانشنامہ شبہ قارہ۔ تہران، ایران کے لئے سپرد قلم کیا ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338). The identification of the *Hadiqat*'s saint with Peer Makki is therefore the editor's.

The editor also weighs the dates. He rejects a death year of 1048 AH given by Nur Ahmad Chishti, writing that Chishti set it down without any reference and that it is baseless: "نور احمد چشتی نے تحقیقات چشتی (۶۰۱۔ ۶۰۷) میں بغیر کسی حوالے کے پیر مکی کا سال وفات ۱۰۴۸ھ لکھ دیا ہے جو بے بنیاد ہے" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 351, folio 339). Against it he finds the author's own date the more plausible, without calling it established: "مفتی غلام سرور کا درج کردہ سال وفات ۶۱۲ھ/۱۵۔۱۲۱۶ء زیادہ قرین قیاس معلوم ہوتا ہے" — 612 AH, which he equates with 1215–16 CE, the Common Era span printed in reversed order (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 351, folio 339). Yet a footnote in the same edition, quoting the author's other book, the Persian *Khazinat al-Asfiya*, gives the same man's death as "ف ۷۹۶ھ [OCR?]", the reading of the year uncertain in the printed text (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 191, folio 189 as printed). The edition does not remark on the difference between the author's two books.

The editor's general verdict on what Lahore's historians had written about the saint is severe. They wrote down hearsay and did no research, he says, so that even the years of the conflict between the Ghurid and Ghaznavid sultans are given wrongly: "مورخین لاہور نے اس سلسلے میں محض سماعی باتیں لکھی ہیں کسی نے کوئی تحقیق نہیں کی۔ یہاں تک کہ سلاطین غوریان و غزنویان کی جو چپقلش ہوئی تھی اس کے سنین بھی غلط لکھے ہیں" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338). He includes the author's own *خزینۃ الاصفیاء* in that charge (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 351, folio 339). The saint's entry thus stands, in this edition, against the background of the Ghurid and Ghaznavid struggle for Lahore that is also reported in the account of his life above.

Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, as it is read here, says something different again. At the tomb he writes that the saint's circumstances are not known, "حال اکا معلوم نہیں ہوتا", and reports two opinions: some say he was a disciple of "حضرت داتا[OCR?] گنج[OCR?] صاحب", others that he came to Lahore "محمود غزنوی کی ساتھہ آ ای[OCR?]", in the company of Mahmud of Ghazni (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674). The author adds that he found no account of him in any book he had read, "کسی کسا میں[OCR?] و کرا کا سطالع[OCR?] نہیں آیا" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674).

He then offers an identification, and hedges it. A book he calls "کتاب تذکرہ فقرا" names a "حضرت سعد الدین ملی[OCR?]" — the reading of the epithet uncertain in the printed text — who came from "ملہ[OCR?] معظمہ", visited the *khanqah* of Hujwiri, stayed there in *iʿtikaf*, died, and was buried by the river at Shah Jahan's order, with a *maqbara* raised over him (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675). "شاید بہی حضرت ہوہ[OCR?] ن", Chishti writes, perhaps this is the same holy man; the *maqbara* is not there, but "اگر گیا ہوتو عجب نہین", if it has gone, that would be no wonder. He gives that saint's death as "۱۲[OCR?] ربیع الثانی سنہ[OCR?] [illegible] ہجری", the year illegible in the printed text (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675).

## The Shrine

Kings maintained the shrine after him and added to its beauty, and it is reported that the Auqaf Department took responsibility for it in 1958. The shrine complex includes the adjoining Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid, the mosque in which, reportedly, the saint settled on reaching Lahore; its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat.

Chishti's survey of the tombs of Lahore describes the place as it stood in his day. It lies west of the *takia* he has just described, at "کر کوشہ جنوبی شرقی کمیٹی باغ", the south-eastern corner of the garden the text calls the Committee Bagh; a brick wall rises above a man's height, and within it "قبر حضرت مکی[OCR?] رحمتہ اللہ علیہ کی پختہ", the grave of Hazrat Makki, built in brick and mortar, stands on a platform (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674). There were two masonry wells, a *ghusl-khana*, and "چبوترہ نشان مسجد", a platform marking a mosque (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675). The keeper was a *faqir* woman, her age printed as "۵۹[OCR?]", with two sons, "فتح دین" and "کرم دین" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675). The shrine held land: "ارہا ای[OCR?] کنال زمین مزروعہ", cultivated land measured in *kanals*, the number unclear in the printed text, held "تا قیام خانقاہ معاف", free of revenue for as long as the *khanqah* stands (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675). Elsewhere in the same book the shrine appears in passing beside its great neighbour: describing the garden of Zeb-un-Nisa, Chishti says its wall can be seen, "مثل [OCR?] مکان دا[تا] [OCR?] گنج بخش صاحب و پیر مکی صاحب" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 342).

Lahori's edition locates the tomb in its appendix of the saints' resting places as they stood when the edition was made. Row 49 reads "سید شیخ عزیز الدین مکی لاہوری قدس سرہ | لاہور | راوی روڈ پیر مکی سٹریٹ": Lahore, Ravi Road, Pir Makki Street (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 290, folio 278). The site's own account places the shrine in the Bhati Gate area near Data Darbar; the two descriptions are not shown to conflict, and not shown to agree. The same appendix gives, under another row, a mosque in Anarkali whose name contains "مکی"; it is a different place (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 291).

Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* of 1884 promises an entry on the tomb. Its table of contents lists "مزار پیر مکی" in the section on the Muslim sites outside the city, the page number printed beside it, ۳۲۵[OCR?], uncertain in the printed text; the entry itself is not among the passages of the book consulted here (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 5, folio 4).

## Devotion and Practice

Devotional custom in Lahore holds that pilgrims should pay their respects at Peer Makki's tomb before proceeding to Data Darbar, honouring him as a spiritual forerunner in the same sacred locale. Peer Makki's own tomb receives some 3,500 to 4,000 pilgrims on an ordinary day, though Thursday-night gatherings draw larger crowds, and the narrow street and surrounding Peer Makki Bazaar can make access difficult.

The annual urs, held on the 9th to the 11th of Rabi-ul-Awal, fills the quarter with gatherings and dhikr, drums and dhamal, qawwali, the ritual bathing of the shrine and the distribution of offerings, and draws on the order of 400,000 to 500,000 devotees.

Chishti, in his own day, records the *ʿurs* in the month of Rabi al-Awwal, the printed text reading "بارہ مین بیع الاول", which appears to give the twelfth of the month; *halwa* and *kheer* were served (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675). He adds that in earlier days "آگی برا سیلہ[OCR?] ہوتا تہا", a great fair used to be held, and that fewer people came in his own time (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675).

## Legends and Miracles

A well-loved anecdote recalls that during Sultan Muhammad Ghori's 1178 siege of Lahore, the besieged governor Khusro Malik sought Peer Makki's prayers, and the saint assured him of six further years of safety. The fuller account reported of the two sieges, the twice-promised respite and Ghori's visit to the saint's door is given above.

The popular claim that he personally tutored Data Ganj Bakhsh sits awkwardly with the conventional dating of Ali Hujwiri's death around 1072, a century before Peer Makki's own arrival, and should be understood as devotional tradition rather than strict chronology. A tradition recorded at the shrine itself runs the other way about: when Ali Hujwiri was ordered to migrate to Lahore, he is said to have objected that "Peer Makki is present there, who is enough for Lahore" — only to arrive and find Peer Makki's funeral already underway. Like the tutoring claim, the story fits loosely with the dates, but it carries the shrine's essential teaching: that Lahore has never been without a saint of Allah.

Chishti knew yet another version of the two saints' bond, and reports it only as what some say: that Peer Makki was Data Ganj Bakhsh's disciple (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674). The saint he tentatively identifies with Peer Makki likewise comes to Hujwiri's *khanqah* as a visitor (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675).

## Setting: Ghaznavid and Ghurid Lahore

The books consulted tell the history of the city in which the saint's prophecies are reported to have been made, without naming him in it; what follows is about Lahore, not about the shrine.

Of the neighbouring shrine, and not of this one, Annemarie Schimmel writes that Lahore was "the capital of the Ghaznawids in India", where Hujwiri "died there in 1071", and that "His shrine, called that of Data Ganj Bakhsh, is still a popular place of pilgrimage in Lahore" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi has Hujwiri reach Lahore "in c. 1035, while Sultan Mas'ud I (1031-41) reigned in Ghazna" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 130, folio 112).

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, written under Aurangzeb, gives the last Ghaznavid rulers of Lahore. Khusraw Shah, son of Bahram Shah, driven from Ghazni by the Ghurid sultan, took Lahore and governed the Punjab until his death in 555; his son "سلطان خسرو ملک بن خسروشاه" succeeded him, and his rule in Lahore lasted twenty-eight years, "مدت حکومت او درلاهور بست وهشت سال" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405). Bhandari dates Shihab al-Din's third campaign, the one directed at Lahore, to "درسنه ۵۷۵[OCR?]", the year as printed uncertain: "سلطان ملک خسرو ازنسل سلطان محمود غزنوی ... حکومت لاهور داشت"; the fort was nearly taken after siege and battle, and Khusraw Malik sent his son with an elephant as tribute and made peace (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404). In the fifth campaign, "درسنه ۵۸۰[OCR?]", the sultan besieged Lahore again and Khusraw Malik shut himself in the fort (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404); the book's account of the suba of Lahore says of the same year that Shihab al-Din came to take Lahore, besieged it, "و بران دست نیافت" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 517). In the sixth, "درسنه ۵۸۲[OCR?]", Khusraw Malik submitted, was taken to Ghazni and died there, and the sultan set his own deputy over Lahore (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404).

Kanhaiya Lal tells the end of the dynasty in the same terms: when the Ghurids drove the house from Ghazni, "خسرو شاہ خسرو ملک کے باپ نے پنجاب مین اپنی حکومت قایم کر لی", and with Khusrau Malik's surrender "سلاطین غوریہ کی سلطنت کا ہند مین آغاز ہوا اور غزنویہ حکومت با اختتام پہنچی", the rule of the Ghurid sultans in Hind began and that of the Ghaznavids came to an end (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19). Chishti, too, has Khusrau Shah son of Bahram make Lahore his capital, his son Khusrau Malik succeed him, and the Ghurids take the land from Khusrau "بہزار مکر و فریب" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 808–809). Rizvi dates the Ghurid seizure of Multan to 1175, when "Mu'izzu'd-Din Muhammad bin Sam seized Multan, establishing firm control and Sunni rule over the southern part of the Panjab" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 128, folio 110). Harish Dhillon, on the other hand, writes that Ghori "was not able to conquer Lahore" when he captured the Punjab in 1192 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 136, folio 151).

## Setting: Bhati Gate and the Name Makki

Bhati Gate, where the site's account places the shrine, is one of the twelve gates of the walled city: Chishti's list of them ends "بہاٹی دروازہ ٭ موری دروازہ" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 498), and Haroon Khalid writes of "the walled city of Lahore, of which Bhatti gate is one of the twelve entry points" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 12, ch. 6, folio not stated). Kanhaiya Lal describes Bhati as the city's seventh gate and names no shrine in it (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13).

Two other names in Kanhaiya Lal's history echo this one and belong to other people. His contents list, apart from the tomb of Peer Makki, a "مقبرہ عبدالرزاق مکی[OCR?]" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 4, folio 3). And he heads one passage "تیرہوان ذکی دروازہ المعروف مکی دروازہ" (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 20, folio 15): the thirteenth gate, Zaki Gate, known as Makki Gate, named for a Pir Zaki, a gate guard of Mughal times who was martyred at the gate; Kanhaiya Lal gives him no Syed descent, no date and no Sufi order, and presents the form Makki as a corruption of Zaki. In a later passage both the man's name and the gate's, "پیر ذکی[OCR?]" and "ذکی[OCR?] دروازہ", are uncertain readings in the printed text (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 164, folio 167). The book does not connect either figure with Hazrat Syed Azizuddin.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Where the tomb stands.** The site's account places it in the Walled City's Bhati Gate quarter, close to Data Darbar. Lahori's edition gives "راوی روڈ پیر مکی سٹریٹ", Ravi Road, Pir Makki Street (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 290, folio 278). Chishti sets it west of a *takia*, at the south-eastern corner of the Committee Bagh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674). Kanhaiya Lal's contents list it among the sites outside the city (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 5, folio 4), and his account of Bhati Gate names no shrine there (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 18, folio 13).
- **When the saint died.** The site's account and the survey give 612 AH (1215 CE). Lahori's text gives 612 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 201, folio 189), and his editor calls "۶۱۲ھ/۱۵۔۱۲۱۶ء" the more plausible (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 351, folio 339). A footnote in the same edition quoting Lahori's *Khazinat al-Asfiya* gives "ف ۷۹۶ھ [OCR?]" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 191, folio 189 as printed). The editor reports that Nur Ahmad Chishti gave 1048 AH, and rejects it as baseless (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 351, folio 339). In Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* as read here, the author gives no date for Peer Makki himself, and for the saint he tentatively identifies with him gives "۱۲[OCR?] ربیع الثانی سنہ[OCR?] [illegible] ہجری", the year illegible (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675).
- **Who he was and when he came.** The site's account and the survey make him Hazrat Syed Azizuddin of Baghdad, who reached Lahore from Mecca in 575 AH. Lahori's editor identifies the *Hadiqat*'s "شیخ عزیز الدین مکی لاہوری" with Peer Makki (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338). Chishti writes that his circumstances are not known; some say he came with Mahmud of Ghazni; and Chishti himself suggests, with a "perhaps", a saint from Mecca who was buried by the river at Shah Jahan's order (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674; p. 675).
- **Peer Makki and Data Ganj Bakhsh.** Popular claim has Peer Makki tutor Data Ganj Bakhsh; a tradition recorded at the shrine has Hujwiri arrive in Lahore to find Peer Makki's funeral under way; Alam Faqri has Peer Makki go first to the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh on reaching Lahore. Chishti reports that some call Peer Makki Data Ganj Bakhsh's disciple (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674).
- **Hujwiri's death.** The site's account gives the conventional date of Ali Hujwiri's death as around 1072. Schimmel writes that he "died there in 1071" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 119, folio 88).
- **The date of the urs.** The site's account gives the 9th to the 11th of Rabi-ul-Awal. Chishti's printed text reads "بارہ مین بیع الاول" (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 675).
- **Ghori and Lahore.** The site's account dates Ghori's siege, in which the governor sought the saint's prayers, to 1178, and the survey has Ghori return exactly six years later and at last take the city, with Khusrau Malik taken prisoner and later killed. Bhandari dates the Ghurid campaigns against Lahore to 575, 580 and 582, the years uncertain in the printed text, and has Khusraw Malik submit in 582 and die at Ghazni (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404). Dhillon writes that Ghori "was not able to conquer Lahore" when he captured the Punjab in 1192 (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 136, folio 151). Lahori's editor holds that Lahore's historians wrote even the years of the Ghurid–Ghaznavid conflict wrongly (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338).
- **When the Auqaf took charge.** The field survey says the Auqaf Department took charge of the shrine in 1958. No book consulted gives a year.

## Legacy

Many writers — including, it is said at the shrine, authors from the Hindu and Christian communities — have written books about the saint that are still read with interest today. The books consulted here show how unsettled that literature has been: a tomb that Chishti could describe in detail while finding no account of its saint in any book (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 674); an identification and a date that Lahori's modern editor offers as the more plausible, against a footnote in his own edition that puts the same man nearly two centuries later (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338; p. 351, folio 339); and the editor's own judgement that Lahore's historians had written hearsay about him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 350, folio 338). Through all of it the shrine has kept its name and its place beside Data Darbar, and the quarter, Peer Makki Bazaar and Pir Makki Street, carries the title Makki that his years in Mecca are said to have given him.

Name: Shrine of Pir Baba (Syed Ali Tirmizi)
Location: Pacha Kalay, Buner District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 16th century (saint died 1583 CE; shrine developed thereafter)
Events: Annual urs (24-26 Rajab)
Description:
The Shrine of Pir Baba at Pacha Kalay, in the mountainous Buner District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, honours *Syed Ali Tirmizi* (c. 1502–1583), the Sufi saint universally known as *Pir Baba*, one of the most revered holy figures of the Pashtun lands. Of *Sayyid* descent, he was traditionally said to have been born at Tirmiz in Central Asia (in present-day Uzbekistan) — though some accounts instead give Fergana as his birthplace — and, according to tradition, came to the region in the train of the Mughal advance, settling at Pacha in Buner around the middle of the sixteenth century. From there his spiritual influence spread widely, and he is remembered as a supporter of the early Mughals — the emperor Humayun is said to have granted him lands in Kunar — and as an opponent of the heterodox teacher Bayazid Ansari, the "Pir Roshan." A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, gives his fuller name as Syed Ali Ghawwas Tirmizi and names Akhund Darweza — the Peshawar-based Chishti saint venerated at the Shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba elsewhere in this archive — as his most renowned khalifa (successor). His green-domed mausoleum, which also holds the grave of his son Syed Habibullah, became the nucleus of a devotional complex; an adjoining mosque was raised in the twentieth century, between about 1938 and 1965, under the care of his descendants. The shrine draws great crowds of pilgrims, above all at the annual *urs* commemorating the saint, held from 24 to 26 of the Islamic month of Rajab. Its prominence made it a target during the militancy that afflicted the region: in December 2008 militants attacked the shrine, destroying religious inscriptions and hoardings, and in 2009 it was briefly closed when Taliban fighters seized control of Buner, before being reopened as security was restored. It remains among the most important Sufi shrines of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Name: Shrine of Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani
Location: Near Naulung (Moola gorge), Gandava area, Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Visited year-round by Muslim and Hindu pilgrims; no fixed urs recorded
Description:
The shrine of *Pir* Chhatal Shah Noorani stands at a spring-fed oasis near the mouth of the Moola gorge, where the Moola River shears clear across the Kirthar range to reach the Kachhi plain at Gandava, in the Jhal Magsi district of Balochistan. The point where the river debouches from the hills is known as *Naulung* ("Nine Fords") or, among the highland Baloch, *Punjmunh* ("Five Mouths"); for thousands of years this was the most convenient passage between the Indus valley and the Kalat uplands. The site is celebrated for a small, clear pond, fed by a copious spring bursting from the rock, that teems with large *mahseer* fish. By long tradition the fish were the saint's pets and no one has ever eaten them; local lore holds that any fish caught and cooked would emerge again alive, a taboo that has in effect made the pond one of the oldest fish-conservation sanctuaries in the region. Chhatal Shah Noorani is remembered as a granter of wishes to whom Hindus and Muslims alike came to have their hearts' desires fulfilled. The tomb sits on a low knoll: in 1831 the traveller Charles Masson (James Lewis) recorded it as a conspicuous *gumbaz*, or domed building, that served as the usual halting-place for caravans crossing between Kalat and Kachhi, though the dome has since collapsed and the grave now stands within plain modern walls. In recent years improved access has turned the once-remote spot into a popular picnic destination. Salman Rashid, who first visited the site in 2003, described the pond as "teeming with mahseer fish, nearly 60 cm long," and recorded a keeper's own account of the saint's identity: asked who Chhatal Shah Noorani had been, the man replied simply, "Only Allah knows!" — adding only that he was "a granter of wishes" to Hindus and Muslims alike. The Jhal Magsi district government's own heritage listing independently confirms the shrine, naming it among the district's principal shrines and placing it "near Kotra."

Name: Shrine of Pir Lakha (Aab-e-Shifa), Jhal Magsi
Location: Near Kotra (Moola gorge area), Jhal Magsi District, Balochistan, Pakistan
Events: Year-round pilgrimage; ritual bathing in the hot springs
Description:
The shrine of Pir Lakha lies in the north-western uplands of the Jhal Magsi District of Balochistan, in the broken country near Kotra where the Moola river descends through its gorge — the same tract that holds the shrine of Pir Chhatal Shah Noorani (a separate entry in this dataset). District heritage listings count Pir Lakha among the principal shrines of Jhal Magsi, alongside the *dargahs* of Rakhyal Shah at Fatehpur and Muhammad Ayub Shah Bukhari at Gandava. Its particular fame rests less on a documented saintly biography — of which little is recorded — than on the hot springs beside it, known as *Aab-e-Shifa*, "the water of healing." Pilgrims travel from far-flung parts of Balochistan and Sindh to bathe in these thermal waters, which are believed to cure skin ailments and other afflictions, so that the site functions at once as a shrine and as a place of folk therapeutics. Like several shrines of the Kachhi–Gandava plain, it draws Muslim and Hindu visitors alike. Because the life of the eponymous *pir* is essentially undocumented in accessible sources, only the shrine's living role as a pilgrimage-and-healing centre can be stated with confidence. This listing is independently confirmed by the Jhal Magsi district government's own Culture & Heritage page, which names "Pir Lakha" both as a page heading and among the district's main shrines. That official listing, however, does not mention the Aab-e-Shifa hot springs at all; no citable source consulted for this entry corroborates the healing-spring claim that gives the site its popular name, which currently rests only on social-media and blog accounts.

Name: Shrine of Pir Mangho
Events: Annual urs; Sheedi Mela (drumming, dance, offerings to the crocodiles)
Description:
## Overview

On the northern outskirts of Karachi lies Mangho Pir, one of the most unusual and atmospheric shrines in Pakistan, famous for three things that meet nowhere else: a medieval Sufi saint, a pool of sacred crocodiles, and hot sulphur springs believed to heal. The darbar of Pir Mangho (Hazrat Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan) is a centre of pilgrimage of great antiquity, and it is bound up with the culture of Karachi’s Sheedi community, the Afro-Pakistani descendants of East Africa, whose annual festival at the shrine is one of the city’s most distinctive traditions.

The books consulted here name the shrine, but in other spellings, and none of them gives the name Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan. Jürgen Schaflechner's study of the Hinglaj pilgrimage speaks of "the shrine of Magho Pir, which is now located in the northern part of Karachi" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 78, folio not stated), of "the dargāh (Urd.) of the Sufi saint Mango Pir, in northern Karachi" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 211, folio not stated), and of "the shrine of Mango Pir in Karachi" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 263, folio not stated); he gives no saint's name, no dates, no Sufi order, no custodian, no *ʿurs*, no ritual and no crocodiles. Shemeem Burney Abbas, writing of the women musicians of Sindh and of its Sidi community, calls it "Manghopir" and "The Mangopir shrine", and dedicates it to a different saint, Bava Gor (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated). Annemarie Schimmel names "Mango Pir near Karachi" once, in a short parenthesis (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 238, folio 207). Michel Boivin uses the name "Mangho Pir" for the locality, in connection with a leper asylum, not the shrine (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 104, folio 91). Each of these identifications rests on the name and the place; none of the books says more about the saint than is set out below.

## The Saint

The saint of Mangho Pir is remembered as a holy man of the medieval centuries who settled at this spot in the hills above Karachi. The site's account names him Pir Mangho, Hazrat Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan. The books consulted here record no year of birth or death for him, no teacher and no Sufi order.

Abbas gives the shrine a different dedication: "The Mangopir shrine is associated with crocodiles and is dedicated to Bava Gor, the African Muslim saint" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated). On the same page she places Bava Gor's shrine in India: "Bava Gor is the Abyssinian saint of the Sidi in Gujrat in India, where a shrine is dedicated to him, his brother Bava Habash, and his sister Mai Misra" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated). She does not reconcile the two statements. Elsewhere she records that "In Karachi there is also a memorial shrine, and everywhere that Bava Gor stopped on his journey a shrine was created and each time one of the Sidis from his army remained in the place" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 73, folio not stated); she does not name that Karachi memorial shrine, and the sentence speaks of the city, not of Mangho Pir.

To Abbas's informant Qalandar Shah, the saint of the place is known by what lives in his pool: "Manghopir is the pir of the crocodiles" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 70, folio not stated).

Schaflechner names no saint of his own. He notes that an earlier writer whom he cites as Hart (Hart 1839) called the saint "Peer Moogha" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 263, folio not stated), and he raises, as a possibility, an older association of the shrine with Lalu Jasraj, a figure of the Kapri narratives he recorded (see Legends and Miracles below).

## The Shrine

Below the tomb lies a pond inhabited by crocodiles, held sacred and cared for by the shrine’s attendants; the eldest and largest is honoured with the title *Mor Sahib*, and pilgrims make offerings of meat, for the crocodiles are believed to be under the saint’s protection and their favour a sign of blessing. Abbas, too, describes the shrine as one that "is associated with crocodiles" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated).

Nearby, hot sulphur springs rise from the earth, and bathing in their waters is believed to cure skin ailments and other diseases, so that the shrine is a place of healing as much as of prayer. Schaflechner mentions the springs as a natural phenomenon. In a comparison with Chandrakup, he writes: "Other examples of similar thermic phenomena also exist on this anticline, such as at the dargāh (Urd.) of the Sufi saint Mango Pir, in northern Karachi (Snead 1964, 549)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 211, folio not stated) Elsewhere he speaks of "a hermitage near the hot springs" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 263, folio not stated).

The site's account places the shrine on the northern outskirts of Karachi, in the hills above the city; Schaflechner says only that it is "now located in the northern part of Karachi" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 78, folio not stated). The books consulted here do not describe the tomb or its buildings, and they record no founder, builder, custodian or endowment.

## Devotion and Practice

Mangho Pir holds a special place for the Sheedi community of Karachi, the descendants of Africans brought to the subcontinent over the centuries, who regard the saint as their own and the shrine as a spiritual home. Their annual *Sheedi Mela* at Mangho Pir, with its drumming, dance, and offerings to the sacred crocodiles, is a vivid survival of African-rooted culture in Pakistan and one of the most striking festivals of Karachi, binding the shrine to a living community and its heritage.

Abbas's informants describe this gathering, which they place in April. Qalandar Shah, speaking to the singer Kubra, said of the Sidis (the book's spelling of Sheedi): "They have a big congregation in Karachi at Manghopir—in April—Manghopir is the pir of the crocodiles—they have a large conference and Sidis from all over come there—they get a big press coverage—Have you been there?" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 70, folio not stated). Kubra answered that the festival lay outside her own circle: "No, that is in Karachi—we sing at weddings" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 71, folio not stated). Abbas adds that "The women musicians Karima and Kubra also explained that the Sidis have a huge melā of another pir at Manghopir in Karachi", and that "Qalandar Shah had talked about the annual festival at this shrine in his interview" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 71, folio not stated). April is the only date the books give for the festival; they give no day and no year.

The site's account also speaks of an annual *ʿurs*. The books consulted here give no date for it.

## Legends and Miracles

Tradition weaves the crocodiles and the springs into the miracles of the saint himself.

Schimmel's *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* touches on such a miracle only in passing. In a passage on a wonder involving an alligator she adds, in a parenthesis of ten words and without a note, "(as happened in Mango Pir near Karachi)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 238, folio 207). She names no saint and gives no date. Her index lists the place as "Mango Pir" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 520, folio 489).

Schaflechner offers a conjecture of his own, and hedges it each time he makes it. "It seems rather likely that the shrine of Magho Pir, which is now located in the northern part of Karachi, was once associated with Lalu Jasraj (Burton 1851, 326)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 78, folio not stated) In the narratives of the Kapri community that he recorded, Lalu Jasraj is "Rama's aguā (Hin. guide)" and "the founder of the Kapris" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 74, 78, folios not stated), and elsewhere "the chaṛīdār (Hin. stickbearer) of Rama and his entourage" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 209, folio not stated). In a note he sets out his reasoning: "Hart's description allows for an association of the mythological figure Lalu Jasraj with the shrine of Mango Pir in Karachi. Notwithstanding the fact that Hart calls the saint 'Peer Moogha,' knowing that it is said that Lalu Jasraj stayed at a hermitage near the hot springs makes the association possible (Hart 1839, 80)." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 263, folio not stated) The association is his suggestion, not a statement of fact. He is also cautious about how widely the Lalu Jasraj stories are known: "I came across this narrative mainly during my conversations with Dayaram Kapri from Gujarat… who claimed that this reference is found in the Hiṃgulā Purāṇ. Unfortunately, I was not able to locate the story there, and only a few of my other informants in Pakistan mentioned this myth about Liari, so it is questionable how widespread it is outside the Gujarati Kapri community." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 209, folio not stated)

## In Verse

The books consulted here quote no verse by the saint of Mangho Pir or about the shrine, and record no hymn, chronogram or inscription from it.

## Setting

The books' wider accounts of Karachi, of Sindh and of the Sidi community speak of the city, the province and the people, not of this shrine, but they help to place it.

**The Sidi community.** Abbas's glossary gives "Sidi Also known as Sheedi or Syedi in Sind and Gujrat" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 188, folio not stated). From her fieldwork among the Sidi she writes that they "were initially brought as slaves from Africa to work in the subcontinent of Pakistan and India. Although they are now free, some of them are attached to the feudal households in the Sind province of Pakistan. Their native language is Sindhi" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 67–68, folios not stated). Qalandar Shah told her that "the Africans are present in the Sind in large numbers—because of the slave trade—they were brought here in large numbers—and then—with the abolition of slavery—here too they were set free", and that "They had been coming continuously—through the ages" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 69, folio not stated). She records that "the Sidis in Sind and Kacch claim descent from Hazrat Bilal" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 167, folio not stated).

**Sidi music and ritual.** The drumming of the Sheedi festival has its context in what Abbas writes of the Sidi drum, the *mugarmān*, "held sacred by the Sidi communities in Sind, Baluchistan, Rajasthan, and Gujrat who use them in their shrines and for rituals" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 185, folio not stated). "In Sind," she writes, "the Sidis of African descent and the Manganhar musicians render the ceremonial singing of devotional narratives" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 169, folio not stated), and "Sidi women render ritual musical services in the households in the Sind" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 167, folio not stated).

**Karachi and its shrines.** Regula Burckhardt Qureshi names Karachi as one of "two important urban centres of Sufism", with Hyderabad in India, "where members of the same Qawwal Bachche lineage actively maintain their special Qawwali heritage" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 33, folio 13). Omar Kasmani describes the city's shrines as a stage in the fakirs' round: after the three-day annual fair of Sehwan, fakirs "follow other fakirs and proceed to shrines in Karachi" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 114, folio 97). Haroon Khalid gives a legend of the city's name: the area was "known as the area of [Mai] Kolachi", after an old woman "known as Mai Kolachi" whose son "was killed [by] a fish"; she "tore apart the fish and retrieved" him, and the city "came to be known as Kolachi" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 225, folio 199). "At the time of Partition", he writes, "Karachi was a minor port city", and migrants from India made it "the largest city of Pakistan" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 226, folio 200).

**The locality and the road to Hinglaj.** Boivin mentions the locality of Mangho Pir once, for a charitable institution: "Among these were the leper asylum in Mangho Pir and an orphanage in Sukkur." (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 104, folio 91) Schaflechner, whose conjecture about Lalu Jasraj ties the shrine to the Hinglaj pilgrimage, describes Karachi as the start of the road route to Hinglaj, "about 240 kilometers long" from Narayanpur (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 158, folio not stated), and writes that "The ongoing growth of Karachi and the corresponding urbanization of the areas where the early stops occurred caused all but a few of the resting places to completely disappear." (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 121, folio not stated)

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **To whom the shrine is dedicated.** The site's account names the saint Pir Mangho, Hazrat Haji Syed Sakhi Sultan, a medieval holy man who settled at the spot. Abbas writes that "The Mangopir shrine is associated with crocodiles and is dedicated to Bava Gor, the African Muslim saint" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated). Schaflechner names no saint, reports that Hart called him "Peer Moogha", and suggests that the shrine "was once associated with Lalu Jasraj" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 78, folio not stated; Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 263, folio not stated).
- **Where Bava Gor's shrine is.** On the same page on which she dedicates the Mangopir shrine to Bava Gor, Abbas writes that "Bava Gor is the Abyssinian saint of the Sidi in Gujrat in India, where a shrine is dedicated to him, his brother Bava Habash, and his sister Mai Misra" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated).
- **The name of the place.** The site's account writes Pir Mangho and Mangho Pir. Schaflechner prints "Magho Pir" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 78, folio not stated) and "Mango Pir" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 211, folio not stated); Abbas prints "Manghopir" and "Mangopir" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 70, folio not stated; Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 200, folio not stated); Schimmel prints "Mango Pir" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 238, folio 207); Boivin prints "Mangho Pir" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 104, folio 91).

## Legacy

Pir Mangho is unlike any other shrine in Pakistan: a place where Sufi devotion, a pool of sacred crocodiles, healing sulphur springs, and the African-descended culture of the Sheedis come together. Ancient, strange, and beloved, the darbar remains a centre of pilgrimage, healing, and festival on the edge of the great city, and a monument to the many strands that weave through the popular religion of Sindh. The books that mention it carry those strands further: a dedication to Bava Gor, "the African Muslim saint", in Abbas's account, and in Schaflechner's a possible link to the Hindu pilgrimage to Hinglaj.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- General established accounts of Mangho Pir, its crocodiles and springs, and the Sheedi community.
- Jürgen Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi: Identity, Change, and Solidification at a Hindu Temple in Pakistan* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2018; print line 2017).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series, published with the Center for Middle Eastern Studies, University of Texas at Austin).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, 2019).
- Regula Burckhardt Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan: Sound, Context and Meaning in Qawwali* (1986; 1995 edition).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).

Description:
## Overview

At Sharaqpur Sharif, north-west of Lahore, stands the shrine of Hazrat Mian Pir Sher Muhammad Sharaqpuri (1865–1928) — a widely revered Sufi master of the Qadiri-Chishti tradition and one of the notable saints of the Punjab in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Known for his piety, his learning, and the great number of disciples he guided, Pir Sher Muhammad made Sharaqpur a centre of devotion and religious teaching, and his darbar remains an important place of pilgrimage in central Punjab.

None of the books consulted here mentions the shrine or Pir Sher Muhammad himself. What they offer is the town and the province. Two of them name Sharaqpur: Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, whose only saint of Sharaqpur is a different and much earlier man (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 121–122, folios 109–110), and Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, which mentions a grant of land in the Sharaqpur area (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 870). The rest of what follows from the books concerns the Punjab at large, the province in which the shrine stands, and is given as such: it describes the Sufi orders, the shrines and the poetry of the region, not this shrine.

## The Life of the Saint

Mian Sher Muhammad was born in 1865 at Sharaqpur into a devout family, and from his youth turned to the religious sciences and the Sufi path. Trained in both the outward learning of the seminary and the inward discipline of the orders, he became a spiritual guide of great reputation, uniting the Qadiri and Chishti lineages, and drew disciples from across the Punjab and beyond.

He was among the teachers whose light shaped the next generation of Punjabi Sufis — the saint Abul Faiz Qalandar Ali Suhrawardi of Lahore, for instance, is remembered as having received knowledge from him. He is remembered for a life of prayer, austerity, and service, and for the reforming, sober devotion he taught. He died in 1928 and was buried at Sharaqpur.

The books consulted here record none of this. They give no year of his birth or death, no teacher, no line of succession and no disciple, and the account above is the site's own.

## The Shrine and its Devotion

The shrine of Pir Sher Muhammad at Sharaqpur Sharif is a large complex kept by his successors, and a busy centre of pilgrimage. It maintains the five daily prayers, gatherings of *naat* and qawwali, and the free kitchen, and its annual *ʿurs* draws great crowds of devotees who come to honour the saint and seek his blessing.

The town of Sharaqpur Sharif takes its very identity from the darbar, and the saint's line has continued as its custodians and as respected religious figures.

The sources consulted do not record when or by whom the tomb was built, the date of the *ʿurs*, or the names of the custodians.

## Sharaqpur in the Books

Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, composed in 1875, lists Sharaqpur in its index of places at two places in the book, "شرقپور | ۱۰۹ ، ۱۴۴" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 334, folio 322). Neither names Pir Sher Muhammad.

The first is the notice, entry no. 74, of Shaikh Muhammad Saeed Chishti Sabri Sharaqpuri, whose tomb the book places in Sharaqpur and whose death it gives as 1214 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 121–122, folios 109–110). The book's index lists him as "محمد سعید صابری شرقپوری | ۱۰۹" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 328, folio 316). He is not the saint of this shrine: he is a Chishti Sabiri of the same town, and his death and Pir Sher Muhammad's, which the site's account places in 1928, fall more than a century apart (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 121–122, folios 109–110).

The second mention is on a page that also names Makan Sharif, Rawalpindi, Peshawar and Gurdaspur, and on which Sharaqpur appears as the place of publication of a work cited there, the *Khazina-e Marifat* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 156, folio 144). Nothing on that page concerns a shrine.

The bibliography of the modern edition ties the town to the book twice more. One item is a manuscript of Lal Beg Lali's *Thamarat al-Quds* held at Sharaqpur, "لعلی، لعل بیگ : ثمرات القدس (لبعد ۱۰۱۷ھ) مملوکہ مولانا نصرت نوشاہی شرقپور پاکستان", in the possession of Maulana Nusrat Naushahi of Sharaqpur (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 294, folio 282). The other is the same *Khazina-e Marifat*, by Muhammad Ibrahim Qasuri, "محمد ابراہیم قصوری : خزینۂ معرفت شرقپور (س۔ن)", printed at Sharaqpur and undated (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 303, folio 291).

Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* names the Sharaqpur area once. Rani Jindan, it says, gave Bhai Budh Singh a jagir in the Sharaqpur area, "مبلغ پندرہ [OCR?] سو روپیہ کی جاگیر علاقہ شرقپور مین", to feed travellers at the samadhi of Jawahar Singh (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 870). The reading of the sum is uncertain in the printed text. The grant has nothing to do with the shrine.

## Setting: The Sufi Orders in the Punjab

The site's account places Pir Sher Muhammad in the Qadiri and Chishti traditions. The books say nothing of him, but several speak of those orders in the Punjab, the province as a whole.

Lahori wrote his *Hadiqat al-Awliya* for readers who wanted the saints of the Punjab in a short Urdu book, and he defined his Punjab as the whole country "دہلی سے پشاور تک جس قدر علاقہ اس وقت پنجاب کے ساتھ متعلق ہے", from Delhi to Peshawar, as it stood in his own day (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 37, folio 25). Its modern editor counts in it the lives of 244 Sufis of the Punjab, the figure uncertain in the printed text, in seven sections (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 31, folio 19).

Of the Qadiri line, Lahori writes that the first of it to come to the Punjab was Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus of Uch: "حضرت کے سلسلہ میں سے حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی اول پنجاب میں آئے". The same passage has him come by way of Khurasan to Multan and settle at Uch, after his ancestors left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan; Lahori gives no year, and the year in the modern editor's footnote, "بقول علی اصغر گیلانی آپ ۸۸۷ھ میں اوچ میں داخل ہوئے", is the editor's (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28). Lahori writes that the Naushahi order spread in the Punjab through Shah Ma'ruf Chishti and Qadiri, or through Sayyid Mubarak Haqqani, named just before him; the text does not settle which (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 50, folio 38). Of Hazrat Naushah Ganj Bakhsh, he says: "طریقہ نوشاہیہ جس کے فقیر پنجاب میں ہزاروں ہیں۔ ان سے شروع ہوا", the Naushahi way, whose faqirs in the Punjab number in the thousands, began with him (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 70, folio 58). Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, writing of the time of Guru Nanak, speaks of "the Qadiris who had made the Panjab the main centre of their activities" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 420, folio 396).

Of the Chishti order, Lahori opens his account with the statement "یہ سلسلہ ہند اور پنجاب میں حضرت خواجہ معین الدین حسن سجزی سے شائع ہوا", that it spread in Hind and the Punjab from Khwaja Muin al-Din Hasan Sijzi (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 85, folio 73). The modern editor adds in a footnote that its Nizami Fakhri branch spread in the Punjab chiefly through Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi: "پنجاب میں سلسلہ چشتیہ نظامیہ فخریہ کی زیادہ اشاعت حضرت خواجہ سلیمان تونسوی کے ذریعہ ہوئی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108). Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence write that "The Nizami Chishtis came to prominence in the eighteenth century, principally in Delhi, the Deccan, and Punjab, through masters who were related to but in tension with local political leaders" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 119, folio 106). Taunsawi, they say, "consolidated the order by stressing learning through establishment of institutions", the academy at Taunsa and "other religious schools throughout the Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, pp. 121–122, folios 108–109); and in the nineteenth century the line resurfaces, "marking the expansion of the Nizami branch of Chishti Sufism through disciples of Shaykh Sulayman Taunsawi in the upper Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 71, folio 57). Michel Boivin writes that "The Chishtiyya is usually considered to be one of the most powerful Sufi orders in Northern India and Punjab" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 227, folio 214).

Richard M. Eaton observes that "Islam took root much more readily in Bengal or the Punjab than in upper India" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 14, folio 2). Christopher Shackle writes that the Muslim conquest of northern India carried the Persianate world to the Punjab, "where Persian remained the dominant literary language of the ruling elite through the Mughal period and beyond", and that a strong Sufi presence was quickly established there with the coming of figures of the main Sufi orders (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 11, folio x).

## Setting: The Punjab in the Saint's Century

The site's account sets Pir Sher Muhammad's life between 1865 and 1928. The books say a good deal about the Punjab of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, none of it about Sharaqpur.

Nur Ahmad Chishti records the British annexation: "۲۹[OCR?] مارچ سنہ ۱۸۴۹[OCR?]ء تمام ملک سلطنت انگریزی مین داخل ہو گیا", with the day and the year uncertain in the printed text; the book says "تمام ملک", the whole country, not the Punjab (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592). Kanhaiya Lal, writing in 1884, calls Lahore "صوبہ پنجاب کا دار الحکومت", the capital of the province of the Punjab, where the Lieutenant-Governor held his court (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 60, folio 63); in the Sikh period, he says, no printed book came into the Punjab from Hindustan, and scribes copied books by hand for sale (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 42, folio 45).

Shackle writes that "Only with the British conquest of Panjab in the 1840s did the literary culture of the Sufi tradition come to be overlaid by new patterns of modernity": Persian gave way to Urdu and English, and publishers in Lahore brought the older Sufi poetry into print (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 11–12, folios x–xi). The lyrics of the Punjab's Sufi poets, he notes, were for the most part collected in printed form only in the late nineteenth century (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 9–10, folios viii–ix). Annemarie Schimmel writes that "In the Punjab, the literary heritage of Panjabi was rarely continued by Muslims after 1800", though "in the twentieth century a number of mystical treatises have been written and published in Panjabi"; the Panjabi Muslims, she says, turned to Urdu (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 427, folio 396).

Robert Rozehnal quotes Katherine Ewing on the colonial treatment of the hereditary saints: "British policy, especially in the Punjab and Sind, was to treat them in essentially the same way that landlords and tribal leaders were treated" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 33, folio 23). Jamal Malik, writing in the volume edited by Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu, says of the countryside of Punjab and Sindh: "In many cases, the local pîr represents the local landlord or is at least closely related to him" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 199, folio 188). Eaton quotes Major Aubrey O'Brien's "The Mohammedan Saints of the Western Punjab", of 1911, on the riverain folk: "Thus, all human beings require an intervener between them and God" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 216, folio 204).

Haroon Khalid describes the canal colonies of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when "the British connected the five rivers of Punjab with each other through canals, turning several acres of jungle land into agricultural land", thousands of new villages were founded, and "farming families from all over Punjab were invited to settle" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated). He writes too that in the early twentieth century Muhammad Ilyas, founder of the Tableeghi Jamaat, "worked in undivided rural Punjab, exhorting Muslims to 'purify' their religious practices which he argued were corrupted due to the influence of the dominant Hindu culture" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 10, ch. 4, folio not stated).

## Setting: Devotion at the Shrines of the Punjab

The site's account speaks of *naat*, qawwali and the free kitchen at Sharaqpur. The books describe the music and practice of the Punjab's shrines in general terms. Regula Burckhardt Qureshi distinguishes the qawwali tunes of the Punjab from those of Uttar Pradesh by their rhythm: "Panjabi tunes tend to be rhythmically organized according to 'quality' or stress" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 73, folio 53). Ernst and Lawrence write that "The name Qalandar continues to be intoned in popular qawwali lyrics of the Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 36, folio 22). Shemeem Burney Abbas defines *dhammāl* as "The vigorous ritual dance performed at Sufi shrines in Panjab and Sind" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 180, folio not stated).

Eaton writes that the writing of *taʿwidh*, amulets, for the people has not changed since the thirteenth century: "even now the successors of Baba Farid and his assistants, in common with those of other shrines in the Punjab, continue to write ta'widh for the masses" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 218, folio 206). And Schimmel notes that the Punjab and Sind "have also produced hymns extolling the great masters of the mystical orders", particularly ʿAbd al-Qadir Gilani (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 417, folio 386).

## The Punjab in Verse

No verse by or about Pir Sher Muhammad, and none about Sharaqpur, appears in the books consulted here. They do carry verse about the Punjab, the province in which the shrine stands.

Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* closes with chronograms giving the year of its completion, 1292 AH. One, by the author's son Mufti Ghulam Safdar Lahori, is on the book's scope, the saints of the Punjab:

جو خدا کے دوست تھے پنجاب میں
حال ان کا اس سے ہوتا ہے عیان

The lines are quoted as the book prints them, without a translation (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 282, folio 270).

Waris Shah's *Hir and Ranjha*, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, opens with an invocation that praises Baba Farid of Pakpattan:

*When Shakarganj made his abode at Pakpattan, the Punjab was delivered of all its troubles.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 2, folio 1)

In the epilogue, on the page where the poet dates his poem to the year 1180 Hijri, Waris Shah laments the disorder of the country and turns to a single town:

*Of all the wretched Punjab I am most concerned for Kasur.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 56, folio 55)

Bulleh Shah's verse names the Punjab of the eighteenth century in the same troubled terms. In one *kafi*, in Shackle's translation, the twelfth century, which his note takes as the twelfth century of the Hijri era, 'has come with gaping mouth':

*The door of doom and torment has opened, and Panjab is in a bad state. It has been struck by fear of the pit of hell.* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 52, folio 27)

Shackle's note reads the poem as referring to a separation of Bulleh Shah from Shah Inayat "due to the troubled conditions then prevailing in Panjab" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 165–166, folios 140–141). Taufiq Rafat renders another poem:

*Now hell has opened its bogs. / Punjab has gone to the dogs. / This hell is the nethermost hell.* (Rafat, *Bulleh Shah: A Selection*, p. 149, folio 129)

Nur Ahmad Chishti's account of the end of Sikh rule carries a *qitʿa* on the departure of Maharaja Dalip Singh, with the lines "چون شمع[OCR?] پنجاب از پنجاب رفت" and "نو گلی از گلشن پنجاب رفت"; the reading of one word is uncertain in the printed text, and the book gives no translation (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 592).

## Where the Sources Disagree

None of the books consulted mentions Pir Sher Muhammad or his shrine, so none of them disputes anything the site's account says of him. The disagreements below concern the province only.

- **Whether the Punjab's troubles ended with Baba Farid.** Waris Shah's verse says that when Shakarganj settled at Pakpattan "the Punjab was delivered of all its troubles". The book's later annotator replies: "Much as one would like to agree with Waris Shah this is not historically correct. The Punjab has had plenty of troubles even after Baba Farid honoured it by making it his home and his place of burial!" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 2, folio 1).
- **The Sufism of the Punjab in Guru Nanak's time.** W. H. McLeod, as Rizvi quotes him, held that "the Panjabi sufism of Guru Nanak's period had evidently departed radically from the classical pattern of Arab and Persian Sufism" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 419–420, folios 395–396). Rizvi answers that "all literate Panjabis, both Hindus and Muslims, at the time of Guru Nanak were conversant with" ʿAttar, Rumi and Saʿdi, and that McLeod "seems to be unaware of" Shaikh ʿAbd al-Quddus Gangohi, his disciple Shaikh Jalal of Thaneswar, and "the Qadiris who had made the Panjab the main centre of their activities" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 420, folio 396).

## Legacy

Pir Sher Muhammad Sharaqpuri is remembered as one of the influential Sufi masters of modern Punjab — a guide of many thousands whose teaching joined the Qadiri and Chishti ways and whose disciples carried his influence onward. His shrine at Sharaqpur Sharif remains a centre of the devotion he inspired, and his memory endures among the notable saints of the Lahore region.

- Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love: Chishti Sufism in South Asia and Beyond* (2002).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Richard M. Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History* (Oxford University Press, 2000; 2003 impression).

Name: Shrine of Qalandar Baba Auliya
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

In Karachi lies the shrine of Hazrat Qalandar Baba Auliya — Sayyid Muhammad Azeem Barkhiya (1898–1979) — a modern Sufi master and the founder of the Azeemia Sufi order. Unusual among the saints for the intellectual character of his teaching, Qalandar Baba Auliya sought to present the inner science of Sufism in a form intelligible to the modern mind, and through his order and his writings his influence has spread widely in Pakistan and abroad. His darbar is a contemporary shrine and the centre of a living Sufi movement.

## The Life of the Saint

Muhammad Azeem was born in 1898 at Khurja, in the United Provinces of British India, into a Sayyid family, and is known by the spiritual title *Qalandar Baba Auliya*. After the creation of Pakistan he settled in Karachi. He is remembered as a saint of deep contemplative attainment who devoted himself to expounding the inner realities of the Sufi path — the science of the soul, of thought, and of the unseen — and to guiding disciples. His best-known work, *Loh-o-Qalam* (“The Tablet and the Pen”), sets out his teaching on metaphysics and the workings of the mind and spirit, and is studied as a foundational text by his followers. He died in 1979 and was buried in Karachi, where his shrine arose.

## The Azeemia Order

Qalandar Baba Auliya’s lasting legacy is the Azeemia Sufi order, which he founded and which was carried on and spread by his foremost disciple, Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi. The order is distinctive for its emphasis on the systematic teaching of Sufi inner science — meditation, spiritual healing, and the understanding of consciousness — presented in a modern idiom, and it has established centres in Pakistan and among the diaspora. The shrine in Karachi is the spiritual centre of this living movement, a place of both devotion and study.

## Legacy

Qalandar Baba Auliya represents the continuation of the Sufi tradition into the twentieth century and its meeting with the modern world — a saint who framed the ancient inner science of the mystics for contemporary seekers, and founded an order that carries his teaching still. His shrine in Karachi is at once a place of pilgrimage and the heart of the Azeemia order he brought into being.

## Bibliography

- Qalandar Baba Auliya, *Loh-o-Qalam* — the saint's principal work.
- Established histories of the Azeemia Sufi order (and the writings of Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi).
- (This saint post-dates the Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan compendium; entry based on established modern accounts.)
