Name: Shrine of Syed Musa Pak
Events: Annual urs; qawwali; langar
Description:
## Overview

In Multan stands the shrine of Hazrat Syed Musa Pak Shaheed — a revered Qadiri saint of the sixteenth century and the ancestor of the Gilani (Musa Pak) sayyids, one of Multan’s most eminent religious families. Honoured with the titles *Pak* (“the pure”) and *Shaheed* (“the martyr”), Musa Pak carried the Qadiri order of Abd al-Qadir Jilani in Multan and founded a spiritual line that remained influential in the city for centuries. His darbar is among the notable shrines of the ‘City of Saints’.

Among the books consulted here, Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* gives him a full entry, no. 15, headed "سید موسیٰ پاک شہید" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 52–53, folios 40–41). It supplies his fuller name and his father's, a famous disciple in Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, a printed work of his own, and a martyrdom at the hands of the Langah, and it calls his tomb in Multan a place of pilgrimage (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). Its author and its modern editor disagree on the year of his death. Sujan Rai Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* names a Shaikh Musa Gilani in its list of the saints buried in Multan, and says nothing more (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). None of the books describes the building, its *ʿurs* or its custodians.

## The Life of the Saint

Syed Musa, called Musa Pak Shaheed, was a Sayyid of the Gilani line — descendants of the great Baghdad saint Shaikh Abd al-Qadir Jilani — who flourished in Multan in the sixteenth century. Learned and devout, he was a shaykh of the Qadiri order and a guide of many disciples, and he is remembered for a life of piety and for the sanctity that earned him the epithet *Pak*, ‘the pure’. Tradition honours him as a *shaheed*, a martyr. Through him and his descendants the Qadiri-Gilani presence was firmly established in Multan, and the Musa Pak Gilani family became one of the leading religious and landed houses of the region. He was buried in Multan, where his shrine arose.

Lahori calls him the beloved son of Sayyid Hamid Ganj Bakhsh Gilani Uchi, and writes that when he had completed his training before his father he was given the title "جمال الدین ابوالحسن", Jamal al-Din Abul Hasan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 52–53, folios 40–41). In a later entry, no. 141, the book gives his name at full length, "سید جمال الدین ابو الحسن موسیٰ پاک شہید گیلانی ملتانی خلف الصدق … شیخ سید حامد گیلانی", and praises his father as "قدوہ سادات کرام، زبدہ مشائخ عظام" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194). The book's index lists him as "موسیٰ پاک شہید ملتانی" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 330, folio 318).

Of his inner life Lahori writes that he had a special *nisbat* with the spirituality of Ghaus al-Azam, so that its presence was constant with him, and that "صدہا دفعہ", hundreds of times, he was blessed with visions of the Prophet, waking and sleeping. His whole life, the book says, passed in austerity, struggle, worship, teaching and instruction (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41).

The book does not speak with one voice on how he came to his father's seat. Its text says that Sayyid Jamal al-Din Musa succeeded to the *masnad* after his father's death (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48, folio 36), while the editor's note to his own entry records a dispute over that same succession lasting 'long years' (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41).

## His Disciple Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi

Great *ulama*, Lahori writes, became his disciples: "چنانچہ شیخ عبد الحق محدث دہلوی بھی انہیں کے مرید با اخلاص تھے", Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi among them. The editor dates that attachment precisely, to 6 Shawwal 985 AH / 1577 CE, and adds that the shaikh gave his disciple special attention (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). The book tells the same relation from the other side in its entry no. 141, where Abdul Haq's *bai'at* is at Musa Pak's hand (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194).

The same entry follows the disciple onward: "ان کی وفات کے بعد پھر یہ شیخ عبد الوہاب خلیفہ شیخ علی متقی کی خدمت میں حاضر ہوئے" — after the saint's death Abdul Haq went to Shaikh Abd al-Wahhab, the *khalifa* of Shaikh Ali Muttaqi, and received from him *faiz* and a *khirqa-e tabarruk* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194). The editor dates that next stage: "شیخ عبد الحق محدث دہلویؒ ۹۹۶ھ میں حجاز مقدس پہنچے اور ۹۹۹ھ تک وہیں قیام کیا", Abdul Haq reached the Hijaz in 996 AH and stayed there until 999 AH, passing almost all of that time with Abd al-Wahhab (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, حاشیہ 1).

## His Writings

A work of his own, *Taisir al-Thaqalain*, on litanies and observances (*awrad* and *ma'mulat*), was printed at Ferozepur in 1309 AH, as the editor notes (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 2). The edition's bibliography lists it again: "موسیٰ پاک شہید ملتانی : تیسیر الثقلین۔ فیروز پور ۱۳۰۹ھ" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 300, folio 288). For his life the editor points further to *Bahr al-Sarair*, on his conditions and practices, in a manuscript owned by Maulvi Hakim Allah Bakhsh Ansari; to the *Akhbar al-Akhyar*; and to Badayuni's *Muntakhab al-Tawarikh* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 2).

## His Martyrdom and Its Date

Lahori's author is the one source here that tells how he died: "آخر سال ایک ہزار ایک ہجری میں بدخواہان قوم لنگاہ کے ہاتھ سے شہید ہوئے" — he was martyred in the year 1001 AH at the hands of the ill-wishers of the Langah tribe (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). The book says nothing more of the circumstances, and in its later entry the word "شہید" stands in his name without explanation (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194).

The edition's editor rejects the author's year outright: "حضرت موسیٰ پاک شہید کا سال وفات ۱۰۰۱ھ غلط ہے", the year 1001 AH is wrong. He gives instead the year 998 AH, which Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, the saint's own disciple, derived from a chronogram on his death, preserved in a manuscript *bayaz* in the Punjab University library (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 1). The chronogram is a phrase of three words:

شمع جمع سیادت

*The chronogram on the saint's death, by Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi, which the editor reports as yielding 998 AH.* (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 1)

A third reading can be drawn from the book, though the book does not draw it. Its text has Abdul Haq go on to Abd al-Wahhab after the saint's death, and its editor dates Abdul Haq's arrival in the Hijaz to 996 AH; read together, the two statements would place the death before 996 AH. This is an inference from two sentences, one the author's and one the editor's, and the book does not say that the two events followed one another directly (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, حاشیہ 1).

## The Shrine and its Devotion

The shrine of Syed Musa Pak in Multan is kept by his Gilani descendants and is a continuous place of pilgrimage, where devotees come to recite the Fatiha, seek intercession, and honour the saint. It maintains the customary devotions of a Multan darbar — prayer, qawwali, and the free kitchen — and its annual *ʿurs* gathers the faithful. It forms part of the great constellation of shrines that gives Multan its identity.

Lahori's account bears witness to the tomb as a place of pilgrimage in his own day: "روضہ حضرت کا ملتان میں زیارت گاہ خلق اللہ ہے", his *rauza* in Multan is a place of pilgrimage for God's creatures (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). He says nothing of the building, its *ʿurs* or its keepers, and neither does his later entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194). The books consulted here do not record who built the tomb, or when, or the date of the *ʿurs*.

In its account of the suba of Multan, Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* includes "شیخ موسی گیلانی", Shaikh Musa Gilani, in its list of the saints buried in the city, and says nothing more about him (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). The name is taken to be this saint's on the strength of the name Musa and the city alone: the book calls him Shaikh, not Sayyid, and gives him neither Pak nor Shaheed (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). Of the city's saints beyond those it names, the book says: "بسیاری از اولیاے دران شهر سعادت بهر اسوده اند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528).

## A Former Grave at Uch

Haroon Khalid's travelogue records, at Uch Sharif and not at Multan, a structure that may bear on this saint. The Gilani shrine there, he writes, "is situated next to a fifteenth century structure, where the grave of Moosa Pak Shaheed once existed", and "According to a board next to the structure, put up by the Department of Archaeology, his body was later shifted to Multan"; the building is "octagonal, constructed in typical Multani fashion with blue tiles. In a dilapidated condition now" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252). Khalid himself adds of this Moosa Pak Shaheed, "It's unclear who he was" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252). The link to the Multan shrine rests on the name and on the board's statement that the body went to Multan; the Uch structure is a separate building from the shrine described here.

## Setting

The books' wider accounts of the Qadiri order, of the Langah and of Multan speak of the order, the tribe and the city, not of this shrine, but they help to place the saint's story.

Lahori's account of the coming of the Qadiri line to the Punjab says that Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Jili Gilani was its first to arrive, after his ancestors had left Baghdad in the time of Hulagu Khan: "حضرت کے سلسلہ میں سے حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی اول پنجاب میں آئے". He came "خراسان کے راستے ملتان میں" and settled "اوچ کے مقام پر"; the editor adds, citing Ali Asghar Gilani, that he entered Uch in 887 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28). This is said of the order, not of Musa Pak's own household. Rizvi, writing of the age of Guru Nanak, speaks of "the Qadiris who had made the Panjab the main centre of their activities" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 420, folio 396). Schimmel writes that Sind and the Punjab "have also produced hymns extolling the great masters of the mystical orders", naming Abd al-Qadir Gilani above them all (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 417, folio 386).

The Langah, at whose hands Lahori's author has the saint die, appear in Bhandari's history of Multan as a tribe that once ruled the city. Bhandari writes "درین ایام جماعة لنگاه در ملتان بغی[OCR?] ورزیده لوائے سروری بر افراشت" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 324). He tells how "راۓ سنهره [OCR?] که سردار جماعت لنگاهان بود" seized the fort of Multan from Shaikh Yusuf Qureshi by a ruse and took a royal title, and he lists the Langah sultans who followed (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 296–297). Their rule ended with the Arghun conquest, after which, Bhandari writes, "ملتان آنچنان خراب شد که بخاطر هیچکس نبود که باز آباد گردد" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 294). He does not connect the Langah with the saint.

Bhandari also names a later governor of Multan with a like name: "شیخ موسے گیلانی[OCR?] که از طرف دارا شکوه حکومت ملتان داشت", the man who held Multan for Dara Shikoh and submitted to the pursuing emperor (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 66). The reading of the name is uncertain in the printed text, and the book does not say whether this governor was of the saint's family.

Of the city in Guru Nanak's time, Haroon Khalid writes that "At that time Multan was one of the biggest cities of Punjab and was known for the religious shrines of Muslim saints, and Jain and Hindu temples. It was a sacred space for people of all religious denominations" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 123, folio 105). Harish Dhillon writes that "By the time Nanak came to Multan, the city was famous as a major centre of Sufi learning and philosophy" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 167, folio 183).

Shemeem Burney Abbas describes, without naming any shrine or family, the place of the Syed houses in the city's devotional life: "Musicians such as Surraiya Multanikar are associated with the powerful landowning Syeds of Multan and Bahawalpur who claim descent from the prophet Muhammad's family. Their training is supported by the Syed households, and these musicians perform in the family shrines of the Syeds. This is partly because of the large landholdings where the affluent Syeds support the shrines of their ancestors. They arrange annual rituals such as the Eid and the Muharram ceremonies marking the tragedy of Kerbala" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, pp. 168–169, folios not stated).

Multan had its place in the region's poetry as well. Writing of the vernacular poets, Schimmel says that "Mecca and Medina (and for the Sindhi and Panjabi, also Multan) are inside the heart" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 178, folio 160). In Madho Lal Hussein's verse the city appears as a market, in a bride's trousseau:

*The dress / someone carried across the snows / all the way from Kashmir. The dress / someone brought from Gujarat… The dress bought in Multan* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 51, folio 51, kafi 29)

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives no year, placing him in the sixteenth century. Lahori's author gives 1001 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). His editor calls 1001 AH wrong and gives 998 AH, from Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi's chronogram "شمع جمع سیادت" (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 1). The book's account of Abdul Haq, read with the editor's date for his arrival in the Hijaz, would put the death before 996 AH, though the book does not say so (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, حاشیہ 1).
- **The succession to his father.** Lahori's text has Sayyid Jamal al-Din Musa succeed to the *masnad* after his father's death (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 48, folio 36); the editor's note records a dispute of 'long years' over that succession (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41).
- **His name and title.** The site's account calls him Syed Musa Pak Shaheed. Lahori gives "سید موسیٰ پاک شہید" as the heading of his entry (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, pp. 52–53, folios 40–41) and, in a later entry, the fuller Sayyid Jamal al-Din Abu al-Hasan Musa Pak Shaheed Gilani Multani (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 206, folio 194). Bhandari's list of the saints of Multan has "شیخ موسی گیلانی", Shaikh rather than Sayyid, with neither Pak nor Shaheed (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 528). Khalid writes "Moosa Pak Shaheed", and of him "It's unclear who he was" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).
- **Where he was first buried.** The site's account has him buried in Multan, where his shrine arose, and Lahori places his tomb in Multan (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41). An Archaeology Department board at Uch Sharif, as Khalid reports it, says that the grave of a Moosa Pak Shaheed once lay in a fifteenth-century structure there and that his body was later shifted to Multan (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 278, folio 252).

## Legacy

Syed Musa Pak Shaheed is remembered as a chief bearer of the Qadiri order in Multan and the founder of the distinguished Musa Pak Gilani line — a saint whose purity and martyrdom won him lasting veneration, and whose family carried his influence through the later history of the city. His shrine remains a revered darbar of the ‘City of Saints’.

The books add to that memory a famous disciple and a written legacy: Lahori counts Shaikh Abdul Haq Muhaddith Dehlvi among his disciples, and his editor records the printing of the saint's *Taisir al-Thaqalain* at Ferozepur in 1309 AH (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41; p. 53, folio 41, حاشیہ 2). In Lahori's own day his tomb in Multan was a place of pilgrimage (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 53, folio 41).

Name: Sial Sharif
Location: Sial Sharif, Sial Sharif (Sargodha District), Punjab
Events: Annual urs; naat and qawwali; daily langar
Description:
## Overview

At Sial Sharif, in the Sargodha district of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Khwaja Muhammad Shamsuddin Sialvi (1799–1883), a leading Chishti saint of the nineteenth century whose khanqah became one of the most influential centres of the order in the region. Heir to the great Chishti revival that flowed from Taunsa Sharif, Shamsuddin Sialvi guided a wide following and trained saints of the first rank, among them Pir Meher Ali Shah of Golra, and his darbar at Sial Sharif remains a major place of pilgrimage in central Punjab.

The books consulted here say very little about him, and none of them names the shrine or the settlement of Sial Sharif. Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence's *Sufi Martyrs of Love* mentions him in a single clause, as the direct pir of Meher Ali Shah, and gives his year of death as 1882 rather than 1883 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111). Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, written in 1875, has no entry under his name in its index (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 320). The other passages gathered below speak of the Chishti line in the Punjab and of the Sargodha district and the city of Sargodha; they are context for the saint and his country, not accounts of this shrine.

## The Life of the Saint

Khwaja Muhammad Shamsuddin was born in 1799 at Sial Sharif into a devout family, and from his youth pursued the religious sciences and the Sufi path. He was initiated in the Chishti order and became a spiritual heir within the line of Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi, rising to be among the foremost Chishti shaykhs of his age. From his khanqah at Sial Sharif he taught, guided disciples, and kept a great *langar*, and his spiritual authority drew seekers from across the Punjab.

Among those who took his guidance was Pir Sayyid Meher Ali Shah of Golra Sharif, through whom the Sial Sharif line reached into the next generation of Punjabi Sufism. Ernst and Lawrence, who spell the names Mihr 'Ali Shah and Shams ad-Din Siyal, record the bond in these words: "Mihr 'Ali Shah's direct pir was Shams ad-Din Siyal (d. 1882)" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111). The clause names no shrine, no place and no order, and says nothing of his succession (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111).

He died in 1883 and was buried at Sial Sharif. Ernst and Lawrence give the year of his death as 1882 (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111). None of the books consulted here records his year of birth, his teachers or the place of his burial.

## The Shrine and its Devotion

The shrine of Shamsuddin Sialvi at Sial Sharif is a large complex kept by his successors, who have continued as its *sajjada-nashins* and as prominent religious figures. It maintains the daily prayers, gatherings of *naat* and qawwali, and the free kitchen, and its annual *urs* gathers great crowds of devotees. The town of Sial Sharif takes its identity from the darbar, a continuing seat of Chishti teaching and devotion.

The books consulted here do not describe the shrine. They give no date for the *urs*, do not say who built the tomb or when, and do not name its *sajjada-nashins*.

## The Chishti Line in the Punjab

The site's account places Shamsuddin Sialvi within the line of Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi. The books do not speak of Sial Sharif, but several of them describe the Chishti revival in the Punjab to which that line belongs. Their statements concern the order and the province, not this shrine.

In a footnote to the modern edition of the *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, its editor, محمد اقبال مجددی, writes that the wider spread of the Chishti Nizami Fakhri line in the Punjab came through Khwaja Sulaiman Taunsvi: "پنجاب میں سلسلہ چشتیہ نظامیہ فخریہ کی زیادہ اشاعت حضرت خواجہ سلیمان تونسوی کے ذریعہ ہوئی". The same footnote gives Taunsvi's birth as ۱۱۸۴ھ and his death as ۱۲۶۷ھ (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 120, folio 108).

Ernst and Lawrence write that "The Nizami Chishtis came to prominence in the eighteenth century, principally in Delhi, the Deccan, and Punjab, through masters who were related to but in tension with local political leaders" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 119, folio 106). Of Shaykh Sulayman Taunsawi, whom they date "(d. 1850)", they say that he "consolidated the order by stressing learning through establishment of institutions: not only the academy called Dar al- 'Ulum at Taunsa on the upper Indus, but also other religious schools throughout the Punjab" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, pp. 121–122, folios 108–109). They add that he "urged his followers to participate in resistance against Sikh aggression in the Punjab", and that "Notable, however, is the effort of Shah Sulayman to maintain cordial relations with Punjabi Hindus even while he opposed their Sikh neighbors" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 121, folio 108). Elsewhere they describe "the expansion of the Nizami branch of Chishti Sufism through disciples of Shaykh Sulayman Taunsawi in the upper Punjab" in the nineteenth century (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 71, folio 57).

On the page where they name Shams ad-Din Siyal, Ernst and Lawrence turn to the later history of this lineage: "If we were to follow only the dictates of political history and the criteria of social science, the test case for the Chishti Nizami Sulaymaniyya lineage in the colonial period might seem to be the battles over shrines in the Punjab". Their example is Taunsa, and they write that "Political power struggles internal to the Sulaymaniyya can be traced to British manipulation and also the rivalry of local Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslim reformers"; they then add that "political contestation is only part of the narrative" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111).

Michel Boivin writes in general terms that "The Chishtiyya is usually considered to be one of the most powerful Sufi orders in Northern India and Punjab" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 227, folio 214). Of the qawwali that the site's account names among the shrine's gatherings, Regula Burckhardt Qureshi writes, of the music of the region as a whole, that "tunes from the two principal regions of the Qawwali tradition, Uttar Pradesh and Panjab, can be distinguished mainly by their rhythmic setting", and that "Panjabi tunes tend to be rhythmically organized according to 'quality' or stress" (Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan*, p. 73, folio 53). Neither book mentions Sial Sharif.

## Setting

Sial Sharif is a settlement in the Sargodha district, distinct from the city of Sargodha. The books that mention Sargodha speak of the district or the city, and none of them names Sial Sharif, its shrine or its saint.

In a chapter of *Embodying Charisma*, Jamal Malik writes of the Punjab that "The cult of the holy man (pîr) and the associated folk piety is particularly evident in the countryside, where major landlords and large-scale land concentrations are crucial features, especially in Punjab and Sindh. In many cases, the local pîr represents the local landlord or is at least closely related to him" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 199, folio 188). In the same chapter he refers to "the tomb to which his ancestors were attached" in the Sargodha district, without naming the tomb, the village or Sial Sharif (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 203, folio 192).

The district also has a place in the Punjab's most famous romance. Annemarie Schimmel, retelling the plot of Hir and Ranjha, writes: "Ranjha, the son of a landlord of the Sargodha district, falls in love with Hir, the daughter of the ruler of Djang." She says nothing further about the district or about any shrine in it (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 419, folio 388).

Of the city of Sargodha, several modern writers give glimpses. Omar Kasmani writes of Zaheda, whose family lived there, that her "stay at the shrine of Se-hwan at the expense of Sargodha, a city in the Punjab where her family lived, demanded explaining"; she stayed at Sehwan "for months at a stretch, a thousand or so kilometers away from home" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 26, folio 9). Her husband Zafar "lived in Sargodha" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 113, folio 96). Haroon Khalid recalls that "in my ancestral house in Sargodha, the arches were three-cusped, hence Sikh, even though we were a Muslim family" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 309, folio not stated). In another book, an uncle of his from Sargodha tells of "another fakir in Sargodha who roams around the city all day long surrounded by dogs, and refuses to talk to any human being. Like Peer Abbas, he offers his food to the dogs first" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 11, ch. 5, folio not stated). Khalid also writes that sectarian conflict at Eid Milad-Un-Nabi processions "remains a problem particularly in cities like Sargodha, Faisalabad and Dera Ismael Khan, where ultra-orthodox Sunni organizations have a large support base", though "until now these incidents have been minor" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 13, ch. 7, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The site's account gives his dates as 1799–1883 and says he died in 1883. Ernst and Lawrence give "(d. 1882)" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111).
- **The form of his name.** The site's account calls him Hazrat Khwaja Muhammad Shamsuddin Sialvi. Ernst and Lawrence call him Shams ad-Din Siyal, without Muhammad or a title (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111).

## Legacy

Khwaja Shamsuddin Sialvi holds an important place in the Chishti revival of nineteenth-century Punjab, a master whose khanqah at Sial Sharif carried the tradition forward and trained saints, above all Meher Ali Shah of Golra, who would shape the religious life of the region into the twentieth century. It is as Meher Ali Shah's own master that he appears in Ernst and Lawrence's history of the Chishti order (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 124, folio 111). His shrine remains a great Chishti centre of central Punjab.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- General established histories of the Chishti revival in nineteenth-century Punjab.
- Carl W. Ernst and Bruce B. Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love: Chishti Sufism in South Asia and Beyond* (2002).
- Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya* (Persian, composed 1292 AH / 1875 CE; read in an Urdu edition annotated by محمد اقبال مجددی and issued by تصوّف فاؤنڈیشن).
- Michel Boivin, *The Hindu Sufis of South Asia: Partition, Shrine Culture and the Sindhis in India* (London and New York: I.B. Tauris / Bloomsbury Publishing Plc, first published 2019).
- Regula Burckhardt Qureshi, *Sufi Music of India and Pakistan: Sound, Context and Meaning in Qawwali* (1986; 1995 edition).
- Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu (eds.), *Embodying Charisma: Modernity, Locality and the Performance of Emotion in Sufi Cults* (1998).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, with a new Foreword by Carl W. Ernst, 2011).
- Omar Kasmani, *Queer Companions* (Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2022).
- Haroon Khalid, *Walking with Nanak* (2016).
- Haroon Khalid, *In Search of Shiva: A Study of Folk Religious Practices in Pakistan* (New Delhi: Rupa Publications India, first impression 2015).

Name: Swami Dharmdas Darbar, Larkana (Kennedy Market)
Location: Kennedy Market area, Larkana, Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan
Events: No events documented
Description:
The darbar of Swami Dharmdas at Larkana is one of the *Nanakpanthi* shrines of the Larkana country of upper Sindh, recorded by the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro in his survey of the region's Hindu–Sikh saints. Swami Dharamdas is remembered as a disciple of Sant Bhai Wasan Shah of Rohri; according to Kalhoro he first established a darbar at the village of Mena and afterwards founded the shrine at Larkana with which his name is chiefly associated, said to lie in the Kennedy Market quarter of the town. He was a contemporary of Sain Vali Vilayat Rai of Kambar (a separate entry in this dataset), one of a group of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century *sants* who spread a message of love, harmony and tolerance among the Hindu, Muslim and Sikh communities of Sindh. In the Nanakpanthi manner, such darbars house a copy of the *Guru Granth Sahib* alongside images of Hindu deities, and honour Baba Guru Nanak without a firm confessional boundary. The saint's dates and the darbar's detailed history are only thinly documented in accessible sources, and — as with most Sindhi Hindu shrines — the size and present condition of the site are uncertain; the entry is offered on the authority of Kalhoro's fieldwork and should be treated as provisional. Kalhoro records this lineage directly, writing that "Swami Dharamdas was a disciple of Sant Bhai Wasan Shah in Rohri. First, he established a darbar in Mena village and later in Larkana," and identifying him as "Swami Dharmdas who founded a darbar in Kennedy Market in Larkana." Beyond this single account, no second independent source, and no dates for the founder or the darbar, could be located.

## Bibliography

- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Nanakpanthi Saints of Sindh," *The Friday Times*, 13 April 2018.

Name: Tilla Jogian
Founded/Opened: Traditional founding date uncertain/legendary (accounts range from antiquity to the 11th–12th century CE); abandoned 1947
Events: None - abandoned since 1947
Description:
## Overview

Tilla Jogian — the "Hill of the Ascetics" — crowns the highest peak of the eastern Salt Range, rising to some 975 metres above sea level, in the Jhelum District of the Punjab. On its summit lie the ruins of an ancient temple and monastic complex that was, before 1947, the foremost centre of Hindu yogis in the whole of the Punjab. Cooler and greener than the parched country below, the hilltop has for many centuries been a retreat for renunciants seeking solitude, and its long association with the *Nath* order of yogis, with Guru Nanak, and with the lovers of Punjabi legend has made it one of the most storied heights in the region.

The books bear out that reputation from several sides. Christopher Shackle, annotating the lyrics of Bulleh Shah, calls the hill the headquarters of the order of *Kanphat* yogis (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). Haroon Khalid calls it the most important pilgrimage site for jogis in the Punjab (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, in its account of the suba of Lahore, sets on the salt mountain the place of austerity of the jogi Bal Nath (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514), and records a gathering there on the day of Shivrat (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 514–513). And in Waris Shah's romance of Heer and Ranjha, in Charles Frederick Usborne's English, Tilla is the hill to which Ranjha comes to take *jog* from Bal Nath, whom Usborne spells Balnath (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30).

## Gorakhnath and the Nath Yogis

Tradition traces the sanctity of Tilla Jogian back some two thousand years and links its foundation to *Gorakhnath*, the revered yogi and organiser of the *Nath* tradition — though this popular chronology is internally inconsistent (scholarship usually places the historical Gorakhnath centuries later, c. 11th–12th century CE) and should be read as legend rather than settled history.

Shackle's notes to Bulleh Shah place Gorakhnath at the head of the order the hill housed. Where the poet names 'guru Gorakh', Shackle explains "Gorakhnath, the head of the Kanphat yogis" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 12 on 122); the name on which the poem's initiate meditates is "Presumably the name of the yogis' guru Gorakhnath" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 11 on 122); and his glossary describes "the great yogi Gorakhnath, from whom Ranjha sought initiation as a yogi" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173). Shackle gives Gorakhnath no date and no lineage.

Michel Boivin, whose study names no Nath site in Sindh or in the Salt Range, describes the Nathpanthis as "the followers of Gorakhnath, who is believed to be an avatar of Shiva" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 77, folio 64). He observes that "in the Persian sources, the main Hindu figure is the jogi", a term "usually employed for the Nathpanthis, a Shivaite school of renunciants who were the followers of Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 21, folio 8); he speaks of "an ascetic order founded by Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107); and his glossary defines the jogis as "wandering Shivaite ascetics who meditate on One, usually affiliated with the Nathpanth" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 219, folio 206). In one tradition he reports, "Gorakhnath would have sent an invisible army to help Goga Pir against Rai Pithora" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 188, folio 175).

Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's history of Sufism in India, which nowhere mentions Tilla Jogian, says of the Naths in general that they "lived in forests, wandered in towns and also established permanent monasteries" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 376, folio 354). Harish Dhillon notes that in the Puratan Janamsakhis the account of the anointment of Guru Angad has Gorakhnath "in conversation with Guru Nanak", and comments: "Historically, Gorakhnath lived and preached long before Nanak's time (in the eleventh century)" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 10, folio not stated).

Gorakhnath's name also reaches the cult of the goddess Hinglaj, the subject of Jürgen Schaflechner's study: "Tradition has it that Hinglaj was very fond of the Nath community, especially of Guru Gorakhnath. So the Goddess waited day after day in Thatta for Gorakhnath to come to meet her" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 205, folio not stated). Schaflechner records 'the dhūnī of Guru Gorakhnath' there (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 256, folio not stated) and writes that "The fireplace of Goraknath dates back to the long-standing tradition of Nath Yogis who made the journey to Hinglaj", citing Briggs's study of 1938 (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, pp. 256–257, folio not stated); "two texts describe the pilgrimage of Guru Gorakhnath to Hinglaj: the Gorakh Caritra and the Gorakhpurāṇa" (Schaflechner, *Hinglaj Devi*, p. 257, folio not stated). What Boivin, Rizvi, Dhillon and Schaflechner say here is said of Gorakhnath and the Naths, not of this hill; Boivin and Rizvi name no Nath site in the Salt Range at all.

## The Seat of the Jogis

Tilla Jogian became the principal seat of the *Kanphata* yogis — the 'split-eared' ascetics, so called from the great rings inserted through the cartilage of their ears at initiation — an order that looked to Gorakhnath as its master. On the hilltop the *jogis* maintained shrines, cells, and reservoirs of water, and the complex is said at its height to have sheltered hundreds of ascetics who came to meditate in its heights. The site formed the easternmost of a string of ancient Hindu sanctuaries strung along the Salt Range, a chain that also includes the temples of Katas Raj and, at its western end, the Amb temples above the Soon Valley.

Shackle's note on the 'Tilla' of Bulleh Shah's lyric reads: "Tilla Jogian high up in the hills of District Jhelum was the headquarters of the order of Kanphat ('split-eared') yogis, who were initiated by having the cartilage of their ears pierced to allow the insertion of a wooden ring" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). It describes the order rather than the buildings: Shackle names no temple, building, date, custodian or endowment.

Bhandari's *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* places the hill on the salt mountain. "بالاے همین کوه بهفت کروهے قلعه رهتاس": on top of this same mountain, seven kos from the fort of Rohtas, is the place of austerity of the jogi Bal Nath (بالناتهه[OCR?] جوگی, the reading of the name uncertain in the printed text), called تله[OCR?], for which the editor's footnote gives the variant بله[OCR?]; the book gives its height in kos as چهار کروه بلند (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Waris Shah's romance, in Usborne's translation, calls the hill simply 'Tilla' and 'your hill of Tilla'; it never writes 'Tilla Jogian', and it names neither the Salt Range nor Gorakhnath. Beyond the name Tilla, its chief tie to this hill is a note by a later, unnamed annotator: "According to tradition, Balnath was the fourth Guru of 'Tilla Guruan' (the mound of the Gurus) on the banks of the river Jhelum" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). The same note goes on, in the annotator's own present tense: "The place is still preserved, and the 'Jog Mat' or the cult of the wandering mystics, with its emphasis on pantheism, is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). It gives no building, structure, custodian, date or district.

The poem peoples the hill with Bal Nath's *chelas*, who keep the jogi's house and kitchen. When Ranjha arrives, "They were all engaged in religious contemplation and prayers. They were reading Gayan Gita Bhagvat and Bharat" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). Their service runs for a fixed term, and they complain of it: "For eighteen years we have been serving him. We have given up all and live by begging. All day and night we remember God. Yet he does not give us Jog" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). The annotator explains the guru by his Muslim counterpart: "Guru — the Hindu holy man, the teacher, the Hindu counterpart of the Muslim Murshid" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 5).

## Festival and Practice

Bhandari records the one festival that any of these sources sets on the hill. On the appointed days, and above all on the day of Shivrat, "روز شیورات که روزه است منسوب بمهادیو[OCR?]", at the end of winter (دربرامد[OCR?] زمستان), the book says, "خلایق کثیر و طوایف جوگیان" gather there "و نمایش گری بکاری برند" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 514–513). The sources consulted record no other festival there.

Shackle's notes, which speak of yogis at large rather than of this hill, gloss the rest of the yogi's equipment as Bulleh Shah's lyrics present it: the ochre dress (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 165, folio 140); the bonfire and its ashes, for "Yogis sit in front of a bonfire (dhūāñ) and rub its ashes (bhabūt) on their bodies" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 190, folio 165, n. 3 on 137); the deerskin, skull-cup, matted hair and ashes (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 156, folio 131); the forehead mark (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 190, folio 165, n. 1 on 137); and the horn, bowl and beads (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, pp. 124, 141; folios 99, 116). He explains, too, that "The tenth door is the hidden aperture in the skull that is opened at the climax of the yogic process" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 173, folio 148, n. 2 on 63).

## Guru Nanak and the Hill

Such was its renown as a place of Hindu spiritual power that it drew, in the early sixteenth century, *Guru Nanak*, the founder of the Sikh faith, who is remembered in tradition as having spent forty days in meditation upon the hill during his travels. The episode became part of the sacred memory of the site for Sikhs, adding another layer to a place already venerated by yogis and by Hindu pilgrims from across the Punjab.

The books consulted add no account of Nanak's own stay on the hill. Haroon Khalid's reconstruction in *Walking with Nanak* brings the hill into the story by another road: Tripta accompanied her husband "to Tilla Jogian, the most important pilgrimage site for jogis in the Punjab. There the couple paid for the jogis' food for one day, as a result of which the jogis prayed all night to bless this young couple" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 21, folio 3).

## Ranjha Takes Jog

Tilla Jogian occupies a special place in Punjabi folklore through the tragic romance of *Heer and Ranjha*, immortalised in the eighteenth century by the Sufi poet *Waris Shah*. In the tale, Ranjha, parted from his beloved Heer, climbs to Tilla Jogian in his grief and there renounces the world: the ascetic *Bal Nath*, master of the hill, pierces his ears and initiates him into the order of the *jogis*, granting him *jog*, the discipline of renunciation. Through this episode the hill entered the imaginative life of the Punjab as the very emblem of the lover-turned-ascetic, and generations who never climbed its slopes knew its name from the recitation of Waris Shah's verses.

Waris Shah dates his poem "in the year 1180 Hijri" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 56, folio 55). In Usborne's English, Ranjha sets out for Tilla telling himself that "Balnath surely knows the way of salvation", and "after many days' journeying, Ranjha reached Tilla the hill on which Balnath lived" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). He "bowed his head and placed a piece of gur" before the guru "as an offering, and clasped the feet of all the Jogis" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). The annotator explains the gift: "Gur is raw sugar. It is well known as a ceremonial offering in the Punjab countryside" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32).

The poem sets caste against the vocation: "You Jats cannot attain Jog" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30), and "What can a Jat do with a beggars bowl or horn, whose heart is set only on ploughing?" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). Ranjha's own name, the annotator notes, is a caste: "Ranjha is still a well-known caste of the Jats in the old Punjab" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 3, folio 2). Bal Nath sets out the conditions of *jog*: "You will have to dress as a Jogi, to wear dirty clothes, long hair, cropped skull and to beg your way through life. You will have to give up the pleasures of birth, to cease to rejoice when friends come or to grieve when they die. You will have to abstain from casting eyes on women. You will have to become divinely intoxicated by taking kand, mul, post, opium and other narcotic drugs" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). A jogi must travel as well: "You will have to go on long pilgrimages to Jagannath, Godavari, Ganges and Jamna" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30). Ranjha, for his part, admits that the vocation is a means to his love: "Had I been only a lover of God, I should have sought only Him… Hir has captivated my heart. That is why I have become a Jogi" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

The rite of initiation is the fullest ritual description in the book. "They obeyed the orders of their Guru and brought Balnath the earrings as he had told them, and the razor wherewith to shave Ranjha. And the Guru took off Ranjha's clothes and having rubbed him in ashes and embraced him, made him sit by his side. Then he took the razor of separation and shaved him completely. Then he bored his ears and put earrings on him. He gave him the beggar's bowl, the rosary, the horn and the shell in his hands", and last he taught him the word Allah (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). With the rite came a moral rule: "An old woman should be treated as your mother and a young woman as your sister" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

The annotator stresses what the scene shows of its time: "Here Ranjha, a Muslim, becomes a spiritual disciple of Balnath, a Hindu yogi. This may seem strange today, but was by no means unusual at the time" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 4). In the same note he adds that "A Murshid is a spiritual teacher" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 4).

The *chelas* turn on their guru: "They left the Jogi's house and kitchen. They pierced the Guru with their shameless taunts" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). Bal Nath himself comes to regret his gift: "Verily I repent and am sorry for having given Jog to this youth. He has got the treasures of jog without spending a single farthing" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). A protest in the poem names the hill again: "Had I known that you would try to keep me from my Love, I would never have set foot on your hill of Tilla" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31). At last "Ranjha made haste to leave Tilla and he collected strange herbs and potent roots from the woods" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 34, folio 33).

Ear-boring is the act that makes a jogi, and the poem returns to it again and again after Ranjha leaves the hill: "Perhaps he has obeyed my word and got his ears bored" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 40, folio 39); "He went to Tilla and got his ears bored and became a Jogi. He has today entered your village" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 41, folio 40); "Fate has shaved your beard and bored your ears" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 43, folio 42); "He has bored his ears and has become a Jogi for my sake" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 45, folio 44). At the end the marks are removed: "They took the Jogi's rings out of his ears" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 54, folio 53).

## Legends and Miracles

Waris Shah's guru commands by enchantment. When the *chelas* rebel, "Whereupon the Guru rebuked them and his anger blazed from his eyes. The Chelas instantly obeyed him, so powerful was the enchantment that the Guru laid upon them. All ill feeling vanished from their minds" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31).

At the hill, too, a prayer is answered aloud. Bal Nath "prayed and poured ashes over his body and plunged his soul into the deep waters of meditation"; then "there came a reply from the Darbar of God": "Hir has been bestowed on Ranjha and his boat has been taken ashore" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32).

The annotator denies the guru two powers. "Balnath obviously could not read Ranjha's thoughts", he writes, as jogis often claim to do (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 6); and "Balnath apparently had no power to take back what he had given" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 34, folio 33, note 16). He also records a popular belief: "According to popular superstition in the Punjab countryside", Pirs, Fakirs and Jogis can, by the force of their piety, "make the Moving Finger of Destiny cancel what it has written" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30, note 7).

## In Verse

Bulleh Shah's lyric, in Shackle's translation, follows the initiate to Tilla step by step:

*Casting aside his drum, he goes toward Tilla, he sits and meditates on his name. He has his ears split and the earrings inserted, and is initiated by the guru* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 123, folio 98)

The lyric then names the authority a Pir must satisfy:

*My Pir gains the approval of guru Gorakh. He keeps crying 'Hir, Hir.'* (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 124, folio 99)

Shackle glosses the yogic vocabulary of Bulleh Shah's verse: "The 'unstruck music' (anhad nād) is the mystical sound heard at the climax of the yogic process"; "The 'circle of nectar' (amrit manḍal) is another traditional image for the ecstatic state that is the goal of yoga"; and the phrase 'make the Ganges flow backward' (ulṭī gangā bahāio) is "an idiom meaning 'to do the opposite of the usual,' which here refers to the drawing up of psychic energy during the yogic process" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 155, folio 130). Again: "The 'fourth state' (cauthā pad, Skt. turīyāvasthā-) is a yogic term that denotes the state of liberation achieved through transcending the three guṇas that govern worldly existence" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 176, folio 151, n. 2 on 71).

Waris Shah's poem, in Usborne's English, defines *jog* in its own terms:

*Jog means to be dead while alive. One has to sing the song of nonentity using ones meagre body as a guitar. One's self has to be entirely absorbed. It is no child's play.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30)

*God has made his abode in this body of dust He is in every thing as a thread runs through the beads.* (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 31, folio 30)

The annotator reads the 'Song of Nonentity' through Sufi eyes: "this is the doctrine of annihilation in God (fana fillah) as practised by the Muslim Sufis, which has strong spiritual affiliations with the 'Nirvana' of the Hindus and Buddhists" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 10). The poem also names a degree of *jog* called Chit Akas, reached "after passing through the stages of Bhut Kas and Juda Kas" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 32, folio 31), which the annotator glosses only as "The three different planes of Jog Philosophy" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 13).

## Setting: The Salt Mountain

Bhandari's account of the salt mountain on which he places Tilla speaks of the range, not of the hill itself. In the Sind Sagar doab (دوابه سندساگر), rock salt (نمک سنگ) is dug at the foot of the hills near Shamsabad, famous above all other salts and called نمک سندهه[OCR?] because it is produced in that doab (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). The miners, called الاشه کش[OCR?], dig tunnels "زیاده از دو صد سیصد درعه[OCR?] عمیق"; each goes in naked with a lamp in his hand and a pick on his shoulder, cuts a lump of about سه من and carries it out on his back; he is paid, "از ناظمان این امر اجرت گرفته", and the men feel no fear. The tunnels, the book adds بحکمت الهی, are not hot in summer or cold in winter (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Two large tunnels near Shamsabad, کهوهره[OCR?] و کهیوره[OCR?], yield "هر سال چندان لکهه من نمک", and their revenue, with that of other places, "بسرکار بادشاهی ضبط می شود" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). Craftsmen make trays, dishes, covers and lamp-stands of salt; the گچ شیرین found next to it is used for whitewash inside the houses of the great; and the stone is also made into dishes and انجوره[OCR?] (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Bhandari also reports a Hindu belief. The Kahyala pool, "کهنتا[OCR?] چهه[OCR?] کولابی[OCR?]", whose depth no one can tell, is held to be an ancient temple; on great days such as the sun's entry into Aries, Hindus crowd there بقصد تغسل[OCR?]. They believe the earth has two eyes: the right is the pool of بهکر[OCR?] near Ajmer, the left this pool (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514). He cites the *Zafarnama* and the *Akbarnama*, "درظفرنامه و اکبرنامه ان راکوه جوده نوشته اند"; Jud was رئیس قوم جنجوهه, whose descendants still live and rule at the foot of the hills in the parganas "کرچاک[OCR?] و نندنه[OCR?] و کهیاله(۱)[OCR?]", the editor giving کهتاز[OCR?] as a variant for the last (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).

Writing of the Sind Sagar doab as a whole, Richard Eaton notes: "Only in the extreme western Punjab, in the Sind Sagar doab, where the Janjua Rajputs and Ghakkars dominated, were the Jats conspicuously absent as zamindars" (Eaton, *Essays on Islam and Indian History*, p. 225, folio 213). Lukas Werth, whose chapter in Werbner and Basu's *Embodying Charisma* studies the anonymous saints' shrines of a village in the range to which he gives a pseudonym, sets that village "In the mountains dividing the plains of the Punjab from the slightly elevated plateau of the Potwar" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 88, folio 77), and writes of "the salt range where there is no irrigation" (Werbner and Basu, *Embodying Charisma*, p. 93, folio 82).

## Decline and Present State

The complex flourished until the Partition of 1947, when the departure of its Hindu and yogi custodians for India left it without a resident community. Deprived of care, the buildings fell into decay; the reservoirs silted, the shrines crumbled, and in the decades since the site has been steadily overgrown — by the early twenty-first century much of it lay beneath a spread of wild olive and scrub, its masonry slipping into ruin. Conservationists and writers have repeatedly warned that this remarkable monument, at once archaeological site, sacred summit, and literary landmark, risks being lost altogether without deliberate protection. Its remoteness has spared it the crowds that press upon lower shrines, but that same isolation has hastened its neglect.

Against this stands the present-tense note of Usborne's later, unnamed annotator: "The place is still preserved, and the 'Jog Mat' or the cult of the wandering mystics, with its emphasis on pantheism, is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1).

For the fate of such places after the division of the Punjab, Haroon Khalid, writing of the country at large and not of this hill, says: "I have seen several gurdwaras and temples being taken over and destroyed by the migrants" (Khalid, *In Search of Shiva*, p. 8, ch. 2, folio not stated).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Who initiated Ranjha.** The site's account names Bal Nath, master of the hill. Usborne's translation of Waris Shah agrees, and its annotator calls Bal Nath "the fourth Guru of 'Tilla Guruan'" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). Shackle's glossary to Bulleh Shah instead names "the great yogi Gorakhnath, from whom Ranjha sought initiation as a yogi" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 198, folio 173), and Bulleh Shah's lyric says that the initiate "is initiated by the guru" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 123, folio 98).
- **Gorakhnath's date.** The site's account says that tradition traces the hill's sanctity back some two thousand years and links its foundation to Gorakhnath, while scholarship usually places him c. 11th–12th century CE. Dhillon puts him "in the eleventh century" (Dhillon, *Janamsakhis*, p. 10, folio not stated), while the Puratan Janamsakhis, as he reports them, set him in conversation with Guru Nanak.
- **Gorakhnath's place in the order.** The site's account calls him the organiser of the Nath tradition. Boivin speaks of "an ascetic order founded by Gorakhnath" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 120, folio 107) and reports the belief that he is an avatar of Shiva (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 77, folio 64); Shackle calls him "the head of the Kanphat yogis" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 12 on 122).
- **The name of the hill and where it stands.** The site's account gives Tilla Jogian, the "Hill of the Ascetics", on the highest peak of the eastern Salt Range in Jhelum District. Shackle has Tilla Jogian "high up in the hills of District Jhelum" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122). Usborne's translation says only 'Tilla', and its annotator gives 'Tilla Guruan', "the mound of the Gurus", "on the banks of the river Jhelum" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1). Bhandari calls the place تله[OCR?], with the editor's variant بله[OCR?], and sets it on the salt mountain seven kos from the fort of Rohtas (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 514).
- **The ear-ring.** The site's account speaks of great rings through the cartilage of the ear; Shackle of the cartilage pierced "to allow the insertion of a wooden ring" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 187, folio 162, n. 10 on 122).
- **The hill since 1947.** The site's account has the complex abandoned at Partition, without a resident community, and its buildings in ruin. Usborne's annotator, writing in the present tense, says that "The place is still preserved" and that the 'Jog Mat' "is still practised there" (Waris Shah, *Hir and Ranjha*, p. 33, folio 32, note 1).

## Legacy

Tilla Jogian gathers into one windswept hilltop several of the great strands of Punjabi religious and cultural history: the antiquity of the *Nath* yogis and their Kanphata order; the pilgrim memory of Guru Nanak; and the deathless romance of Heer and Ranjha. As one of the trio of Salt Range sanctuaries alongside Katas Raj and the Amb temples, it testifies to a landscape once dense with Hindu holiness. For the modern traveller it offers a rare and melancholy grandeur — ruined shrines amid olive groves, commanding a vast prospect over the Jhelum plains — and stands as a reminder of a plural sacred past that survives now chiefly in stone and in song.

Writers on the romance, who speak of the tale rather than of the hill, show how it lives on in song. Shackle writes: "The greatest of these local legends is the story of Hir and Ranjha, which is set in the world of the Jat pastoral tribes of western Panjab" (Shackle, *Sufi Lyrics*, p. 20, folio xix). Annemarie Schimmel writes that the romance, "elaborated in more than a hundred versions in Panjabi, Urdu, Sindhi, and Persian, was given its final form in the late eighteenth century by Warith Shah. It is his verse which is sung, time and again, wherever Panjabis meet" (Schimmel, *As Through a Veil*, p. 171, folio 153), and that "The visitor who stays in a Panjabi village will certainly find somebody to sing for him the old romance of Hir Ranjha in the classical form given it by Warith Shah" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 414, folio 383). Shemeem Burney Abbas records that Waris Shah "is said to have recited it with great emotion among his speech communities in the Panjab", and that "Many renowned folk artists in the Panjab, such as Reshma, Zahida Parvin, Nazir Begum, Sabiha Khanum, Tufail Niazi, and Iqbal Bahu, have sung it" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 123, folio not stated). Scott Kugle compares its place in Punjabi devotion with that of Radha and Krishna: "Punjabi poets and their eager audiences poured into Hir and Ranjha the same erotic emotion that was invested in Radha and Krishna in regions closer to the Ganges. The story of Hir and Ranjha became a favorite Sufi device for conveying the value of erotic passion in spiritual life" (Kugle, *Sufis and Saints' Bodies*, p. 228, folio 207). Bhandari, in his account of the suba of Lahore, already records that wonderful verses and designs on the love of Heer and Ranjha were composed and sung there (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 512–511).

- Pnina Werbner and Helene Basu (eds.), *Embodying Charisma: Modernity, Locality and the Performance of Emotion in Sufi Cults* (1998).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *As Through a Veil: Mystical Poetry in Islam* (New York: Columbia University Press, 1982; Lectures on the History of Religions, New Series 12).
- Annemarie Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam* (Chapel Hill: The University of North Carolina Press, 1975; 35th Anniversary Edition, 2011).
- Shemeem Burney Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual* (Austin: University of Texas Press, 2002; Modern Middle East Series).
