Name: Tomb of Javindi Bibi
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

The Tomb of Bibi Jawindi at Uch Sharif is among the most beautiful — and most poignant — monuments of Islamic architecture in Pakistan: a jewel of blue-and-white glazed tilework, half-ruined by the flooding of the river, that has become the very emblem of Uch Sharif’s medieval glory. Bibi Jawindi was a saintly woman of the great Bukhari sayyid family of Uch, a descendant of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht, and her ornate mausoleum, raised in the late fifteenth century, stands within the famous cluster of tombs in the Bukhari quarter of the town.

Two of the books consulted for this article name the tomb, and both saw it. Haroon Khalid, travelling with Iqbal Qaiser, came to "the shrine of Bibi Jiwindi" on a mound outside the town and calls it "arguably the most important" of the three buildings that stand there (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255; Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Robert Rozehnal passed "near the crumbling tomb of Bibi Jawindi" on a day's visit to Uch Sharif in April 1996, and there met the stranger whose story opens his book (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). The two books spell her name differently, Jiwindi and Jawindi, and they do not agree with each other, or with the site's account, on whose kinswoman she was, on when the tomb was built, or on when the flood that ruined it came. Each account is set out below as its author gives it, and the differences are gathered under 'Where the Sources Disagree'.

The other histories and studies consulted speak of Uch Sharif, its saints and its Suhrawardi past, but none of them names Bibi Jawindi. Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi's account of the Sufis of Uch, the longest treatment of the town among them, names no woman and no builder or craftsman (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 299–304, folios 277–282). What those books say of the town is gathered under 'Setting', as context for the tomb and not as a statement about it.

## Bibi Jawindi and her Tomb

Bibi Jawindi is remembered as a pious woman of the Jalali Bukhari line — by tradition a great-granddaughter of the celebrated saint Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht — venerated for her holiness. Her tomb was built around 1493, tradition holds, by an Iranian prince, Dilshad, in her honour. It is an octagonal, tiered structure crowned by a dome, its surfaces sheathed in the exquisite cobalt-blue, turquoise, and white *kashi* tilework for which Uch and Multan are famed, and adorned with corner turrets — a masterpiece of the regional style that flourished around the tombs of the Suhrawardi saints. Over the centuries the changing course of the river undermined the structure, and a great part of it collapsed (by tradition in a flood in the nineteenth century), leaving the ravishing half-tomb that visitors see today — a fragment whose surviving beauty only sharpens the sense of what has been lost.

Khalid, too, makes her a great-granddaughter, but of another man: the tomb, he writes, "belonged to the great granddaughter of Syed Jalaludin Bokhari" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Rozehnal makes her a wife, not a descendant: she is "the wife of the renowned fourteenth-century Suhrawardi shaykh, Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). That relation is all Rozehnal gives of her. His book records no date of death for her, no date of building, no custodian, no *ʿurs* and no measurements, and it calls her by no name other than Bibi Jawindi (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10).

Of her death Khalid's book preserves only the beginning of a sentence. Iqbal Qaiser, standing at the tomb, says "that Bibi Jiwindi died during the …", and the rest of the line cannot be read in the printed text (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). No other book consulted gives the date or the manner of her death.

Khalid describes the tomb as he found it. The shrines on the mound needed a car to reach; they lay "on the outskirts, situated on top of a mound, which was being used as a graveyard" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255). "Half the structures of the shrine had been razed and were protected by iron rods", and what remained was "made out of glazed Multani tiles, coloured in blue and white", with "a white dome on top" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255). Of the building's date he reports what was posted at the site: "The last shrine on this mound was that of Bibi Jiwindi and it is arguably the most important of these three buildings. According to the board here, this tomb was built in 1494" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Of its ruin Iqbal Qaiser gives a different century from the site's account: "There was a huge flood here in the sixteenth century and these buildings were destroyed at that time" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).

On the same mound, Khalid writes, there were "several graves … which were covered arbitrarily with the blue and white Multani tiles that had been recovered from these historical shrines" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). He calls the whole group "thirteenth and fourteenth century shrines", reached through "the market", and Iqbal Qaiser, who had been there before, remarked: "This place has changed since the last time I came here" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255). Looking at the ruins, Khalid recalls the river that once ran beside them: "River Sutlej, the lost river of Pakistan, used to flow from here before it was lost forever after the Indus Water Treaty was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960", and he imagines that "Nanak must have seen these buildings intact with a mighty river flowing next to it" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, pp. 281–282, folios 255–256).

Khalid's pages on the mound do not themselves name the town. They are read as describing Uch Sharif from the shrines they name and from his later mention of "the shrine of Jalaludin Bokhari at Uch Sharif" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 288, folio 262). Rozehnal's single word for the tomb is "crumbling", and his only description of its surroundings is of the town as a whole (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10).

## The Monuments of Uch Sharif

Bibi Jawindi’s tomb does not stand alone: it is the finest of a group of contiguous mausolea in the Bukhari quarter of Uch — including those associated with Baha al-Halim (a teacher of the line) and the tomb’s own builder — that together form one of the most important surviving ensembles of pre-Mughal funerary architecture in the subcontinent. So exceptional are they that the monuments of Uch Sharif have been placed on UNESCO’s Tentative List of World Heritage sites, and they have been the subject of international conservation efforts. The tombs make Uch Sharif a destination for lovers of architecture and history as much as for pilgrims.

Khalid counts three buildings on the mound and ranks hers the most important of them (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). He found the surviving halves of the shrines "protected by iron rods" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255). Rozehnal, who names no tomb at Uch but hers, writes of "the magnificent blue and white tiled mosques and desolate tombs of this ancient center of learning, trade, and pilgrimage built on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab rivers" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10).

## An Encounter at the Tomb

Rozehnal's book begins at this tomb. In April 1996, on a day's journey from the *ʿurs* at Allahabad, "the rural village of Allahabad—sixty miles southwest of the city of Bahawalpur—in southern Punjab", he spent a day wandering through Uch Sharif, and he writes that "near the crumbling tomb of Bibi Jawindi—the wife of the renowned fourteenth-century Suhrawardi shaykh, Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)—we were approached by an elderly gentleman" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). He photographed the stranger. Disciples in Lahore later identified the man in the photograph as "the deceased spiritual master Shaykh Wahid Bakhsh Sial Rabbani", and Rozehnal records that "the shaykh had been deceased for more than a year when the photograph was taken" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, pp. 21–22, folios 10–11). The story is the author's own, and his book presents it as its founding anecdote; it makes no claim for the tomb itself beyond its being the place where the meeting happened.

## Setting

The books that do not name the tomb speak of Uch Sharif, the town around it. What follows is about the town and its saints, not about Bibi Jawindi or her tomb.

Rozehnal places Uch "seventy miles southwest of Multan in Pakistan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202). Annemarie Schimmel places 'Ucch' northeast of Multan, and writes that "Ucch was, for a while, the center of the Suhrawardiyya, thanks chiefly to the active and pious Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Michel Boivin speaks of "one of the masters of the second Sohrawardiyya period, then based in Utch near Bahawalpur in Punjab" (Boivin, *Hindu Sufis of South Asia*, p. 56, folio 43). Omar Kasmani's only words on the town name its first Bukhari saint, "Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari (d. 1291) of Uchh", and add: "Their shrines are spread across southern Punjab in Pakistan" (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17). Shemeem Burney Abbas calls Uch Gilanian "the city of saints in Bahawalpur" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 107, folio not stated).

Rizvi records a foundation legend for the town, in a passage on Shaikh Safiu'd-Din Kaziruni. A shaikh is ordered "to mount a camel and travel in whatever direction the animal led him; he was then to remain where the camel finally halted"; the camel halted "in the middle of a desert", and "the Shaikh founded a town later called Uch" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 129, folio 111). Rizvi's own verdict on the tale is: "Although this story would appear mythical, it is typical of medieval tales relating to sufis" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 129, folio 111). He tells, too, of a flying contest with a yogi at Uch (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, pp. 129–130, folios 111–112), and writes that "all the stories dealing with three generations of these 'sufis in Uch recount conflicts with Hindu Yogis" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 304, folio 282). He writes that "The Baba found a lonely mosque in Uch" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 158, folio 140), and of one Sufi that "he went to Multan and Uch. At Uch it is possible that he was formally initiated into the Suhrawardiyya order as is suggested by local legends" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 337, folio 315). Carl Ernst and Bruce Lawrence place at Uch, in the well of its Hajj mosque, Farid ad-Din's 'inverted 40-day fast': "For 40 days they would suspend him from a branch of the tree that overhung the well every night. At daybreak they would pull him out" (Ernst and Lawrence, *Sufi Martyrs of Love*, p. 168, folio 156).

Uch was also the gate by which, in the books' accounts, the Qadiri order entered the subcontinent. Schimmel writes: "It was in Ucch that the first missionaries of the Qadiriyya settled in the late fifteenth century; from there this order spread into the Subcontinent" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354). Mufti Ghulam Sarwar Lahori's *Hadiqat al-Awliya* writes that of this line "حضرت کے سلسلہ میں سے حضرت سید محمد غوث اوچی جیلی گیلانی اول پنجاب میں آئے", that Hazrat Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus Uchi Jili Gilani was the first of it to come to the Punjab, coming by way of Khurasan to Multan and settling at Uch; the date given for his arrival, 887 AH, is the editor's, citing Ali Asghar Gilani, and not the author's (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28). Rozehnal calls Shaykh Muhammad al-Husseini al-Jilani "the founder of the first Qadiriyya khanaqah at Uch", a native of Turkey who travelled to Khurasan and Multan "before settling with his family in Uch", and says of his son 'Abd al-Qadir Jilani Thani, "the famous Qadiri saint of Uch Sharif", that "there seems to be no extant archive of the saint, no textual record to document his life and legacy" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 259, folio 252; Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202). Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's *Tahqiqat-e Chishti* writes that the four sons of Hazrat Muhammad Ghaus "بمقام اوچ شریف آسودہ ہین", lie at rest at Uch Sharif, beside the tomb of Shah Muhammad Ghaus (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 527), and that the "سادات اوچ" are famous, their word being final on any disputed descent (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 526–527).

Khalid's own approach to the town gives its present. The road ran "through Bahawalpur, heading towards our destination at Uch Sharif", where "the cultures of Punjab and Sindh merge" and the language is Siraiki (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). The older city stands on a mound, with "massive havelis" of "the current caretakers of the shrine, the Gilanis and the Makhdooms" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 276, folio 250). He writes that "The southern region of Punjab, where Uch Sharif lies, has more traces of religious and cultural syncretism compared to the northern and central region" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 277, folio 251). Khalid's book follows Guru Nanak, and in his reconstruction of Nanak's visit, "Uch Sharif was one of the most famous Muslim shrines in Southern Punjab and Nanak had arrived here only a day ago, travelling from Kartarpur" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 288, folio 262). Of Nanak's traces Iqbal Qaiser showed him a well hidden in a field, "abandoned and juice tetrapaks and wrappers were floating in the black water", and beside it a grassy mound: "This was the Gurdwara of Nanak … Now nothing remained" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 286, folio 260).

Abbas records a hereditary *qawwal* family that left Uch with a saint's household. "We came with Bulle Shah's family from Uch Sharif, and we have learned his poetry from our ancestors, who have always sung here", in the words of Muhammad Bakhsh at Kasur (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 112, folio not stated). She quotes the line "Thou art an inhabitant of Uch city", glossing the name, "[Uch literally means high/great]", and says in prose that Bulle Shah's mentor Inayat Shah "belonged to Uch city" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 104, folio not stated).

Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, composed in the fortieth regnal year of Aurangzeb, calls the place "قصبه اوچ", the township of Uch (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 527), and in describing the suba of Thatta takes "حدود ملتان و اوچ", the bounds of Multan and Uch, as one of its limits (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 529). In its pages armies pass through it again and again: Shihab al-Din took Uch on his first campaign and returned by Multan and Uch on his second (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405); Mirza Pir Muhammad brought "حصار اوچ و ملتان" into his possession (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 333); and Khawas Khan's pursuit went "تا ملتان و اوچ" (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 285). It names no saint and no tomb at Uch in these passages.

## Devotion and Legacy

As the resting place of a holy woman of the revered Bukhari line, Bibi Jawindi’s tomb is honoured by pilgrims who come to Uch to visit the shrines of the sayyids, and it forms part of the sacred fabric of the town. But its fame today is above all as a monument — a breathtaking, wounded masterpiece that stands for the vanished splendour of medieval Uch and for the artistry of the tile-workers who adorned the shrines of the Punjab’s saints. It is, at once, a place of devotion, a heritage treasure, and an elegy in brick and glaze.

Neither book that names the tomb describes devotion at it. Khalid came to it as a visitor to the monuments and found its fallen half secured with iron and the tiles of the ruined shrines reused on the graves around it (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255; Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Rozehnal records no *ʿurs* or custodian there (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). For him the tomb is remembered as the place where his book began.

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **Whose kinswoman she was.** The site's account makes her a woman of the Jalali Bukhari line and, by tradition, a great-granddaughter of Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht. Khalid makes her "the great granddaughter of Syed Jalaludin Bokhari" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Rozehnal makes her the wife of "Sayyid Jalal ad-Din Bukhari (1303–1383)" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10). Schimmel gives Jalaluddin Makhdum-i Jahaniyan's death as 1383 (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), and Rizvi the birth of Saiyid Jalalu'd-Din Bukhari, Makhdum-i Jahaniyan, as 9 February 1308 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 299, folio 277); Kasmani gives the death of Jalaluddin Surkhposh Bukhari as 1291 (Kasmani, *Queer Companions*, p. 188, folio 171, ch. 1 n. 17).
- **When the tomb was built.** The site's account gives around 1493, by tradition. The board at the site, as Khalid reports it, gives 1494 (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 285, folio not stated). Khalid calls the group of buildings on the mound "thirteenth and fourteenth century shrines" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).
- **When the flood came.** The site's account places the collapse, by tradition, in a flood in the nineteenth century. Iqbal Qaiser, in Khalid's book, says: "There was a huge flood here in the sixteenth century and these buildings were destroyed at that time" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).
- **Where the tomb stands.** The site's account sets it in the Bukhari quarter of the town. Khalid's shrines lie "on the outskirts, situated on top of a mound, which was being used as a graveyard" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).
- **The tilework.** The site's account describes cobalt-blue, turquoise and white *kashi* tilework. Khalid describes "glazed Multani tiles, coloured in blue and white" and "a white dome on top" (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).
- **Her name.** The site's account writes Bibi Jawindi, as does Rozehnal (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10); Khalid writes Bibi Jiwindi (Khalid, *Walking with Nanak*, p. 281, folio 255).
- **Where Uch lies.** Rozehnal sets the town on a hill overlooking the confluence of the Sutlej and Chenab (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 21, folio 10) and "seventy miles southwest of Multan" (Rozehnal, *Islamic Sufism Unbound*, p. 210, folio 202); Schimmel puts it 'northeast of Multan' (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354).
- **When the Qadiriyya came.** Schimmel has the first Qadiri missionaries settle in Ucch "in the late fifteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 385, folio 354), and elsewhere has the order introduced into the subcontinent "in the late fourteenth century" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 278, folio 247). The editor of Lahori's book, citing Ali Asghar Gilani, has Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus enter Uch in ۸۸۷ھ (Lahori, *Hadiqat al-Awliya*, p. 40, folio 28).

Location: Aibak Road, Anarkali, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: None - heritage site, no devotional programme
Description:
## Overview

Tucked amid the crowded lanes of Aibak Road in the Anarkali quarter of Lahore, a modest garden tomb marks the burial place of Sultan Qutb ud-Din Aibak, founder of the Mamluk, or "Slave," dynasty and the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. A slave who rose through service to the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, he established independent rule based in Lahore after Ghori's death, laying the foundations of Muslim dynastic government in the subcontinent, and he is remembered too as the patron who commissioned Delhi's Qutb Minar. He died in Lahore in November 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing *chaugan*, an early form of polo. The tomb is not a Sufi shrine: it hosts no *ʿurs*, no pilgrimage tradition and no ongoing devotional practice, and it is maintained as a protected historical monument, valued chiefly for its symbolic role marking the thirteenth-century founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself.

The tomb's physical history has been anything but continuous. Historians dispute whether a substantial mausoleum ever stood over the grave in the medieval period; for long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar; and the structure visitors see today is essentially a reconstruction of the 1970s, though one official account dates it to 1990.

The books consulted add a good deal to this picture. Maulvi Nur Ahmad Chishti's survey of the tombs and buildings of Lahore, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, is the only one of them to describe the grave itself: he places it in the Sadr Bazaar of Anarkali, records a lost two-storey dome of marble that old people remembered, and says the Maharaja of his day demolished the buildings and sent their stone to Amritsar (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271). Sujan Rai Bhandari's Persian *Khulasat al-Tawarikh* gives the fullest account of the life: the purchased slave made viceroy, his campaigns, his accession at Lahore, his generosity, his name and his death at *chaugan* (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402). Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* places his death at Lahore and explains his title Lakh Bakhsh, but names no grave for him (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Naveed Alam's translation of Madho Lal Hussein, Saiyid Athar Abbas Rizvi, Shemeem Burney Abbas and Annemarie Schimmel mention him in passing, and the year of his death is given in more than one way.

## The Life of the Sultan

Aibak was born around 1150 in Turkestan and sold into slavery as a child. He rose through service to the Ghurid ruler Muhammad Ghori, and came to command Ghurid territories in northern India following the decisive Second Battle of Tarain in 1192.

Bhandari calls him plainly 'سلطان قطب الدین ایبک غلام زرخرید سلطان شهاب الدین نیابتاً حکومت هندوستان داشت', the Sultan's purchased slave, governing Hindustan as his deputy (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). After the victory at 'نراین', he writes, Sultan Shihab al-Din left 'ملک قطب الدین ایبک را که غلام برگزیده او بود درقصبه کهرام هفتاد کروهے دهلی نایب سلطنت': his chosen slave was made viceroy at the *qasba* of Kuhram, seventy *kos* from Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 402). Rizvi's history of Sufism tells it differently: "Mu‘izzu’d-Din Muhammad bin Sam had conquered Delhi and, departing for Ghazni, left his favourite slave, Qutbu’d-Din Aibak, as head of his forces in the occupied city" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121).

As deputy, 'نیابتاً', after the Sultan went back to Ghazni, Bhandari continues, he 'دراسرع اوقات قلعه دهلی ومیرته تسخیر نموده بهرجا حکام نصب گردانید', in the shortest time took the forts of Delhi and Meerut and set governors in every place; in the second year he took 'قلعه کول', and then the forts of Gwalior, Budaun 'ودیگر قلاع', and other forts (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402). He marched on Gujarat and took revenge on 'راۓ بهیم دیو گجراتی' for the Sultan's earlier defeat, 'انتقام شکست سلطان که سابقاً بتحریر درامده', plundered the country, returned to Delhi and 'خطبه وسکه بنام سلطان رواج داد', put the *khutba* and the coin into currency in the Sultan's name (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). In the Sultan's tenth campaign, against the Khokhars near Lahore, 'ملک قطب الدین نیز از دهلی بخدمت سلطان رسیده باتفاق یکدیگر گوشمال انجماعت ... کردند': Malik Qutb al-Din too came from Delhi to the Sultan's service, and together they chastised that tribe (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).

Rizvi describes the occupation: "Occupying troops stationed at Indraprastha near Delhi under Qutbu’d-Din Aibak were forced to make several invasions in the Doab and the regions around Ajmer to consolidate their power" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 140, folio 122). In the same account he records that "Qutbu’d-Din had appointed Saiyid Husain Mashhadi as the darogha (military governor) of the area. The Saiyid served the Khwaja with great devotion" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 140, folio 122).

His captains carried the conquest east. In Bhandari's words, 'در بلاد بنگاله آغاز ظهور اسلام از ملک محمد بختیار که از امراے بزرگ سلطان قطب الدین ایبک بود گردیده وازان زمان آن ولایت درتصرف[OCR?] سلطان دهلی گشت': Islam in Bengal began with Malik Muhammad Bakhtiyar, one of Aibak's great amirs, and from that time the province was in the hands of the Sultan of Delhi (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 208). Chishti tells of a general who sent his booty from Bihar 'اپنے مالک کی پاس دہلی مین', to his master at Delhi, of a 'مست ہاتہی', a rutting elephant, and of the governorship of Bihar and an order to take Bengal (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

Delhi was his seat. Bhandari records that 'سلطان قطب الدین ایبک و سلطان شمس الدین التمش در قلعه رائے پتهورا می بودند', he and Iltutmish lived in Rai Pithora's fort (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 561), and that 'ازان تاریخ شهر دهلی دارالخلافت سلاطین مسلمین مقرر گردیده', from then on Delhi was the capital of the Muslim sultans (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). He is remembered as the patron who commissioned Delhi's Qutb Minar, and Alam's note calls him "known for the famous Qutb Minar" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Schimmel, writing of the death of Muʿinuddin in 1236, places it "not far from the beautiful mosque" that Aibak, whom she calls 'of Delhi', "had erected in Ajmer" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346).

## The Accession

After Ghori's assassination in 1206, Aibak established independent rule based in Lahore. Chishti's history gives Muhammad Ghori's death as 'سن بارہ سو چہہ [OCR?]', the year twelve hundred and six, and says he died without a son; 'قطب الدین حاکم دہلی', Qutb al-Din the ruler of Delhi, then claimed Hindustan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Elsewhere Chishti sets the accession in 'چھ سو دو[OCR?]', six hundred and two, with the figure ۶۰۲ in the margin, when he 'تخت دہلی پر جلوس فرمایا', took his seat on the throne of Delhi; before that, he writes, 'ملک ہندوستان ... بے چراغ تھا', the land of Hindustan was without a lamp (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267). Kanhaiya Lal states his status plainly: Shahab-ud-Din Ghori 'دہلی کا تخت سلطان [illegible] قطب الدین ایبک اپنے غلام کے سپرد کر دیا', handed the throne of Delhi to Qutb al-Din Aibak, his own slave (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19).

Bhandari puts the moment of sovereignty at Lahore: 'بعد ازانکه سلطان درجه شهادت یافت از دهلی برامده درلاهور رسید اصالتاً سریراراۓ خلافت گشت ویازدهم ربیع الاول سنه ۶۰۳[OCR?] سکه وخطبه بنام خود کرد'. After the Sultan attained martyrdom, he came out of Delhi, reached Lahore and took the throne in his own right, and on the eleventh of Rabiʿ al-Awwal of the year 603 had the coin struck and the *khutba* read in his own name; the reading of the year is uncertain in the printed text (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). 'سلطان غیاث الدین محمود[OCR?] برادرزاده سلطان شهاب الدین از فیروزه کوه', Sultan Ghiyas al-Din Mahmud, Shihab al-Din's nephew, sent him from Firozkoh 'چتر وتجملات بادشاهی', the parasol and the trappings of kingship, and 'بخطاب سلطانی مخاطب ساخت', addressed him with the title of Sultan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 400–401).

## The Contest with Yildiz

His rival for the Ghurid inheritance was Taj al-Din Yildiz, whom the books spell variously. Bhandari calls 'تاج الدین یلدوز' one of Shihab al-Din's 'بندهاۓ خاص', his special slaves, who had been given the name of sultan in Ghazni after Shihab al-Din's death; a dispute arose between the two 'برسر لاهور', over Lahore, and they fought a pitched battle: 'بالآخر تاج الدین تاب مقاومت نیاورده منهزم گشته درکرمان اقامت ورزید وسلطان مظفر ومنصور شده باستقلال کمال بسلطنت پرداخت'. At last Taj al-Din could not hold out, was routed and settled in Kirman, and the Sultan, victorious, gave himself to rule in complete independence (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).

In Kanhaiya Lal's history Yalduz, having seized Ghazni, 'پھر پنجاب کو آیا', came on to the Punjab to take the throne of Hind from Qutb al-Din (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Aibak defeated him in the field and pursued him to Ghazni, and then 'قطب الدین وہاں سے لاہور کو آ گیا', Qutb al-Din came from there to Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Chishti, for his part, has him defeat 'الدوز [OCR?]' and be crowned at Ghazni, where he grew 'آرام طلب', a lover of ease, and was driven back (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

## His Rule and His Household

Chishti says he ruled 'بہت لیاقت سی', with great ability, and lived five years after his master, the reading of the number being uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Bhandari reckons the whole of his government thus: 'مدت بست سال حکومت هندوستان نمود ازانجمله سلطنت غزنین چهار سال', he governed Hindustan for twenty years, the sultanate of Ghazni among them for four (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi's index gives the bracket "(1206-1210)" after his name (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).

Iltutmish, who would follow him, was his slave before he was his son-in-law. Rizvi writes that "Sultan Qutbu'd-Din Aibak, also a former slave, during a visit to Ghazna after his Anhilwara expedition in 1196, took a fancy to Iltutmish and was able to buy him in Delhi, and between 1197 or 1198 to 1206 Iltutmish rose to prominence" (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 153, folio 135, footnote 2). In Bhandari's account, 'اورا سلطان قطب الدین ایبک به[OCR?] لک جیتل خریده بفرزندی گرفته دختر خود را درمناکحت او درآورده بود': Aibak bought him for a lakh of *jitals*, adopted him and married him to his daughter. 'بعد فتح گوالیار امارت انجا باو ارزانی داشت', after the conquest of Gwalior he granted him its command; then he gave him 'برن[OCR?]' and its region and, step by step, Budaun, until Iltutmish rose to be *amir al-umara* and 'خط آزادی از سلطان یافت', received his letter of manumission from the Sultan (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). Shemeem Burney Abbas, recounting her own ancestors' appointment as muftis of Lahore under "the Muslim slave king Shamsuddin Iltutmish", adds that "Qutubuddin Aibek was himself a slave king" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).

He was succeeded eventually by his son-in-law Iltutmish. The books differ on what came between. Bhandari writes that 'سلطان مرحوم پسر صلبی که سزاوار جهانبانی تواند بود نداشت', the late Sultan had no son of his own body fit to rule; the nobles therefore seated 'آرام بخش پسرخوانده سلطان', Aram Bakhsh, the Sultan's adopted son and the only heir, 'درسنه ۶۰۷[OCR?] درخطه دل کشاۓ لاهور', in the year 607 in the delightful region of Lahore, as Sultan Aram Shah (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400); but 'از سلطان آرام شاه امور خلافت تمشیت نیافت', under Aram Shah the affairs of state did not prosper (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). Chishti calls 'آرام' his son, deposed after a year by 'شمس الدین', who was Aibak's slave and son-in-law (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal names his successor on the throne of Delhi as 'سلطان شمس الدین التمش' (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and Abbas has Iltutmish ascend the throne of Delhi "after the death of his master, Qutubuddin Aibek" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).

A different Qutbuddin must not be confused with him. On the same page as her mention of Aibak's mosque, Schimmel writes of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki of Farghana, who died in 1235 and whose "rather modest compound in Merauli near the Qutb Minar in Delhi is usually filled with pious pilgrims" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346); her index lists him separately (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 513, folio 482).

## Lakh Bakhsh: His Names and His Giving

Bhandari explains the name Aibak: 'چون انگشت خنصر او شکسته بود ازینجهت اورا ایبک گفتندے', because his little finger was broken, he was called Aibak (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).

His title Lakh Bakhsh, the giver of lakhs, is explained by his largesse. Kanhaiya Lal ties it to Lahore: there he 'بہت [illegible] رعایا کو [illegible] خوش کیا اور کثرت داد و دہش سے سلطان لکھ بخش خطاب لیا', pleased the subjects and, by the abundance of his giving, took the title Sultan Lakh Bakhsh (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari gives a long passage in praise of his giving, 'دست جود وسخایش گرد افلاس ازچهره مفلسان برافشاندی', which ends 'چون لکها باهل احتیاج انعام دادی ازینجهت درهند اورا لکهه بخش گفتندی': because he gave lakhs to the needy, in Hind they called him Lakh-bakhsh (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). A couplet in his praise follows:

باهمت او حوصله دریا تنگ
بارفعت او مرتبه گردون پست

The couplet closes Bhandari's praise of the Sultan's generosity (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).

The books write his name in several forms: 'قطب الدین ایبک' in Kanhaiya Lal and Bhandari (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19; Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401), "Sultan Qutub-uddin Aibak" in Alam's note (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185), Qutbu’d-Din Aibak in Rizvi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121), Qutubuddin Aibek in Abbas (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated) and Aybek in Schimmel (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 377, folio 346).

## Death at Chaugan

He died in Lahore in November 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing *chaugan*, an early form of polo. Kanhaiya Lal tells it in one line: 'اور لاہور ہی کے مقام پر گیند کھیلتے ہوئے گھوڑے سے گر کر مر گیا', and at Lahore itself, playing ball, he fell from his horse and died; he gives no year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari has 'درسنه [illegible] درچوگان بازی از اسپ افتاده گوۓ زندگی بجولانگاه آخرت رسانید', that he fell from his horse at *chaugan* and died; the year cannot be read, and Bhandari names no place of death (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Chishti gives the year as 'سن بارہ سو دس [OCR?]', twelve hundred and ten, the reading flagged as uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).

Naveed Alam's translation of Madho Lal Hussein recalls the death in a note on the game itself: "The game was brought to the subcontinent by the Central Asian armies. Sultan Qutub-uddin Aibak, known for the famous Qutb Minar, died playing polo in Lahore in AD 1210." (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). The verse is Hussein's own, a *kafi* that watches a polo match and does not name the Sultan:

*Let me stand and watch for a few days / the polo tournament. Who wins, who loses, / whose brisk horse makes a clever move? … Let's see who hits the ball / across the field. The crowd cheers and jeers* (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, p. 113, folio 113, kafi 90)

## The Tomb

Chishti's survey of Lahore's tombs is the only book consulted that describes the grave. He places it 'دروازہ لاہوری کے باہر بطرف شمال', outside the Lahori Gate on the north side, east of a 'گودام [OCR?] شراب', a liquor godown, 'واقعہ صدر بازار انار کلی', situated in the Sadr Bazaar of Anarkali. In his day a 'قصاب [OCR?] خانہ', a butcher's house, stood on its land, and 'طوائف لوگوں', courtesans, occupied it (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271).

He records what had been lost. Under Sikh rule there stood 'عمارات عالیشان سنگ [illegible]', lofty buildings of stone; 'مہاراجہ نے سب مسمار کرکے روانہ امرتسر کر دین', the Maharaja demolished them all and sent them off to Amritsar; and there remained 'ایک قبر خشتی [OCR?] بلند چبوترہ پر', a single brick grave on a raised platform. Old people, he writes, had seen a 'گنبد دو منزلہ سنگ مرمر کا', a two-storey dome of marble, unmatched anywhere round Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271).

Chishti judged that no building near Lahore was older than this grave, because Qutb al-Din was '[illegible] سی', and because 'سلطنت عوریہ یہاں چغتائی [OCR?] سے بہت مدت پہلے تھی', the Ghurid sultanate was here long before the Chaghatai; for the fuller story he refers the reader to 'تواریخ ہند', the histories of Hind. He left more unsaid on purpose: because of the courtesans, what might have been written, '[illegible] لکھا جاوے قلم انداز کیا گیا', was omitted (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 271–272).

The modern accounts tell the story another way. Punjab's Directorate General of Archaeology states that the grave was "originally... only one grave without any tomb or structure," that a marble tomb was later "pulled down by Ranjit Singh," and that the department itself "built the present tomb over the grave in 1990." Earlier still, according to Dawn's "Harking Back" column, Sultan Iltutmish had ordered "a simple small room, one barely able to enclose the grave": at first a mud room, it was later bricked in during Akbar's reign. For long the site was a simple, informal grave hemmed in by the houses of the Anarkali bazaar.

The same column dates the present mausoleum's actual construction to 1972, ordered by Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto after the Bangladesh war, who is quoted remarking that Aibak "was a great and kind ruler and deserved the respect of the poor"; the design was led by the architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz. Daily Times likewise places the rebuilding "during the 1970s," rather than in 1990 as the Archaeology Department's own page states. The structure visitors see today is essentially this 1970s reconstruction by Pakistan's Department of Archaeology and Museums, deliberately evoking early Sultanate-period style within a small walled garden.

The other books are silent on the tomb. Kanhaiya Lal's history of Lahore names no grave for him, and its table of contents lists no tomb of his (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 2–5); Bhandari names no burial (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400); and Rizvi, Abbas, Schimmel and Alam mention none.

## The Tomb Today

Unlike Lahore's Sufi shrines, the tomb hosts no *ʿurs*, no pilgrimage tradition and no ongoing devotional practice. It is maintained purely as a protected historical monument, and none of the books consulted records any observance at the grave.

## Setting: Anarkali and Ghurid Lahore

What the books say of the quarter and the city is context, not a description of the tomb. Kanhaiya Lal's *Tarikh-e Lahore* knows Anarkali only as a cantonment and a bazaar (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, pp. 34–35, folios 37–38). Haroon Khalid's *A White Trail* says that the Anarkali market "is named after the legendary lover of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir", that the area "over the years has become the largest tyre market in the city", and that "The Pak Tea House, just a few shops away, once famed for its gatherings of the leading intelligentsia of the city, is now on its way to becoming yet another tyre shop" (Khalid, *A White Trail*, p. 66, folio not stated).

Aibak's Lahore was a city the Ghurids had only lately taken. Bhandari tells how 'خسروشاه بن بهرام شاه', driven from Ghazni by the Ghurids, took Lahore and died there in 555 (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405); his son Khusraw Malik held it for twenty-eight years, 'مدت حکومت او درلاهور بست وهشت سال', while Shihab al-Din attacked Lahore again and again (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 405). In the campaign Bhandari dates 582, Khusraw Malik submitted and was taken to Ghazni, where he died, and the Sultan 'ودرلاهور نایب خود نصب کرد', set his own deputy in Lahore (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 404). Kanhaiya Lal marks the same turn: with Khusrau Malik's surrender, 'سلاطین غوریہ کی سلطنت کا ہند میں آغاز ہوا اور غزنویہ حکومت با اختتام پہنچی', the rule of the Ghurid sultans in Hind began and the Ghaznavid government came to its end (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19).

After Aibak's death Lahore was briefly a royal seat again: his heir Aram Shah was enthroned there, and when Iltutmish came, Aram Shah moved 'از لاهور', from Lahore, toward Delhi, drew up his ranks and fled 'باندک محاربه', after little fighting (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399). In Kanhaiya Lal's account Yalduz rose again in Iltutmish's reign, took Multan and came to Lahore 'اور اُس نے دل کھول کر پنجاب کو غارت کیا', and plundered the Punjab freely (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20).

Chishti's general account of the city sets the loss of old Lahore's monuments in the Sikh period, which is the setting for his report of this tomb's demolition. In Ranjit Singh's time, he writes, red, black and marble stones 'گرد و نواح لاہور کے', in the neighbourhood of Lahore, were torn down (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 296); when the cantonments of Ranjit Singh's armies were built the bricks of old tombs and houses were pulled out, and 'ہزار ہا مقابر و گنبد و مساجد و باغات و حویلیہائے[OCR?] قدیمہ جو یادگار امرائے سلف تھیں گم گشتیں[OCR?]', thousands of tombs, domes, mosques, gardens and old mansions that were memorials of the nobles of the past were lost (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 431).

## Where the Sources Disagree

- **The year of his death.** The current account gives November 1210. Chishti gives 'سن بارہ سو دس [OCR?]', 1210, the reading flagged as uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809), and Alam's note gives "AD 1210" (Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Kanhaiya Lal gives no year (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and in Bhandari the year is illegible (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Schimmel's index prints "(d. 1206)" (Schimmel, *Mystical Dimensions of Islam*, p. 523). Rizvi's index prints "(1206-1210)", a span of rule, and gives no death date (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457). Abbas prints a year at this point that cannot be read in the copy consulted (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).
- **Where he died.** The current account, Kanhaiya Lal and Alam place his death at Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20; Madho Lal Hussein, *Verses of a Lowly Fakir*, pp. 184–185, folios 184–185). Bhandari tells the fall at *chaugan* but names no place (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi places him at Delhi and Ghazni only and has no Lahore for him (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).
- **Where Ghori left him.** Rizvi has Muhammad bin Sam leave him "as head of his forces in the occupied city" of Delhi (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 139, folio 121). Bhandari has him made viceroy at Kuhram, seventy *kos* from Delhi, taking Delhi himself afterwards (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, pp. 401–402).
- **When and where he became sovereign.** The current account has him establish independent rule based in Lahore after Ghori's assassination in 1206. Chishti has him take his seat on the throne of Delhi in 'چھ سو دو[OCR?]', 602 (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267), and elsewhere has Ghori die in 1206 and Aibak, ruler of Delhi, claim Hindustan (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal has Ghori hand him the throne of Delhi (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 24, folio 19). Bhandari has him come from Delhi to Lahore and strike coin and read the *khutba* in his own name on 11 Rabiʿ al-Awwal 603, the year's reading uncertain (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401).
- **Yildiz and Ghazni.** Bhandari has Yildiz contest Lahore, lose a pitched battle and settle in Kirman, and gives Aibak four years of the sultanate of Ghazni (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Kanhaiya Lal has Aibak defeat Yalduz, pursue him to Ghazni and come back to Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Chishti has him crowned at Ghazni, grow 'آرام طلب', a lover of ease, and be driven back (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809).
- **How long he ruled.** Chishti says he lived five years after his master, the number's reading uncertain (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Bhandari says he governed Hindustan for twenty years (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Rizvi's index brackets his name with 1206 and 1210 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 481, folio 457).
- **His successor.** The current account has him succeeded eventually by his son-in-law Iltutmish. Bhandari has the nobles seat Aram Bakhsh, his adopted son, at Lahore as Aram Shah, saying the Sultan had no son of his own body (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400). Chishti calls 'آرام' his son, deposed after a year by Shams al-Din (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 809). Kanhaiya Lal names Iltutmish as his successor on the throne of Delhi with no reign between (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20), and Abbas has Iltutmish ascend "after the death of his master" (Abbas, *The Female Voice in Sufi Ritual*, p. 25, folio not stated).
- **How he acquired Iltutmish.** Rizvi has him buy Iltutmish in Delhi, having taken a fancy to him on a visit to Ghazna after the Anhilwara expedition of 1196 (Rizvi, *A History of Sufism in India*, p. 153, folio 135, footnote 2). Bhandari has him buy Iltutmish for a lakh of *jitals*, adopt him and marry him to his daughter, and names no place (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 399).
- **Where he was called Lakh Bakhsh.** Kanhaiya Lal ties the title to his largesse at Lahore (Kanhaiya Lal, *Tarikh-e Lahore*, p. 25, folio 20). Bhandari says that 'درهند', in Hind, he was called Lakh-bakhsh (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).
- **What once stood over the grave.** The Directorate General of Archaeology says it was originally only a grave without any tomb or structure, and that a marble tomb was later pulled down by Ranjit Singh. Dawn's column has Iltutmish order a simple small room, first of mud and bricked in under Akbar. Chishti reports lofty buildings of stone under Sikh rule, demolished by the Maharaja and sent to Amritsar, and a two-storey marble dome that old people remembered (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 271). The current account adds that historians dispute whether a substantial mausoleum ever stood over the grave in the medieval period.
- **When the present tomb was built.** The Directorate General of Archaeology says its department built the present tomb in 1990. Dawn's column dates the construction to 1972, under Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, and Daily Times places the rebuilding in the 1970s.

## Legacy

The tomb is valued chiefly for its symbolic role, marking the thirteenth-century founding moment of Muslim dynastic rule in South Asia, centred, briefly, on Lahore itself. Bhandari makes the same claim for Delhi: from his time, 'ازان تاریخ شهر دهلی دارالخلافت سلاطین مسلمین مقرر گردیده', Delhi was fixed as the capital of the Muslim sultans (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 401). Chishti, for whom the land of Hindustan had been 'بے چراغ' before him (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, p. 267), held his grave to be older than any other building near Lahore (Chishti, *Tahqiqat-e Chishti*, pp. 271–272).

Aibak, according to Dawn's column, had also wanted Lahore's dead buried together, designating land south of Mozang village as a graveyard for "at least 150,000 dead," the origin of the present Miani Sahib graveyard.

Bhutto's remark, as Dawn reports it, that Aibak "was a great and kind ruler and deserved the respect of the poor" stands beside the older memory of the Lakh Bakhsh, whose giving Bhandari praises in prose and verse (Bhandari, *Khulasat al-Tawarikh*, p. 400).

Name: Tomb of Ustad Nuriya
Location: Bukhari mound, Uch Sharif, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: None - heritage site, no devotional programme
Description:
The Tomb of Ustad Nuriya is the smallest and plainest of the celebrated funerary monuments clustered on the Bukhari mound at Uch Sharif, an ancient town in the Bahawalpur district of southern Punjab long renowned as a centre of Suhrawardi Sufism. It stands beside the far more famous tombs of Bibi Jawindi and Baha'al-Halim (both octagonal and blue-tiled) and the flat-roofed brick tomb-and-mosque of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari, with which it forms an ensemble of five monuments placed on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites. Tradition holds that the tomb honours Ustad Nuriya — the master-builder, or ustad, credited with designing the exquisite tomb of Bibi Jawindi, itself usually dated to the late fifteenth century. Because it was raised for a craftsman rather than a saint, the tomb departs from the octagonal, tiered form of its neighbours: it is smaller and broadly rectangular in plan, and it lacks the lavish glazed-tile revetment for which Uch is famous. Like the rest of the group it has suffered severe structural loss over the centuries — a great flood in 1817 is traditionally blamed for the collapse of much of the complex — and part of its rear structure is gone. Its interest lies precisely in its dedication: in an architectural tradition that seldom named its makers, the survival of a monument to the builder himself is remarkable, and it underlines the extraordinary artistic reputation of the Uch workshops. Filed here under the Muslim-shrine category as an integral part of the Suhrawardi funerary complex, the tomb draws the heritage traveller and the historian of Indo-Islamic architecture rather than the pilgrim.

An academic study of the Uch Sharif funerary complex places the tomb specifically in the northwest corner of the town, on the sloping side of a hill that was once the site of a historic fortress, amid the ruins of other architecturally significant shrines — among them those of Bibi Jawindi and Baha'al-Halim. The tomb is also listed as a protected monument in the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology's register of religious monuments, where it is classified under the heading "Early Muslim Period (8th–12th Century)."

- Directorate General of Archaeology, Government of Punjab, "Religious Monuments," https://archaeology.punjab.gov.pk/religious_monuments, accessed 16 August 2026.

Name: Umarkot (Amarkot) Shiv Mandir
Events: Maha Shivratri (three-day festival)
Description:
## Overview

The Shiv Mandir at *Umarkot* (historically *Amarkot*), in the desert district of the same name in eastern Sindh, is among the oldest and most venerated Hindu temples in Pakistan, and the setting each year of one of the largest Hindu festivals in the country. Dedicated to *Shiva* and enshrining a much-revered *lingam*, it draws tens of thousands of pilgrims from across Sindh to the annual celebration of *Maha Shivaratri*, and it stands as a living centre of the Hindu devotional life that has flourished in this corner of the Thar borderlands for centuries.

## Antiquity and Sacred Legend

Tradition ascribes to the temple a very great age — some accounts speak of two thousand years and more — though such claims belong to legend rather than to documented history and are best treated with due caution. The origin story most often told is a pastoral one: a herdsman, it is said, noticed that one of his cows would slip away each day to a particular spot and there let down her milk of her own accord upon a stone. When the people investigated, they found the stone to be a *Shiva lingam*, self-manifested from the earth, and upon that spot the temple was raised. A further tradition holds that the lingam continued to grow over time, so that devotees marked its height to observe the increase — again a matter of devotional legend rather than record.

## The Temple and Interfaith Custom

The structure standing today is said to have been built roughly a century ago, and — in a detail often recounted as an emblem of Sindh's tradition of religious coexistence — the building is attributed to the piety and patronage of a local Muslim. Such interweaving of communities is characteristic of the region: Umarkot itself is celebrated in history as the birthplace, in 1542, of the Mughal emperor *Akbar*, born there while his fugitive father Humayun sheltered under the protection of the local Hindu Rana — a memory that underlines the district's long entanglement of faiths and rulers.

## Maha Shivaratri at Umarkot

The temple comes most fully to life at *Maha Shivaratri*, the great night of Shiva, when a festival lasting some three days transforms the town. Pilgrims from the length of Sindh, from the lower delta to the upper districts, converge upon the shrine, many staying for the duration of the celebrations; estimates of attendance run into the hundreds of thousands, making it one of the very largest religious gatherings of Pakistan's Hindu community. The festival is at once an act of collective worship and a great affirmation of the community's identity and continuity in the land of its ancestors.

## Legacy

The Umarkot Shiv Mandir is far more than an ancient building; it is a beating heart of Hindu devotion in Pakistan, where legend, landscape, and living faith meet. Its origin-tale of the milk-giving cow and the self-born lingam, its association with the tolerant history of the Sindhi borderland, and above all the vast annual pilgrimage that it sustains, together make it one of the most significant Hindu sacred sites in the country and a proud symbol of the endurance of Sindh's Hindu heritage.

## Bibliography

- Cousens, Henry. *The Antiquities of Sindh, with Historical Outline*. Archaeological Survey of India.
- Raikes, S. N. *Memoir on the Thurr and Parkur Districts of Sindh*.
- Contemporary press reporting (Dawn, "The thriving Shiva festival in Umarkot") on Maha Shivaratri at the temple.
- Studies of Hindu communities and pilgrimage in modern Sindh.
- Local histories of Umarkot (Amarkot) and the birth of Akbar.

Name: Valmik Mandir (Naqi Road)
Events: Holi; Diwali; Valmiki Jayanti
Description:
## Overview

The Valmik Mandir of Lahore, dedicated to the sage *Valmiki* (also written *Balmiki*), is one of only two functioning Hindu temples in a city that once counted them in the dozens. It stands in the *Neela Gumbad* quarter on the edge of the old Anarkali bazaar — the address recorded in this dataset as Naqi Road belongs to the same dense grid of lanes near Bhim Street — and it serves as the principal place of worship and communal gathering for Lahore's small but tenacious Valmiki community. Regarded by local heritage accounts as among the oldest surviving Hindu sacred sites in the city, the temple carries an importance out of all proportion to its modest size, for it is a living link to the pre-Partition religious plurality of the Punjab.

## Maharishi Valmiki and the Balmiki Community

Valmiki is revered across the Hindu world as the *Adi Kavi*, the "first poet", to whom tradition ascribes the composition of the *Ramayana*, the great Sanskrit epic of Rama. In the Punjab he is venerated with special devotion by the Valmiki (or Balmiki) community, who look to him as their patron and spiritual founder. Historically associated with sanitation work and counted among the most marginalised groups of society, the Valmikis have made the figure of the sage a source of dignity and collective identity; a portion of the community follows Hindu practice while others have embraced Christianity or Sikh usages, and the temple has at times served worshippers of more than one persuasion. The reverence for Valmiki thus binds together a scattered and often disadvantaged people, and the Lahore temple is the emotional centre of that devotion in the city.

## The Temple and its History

By tradition the shrine on this site is very ancient; some heritage accounts, difficult to verify, trace a place of worship here back roughly twelve hundred years, which would make the structure — or at least its site — one of the oldest in Lahore. What is certain is that the temple was an established feature of the Neela Gumbad locality well before the Partition of 1947, when Lahore still possessed a large and prosperous Hindu population. After Partition the great majority of the city's Hindus departed for India, temples were abandoned, encroached upon or converted to other uses, and the Valmik Mandir became one of a mere handful to remain in worship. Today it is looked after in conjunction with the *Evacuee Trust Property Board*, the state body that administers the religious properties left by those who migrated, and the Pakistan Hindu Council, which has taken an increasing role in the welfare of functioning temples.

## Attack, Survival and Renewal

The temple's continued existence has not been untroubled. In December 1992, in the violent reaction across the subcontinent to the demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, mobs attacked Hindu temples in Pakistan; the Valmik Mandir was among those assaulted, its images broken, its valuables looted and parts of it set alight. That the community rebuilt and returned is a measure of its attachment to the site. In more recent years the temple has again become a place of open and confident celebration: the festivals of *Holi* and *Diwali*, and the birth anniversary of Valmiki, are marked here, and worshippers who had stayed away for years have returned to its courtyard. Government-approved renovation, including work on the entrance and interior rooms, has sought to repair the fabric of the building and to acknowledge its standing as a heritage site.

## Significance Today

For a city whose Hindu heritage survives largely in ruined *havelis*, disused shrines and the memory of old street-names, the Valmik Mandir is a rare instance of continuity — a temple that has weathered Partition, communal violence and decades of neglect and yet still opens its doors. It is at once a working place of worship, a symbol of the resilience of the Valmiki community, and a monument to the older, more plural Lahore that lay behind the border of 1947. Its modest survival, alongside the nearby Krishna Mandir, keeps alive a thread of Hindu devotional life in the heart of the Pakistani Punjab.

Name: Valmiki Swamiji Mandir (Gracy Lines), Rawalpindi
Location: Gracy Lines, Chaklala Cantonment, Rawalpindi, Punjab, Pakistan
Events: Diwali; Holi
Description:
The Valmik Swamiji Mandir — also called the Valmiki Mandir or *Balaknash* Temple — lies in the Gracy Lines neighbourhood of Chaklala Cantonment, in the south-eastern part of Rawalpindi. Reported to have been built in 1935, it has served since the pre-Partition era as one of the principal places of worship for the city's Hindu residents, and is counted among the three main Hindu temples of Rawalpindi district alongside the Krishna Mandir of Saddar and the Lal Kurti (Balmiki) Temple. Like the Lalkurti shrine it is dedicated to the sage-poet *Valmik* (Valmiki), author of the *Ramayana*, particularly venerated by the Balmiki community, and it remains active, celebrating festivals such as *Diwali* and *Holi*. In August 2014 the temple drew national and international attention when cantonment authorities issued notices for residents of Block 141, Gracy Lines, to vacate the area for a development scheme, raising fears that the temple and adjoining Hindu homes might be demolished. Members of the community petitioned the courts and obtained a stay against immediate demolition; authorities reportedly indicated that a replacement temple would be provided if relocation went ahead, and residents were said to have been offered alternative accommodation. In the event the temple was not demolished and continues in worship — a reminder of the precarious position of the small Hindu community's heritage in the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad.

Reporting on the temple's more recent history, profiles in *Dawn* and *Arab News* quote its longtime custodian, Budh Raj, confirming the 1935 founding and describing a congregation that now draws worshippers from well beyond Rawalpindi: because Islamabad itself has no functional Hindu temple, many of the capital's Hindu residents travel here to worship. By 2025 the building was showing its age, with "worn carpet" covering "broken cement and chapped walls"; Budh Raj recalled that the cantonment once held "two to three mandirs," left vacant after the Hindu population migrated at Partition. A 2023 profile in *The Express Tribune* described it simply as "ancient and small," and a 2025 survey of Rawalpindi's Hindu heritage counted it, alongside the Krishna Temple of Saddar and the Lal Kurti Temple, as one of only three temples still functional in the city — characterising all three, including this one, as "over a century old," a description at odds with the 1935 construction date reported elsewhere. The temple continues to host community festivals, with Diwali celebrations reported here as recently as November 2024.

Name: Wadpagga Sharif
Sufi Saint: Ghazi Syed Shah Fateh Muhammad Bukhari
Events: Annual urs
Description:
## Overview

Wadpagga Sharif is a village and shrine on the outskirts of Peshawar, in the historic vale that has for centuries been a meeting-ground of Pashtun, Persian, and Central Asian devotion. It is remembered above all as the seat of a family of *sayyids* — descendants of the Prophet Muhammad — of the *Bukhari* line, and as the resting place of the saint the local tradition calls *Ghazi Baba*. The very name of the place is said to preserve the memory of these holy men: *Wadpagga*, in the popular etymology, derives from words meaning "big turbans," for the *sayyids* who settled here wore the large turbans that marked their dignity, and the village took its name from them.

## The Sayyids of Wadpagga

According to the traditions of the family, the saint honoured at Wadpagga, Ghazi Baba, belonged to the *Bukhari sayyids*, that widely revered lineage which traces its descent through the great Suhrawardi saints of the medieval Punjab and Sindh — *Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari* and his grandson *Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht* of Uch, both of whom are venerated at their own shrines elsewhere in this collection. Ghazi Baba is remembered as a descendant, some fifteen generations removed, of Syed Nasiruddin Mahmud, and thus as an inheritor of that Bukhari spiritual patrimony, which he carried into the Pashtun country around Peshawar. He is said to have been a contemporary of other saints of the valley, among them Mian Umar, remembered at the village of Chamkani, so that his life is placed within a whole network of holy men who flourished in the region in the later medieval and early modern centuries. Because the detailed record of his life survives chiefly in family and devotional tradition rather than in independent chronicle, the particulars of his dates and deeds are best received as the community remembers them, with the caution proper to hagiography.

## Devotional Life

The shrine of Ghazi Baba at Wadpagga is a site of pilgrimage, drawing devotees who come to offer *fatiha* at the tomb, to seek the intercession and blessing (*baraka*) of the saint, and to honour the wider circle of his descendants who are buried in the village. As at the other Bukhari shrines of the subcontinent, the devotion here is bound up with the prestige of *sayyid* descent — the belief that the family carries the light of prophetic lineage — and with the memory of a saint who brought that heritage from the Indus valley into the hills of the frontier. The rhythms of the shrine follow the familiar pattern of the Pashtun *ziyarat*: gatherings on the days of remembrance, the recitation of the Qur'an and of devotional poetry, and the quiet daily traffic of local people who bring their hopes and troubles to the saint's threshold.

## Legacy

Wadpagga Sharif is a characteristic example of the smaller sacred places that stud the countryside around Peshawar, where the great movements of Islamic mysticism — Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi — took root through the settlement of *sayyid* and saintly families who married into the local society and became, in time, the spiritual anchors of their villages. The shrine's link to the Bukhari lineage ties this frontier settlement to the far older centres of Suhrawardi devotion at Uch and Multan, and reminds the visitor that the religious landscape of the Peshawar valley was shaped not only by the celebrated poets and warriors of Pashtun tradition but also by these quieter dynasties of the holy. For the people of Wadpagga and the surrounding district, Ghazi Baba remains a protector and patron, and his turban-crowned forebears are honoured in the very name their descendants still bear.

Name: Ziarat Kaka Sahib
Location: Ziarat Kaka Sahib, Nowshera District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: c. 1661 (mausoleum, built by his son); saint traditionally born 1575 CE, died 1653
Events: Annual urs; regular pilgrimage
Description:
Ziarat Kaka Sahib, set among rugged hills roughly twelve kilometres south of Nowshera city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is the shrine of the sixteenth-century Sufi saint *Kaka Sahib*, whose given name was *Syed Kasteer Gul* and who is also remembered by the honorific *Sheikh Rahmkar*. Born, by tradition, on the first of Ramazan in 1575 (sometimes given as 1576), he received his religious education from his Sufi father and from the scholars of his day, and his forefathers are remembered as affiliated with all four of the great Sufi orders — the *Naqshbandi*, *Suhrawardi*, *Chishti*, and *Qadiri* — an inheritance tradition credits him with carrying forward, though he himself is remembered in the *Uwaisi* style of not naming a personal living guide. Tradition names his teachers as Qazi Abul Aala, Abdullah Ansari Sultanpuri, Maulana Abdul Lateef Sultanpuri, and Sheikh Akhuddeen Seljuki; the nearby saint Akhund Panju Baba was a respected contemporary he is said to have met, rather than a personal teacher — Panju Baba's own disciple, by tradition, was Kaka Sahib's father, Bahadur Baba. A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates his name (there rendered Sheikh Rahm Kar) and adds a specific detail of place: at the time of his birth, his father was living in forest roughly six miles south of the site later known as Ziarat Kaka Sahib. So great was his renown for piety that his resting place became one of the most frequented religious sites of the province, and the town that grew around it took his name. His white mausoleum, raised by his son Sheikh Abdul Haleem around 1661, is a fine example of Mughal-era funerary architecture, richly ornamented within by mosaic work, floral patterns, and painted stucco decoration. The descendants of his teacher and of the saint's own line have long lived in the settlement, tending the shrine and its traditions. Today Ziarat Kaka Sahib remains a much-visited place of pilgrimage, its annual observances drawing devotees from across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa who come to seek blessing at the tomb of a saint whose memory has endured for more than four centuries.
